qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 190, tip 24 'A logo is not a brand'; and printed pp. 161-162, 'Usage rights'
qa_items.question: Airey draws a three-level distinction that his book keeps returning to. Name the three levels, say what belongs at each, and state the limit he draws from the distinction.
qa_items.answer: The LOGO is one mark, and he says explicitly it is only one part of a company's brand identity. The BRAND IDENTITY — which he also calls the visual identity — is the applied system: he enumerates business cards, compliment slips, vehicle graphics and signage design, and elsewhere adds packaging, marketing materials, the website and company vehicles. The BRAND as a whole is larger again and is not a design artefact at all: the company's mission, its history, and people's perception of it. The limit he draws is a limit on his own trade — an effective logo plays an important role but will not save a poor product or service, or a company with a weak mission. He uses the same distinction in the other direction too, to argue that a client asking for a logo in isolation should be advised to take guidance on applying it across the full range of corporate literature.
qa_items.support: Tip 24 states the three levels and the limit; printed pp. 161-162 gives the enumeration of what an identity project covers. The exact English wording could not be verified from this copy, which is a Spanish translation, so the substance is given rather than a quotation.
confounders: collapsing identity and brand into one, which is the error the tip exists to correct
reading 'a logo is not a brand' as meaning the logo does not matter — he says it plays an important role
assuming the brand level is something a designer delivers; in his account it includes perception, which nobody delivers

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 34 'Think small', restated at printed p. 187 tip 17
qa_items.question: Airey gives one numeric target for a mark's reproduction. What is it, what condition attaches to it, and what does he say is the only way to meet it?
qa_items.answer: The design should work at a minimum of around one inch, and the condition attached is "with no loss of detail". The only route he offers to meeting it is simplicity — he states plainly that the only way to achieve this is to keep the mark simple, and he ties it to the same claim everywhere else in the chapter, that simplicity is what makes the other requirements reachable. He states the figure twice, in the "Think small" section and again in tip 17. It is a practitioner's rule of thumb: no viewing distance, no substrate, no reproduction process and no derivation is given anywhere.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 34 states the one-inch minimum and the "no loss of detail" condition; printed p. 187 repeats it. No derivation appears anywhere in the book.
confounders: treating one inch as a measured threshold rather than a rule of thumb
confusing it with a screen or pixel dimension — the figure is stated in inches and is print-era
assuming the condition is legibility; the condition he states is loss of detail

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 186-188, tips 15, 16, 19 and 20
qa_items.question: Four of Airey's twenty-five tips concern variants and checks on a finished mark rather than on its design. Name them and, for each, say what he asks for.
qa_items.answer: Tip 15, offer a one-colour version: whatever colours the mark carries, also supply one using only one. Tip 16, pay attention to contrast in the medium: keep an eye on the contrast between the logo and its background AND between the actual elements inside the logo, with the tonal range contrasting enough for the mark to be clearly identified. Tip 19, reverse it: offer an option that works on dark backgrounds, which he glosses as supplying a version in white. Tip 20, place it upside down: a design that looks right the correct way up may not look right inverted, so consider it from every angle before finalising. The internal-contrast half of tip 16 is the least obvious of the four and is the one a designer working only against white will not have tested.
qa_items.support: The four tips are printed consecutively across printed pp. 186-188. Tip 16 names two contrast relationships, not one, which is the detail most summaries drop.
confounders: remembering only the logo-versus-background contrast and dropping the element-versus-element half
treating the one-colour version as an optional extra; he presents it as something you should supply
confusing tip 18's print-and-inspect instruction, which is a physical paper check, with these four

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 38-39, 'The seven ingredients on the plate'
qa_items.question: Airey's central chapter closes with a recap list. What are the seven headings, and what discrepancy is there between that list and the adjectives he opens the chapter with?
qa_items.answer: The seven are: keep it simple; make it relevant; incorporate tradition; aim for distinction; commit to memory; think small; focus on one thing. The chapter opens instead with six adjectives — an iconic design will be simple, relevant, enduring, distinctive, memorable and adaptable. The two lists do not line up: "incorporate tradition" and "think small" are headings with no matching adjective, and "enduring" is an adjective with no heading of its own. The mismatch is the book's, not a reading error, and it matters because it shows the seven are a teaching sequence rather than a specification. The chapter's final section confirms that reading by telling the reader rules are made to be broken.
qa_items.support: The adjective list is at printed p. 22; the seven headings run from p. 22 to p. 37 and are recapped at pp. 38-39; the exemption is at p. 39.
confounders: assuming the six adjectives and the seven headings are the same list stated twice
treating the seven as a specification, which the chapter's own closing paragraph withdraws
adding 'legible' or 'timeless' to the list — legibility is tip 12, in a different chapter

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 30, 'Aim for distinction'
qa_items.question: Airey states an ordering between colour and form. What is the ordering, what working practice does he derive from it, and what does he say that practice does?
qa_items.answer: The ordering is that colour is secondary to the form and the shape of the design. The practice he derives is to work only in black and white, and what he says it does is create more distinctive marks, because the contrast puts the emphasis on the shape or the idea. He offers this inside the distinctiveness section, as his answer to the question "how do you create a logo that is unique?" — so in his account working in black is not a presentation convention but a generation method. He restates the point negatively in tip 10: no amount of fancy gradients or colour options will rescue a badly designed mark.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 30 states both the ordering and the working practice; printed p. 184 (tip 10) gives the negative formulation. No comparison of marks developed in colour against marks developed in black appears anywhere.
confounders: reading this as the presentation argument from printed p. 111, which is a different claim about the client's attention
concluding that finished marks should be monochrome — his own examples on the facing pages are two-colour
treating it as a claim about colour psychology; it is a claim about which channel carries distinctiveness

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 62, opening of Ch. 5 'Skirting the dangers of a redesign'
qa_items.question: Airey splits identity projects into two categories with different risk profiles. What are they, and what is the comparison he uses to make the difference concrete?
qa_items.answer: Either a newly formed company needing a first identity, or an established company wanting its identity redesigned or refined. He says designing from scratch is the much simpler case, because there is no brand equity for either the designer or the client to take into account. The comparison is Nike abandoning its internationally recognised swoosh in favour of, say, the outline of a shoe, versus a new business called "Pete" commissioning a visual identity to help sell custom T-shirts — because of Nike's stature, standing and visibility in the market, the potential damage is far greater. He adds two consequences: the redesign process is necessarily longer and stricter, with more thought and discussion per decision, and it therefore tends to be the more lucrative of the two for the designer.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 62 sets out both categories, the Nike-versus-Pete comparison, and the observation about process length and fees.
confounders: assuming the risk is to the designer's reputation; he frames it as damage to the company's identity
reading 'no brand equity' as meaning a start-up project is low-stakes rather than structurally simpler
confusing this with the separate refine-versus-replace decision at printed pp. 72-73

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 185, tip 13 'Be consistent'
qa_items.question: Whose responsibility does Airey say brand style guides are, and what chain of consequences does he attach to consistency?
qa_items.answer: The designer's — he states that many logos are accompanied by style guides and that creating them is your responsibility. Their function is to make sure anyone inside the client's company who uses the design does so consistently. The chain he attaches is two links and he states it compactly: consistency breeds trust, and trust wins customers. He makes the same claim in the earlier chapter, that the same visual identity seen over and over generates trust and trust makes customers come back for more, and his historical case is the Kellogg signature, used on the front of every packet since 1906. Neither link is evidenced; Kellogg is a survivorship case with a century of confounded marketing behind it.
qa_items.support: Tip 13 at printed p. 185 assigns the responsibility and states the chain; printed pp. 9 and 21 give the earlier statement and the Kellogg case.
confounders: assuming the client or their marketing team writes the guide
treating the trust-to-customers chain as an established finding rather than this author's assertion
confusing consistency with the template-per-application practice he praises at printed p. 15, which pulls the other way

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 22-24, 'Keep it simple'
qa_items.question: Airey does not treat simplicity as one requirement among seven equals. What does he say it does, and what are the three specific consequences he works through?
qa_items.answer: He states that a simple logo helps satisfy most of the other requirements of iconic design — so on his own account simplicity is the member of the set that buys the others, not a peer of them. The three consequences he works through in order are: versatility, because a minimalist approach lets the mark be used across a wide range of media, from posters down to a website favicon; recognisability, which he says raises the chance of achieving a timeless, lasting quality; and memorability, because it is much easier to remember a single detail than five. He extends the dependency elsewhere — the small-size requirement is met only by simplifying, and the distinctiveness route he recommends works by removing colour so that shape carries the mark.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 22 states the enabling claim and the versatility consequence; p. 23 gives recognisability and memorability; p. 34 makes the small-size dependency explicit.
confounders: listing the seven elements as unstructured peers, which loses the one piece of structure he supplies
attributing to him a mechanism for WHY recognisability produces longevity — he asserts the link without arguing it
confusing versatility with adaptability across cultures; his versatility claim is about media and carriers

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 37, the French Property Exhibition case, 'Focus on one thing'
qa_items.question: Airey argues that an element can be genuinely relevant to the subject and still be wrong to include. What is the case he uses, and what is the mechanism that makes relevance insufficient?
qa_items.answer: The case is a counterfactual, not an example: the redesigned French Property Exhibition mark focuses on one attribute, an open door read out of the tricolour. He observes that the designer could have added an Eiffel Tower, that everyone would immediately associate an Eiffel Tower with France — and that this is exactly why it would have been wrong. The mechanism he gives is processing cost inside a glance: the viewer would then have been forced to consider an unnecessary element, which would make the design less memorable. So relevance does not buy back the attention an element costs. This is the argument that makes his one-feature rule non-obvious; without it the rule reads as a preference for minimalism, and with it, it is a claim about what a second element does to the first.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 37 gives the Eiffel Tower counterfactual and the "forced to consider an unnecessary element" reasoning. The counterfactual is asserted; no version with the tower was made or shown.
confounders: reading the rule as 'keep it minimal', which misses that the excluded element is relevant
assuming the Eiffel Tower version exists and was tested; it was neither made nor shown
confusing this with the relevance requirement at printed p. 25, which the one-thing rule here overrides

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 111-113, 'Black and white before colour'; and printed p. 184, tip 10
qa_items.question: Airey gives two entirely different reasons for withholding colour, from two places in the book. Distinguish them, and say which one is about the client rather than about the mark.
qa_items.answer: The first is about the client's attention and is the agency practice he reports at printed p. 111: present concepts initially in black and white only, because their designers have found that colour skews a client's ability to focus on the form and on the ideas the logo communicates. He adds the scheduling version of the same point — colour is a detail that can easily be changed, and the last thing you want is a client turned off an effective idea because they dislike the colour scheme. The second is about the work and is tip 10: no amount of fancy gradients or colour options will rescue a badly designed mark. The first is the client-facing reason; the second is a claim about the artefact. They are usually collapsed into one and they are not one — a designer could honour the second while breaking the first, by developing in black and then presenting in colour.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 111 gives the client-attention reason and attributes it to one agency's standing practice; printed p. 113 gives the easily-changed-detail reason; printed p. 184 gives the gradients claim. There is a third, separate argument at printed p. 30, about working in black producing more distinctive marks.
confounders: collapsing all of these into one 'work in black and white' rule
missing that the presentation reason is attributed to an agency's own experience, not to any study
assuming the mark must be delivered in black and white; the sequence ends with colour and Pantone swatches

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 110, 'Dressing for success', the Circle project
qa_items.question: Airey gives a sharper reason than "it looks unprofessional" for not showing a client every idea. What is it, and what happened when he broke his own rule?
qa_items.answer: The sharp reason is that anything you show can be chosen: including ideas you are unsure of introduces the possibility that the client will pick the weakest candidate out of an otherwise strong set. The dilution point — that sub-par possibilities drag down the quality of the set — is the softer, secondary reason. When he broke it, on an early project for a South African web hosting company called Circle, he presented all his ideas for feedback in his eagerness to please. The effect he reports was not a bad choice but no choice: he overwhelmed the client, made it impossible to pick one idea out of so many possibilities, and the project stalled and was never completed. It is one narrated failure with no control, told by the person it happened to, and the stall may have had other causes.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 110 gives both reasons and the Circle account. The rule is restated in the chapter recap at printed p. 117.
confounders: giving only the dilution reason, which is the weaker of the two
assuming the failure was that the client chose badly; the reported failure was paralysis
confusing this with the separate 'how many concepts' answer at printed pp. 169-170, which is about a number

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 63-65, 'Don't squeeze too hard', the Tropicana rebrand
qa_items.question: In Airey's account of the Tropicana packaging redesign, what specifically was lost, and what outcome does he report? What should a careful reader not conclude from it?
qa_items.answer: What was lost was a finding device. He notes that PepsiCo had for years used the "straw stuck in an orange" symbol, that consumers were used to it, and that brand-loyal customers could easily spot the packaging when shopping — and the redesign removed it, producing what he calls a diluted, almost generic identity. The outcome he reports is that sales of the Tropicana Pure Premium line fell 20 per cent in less than two months, costing PepsiCo $33 million in lost sales, and that the company reverted to the old packaging about two months after the launch. A careful reader should not conclude that the book establishes the causal link: both figures are cited to trade press, no controls exist, no alternative explanation is examined, and Airey himself floats an open speculation that the dilution may have been a deliberate alignment with generic store-brand packaging. He also says most redesigns do not go this badly and that both PepsiCo and Coca-Cola have probably had successful ones.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 63-65. The 20 per cent figure is footnoted to AdAge and the $33 million to a branding blog; the reversion and the store-brand speculation are on printed p. 65.
confounders: treating the 20 per cent figure as evidence that simplicity or genericness causes sales loss
identifying the lost element as the brand name; the name remained, set small and rotated vertically
confusing this with New Coke at printed pp. 66-68, where he says outright he does not know whether it was a deliberate manoeuvre or a genuine error

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 139-140, the Yellow Pages dart concept, 'Swallow that pride'
qa_items.question: A client group is convinced an element should be added that you believe will weaken the mark. What does Airey do instead of arguing, and what is the mechanism he says makes it work?
qa_items.answer: He builds their request. On a Yellow Pages redesign, committee members were convinced that adding a dart beside the walking fingers would improve the design and he was sure it would not. Rather than becoming defensive, he executed the dart version — and paired it with another idea he believed was a better improvement, explaining why when he presented it. He reports that once the two results could be compared, it was easier for the committee to see that its own idea was unsuitable. The mechanism he generalises is that clients are much less likely to resist your ideas going forward if they have seen a graphic representation of how their own strategic interpretation filters out. He also records the reason the demonstration was needed: the committee was unaware of the "focus on one thing" idea from Chapter 3 — which is as much an argument for explaining the principle as for showing the comparison.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 139-140. Both concepts are printed on p. 140, the dart version above and the alternative below. One narrated project, no measurement of whether the method changes outcomes.
confounders: assuming he refused and defended his position, which is the move he explicitly rejects
assuming he simply complied — he coupled the client's request with an alternative
reading this as always deferring to the client; he narrates the opposite case at printed p. 136, where the committee was right and he was wrong

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 90-94, 'Mind mapping'; and printed pp. 96-97, 'The fundamental need for the sketchpad'
qa_items.question: Airey puts two stages before any use of a computer. What does he say each is FOR — not what each is — and what does he demonstrate rather than merely assert?
qa_items.answer: Mind mapping is for considering as many different design directions as possible, at the stage where that matters most: you write a word central to the brief, branch outward, and build the largest thought cloud you can. Sketching is for volume and freedom: paper is less restrictive and adds no intermediate steps, so more ideas get out before the computer is opened, and he says drawing skill is irrelevant because the point is documenting ideas so they can be built on or discarded. What he demonstrates rather than asserts is the mapping chain on the Ecometrica project: from "science" he associated to "DNA", from DNA to "personal", from personal to "fingerprint" — and basing the mark on a fingerprint became his central concept possibility. That chain is the evidence that word association moves the imagination into directions it would not otherwise take.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 90-91 state the purpose of mapping; pp. 93-94 give the Ecometrica chain; pp. 96-97 give the sketching argument. One designer's practice throughout, with no comparison against work produced without it.
confounders: describing the stages without giving the purpose, which is the reusable half
treating the two-day mapping figure as a finding; it is his habit, chosen so a night's sleep falls inside the stage
assuming he bans the computer outright; he excludes it until a concept has developed structure

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 33, 'Commit to memory'; and printed p. 36, 'Focus on one thing'
qa_items.question: Airey converts a claim about how a mark is SEEN into a constraint on how the designer WORKS. What is the exposure claim, what is the working constraint, and what is the inferential step between them that he does not defend?
qa_items.answer: The exposure claim is that very often a quick glance is all the time you get to make an impression — his examples are a bus passenger looking out of the window at a billboard and a pedestrian looking up as a branded truck drives past, and he adds that the client's customers are not going to spend long studying the logo. The working constraint is to limit the time spent on each idea sketch, trying about thirty seconds. The step between them is his rhetorical question: otherwise, how can you expect a viewer to remember it with a quick glance? That equates the designer's sketching time with the viewer's processing time, which is an assumption, not an argument — and it plainly would not hold for a viewer who already knows the mark. The exposure claim itself is offered with no evidence and its examples are outdoor media of 2010.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 33 gives the exposure claim and the thirty-second sketching cap; printed p. 36 restates the brief-glance premise; printed p. 39 recaps it. No evidence is offered for either.
confounders: treating thirty seconds as a claim about viewer attention rather than about sketching time
assuming the glance claim is measured; it is asserted
confusing it with the one-or-two-second reading window in tip 12, which is about legibility of lettering

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 31, the NAAs mark, 'Aim for distinction'
qa_items.question: Airey slips in a test a designer can run on their own prose rather than on the artwork. What is it, what does he claim, and in which direction does the claim actually run?
qa_items.answer: Having described a mark in a single clause — an "open newspaper" symbol in the form of the letter A — he draws attention to how easy the description was and asserts a rule: distinctive marks are almost always simple enough to be described easily. The claim as stated runs only one way, from distinctiveness to describability. The useful diagnostic runs the other way — if you cannot describe your mark in a short phrase, it is probably carrying more than one idea — and that inversion is a reader's inference, not his claim. Two further limits are worth keeping: he hedges with "almost always", and the single demonstration is the author describing a mark whose intended meaning he had just been told, which is the opposite of the blind condition that would make the test informative.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 31. The mark was rendered and inspected during extraction: a solid black form built from splayed page-fans that resolves into a capital A.
confounders: attributing the reverse entailment to Airey; he states only that distinctive marks are describable
dropping his 'almost always' hedge
treating one self-administered description as evidence

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 129-130, 'Outlining the ground rules'
qa_items.question: Airey gives a phrase for the boundary he sets on client feedback. What is the boundary, what does he say happens if it is not held, and what does he suggest saying to make it concrete?
qa_items.answer: The boundary is that what he needs from the client group is strategic input and execution freedom. If it is not held — if the discussion collapses into them telling you which colours or typefaces to use — he says the identity will inevitably be weakened, because you are taking design decisions from too many non-designers. To make it concrete he scripts both halves for the client: saying you think a blue is too weak for an organisation trying to present strength, or that a typeface feels too old-fashioned, is exactly what he wants — expressing those impressions is critical to a project's success. Saying "make the blue darker" or "why not try a modern typeface" is what he asks them to stop at, with the reason given as trust: you have to trust that I can find the right design solution based on your feedback.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 129-130. The two paired examples — the impression is welcome, the fix is not — are the operative part and are the half most summaries drop.
confounders: reading it as a rule against client feedback; he says expressing impressions is critical
treating it as a claim about client competence rather than about where the boundary sits
confusing it with the separate instruction to keep the presentation on the idea rather than the details

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 25, 'Make it relevant'; and printed p. 106, the La Internacional case
qa_items.question: Airey holds two positions on literal depiction that look contradictory. State both, and state the condition that reconciles them.
qa_items.answer: Position one, at printed p. 25 and again as tip 4: a logo does not have to say what a company does. The BMW logo is not a car, the Hawaiian Airlines logo is not a plane, and he generalises — computer logos need not show computers, dentist logos need not show teeth, furniture shop logos need not show furniture. Position two, at printed p. 106: a logo does not have to reflect literally what the business is about, but when it does, and especially when it manages to do so without hitting you over the head with the idea, it can really be a winner. The reconciling condition is about MANNER, not about the fact of depiction: literalness is allowed provided it is not overstated. His approved case is a natural-medicine pharmacy whose chosen mark builds a capsule into the letterform and sets it in a green circle — literal twice over, and praised. Note that the criterion "without hitting you over the head" is taste, not a test.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 25 and tip 4 at printed p. 180 give the first position; printed p. 106 gives the second and the pharmacy case. The pharmacy page was rendered and inspected during extraction.
confounders: reading the first position as a prohibition on depiction
assuming the reconciling condition is about how much of the mark is literal; it is about how overstated the reference is
missing that every non-depicting exemplar he names is a large established brand

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 22-39 (Ch. 3) against printed p. 145, Ivan Chermayeff quoted
qa_items.question: Somewhere outside the criteria chapter, Airey prints a quotation that demotes that chapter's central requirements. Whose is it, what does it say, and why does it matter?
qa_items.answer: Ivan Chermayeff, quoted in the motivation chapter at printed p. 145: to be effective for a reasonably long lifetime, all identities must be simple and appropriate — however, if they are not original or in any way provocative, thought-provoking and remarkable, they will not do their job. It matters because Chapter 3 treats simple and relevant as the goal, and this reduces them to entry conditions. It is the only place in the book where the criteria are declared insufficient rather than merely defeasible, and Airey never carries the qualification back into Chapter 3 or reconciles the two. It also matters practically: the four sufficiency conditions are entirely unoperationalised, so nothing in the book tells you how to check them, whereas the necessary conditions come with reproduction tests attached.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 145, in 'Never stop learning'. The criteria chapter runs printed pp. 22-39 and is never revised in light of it.
confounders: attributing the qualification to Airey; it is a quoted designer's, printed without comment
reading it as agreeing with Ch. 3 — it grants the premise and then denies sufficiency
confusing it with the 'rules are made to be broken' passage at printed p. 39, which withdraws necessity rather than sufficiency

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 180, tip 5, against printed p. 13, 'Symbols transcend borders'
qa_items.question: Airey states two incompatible things about symbols and international expansion. Set them out, and say what the book does about the conflict.
qa_items.answer: Tip 5, at printed p. 180: if the company is entertaining ideas about expanding into other markets, it might be better to opt for a distinctive logotype, because a mark or identifying symbol could prove restrictive. Chapter 2, at printed p. 13: to sell products internationally your brand has to speak a lot of languages, and easily identified symbols need no translation — recognisable regardless of culture or language, symbols let companies cross language barriers, compete globally and maintain consistency across a wide range of media. Under the same condition, planned expansion, one passage recommends the wordmark and the other recommends the symbol. The book does nothing about it: the two sit 167 pages apart and neither refers to the other, and Airey gives no reason for the restrictiveness claim in tip 5. Anyone citing him on this should cite both.
qa_items.support: Tip 5 at printed p. 180; the symbols argument at printed p. 13. The conflict is genuine and unresolved in the source; neither passage cross-references the other.
confounders: picking one passage and presenting it as his settled position
resolving the conflict by inventing a distinction he does not draw, such as one being about market entry and the other about market breadth
assuming tip 5's restrictiveness claim comes with a reason; it does not

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 72-73, 'Maybe just a few adjustments?', the JCJ Architecture case
qa_items.question: Airey names the condition under which refinement beats a full redesign. What is the condition, and what does the JCJ case keep and what does it change?
qa_items.answer: The condition is a conjunction, and both halves must hold: refinement is the good option when the client's identity has become somewhat dated over recent years BUT consumer familiarity with it is high. He is explicit that a complete redesign could be a step too far when a few adjustments would do while still preserving the equity behind the visual. In the JCJ case what changes is the typeface — the old mark used Helvetica Neue, which he notes is a well-crafted face with nothing spectacularly wrong with it beyond some tight kerning, but which was used on seemingly every new design through a period in the nineties. What is kept is the distinctive red lettering, and he says explicitly that this is why the brand equity around the old design remains intact. The refined mark also establishes consistency and allows flexibility across print methods, from brochures to offset to office laser output.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 72-73. Both marks are printed on p. 73 and were rendered and inspected during extraction; they differ subtly, which is itself the evidence for the refinement claim.
confounders: giving only the 'dated' half of the condition and dropping the familiarity half
assuming refinement means changing less of the artwork; the criterion is what carries the equity, not how much changes
confusing this with the Tropicana case, which is the failure of the opposite decision

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 169-170, 'How many concepts?'; and printed pp. 171-172, 'Design revisions'
qa_items.question: Airey gives a working number for how many concepts to present and then attacks the question itself. Give both, and give the argument that makes the attack more than a dodge.
qa_items.answer: The working number: sometimes one is all you need, but more often than not he gives clients a choice of two or three, on the reasoning that a client is happier with a choice than with a single design handed to them — while warning that it is much easier to choose one from two than one from ten, even if all ten ideas are good. The attack: quoting a fixed number in advance, as online client questionnaires do when they ask the client to pick one, two, three or four, is bad practice, because neither party can know how many ideas are needed before the right one exists, and the designer cannot answer it until the design has started. What makes it more than a dodge is the incentive he identifies: promising four creates pressure to present a weak idea to fill the quota. He runs the same argument for revision rounds — specifying a number at the outset only limits the outcome — and refuses the implied bargain outright: you do not hand over a poor design because the client has not paid for more. His preferred formulation to a client is "between one and four".
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 169-170 for the concept count and the questionnaire criticism; printed pp. 171-172 for revisions and the refusal. "Two or three" and "between one and four" are his habits, not derived numbers.
confounders: reporting 'two or three' as a rule; he presents it as his practice and then argues no number can be fixed
assuming the objection is commercial; his stated objection is that the count is unknowable before the work starts
confusing this with the separate rule about not showing ideas you would not accept

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 15, 'Symbols transcend borders', against printed p. 185, tip 13
qa_items.question: The Bethnal Green project is Airey's model of versatility, and the practice it demonstrates pulls against another of his own requirements. Explain both sides.
qa_items.answer: The versatility side: the chosen star was picked over the team's other variations not only because it was a good design but because it could be used as a template and MODIFIED to suit any application or theme. The simplest form of the star is engraved into the pub's pint glasses; the screen-printed paper carries the same design drawn by hand. He calls the project a classic lesson in versatility and turns it into a standing question — always ask whether your logo can adapt to different media. The tension: tip 13 requires consistency, backed by a style guide whose job is to make sure everyone in the client's company uses the design the same way. Deliberate per-application modification and strict consistency are not the same instruction, and the book never says how much a template may vary before it stops being one mark — which is exactly the question a style guide has to answer.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 13-15 for the template practice and the engraved and screen-printed applications; printed p. 185 for the consistency requirement. Printed p. 15 was rendered and inspected during extraction.
confounders: reading versatility as one fixed artwork appearing everywhere, which is what the project is NOT
assuming Airey addresses the tension; he does not raise it
treating the engraved application as decorative; it is the case with no colour at all, so only form survives

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 29, Malcolm Grear quoted, against printed pp. 136-137, 'Swallow that pride'
qa_items.question: Airey prints a demanding statement about the designer's own standard and, a hundred pages later, a story that cuts against it. Give both and say how they can be held together.
qa_items.answer: Grear, at printed p. 29: the most difficult person to please on any logo design project should be the designer creating the mark — it is a challenge because the work has to be memorable and as timeless as possible, and "I don't want to be in vogue, I want to set the standard and not follow others." Against that, at printed pp. 136-137, Airey produced two strong concepts for Berthier Associates; the committee judged his preferred, more organic option too organic to represent the firm's structured approach and chose the other. Looking back, he says their choice was much better suited to the firm, and adds that it looks very good on their business cards. They can be held together only by separating two things Airey keeps separate himself: the standard applied while making the work, which is where Grear's demand belongs, and the openness applied while receiving feedback on it — even when everything inside you is saying no, it is always worth listening carefully and keeping an open mind.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 29 for the Grear quotation; printed pp. 136-137 for the Berthier account and Airey's retrospective concession. Both are practitioner accounts, neither tested.
confounders: reading Grear's standard as licence to override the client
reading the Berthier story as saying the client is usually right; it is one case, and the Yellow Pages case runs the other way
attributing Grear's words to Airey

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 34 'Think small'; printed p. 186 tip 15; printed p. 187 tips 16 and 18; printed p. 188 tips 19 and 20
qa_items.question: You have a finished wordmark for a new company and a single afternoon. Using only checks Airey actually specifies, what do you run, and which of your results are determinate and which are judgements?
qa_items.answer: Six checks come straight from him. Reduce it to about one inch and confirm no detail is lost. Flatten it to one colour and confirm the one-colour version he requires actually works. Put it on a dark ground and confirm the reversed version reads. Check both contrast relationships he names — mark against ground, and element against element within the mark. Print it, replicated across a range of sizes and colours on one sheet, and confirm on paper that it is clean, holds contrast and is not pixelated. Turn it upside down and look. Determinate: the reduction, the flatten, the inversion, and the print sweep — something either survives or it does not, and you can say which elements were lost. Judgements: the two contrast checks, because his only pass condition is that the mark be "clearly identified", which is not a measurement — and, if the mark carries lettering, his legibility gate, which asks whether most people can read it straight away and specifies no population, no exposure time and no distance. Nothing in the book supplies a threshold for any of the judgements, so a result stated as a number would be yours, not his.
qa_items.support: The checks are at printed p. 34 (one inch), p. 186 (one colour), p. 187 (contrast; print sweep), p. 188 (reverse; upside down), p. 185 (legibility). The determinate-versus-judgement split is a reading of what he does and does not supply a pass condition for.
confounders: adding a numeric contrast ratio, which comes from accessibility standards and not from this source
treating the print sweep as a screen check; he specifies printing and inspecting paper
assuming the one-colour check is a mechanical desaturation; he asks for a supplied version, which a designer would redraw

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 185, tip 12 'Remember legibility'
qa_items.question: Two clients bring you a script wordmark that is hard to read at a glance. One is an unknown start-up; the other is a household name. What does Airey's legibility tip imply for each, and what is the sentence that makes the difference?
qa_items.answer: For the start-up, his gate applies at full force: if most people cannot read it straight away, do not consider using it as a logo — his named failing case is a client's handwriting that may look pretty and still fails. For the household name, the gate is loosened by his own scoping clause, which is the sentence that makes the difference: legibility is key, "especially when the brand isn't well known". That concedes that recognition can substitute for reading, so an established mark can carry lettering that is not immediately readable. The reason he gives for the gate is exposure: the audience will most likely look at the logos you design for only one or two seconds before moving on. Note what he does not supply — no test population, no exposure timing and no viewing distance — so any specific test you run is yours, not his.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 185. The scoping clause "especially when the brand isn't well known" is the operative qualification and is the half most often dropped.
confounders: applying the gate identically to both, which ignores his own scoping clause
reading the one-or-two-second figure as measured; it is asserted
concluding that script faces are ruled out; his criterion is immediate readability, not the class of typeface

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 36-37, 'Focus on one thing'
qa_items.question: A client for a Himalayan eco-resort asks you to add a mountain silhouette to a mark that already has a single leaf device. The mountain is genuinely relevant. What does Airey's reasoning say, and what is the strongest counter-consideration from his own book?
qa_items.answer: His reasoning rules against it, and rules against it precisely BECAUSE the mountain is relevant. The one-thing rule requires exactly one feature doing the work of standing out — one, not two, three or four — and the Eiffel Tower counterfactual at printed p. 37 is the same shape of case: an element everyone would immediately associate with the subject, excluded because the viewer would then be forced to consider an unnecessary element, making the design less memorable. So relevance is not a defence. The strongest counter-consideration from the same book is his own Tenth Church example at printed p. 101, a simple wordmark he praises for incorporating multiple conceptual themes — worship, welcome, transformation, outreach and the cross — in one graphic icon. That shows his rule counts DEVICES, not meanings: one device may legitimately carry several readings, and adding a second device is what he forbids. A mountain silhouette beside a leaf is a second device; a leaf whose outline also reads as a peak would not be.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 36-37 for the rule and the Eiffel Tower counterfactual; printed p. 101 for the Tenth Church wordmark and its five stated themes. The device-versus-meaning distinction is a reading that reconciles the two passages; Airey does not draw it explicitly.
confounders: allowing the mountain because it is relevant, which is the exact error the counterfactual targets
reading the rule as forbidding multiple meanings, which his own Tenth Church example contradicts
treating this as a minimalism preference rather than a claim about processing cost inside a glance

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 111-113, 'Black and white before colour', the Woodmere Art Museum case
qa_items.question: You are about to send a client three concepts for a new wordmark, each already coloured because the palette is part of the idea. Following the practice Airey documents at Woodmere, what would you change, at which point would colour re-enter, and what does he say the risk is if you do not?
qa_items.answer: You would present all three in black and white only, and hold colour back until the client is firmly behind one direction — at Woodmere the agency presented three concept families (monogram, signature, perspective) in black and white, and only once the client had settled on the monogram did its designers render in colour, delivering the final colours as Pantone swatches. The stated reason for the order is that colour skews a client's ability to focus on the form and on the ideas the logo communicates. The risk he names for doing otherwise is specific and not the obvious one: it is not that the client will choose a bad colour, it is that the client will be turned off an effective IDEA simply because they dislike the colour scheme — and colour, he points out, is a detail that can easily be changed afterwards, so it is the cheap variable being allowed to decide the expensive one. If the palette really is inseparable from the idea, you have a case his account does not cover, and you should say so rather than claim his support.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 111-113. The pages were rendered and inspected during extraction: thirty-two concepts across pp. 111-112, every one in black, white and grey, and the chosen mark in colour with three Pantone chips on p. 113.
confounders: keeping colour because it 'is part of the brand', which is the objection his sequence is designed to defer, not to answer
presenting one concept in black and white and the rest in colour, which reintroduces exactly the skew
assuming the deliverable is monochrome; the sequence ends in colour

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 46-47, 'Asking the tougher questions'; and printed p. 179, tip 2
qa_items.question: A client mentions in passing that they promote themselves mainly through leaflets handed out at trade events. Airey treats that answer as changing the design, not just the media plan. What follows from it, and what should you have asked before designing?
qa_items.answer: It changes the colour decision, and it changes it before any concept exists. He uses almost this exact case: if the company promotes itself through leaflets at trade events, you may need to remind the decision-maker that a multicoloured rainbow effect will cost more to produce than, say, a cool monotone grey design. The question you should have asked, and asked very early, is whether a print budget has been set — because colour usually costs more and can limit the scope of the design. He also warns not to assume: every printer's prices are unique, and with some the full-colour cost comes close to a one-colour job, though he says this is usually infrequent. He puts the duty on the designer: it is your job to inform the client about commercial print requirements and limitations at the start of the process. This is print economics of 2010, not a claim about any digital pipeline; the transferable part is the ordering — find out the constraint before you choose the palette.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 46 gives the leaflet case and the rainbow-versus-monotone comparison; printed p. 179 (tip 2) gives the print-budget question, the printer-pricing warning and the duty. He gives no figures and says so.
confounders: treating the promotional-channel question as market research rather than as a production constraint
assuming full colour always costs substantially more; he explicitly allows the exception
delaying the question to the artwork-delivery stage, which is after the decision it should govern

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 160-161, 'Similar-looking logos'
qa_items.question: A designer is accused of copying a mark that does look similar to theirs. Reconstruct Airey's answer, including the discriminator he reports and the two things you should not take from it.
qa_items.answer: His answer starts by normalising the resemblance: with millions of companies in existence and most iconic logos being simple in appearance, it is almost certain that if you search hard enough you will find a design similar to any other. Note the sting in that — the simplicity his own book demands is what shrinks the space of forms and makes collision likely. The discriminator he reports is what a trademark lawyer weighs most heavily: whether the two logos are used in the same industry or by the same profession. If they are not, he says the lawyer will probably tell you there is no case; if they are, he warns that lawyers are not cheap, so research well and be prepared to spend. Two things not to take from it. First, this is not legal advice: it is a designer's second-hand summary from 2010, tied to no jurisdiction or statute, and it moves between copyright infringement and trademark confusion inside one passage. Second, it is not absolution for the design process — he pairs it with Mike Davidson's discipline of telling yourself at every step that someone has surely already thought of this, and then asking what you can do to set yours apart, and with his own rule never to settle on an idea you have seen elsewhere.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 160-161. The Davidson quotation and Airey's "original to the best of your knowledge" formulation are on p. 161. Tip 1 at printed p. 178 adds the preventive version — ask the client early about competitors and previous identities.
confounders: treating the same-industry test as a statement of trademark law
reading the inevitability argument as meaning resemblance never matters
missing that the collision risk is a direct cost of the simplicity the book requires

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 63-65 and 72-73, Ch. 5
qa_items.question: A twelve-year-old regional food brand asks for a fresh identity. Its packaging is dated, but shoppers find it on the shelf by one distinctive device. Using Airey's Chapter 5 reasoning, what do you recommend and what is the specific failure you are avoiding?
qa_items.answer: You recommend refinement, not replacement — his stated condition is exactly this pair: the identity has become somewhat dated over recent years, but consumer familiarity with it is high. A complete redesign would be going a step too far when a few adjustments would do while keeping the equity behind the visual intact, and his JCJ case shows the shape of it: change the typeface, keep the distinctive red lettering, and the equity around the old design survives. The specific failure you are avoiding is the Tropicana one: consumers were used to the "straw stuck in an orange" device and brand-loyal customers could easily spot the packaging when shopping; the redesign removed it, and he reports sales of the line falling 20 per cent in less than two months and the company reverting to the old packaging. Before designing anything, he would have you establish the client's actual reasons for rebranding, and ask early whether any focus groups have been run — if not, suggest that questioning existing and potential customers about brand perception should be the first order of business. State the reported outcome as this source's claim: it is cited to trade press, with no controls.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 63-65 (Tropicana), pp. 67-68 (focus groups), pp. 72-73 (refinement and JCJ). The Tropicana and JCJ pages were rendered and inspected during extraction.
confounders: recommending a full redesign because the identity is dated, which uses only half his condition
assuming refinement means a small change; the criterion is preserving what carries the equity
presenting the 20 per cent figure as demonstrated causation rather than as this source's uncontrolled claim

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 34, 'Think small'; and printed p. 35, the Sugoi applications
qa_items.question: A client insists the mark will only ever appear on a website and on large exhibition panels, so small-size behaviour does not matter. What is Airey's argument against accepting that, and what is his commercial argument rather than his aesthetic one?
qa_items.answer: His argument is that the ambition to see work on billboards is exactly what makes designers forget the other end, and that the design may also need to accommodate smaller applications — his named cases are zip pulls and clothing labels, and the Sugoi mark is photographed on both a zip pull and a woven garment label. His commercial argument, which is the one to put to a client, is not about craft: an adaptable mark saves the client a considerable amount of money on print costs, brand-application meetings and potential redesigns, which is why he says clients are typically enthusiastic about and demanding of adaptability. Note the honest limit — he never quantifies that saving. Note also what your client is really asserting: that the set of future applications is known now, which is the assumption an identity designed to last the lifetime of the company cannot safely make.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 34 for the argument and the client-cost reasoning; printed p. 35 for the Sugoi applications, which were rendered and inspected during extraction. The cost saving is asserted and never quantified.
confounders: arguing only from craft, which gives the client nothing to weigh
citing the one-inch figure as a standard rather than as this author's rule of thumb
assuming a favicon is the small case he has in mind; his small cases are physical merchandise

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 44-47, 'Gathering preliminary information' and 'Asking the tougher questions'
qa_items.question: Airey gives a reason for each briefing question rather than just a list. Take three of his questions and state what each is actually FOR.
qa_items.answer: "What does your audience care about?" — it focuses and directs the creative effort onto whatever appeals to the client's customers, and it demonstrates to the client that you have an interest in their customers rather than merely a wish to please personal tastes. "Which logos do you think will appeal to your customers, and why?" — the point is the redirection: by shifting the focus off the client's individual design tastes and onto their customers', the process stays oriented to the interest of the business as a whole rather than one person's preference. "Why does your audience need a new brand identity?" — it forces the client to justify the project, and it often exposes a knee-jerk response to a competitor's relaunch, in which case he instructs you to encourage the client to proceed slowly and carefully, because the company may have built enormous equity around a long-standing identity. His summary of why all this matters: logos that are pretty can win awards, but they do not always win market share.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 45-47 give the questions with their stated purposes; printed p. 48 gives the awards-versus-market-share line. He explicitly presents the set as a starting point, not a standard.
confounders: reciting the questions without their purposes, which is the reusable half
treating the list as fixed; he says each sector and company varies and the reader should form their own
assuming the taste question is about gathering references; it is about moving the decision off one person's preference

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 57-58, the New Mexico Heart Hospital and Zia Pueblo
qa_items.question: A client wants their mark built on a symbol sacred to a living community. What does Airey's one worked case actually recommend, what harm does the designer in it name, and what should you be careful not to generalise?
qa_items.answer: It recommends asking, through the client. The designer, aware that the Zia sun symbol was an ancient and sacred design belonging to Zia Pueblo, encouraged the doctors to request an audience with the elders at Zia Pueblo to ask for permission to use their identifying mark, rather than simply using it. The harm she names is concrete and current: people slapping the Zia at random onto the side of any old work van as an identity, which she says happens often in New Mexico — so the objection is not abstract offence but a pattern of appropriation she could see. Airey generalises it only as far as being sensitive to that kind of thing, adding that respecting traditions and differences can bring unexpected parties together, which matters for collective acceptance. What not to generalise: this is one narrated project with a favourable outcome recounted rather than tested, the Pueblo granted use and blessed the hospital grounds, and Airey frankly notes the public-relations benefit — so the case cannot be read as evidence that asking pays. It is a boundary condition on borrowing heritage symbols, and it is specific to a community that can be identified and asked.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 57-58. One project; the outcome is narrated, not tested, and no general procedure for identifying who holds a symbol is offered.
confounders: generalising to any pre-existing symbol; his other heritage case, Vanderbilt's oak leaf, involves no living rights-holder to ask
reading the good outcome as evidence that permission-seeking is commercially advantageous
treating the designer's route as direct — she had the CLIENT request the audience

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 30, 'Aim for distinction'; and printed pp. 48-49, 'Homework time'
qa_items.question: A founder says their mark must "stand out". Using Airey, turn that into two things you can actually do, and name what each requires that the founder has not supplied.
qa_items.answer: First: pursue outline recognisability. His stated best strategy is to focus initially on a design that is recognisable — so recognisable, in fact, that its shape or outline alone gives it away — and the route he recommends is working only in black and white, because the contrast puts the emphasis on the shape or idea, colour being secondary to form. What that requires and the founder has not supplied is a way to administer the test: he offers no protocol for who is shown the outline, against what, or what counts as passing. Second: define "out" as a set. He is explicit that a distinctive logo is one that can easily be separated from the competition, and his research instruction is to focus on how the client's competitors brand themselves, picking up any weaknesses you perceive and using them to your advantage — with the blunt framing that if your client is to win, there has to be a loser. What that requires and the founder has not supplied is the competitor set: without a named set there is nothing for distinctiveness to be relative to.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 30 for the outline standard and working in black; printed pp. 48-49 for the competitor instruction and the zero-sum framing; printed p. 173 for his refusal to quantify how much research is enough.
confounders: treating 'stand out' as a property of the mark alone rather than relative to a named set
supplying a numeric distinctiveness score; the source has none and inventing one attributes it to him
confusing the outline test with the small-size reduction; they fail for different reasons

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 180, tip 5 'Not every brand needs a logo mark'
qa_items.question: A two-person consultancy asks for a symbol because "every real brand has one". What does Airey's tip 5 actually make you decide, when should you decide it, and what does his reason not include?
qa_items.answer: It makes you decide whether there should be a symbol at all, rather than assuming there should. He states that sometimes the client just needs a professional logotype to identify the business and that using a symbol can be an unnecessary addition, and he tells you to ask the client whether they have a preference one way or the other. When: he is explicit that this is something to determine at the start of the project, before concept work, not something to arrive at. What his reason does not include is any argument. His one directional rule — if the company is entertaining ideas about expanding into other markets, it might be better to opt for a distinctive logotype, because a mark or identifying symbol could prove restrictive — is stated as a conclusion with no reasoning attached, and it is contradicted by his own earlier chapter, where symbols are what let companies cross language barriers and compete globally. So the usable part of tip 5 is the decision and its timing; the expansion rule is unsupported and disputed inside the same book.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 180. The conflicting passage is at printed p. 13. Neither refers to the other and no reason is given for the restrictiveness claim.
confounders: applying the expansion rule as settled advice without noting the contradiction at printed p. 13
treating a symbol as the default and the wordmark as the exception, which reverses his framing
deferring the decision until concepts exist; he places it at the start

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 96-97, 'The fundamental need for the sketchpad'; printed p. 149; printed p. 155
qa_items.question: A designer says they think faster on screen than on paper. Reconstruct Airey's reasons for excluding the computer anyway, and state precisely where his exclusion stops.
qa_items.answer: Three reasons, from three places. Friction: translating the same process to a computer requires unnecessary intermediate steps that hinder creative flow, whereas on paper you want a circle here, a stroke there — no problem, just do it. Volume: what matters is beating out as many ideas as possible before turning to the computer, sketching from a single mapped word, then combining two, then a group. Disinhibition: keep an open mind and do not limit yourself, make a visual note of every thought that passes even if the ideas seem far-fetched, and do not let weak drawing skill stop you, because the point is documenting ideas so you can build on them or discard them. He repeats it at printed p. 149 with a designer's addition that drawing "will teach you how to see". Where the exclusion stops is stated precisely: eventually your concept develops structure, and only then are you ready to use a computer. It is a stage rule, not a prohibition — and it is practitioner assertion throughout, with no comparison and no measurement anywhere in the book.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 96-97 for all three reasons and the stopping point; printed p. 149 for the repeat and the Huerta quotation; printed p. 182 (tip 7) for the compressed version.
confounders: reading it as a general ban on digital tools rather than a stage rule
assuming the argument is about craft or nostalgia; his stated argument is throughput and freedom
treating 'drawing skills are not important' as encouragement; it is a claim about what the stage is for

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 187, tip 18 'Test at a variety of sizes'
qa_items.question: Airey's size test is a physical procedure with a specific layout instruction. State the procedure, the three properties checked, and the layout instruction with its reason.
qa_items.answer: The procedure is to PRINT the work — this is a paper check, not a screen check. The three properties to confirm on the paper are that it is clean, that it has a good level of contrast, and that it is not pixelated. The layout instruction is not to print a single logo: replicate the design across a variety of sizes and colours on the sheet for variation, and his stated reason is that there is no point in using a full page of paper on one tiny design. The value of the instruction is that it makes the test a comparison across a range in one look rather than a sequence of single verdicts. What he does not supply is any pass criterion for the three properties; "clean", "good contrast" and "not pixelated" are left to the designer's eye.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 187. Explicitly a print-and-inspect instruction on paper output; it is production advice in the source's own frame and is not a rendering instruction.
confounders: substituting an on-screen contact sheet, which is a different act with different failure modes
checking one size, which the instruction exists to prevent
assuming a numeric contrast criterion; he gives none

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 190, tip 22 'Don't neglect the substrate'; and printed pp. 175-176, 'Tools of the trade'
qa_items.question: Two of Airey's cautions are about the artwork's physical fate rather than its design. What are they, and why does he say each matters?
qa_items.answer: The substrate: the paper or card a logo appears on can make a big difference to how it appears in the final presentation, because the colour and the sharpness of the mark can change drastically — so discuss all the possibilities for variation with the commercial printer, or advise the client to, before final production. And scalability: the delivered artwork must be scalable to any size, for use on posters or on the side of buildings, which is his reason for producing marks as vector artwork rather than in a photo editor. The failure case for the second is named earlier and is the sharper illustration: a low-resolution "save for web" logo file scaled up and used on the cover of a printed sales manual, which he says defeats the purpose of hiring a specialist. Both are physical-production cautions in his own frame, tied to 2010 commercial print, and neither comes with a method or a tolerance.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 190 (tip 22) for the substrate; printed pp. 175-176 for scalable vector artwork; the low-resolution failure case is at printed p. 47. Tool recommendations in the same passage are deliberately not treated as knowledge here.
confounders: reading the substrate caution as being about paper quality rather than about colour and sharpness shifting
treating the scalability point as a software preference; his stated reason is size range
assuming he gives tolerances or a method; he gives neither

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 39, 'Remember that rules are made to be broken'
qa_items.question: Airey ends his criteria chapter by weakening it. What exactly does he withdraw, what precondition does he attach, and what does he claim the benefit is?
qa_items.answer: He withdraws necessity. Having given the seven elements, he asks whether you always have to play by the rules and answers that rules are made to be broken — it is up to you to break new ground and cross boundaries in attempting designs that are a cut above the rest. The precondition is stated a chapter-opening earlier and is not decorative: you have to know the rules in any creative endeavour before you can successfully break them, illustrated by a Michelin-starred chef who does not pull ingredients out of thin air but takes a proven recipe and adapts it. The benefit he claims is not a better outcome — he is explicit that whether your results are successful will obviously be an open question — but a faster one: you will learn much more and much faster when the potential mistakes are your own rather than someone else's. The consequence for anyone quoting the seven elements as a specification is that they are reading the book against its own closing paragraph.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 39 for the withdrawal and the open question; printed p. 22 for the know-the-rules precondition and the chef analogy.
confounders: reading it as licence to ignore the criteria; the licence is scoped to a designer who knows them
assuming he claims rule-breaking produces better marks; he says the outcome is an open question
confusing this weakening of necessity with Chermayeff's denial of sufficiency at printed p. 145

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 188, tip 19 'Reverse it'
qa_items.question: You supply a reversed version of a mark as Airey instructs, and it fails. What kind of mark fails, and does Airey give you a test for it?
qa_items.answer: The kind that fails is a mark whose meaning lives in its own internal negative space, because inverting figure and ground can invert the reading. His own book is full of such marks — the Food Writers Guild nib containing a spoon, Ed's Electric where the white gaps between two black forms make the letters, the New Bedford Whaling Museum where the whale's fluke is white space between sails — and a naive reversal turns the negative shape into the positive one. He does NOT give you a test for it. Tip 19 states only that you should offer a version that works on dark backgrounds, glossed as supplying a version in white, with the stated reason being flexibility and the client appreciating you for it. It raises no possibility of failure at all. Worth adding: the mark printed on that very page, the "amp" wordmark, is shown in black on white, so the page does not demonstrate its own instruction. The best you can do with him is combine tip 19 with tip 16's requirement that the elements inside the mark stay separable — which turns the reversal into a check rather than a deliverable.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 188. The page was rendered and inspected during extraction: the 'amp' mark is printed black on white and not reversed. The negative-space marks named are at printed pp. 7, 26 and 32, all rendered and inspected.
confounders: assuming Airey addresses reversal failure; he does not raise it
treating the reversed version as automatic — a mechanical inversion is not what a designer would supply
confusing reversal with the one-colour reduction; a mark can survive one and fail the other

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 25, 'Make it relevant'; and printed p. 184, tip 11
qa_items.question: Airey teaches relevance almost entirely through negative examples. List the ones he gives, and say what kind of judgement they all are.
qa_items.answer: From printed p. 25: drop the fun approach if you are designing for a lawyer; no beach balls for a winter-holiday television programme; a smiling face clearly will not work for a cancer organisation. From the chapter recap at printed p. 38: however much you might want to use a fun design that makes everyone smile, it is not ideal for the local crematorium. From tip 11 at printed p. 184: ditch the fun approach for a law firm; nothing too serious for a children's television programme; muted colours rather than bright fluorescents for a Michelin-starred restaurant. They are all the same kind of judgement — REGISTER violations, where the mark's tone is wrong for the category rather than its form being badly made. That is worth naming because it means the relevance requirement is not checkable the way his reproduction tests are: you can verify a one-inch reduction, and you cannot verify that a register is appropriate. It also means the examples are culturally bounded to Western commercial categories around 2010, which he does not say.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 25, the recap at p. 38, and tip 11 at p. 184. All the examples are register judgements; none is a formal property of a mark.
confounders: treating relevance as checkable in the way the reproduction tests are
reading the examples as being about subject matter rather than tone
assuming he flags the cultural boundedness; he does not

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 24, the NHS case, 'Keep it simple'
qa_items.question: Airey offers the NHS mark as evidence for simplicity. What does the designer actually give as his three reasons, and what does that do to the aesthetic reading of the case?
qa_items.answer: Richard Moon's three stated reasons for keeping the design deliberately simple were: to make it easy to implement; to last as long as possible; and to avoid being attacked by the British media, which often view identity programmes of that kind as an extravagant use of public funds. Only the second is an aesthetic or design-longevity reason at all. The first is operational and the third is political — a simple mark is cheap-looking in the sense that matters when a newspaper is costing your identity programme. That complicates the case considerably as evidence for simplicity as a design virtue: the mark is simple partly for reasons that have nothing to do with how it is perceived by its audience. Airey's own framing around it is separate — the design going essentially unchanged for nearly twenty years is a testament to its success — which is a survivorship argument, using longevity as the evidence of quality and quality as the explanation of longevity.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 24, quoting Richard Moon of Moon Brand. The saving claim in the same passage — tens of millions of pounds by the NHS's own calculations — is an outcome asserted by a party to the project with no controls.
confounders: reporting only the longevity reason and dropping the implementation and press reasons
reading the twenty-year survival as evidence that simplicity caused it
treating the NHS's own savings estimate as independent evidence

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 141, 'Swallow that pride'
qa_items.question: At the presentation itself, Airey says you are selling one thing and not another. What is the distinction, and what specific cost does he say you pay for getting it wrong?
qa_items.answer: What you are selling at that stage is the IDEA behind your best designs — the story behind the concepts — and not the intricacies of the mark or the particular choice of typeface. He tells you to remind the client as often as necessary to focus on the idea alone, and says those minor details can be settled once a single direction has been agreed. The specific cost of getting it wrong is not vague dilution: you could end up supplying revisions on more than one direction, which is an unnecessary expense for both parties. That is the argument's strength — it gives the client a reason too, not just the designer. He follows it immediately with an honest admission that things do not always work out: of the sixty or seventy clients he had presented brand identity projects to, two or three of his earliest presentations were so unsuccessful that they stalled the process and both sides lost out.
