qa_items.support: Printed p. 141. The revisions-on-more-than-one-direction cost is his stated reason; the sixty to seventy client figure and the two or three failures are on the same page.
confounders: reading it as advice to withhold detail from the client rather than to sequence the decisions
assuming the cost is aesthetic; the cost he names is duplicated revision work
confusing it with the ground-rules passage at printed pp. 129-130, which is about the boundary on feedback

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 155, 'Think laterally'
qa_items.question: You have produced twenty sketches for a wordmark and they all look like each other. Which of Airey's moves apply, and what account does he give of why you are stuck?
qa_items.answer: His account of the problem is mechanical rather than mystical: the brain forms routine patterns, and the more often you perform the same task the more entrenched and natural the pattern becomes, so before you know it you are in a rut. Four moves follow. Turn your design concepts upside down. Look at them from a distance. Ask someone else to share some thoughts on your sketches. And the one from his own practice: sketch every idea that comes, then study those sketches WITH THE DESIGN BRIEF IN HAND, which he says produces further sketches that would not have come to mind without that analysis. Each works by presenting the same material under a condition the entrenched pattern does not cover — different orientation, different distance, different observer, or a re-reading against the brief. He frames all of it against the romantic view, quoting de Bono that creative thinking is a skill rather than a matter of individual talent, and not a matter of sitting by the river playing baroque music and hoping to be inspired.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 155. The pattern-formation account is asserted without evidence and the de Bono quotation is an appeal to authority.
confounders: reaching for inspiration or reference-hunting, which is the approach the passage argues against
missing the brief-in-hand move, which is the only one specific to identity work
confusing the upside-down move here, which is for generating ideas, with tip 20, which is a finishing check

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 53-55, the FedEx renaming, 'Field research to the rescue'
qa_items.question: In Airey's FedEx account, research changed something bigger than the mark. What did the research find, what did it change, and what makes this his strongest example of research?
qa_items.answer: A nine-month global study by the two organisations' research groups found that businesses and consumers were unaware of the company's global reach and full-service capabilities, believing it shipped only overnight and only within the United States. Further research on the name itself found that many people associated "federal" negatively with government and bureaucracy, and that "express" was over-used — more than 900 company names in the US alone employed it. On the positive side, people had already shortened the name into a generic verb ("I need to FedEx a package") regardless of which carrier they used, and testing with the target public confirmed that the short form conveyed more speed, technology and innovation than the formal name. What it changed was the name: Landor advised adopting "FedEx" as the communicative name while keeping "Federal Express Corporation" as the legal one. It is his strongest research example because it is the only place in the book where a finding contradicted the obvious move and the research output was a decision above the designer's own remit — with over 300 designs then created in the exploratory phase, ranging from evolutionary to revolutionary.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 53-55. This is the only reported measurement in the extracted span; everything else in the book is practitioner assertion or narrated case.
confounders: remembering the FedEx arrow, which Airey does not mention anywhere
assuming the research validated a design; it changed the name
treating the 300 explorations as a recommended concept count; his own guidance is two or three shown to the client

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 114-116, 'Where Photoshop comes into play'
qa_items.question: Airey requires concepts to be shown in context. What is his analogy, what is his stated reason, and what does he concede about what the practice is for?
qa_items.answer: The analogy is a car: it might have a fresh paint job and that new-car smell, but unless you take a test drive you will not be entirely convinced. The stated reason is about the client's attention rather than the design's quality — most clients do not have the time to follow every step of the process and will be focused on the final result, so the more tangible your concepts appear, the more the client will be able to visualise the benefits. He also claims a variety effect: the greater the range of applications you create, the more consistent the use appears and the more attractive the result. What he concedes, and it is worth keeping, is the purpose: showing your logo designs in context may be what finally seals the deal with the client. That is a persuasion claim, not a decision-quality claim — and the obvious corollary he does not raise is that a well-made mock-up can make a weak mark look convincing too.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 114-116, including the test-drive analogy, the variety claim and the seals-the-deal concession. The Kerling mock-up pages were not rendered during extraction, so nothing is claimed here about what they show.
confounders: reading it as improving the client's judgement; his stated function is helping them visualise and closing the sale
assuming he warns about flattering mock-ups; he does not
treating the tools named in the passage as part of the knowledge; they are 2010 tool recommendations

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 43-44, 'It's all in the design brief'
qa_items.question: Airey's argument for a written brief is not that it records requirements. What is it, and what does he explicitly say the brief does NOT let you do?
qa_items.answer: It is that the brief settles disputes. He says pitfalls may arise along the way — your client may disagree with a decision you have taken — and it is at moments like that that you can return to the details of the brief to back up your position. What he explicitly says it does not let you do is refuse to change: that does not mean you will not make design changes as a result of a disagreement, since you want to please your client after all. The brief exists to provide BOTH parties with concrete reasons for the decisions taken throughout the process — so its function is to convert a clash of taste into a check against a shared prior commitment, not to give the designer a veto. He names a second function too: keeping his own work in bounds, admitting he has entertained some far-fetched ideas from time to time and that the brief helps keep relevance on course.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 43-44 for the arbitration function and the explicit qualification; printed p. 50 for the keeping-your-own-work-in-bounds function.
confounders: reading the brief as a contract that lets the designer refuse changes, which he rules out in the next sentence
treating it as a requirements document, which is the function he does not emphasise
assuming it protects only the designer; he says it gives both parties concrete reasons

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 185, tip 13; printed p. 15, the Bethnal Green applications; printed p. 47
qa_items.question: A client will produce their own social posts, decks and signage using your mark. Using Airey, what do you deliver beyond the artwork, what failure are you preventing, and where does his own advice complicate the answer?
qa_items.answer: You deliver a style guide. He says many logos are accompanied by style guides, that creating them is your responsibility, and that they exist so anyone within the client's company who uses the design does so consistently — and at printed p. 47 he frames the trigger as a briefing question, asking how many people are responsible for using the brand identity, which invites the follow-up conversation about guidelines and may lead you to offer a guide showing how to use, and how not to use, the design. The failure being prevented is stated as an extreme case: a low-resolution "save for web" logo file scaled up and used on the cover of a printed sales manual, which defeats the purpose of hiring a specialist. Where his own advice complicates it: at printed p. 15 the practice he praises is a mark used as a TEMPLATE and modified to suit any application — the same star engraved on glass and hand-drawn on screen-printed paper. Deliberate per-application variation and strict consistency are not the same instruction, and the book never says how much variation is still one mark, which is precisely what your guide has to decide.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 185 for the guide and the responsibility; printed p. 47 for the briefing question and the low-resolution failure; printed p. 15 for the template practice. He never reconciles the two.
confounders: delivering artwork alone, which leaves the consistency requirement with no instrument
assuming consistency means one immutable lockup, which his own Bethnal Green case contradicts
treating the guide as optional; he assigns it to the designer as a responsibility

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 186, tip 14 'Match the type to the mark'; and printed p. 37, the French Property Exhibition typeface note
qa_items.question: Airey's only direct instruction about typeface selection is one line. What is it, and what does a designer on the facing side of the same book actually do?
qa_items.answer: Tip 14: show a level of unity across your design — for example, if you show a playful mark, try matching it with a playful typeface. That is the whole of it: one example, one direction, no mechanism, and no treatment of the deliberate mismatch a designer might use for tension. What the designer of the French Property Exhibition mark actually says he did is different in kind: with three lines of text he chose regular, evenly weighted Avenir caps in order to keep the type flush with the lines of the mark. That is a proportion and alignment argument, not a register-matching one. Both are in the book and only the weaker of the two is elevated into a tip. The practical reading is that "match the type to the mark" underdetermines almost every real decision, and Airey's other constraint on lettering — tip 12's immediate-legibility gate — does more work.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 186 for tip 14; printed p. 37 for Roy Smith's stated reasoning about Avenir caps. The two are different kinds of argument and the book does not connect them.
confounders: elaborating tip 14 into a theory of type pairing; the book contains one sentence
assuming register-matching is his general position on type; the worked case reasons about alignment
confusing it with tip 12, which is a legibility gate rather than a matching rule

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 28, 'Incorporate tradition'; and printed p. 183, tip 8
qa_items.question: Airey rules against trends and then makes one concession that keeps the rule workable. State the rule, the standard it replaces, the concession, and the problem the rule cannot solve.
qa_items.answer: The rule: leave trends to the fashion industry — trends come and go like the wind, and the last thing you want is to invest a significant amount of your time and your client's money in a design that will look dated overnight. The standard it replaces: longevity is key, and a logo should last the lifetime of the company it represents. The concession, without which the rule would forbid all change: the mark may be refined after a certain time to add some freshness, but the underlying idea must remain intact. The problem it cannot solve is telling a trend from a current convention while you are inside it. His own example of the error — the period in the nineties when Helvetica Neue seemed to be used on every new design — is identified only in retrospect, and the book offers no way to make that identification prospectively. The quoted designer's version, "I don't want to be in vogue, I want to set the standard and not follow others", is a statement of ambition, not a test.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 28 for the rule, the standard and the refinement concession; printed p. 183 for tip 8; printed p. 73 for the Helvetica Neue observation; printed p. 29 for the Grear quotation.
confounders: stating the rule without the refinement concession, which makes it unworkable
assuming he offers a way to identify a trend prospectively; his own example is retrospective
reading 'the underlying idea should remain intact' as forbidding visual change

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 25 and printed p. 180, tip 4, against printed pp. 10 and 21
qa_items.question: Airey's examples of marks that do not depict the business are BMW, Xerox, Virgin Atlantic, Tiger Woods and Hawaiian Airlines. Using something he says elsewhere in the same book, explain why that example set is weak support for a new brand, and what still survives of the claim.
qa_items.answer: Every one of them is a large, long-established brand. At printed p. 10 he concedes the point himself, in a different context: for products and services with a strong brand identity it is the identity people often think of first rather than the product itself — but of course a huge marketing budget is needed to reach the recognition rates of organisations like those. So the examples show that a non-depicting mark can work AFTER decades of exposure, not that a new brand can carry one. The example set is survivorship-selected in the ordinary way — famous surviving marks chosen after the fact, with no unsuccessful non-depicting marks shown anywhere. What survives is the narrower and still useful claim: depiction is not a REQUIREMENT of relevance, which he demonstrates by separating the two ideas cleanly and by allowing a literal mark that does not overstate its idea. What does not survive is any inference about how a new brand with no recognition should choose.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 25 and tip 4 at printed p. 180 for the example set; printed p. 10 for the marketing-budget concession. Only Hawaiian Airlines is actually printed in the book; the rest are named in prose and the reader is asked to recall them.
confounders: taking the example set as evidence for a start-up's choice
concluding depiction is therefore required for a new brand, which he never says
missing that four of the five marks are not reproduced in the book at all

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 22-24, 'Keep it simple'; and printed p. 8, Ch. 2 opening
qa_items.question: Airey's argument for simplicity rests on a memory claim and his argument for brand identity rests on a value claim. State each, and state what evidence he offers for either.
qa_items.answer: The memory claim: it is much easier to remember a single detail than five — his illustration is the Mona Lisa, where the smile is recalled and the clothing, the hand position, the eye colour, the background and the artist are not, and he proposes a self-test, asking which you would draw more accurately, the McDonald's mark or the Mona Lisa. The value claim: people usually choose products based on their perceived value rather than their actual value — his illustration is a celebrity driving an Aston Martin rather than a Škoda, which he concedes is consistently rated car of the year in many European countries, offers much better mileage and is significantly cheaper, and is the logical choice, while the Aston Martin identity, evoking luxury and status, usually takes the sale. The evidence he offers for either is none. Both are stated as facts about how minds and markets work, with no citation, no measurement, and no reported result from the self-test he proposes. They are the two load-bearing premises of the book and both are assertions.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 23 for the memory claim and the Mona Lisa test; printed p. 8 for the perceived-value claim and the Aston Martin comparison. Neither carries a citation anywhere in the book.
confounders: treating the memory claim as drawing on cognitive research; he cites none
assuming the drawing test was actually run; it is proposed rhetorically and no result is reported
reading the perceived-value claim as a finding rather than as the premise the book is built on

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 30-31, 'Aim for distinction'; printed p. 34; printed p. 186; printed p. 188
qa_items.question: You are briefed to make a wordmark for a new prepaid-billing product with no existing recognition, to be used at favicon size, on a dark dashboard, in a one-colour invoice header, and on printed collateral. Which of Airey's requirements bind hardest here, and where does his advice stop being usable?
qa_items.answer: Four bind hard and they compound. The dark dashboard and the one-colour header together mean the mark must be designed for the reduced case, not adapted to it: he requires a supplied one-colour version (tip 15) and a version that works on dark backgrounds (tip 19), and his generation argument at printed p. 30 says to work only in black and white anyway, because contrast puts the emphasis on the shape and colour is secondary to form. Favicon size is the extreme of his "think small" case — he names the favicon explicitly as the small end of the media range, and his one-inch rule with no loss of detail sets the floor. And because the brand is unknown, tip 12's legibility gate applies at full strength by his own scoping — if most people cannot read it straight away, do not use it as a logo. Where his advice stops being usable: he gives no threshold for the dark-ground case beyond "clearly identified", no test for whether a mark survives reversal at all, nothing about screen rendering below one inch, and no way to administer the legibility gate — no population, no exposure time, no distance. Everything past those points is your judgement and must not be attributed to him.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 30 (work in black; colour secondary to form), p. 34 (think small; favicon; one inch), p. 185 (legibility gate and its scoping clause), p. 186 (one-colour version), pp. 187-188 (contrast; reverse it). The gaps named are gaps in the source, not omissions from the answer.
confounders: importing a numeric contrast threshold from an accessibility standard and presenting it as Airey's
treating the dark-ground and one-colour requirements as delivery formats rather than as constraints on the design
dropping the legibility gate because the mark is a wordmark; the unknown-brand condition is exactly when he says it binds hardest

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 31, the NAAs mark; and printed p. 30, 'Aim for distinction'
qa_items.question: You have three candidate symbols and no way to test them on an audience. Using two checks Airey supplies that need neither a client nor a budget, how would you separate them, and what may you NOT report from the result?
qa_items.answer: Two checks, both administered on the artwork and both free. The outline check: reduce each candidate to a filled silhouette and see whether the shape alone still gives it away — his stated strategy is to focus on a design that is recognisable, so recognisable in fact that only its shape or outline betrays it. The description check: try to describe each candidate in one short phrase, on his observation that distinctive marks are almost always simple enough to be described easily, demonstrated by his own one-clause description of the NAAs mark as an "open newspaper" symbol in the form of the letter A. A candidate that needs three clauses is carrying more than one idea, which is also what the "focus on one thing" rule forbids. What you may NOT report is a result as his. He gives no protocol for the outline check — no assessor, no comparison set, no pass mark — and the description claim runs only from distinctiveness to describability, hedged with "almost always", demonstrated once by an author who already knew what the mark meant. Any score you attach is yours.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 30 for the outline standard and its restatement at p. 38; printed p. 31 for the describability observation and its single demonstration. Printed pp. 30-31 were rendered and inspected during extraction.
confounders: reporting a numeric distinctiveness score as though it came from this source
using the description check on someone who has been told the intended meaning, which is his flawed demonstration condition
treating the silhouette check as the same as the small-size reduction; the two fail for different reasons

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 132-133, 'Keep the committee in question', the landscape gardening project
qa_items.question: A client's team already has a firm idea of the design they want and does not tell you. Airey lost a month to exactly this. What did he conclude he should have set up, and what does his account reveal about why they stayed quiet?
qa_items.answer: He concluded he should have set the ground rules at the start, and he scripts what he should have said: with your help, we will create a number of possible design directions that suit your prospective customers perfectly; once the different ideas have been presented, we can choose the most effective option and either move ahead with it or adjust it slightly after your feedback. He adds a second, blunter omission — he should also have asked at the initial meeting whether the client had any preconceived design ideas, and did not. What his account reveals about the silence is the useful part and is not what you would guess: they were not being obstructive. They stayed quiet because they considered the possibility that he might create a design they liked even better, so they decided to keep it to themselves. The cost was a month of research, brainstorming, sketching and conceptualising that did not matter to them, because by then the committee members had already attached themselves to their own original idea.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 132-133. One narrated project told by the person it happened to, with no control; the reason for the silence is his reconstruction of their reasoning.
confounders: assuming the client was acting in bad faith; his account says the opposite
concluding the fix is a stricter contract rather than a question asked at the first meeting
reading it as an argument against committee involvement; he argues elsewhere that committee input made a project stronger

qa_items.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 187, tips 16 and 18; printed p. 190, tip 22
qa_items.question: Three of Airey's checks are about physical output rather than about the design. Identify them, and say why it matters that they are kept in his frame rather than translated into a digital one.
qa_items.answer: Printing the mark replicated across a range of sizes and colours on one sheet and inspecting the paper for cleanliness, contrast and pixelation (tip 18). Watching the contrast between the mark and its background and between its own elements when the mark is applied to promotional material and corporate stationery (tip 16). And discussing the substrate with the commercial printer before final production, because the paper or card can drastically change the mark's colour and sharpness (tip 22). It matters because each is defined on ink and stock and each has failure modes that do not exist elsewhere: dot gain, absorbency, sharpness loss on uncoated board. Rendering an on-screen contact sheet is a DIFFERENT act, and the source does not endorse it as a substitute — treating it as one would silently convert a press check into something it is not, and would attribute to Airey a claim about a pipeline he never discusses. The transferable content of all three is the ordering and the fact that the check exists, not the tolerances, of which he gives none.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 187 (tips 16 and 18) and printed p. 190 (tip 22). All three are stated as physical acts and none carries a numeric criterion.
confounders: restating tip 18 as an on-screen size check, which loses the paper-specific failure modes
assuming tip 16 is a design-stage rule; he scopes it to when the mark is applied to material
inventing tolerances for any of the three; the source supplies none

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction, section 'Generating Word of Mouth' (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Berger opens by claiming practitioners systematically misjudge where word of mouth happens. What figure does he report, what do audiences typically guess, and what two reasons does he give for the gap?
qa_items.answer: He reports that only about 7 percent of word of mouth happens online, against a typical estimate of around 50 percent. Two reasons for the overestimate. First, time: people spend roughly eight times as long offline as online, which creates far more occasions for offline conversation. Second, and the more interesting one, visibility — online conversation leaves a written record and offline conversation leaves none, so the countable channel is mistaken for the large one. He also disputes the assumption that online reach is larger in practice: potential reach is larger, but most recipients never see any given message.
qa_items.support: The 7 percent figure is NOT Berger's measurement — he attributes it to the Keller Fay Group and points to Keller and Fay's The Face-to-Face Book, with no design described. The counter-estimate of around 50 percent IS his own reported measurement, but it is an informal poll of hundreds of students and executives, with no control or sampling frame. Sharply period-bound to roughly 2011-2012.
confounders: reading this as a claim that online word of mouth is unimportant, which he does not say — his endnote adds that online is the better channel when the desired action is a click away
assuming the 7 percent figure is one of Berger's own studies; it is not, and the book gives no design for it
treating the 50 percent figure as a survey finding rather than as an informal classroom poll

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction, the passage on viral 'theories' in 'Generating Word of Mouth' (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Berger says the popular theories of what makes content viral — that it must be funny or cute — are built on a specific methodological error. What is the error, what is his illustration of it, and what standard does he say a proper account must meet?
qa_items.answer: The error is selecting cases on the outcome: the theories are induced from a handful of hits, and the features they identify are equally present in the vast population of content that failed. His illustration is that Bill Clinton, Bill Gates and Bill Cosby are all famous, so changing your name to Bill is the route to fame — where, as he puts it, the initial observation is correct and the conclusion is patently ludicrous. The standard he sets is that you must examine successes and failures together and ask whether a characteristic is more often than not linked to success. He notes that most cute cat clips get fewer than a few dozen views; the million-view ones are the outliers.
qa_items.support: A methodological argument, not a measurement. Note that Berger states this standard and does not demonstrate that his own analyses meet it; establishing that requires checking each study, and two of his datasets — the BzzAgent campaigns and six months of New York Times articles — are populations rather than hit lists.
confounders: reading it as a claim that humour and cuteness do not help, which is not the claim — the claim is that the inference is invalid
confusing this with the separate argument about influentials, which is about the messenger rather than about method
assuming Berger exempts himself; he states the standard and never shows his own work satisfies it

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction, section 'Generating Word of Mouth' and its endnote on 'making things go viral'; Epilogue, second point (spine 5, spine 12, spine 17)
qa_items.question: Berger rejects the influentials thesis in the body text and states something noticeably weaker in his endnote. What does each say, and why does the difference matter?
qa_items.answer: The body text says conventional wisdom is wrong: some people are more persuasive and some have more friends, but in most cases that does not make them more influential in spreading things, and contagious content spreads regardless of whether the messenger has ten friends or ten thousand. The endnote says something different in kind — that right now there is little good empirical evidence that better-connected or more persuasive people have a bigger impact. That is an absence-of-evidence statement, not a demonstration that messengers do not matter. The difference matters because the body text's confident refutation is not what the endnote supports, and the book's whole shift of attention to the message rests on it. Berger does not deny that individuals supply an initial spark; his borrowed comparison, from Duncan Watts, is that big forest fires are not caused by big sparks.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument, with the empirical support cited only in the Notes and all of it third-party: Bakshy, Hofman, Mason and Watts's Twitter influence study, and Watts and Dodds. The forest-fire comparison is Watts's, and Berger attributes it.
confounders: reporting the body text alone, which overstates what the source establishes
reading the claim as 'messengers never matter'; he explicitly allows that individuals provide the spark
attributing the forest-fire argument to Berger; he credits Duncan Watts for it

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction, the author's first footnote defining 'viral' (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Berger uses the word "viral" constantly. In his own footnote he narrows it. What does he say it does and does not mean, and what does that narrowing do to the rest of the book's promises?
qa_items.answer: He says that when he claims something will make an idea more viral, he means only that it will be more likely to spread from one person to another — and expressly not that one person will generate a long chain that infects a population. He says the disease analogy holds only up to a point, that the key difference is expected chain length, and that long chains may be less common with products and ideas than the analogy implies. The effect on the book is substantial: every promise to make something contagious means raising the probability of a single pass-on, not producing an epidemic. He hedges the empirical half — long chains "may be" less common — and cites Goel, Watts and Goldstein for it.
qa_items.support: Berger's own explicit definition, placed in a footnote to the Introduction, with a single parenthetical third-party citation. He does not claim to have established the short-chain point himself.
confounders: assuming 'viral' in this book means what it means in ordinary usage, namely explosive population-wide spread
missing the placement: the book's most important self-limitation is in a footnote, and the body text never repeats it
treating the short-chain claim as Berger's finding rather than as a hedged citation

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction, the author's second footnote on the recipe analogy, and 'A Conversation with Jonah Berger', question 9 (spine 5, spine 14)
qa_items.question: What does Berger actually claim about how his six drivers relate to one another — are they jointly necessary, individually sufficient, ranked, or something else? Quote his own framing and note where the book contradicts it.
qa_items.answer: A menu, not a recipe. He states that not all six ingredients are required; that a product which is Public will not fail because it is not wrapped in a Story; that the principles are relatively independent so you can pick and choose; and that more is better. His own image is that they are "less like a recipe and more like tasty salad toppings" — a Cobb salad with just cheese and bacon is still delicious. In the back-matter interview he adds that no one of the drivers is most important, though some are easier to apply in some categories, and that the payoff lies in attempting the difficult ones. The contradiction is in his own Epilogue, which says "there is a recipe for success" and closes that following the six will make any product or idea contagious — a sufficiency claim the footnote denies — while also saying "or even just a few of them" two paragraphs earlier.
qa_items.support: The Introduction footnote and the Readers Group Guide interview, both explicit. Note that the independence claim is ASSERTED and never tested: no analysis in the book measures the six jointly and checks whether their contributions separate.
confounders: the checklist reading — treating the six as boxes all of which must be ticked, which the Epilogue's diagnostic checklist invites and the footnote forbids
reading STEPPS as a priority order or a sequence; Berger says the ordering is a memory aid
taking the Epilogue's 'recipe for success' as the source's position; it contradicts his own footnote
assuming independence is a finding; it is an assertion with no supporting analysis in the book

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction, section 'Six Principles of Contagiousness'; restated in the Epilogue checklist (spine 5, spine 12)
qa_items.question: Name Berger's six drivers in his own terms and give the diagnostic question he attaches to each in the closing checklist.
qa_items.answer: Social Currency — does talking about your product or idea make people look good. Triggers — what cues make people think about it, and how can you grow the habitat so it comes to mind more often. Emotion — does talking about it generate feeling, and how can you kindle the fire. Public — does it advertise itself, can people see when others are using it, and can you create behavioural residue that persists after use. Practical Value — does talking about it help people help others, and can you package your expertise into useful information others will pass on. Stories — what is your Trojan Horse, and is the story not only viral but valuable. The initials spell STEPPS, which Berger says is a memory aid rather than an order.
qa_items.support: Berger's own framework, stated in the Introduction and restated as a checklist in the Epilogue. The six were derived inductively by noticing common themes across contagious content; he does not claim the set is exhaustive and offers no test that would reveal a missing seventh.
confounders: substituting the Heaths' six principles from Made to Stick, which is a different framework aimed at a different outcome — being remembered rather than being passed on
reading 'Public' as meaning publicity rather than observability of use
reading 'Stories' as meaning storytelling craft rather than as a carrier for information

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction, the passage beginning 'Word of mouth is more effective than traditional advertising for two key reasons' (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Berger gives two reasons word of mouth beats advertising. The second is the less obvious one. What is it, and what is his image for how it works?
qa_items.answer: The second is targeting. Advertising can buy proximity to an interested audience but not knowledge of who within it actually needs the thing now; word of mouth is naturally directed, because a sharer selects the specific person they judge would find the information relevant and skips everyone else. His image is a searchlight: each recipient sweeps their own network for the one person the thing suits. His example is a publisher who sent him two copies of a book with a note suggesting he pass the second to a colleague — outsourcing the targeting to someone with private knowledge no media buy could purchase. The first reason is credibility: advertising will always argue its product is best, so it is discounted, whereas a friend will report a negative as readily as a positive.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument from premises about incentives and private knowledge, illustrated by one personal anecdote. Every supporting figure in this passage is third-party and appears only in the Notes — the twenty-to-fifty-percent purchasing figure is a McKinsey white paper, the restaurant and Amazon figures are Godes and Mayzlin and Chevalier and Mayzlin.
confounders: giving only the credibility reason, which is the one most accounts remember
reading targeting as demographic targeting; his point is that the sharer holds private knowledge about relevance that no targeting system has
treating the 'ten times more effective' figure as Berger's measurement; it rests on third-party work cited only in the Notes

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Inner Remarkability' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Berger defines "remarkable" and insists on a particular emphasis in the word. What is the definition, what is the emphasis, and what does he report about how remarkability relates to being discussed?
qa_items.answer: Remarkable things are unusual, extraordinary, or worthy of notice or attention — novel, surprising, extreme, or just plain interesting. His emphasis is on the second half of the word: the most important aspect is that they are worthy of REMARK, worthy of mention. The test is whether a thing is worth saying out loud, not whether it is impressive. He reports his own analysis, with Raghu Iyengar, of 6,500 products and brands scored for perceived remarkability against how frequently each was discussed online: more remarkable brands were talked about almost twice as often as less remarkable ones. The mechanism he gives is transfer — telling someone a remarkable thing makes the teller seem remarkable.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Raghu Iyengar, cited in the Notes as a Wharton working paper at the time of writing. The design is CORRELATIONAL — remarkability was rated and discussion counted, nothing manipulated — and the outcome measured is ONLINE discussion, which by the book's own account is about 7 percent of word of mouth.
confounders: reading remarkability as impressiveness or quality; his test is mentionability
treating the 'almost twice as often' result as causal; the design is correlational and the source's narration does not mark that
missing that this finding sits in unreconciled tension with the BzzAgent null in the next chapter, where interest, novelty and surprise showed no relationship with word of mouth

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', the University of Illinois cockroach study in 'Inner Remarkability' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A study in this chapter shows that how a story is retold depends on who is listening. Describe the design and the result, and say whose study it is.
qa_items.answer: It is not Berger's — it is by a group of psychologists at the University of Illinois. Pairs of students were brought to a working kitchen for what appeared to be a study of group cooking, with vegetables, chicken and shrimp laid out. Live cockroaches had been planted among the ingredients. After the students recoiled, the experimenter cancelled the study and sent them to another one supposedly next door. On the way, half were questioned about what had happened by the experimenter and half by someone who appeared to be another student but was working with the experimenter. That is the manipulated variable: the audience. Those talking to a peer described larger and more numerous cockroaches and a more disgusting experience. When the goal was to impress and entertain rather than to report, the details were amplified.
qa_items.support: Third-party research, reported by Berger. It IS a genuine manipulated comparison — audience type varied, everything else held. Note the reported outcome is a difference in a SINGLE retelling, not a measured drift across a chain; the game-of-telephone extrapolation is Berger's.
confounders: attributing the study to Berger; the audience manipulation is one of the cleanest designs in the book and it belongs to someone else
assuming the amplification is deliberate lying — Berger gives a second, non-strategic route through reconstructive memory

reading this as showing stories grow richer as they travel, which conflicts with the Allport and Postman result Berger reports later, where about 70 percent of detail is lost in five or six transmissions

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', sub-section 'Building a Good Game' within 'Leverage Game Mechanics' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A membership scheme awards more than a hundred differently named badges for different kinds of activity, and users are proud of them. On Berger's account, what is wrong with it and what is his contrasting case?
qa_items.answer: It fails his legibility requirement. Berger says effective status systems are easy to understand even by people unfamiliar with the domain, and a scheme with a hundred unrankable badges fails that: he asks whether anyone on the street could say whether being the mayor of a location beats a School Night badge or a Super User badge. Since the whole payoff of a status system is being SEEN to be ahead, standing that an outsider cannot read confers no social currency, and the achievement produces no talk. His contrasting case is Olympic medals — tell someone you won silver and they know exactly how you did, even if they know nothing about the sport. He gives credit card tiers as the same failure: once gold was issued broadly, companies added platinum, sapphire and diamond, and nobody can rank them, producing what he calls a chaos of consumer confusion. He also cites British supermarket traffic-light nutrition labels as an intuitive system anyone can read immediately.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument from constructed contrasts, not measured. No comparison of outcomes between legible and illegible schemes is reported anywhere. Heavily period-bound to roughly 2011-2012.
confounders: diagnosing the problem as too many badges rather than as unrankable ones; Berger's criterion is legibility to outsiders, not count
assuming internal satisfaction is enough — his mechanism runs through interpersonal comparison, so private pride produces no word of mouth
recommending better badge design or naming without addressing whether a stranger can rank the levels

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Make People Feel Like Insiders' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Berger distinguishes scarcity from exclusivity, which are usually run together. What is the distinction, and what does he insist about what can serve as the basis for exclusivity?
qa_items.answer: Scarcity restricts HOW MUCH is offered — through high demand, limited production, or limits on the time or place something can be acquired. Exclusivity restricts WHO may have it, by criteria. His insistence is that the criterion need not be money or celebrity: exclusivity is also about knowledge — knowing certain information, or being connected to people who do. That is why a bar with no sign, reachable only through a phone booth inside a hot dog restaurant, is exclusive without being expensive, and why an invitation-only site is exclusive in a way money cannot purchase. Both raise perceived desirability, by two inferences he names: difficulty of acquisition is read as evidence of worth, and unavailability is read as evidence that many other people wanted it.
qa_items.support: Berger's distinction, illustrated by recounted business cases with uncontrolled outcomes. The supporting effects he lists — cookbooks rated better in limited supply, cookies tasting better when scarce — are third-party findings compressed to a clause each with no citation in the body text.
confounders: collapsing the two into 'limited availability', which loses the knowledge-based route to exclusivity that his best cases depend on
assuming exclusivity requires price or status; he explicitly rejects that
treating the Rue La La versus SmartBargains comparison as controlled; the two also differed in timing, brand and merchandising

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', the author's footnote following the Disney Vault passage (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A restaurant reads the chapter on scarcity and starts turning away most callers, on the grounds that difficulty of access builds demand. Bookings rise briefly and then customers stop calling. What does Berger's own footnote say about this, and what operating rule does he report?
qa_items.answer: His footnote bounds exactly this. Making access difficult is different from making it impossible: getting a reservation at Please Don't Tell is hard, but people who keep calling should be able to get one. He warns that restricting availability can come off as snooty or standoffish, and that people are used to getting what they want and will go elsewhere if they hear no too often. The operating rule he reports, from Jim Meehan, is to convert every refusal into a "no, but" — no at eight-thirty, but how about eleven; no to that brand, but would you try this one. Managing the disappointment preserves the allure while preserving satisfaction. He also adds a lifecycle qualification: using scarcity and exclusivity early and relaxing them later is a particularly good way to build demand, which makes restriction a launch phase rather than a permanent setting.
qa_items.support: Berger's own stated boundary condition on his own advice — but placed in a FOOTNOTE, so a reader taking the chapter from its body text and summary would never meet it. No evidence is offered for the boundary or the rule; both are a practitioner's operating procedure attributed to Jim Meehan.
confounders: doubling down on scarcity on the grounds that demand takes time; the footnote says the opposite
reading the fix as better communication of the scarcity rather than as an alternative offered with each refusal
missing the lifecycle point — that the restriction is meant to be relaxed later, not held forever

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'A Brief Note on Motivation' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A company is deciding whether to pay customers a hundred dollars per successful referral. Berger's objection is not that it is expensive. What is it, and what does he propose instead?
qa_items.answer: His objection is substitution. People already talk about products they like, for free and unprompted, and as soon as you pay them for doing it you crowd out the intrinsic motivation. The consequence is that sharing decisions stop tracking how good the product is: the quality and quantity of buzz becomes proportional to the money received rather than to the customer's opinion, so the referral stops carrying the signal that made it valuable. He grants that paying works in the narrow sense — lots of people will refer for a hundred dollars — and that it scales in cost rather than in quality. His alternative is social incentives: harness the desire to look good, which is what makes people publicise airline status and check-ins without being paid, and which he says is more effective in the long term.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument, carried entirely by a personal anecdote about playing fantasy football unpaid. NO evidence is cited — the crowding-out literature is large and he cites none of it — and the anecdote does not test the claim, since enjoying an unpaid game does not show that payment would have reduced motivation. He states it absolutely, with no boundary conditions on payment size or context.
confounders: objecting on cost grounds, which is not his argument
assuming a smaller payment avoids the problem; he states the effect without any threshold, though he also offers no evidence for that absoluteness
confusing crowding out with the separate claim that paid endorsements lack credibility

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Minting a New Type of Currency', the Mitchell and Tamir studies (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Berger reports two studies about the reward value of talking about oneself. What did each find, whose studies are they, and what inferential step does Berger take that the studies do not test?
qa_items.answer: They are by Harvard neuroscientists Jason Mitchell and Diana Tamir, not by Berger. In the first, subjects in brain scanners shared either their own opinions ("I like snowboarding") or another person's ("He likes puppies"); sharing personal opinions activated the same reward circuits that respond to food and money. In the second, participants made hundreds of quick choices between waiting a few seconds and answering a question about themselves, with small payments varied across trials; people accepted a 25 percent pay cut in order to share their opinions, valuing an act of self-disclosure at just under a cent against five seconds of doing nothing. The step Berger takes that the studies do not test is the one that matters for his book: from self-disclosure being rewarding to people therefore sharing products and brands. What was measured was disclosure of personal opinions, not transmission of commercial content.
qa_items.support: Third-party research — Tamir and Mitchell (2012) — reported by Berger. The supporting base rates are also third-party: the 40-percent conversation figure is Dunbar, Marriott and Duncan, and the tweet figure is Naaman, Boase and Lai.
confounders: attributing the brain-scanner work to Berger
reading the 25 percent pay cut as a large sum; the absolute value was just under a cent
assuming the studies show people enjoy sharing content about products; they measured self-disclosure only

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Inner Remarkability', the passages on breaking expected patterns and on mystery (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A brand in a category with rigid customer expectations wants remarkability and has no unusual product feature to point at. What two constructive routes does Berger offer, and what does each exploit?
qa_items.answer: First, break an expected pattern. Remarkability is relative to an expectation, so the expectation itself is the raw material — which means a category with a firm norm is an advantage rather than an obstacle. His cases are a low-cost airline supplying a comfortable seat, varied snacks and seat-back television against no-frills expectations, and a hundred-dollar cheesesteak against what a cheesesteak is. Second, unresolved mystery or controversy, which works by a different mechanism: an open question that undermines a settled belief gives people a reason to ask others to help settle it, and the disagreement itself generates more discussion. His case is the 1999 film whose viewers could not tell whether the footage was real. He insists remarkability can be found in anything, and offers black toilet paper at a party as his cheapest demonstration.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument, supported by recounted cases with press-reported outcomes — the film shot for about $35,000 grossing more than $248 million worldwide. No control case is examined, and the many pattern-breaking products that failed are not counted, which is the error his own Introduction warns against. The mystery route is period-bound: the 1999 ambiguity depended on an information environment in which the question could not be settled quickly.
confounders: reaching for a striking execution rather than for the category expectation the audience actually holds
treating mystery as the same mechanism as pattern-breaking; his mystery route works by prompting people to consult each other, not by surprising them
assuming a strong category norm is a constraint; on his account it is the material

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', sections 'Why Do People Buzz About Some Products More Than Others?' and 'The Difference Between Immediate and Ongoing Word of Mouth' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Berger set out to test the most intuitive hypothesis in word-of-mouth marketing and got a null. Describe the sequence of what he tested, what he found each time, and how the null was eventually resolved.
qa_items.answer: With Eric Schwartz he analysed several hundred BzzAgent campaigns. First test: how interesting a product was rated against how much word of mouth it got over a ten-week campaign. No relationship. Second: suspecting "interest" was too vague, he rescored the products on more concrete dimensions — novelty and surprise. Still no relationship. Third: suspecting the raters, he replaced the undergraduate scorers with a new set of people of all ages and backgrounds. Still nothing. The resolution was not that interest fails but that the outcome was the wrong one. Splitting word of mouth into immediate — soon after the experience — and ongoing — in the weeks and months after — showed that interesting products got more IMMEDIATE word of mouth and no more ONGOING word of mouth than boring ones. His own image is arriving at work dressed as a pirate: discussed all day, not discussed the following month.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Eric Schwartz, published in the Journal of Marketing (2011). The strongest empirical item in the book and it is his. Limits: the design is observational, not experimental — interest was rated, not assigned; the outcome is conversations self-reported by people who received free product; and the immediate/ongoing split was made AFTER the null, so it was not pre-specified.
confounders: reporting only the null, which misstates the finding — interest does predict immediate talk
reporting only the split result, which loses the three failed tests that make the null credible
treating this as an experiment; nothing was manipulated in this dataset
assuming the finding generalises beyond consumer products discussed by volunteer product-testers over ten weeks

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', sections 'Triggered to Talk' and 'Why Cheerios Gets More Word of Mouth Than Disney World' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: In the same dataset that produced the interest null, what did predict word of mouth, by how much, and what mechanism does Berger give for why dull products can out-talk exciting ones?
qa_items.answer: Trigger frequency. More frequently triggered products got 15 percent more word of mouth — and, unlike interest, they got more of BOTH kinds, immediate and ongoing. His mechanism is that most conversation is small talk whose purpose is to fill conversational space rather than to impress, and what fills it is whatever is accessible. If something is top of mind it is usually relevant to the situation at hand, so it is what people reach for. Frequent use or frequent environmental cues keep a thing accessible, so it keeps being reached for. This is why Ziploc bags and moisturiser get discussed week after week while a theme park visited once a year does not: the park has high social currency and emotion and almost no triggers. His summary is that social currency gets people talking and triggers keep them talking — top of mind means tip of tongue.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Eric Schwartz, same dataset. Limits: 15 percent is the only figure given, with no baseline rate and no statement of how trigger frequency was operationalised per product; the design is observational; and the Cheerios-versus-theme-park comparison switches instrument mid-argument, resting partly on this dataset and partly on counted Twitter mentions.
confounders: assuming the mechanism is that people love the product; his mechanism is accessibility in low-stakes conversation, which is indifferent to enthusiasm
reading the 15 percent as an effect of an intervention; nothing was manipulated in this dataset
concluding that boring is better; the claim is that frequency of cueing beats interest for sustained talk, not that dullness helps

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', the dining-hall tray experiment in 'From Mars Bars to Voting: How Triggers Affect Behavior' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Berger reports an experiment in which the less-liked message won. Describe the design, what participants said about the two messages, and what they actually did — and say what the result implies about testing messages by asking audiences which they prefer.
qa_items.answer: With Gráinne Fitzsimons he paid students to record everything they ate for two weeks. Halfway through, framed as an unrelated study by a different researcher, students were shown a public-health slogan more than twenty times in varied colours and fonts. One group saw "Live the healthy way, eat five fruits and veggies a day"; the other saw "Each and every dining-hall tray needs five fruits and veggies a day". Both encourage the same behaviour; only the second uses a trigger the students physically encounter at the moment of the decision. Students called the tray slogan corny and rated it less than half as attractive, and those shown it were significantly more likely to say it would not influence them. Behaviour ran the other way: the generic slogan changed nothing, and students who saw the tray slogan and used trays ate 25 percent more fruit and vegetables. The implication is that preference and self-prediction are poor instruments — the audience disliked the message that worked and correctly identified neither.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN experiment with Gráinne Fitzsimons, published in the Journal of Marketing Research (2008). A genuine manipulated comparison with a behavioural outcome. Limits: the effect is CONDITIONAL on the cue being present — it holds for students who saw the slogan AND used trays — and the book gives no sample size, no interval and no attrition, with intake self-reported.
confounders: reporting the behaviour change without the liking result, which is the transferable half
assuming the tray slogan worked because it was more specific or more memorable, rather than because the cue was physically present at the decision
dropping the conditionality: the effect holds for tray users, not for everyone shown the slogan

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', the Arizona polling-place study in 'From Mars Bars to Voting: How Triggers Affect Behavior' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Berger reports a field study on where people vote. Describe the data, the result, and the two steps he took to rule out the obvious alternative explanations.
qa_items.answer: With Marc Meredith and Christian Wheeler he took every polling place in Arizona's 2000 general election and classified it by building type from its name and address — 40 percent churches, 26 percent schools, 10 percent community centres, the rest apartment buildings, golf courses and even RV parks. He then examined support for a contested initiative raising sales tax from 5.0 to 5.6 percent to fund public schools. More than ten thousand additional votes were cast in favour where the polling place was a school. Two steps against alternatives: the difference persisted after controlling for regional political preference and demographics; and he compared two similar groups directly — people who lived near schools and were assigned to vote in one, against people who lived near schools and were assigned to a different building type such as a firehouse. The school group was significantly more supportive. The initiative passed.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Marc Meredith and S. Christian Wheeler, published in PNAS (2008). Important limit the book does not state: it is OBSERVATIONAL. Voters were not randomly assigned by the researchers; assignment was administrative. The matched near-school comparison is a real design strength and is not random assignment.
confounders: treating this as a randomised experiment; assignment was administrative, not researcher-controlled
generalising to issues with no match between building and ballot content; the tested initiative matched the building type exactly
reading the comparison with the 2000 presidential margin as an effect size; the book never reports the effect in proportional terms

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', section 'What Makes for an Effective Trigger?' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: A team is choosing a cue to link a product to and proposes the colour red because everyone sees red constantly. State the trade-off Berger names, his image for it, and what he says about how to resolve it.
qa_items.answer: The trade-off is frequency against strength of link. A cue must occur often or it will rarely fire — his case is a beer brand moving from "Holidays are made for Michelob" to "Weekends are made for Michelob" because holidays are too rare. But the more things a cue is already associated with, the weaker any one association becomes, and red is his own example of the failure: roses, love, Coca-Cola, fast cars, so it retrieves none of them strongly. His image is a paper cup with holes punched in the bottom — one hole gives a strong stream, many holes give a trickle from each. His recommendation is a fresher, more original link, with peanut butter reliably retrieving jelly as the standard to aim at. On how to resolve it: he names the two failure modes and stops. He gives no procedure for locating the balance point, which is exactly the decision a practitioner faces.
qa_items.support: Berger's stated trade-off, supported by an analogy and an advertising history that is credited in his Notes to Cialdini's Influence rather than to a study. No measurement is offered for either side of the trade-off or for the optimum.
confounders: optimising for frequency alone, which is what makes red look attractive
optimising for distinctiveness alone, which is the holidays failure
expecting Berger to supply a method for finding the balance; he does not, and treating his advice as operable overstates it

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', the bath-mat and 'Man Drinks Fat' comparison in 'What Makes for an Effective Trigger?', and the reusable-bag passage in 'Consider the Context' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: A public safety film is vivid, memorable, and viewers report thinking about it often. Berger would still call it a failed trigger. Why, and what is his contrasting case?
qa_items.answer: Because the trigger fires where the person cannot act. His example is a New Zealand spot about bathroom slips that is so memorable he says he thinks of it every time he showers in a room without a mat — and, as he puts it, you cannot buy a bath mat in a bathroom. The message is physically removed from the desired behaviour, so it must survive unaided until the action becomes possible, which is the failure the trigger was supposed to prevent. His contrast is a New York City health video showing fat pouring from a soda can, which fires the message at precisely the moment someone is about to drink one. He gives the same structure for reusable shopping bags: the supermarket is a strong cue for the bags and a badly timed one, since the bags are at home. The useful cue is the shopping list, seen before leaving the house. He adds the corollary that the longer the delay between exposure and action, the more the trigger matters — and that market research measuring immediate reaction is measuring the wrong moment.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument. NO measurement supports the proximity condition: both films are analysed by the author from the armchair and neither is compared on outcomes. The reusable-bag case, which states the condition most cleanly, is an invented illustration.
confounders: treating memorability as evidence the trigger works; on his account the bath-mat spot is memorable and useless
proposing a more striking execution rather than moving the cue to the point of action
confusing this with the frequency condition; a bathroom is encountered daily, so the spot passes on frequency and fails on proximity

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', section 'Kit Kat and Coffee: Growing the Habitat', including the Boston Market experiment (spine 7)
qa_items.question: What does Berger mean by a habitat, and what evidence does he offer that one can be deliberately grown rather than inherited? Be precise about who the reported effect applies to.
qa_items.answer: A habitat is the set of triggers that cause people to think of a product or idea, on an analogy with the environment that sustains an organism. Hot dogs have a thick habitat — barbecues, summer, baseball, dachshunds; he says Ethiopian food has a thin one. Some habitats are inherited: a chocolate bar shares a name with a planet, and a song called "Friday" is cued by the day. He claims a habitat can be grown by repeated pairing with a cue already prevalent in the audience's environment, and his manipulated evidence is a six-week campaign for a fast-casual restaurant: one group received messages pairing it with dinner, another a generic "thinking about a place to eat" message. Precision matters here — the reported 20 percent increase in word of mouth is for a SUBGROUP, people who had previously associated the brand only with lunch. He does not report the effect in the whole sample.
qa_items.support: The restaurant test is Berger's OWN, run with BzzAgent and reported in Berger and Schwartz (2011), and it is a genuine manipulated comparison with a control message. The confectionery case that opens the section is an uncontrolled business outcome, and Berger himself lists competing causes and says only that he would like to ADD triggers to the list.
confounders: reporting the 20 percent as a whole-sample effect; it is conditional on prior single-occasion association
citing the confectionery campaign as evidence; the author explicitly declines to claim he has isolated the trigger effect there
assuming any repeated pairing works, without the frequency and strength constraints stated two sections later

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', section 'Consider the Context', with the caveman and 'Wassup' comparison from 'Triggered to Talk' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Two campaigns are both witty and well made. One is built on prehistoric characters, the other on a greeting young men were using at the time. On Berger's account, what separates them, and what does that imply about whether a trigger is a property of the work?
qa_items.answer: The cue has to be something the specific audience actually encounters. Cavemen are not met in daily life, so the advertisement is unlikely to come to mind and unlikely to be talked about; the greeting was in constant use in the target demographic, so greeting a friend cued the brand. The implication is the important part: trigger value is not a property of the work at all. It is a property of the relationship between the work and the environment the audience inhabits, which is why the same idea has different value in different places and at different times. Berger gives both variants — a hundred-dollar cheesesteak is remarkable anywhere but frequently cued only where cheesesteaks are everywhere; and he reports his own finding that people were far more likely to think of orange-coloured products the day before Halloween than a week after, because the orange cues in the environment disappeared with the holiday.
qa_items.support: The seasonal finding is Berger's own, from Berger and Fitzsimons (2008), and what it measured is a change in what people THOUGHT OF, not in what they bought or discussed. The campaign comparison is the author's analysis, not a measured comparison, and he never reports how the caveman campaign actually performed. He hedges the greeting explanation — "at least part of its success" — and the chapter summary drops the hedge.
confounders: judging the two campaigns on wit or craft, which is the dimension on which they are hard to separate
treating the caveman verdict as a measured result; it is an armchair analysis and no performance data is given
assuming a trigger, once chosen, travels with the work to any audience

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', the New York Times book-review analysis at the end of 'Triggered to Talk' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Berger tests the slogan that any publicity is good publicity and finds it is conditionally true. What did he find, what is the moderator, and what mechanism does he propose?
qa_items.answer: With Alan Sorensen and Scott Rasmussen he analysed hundreds of New York Times book reviews against sales. Negative reviews HURT sales for some books — which contradicts the slogan outright. But for books by new or relatively unknown authors, negative reviews INCREASED sales by 45 percent. The moderator is prior awareness. His mechanism runs through triggers rather than persuasion: negative attention has two effects that pull in opposite directions, lowering evaluation and raising accessibility, and where nobody knew the thing existed the accessibility gain dominates because there was nothing to lower. One book given a hostile review sold more than four times as many copies afterwards.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Alan Sorensen and Scott Rasmussen, published in Marketing Science (2010). Limit: the moderator is stated and NOT quantified — "new or relatively unknown" has no threshold anywhere in the book. The mechanism is his reading, not something the study tests; the study establishes the moderated effect.
confounders: reporting the 45 percent without the moderator, which turns a conditional finding into the slogan it refutes
assuming the mechanism is curiosity or contrarian appeal; his account is accessibility, and the study does not distinguish them
citing the wine and exercise-gadget examples as evidence for the moderator; they are single cases with press figures

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Emotion', section 'Does Any Emotion Boost Sharing?' (spine 8)
qa_items.question: This is the most misremembered finding in the book. State all three of Berger's valence results with their figures and directions, and say what the correct conclusion is.
qa_items.answer: Three results, from the same corpus of almost seven thousand New York Times articles. One: sadness, a negative emotion, made an article 16 percent LESS likely to make the Most E-Mailed list. Two: overall positivity, measured by counting emotion words with Jamie Pennebaker's textual analysis program, RAISED sharing — positive articles were on average 13 percent more likely to make the list than negative ones. Three: anger and anxiety, also negative, INCREASED sharing. Berger states plainly that this left him confused. The correct conclusion is neither of the two things the book is usually quoted for. He does NOT report that negative content spreads more — his positivity effect runs the other way. And he does NOT report that positive content is what spreads — his anger and anxiety results are precisely why he abandoned valence. The conclusion is that valence has a real but small association and is not the organising variable; arousal is.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Katherine Milkman, published in the Journal of Marketing Research (2012). Two limits that bear directly on the figures: the predictors are measured by DIFFERENT instruments — sadness, anger and anxiety by human research assistants, positivity mechanically by word count — so the 13 and 16 percent figures are not commensurable; and no effect size is given for anger or anxiety at all, only the direction.
confounders: 'negativity spreads' — refuted by his own +13 percent positivity result
'positivity spreads' — refuted by his own anger and anxiety results, which are why he dropped valence
quoting a figure for anger; the book gives none
assuming the three figures are directly comparable; they come from two different measurement instruments

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Emotion', section 'Kindling the Fire: The Science of Physiological Arousal' (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Set out Berger's two-dimensional classification of emotion with the contents of each cell as he gives them, and state which dimension he says does the predicting and why.
qa_items.answer: Two axes: valence, positive or negative, and physiological arousal, high or low. Positive and high-arousal: awe, excitement, amusement. Positive and low-arousal: contentment. Negative and high-arousal: anger, anxiety. Negative and low-arousal: sadness. Arousal is the dimension that predicts. His reason is what arousal is — a state of activation and readiness for action, evolved for fight or flight, in which heart rate and blood pressure rise. Activation drives doing things generally, and sharing is one of the things done. Low-arousal states do the opposite: sad people power down and content people relax, and neither disposes anyone to act. His practical form is to kindle the fire — excite or inspire on the positive side, and on the negative side make people mad, not sad.
qa_items.support: Berger's own model, built on his own published research with Katherine Milkman and his own 2011 arousal experiment; the two-dimensional classification of emotion is imported from existing psychology and he says so. Note that two cells carry no measurement in the book — excitement and contentment are placed on theoretical grounds — and disgust, used later to justify a public health film, never appears in the grid at all.
confounders: treating high-arousal as a synonym for negative; anger and awe sit in different valence cells and both raise sharing
treating contentment as a mild positive that helps a little; on his account it deactivates and reduces sharing
assuming every cell is measured; excitement and contentment are placed theoretically

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Emotion', sections 'Systematically Analyzing the Most E-Mailed List' and 'The Power of Awe' (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Berger describes an anomaly in his data that led him to awe. What was the anomaly, how did he build the dataset, and what did awe turn out to be worth?
qa_items.answer: The anomaly was science articles. They out-shared politics, fashion and business news while scoring low on both social currency and practical value — his opening case is a piece on a photographic technique that renders a cough visible, which readers rated as neither useful nor especially interesting and shared anyway. The dataset was built with a web crawler, suggested by Katherine Milkman after he had been clipping most-emailed lists out of newspapers by hand: it scanned the New York Times home page every fifteen minutes for six months and recorded almost seven thousand articles with author, section and page placement, plus which made the Most E-Mailed list. Research assistants then scored articles for the constructs. More interesting articles were 25 percent more likely to make the list, more useful articles 30 percent, and awe-inspiring articles 30 percent. Awe is what explained the science anomaly.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Katherine Milkman. The dataset is a whole population over a window, not a sample of hits, which meets the standard his own Introduction sets. Limits: correlational and single-outlet; the predictor is human-rated awe applied after the fact, which measures raters' judgements about articles rather than readers' states. The DEFINITION of awe is not his — he credits psychologists Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt.
confounders: attributing the definition of awe to Berger; it is Keltner and Haidt's
assuming awe was measured in readers; research assistants scored articles
treating the singing-competition video as data; it is an illustration with no comparison content

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Emotion', section 'Exercise Makes People Share' (spine 8)
