qa_items.question: Berger's correlational data could not show that arousal causes sharing rather than merely accompanying it. Describe the experiment he ran to separate them, and say precisely what it establishes.
qa_items.answer: In a behavioural lab, half of participants were asked to sit still and relax for sixty seconds and half to jog lightly in place for sixty seconds, in whatever clothes they had come in. Both groups then took part in an apparently unrelated second study, read an article from the school newspaper, and were offered the chance to email it to anyone they liked. Seventy-five percent of the joggers shared it — more than twice the rate of the relaxed group. The point of jogging is that it evokes no emotion at all while raising heart rate and blood pressure, so the design separates arousal from emotional content completely. What it establishes is that arousal alone increases transmission, even when the aroused state has nothing whatever to do with what is being shared. Berger draws the further consequence that situational arousal explains oversharing — after a turbulent flight, a near-accident, or a treadmill.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN experiment, published in Psychological Science (2011). Randomised two-condition design with a behavioural outcome — the cleanest identification in the book. Limits: one laboratory study, a student pool, one stimulus, one channel, and no replication reported; the control rate is given only as "less than half".
confounders: assuming the jogging made the article more interesting; the content was identical across conditions
reading it as showing that exercise makes people talkative in general; the measured outcome was sharing one specific article
extending it confidently to advertising placement — Berger's own applications here are hedged with 'should' and 'may', and no media test is reported

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Emotion', section 'Kindling the Fire with High-Arousal Emotions' (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Berger reports two experiments that manipulate arousal directly. What were they, what did they find, and what is notable about how they are reported?
qa_items.answer: In one, the details of a story were changed to make it evoke more anger; in the other, an advertisement was made funnier. In both, the higher-arousal version was shared more, and Berger attributes the increase specifically to the added arousal rather than to the content change as such. What is notable is the reporting. These are the book's cleanest minimal pairs — one variable changed, everything else held — and they get two sentences with no figures, no sample sizes, and no description of what was altered in either stimulus. For the book's most decisive designs, that is the thinnest reporting in it: a practitioner cannot tell how much arousal was added or how much sharing resulted.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN experiments, reported in Berger and Milkman (2012). Two experiments, two emotions, on stimuli of the authors' construction; nothing establishes that arousal can be raised without limit or that the relationship is monotonic.
confounders: supplying a figure; the book gives none for either experiment
assuming these are the same studies as the Most E-Mailed analysis; those are correlational and these are manipulated
concluding that maximum arousal is optimal; no dose-response relationship is reported

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Emotion', section 'Focus on Feelings' (spine 8)
qa_items.question: A campaign wants to reduce a harmful behaviour and plans to publish clearer, better-designed information about its risks. What is Berger's objection, what does he propose instead, and whose technique does he credit for finding it?
qa_items.answer: His objection is that information is the wrong instrument in the common case where the audience already holds it. Teenagers do not smoke because they think it is healthy; people eating a supersized meal are not unaware of the risks. Where the fact is already held, adding more of it changes nothing, and what is missing is the motivation to act, which is emotional. He proposes focusing on feelings rather than features or facts — and, given the previous section, on a high-arousal feeling specifically, since the choice of which emotion is not free. For finding the emotional core he credits the "Three Whys" explicitly to Chip and Dan Heath's Made to Stick, by name: write down why people do something, then ask why that is important three times, noting each answer. His own worked example runs from search being quick, to getting answers, to connecting with people and fulfilling dreams.
qa_items.support: An argument from premises about smoking and fast food; NO measurement supports it. The search- engine case he offers is a recounted production history whose reported outcome is internal enthusiasm and a decision to release the film, not a comparison against an informational version. Note also that the argument as stated is broader than what it establishes: that information is insufficient WHERE ALREADY HELD does not show it is generally the wrong instrument.
confounders: attributing the Three Whys to Berger; he credits the Heaths by name in the text
choosing any emotion; his own model says the emotion must be high-arousal, so a sad appeal satisfies this advice and defeats the aim
reading the claim as 'facts never matter' rather than as 'facts the audience already has do not move them'

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', the laptop logo decision in the opening and the shirts-and-socks argument in 'The Power of Observability' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Berger opens this chapter with a company deliberately making its product worse for the person who bought it. What was the decision, what was traded for what, and what general claim does he build on it?
qa_items.answer: The laptop logo. It had faced the owner when the machine was closed, so that a person pulling it from a bag could tell which way up it went — a small usability gain, consistent with the company's obsession with the buyer's experience. But once opened, the logo was upside down to everyone else in the room. The trade was made explicitly: the customer's orientation cue was given up so that the logo read correctly to onlookers. The general claim is that seeing others do something makes people more likely to do it themselves, and the operative word is SEEING — if it is hard to see what others are doing, it is hard to imitate it. So observability bounds how far social influence can carry anything, which he compresses into: if something is built to show, it is built to grow. His category test is shirts against socks, cars against toothpaste.
qa_items.support: A recounted decision, told through the agency creative director who was in the room, with NO outcome measurement — what is reported is that the logo was flipped and why, not what it produced. The shirts-versus-socks contrasts are illustrative categories chosen by the author. The measured evidence for observability arrives separately, in the car-sales study.
confounders: reading the chapter as being about publicity or PR rather than about whether use is visible
treating the logo case as evidence; no outcome is reported for it
assuming the claim is only about imitation — he adds a second channel, that visible things are easier to bring up in conversation

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', section 'The Power of Observability', the 1.5 million car sales analysis (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Berger reports a study that measures both the size of social influence and its dependence on visibility. Describe the design and both results, and say what carries the identification of the second one.
qa_items.answer: With Blake McShane and Eric Bradlow he analysed data on 1.5 million car sales. First result: people were more likely to buy a new car if neighbours had recently bought one, and roughly one in every eight cars sold was attributable to social influence. Second, and the more interesting one: the effect varied by city in a patterned way. Influence was stronger in Los Angeles and Miami, where people commute by car and the weather is clear, than in New York, where people commute by subway, and Seattle, where it rains. What carries the identification is that commuting mode and weather are being used as PROXIES for how easily cars can be seen — natural variation in observability, holding the product category constant. Where behaviour was more observable, social influence was larger.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN study with Blakely McShane and Eric Bradlow, forthcoming in the Journal of Marketing Research at the time of writing. Limits the book does not state: it is OBSERVATIONAL, nothing was manipulated, and both proxies are confounded with a great deal else — density, income, dealer networks, model mix, replacement cycles. "One in eight cars sold was because of social influence" is a causal statement from a model applied to observational data, and the identifying assumptions are not given.
confounders: treating the city comparison as a controlled experiment; it is natural variation with confounded proxies
reporting the one-in-eight figure as a measured count rather than a model output
assuming the study manipulated visibility; it inferred it from commuting mode and weather

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', the campus drinking case in 'The Power of Observability' and the remedy in 'Making the Private Public . . . with Moustaches' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Most students on a campus privately dislike heavy drinking and heavy drinking is nonetheless the norm. Explain the mechanism Berger gives for this and the intervention he reports, and state the condition that the intervention silently depends on.
qa_items.answer: The mechanism is an asymmetry: behaviour is public and thoughts are private. Each student sees the drinking, cannot see anyone's discomfort with it, and concludes they are the outlier — so they drink more, which becomes part of what the next student sees. The error sustains itself because everyone's visible behaviour is already an accommodation to it. His second illustration is the silence after a bewildering presentation, where the absence of questions is read by everyone present as evidence that they alone failed to understand. The intervention was to publish the true private norm: newspaper advertisements stating that most students had one or two drinks and 69 percent had four or fewer when they partied, with heavy drinking reported to have fallen by almost 30 percent. The silent condition is that THE TRUE NORM HAPPENS TO FAVOUR THE DESIRED BEHAVIOUR. The same chapter's final section shows what publishing a norm does when it does not, and Berger never states the distinguishing variable as a rule.
qa_items.support: The intervention outcome is a PRACTITIONER'S REPORT of a campus campaign, not a study Berger conducted: no control campus, no control period, no design described. The nearest controlled evidence, cited only in his Notes, is third-party — Schroeder and Prentice on pluralistic ignorance and college alcohol use. The evidence that students privately disliked the culture is the practitioner's own asking, reported at second hand.
confounders: recommending more information about health consequences, which is what the same practitioner had already tried without effect
generalising 'publish the true norm' as a rule; it works only where the true norm favours the desired behaviour, which the source never states
treating the 30 percent reduction as a measured effect; it is an uncontrolled outcome report

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', section 'Anti-Drug Commercials?' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: This chapter's own disconfirmation. What happened when large anti-drug campaigns were evaluated, what mechanism does Berger give, and whose research is it?
qa_items.answer: The campaigns did not merely fail — they appear to have backfired. Communications professor Bob Hornik, not Berger, collected data on thousands of teenagers over the period the National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign ran, recording exposure to the advertisements and marijuana use; twelve-and-a-half to eighteen-year-olds who saw the advertisements were MORE likely to smoke marijuana. Berger's mechanism is that such an advertisement says two things at once — drugs are bad, and other people are taking them — and social proof does not distinguish approval from prevalence, so the second is the one that transmits. He adds a second route: the existence of the campaign is itself evidence of prevalence, since nobody makes announcements about not cutting your hand off with a saw. Hornik's own quoted hypothesis is the same: the more kids saw the ads, the more they believed other kids were using, and the more interested they became.
qa_items.support: NOT Berger's research — Hornik, Jacobsohn, Orwin, Piesse and Kalton (2008), American Journal of Public Health. The design is observational and exposure was not assigned, which Berger does not note while reporting the causal reading. Almost $1 billion was appropriated for the campaign between 1998 and 2004.
confounders: attributing the study to Berger
diagnosing the failure as poor execution or unpersuasive creative; the mechanism is that the message is accurate about prevalence
reading the finding as causal without noting that exposure was self-selected

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', the Petrified Forest sign comparison in 'Anti-Drug Commercials?' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: A park is losing wood to visitors taking souvenirs. Two signs are trialled on different trails. One reports how many past visitors have removed wood; one asks visitors not to remove it in order to preserve the park. What happened, whose study is it, and what is the general rule?
qa_items.answer: The sign reporting how many past visitors had removed wood ALMOST DOUBLED the theft. The sign asking visitors not to remove it, and giving the reason, reduced it. The study is Bob Cialdini and colleagues', not Berger's, and it is a genuine field comparison — different signs on different trails, everything else held. The general rule Berger states is that if you want to get people not to do something, do not tell them that lots of their peers are doing it, and that preventing a behaviour requires the inverse of his own chapter: making the public private, making others' behaviour less observable. The constructive form is to highlight what people should be doing rather than to report what they are doing. He extends the diagnosis to a music industry site warning that only 37 percent of music was paid for — a message he says he suspects has the opposite of the intended effect.
qa_items.support: NOT Berger's research — Cialdini and colleagues (2006). This is the stronger of the two pieces of evidence in the section because it IS a manipulated field comparison, where the anti-drug analysis is observational. The music-industry example is the author's reasoning about a message he expects to backfire, and he says himself he is not sure; it is not a measured case.
confounders: assuming the reporting sign failed because it was too weak or too polite; it worked, in the wrong direction, by supplying social proof
attributing the sign study to Berger
concluding that the fix is a stronger prohibition; the effective sign was a request with a reason, not a stronger warning

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', sections 'Making the Private Public . . . with Moustaches' and 'Anti-Drug Commercials?' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Berger gives two opposite instructions in one chapter — make the private public, and make the public private. When does each apply, and what does he leave unsaid?
qa_items.answer: Make the private public when you want a behaviour to SPREAD: generate public signals for private choices, actions and opinions, so others can see and imitate them. His case is a men's health campaign in which participants grow moustaches for a month, turning support for an abstract cause into something visible that provokes the question and then the conversation. Make the public private when you want a behaviour PREVENTED: make others' behaviour less observable and stop reporting how many people do the thing you oppose. What he leaves unsaid is the variable that selects between them in the hard case. Publishing the true norm HELPED on the campus drinking campaign and HARMED in the anti-drug campaigns, and the difference is whether the true norm favours the desired behaviour — which is visible in his own two cases and is never stated as the rule. Applied without that condition, the make-it-private instruction would forbid the intervention that worked.
qa_items.support: Both instructions are Berger's, stated explicitly, in the same chapter. The gap between them is an extractor observation: the source never puts the campus case and the anti-drug case side by side, and never names the condition that reconciles them.
confounders: treating 'make the private public' as a general rule; it is signed and reverses
assuming the reversal turns on whether the behaviour is good or bad; it turns on which way the TRUE NORM points, which is a different question
expecting the source to supply the selection rule; he does not, and this is a gap rather than a subtlety

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', section 'Advertising Itself: Sharing Hotmail with the World' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: A small organisation with no advertising budget wants existing users to generate awareness. Berger's remedy is not to ask them to. What is it, and what are the non-textual forms he gives?
qa_items.answer: Build the signal into the act of use, so that consumption broadcasts without anyone being asked to do anything. His paradigm case is the free email service that appended a line and a link to every outgoing message, so each user sent prospective customers an implicit endorsement in the course of writing to exactly the people they already wrote to. The non-textual forms matter more for his general claim: distinctive shape, in a crisp packaging tube; distinctive sound, in an operating system's startup chime; unexpected colour, in white earphone cords in a market where every competitor shipped black ones, and in red-lacquered shoe soles that make a brand recognisable to people who know nothing about it; and enlarged logos. He notes the white cords did double duty — they also supplied visible social proof of how many people had switched, in a market where the standard was contested. He stresses this is disproportionately valuable to organisations with no advertising money, because existing customers become the medium.
qa_items.support: Recounted business cases with company and press outcome figures that are uncontrolled and given for the whole business rather than for the mechanism. Berger concedes in passing that such signals can be switched off — device signature lines can be changed and mostly are not — which makes the mechanism partly a default-setting effect; he attributes the low switch-off rate to social currency without evidence. Period-bound to the late 1990s and early 2000s.
confounders: reading the remedy as asking customers to advertise, which is what he is offering an alternative to
treating it as a text-and-logo tactic; his stronger examples are shape, sound and colour
assuming the business outcome figures isolate the mechanism; they are whole-business figures

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', section 'Livestrong Wristbands as Behavioral Residue' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: A cause has budget for either a large national event or a cheap durable object. Berger reports exactly this decision. What is the concept that settled it, how does he define it, and what is unusual about how honestly he handles the case?
qa_items.answer: Behavioural residue — the physical traces or remnants that most actions leave in their wake. The argument that settled it is stated by the person who made the call: the wristband lives on and the ride does not; there will be photographs of the ride and people will talk about the ride, but even repeated annually it does not act as a daily reminder, and the band does. The concept generalises: a sticker worn after voting converts a private act into a visible one, and a shopping bag built to be reused keeps generating social proof on other errands. He extracts a selection rule for giveaways — choose the item whose use is public over the item whose use is frequent, so a gym bag over a make-up case. What is unusual is his handling: he says outright that it is hard to know how the ride would have done, and easy to declare a successful strategy obviously correct after the fact. That is the book's most honest treatment of a selected success.
qa_items.support: A recounted decision with press-reported outcomes and an explicit concession from the author that the counterfactual is unknown. The TERM is not his — he credits it in the Notes to psychologist Sam Gosling. His own endnote lists competing causes he does not weigh in the text, including a one-dollar price and the fact that a band, unlike a pinned ribbon, could be worn continuously — while the body text presents colour as decisive.
confounders: attributing 'behavioural residue' to Berger; the term is Sam Gosling's
reading the case as proof the object beat the event; the author explicitly declines that claim
choosing the giveaway that gets used most often rather than the one whose use is seen

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', section 'The Psychology of Imitation', the kidney study (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Berger reports a case where social proof kills people. Describe the situation, the two figures, and which of them is actually the social-proof result.
qa_items.answer: Organ waiting lists are strictly ordered, so a patient low on the list who is offered a kidney knows the organ has already been refused by everyone above them. That refusal history is visible; the reasons for it are not. Patients infer from the sequence of refusals that the organ must be poor quality, and refuse it themselves. The two figures are 97.1 percent of kidney offers refused, and one in every ten refusals made in ERROR because of this inference — thousands of patients turning down organs they should have accepted. Only the second is the social-proof result. The 97.1 percent headline is mostly tissue and blood-type mismatch, which Berger says, but the two figures sit close enough together to be conflated. The general point is that social proof is an inference under uncertainty and it is fallible in a specific way: observers see the choice and not the reason for it, so a decision made for a private reason is read as a verdict on quality.
qa_items.support: NOT Berger's research — MIT professor Juanjuan Zhang, published in Marketing Science (2010), from an examination of hundreds of kidney donations. The 'social proof' term is credited by Berger to Cialdini, not claimed.
confounders: quoting 97.1 percent as the social-proof effect; the social-proof result is the one-in-ten error rate
attributing the study to Berger
reading social proof as irrationality; his account is that it is a valid inference applied to information the observer cannot fully see

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', the author's footnote following 'Most products, ideas, and behaviors are consumed privately' (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Berger's footnote to this chapter addresses a category where invisibility has a specific cause rather than being incidental. What is the category, and what does he say the remedy has to do differently?
qa_items.answer: Behaviour people are not comfortable being seen doing — stigmatised behaviour. His examples are online dating, which many people had tried and which remained socially awkward; erectile dysfunction, where he notes the makers of a drug coined a term precisely to make the subject speakable; and campus "wear jeans if you're gay" days run partly to raise visibility and discussion. The difference is in the direction of causation. Ordinary invisibility is a property of the product — socks are worn inside shoes. Stigma-driven invisibility is self-sustaining in the same way as the misread drinking norm: people do not know how many others have done it BECAUSE nobody says, and nobody says because they do not know how many others have. So the remedy is not to make use more visible but to make the prevalence known, which the footnote says is what such categories need.
qa_items.support: Berger's own footnote, argued rather than measured, with three illustrative cases and no study. Period-bound and culturally specific in its examples.
confounders: treating stigma as ordinary low observability, which would suggest making individual use more visible — a remedy that runs against the reason for the invisibility
confusing this with 'make the public private', which is the instruction for behaviours you want to prevent
reading the coined-term example as a naming tactic rather than as a move to make a subject speakable

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Public', section 'The Psychology of Imitation', the MBA cohort exercise (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Berger runs an annual exercise with his own students that he presents as evidence of social influence. Describe the design, the result, and the alternative explanation he concedes.
qa_items.answer: Every year he asks his second-year MBA students a question, splitting the class in half. One half is asked what they thought they wanted to do with their life when they STARTED the programme; the other is asked what they want to do NOW. Neither half sees the other's question and responses are anonymous. The result: the pre-programme answers are diverse — reforming health care, building a travel site, entertainment, politics, entrepreneurship, with a handful naming investment banking or consulting. The current answers are concentrated, with more than two-thirds naming banking or consulting. He describes the mechanism as snowballing: fewer than 20 percent were interested initially, but that was still larger than any other option, so a few switched, which made others more likely to switch. The alternative he concedes is that students genuinely learn about opportunities during the programme; he attributes only part of the convergence to social influence.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN reported measurement, and a two-condition design with a sensible blinding — but an informal annual classroom exercise, not a study: one institution, one cohort type, no sampling frame, recall-based for the pre-programme half. He concedes an alternative explanation before attributing the remainder.
confounders: citing it as a study; it is a classroom exercise
ignoring the recall problem — the pre-programme half are remembering, not reporting at the time
reading the concession as decorative; it is the alternative explanation and he does not rule it out

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the opening cases and the barn-raising passage (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Berger's fifth driver overlaps heavily with his first — both explain why people pass things on. How does he distinguish them, and what does he choose as his opening cases to make the point?
qa_items.answer: He distinguishes them by whose interests the sharing serves. Social Currency is about the SENDER and how sharing makes them look; Practical Value is about the RECEIVER, and it transmits because people want to help — saving someone time or money or trouble. He concedes the sender still benefits, since helping feels good and reflects well, but says the core of the mechanism is other-directed, and his analogy is a barn raising: mutual help that distance has made rare in physical form and that useful information restores. His opening cases are chosen to be unglamorous on purpose, because glamour would let social currency explain them: an eighty-six- year-old's video about removing silk from corn, watched more than five million times and skewing to viewers over fifty-five, and hikers on a mountain trail discussing vacuum cleaner models. He goes through the other drivers explicitly to show none of them accounts for the vacuum conversation.
qa_items.support: No measurement supports the sender-versus-receiver distinction; it is an interpretive framing, and the same act is compatible with either motive, which Berger concedes without separating them. The one measurement bearing on the driver is his own New York Times finding, reported in the previous chapter, that more useful articles were 30 percent more likely to make the Most E-Mailed list — which establishes the association, not the helping motive behind it. He ranks this driver the easiest of the six to apply, as a judgement without a cross-driver comparison.
confounders: collapsing the two drivers because both make the sharer look good; his distinction is about who the content is for
reading the opening cases as evidence; they are anecdotes, and the driver is assigned to them by elimination
treating 'easiest to apply' as a measured ranking

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the barbecue grill scenarios in 'Saving a Couple of Bucks' and their explanation in 'The Psychology of Deals' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Berger reports a pair of scenarios in which people preferred to pay MORE. Give the two scenarios, both figures, and the principle that explains the result.
qa_items.answer: One hundred people were shown a grill reduced from $350 to $250; another hundred saw the same grill reduced from $255 to $240. Seventy-five percent of the first group said they would buy rather than keep looking; 22 percent of the second group did. The second group would have paid ten dollars less. The principle is the reference point: people do not evaluate in absolute terms but against a comparison standard, usually the price they expect to pay, so a larger apparent reduction from a higher starting point beats a lower final price. Berger draws the practical consequence — whoever sets the standard controls the judgement, which is why infomercials name a price you "might expect to pay" before naming theirs, and why retailers print a regular price beside a sale price. His summary is that consumers are so focused on getting a good deal that they sometimes end up paying more to get it.
qa_items.support: The figures ARE Berger's own reported measurement — he states he gave each scenario to one hundred different people. The scenarios are not his: the Notes credit them to Richard Thaler's work on mental accounting, and the theory to Kahneman and Tversky. Note the mismatch: the outcome is a STATED INTENTION in a hypothetical, no money changed hands, and yet these are among the most precisely reported figures in the book. No sampling frame or interval is given.
confounders: attributing prospect theory or the scenarios to Berger; both are borrowed and he says so
treating stated intention as purchase behaviour
reading the effect as being about discount size rather than about the reference point that makes a discount look large

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the clock radio and television scenarios in 'The Psychology of Deals' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Berger presents two situations that are identical in substance and produce opposite decisions. Describe them, give his figures, and name the principle. Then note the objection he does not consider.
qa_items.answer: A $35 clock radio is $25 at a branch twenty minutes away, or a $650 television is $640 at the same branch. Both are twenty minutes to save ten dollars. He reports that 87 percent said they would buy the television at the first store, while only 17 percent said the same of the clock radio — so almost everyone drives for the radio and almost nobody for the television. The principle is diminishing sensitivity: the same absolute change has a smaller felt impact the further it lies from the reference point, which he illustrates with lottery winnings — $20 instead of $10 feels much better, $1,020 instead of $1,010 is not noticed. The objection he does not consider is that the two situations may not be equivalent in substance after all: a buyer making a six-hundred-dollar purchase may reasonably value twenty minutes differently, and the framing of the result as an irrationality is his.
qa_items.support: Berger's OWN reported measurement of one hundred people per scenario, with the scenarios again adapted from Thaler rather than devised for this purpose. Hypothetical stated intentions, not observed behaviour.
confounders: reading the result as showing people are bad at arithmetic; the arithmetic is trivially available in both scenarios
reversing the figures — the low percentage is the one where people take the drive
assuming Berger tests the opportunity-cost defence; he does not raise it

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the catalogue experiment in 'The Psychology of Deals' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Describe the study Berger reports on sale signs, its scale, its result — and the boundary condition that is in the study's own title and not in his body text.
qa_items.answer: Two versions of a real clothing catalogue were mailed to more than fifty thousand people each, identical except that in one version certain items carried a "Pre-Season SALE" sign. Prices were the same in both versions. Demand for the labelled items rose by more than 50 percent — the word did work the price did not. The boundary condition is in the paper's title, which asks whether sale signs are LESS effective when more products have them, and the answer is that they are. Berger does state that limit later in the chapter, in a different section, when discussing over-use of promotions — but he never connects it back to this result, so a reader taking the catalogue finding on its own gets an unbounded version of a conditional effect.
qa_items.support: NOT Berger's research — marketing scientists Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester, in Marketing Science (2001). It is a large randomised field experiment and it is theirs. Period-bound to printed catalogue retail before 2001.
confounders: attributing the catalogue experiment to Berger
reporting the 50 percent increase without the saturation condition that the source's own citation carries in its title
assuming the prices differed; the whole point is that they did not

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', section 'Highlighting Incredible Value' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: A retailer runs a discount every week and finds the discounts stop working. Using Berger's material, explain what has happened and what the counter-intuitive alternative is.
qa_items.answer: The reference point has migrated. When a product is always on sale, the sale price becomes the price people expect, so there is no longer a gap for them to perceive as a deal — his case is a rug store permanently advertising seventy percent off, where customers have learned that sales are the norm. He adds a second version of the same erosion: if too many items in a store carry a sale sign, purchase actually falls. The counter-intuitive alternative is restriction rather than repetition. Making a promotion MORE restrictive makes it more effective: limits on time, limits on quantity per customer, or limits on who may access it. He reports that quantity purchase limits increase sales by more than 50 percent, and the inference doing the work is that a limit is read as a signal — the store must be worried about running out, so the deal must be good.
qa_items.support: The quantity-limit figure is NOT Berger's — the Notes credit Inman, Peter and Raghubir (1997); the access-restriction claim is credited to Schindler (1998). The erosion side is asserted with no figure at all, and no criterion is given for where the boundary lies — how often, how many items, how long — so the trade-off is named and not made operable.
confounders: deepening the discount, which accelerates the erosion
reading restriction as reducing demand, which is the intuition the source is contradicting
confusing this with the Social Currency chapter's scarcity, which buys status for the holder rather than changing perceived monetary value

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the sub-section 'The Rule of 100' within 'Highlighting Incredible Value' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Two offers need framing: twenty percent off a twenty-five-dollar shirt, and two hundred dollars off a two-thousand-dollar laptop. State Berger's rule, apply it to both, and give the limitation that his statement of it hides.
qa_items.answer: The Rule of 100. Below a price of one hundred dollars, express the discount as a PERCENTAGE; above one hundred, express it as an AMOUNT. So the shirt is advertised as twenty percent off rather than five dollars off, and the laptop as two hundred dollars off rather than ten percent off. The mechanism is that whichever framing yields the larger NUMBER feels larger, and which framing does that flips at a base price of one hundred. The hidden limitation is that the threshold is an artefact of arithmetic in a currency quoted in units of one, not a psychological constant. Applied in a currency of a different scale the crossover sits at a different number, and Berger does not say so — he presents one hundred as a rule. A second limit: the rule is about which framing SEEMS larger, and no evidence here shows the framing choice changes purchase or sharing.
qa_items.support: NOT Berger's research — the underlying finding is credited in the Notes to Chen, Monroe and Lou (1998) in the Journal of Retailing, and his body text says only "researchers find". The packaging of it as a hundred-dollar rule is his presentation. The currency-scale limitation is an extractor observation; the source states the threshold without qualification.
confounders: inverting the rule, which is easy to do and produces the smaller number in both cases
treating one hundred as a psychological threshold that transfers across currencies
assuming the finding is Berger's; the body text attributes it only to 'researchers'

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the loyalty-card passage closing 'Highlighting Incredible Value' and the packaging discussion in 'More Than Money' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: A supermarket loyalty scheme saves customers real money and generates almost no word of mouth. Berger gives two form conditions that explain it. What are they, and what does his proposed fix for the first one actually change?
qa_items.answer: First, visibility. The saving is real but it is printed among half a dozen other items on a till receipt, and since nobody shows anyone their receipts, no one but the card holder ever sees it — so there is nothing to talk about and nothing for a non-holder to observe. His proposed fix is to surface it at the checkout: a sign showing the queue how much the current customer saved, or a bell rung when someone saves more than twenty-five dollars. That changes two things at once — it demonstrates the value to people who have no card, and it gives the card holder a remarkable figure worth repeating. Second, packaging. Useful information travels when it is bounded and scannable, so it can be passed on whole: a one-page note with a header item and three or four links rather than a rambling multi-page mailing across fifteen topics, which is also why so many heavily shared articles are short lists built around one topic.
qa_items.support: NO measurement anywhere in this passage. The checkout proposal is a hypothetical Berger invents and does not test; the packaging case is his own forwarding behaviour, reported as an anecdote about himself; and the observation about list-structured articles is stated without checking it against his own dataset, which recorded article features and presumably could have.
confounders: diagnosing the problem as insufficient savings rather than invisible ones
treating the checkout proposal as a reported case; it is invented and untested
reading packaging as a matter of tone or clarity rather than of being a bounded unit that can be forwarded whole

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', the audience-breadth passage near the end of 'More Than Money' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Berger makes a counter-intuitive claim about audience breadth, and he hedges it. State the claim, the mechanism, the hedge, and the arithmetic problem he does not address.
qa_items.answer: The claim is that narrowly relevant content may actually be MORE likely to be shared than broadly relevant content — an article about water polo or an Ethiopian restaurant over one about professional football or an American restaurant. The mechanism is that sharing requires a recipient to come to mind: a topic many friends like activates no one in particular, whereas a topic only one friend cares about summons that friend immediately, and the sense that it is uniquely perfect for them converts the thought into an act. The hedge is consistent and deliberate — broadly relevant content COULD be shared more, narrowly relevant content MAY actually be more viral. The arithmetic problem he does not address is that a higher per-person share rate over a smaller audience does not entail more total transmission, and his claim concerns the probability an individual passes something on, not reach.
qa_items.support: NO EVIDENCE IS OFFERED FOR THIS AT ALL — no study of Berger's, no third-party citation, and no note. It is an argument from a plausible mechanism and is the least supported claim in the chapter. The hedging is the source's own and is preserved here.
confounders: reporting 'niche beats broad' as an established finding of this book; it is a hedged argument with no evidence
reading it as a claim about total reach rather than about per-person share probability
assuming it follows from his Most E-Mailed data; that dataset is never brought to bear on it

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Practical Value', section 'A Note on Truth' (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Berger names a failure mode of his own driver. What is it, what is his case, and what asymmetry makes it durable? Note where his prescription stops short of his own material.
qa_items.answer: Practical value selects for perceived usefulness, not for truth, so a false claim that seems useful spreads by exactly the same mechanism and at the same speed — as he puts it, the desire to share helpful things is so powerful that it can make even false ideas succeed. His case is the 1998 paper linking the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to autism, later found to be a fraud whose author was found guilty of serious professional misconduct and lost his licence; it spread widely and vaccination rates fell. The asymmetry that makes it durable is that the retraction did not travel as far as the claim, so people went on sharing a narrative that had been discredited — and nobody was trying to spread a falsehood, they heard something they thought was useful and wanted other people's children to be safe. His prescription is a burden on the individual sharer: verify health claims independently before passing them on. That stops short of the harder question his own book is equipped for — how a correction could be given the triggers and arousal it would need to travel as far as the original.
qa_items.support: An argued account of one historical case, not a measurement. Berger reports no study of anyone's on the relative spread of true and false claims, and the assertion that false information spreads "just as quickly as" the truth is not established anywhere in the book. The Notes cite third-party discussion of the episode.
confounders: reading it as a claim about deliberate misinformation; his mechanism runs entirely through good intentions
quoting 'false information spreads just as quickly as the truth' as a finding; it is an assertion with no supporting measurement
assuming the source offers a distribution-side remedy; he offers only individual verification

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', section 'Stories as Vessels' (spine 11)
qa_items.question: A brand has a fact about its product that is genuinely useful and that nobody ever repeats. Berger's diagnosis is not that the fact is dull. What is it, and what does his contrasting case show?
qa_items.answer: The diagnosis is that the fact has no occasion. His example is a sandwich chain's low-fat range: the information is practically valuable to someone trying to lose weight, but nobody walks up to a friend and states it — it would be strange and out of context, and unless weight loss is already the topic or something has cued it, it never comes up. People do not think in terms of information, they think in terms of narratives, so the fact needs a carrier. His contrast is the story of one man losing 245 pounds while eating at that chain, which people bring up even when weight loss is not the subject, because the story is worth telling for its own sake. Listeners take away four things about the brand — that it has healthy options, healthy enough to lose weight on, a lot of weight, and food someone could eat for three months and still want. As he puts it, information travels under the guise of what seems like idle chatter.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument, with NO measurement of any kind anywhere in this chapter's case for the driver. The chain case is a company's promotional history, and the unpacking of what a listener takes away is Berger's own reading — it is not measured that listeners take away any of it.
confounders: diagnosing the fact as insufficiently interesting and trying to make it more striking
reading the remedy as storytelling craft rather than as supplying an occasion for a fact that has none
assuming the listener consciously registers the information; the claim is that it arrives with the plot

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', section 'Learning Through Stories' (spine 11)
qa_items.question: Berger claims narrative is more persuasive than assertion and gives two separate mechanisms rather than one. What are they, and what does he mean by proof by analogy?
qa_items.answer: First, specificity: it is hard to disagree with a particular thing that happened to a particular person — a listener cannot easily tell someone their experience did not occur. Second, engagement: following a narrative consumes the cognitive resources that would otherwise go into counterarguing, so the listener is too caught up in the drama to question it. Proof by analogy is the epistemic function rather than the rhetorical one: a story is evidence that something happened to someone like the listener, which is weaker than a guarantee and stronger than a claim. There is no way to be sure a retailer will replace your coat because it replaced someone else's, but the fact that it happened to a person like you makes it feel likely. He frames the whole thing against the alternatives — trial and error is expensive, direct observation is impractical, and advertising is discounted because the advertiser is selling.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument, not measured here. The Notes point to third-party work on counterarguing (Kardes) and on gossip as cultural learning (Baumeister, Zhang and Vohs); neither design is described in the text.
confounders: giving only the engagement mechanism, which is the one usually cited
reading proof by analogy as a claim that stories constitute evidence; his point is that they supply a defeasible inference
treating suppressed counterargument as purely a benefit — his own Practical Value chapter documents the same property carrying false claims, and he never connects the two

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', section 'Making Virality Valuable', the Olympic stunt and bottled-water cases (spine 11)
qa_items.question: Berger's clearest failure condition. Give both of his cases with their figures, state what the two have in common, and give his one-line diagnosis of the whole error.
qa_items.answer: First, a publicity stunt at the 2004 Olympics: a man in a tutu and polka-dot tights with an online casino's name across his chest interrupted the diving. Millions watched, news outlets worldwide covered it, and the word of mouth was enormous — about Olympic security, about the Chinese divers who flubbed their next dive, about the perpetrator's trial. Nobody talked about the casino. Second, a bottled-water brand's roller-skating babies film: more than 50 million views and declared by Guinness the most viewed online advertisement in history, and the same year the brand lost market share and sales fell almost 25 percent. What the two have in common is that the sponsor was irrelevant to the content — a tutu and roller-skating babies are great story material and neither has anything to do with a casino or with water. His diagnosis is that people focus so much on getting people to talk that they ignore the part that really matters: what people are talking about. There is a big difference between people talking about content and people talking about the company that made it.
qa_items.support: Both cases are recounted with third-party outcome figures and neither is a controlled test. The sales decline is reported from a trade-press piece and is not attributed by anyone to the campaign; a year of falling sales has many possible causes, and Berger's placement of the two facts side by side implies more than the evidence carries. The underlying research is his own but is cited only as an unpublished Wharton working paper whose design the book never describes.
confounders: diagnosing the failures as brand-safety problems or as poor taste; the mechanism is irrelevance
treating the pairing of views with the sales fall as a demonstrated causal relation
assuming high view counts indicate the campaign worked, which is the assumption the section exists to attack

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', the cheese advertisements and blender passages in 'Making Virality Valuable' (spine 11)
qa_items.question: Berger tests his own favourite advertisement destructively before endorsing it. What is the test he applies, what does the destructive step establish, and how do you run the same test on any artefact?
qa_items.answer: The test is whether the thing you want transmitted is load-bearing in the story — whether people can tell the story without mentioning it. The destructive step is that he points out the cheese commercials would be exactly as funny with a chicken suit and a used-car tagline: someone in an animal costume kicking over groceries is funny regardless of which animal or which product. That establishes that the humour is not what makes them work as advertising, because the humour is detachable. The brand passes anyway, on a different ground: the story cannot be told or understood without the panda, so mentioning it is unavoidable. He runs the same test on the blender films — impossible to recount the clip destroying a phone without saying a blender did it, and without conveying that the blender is extraordinarily strong, which is exactly what the company wanted communicated. To run it: retell the artefact aloud without naming the subject. If the account still makes sense and still lands, the subject is detachable and will be dropped.
qa_items.support: Berger's argument, not measured. The claim that audiences remember the brand days or weeks later is asserted rather than measured, and the test as stated is binary with no way to grade partial integration. His counterfactual is unusually rigorous for this book — it holds the entertainment constant and varies only whether the subject is load-bearing — but it is an argument, not an experiment: he did not build the chicken-suit version and measure anything.
confounders: judging the advertisement on how funny or well made it is, which is the dimension the destructive step removes from consideration
assuming heavy branding satisfies the test; a logo can be prominent and still detachable from the plot
grading an artefact as partially integrated; the source's test is binary and gives no way to do that

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', the Telephone study at the end of 'Making Virality Valuable' (spine 11)
qa_items.question: What is the empirical basis for Berger's integration rule? Describe the study, its figure, and the pattern — and say whose study it is and how old.
qa_items.answer: Gordon Allport and Joseph Postman's rumour research, published in 1947 — not Berger's, and more than sixty years old when he wrote. One person viewed a detailed picture of a subway car: an Eighth Avenue Express passing Dyckman Street, advertisements on the walls, five seated passengers including a rabbi and a mother with a baby, and, as the focus, two men arguing with one pointing and holding a knife. That person described it to a second, who described it to a third, and so on to a sixth, none of whom had seen it, across dozens of chains. About 70 percent of the details were lost in the first five or six transmissions. The important part is that the loss was STRUCTURED, not random: across chains the same details were consistently dropped and the same consistently retained, and the account sharpened around the central event. The line and the street went; the argument and the knife stayed. That is why an integrated brand survives and a decorative one does not.
qa_items.support: NOT Berger's research — Allport and Postman, The Psychology of Rumor (1947). Limits: the stimulus is a picture, not an experience, and the transmission is a laboratory chain rather than conversation, so whether the same rates hold for stories people want to tell is not established. Note also that this finding is in tension with Berger's own chapter 1 claim that stories become MORE remarkable as they travel; he never reconciles the two.
confounders: attributing the study to Berger, or assuming it is recent
reading it as showing that transmission garbles stories randomly; the point is that the loss is patterned
reconciling it too quickly with the exaggeration finding in chapter 1; the source does not, and the tension is real

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Stories', the beauty-industry film in 'Build a Trojan Horse' (spine 11)
qa_items.question: A brand wants to enter a conversation about a subject people feel strongly about but are reluctant to raise. Using Berger's account of the beauty-products film, describe how the Trojan Horse worked here and which of his other drivers he says it recruited.
qa_items.answer: The film shows an ordinary-looking woman transformed by makeup, styling, photography and then heavy digital retouching into a billboard image, closing on a line about why our perception of beauty is distorted. Berger's account is that the brand latched onto something people already wanted to talk about — unrealistic beauty norms — and which was emotional but controversial enough that people had been reluctant to raise it. The film gave them the occasion. He explicitly names the other drivers it recruited: it made the issue more PUBLIC, giving people an excuse to discuss what had been private, and it was highly EMOTIONAL. And it got people talking about the brand along the way, because the brand was smuggled in as part of the discussion rather than attached to it. He reports the film cost a little over a hundred thousand dollars, took more than 16 million views, tripled the traffic the brand's own Super Bowl spot had produced, and that the company saw double-digit sales growth.
qa_items.support: A recounted campaign with press-reported outcome figures and no control. The claim that the brand benefited is asserted from the co-occurrence of the campaign and the sales growth. Note that this case is one Berger uses positively while the equally viewed bottled-water film in the next section is his negative case — the difference he identifies is relevance of the sponsor to the subject, not view count.
confounders: reading the case as being about the film's craft or shock value rather than about supplying an occasion for a conversation people wanted to have
treating the sales figures as isolating the campaign's contribution
assuming any emotive social issue works; his own next section shows an equally viewed film that produced nothing for its brand

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Epilogue, the Vietnamese nail-salon account and the three closing points (spine 12)
qa_items.question: Berger closes by running his whole framework over one case. What is the case, and how does he assign each of the six drivers to it?
qa_items.answer: Immigrant occupational clustering — his headline is that 80 percent of manicurists in California are Vietnamese American, traced to twenty women taught manicure skills in a refugee camp in 1975. He notes it is not unique, citing similar concentrations among Cambodian American doughnut shops in Los Angeles, Korean dry cleaners in New York, Irish liquor stores in 1850s Boston and Jewish men's clothing manufacture in the early 1900s. His assignment: employment is a frequent topic among new immigrants looking for work, which supplies TRIGGERS; they can see what work other recent arrivals have taken, which is PUBLIC; the established ones want to look good, which is SOCIAL CURRENCY, and to help, which is PRACTICAL VALUE; and they tell exciting — EMOTION — narratives — STORIES — about people who succeeded. He uses the case to make three closing points: that anything can be contagious, that epidemics are driven by the products and ideas themselves rather than by influentials, and that specific characteristics make things more likely to be shared.
qa_items.support: A historical account assembled from press sources cited in the Notes, with the framework applied to it retrospectively by the author. No measurement, and the assignment of all six drivers to one case after the fact is the least falsifiable use of the framework in the book — worth noting because the Introduction's own methodological standard warns against exactly this shape of reasoning.
confounders: reading the retrospective assignment as evidence that the framework predicts; nothing was predicted
taking the closing 'if you follow these six key STEPPS, you can make any product or idea contagious' at face value, against his own footnote that not all six are required
assuming the six drivers were derived from cases like this; they were derived from research and then applied here

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Social Currency', section 'Inner Remarkability'; Ch. 2 'Triggers', sections 'Why Do People Buzz About Some Products More Than Others?' and 'Triggered to Talk' (spine 6, spine 7)
qa_items.question: A team has built something genuinely remarkable and asks how long the resulting conversation will last. Answer from Berger's own two findings, and note the tension between them that he never resolves.
qa_items.answer: On his BzzAgent evidence: not long, unless something in the audience's environment brings it back. Interesting, novel and surprising products got more IMMEDIATE word of mouth and no more ONGOING word of mouth than boring ones; what predicted ongoing talk was how frequently the thing was cued in the environment. So the practical answer is that remarkability buys the opening and triggers buy the duration, and a remarkable thing with no habitat behaves like his pirate costume — discussed all day and gone by the next month. The tension he never resolves is that his other study, with Raghu Iyengar across 6,500 brands, found more remarkable brands discussed almost twice as often, with no immediate-versus-ongoing split applied. The two findings are never placed side by side, and the resolution he offers later concerns INTEREST rather than REMARKABILITY, and is asserted rather than shown to apply to the brand study.
qa_items.support: Both studies are Berger's own — Berger and Schwartz (2011) for the BzzAgent analysis, Berger and Iyengar (Wharton working paper) for the brand analysis. Both are correlational. The unresolved tension between them is an extractor observation; the source never addresses it.
confounders: answering only from the remarkability finding, which predicts sustained conversation
answering only from the triggers finding, which understates what remarkability does buy
assuming Berger reconciles them; he does not, and asserting a reconciliation on his behalf attributes a claim he never makes

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Triggers', section 'The Difference Between Immediate and Ongoing Word of Mouth' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: A campaign is measured one week after launch, performs well, and is judged a success; a second campaign is measured over four months, looks flat, and is killed. On Berger's account, what might have gone wrong in each judgement, and what does he say determines which window is the right one?
qa_items.answer: Both judgements may be reading the wrong window rather than the wrong campaign. Berger's own research history is the warning: he measured whether a property mattered without asking WHEN it mattered, found nothing, and only recovered a real finding by splitting the outcome into immediate and ongoing. A one-week measure will credit whatever is interesting, which his data say does not persist; a four-month pooled measure can bury a real immediate effect. What determines the right window, on his account, is the product's own economics rather than the campaign: films and new grocery items depend on immediate word of mouth, because theatre bookings and shelf space get reallocated fast, so an early read is the correct one. Anti-bullying campaigns and policy initiatives need people still talking months later, so an early read is meaningless for them. The window is a substantive decision, not a measurement detail.
qa_items.support: Berger's own distinction and his own narrated research history, from Berger and Schwartz (2011). The generalisation that a wrong window produces a confident wrong answer rather than a noisy one is an extractor reading of what happened to him; he narrates the episode and does not state it as a methodological principle.
confounders: assuming a longer measurement window is always better; it can bury a real immediate effect
treating the window as a matter of statistical power rather than of which outcome the product actually needs
attributing the general methodological principle to Berger; he demonstrates it and does not state it

qa_items.source_title: Jonah Berger, Contagious: Why Things Catch On (Simon & Schuster, 2013)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Emotion', sections 'Does Any Emotion Boost Sharing?' and 'Kindling the Fire with High-Arousal Emotions'; Ch. 4 'Public', section 'Anti-Drug Commercials?' (spine 8, spine 9)
qa_items.question: A charity's film about a slow-moving crisis is beautifully made, leaves audiences moved and quiet, and is barely shared. Diagnose it from Berger, give his prescribed direction, and state the cross-chapter constraint that his prescription must not violate.
qa_items.answer: The diagnosis is arousal, not quality or valence. Sadness is a low-arousal emotion: it deactivates, people power down, and his own data put sad articles 16 percent less likely to make the Most E-Mailed list. Being moved and quiet is the symptom. His prescribed direction is to kindle the fire — make people mad rather than sad on the negative side, or excite or inspire them by showing how they can make a difference on the positive side, and he notes that anxiety and disgust also activate, citing a public health film about fat pouring from a soda can. The cross-chapter constraint is from the Public chapter: if the film's aim is to REDUCE a behaviour, it must not do its arousing by reporting how many people currently do it, because that supplies social proof and can increase the behaviour — as, on the evidence he reports, large anti-drug campaigns did. So the anger has to be aimed at the situation, not manufactured by publicising the prevalence of the thing being opposed.
qa_items.support: The arousal material is Berger's own research (Berger and Milkman, 2012; Berger, 2011). The backfire constraint rests on third-party work he reports — Hornik's observational anti-drug analysis and Cialdini's field comparison of park signs. Joining the two chapters is an extractor reading; the source never states the combined constraint, and the disgust claim in particular is made without disgust ever appearing in his own arousal grid.
confounders: prescribing a more emotional film, without distinguishing which emotion — a sadder film satisfies 'more emotional' and makes it worse
reading the fix as making it more positive; contentment is positive and also deactivates
arousing anger by publicising how many people are causing the problem, which satisfies the Emotion chapter and violates the Public chapter

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Leading lines", sub-heading "Look for the leading lines" (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Carroll gives three working rules for leading lines, not one. What are they, and which of the three would a photographer be most likely to get wrong by instinct?
qa_items.answer: The three are: one main leading line is often all you need; a line is at its most powerful when it sweeps in from the edge of the frame; and you should not be shy about making the line very overt. The one that runs against instinct is the third — the beginner's instinct is to be subtle, and Carroll's instruction is the opposite. The first also cuts against the impulse to accumulate devices. Note that "one is often all you need" is stated as a preference; he never says what goes wrong with two and shows no counter-case.
qa_items.support: Leading lines spread: great compositions take you on a journey; use them to give structure and draw the viewer to key elements; one main line is often all you need; strongest sweeping in from the frame edge; don't be shy about making these lines very overt.
confounders: reading 'overt' as a warning against obviousness — he says the opposite
assuming more leading lines means more control of the eye
the modern default that a leading line must be a road or a path; his examples include a tree branch and a crack in rock

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Getting close", sub-heading "Get close. And then get closer." (spine 12)
qa_items.question: A photographer says they will shoot from further back and crop in afterwards to get the same tight frame. On Carroll's account, what have they lost, and what is his stated reason?
qa_items.answer: They have lost the thing he says the picture actually carries. Carroll raises this exact substitution and rejects it: cropping is a fine tuner, not a way to fundamentally alter an image. His reason is relational rather than optical — the photographer's physical exposure to the subject is part of what the picture means. He says of the photographer in his example that it matters that he puts himself in the line of fire, and that if he did not, the pictures would lose their humour and start to feel underhand. So the loss is not resolution; it is the fact of the encounter. Note the scope: he is talking about candid work with people, and elsewhere he recommends a long lens precisely where approach is impossible.
qa_items.support: Getting close spread: nothing kills an image more than keeping your distance; think of cropping as a fine tuner rather than a way of fundamentally altering your image; it's important that the photographer puts himself in the line of fire, or the pictures would feel underhand.
confounders: answering in terms of image quality, resolution or lens sharpness — Carroll's reason is not technical
assuming he forbids cropping; he permits it as a fine tuner
generalising the rule to all subjects; his scope is subjects that could have been approached

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "The rule of thirds", sub-heading "Be offish" (spine 14)
qa_items.question: Carroll names two ways of getting off-centre placement wrong, and they are on opposite sides of each other. What are they, and what does having two of them tell you about how he is using the rule of thirds?
qa_items.answer: A subject positioned too near the edge of the frame looks clumsy, and so does a subject positioned only slightly off centre. Because the two failures sit on either side, the rule is not functioning as a construction method but as a corridor between two errors: it tells you how far to displace a subject once you have decided not to centre it. That is consistent with how he frames it — a rough guideline for maintaining balance when you do not want to centre, not a grid to build on. Neither failure zone is quantified anywhere.
qa_items.support: Rule of thirds spread: if you don't want to centre your subject, the rule helps maintain balance; use it as a rough guideline; be careful not to position your subject too near the edge of the frame, or only slightly off-centre, as this can look a little clumsy.
confounders: naming only the edge failure and missing the slightly-off-centre one
treating the thirds grid as a construction to place elements on rather than a corridor
importing a golden-ratio or geometric justification; Carroll gives none

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Symmetry", sub-heading "It's a primal instinct" (spine 13)
qa_items.question: You have a symmetrical composition that a client calls lifeless. What does Carroll say has gone wrong and what is his prescribed correction — and what does he not tell you?
qa_items.answer: He names this failure directly: there is a fine line between balance and boring, and an image that is too perfectly mirrored can feel soulless and a little too phony. His correction is a dose rather than an abandonment — allow the human elements to creep in, the little things that draw attention without upsetting the balance. What he does not tell you is any threshold: how perfect is too perfect, or how large the saving asymmetry may be before it stops rescuing the picture and starts unbalancing it. The remedy is asserted, never specified.
qa_items.support: Symmetry spread: symmetry satisfies a primal need for order; it isn't a case of composing like an ink blot but of overall harmony and balance; there's a fine line between balance and boring; if everything is too perfectly mirrored an image can feel soulless; allow the human elements to creep in.
confounders: prescribing that the composition be made asymmetric — his fix is a small element, not a restructure
assuming he supplies a threshold or ratio; he supplies neither
confusing this with the rule-of-thirds guidance, which is about off-centre placement, not about rescuing symmetry

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Working the frame", sub-heading "Make every inch count" (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Carroll's remedy for a composition that is not quite working is to change position "even very slightly". Why does such a small movement do anything at all, on his account?
qa_items.answer: Because the elements in the frame do not move together. They lie at different distances from the camera, so as the camera shifts they move relative to one another at different rates. A small change of viewpoint therefore re-arranges the relationships inside the frame without changing the subject at all — which is why the instrument is a couple of steps rather than a different picture. His instruction is to change position slightly and keep an eye on how all the elements move around in relation to each other.
qa_items.support: Working the frame spread: a little lower, a touch to the left, a couple of steps back; these minor adjustments make the fencepost vertical, frame the taxi rather than cut it in two, and ensure nothing is creeping into the frame; change position even very slightly and watch how the elements move in relation to each other.
confounders: explaining it as a change of perspective distortion or focal length; neither changes here
assuming the point is to find a better subject rather than a better arrangement of the same one

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Working the frame", sub-heading "Make every inch count" (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Give the concrete checks Carroll runs before releasing the shutter, and name the fault he says the whole procedure exists to prevent.
qa_items.answer: The fault is a "passive" area — a region of the frame that does not add much. The checks he names are specific: is a foreground vertical actually vertical; is a passing object framed rather than cut in two; do the colours balance without one becoming overpowering; is anything creeping into the frame that does not belong. The procedure is to pause just when you think you are ready and glance around the frame asking whether everything is where it should be and whether the composition is working as a whole. He says pictures like this cannot be snapped — which is the honest limit of the method.
qa_items.support: Working the frame spread: knowing exactly what's going on in every part of your frame; the named checks; avoid passive areas that don't add much; pause and glance around your frame before shooting.
confounders: listing generic composition rules instead of his named checks
assuming this scan is compatible with catching a decisive moment; Carroll says these pictures can't be snapped

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Visual weight", sub-heading "Reducing it down" (spine 16)
qa_items.question: "Don't see the world as it is. See it as a photograph." What is Carroll actually instructing the photographer to do, and what does he claim about how hard it is?
qa_items.answer: He is instructing the photographer to stop seeing objects and start seeing the two-dimensional shapes and tones they will become, because it is tone that carries visual weight — he says a dark ground reads as heavier than a light wall, and the amount of frame each element is given has to answer to that. On difficulty he makes an unusual claim: the skill is not new. He says the eyes are already effective weighing scales, used every time you decide where to hang a picture or how to arrange food on a plate, so the task is transferring an existing judgement rather than acquiring one. That transfer is asserted with no support.
qa_items.support: Visual weight spread: he reduced everything down to two-dimensional shapes and tones; notice how much heavier the dark ground seems than the light wall and how this influenced the space given to each; your eyes are already pretty effective weighing scales.
confounders: reading 'visual weight' as physical size or as subject importance; Carroll grounds it in tone
assuming he provides a method for computing balance; he provides an analogy

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Breaking the rules", sub-heading "Throw the rule book out the window" (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Carroll writes that good photographs conform to the rules and really great ones often break them. What warrant does he give for a break, and why is that warrant a weak test?
qa_items.answer: The warrant is correspondence with the subject: rather than making sure everything conforms, concentrate on creating compositions that capture the essence of the subject. Where the subject is not settled, a settled composition misdescribes it, so the discomfort a broken rule produces can be the true reading. He also warns that too much conformity makes photographs feel safe and predictable. The test is weak because it is unfalsifiable as stated — any broken rule can be justified after the fact by asserting the discomfort suits the subject — and because every case he can show is already a famous photograph, so nothing that broke the same rules and failed is in the book.
qa_items.support: Breaking the rules spread: compositional techniques serve as essential building blocks but too much of that makes photographs feel safe and predictable; rather than making sure everything conforms, concentrate on capturing the essence of your subject.
confounders: reading it as a licence for novelty; his warrant is correspondence with the subject, not difference
