treating 'break the rules' as advice for beginners; he presents the techniques as prerequisites
missing the survivorship problem in his evidence base

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Breaking the rules", sub-heading "Throw the rule book out the window" (spine 17)
qa_items.question: In the course of the rule-breaking spread Carroll lists the things that ordinarily read as compositionally wrong. What is on that list, and what should stop you from using it as a scorecard?
qa_items.answer: Four things: the eye pulled out of the picture by a path running off the frame; an element awkwardly making contact with the very top of the frame; the subject positioned at the extreme edge with its gaze cut short by that edge; and a horizon line cutting right through the subject's head. What stops it being a scorecard is that he lists them in order to defend them — in the same passage he argues that because the resulting tension and anxiety match this particular sitter, the composition is right. So a cue found is a question about whether the register suits the subject, never a verdict.
qa_items.support: Breaking the rules spread: the eyes pulled out of the image by the path; the off-kilter lamppost meeting the top of the frame; the subject at the extreme left with his gaze cut short by the frame edge; a horizon line cutting through the subject's head; and then — on second thoughts, everything about this image is so right.
confounders: treating the four cues as defects to be corrected; Carroll's whole point is that they were not
assuming the cues came from a rule list rather than from his reading of one image
adding modern checklist items (leading room, headroom, rule-of-thirds crops) that he does not name here

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Foreground interest", sub-heading "The layered look" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: What does Carroll claim foreground interest does, and what does he say about how it gets into the picture?
qa_items.answer: It offers the viewer a stepping stone into the image and heightens its sense of depth; without it, the eye feels too separated from the middle distance and background and the picture loses depth. The second half is the part that is easy to miss: it does not get into the picture by being noticed, it gets there by the photographer moving. He is explicit that the near material in his example is not there by chance, that the photographer positioned himself to make it an essential part of the composition, and that landscape photographers do not plonk a tripod anywhere — it is a case of exactly here, not around about here.
qa_items.support: Foreground interest spread: foreground interest offers a stepping stone into your image and heightens its sense of depth; without it our eyes would feel too separated from the middle distance and background; the mud isn't there by chance, the photographer positioned himself.
confounders: describing it as a framing device; it is a depth and entry device
assuming it means anything in the foreground; Carroll requires it to be positioned for

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Section opener "EXPOSURE", sub-heading "Seeing through the science" (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Carroll writes that "correct exposure" is just a matter of opinion. What is he actually claiming, and which later positions in the book depend on it?
qa_items.answer: He is claiming that because shutter, aperture and ISO all act on the same quantity of light, several different balances satisfy any given scene, and the camera reports one of them rather than the right one. Which balance you want is a question about the picture — blur or freeze, shallow or deep — not about the light. Two later positions rest on this. His case against manual mode rests on the camera's exposure being a proposal that manual does not improve on, and his whole treatment of exposure compensation rests on it being legitimate to depart from that proposal on purpose. This is his stated position, not a finding.
qa_items.support: Exposure opener: shutter speed controls the length of time light enters, aperture how much, ISO how sensitive; the trio is inseparable because each relies on the others; adjusting them is as much an exercise in creativity as in controlling light; "correct exposure" is just a matter of opinion.
confounders: reading it as saying exposure doesn't matter; he means several exposures are defensible, not that any is
attributing to him the idea that the meter is inaccurate — his claim is that it is answering a different question

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Appendix "Troubleshooting", question "Why does my whole picture look out of focus?" and Ch. "Slow shutter speeds at night" (spines 67, 23)
qa_items.question: A handheld frame comes back and the entire image looks soft, not just the moving parts. What is Carroll's diagnosis, what is the tell, and what are his three responses in order of strength?
qa_items.answer: His diagnosis is that this is almost certainly not a focusing fault but camera shake from too slow a shutter speed. The tell is exactly the one in the question: with subject blur only the moving parts smear, whereas with camera shake everything in the frame is blurred, because it was the camera that moved. His check is whether the shutter speed dropped below about 1/60 handheld. The responses run: switch on stabilisation, which lets you hand-hold at slower speeds; raise the ISO enough to lift the shutter speed back over that marker, nudging it rather than maxing it out because of noise; and, at genuinely slow speeds, a tripod, which he calls the only cure.
qa_items.support: Troubleshooting: chances are it's not a focusing issue, it's camera shake caused by a slow shutter speed; check the speed isn't below 1/60; increase ISO or use a tripod. Night spread: hand-holding is the most common cause of death for night shots; IS/VR helps; at this speed a tripod is the only cure. ISO spread: nudge the ISO just enough to tip over that marker.
confounders: diagnosing a focus or autofocus-mode problem, which is what the symptom superficially suggests
raising ISO as far as it will go; he warns explicitly against that because of noise
assuming stabilisation makes a tripod unnecessary at any speed

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Shallow depth of field", sub-heading "Stand out by being shallow" (spine 26)
qa_items.question: Carroll explains why a shallow depth of field makes a subject stand out. His mechanism is subtractive rather than additive. What is it, and why does the distinction matter?
qa_items.answer: His mechanism is that by throwing an area of the image out of focus you are effectively getting rid of detail, and it is the removal of detail that causes the subject to stand out. Nothing is added to the subject at all. The distinction matters because it tells you where the technique fails: it works by removing competitors for attention, so it does nothing in a scene that has no competing detail to remove, and it does nothing to a subject that is not itself worth attention once the competition is gone.
qa_items.support: Shallow depth of field spread: to achieve it select Aperture Priority and a wide open aperture (low f-number); by throwing an area of your image out of focus you're effectively getting rid of detail, which causes your subject to really stand out.
confounders: explaining it as the subject being made sharper or brighter; nothing is added
attributing the effect to the lens rather than to the removal of competing detail

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Shallow depth of field", second spread, sub-heading "Compelling close-ups" (spine 27)
qa_items.question: A photographer opens the aperture as wide as it will go and gets almost no background blur. Carroll names the condition they have violated. What is it?
qa_items.answer: There is nothing at a different distance for the shallow depth of field to act on. He states it as a requirement: make sure there is a good amount of distance behind or in front of your subject, otherwise there will not be anything to actually fall out of focus. His reason is that focus is all about distance from the camera, so the effect is a property of the scene's depth as much as of the lens setting. He adds the compounding factor in the other direction — depth of field is at its shallowest in close-up, so proximity, a wide aperture and some zoom stack.
qa_items.support: Compelling close-ups spread: depth of field is at its most shallow when shooting close-ups; focus is all about distance from the camera; make sure there's a good amount of distance behind or in front of your subject, otherwise there won't be anything to fall out of focus.
confounders: blaming the lens's maximum aperture; the condition is about the scene, not the equipment
assuming a wide aperture guarantees background separation

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Manual", sub-heading "All good photographers use Manual, right?" (spine 31)
qa_items.question: Carroll calls shooting in manual a waste of time. Reconstruct his argument, and state the one exception he allows and why he then removes it.
qa_items.answer: The argument is about time, not quality. In manual the camera is still telling you what it thinks the correct exposure is, exactly as in every other mode; a photographer who then adjusts shutter and aperture to match that reading has shot in Program mode more slowly. So manual adds nothing to the picture while adding confusion and, worst of all, the risk of missing the shot. The exception he allows is wanting to override the camera and deliberately under- or overexpose — and he then removes it by pointing at exposure compensation as a faster and easier route to the same result. This is a deliberately contrarian position against camera-club orthodoxy, argued rather than demonstrated, and he scopes it to general day-to-day shooting.
qa_items.support: Manual spread: in Manual the camera is still telling you what it thinks is correct exposure; people who match it are effectively shooting in P and taking longer; Manual adds nothing to the picture, slows you down and means you risk missing the shot; the one situation is deliberate over- or underexposure, for which exposure compensation is faster.
confounders: the widespread view that manual gives more control; his counter is that it gives the same control more slowly
assuming he rejects manual for all photography; he scopes it to general day-to-day shooting
confusing this with his separate and differently-argued dismissal of scene modes

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Exposure compensation", sub-headings "The alternative to Manual" and "Detail from the shadows" (spines 32-33)
qa_items.question: You are photographing someone standing in front of a bright window and their face comes out as a silhouette. What does Carroll say is happening, what does he tell you to do, and what cost does he tell you to accept?
qa_items.answer: The cause he gives is relative: the light inside is much darker relative to the light outside, so a subject in front of a window is routinely silhouetted and all facial detail is lost. The correction is exposure compensation scrolled towards +, which makes the whole image brighter. The cost he tells you to accept is explicit and is the part that is easy to get wrong — the highlights may well blow out, and he says not to worry too much about that as long as you can see the detail in your subject. He refuses to say how far to go, on the ground that it depends on the specific conditions. And remember to return the compensation to zero or it affects every subsequent frame.
qa_items.support: Exposure compensation spreads: a backlit subject often becomes silhouetted because the light inside is much darker relative to the light outside; to draw out shadow detail scroll towards +; the highlights might well blow out but don't worry too much as long as you can see detail in your subject; the precise amount depends on the conditions; always reset to 0.
confounders: protecting the highlights, which is the modern digital default and the opposite of his instruction
reaching for fill flash, which he treats elsewhere as a different tool with an unnatural look
assuming a specific compensation value exists; he explicitly declines to give one

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Appendix "Troubleshooting", question "Should I use Aperture or Shutter Priority?" (spine 67)
qa_items.question: Carroll gives a one-question rule for choosing between the two semi-automatic modes. What is the question, and what does the rule reveal about how he thinks the decision should be made?
qa_items.answer: The rule is to work backwards and ask: what is my picture about? If it is fundamentally about capturing a moving subject, use shutter priority; if it is more about controlling depth of field, use aperture priority. What it reveals is that he treats the mode decision as downstream of the picture's subject rather than of the lighting conditions — you decide which visual effect the picture depends on, take control of the corresponding variable, and hand the compensating variable to the camera. It is the same move as his case against manual.
qa_items.support: Troubleshooting: work backwards — ask what your picture is about; if it's fundamentally about a moving subject use Shutter Priority, if it's more about controlling depth of field use Aperture Priority. Deep depth of field spread: select Aperture Priority so you're in control while the camera worries about the shutter speed.
confounders: choosing the mode from the light level rather than from the subject of the picture
assuming manual is the answer when both matter; Carroll's position is the opposite

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Fast shutter speeds", sub-heading "The big freeze", and Ch. "Fill flash", sub-heading "Daylight flasher" (spines 24, 45)
qa_items.question: A photograph shows a subject in mid-air, completely frozen. Why does Carroll say you cannot conclude a fast shutter speed was used?
qa_items.answer: Because flash freezes movement independently of the shutter. He makes the point explicitly about a daylight fill-flash photograph: when a flash fires it throws light on a subject that comes and goes in an instant, so any movement within the reach of the flash is frozen, and what you are looking at is the result of the flash rather than of a very fast shutter speed. The frozen appearance is evidence about the duration of the light, not about the duration of the exposure.
qa_items.support: Fill flash spread: when a flash fires it throws light on a subject that comes and goes in an instant, causing any movement within the reach of the flash to be frozen, so what we're looking at is the result of the flash rather than a very fast shutter speed. Fast shutter spread: subjects appear frozen because in the instant the picture is taken nothing has time to move.
confounders: reading frozen motion as a reliable signature of shutter speed
assuming the two mechanisms are equivalent; one limits how long the sensor is open, the other how long the subject is lit

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Modes", sub-heading "The good, the bad and the ugly" (spine 19)
qa_items.question: Carroll calls scene modes "junk". His reason is not that they produce poor results. What is it, and why does it matter for the rest of his book?
qa_items.answer: His reason is that a scene mode is a factory preset that adjusts the camera to shoot a particular subject in a particular way, and — his actual objection — there is no single right way to photograph anything. The complaint is about a fixed answer being encoded, not about the quality of that answer. It matters because it is the same claim as "correct exposure is a matter of opinion", applied to subjects rather than to light: throughout the book he treats every setting as a choice about the picture, so a mode that decides for you removes the choice he is trying to teach.
qa_items.support: Modes spread: P, S (Tv) and A (Av) are the only modes you need; scene modes are junk because they are factory presets that adjust settings to shoot a particular subject in a particular way, and there's no single right way to photograph anything; fully Auto is for quick snapshots.
confounders: assuming he objects to automation as such — he recommends Program mode enthusiastically
confusing his objection to scene modes with his separate objection to fully automatic mode

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Hard light", sub-headings "Hard light creates contrast" and "Hard light creates depth" (spines 36, 38)
qa_items.question: Carroll credits hard light with two different and separable effects. Name both and the single property of the light that produces each.
qa_items.answer: The first is simplification by contrast: because hard light makes anything in its path a highlight and leaves everything else dark, the shadow areas become large masses that mask unnecessary detail, which drives the eye to the lit parts and can be used deliberately to abstract a composition. The second is modelling by shadow: the strong, razor-edged shadows that go with hard light create depth and three-dimensionality by describing the angles of what they fall across. The first comes from the division between lit and unlit; the second from the sharpness of the boundary. He adds the reciprocal reading — shadows tell you where the light is coming from and how intense it is.
qa_items.support: Hard light spreads: comes from one direction, typical of a spotlight or bright sunshine, and its common trait is high contrast; anything in its path becomes a highlight while everything else remains dark; the shadows form large areas of black which mask unnecessary detail; the strong decisive shadows create depth and three-dimensionality; shadows tell us where light is coming from and how intense it is.
confounders: collapsing the two effects into one 'contrast' claim
treating hard light as simply harsh and undesirable; he presents both effects as usable

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Hard light", sub-heading "Hard light creates contrast" (spine 36)
qa_items.question: What cost does Carroll say hard light always carries, and why is his own remedy for it not actually a fix?
qa_items.answer: The cost is that hard light is uneven, so you will lose detail somewhere — the range exceeds what can be held at once. His remedy is exposure compensation: scroll to + to bring out detail in the shadows, to − to bring out detail in the highlights. That is a choice, not a fix. The compensation moves the whole image, so it decides which end of the range you keep; it does not recover both ends. He says as much in the same breath — you will lose detail somewhere.
qa_items.support: Hard light spread: the unevenness of hard light makes it tricky to work with, as you will lose detail somewhere; this is another situation where exposure compensation helps — scroll to + for shadow detail and to − for highlight detail.
confounders: presenting exposure compensation as recovering the full range
confusing this with the backlit-subject case, where the choice is between subject and window

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Soft light", sub-heading "Soft light is flattering", and Ch. "Hard light", sub-heading "Hard light is brutal" (spines 41, 40)
qa_items.question: A brief calls for a flattering portrait. Which light does Carroll prescribe, what physical property of it does the work, and where does his own rule not apply?
qa_items.answer: Soft, diffused light, and his instruction about the alternative is unqualified: if you are looking to flatter a subject then avoid hard light altogether. The property doing the work is the shadow edge — under soft light shadows curve around the lines of the body and their edges slowly fade rather than coming to an abrupt stop, which draws out form and features without being severe. Where it does not apply is where flattery is not the aim: in the same section he praises a photographer for using hard light to be confrontational and unflattering on purpose. So the rule is about matching light to intent, not about soft light being better.
qa_items.support: Soft light spreads: soft light is less intense so there isn't a stark divide between highlights and shadows and detail remains visible; shadows curve around the body with edges slowly fading; portrait photographers love soft diffused light as it draws out form without being severe. Hard light spread: hard light is unforgiving and exposes all; if you're looking to flatter a subject avoid it altogether.
confounders: concluding soft light is generally superior; Carroll treats the choice as intent-driven
explaining the flattery by brightness or exposure rather than by shadow-edge quality

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Soft light" (continued), sub-heading "Soft light can be flat" (spine 39)
qa_items.question: This is the one place in the book where Carroll states an interaction between two of his own chapters. What is the interaction, and what does it imply about how much compositional work a picture needs?
qa_items.answer: The interaction is between light and composition. Flat overcast light is very low in contrast and casts little or no shadow, so there are no dramatic shadows and highlights available to create depth and draw the eye — and therefore, he says, the composition alone has to guide the viewer around the image. The implication is that the amount of compositional work a picture requires is set by its light: under directional light, tone shares the guiding; under flat light, structure carries all of it. Note that he sets the reader an exercise here whose answer sits behind print-edition page references that are unresolvable in this copy.
qa_items.support: Soft light can be flat spread: flat light casts little or no shadow and makes everything seem flatter; the blanket evenness means there are no dramatic shadows and highlights to create depth and draw the eye; this evenness means your composition alone has to guide the viewer around your image.
confounders: treating flat light as simply a quality problem rather than as a shift in where the eye guidance comes from
assuming the fix is to add contrast in post; his answer is compositional

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Inbuilt flash", sub-heading "The light without love" (spine 44)
qa_items.question: Carroll gives a geometric reason why built-in flash produces the snapshot look. What is it, and what second effect does he attribute to its intensity?
qa_items.answer: The geometry is that the flash lights the subject from the same angle you are shooting from. Its shadows are therefore thrown forward, away from the camera and out of sight, so the modelling that shadows normally provide is simply absent. The second effect is that its intensity causes anything in the very foreground, or anything slightly reflective, to become overexposed. Together these dominate the look and feel of the image, and used without skill they produce a snapshot look he calls wholly unflattering. Note the scope: this is about on-axis built-in flash. He says nothing about off-camera or bounced flash.
qa_items.support: Inbuilt flash spread: inbuilt flash dominates the look and feel of an image; as the flash lights your subject from the same angle as the one you're shooting from, harsh shadows are thrown forward and its intensity causes anything in the very foreground, or slightly reflective, to become overexposed; used less skilfully it creates a snapshot look that is wholly unflattering.
confounders: attributing the look to colour temperature rather than to the light's angle
generalising the objection to all flash; his fill-flash spread recommends flash deliberately

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Standard focal length", sub-heading "Far from the standard treatment" (spine 52)
qa_items.question: Carroll's instruction for choosing a focal length has three links in it, and magnification is not one of them. Set out the chain.
qa_items.answer: Think about how the focal length will affect your physical position in relation to your subject, and how that then affects the way people will read your images. So: focal length fixes the distance at which you must stand to get the framing you want; the distance you stand at is your actual relationship to the subject; and that relationship is legible in the finished picture. He works the chain in his example — a wider lens would have forced the photographer physically closer, which would have been invasive; a telephoto would have forced distance, which would have felt predatory; the standard focal length put her close without being too close. The reading claim at the end of the chain is asserted, never demonstrated, and is scoped to work about people.
qa_items.support: Standard focal length spread: a standard focal length gets you close to your subject without being too close; when deciding which to use, think about how this will affect your physical position in relation to your subject, and how that then affects the way people will read your images; a wider lens would have been too invasive, a telephoto would have felt predatory.
confounders: answering in terms of field of view or magnification, which is the link he explicitly bypasses
treating the standard lens as a neutral default rather than as a chosen social distance

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Wide angle / short focal length", sub-headings "It's all about the context" and "Composition is the key" (spines 48-49)
qa_items.question: A wide-angle landscape comes back looking empty, with the point of interest reduced to nothing. What does Carroll say happened, and what two devices does he prescribe?
qa_items.answer: Shorter focal lengths seemingly elongate distance, so points of interest that looked relatively close to the naked eye become insignificant details lost within a wider composition. Wide-angle lenses create a lot of space in an image, so — his phrase — you really have to nail your composition. The two devices he names are leading lines and foreground interest, used to emphasise the focal points and pull the composition together. He also gives a second instruction for the near field: get close to your subject, and watch the periphery, because with a short focal length the edge detail plays an all-important role.
qa_items.support: Wide angle spreads: wide-angle lenses cause periphery details to play an all-important role; shorter focal lengths seemingly elongate distance; points of interest become insignificant details lost within a wider composition; you really have to nail your composition; look for leading lines and foreground interest; make sure you get close to your subject.
confounders: reaching for a longer lens, which solves the emptiness but abandons the wide-angle picture
cropping in, which Carroll treats elsewhere as a fine tuner rather than a fix
assuming the problem is that the lens was too wide rather than that the composition was not built for the space

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Telephoto / long focal length", sub-headings "Are you a predator?" and "The telephoto effect" (spines 50-51)
qa_items.question: Carroll allows telephoto lenses in some circumstances and warns about them in others. What is the condition that separates the two, and what does he say the lens does to the space in the picture?
qa_items.answer: The condition is whether you could have got close. Telephoto lenses are essential where you are unable to get physically close — his examples are sports and wildlife — but when you are able to get close and choose not to, the images can start to feel predatory. So the fault is not in the lens but in a decision the picture records. To the space, the lens gives the illusion of compressing depth: everything seems flatter, a receding avenue reads as a flat vertical strip rather than leading into the distance, and buildings behave like layered cut-out shapes, which he says makes images look more graphic. He calls the compression an illusion and explains it no further.
qa_items.support: Telephoto spreads: telephoto lenses transform you into a hidden observer able to capture subjects unawares; essential when you're unable to get physically close, but when you are able to and choose not to, images can feel quite predatory; telephoto lenses give the illusion of compressing depth, making everything seem flatter and more graphic.
confounders: treating the predatory reading as an absolute objection; Carroll concedes one photographer wanted it
explaining the compression optically; Carroll gives no mechanism and calls it an illusion

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Decisive moments", sub-heading "It's all in the timing" (spine 56)
qa_items.question: What operational consequence does Carroll draw from the decisive moment being fleeting, and how does it collide with the composition discipline he teaches earlier in the same book?
qa_items.answer: The consequence is that the camera must be configured before the moment: when it comes to it you will have no time to think, so set your camera up in advance — for him, shutter priority and a fast shutter speed — leaving only the timing decision live. The collision is with his own frame-scan discipline, where he says you cannot snap pictures like that, that they result from knowing exactly what is going on in every part of the frame, and that you should pause and glance around the frame before shooting. Both are his; he never reconciles them. They belong to different situations, and the honest reading is that the pre-set exists precisely because the scan is unavailable.
qa_items.support: Decisive moments spread: knowing exactly when to press the shutter is one of the single most important aspects of photography; capturing it is all about anticipation and instinct; you'll have no time to think, so set your camera up in advance; use Shutter Priority and a fast shutter speed. Against Working the frame: you can't snap pictures like this.
confounders: treating the decisive moment as fast reaction; Carroll's word is anticipation
assuming the two disciplines are compatible in one situation

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "The dangers of perfection", sub-heading "Perfect is often imperfect", and Ch. "The good from the bad", sub-heading "Photographs without excuses" (spines 57, 61)
qa_items.question: Carroll states one priority that is lenient and one discipline that is severe, and they are about the same photograph. What are they, and how do they fit together without contradicting?
qa_items.answer: The lenient one is a priority between two things you cannot always both have: it is far better to capture the right moment with the wrong settings than the wrong moment with the right settings, because the settings can be better next frame and the moment cannot recur. The severe one is a test applied afterwards: a photograph that comes with an excuse — "just before I took this the light was incredible" — has failed, and the effort a shot cost must not be allowed to warp your idea of its quality. They fit because they apply at different times and to different things. Leniency about technique in the moment; severity about the result afterwards. What the second forbids is using the first as a defence.
qa_items.support: Dangers of perfection spread: sometimes you can't have it all and it's far better to capture the right moment with the wrong settings than the wrong moment with the right settings; the desire for perfection can choke your creativity. The good from the bad spread: a picture that comes without any excuses; shots with excuses require you to be tough with yourself; don't let the sole fact that they were hard to get warp your idea of their quality.
confounders: reading the first as a general licence for technical sloppiness; it is scoped to unrepeatable moments
reading the second as public criticism; he addresses it to your own frames
missing that the second is a check on the first being used as an alibi

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "The good from the bad", sub-heading "Photographs without excuses" (spine 61)
qa_items.question: Apply Carroll's excuse test. A photographer shows you a frame and says, "the animal had been out of the hole for a full minute before this". What does the test say, and what is the reasoning behind it?
qa_items.answer: The frame has failed his test. The excuse is the diagnostic: it is a statement about the picture that was not made, offered in place of the picture that was. His reasoning is that the viewer only ever has the frame, so any quality that has to be supplied by an explanation is not in the photograph. The second half is what makes it hard to apply to your own work — the effort the shot cost carries no information about its quality, so a shot that was difficult to get and did not come off should be written off as one that got away, however expensive it was.
qa_items.support: The good from the bad spread: it's a picture that comes without any excuses; shots that come with excuses like "just before I took this the light was incredible" require you to be tough with yourself; write them off as the ones that got away; don't let the sole fact that they were hard to get warp your idea of their quality.
confounders: accepting effort or difficulty as partial credit, which is exactly what he forbids
treating the excuse as context that helps you read the picture
the modern default of judging a shot against the photographer's intent rather than against the frame

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "A different point of view", sub-heading "Photography yoga" (spine 60)
qa_items.question: Carroll calls head height "boring". What exactly is his complaint, and what does he claim about telling good photographers from bad ones?
qa_items.answer: His complaint is about familiarity, not about aesthetics: head height is an all too familiar point of view of the world, with what he calls a punch-pulling neutrality. Because the viewer occupies that viewpoint every day it carries no information of its own, so it contributes nothing to the reading. His claim about telling photographers apart is that you can do it without even looking at their pictures — good photographers are the contortionists, hunching, squatting, lying on the ground and climbing on benches. That is a rhetorical claim about behaviour offered with no evidence, not an assessment method.
qa_items.support: A different point of view spread: good photographers are contortionists; they're the ones hunching, squatting and bending over backwards, down on the ground and climbing on benches; head height is boring, an all too familiar point of view with a punch pulling neutrality; always be looking for those unfamiliar and surprising viewpoints.
confounders: reading the complaint as being about composition or framing rather than about familiarity
treating the contortionist claim as a real assessment method

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "Unexpected beauty", sub-heading "Don't always look for nice" (spine 58)
qa_items.question: A brief asks for beautiful imagery and the obvious answer is a sunset. On Carroll's argument, why is that the hard option rather than the easy one?
qa_items.answer: Because a conventionally beautiful subject arrives with its beauty already supplied, so the photograph has nothing left to contribute. He says the "nice" subjects — sunsets, pretty flowers, hot air balloons — offer a package deal of conventional beauty, and your photograph will at best act as a substitute for the real thing. Everyone loves a sunset; the picture of it adds nothing to the sunset. His alternative is a selection rule about your own motive: look for subjects that for whatever reason interest you, rather than the ones you think are photogenic. Note that his list of "nice" subjects is a snapshot of one photographic culture around 2014.
qa_items.support: Unexpected beauty spread: it's with the "nice" subjects — sunsets, pretty flowers, hot air balloons — that you'll struggle; they offer a package deal of conventional beauty and your photograph will at best act as a substitute for the real thing; look for subjects that interest you rather than the ones you think are photogenic.
confounders: reading it as a claim that beautiful subjects photograph badly; his claim is that the photograph adds nothing
the slogan 'great photographers create their own beauty', which is the rhetoric rather than the argument

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "The importance of intrigue", sub-heading "Pose questions, not answers" (spine 64)
qa_items.question: What redirection of attention does Carroll prescribe for making a picture that holds a viewer, and what mechanism does he give?
qa_items.answer: The redirection is away from the nominal subject: do not focus too much on "the subject", look instead for the little truths that say more, keep an eye on what is going on in between, and steer clear of "Kodak moments". The mechanism is that a picture which explains itself is finished at the first glance and leaves the viewer nothing to do, whereas holding a little back transfers part of the work to them — their own completion of the picture is what holds them in it. His formula is to pose questions, not answers, and to give the imagination somewhere to go. He gives no boundary between productive withholding and simple obscurity.
qa_items.support: Importance of intrigue spread: don't feel like your photographs have to explain themselves; hold a little back; give our imagination somewhere to go; don't focus too much on "the subject", instead look for those little truths; steer clear of Kodak moments and keep an eye on what's going on in-between.
confounders: reading it as advice to be obscure or to hide the subject; he asks for questions, not concealment
assuming it applies to work that must be understood at a glance; Carroll is writing about pictures made to be looked at

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "The power of a project", sub-heading "Photographs need photographs" (spine 65)
qa_items.question: Carroll reports having judged a famous body of work wrongly as a student. What was his error, what does he say the correct unit of judgement is, and what kind of evidence is this?
qa_items.answer: His error was seeing the book as individual pictures and analysing each one separately, trying to work out why this one or that one was great. The correct unit, he says, is the series: as a series the pictures made sense, and together their style and subject matter carry a message that no single one alone could ever voice. Two properties of the set are load-bearing — the specific style and the order of the photographs are essential to their meaning. The kind of evidence is weak and should be labelled: it is autobiographical, a report of his own change of view two years later, not a demonstration. He also never says how to judge a series while making one.
qa_items.support: The power of a project spread: I'd been seeing the book as individual pictures, analysing each one separately; as a series the pictures suddenly made sense; together their style and subject matter carry a message that no single one alone could ever voice; the specific style and order of photographs is essential to their meaning.
confounders: reading it as advice to shoot more of the same thing; his claim is about style and order carrying meaning
treating the anecdote as evidence that series meaning exists rather than as a report of his own reading

qa_items.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. "The power of a project" (spine 65), against Ch. "The good from the bad" (spine 61)
qa_items.question: You are reviewing twelve images made as one body of work. Which of Carroll's two assessment principles applies, and what does the other one get wrong here?
qa_items.answer: Both are his and they pull in opposite directions, so the answer is that the unit has to be settled first. His excuse test is a per-frame test — this photograph either stands without an account of the circumstances or it does not. His series claim says the frame is the wrong unit for a body of work, because the meaning is carried by style and order across the set and assessing members independently destroys exactly the property being claimed. So for a body of work made and sequenced as one, the series claim governs; applying the excuse test frame by frame would be the error he says he made himself as a student. The honest limit is that he gives no method for judging a series, only for judging a frame.
qa_items.support: The power of a project: seeing the book as individual pictures was looking at it all wrong; the style and order are essential to the meaning. The good from the bad: a photograph that comes with an excuse has failed. The two are stated four spreads apart and are not reconciled.
confounders: applying the excuse test to each image and concluding the set is weak
assuming Carroll offers a method for evaluating a series; he offers only a claim that the unit is different
treating the two principles as compatible without settling the unit of observation

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 3-5 (Ch. 1, 'The Problem with Asking for Feedback' / 'What Is Feedback?')
qa_items.question: Connor and Irizarry argue that the trouble with asking for feedback begins with the word itself, not with the people answering. What do they say "feedback" actually denotes, where do they take that sense from, and what do they say follows from it?
qa_items.answer: They say feedback is nothing more than a reaction or response, and they take the sense directly from the interaction-design idea of a feedback loop, where feedback is the system's noticeable change of state after a user acts. Because the word covers every possible response, a request for feedback constrains nothing about what comes back, and the authors say what returns is an unpredictable mixture: a gut reaction, a list of instructions on what to change, or comments describing how the design differs from what the critic would have made. The consequence they draw is that the sorting work — deciding which of it is usable — falls entirely on the person who asked. Notably they do not prescribe abandoning the word, conceding that giving it up is "damned difficult" and that they use it throughout the book; the remedy is to know which of the three forms you want and shape the request accordingly.
qa_items.support: The authors' own definition and argument, printed pp. 3-5. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism; no measurement of how differently-worded requests perform is offered anywhere.
confounders: reading the complaint as being about rude or unskilled feedback-givers, which is the opposite of the authors' point — their complaint is about the request
assuming they recommend banning the word 'feedback'; they explicitly decline to
confusing their 'feedback loop' derivation with the management-science sense of feedback as performance appraisal

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 5-11 (Ch. 1, 'Three Kinds of Feedback'), restated printed p. 169 (Ch. 7)
qa_items.question: Name the three forms of feedback in this source's taxonomy and state, for each, what the statement is actually about. What single property do the authors say the first two lack?
qa_items.answer: Reaction, direction and critique. A reaction is about the responder's own state — how they felt on seeing the work. A direction is about the responder's preferred solution — what they would do instead. A critique is about the relationship between a specific element of the work and a stated objective, and why that element does or does not serve it. The property the first two lack is the one the authors care about throughout: neither helps you understand whether the design choices made will work toward the product's objectives. Their summary formulation is that reaction and direction "are limited in their ability to help us understand if the design choices we've made might work toward the product's objectives", while critique "is feedback that focuses on exactly that understanding".
qa_items.support: The taxonomy as stated in Ch. 1 and restated in the Ch. 7 summary. Asserted by the authors; no argument is offered that the three forms are exhaustive.
confounders: treating the three as a quality ranking of the same kind of thing rather than three different kinds of statement
assuming reaction and direction are useless — the authors say a reaction tells you something about a subconscious response and a direction may reveal an unstated concern
substituting a positive/negative or constructive/destructive split, which is a different distinction the source explicitly does not use as its primary one

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 9 (Ch. 1, 'Critique: The third form of feedback'), restated printed p. 33 (Ch. 2, 'A Simple Framework for Critique')
qa_items.question: State the three elements the source says good critique is composed of. Which of them is the one most often missing from ordinary design feedback, and why does its absence matter more than it looks?
qa_items.answer: Good critique identifies a specific aspect of the idea or a decision in the design; it relates that aspect or decision to an objective or best practice; and it describes how and why the aspect works to support or not support that objective. The second — naming the objective the judgement is being made against — is the one ordinary feedback almost never supplies, and it is the element that makes the judgement checkable by someone who was not in the room. Without it a statement may still be specific and may still give a reason, but the reason has no external referent, so there is no way for another person to agree or disagree except by preference. The authors demonstrate the decomposition on their own example, splitting it into the clause naming the objective, the clause naming the design choices, and the clause stating that the critic does not believe those choices will be effective and why.
qa_items.support: The three elements as listed at printed p. 9 and again at p. 33. The identification of the second element as the usual omission is drawn from the source's own catalogue of bad critique, where the named defects are missing reasons and missing referents; the source lists the elements without ranking them.
confounders: collapsing the second and third elements — relating to an objective and explaining why are separate requirements here
Catmull's five properties of a good note in Creativity, Inc. cover specificity and not demanding a fix, but contain no requirement to name the objective; do not import the missing element from there
assuming 'best practice' is a weaker substitute for an objective; the source admits it as a legitimate yardstick in its own right

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 5-6 (Ch. 1, 'The first two types of feedback' / 'Why it can be an issue')
qa_items.question: The source describes two varieties of reaction-based feedback, not one. Describe the second, and explain why the authors treat it as a problem even though it sounds like praise.
qa_items.answer: The first variety is the familiar gut reaction: fast, instinctive, driven by the responder's own expectations, desires and values. The second is a reaction driven by the responder's understanding of what they are expected to say — shaped by a cultural sense of the situation or by what they think the presenter wants to hear — and it produces "That's wonderful! Great work!" or "I love what you did with…". The authors' point is that this is not a response to the work at all: it is a response to having been asked for feedback in the first place. It therefore carries no information about any decision in the design, while looking exactly like a favourable judgement. The authors' test for both varieties is a set of questions neither can answer: is the responder representative of the actual audience, are they looking at it as a user would, and does the reaction divulge anything specific about any design decision or its effectiveness.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 5-6; the second variety and the three diagnostic questions are the authors'. The observation that the two varieties are indistinguishable in form is an inference from their own account, not something they state.
confounders: reading it as ordinary flattery or politics rather than as a category of feedback with a stated cause
assuming the authors want positive reactions suppressed; they say elsewhere that reactions are worth understanding, just not usable as iteration guidance
confusing it with the feedback sandwich, where the positives are deliberate rather than reflexive

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 7-8 (Ch. 1, 'Direction' / 'Why it can be an issue')
qa_items.question: A stakeholder says: "Move the balance to the top of the screen and make it larger — I'm suggesting it because I don't think people will notice it where it is." She has given a reason. On this source's account, has she given a critique? Explain precisely what is still missing.
qa_items.answer: No. The authors address this exact case: direction accompanied by an explanation is still direction. The explanation tells the designer what problem the giver believes exists — the authors say "you at least begin to understand the impetus and perhaps the issue she's trying to address" — but it "still does not help you understand how or why the design you have is or is not effective at addressing that problem". What is missing is the analysis of the existing design: nothing has been said about why the current placement fails, only that a different placement is preferred. The finding the designer needs — this element, against this objective, fails for this reason — has been skipped over and replaced by its proposed remedy. The authors are careful that the suggestion may well be a good one; their claim is that at this point it is out of place.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 7-8, where the source distinguishes bare direction from direction with an explanation and holds that both fail the same test. Argument from the authors' stated premises; no evidence is offered about how often reasoned directions turn out to be right.
confounders: treating the presence of any 'because' as sufficient — the source's requirement is a reason about the existing design, not about the proposal
judging it a critique because the reason mentions a plausible user outcome
concluding the suggestion should be rejected; the authors say the direction may be a good idea and is merely misplaced

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 24-25 (Ch. 2, 'The Characteristics of Bad Critique — Incomplete')
qa_items.question: This source defines "actionable" feedback in a narrower and more specific way than the word usually carries. Give its definition, and state the boundary it immediately draws afterwards.
qa_items.answer: Actionable, here, means the designer has enough understanding of what is and is not working, and why, that she can explore alternatives or make other adjustments. It is a property of her understanding, not of the instruction she received. The boundary the authors draw immediately afterwards is that this is different from prescription or direction: "Critique should not tell the designer how to act on something or specifically what changes she should make." So a statement can be fully actionable in this sense while containing no instruction at all, and a detailed instruction can be entirely unactionable in this sense because it leaves the designer unable to explore anything else. The repair the source prescribes for an incomplete critique is to attach the why — "Nobody is going to click on that because the current page design leads the eye down the left side of the screen away from the call-to-action" — not to attach a fix.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 24-25. The definition and the boundary are both stated by the authors in consecutive paragraphs. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism.
confounders: the common industry sense of 'actionable feedback' as feedback specific enough to act on directly, which is what this source excludes
assuming the repair is to make the instruction more detailed
reading the prohibition as absolute; the source concedes elsewhere that some changes are small and obvious

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 33-35 (Ch. 2, 'A Simple Framework for Critique')
qa_items.question: Give the four questions of the source's critique framework in order. What variation in the order does the source explicitly permit, and what does the second question deliberately not care about?
qa_items.answer: What is the objective of the design? What elements of the design are related to the objective? Are those elements effective in achieving the objective? Why or why not? The permitted variation is that the first two may be reversed depending on how the design is being presented. The second question deliberately does not care whether the aspect being analysed was a conscious choice by the designer — the source says so explicitly, "whether the aspect or element is the result of a conscious choice by the designer doesn't matter. We are analyzing the effectiveness of the whole design as it's presented." The fourth question is also more demanding than it sounds: it asks for the result the choice will actually produce and how close that is to the objective, and it admits the case where an element does not achieve the objective on its own but contributes to it in conjunction with other elements.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 33-35, with the four questions also shown as an ordered arrow flow in Figure 2-1 (rendered and inspected for this extraction). The authors call the third question "the crux of critical thinking".
confounders: assuming the order is free; the source fixes it and permits exactly one swap
reading the fourth question as asking for a verdict rather than a predicted result
restricting the second question to intentional decisions, which the source expressly rules out

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 56-57 (Ch. 3, 'Lack of Foundation')
qa_items.question: A team runs regular, well-facilitated critiques and everyone participates, yet the sessions repeatedly appear to reach agreement and then the work that comes back shows people had different ideas of what was decided. What does this source say is most likely wrong, and why would better facilitation not fix it?
qa_items.answer: The source's diagnosis is a missing foundation: the team has not explicitly and jointly agreed what the product's objectives are, so each participant is critiquing against their own. The authors describe this exact symptom — a meeting where everyone seemed to be talking about the same thing and left with their to-dos, and then the work revealed different understandings. The reason facilitation cannot fix it is structural rather than behavioural: critique is a comparison of an element against an objective, so if the objective differs per person the comparisons are not commensurable. The group is not disagreeing about the design at all; it is running several unrelated analyses that happen to be voiced in the same room, and nothing in the conversation surfaces that, because the objective is usually left implicit in each remark. The authors add that when they ask teams what the objectives of the product are, very few people can answer, and those who do rarely give the same answer.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 56-57, plus the Appendix A restatement as "Starting from Disparate Foundations" (printed p. 177). The observation about teams unable to name their objectives is reported from the authors' consulting experience with no count, sample or method — it is the most empirical-sounding statement in the book and it is not a measurement.
confounders: diagnosing a communication or listening problem, which is what the symptom looks like from inside
diagnosing a documentation problem — the authors' own text says agree the objectives, but Kim Goodwin's sidebar warns that writing them down is not the same as sharing them
assuming better note-taking would catch it; the divergence is in the premises, not the record

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 57-58 and 63 (Ch. 3, 'Creating an Effective, Common Foundation')
qa_items.question: Name the four foundational artifacts this source means when it says "objectives", state the single sentence in which it relates them, and give its test for whether a goal is usable.
qa_items.answer: Personas, scenarios, goals and principles. The relating sentence is that the objectives for a product are to reach its goals, for the given audiences (personas), by creating a design with the right behaviours and characteristics (principles), to produce the desired experience when used in the applicable contexts (scenarios). Personas and scenarios supply the setting for the analysis — through whose eyes, with what expectations, in what contexts; goals and principles supply the finish line. The test for a goal is that it must be a desired, measurable outcome correlating to a change in user behaviour, and that binary or output-based goals are to be avoided: adding a "remember me" feature is an output the team either ships or does not, whereas "increase authenticated visits to our site by 15 percent" remains a live test after delivery and can therefore be argued against during design.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 57-58 for the four elements and the relating sentence, p. 63 for the goal test. The example goals in Figure 3-5 (rendered and inspected) are all numeric and outcome-shaped, which is stronger than the prose alone conveys.
confounders: treating the four as documentation deliverables rather than as the yardstick every critique runs against
assuming the source demands quantified goals only; it admits experiential objectives elsewhere (printed p. 10)
including the Mini Creative Brief as a fifth element — it is a container for the four, not one of them

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 63-64 (Ch. 3, 'The end game: goals and principles'), with the negative form at printed p. 165 (Ch. 6, 'Step 4: Critique together')
qa_items.question: A team's design principles are "delightful", "modern" and "fun". Applying this source's own test, what is wrong with them, and what is the test — stated both in its positive and its negative form?
qa_items.answer: They are too broad. The positive form of the test is that a good principle is specific and, by virtue of being specific, eliminates more design ideas than it retains — the source names "fun" and "amusing" as exactly the kind of quality that fails, because every member of a team interprets them differently and none of them rejects any candidate. The negative form appears in Chapter 6 and is the sharper one: "when asking whether design options adhere to a principle, more often the answer should be 'no'." A set of principles that never says no is evidence that the principles are too broad, not that the designs are good. The source's example principles are written instead as first-person constraints with a reason attached — "Be where I am. Don't be just another place I have to go log into" — which is a form the prose does not describe and only the figure carries.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 63-64 for the specificity test and the "fun" counter-example, p. 165 for the negative form. The example principles are in Figure 3-6, rendered and inspected for this extraction.
confounders: judging the principles by whether they describe the brand accurately, which is not the test
assuming the fix is to define each word more precisely; the source's fix is a principle that discriminates, not a glossary
reading 'more often the answer should be no' as a numeric threshold — the source gives none

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 40-42 (Ch. 2, 'Best Practices for Receiving Critique — Return to the foundation')
qa_items.question: In a critique, a comment arrives that you cannot connect to any of the project's objectives. What does this source tell you to do, and what does it say the failure to connect it might mean? Why is that second possibility the interesting one?
qa_items.answer: Try to relate it to the previously agreed objectives, if necessary by asking the giver follow-up questions that do the relating. The source treats both outcomes as informative. If a connection is found, the feedback is now understood and usable. If none can be found, the authors' reading is not that the comment was worthless but that members of the team may hold different views of what the product's objectives are — and they prescribe naming that explicitly, then deciding on the spot whether to resolve it now or table it for a separate conversation. That second possibility is the interesting one because it makes the test bidirectional: a judgement's failure to bind to the stated objectives becomes evidence about the objectives, not only about the judgement. The same aperture appears on the giving side at printed p. 27, where feedback that is neither a best practice nor tied to a stated objective may be revealing an objective or constraint that has not yet been exposed.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 40-42, with the giver-side counterpart at p. 27 and the Appendix A note that a comment unrelatable to the foundation may mean the foundation is incomplete. Argument from the authors' stated premises.
confounders: discarding the comment as off-topic, which is the move the source is arguing against
treating the foundation as fixed and authoritative; the source explicitly allows that it can miss something and that new information can reveal new elements
assuming the divergence must be resolved immediately — the authors leave the resolve-or-table decision to judgement and give no criterion

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 61-62 (Ch. 3, sidebar 'Personas Help Visual Design Discussions, Too' — Kim Goodwin)
qa_items.question: A team has written personas, scenarios, goals and principles, circulated them, and reviewed them in a kickoff meeting. According to the sidebar in this book, what condition may still not be satisfied, and what behaviour does its absence produce?
qa_items.answer: That the criteria are actually shared. Kim Goodwin's sidebar states that evaluation criteria are not truly shared unless everyone both understands them and believes in them, and that teams mistakenly treat "written down somewhere or mentioned in a meeting" as sufficient. The behaviour the absence produces is criteria used as weapons rather than as tools — in her account, interaction designers wielding a persona as a trump card, "Trust us, we did the user research" — which erodes trust rather than settling anything. She attributes the gap to involvement: the visual designer in her story had limited participation in the research and the scenario work, which she notes is sometimes unavoidable on budget grounds but which his teammates could have done more to mitigate. Note that this is Goodwin's contribution, not Connor and Irizarry's own text, and it qualifies their argument rather than restating it.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 61-62, a signed sidebar by Kim Goodwin — a different practitioner's assertion carried inside this book. The evidence is a single coaching anecdote about one three-person team.
confounders: attributing the claim to Connor and Irizarry; their own text argues for establishing and referring back to the foundation and does not raise the belief condition
reading it as a communication problem fixable by better documentation, which is the position it contradicts
missing her closing caution — that using personas and goals 'like hammers to end arguments' backfires, which cuts against the return-to-the-foundation prescription the authors give elsewhere

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 58-59 (Ch. 3, 'The background: personas and scenarios')
qa_items.question: What two specific cautions does this source give about writing personas, and what does it say is wrong with the second thing it warns against?
qa_items.answer: First, state characteristics explicitly rather than hinting at them through narrative detail: the authors ask what it tells the team that a persona has two dogs and enjoys Saturdays in the park, and say not to use flowery stories or superfluous details to imply characteristics or behaviours. Second, do not get hung up on demographics. What is wrong with demographics is that they are used as stereotypes for behaviours and characteristics — the authors' example is assuming a millennial persona must be good with technology — and they note counter-cases in both directions from their own acquaintance. Their positive instruction is to learn the real characteristics of the audience and state them explicitly, so that references to the persona later in the project do not have to be interpreted. They also state a format preference: half-page, succinct personas listing main points that can be read at a glance, rather than deeper narrative ones.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 58-59. Practitioner preference and assertion; the format preference is explicitly labelled by the authors as "our preference".
confounders: assuming the objection to demographics is about fairness or bias in a social sense; the stated objection is that they are unreliable proxies for behaviour
reading the brevity preference as a rule rather than as the authors' stated preference

extending the caution to scenarios unchanged — the scenario caution is different: base them on real observations and make sure included thoughts and emotions are ones the design is meant to address or produce

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 113-114 (Ch. 5, 'Avoid Problem Solving')
qa_items.question: Why does this source hold that someone proposing a fix during a critique damages the session, beyond simply using up time? Give the mechanism, including what it says happens across the rest of the room.
qa_items.answer: Because proposing a solution means that person has switched from analytical to creative thinking, and the source's premise is that a brain does not consciously do both at once — it divides resources and actively switches. When that switch happens in public, the rest of the room scatters: some participants are still analysing the original design, some are analysing the new idea, some are generating alternatives of their own, and some are in a fourth process, simply trying to comprehend what was just proposed, with individuals jumping between them. The authors' summary is that "the coordination becomes lost and everyone heads in different mental directions", and that the paramount thing is to keep everyone in the same mental process. The practical cost is stated separately and additionally: veering into problem solving on item two of five means items three to five are never reached.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 113-114. The cognitive premise about simultaneous analytical and creative thinking is asserted without citation or evidence anywhere in the book, and it carries the weight of the rule; it should be read as the authors' working model.
confounders: explaining it as rudeness, dominance or derailing — the source's account is cognitive, not social
assuming the source thinks the rule can be enforced by willpower; it says explicitly 'we can't' prevent a room from doing it
reading it as a ban on ever exploring solutions — the source permits deliberately switching the whole room to exploration

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 114 (Ch. 5, 'But it's too damned difficult to not solve problems')
qa_items.question: You are facilitating. Half the room has become absorbed in solving one problem in the design and will not return to the analysis, and how it gets solved would change what is worth analysing in the rest. What does this source tell you to do — and how does that differ from what it tells you to do when one person merely keeps elaborating a solution?
qa_items.answer: In this case the source tells you to pause or postpone the remainder of the critique and switch the room right then to exploring solutions. That is the third of its three responses and it is a permitted exit from the analysis, offered precisely for the two conditions described: everyone is stuck on one issue, or the impact of how it might be solved brings further critique of the current design into question. It differs from the single-elaborator case, where you understand the issue already and the instruction is to get that person to hold the idea for a future discussion focused on exploration while the analysis continues. And both differ from the case where someone has jumped to a solution without naming the issue at all, where the instruction is to ask questions that identify the issue and relate it to the objectives. What is common to all three is the stated priority: keep everyone in the same mental process.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 114, where the source gives three distinct responses for three distinct situations. Practitioner prescription; no reported outcome from applying any of the three.
confounders: applying the parking-lot response universally, which is the response for one elaborating individual, not for a stuck room
treating the rule against problem solving as absolute and pressing on with the analysis
assuming the switch means the critique has failed; the source presents it as a legitimate facilitation decision

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 115 (Ch. 5, 'Don't Rush to Make Decisions on the Changes to Be Made')
qa_items.question: State what this source says the output of a critique should be, and the retrospective diagnostic it attaches to that claim. Why does it say deciding during the session costs you something?
qa_items.answer: The output should be a set of new observations and understandings about the design and whether it is meeting the objectives set for it — explicitly not a list of specific changes for the designer to go back and make. The diagnostic follows immediately and is checkable after the fact: "If a list of changes is coming out of a critique session, problem solving is taking the place of analysis." The cost of deciding during the session is that most insights admit numerous possible responses, so committing to one while the analysis is still running means the choice is made on less information than the same choice would have afterwards — "it's likely that we'll miss opportunities for stronger ideas or make premature decisions that cause more problems down the road." The delay also serves the maker: she gets time to digest the feedback against the goals, principles, scenarios and personas and to follow up on specific points. Exploration is not cancelled, only sequenced after the analysis.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 115, with the Appendix A restatement "Critique is not a list of revisions to be carried out like a short-order cook" at printed p. 178. Argument from the authors' premises; the source concedes some changes are small and obvious and gives no criterion for how small.
confounders: assuming the rule forbids acting quickly on anything; Adam's own follow-up routine starts by fixing typos and alignment
reading the diagnostic backwards — a change list is evidence about the session, not evidence that the changes are wrong
conflating 'no decisions' with 'no conclusions'; the session is meant to produce findings

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 162-163 (Ch. 6, 'Dealing with Directive Feedback — Step 1')
qa_items.question: You asked a stakeholder for feedback and she has sent back her own mockup of how the screen should look. How does this source read that act, and what does it say the first thing you should do is — and why that first?
qa_items.answer: The source reads it, in most cases it has encountered or observed, as an articulation failure rather than an insult: the person found it difficult to articulate everything she wanted to say and thought showing would be easier. The authors turn the design community's own maxim back on it — "Show me. Don't tell me" is the mantra designers use to describe the inefficiency of verbal description, so a stakeholder reaching for a picture is doing what designers themselves recommend. The first thing to do is to let your own reaction pass, and the reason is that the source applies its own reaction discipline to you: at that moment you are having an impulse and are not thinking critically yet, so anything you do now is reactive feedback of the kind the book spends five chapters displacing. The authors do not claim the motive is always benign — they say the later steps will reveal whether it is personally motivated, and that even then it is worth understanding, because you never know where a valuable insight might come from.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 162-163. The reframing is the authors' own reading of situations they have encountered; no count is given. Kim Goodwin's sidebar reaches the same explanation independently at printed pp. 61-62, which is corroboration inside the book by a different practitioner, not external evidence.
confounders: treating it as a boundary violation or a challenge to authority to be pushed back on
accepting the mockup and implementing it, which the source says would leave the diagnosis unstated
assuming benign intent is established rather than assumed — the authors recommend the assumption as a stance, not as a finding

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 163-165 (Ch. 6, 'Step 3: Critique the directive feedback' and 'Step 4: Critique together')
qa_items.question: Continuing from a stakeholder's alternative mockup: the source gives a two-stage procedure. What is the pivotal move that turns the meeting from a contest into a critique, and what is the one question about her design that people usually forget to ask?
qa_items.answer: The pivotal move is the comparison target. Instead of comparing the two designs to each other, compare both against what the team previously agreed mattered — the personas, scenarios, goals and principles. The source says this "helps remove some of the my-idea-versus-your-idea atmosphere" and refocuses the conversation on what the right decisions are for the product; without an external referent, a two-design comparison can only be settled by preference or authority.
