The intended output is stated precisely: a critique of your own original design, constructed using her design or change list as a discussion tool. The forgotten question is about what she did not change — ask specifically about the things she is not recommending be altered, and the similarities between her design and yours, and whether she kept them for the same reasons you made them. The first stage, before any of this, is private: five questions asked of the proposal on your own, with the notes kept to yourself.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 163-165. The five private questions and the comparison-against-the-foundation move are both stated by the authors. Practitioner prescription with a stated mechanism; no reported outcome.
confounders: going into the meeting to defend the original design, which the source treats as the failure mode
comparing the two designs feature by feature, which is the move the source is replacing
skipping the private stage — the source is explicit that the notes stay private, which is a deliberate exception to its own transparency norm

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 165 (Ch. 6, 'Step 4: Critique together')
qa_items.question: Halfway through comparing two designs against the project's goals and principles, you find the goals and principles are not helping to settle anything. This source reads that as a finding. About what, and what does it prescribe?
qa_items.answer: About the goals and principles, not about the designs. The source says this can be a sign that the goals and principles you set are too broad, and that the conversation is the chance to refine them: "Remember, when asking whether design options adhere to a principle, more often the answer should be 'no'." It gives a matching test for goals — if, trying to critique against a particular goal, you find you have no way to meaningfully measure whether it has been achieved, the goal needs refining. The diagnostic runs backwards through the method: the criteria are under test by the critiques they are supposed to enable. Where no goals or principles exist at all, the authors treat the same conversation as the occasion to generate some on the fly, using what you learn about which aspects matter most to the other person and how that compares with any research already done.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 165, with the positive form of the principle test at pp. 63-64. Practitioner assertion; the source gives no threshold and no test for the opposite failure of over-narrow criteria.
confounders: concluding the two designs are equally good
concluding critique does not work here and falling back on authority
assuming criteria are fixed inputs to a critique rather than something the critique can test

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 25 (Ch. 2, 'The Characteristics of Bad Critique — Preferential')
qa_items.question: Preferential feedback is a familiar complaint. What does this source say happens to it that makes it more than an isolated annoyance, and under what condition?
qa_items.answer: The condition is that the person with the preference is also in a position of approval. The source says that in that situation the team begins, consciously or subconsciously, to prioritise that individual's tastes alongside or above project and user goals, even where the two conflict. The preference stops being a bad comment in one meeting and becomes a standing criterion the team optimises against — and because it was never written down, it is never subject to the test that written objectives are subject to. The authors' illustration is deliberately absurd, a website design discarded because the colour scheme reminded a stakeholder of a Christmas sweater given to him by his ex-wife, and they concede it "might seem ridiculous"; their claim is that milder versions are common. What the source does not supply is a way to tell a preference from a legitimate but unarticulated expert judgement at the moment it is voiced.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 25. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism and an acknowledged-absurd illustration; no observation of teams drifting toward an approver's taste is reported.
confounders: treating preferential feedback as simply unhelpful, which is the ordinary complaint and not the source's addition
assuming the remedy is to overrule the approver; the source's remedies are to ask which persona, scenario, goal or principle the comment relates to
confusing this with the HiPPO rule, which is about weight given during collection rather than about taste becoming a criterion

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 90-91 (Ch. 4, 'How Often Should You Critique?')
qa_items.question: This source retracts a position its own author took publicly. What was it, what is the position now, and what cues does it offer in place of a number?
qa_items.answer: Asked at a talk whether there is such a thing as too much critique, Adam had answered "No. Not at all!" and gone on at length; the authors write that they wish they could find that audience member and apologise. The position now is that there absolutely is such a thing. In place of a number they give four cues: the advancement between critiques becomes so small that progress feels stalled; critiques circle, with the changes made from the collected insights not advancing the design; formal critiques are required so frequently that the team cannot push the design forward enough between them; and critique begins to be used as a validation mechanism because the team or the designer lacks confidence in the ideas. They decline to give any threshold, calling the judgement "an innate sense or sensitivity that a team or individuals develop over time" and advising teams to try different frequencies, ask each other how it feels, and adjust.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 90-91. Explicitly a self-correction of the authors' earlier enthusiasm, offered with no measurement and no threshold. The fourth cue is a motive rather than an observable.
confounders: assuming a book advocating critique would not bound its own recommendation
supplying a cadence the source does not give — it refuses numbers here as it does for the timing window
reading the fourth cue as being about the design's quality; it is about why the sessions are being held

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 147 (Ch. 6, 'Preventing Surprises from Quiet Participants')
qa_items.question: Why does this source treat a quiet participant as a specific risk rather than as a neutral outcome? Describe the pattern it names, and the limit it puts on chasing them.
qa_items.answer: Because the judgement is not removed, only delayed past the point where it can be used. The pattern is that the person shares the thought with someone else instead — a teammate or a manager — and the comment then travels person to person until it reaches you days or even weeks later, when you may no longer be able to act on it. The source gives two typical causes: feeling overwhelmed by the process and subject matter, or fear of saying something that would be considered wrong. The remedies are to look for who is not saying much, to ask them for feedback directly if necessary, and to frame the request around their specific expertise or skillset, which makes contributing easier. The limit is explicit: do not keep pressing. If you sense the person simply has not found anything useful to say, leave it — they may just be quiet or shy — and try a one-to-one conversation after the session instead.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 147, plus the corresponding session rule at printed p. 112 that non-participation leads to concerns being expressed afterwards when it is too late to act. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism.
confounders: reading silence as agreement, which the source separately warns against in its material on cultural norms
assuming the remedy is to require everyone to speak; the source caps the pressure explicitly
attributing quietness to disengagement — the source's stated causes are being overwhelmed and fearing a wrong answer

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 66-67 (Ch. 3, 'Personal Barriers to Critique — Additional Cultural Influences')
qa_items.question: This source names a bias that acts on the supply of judgement itself, and a matching reading error. Describe both, and say why the reading error is hard to detect.
qa_items.answer: On the supply side: people raised on the principle that if you have nothing nice to say you should say nothing hold back honest critique they fear will upset the recipient — or, the authors say, worse, validate a direction they do not believe in. On the reading side: in communities where challenging or speaking up is seen as rude, silence is not agreement, and participants who assume it is will record a consensus that does not exist; the converse error is also named, that people used to being straightforward can be read as combative. The reading error is hard to detect because the filter is invisible — the observations were removed before they were voiced, so nothing in the room signals their absence. Adam's own account is of a project with a team from India where he repeatedly found afterwards that the alignment he thought he had seen in meetings was not there, and that where he thought there had been disagreement there had been none. The prescription is to say before the session that stepping outside these norms is acceptable, and to clarify such gaps as soon as they are noticed.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 66-67. Explicitly culturally bounded; the source generalises about cultures and its illustration is one person's recollection of one engagement. The related structural barrier — withholding out of intimidation or after repeatedly being told "no" — is at printed p. 55.
confounders: treating it as a translation or language problem; the source's cases are about norms and body language, not vocabulary
assuming the prescription detects the filter in progress — it only pre-empts it, and the source offers no in-session detection
reading the source as making a claim about any particular national culture; it names one anecdote and generalises loosely

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 111-112 (Ch. 5, 'Everyone Is Equal')
qa_items.question: The "everyone is equal" rule is often read as a claim that seniority should not affect decisions. That is not what this source says. What does it say, and what does it explicitly permit — and when?
qa_items.answer: The source concedes that an organisation may legitimately make its decisions on what its leaders think. What it denies is that seniority makes an observation more accurate: "it isn't inherently true that their opinions are more accurate just because they're executives." The rule therefore governs the weight given during collection, not during decision, and the authors' instruction is to keep the two separate and sequenced — "we want to keep that separate, and hopefully after a critique." What is explicitly permitted, and when, is stated plainly: as the collected feedback is reviewed afterwards, an individual's expertise and experience may be taken into consideration rather than only their position in the hierarchy. The harm the rule guards against is suppression: participants sensing inequality either stay quiet or go along with what someone else said, and the group loses information it will not know it lost.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 111-112, with the later weighting permitted explicitly on p. 112 and reappearing at p. 138 as "source of the feedback" among four prioritisation considerations. The authors concede the rule is hard to implement depending on culture.
confounders: reading it as flat decision-making or consensus governance, which the source does not claim
concluding expertise is irrelevant; it is permitted, just later
assuming HiPPO refers to the executive rather than to the weight the room gives their opinion

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 155-157 and 161 (Ch. 6, 'Receiving Unsolicited Feedback' and 'Remember, this applies to positive feedback as well')
qa_items.question: Why does this source insist that a positive reaction needs the same treatment as a negative one? Give its argument, and the additional reason it gives for distrusting praise specifically.
qa_items.answer: Because usability of feedback is a property of its structure, not of its sign. "I love it!" names no aspect of the work and relates it to no objective, so it cannot tell you what to keep, what to expand or what to change — exactly the defect that makes an unexplained rejection useless. The authors put it as a question: someone saying "I like this" might make us feel good, "but the question remains, what does he like?" The additional reason for distrusting praise is that people will often offer positive feedback because they do not want to hurt someone's feelings, not because they think the work is heading in the right direction. The prescribed handling is identical for both signs: thank the person, make sure you understand what is being communicated, review it against your known objectives, and follow up with questions — what do they love about it, why, and how does it apply to the goals, personas, scenarios and principles.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 156-157 and 161. Argument from the authors' own definition of critique; the claim that people praise to avoid hurting feelings is asserted and connects to their culturally bounded material at pp. 66-67 rather than to any observation.
confounders: assuming positive feedback needs no scrutiny because it costs nothing to accept
treating this as the sandwich argument; that is about deliberate framing, this is about unexamined praise
concluding the source distrusts all positive feedback — it argues at length for discussing genuine strengths

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 22 and 37-38 (Ch. 2, 'The Two Sides of Critique' and 'Asking for feedback without listening')
qa_items.question: This source describes a way in which a team's supply of useful feedback can decay over time. Describe the loop, and name the two distinct triggers it gives for it.
qa_items.answer: The loop is that responding to requests for judgement is voluntary, so when responding is seen to be pointless, people stop. The source names two triggers. The first is on the recipient's side in the moment: asking for feedback without being ready to listen — the critics pick up on the disinterest, feel uninterested in sharing their thoughts, and over time become less inclined to participate in these kinds of conversations at all. The second is downstream and slower: if discussions repeatedly fail to produce action and changes, the desire to participate wanes. The authors are careful about what they are claiming for a single session — "everything said in a critique is not going to produce a discrete modification to the design" — and locate the requirement at the level of the pattern: participants should feel overall that the discussion they contributed to will play a role in improving the design, not merely in changing it.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 22 for the action trigger and pp. 37-38 for the listening trigger. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism; the decay is never quantified or observed in the book.
confounders: assuming the fix is to act on every piece of feedback, which the authors explicitly do not require
collapsing the two triggers into one — one is about attention in the room, the other about outcomes over months
reading it as a morale claim rather than a claim about the supply of information

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 118-120 (Ch. 5, 'Avoid Ta-Da Moments')
qa_items.question: You are running a critique on Thursday. This source says showing the work for the first time in the room is a mistake. Give its reason, and state the two constraints it puts on what you send beforehand and the one thing it says you are not trying to achieve by sending it.
qa_items.answer: The reason is temporal: critical thought takes time. Participants need to think through the design, determine the effects they believe it will have, and compare those effects to the objectives — so a room asked to do that on the spot can only supply responses it has not thought through, which is reactive feedback by construction. Send the designs a couple of days ahead, under two constraints: limit what you send to only the aspects you plan to discuss, because sending more invites people to fixate on parts that are irrelevant to the session; and preface them with a few clear notes on what the critique will focus on and what you expect from participants. What you are not trying to achieve is participants arriving with their feedback ready — the source is explicit about this. The aim is to jump-start the critical thinking process before the conversation begins.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 118-120. Practitioner prescription with a stated mechanism; the authors concede that some people will not look at what was sent and that "no matter which route we choose, there will always be people who do their own thing".
confounders: sending the whole design for context, which the source specifically warns against
asking people to come with their feedback prepared, which the source explicitly says it is not doing
concluding you cannot critique at all if nothing could be sent — the source's fallback is to pace the opening slower and start with small, discrete aspects

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 120 (Ch. 5, 'Avoid Ta-Da Moments')
qa_items.question: You sent the designs ahead as instructed, and someone has replied by email with a list of changes — the exact outcome you were warned about. What does this source tell you to do, both now and in the session?
qa_items.answer: Reply acknowledging the feedback, tell the sender you have noted it and that you plan to address it in the critique session. Then in the session, revisit that person's feedback and ask whether it is still relevant now that more of the design has been discussed. The source reports two outcomes from doing this: either the individual understands why the decisions were made and rescinds the feedback, or it gets discussed further and more understanding is gained. The authors' stated reason for handling it this way is that it signals the feedback is not being dismissed while still keeping the conversation facilitated rather than fragmented across email. They are candid that this happened to them — Adam sent the sample notification email reproduced in the book and got feedback back in reply — and that the situation is not ideal, but treat it as an opportunity to improve facilitation rather than as a reason to stop pre-sending.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 120. Practitioner prescription; the two reported outcomes are the authors' experience, not a measured distribution.
confounders: answering the change list on email, which reintroduces the channel problem the source describes at pp. 43-44
ignoring it until the session without acknowledging, which the source says would read as dismissal
concluding the pre-send was a mistake — the source treats this as a known cost of a practice it still recommends

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 121-122 (Ch. 5, 'Present Your Work Quickly and Efficiently')
qa_items.question: Most people presenting work for critique try to explain every decision up front. This source says to do the opposite. Give both reasons it offers, and the rule it gives for choosing what to say instead.
qa_items.answer: The first reason is that pre-empting every question overwhelms participants and eats the meeting's time; the authors read the over-explanation as an attempt to foreclose questioning at all — "it's as if we're trying to avoid the potential for questions." The second is the more interesting one: when the details arrive in answer to questions, they are more closely tied to the participants' own insights and questions, so the explanation lands where someone actually needed it. The rule for what to say instead is to focus on what is not obvious or cannot easily be seen — participants do not need to be told that the navigation is at the top of the page — and the authors' usual way of doing that is to present the design from a user's perspective. Give enough for the team to understand how the design is intended to work, no more, and if you feel the pace ran fast, say so and invite questions.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 121-122. This interlocks deliberately with the giving-side advice at printed p. 26, where the source says the presenter "likely hasn't explained everything. Actually… hopefully he hasn't." Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism.
confounders: assuming the aim is to save time; the authors give the tying-to-questions reason as the more important one
reading it as a licence to present badly or vaguely — the requirement is that the team understand how the design is intended to work
conflating it with the constraints caution, which is a specific case with its own reasoning

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 122-124 (Ch. 5, 'Be Careful When Talking About Constraints')
qa_items.question: A legacy system forced a compromise you are not happy with. Should you explain the constraint when you present? What does this source say, what is its reasoning, and what single exception does it grant?
qa_items.answer: Not up front, in general. The source's reasoning is about how it is received: your motive for mentioning the constraint is usually that it was frustrating and forced a decision you consider less than ideal, and participants often hear that as an excuse or as casting blame, with a negative effect on the tone and energy of the discussion. The prescription is to let the constraint surface through a question about why a choice was made, word it matter-of-factly rather than as blame, and if needed set up separate time for it; in some cases to defer it entirely until after the critique, following up with the person whose insight bears on it and bringing in someone who can explain the constraint and how it might be worked around. The single exception is where the constraint was discussed with the group in a previous conversation and you are presenting your solution to it — then it is part of the context the team needs, with the same caution about wording.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 122-124. Practitioner assertion about how disclosures land; no observation of differently-framed constraint disclosures is reported. The exception is narrow and is the only one granted.
confounders: assuming transparency is always better and stating all constraints up front
concealing the constraint entirely, which the source does not advise — it moves the disclosure, it does not suppress it
generalising the exception to any constraint the team already knows about; the source's exception is specifically about presenting the solution to a previously discussed constraint

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 126-128 (Ch. 5, 'Defining the Critique Scope and Goals')
qa_items.question: This source defines the scope of a critique as two things, not one. What are they, and what does the second one buy you that naming the components alone would not?
qa_items.answer: The scope is the identification of the components of the design the team will be analysing AND the objectives against which they will be analysed. Naming only the components leaves each participant free to bring their own yardstick, which is the condition the source identifies as producing unusable sessions: participants analysing different aspects against their own criteria. Fixing the objective too is what makes the resulting judgements comparable to one another. The source's examples are of the pair: one session focused on critiquing visual styles against a particular set of design principles, another on a specific sequence of screens against the relevant scenario and goals. Having set the pair, you also gain a defined place to steer back to when the conversation leaves it — with anything outside noted for a separate discussion rather than dropped.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 126-127. Practitioner definition with a stated mechanism. The four default session goals that follow from a scope are on p. 127.
confounders: treating scope as an agenda or a list of screens, which is the half the source says is insufficient
assuming out-of-scope comments should be shut down; the source says note them and plan additional discussions
conflating critique scope with product scope — the source distinguishes them when discussing scope creep at p. 35

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 127-128 (Ch. 5, 'Defining the Critique Scope and Goals' — reverse planning)
qa_items.question: A usability study on a new digital claims-filing flow is scheduled in a few weeks. Using this source's reverse planning method, derive what you should critique now and why — and state the three steps of the method in the order it gives them.
qa_items.answer: Reverse planning runs: start from what actions you want to be able to take after the conversation; ask what questions must be answered in the critique to take them; and let those questions tell you which aspects of the design to present and focus on. Applied to the source's own worked case: because a usability study is coming, the action you want afterwards is to have the prototype be the best available reflection of the process and experience before it is tested. Since there is time to iterate before the study, a logical scope is the scenarios that use the new claims process. The goals the source derives are to identify the aspects that do not support the desired experience; to identify the aspects that most effectively produce it, so they can perhaps be expanded; and to identify where there is the most question or disagreement among the team, so the usability study can take those into account and perhaps build them into its plan. That third goal is the one usually missed: disagreement inside the team is treated as an input to the study's design.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 127-128, which is the source's own worked example. Practitioner method; no reported outcome from running it.
confounders: planning forward from what is ready to show, which is what reverse planning replaces
scoping to the whole application because the study will cover the whole application
omitting the disagreement goal — treating internal disagreement as noise rather than as something a study can be pointed at

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 128-129 (Ch. 5, 'Implementing Active Listening')
qa_items.question: What does this source mean by active listening, what does it say the technique verifies, and which follow-up question does it single out as particularly effective when your restatement turns out to be wrong?
qa_items.answer: Replying to a piece of feedback by repeating it back as you have understood it, so the person who gave it can confirm whether your understanding matches what they meant. The stated reason is that vocabulary and understanding of terminology vary among participants, so a piece of feedback cannot be taken at face value as meaning the same thing to everyone. What it verifies is that the words were understood — not that the judgement is correct, which the source does not claim. When the restatement is wrong, the source singles out asking what would happen if the thing were left as it is: the authors say this prompts the participant to describe the effect on the user or the behaviours and actions that are undesirable, which can then be related to the product's objectives. When the restatement is confirmed, the next move is to go into specifics — in their news-feed example, asking what in the current treatment gives it that prominence: placement, type size, something else.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 128-129, including the source's worked dialogue. Practitioner technique with a stated mechanism.
confounders: assuming the restatement establishes that the feedback is right
treating the technique as a politeness device rather than as verification
missing that the source's own worked dialogue ends with the product owner proposing a solution, which the authors do not flag despite their rule against it

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 133-134 (Ch. 5, 'Taking Notes')
qa_items.question: This source rejects the common practice of participants taking their own notes and sharing them afterwards. Why, and what does the alternative buy that a good private record would not? What second, different record does it recommend keeping?
qa_items.answer: Because each person's notes are their own interpretation of what was discussed, and merging notes from a group is confusing and time-consuming. The alternative — one designated note-taker recording where everyone in the discussion can see what is being captured — buys something a private record cannot: participants can look at exactly what is being written and question or clarify it if it does not match their understanding, at the moment it is written and while the speaker is still present. It puts the record itself under the same confirmation loop as active listening. The second, different record is private: notes on how people participated during the session, kept unobtrusively because taking them publicly "would be pretty awkward", and used afterwards to see which facilitation techniques worked, who engaged and who did not, and who to invite to future critiques.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 133-134. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism; the claim that merging notes is confusing is the authors' experience, not a comparison.
confounders: assuming the point is completeness of the record; the point is that the interpretation is checkable while the speaker is present
reading the tools mentioned (an easel pad, Acrobat, InVision) as the requirement — the requirement is visibility during capture
conflating the two records; the participation notes are explicitly not public

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 134-135 (Ch. 5, 'Using Third-Party Facilitators')
qa_items.question: A team new to critique is offered an experienced facilitator from outside the project. What does this source say they gain, what does it say they lose, and what does it recommend over time?
qa_items.answer: They gain a neutral party who guides the conversation and keeps it in scope without contributing feedback, which frees the designer to capture notes, present, clarify points and answer questions. What they lose is specific and is the more interesting half: the designer is the person who will act on the insights and therefore the person best placed to know where clarification is needed and where the focus should shift, while a facilitator unfamiliar with the design decisions or the everyday workings of the project "might not be able to pick up on when something that is useful has been shared, or how to guide reactive or directive feedback to a place of being useful." The practical symptom is a lot of back-and-forth between designer and facilitator during the session. The recommendation over time is that as the team becomes comfortable with critique it should take on the facilitation itself.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 134-135. Practitioner assertion of a trade-off; no comparison of sessions run by insiders and outsiders is reported.
confounders: assuming neutrality is unambiguously good, which is the position the source complicates
reading the recommendation as against outside facilitators generally; the source says they help while a team is starting
attributing the loss to the facilitator's skill rather than to their lack of project knowledge

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 135-136 (Ch. 5, 'Having the Designer Present')
qa_items.question: Designs are circulated and the team is asked to send feedback in a few days; the designer is not in the loop. What does this source say every insight produced that way rests on, and what mitigation does it prescribe when the designer genuinely cannot attend?
qa_items.answer: Assumptions — all of them. The source's claim is that without the designer present, the people giving critique are forced to assume why certain decisions were made and cannot check, and the recipient inherits insights whose premises are unknown: "All the insights shared are based on assumptions, which is a shaky foundation upon which to base our iterations and improvement." The authors dramatise it with two lines a participant might think — that they could ask if she were here, and that they cannot know whether their critique is right because there is no one to state the goals or the problems being solved. The mitigation, where attendance is genuinely impossible, is the same one they prescribe for asynchronous channels generally: note in your feedback the assumption you are making, so the designer can first check whether it matches her actual objectives. They accept the cost explicitly — "there might be some wasted feedback, but that is one of the trade-offs."
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 135-136, connecting to the channel argument at pp. 43-44. Argument from the authors' premises; the source says "whenever possible", which is weaker than a prohibition.
confounders: reading it as a rule against any absentee review; the authors concede such situations occur and give a mitigation
assuming the problem is missing context that better documentation would supply — the missing thing is the ability to ask
treating stated assumptions as resolving the problem rather than as labelling it

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 137-138 (Ch. 5, 'Review the Findings')
qa_items.question: After a critique, this source describes turning notes into work. What is the reframing step, why does it matter to the book's central distinction, and what does the source say about the prioritisation that follows?
qa_items.answer: The reframing step converts each note into an exploration rather than a change: "The news feed is too prominent, because…" becomes "Explore options for decreasing the prominence of the newsfeed…". It matters because it carries the book's central distinction past the end of the session — the to-do that leaves the room is an instruction to explore, not an instruction to change, which keeps the option space open for the same reason the session refused to produce a change list. About the prioritisation that follows, the source is unusually candid: four considerations are offered — relevancy to the product's objectives, immediacy from the project plan, amount of agreement among participants, and the source of the feedback and that person's expertise — and the authors then add, in their own parenthesis, "(As Adam says, this is completely unscientific.)" It is one practitioner's routine, and they say it changes with every project depending on team, culture and timeline.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 137-138. The reframing example and the four considerations are the authors'; the unscientific label is their own. Adam's routine also begins by fixing typos, copy-paste errors and small alignment issues before anything is reframed.
confounders: treating the four considerations as a method the source stands behind, which its own parenthesis disclaims
assuming the agreement heuristic is safe — the source offers no protection against it amplifying a shared blind spot
missing that the source-of-feedback consideration deliberately reintroduces the weighting that the 'everyone is equal' rule excluded during collection

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 138 (Ch. 5, 'Review the Findings', step 4)
qa_items.question: Of the four steps in the source's follow-up routine, which one concerns the items you are NOT going to act on, and what specifically does it require you to do? What is its stated reason?
qa_items.answer: The fourth step. Go through the prioritised list and determine which items will not be addressed — the source is explicit that "just because something is said in a critique does not mean that something will change in the design as a result of it" — and, for those, note why. The stated reason is practical and forward-looking: "I need to be ready to answer why it wasn't changed when it comes up in future discussions." The effect is that a declined item becomes a recorded decision rather than a silent omission, so it can be defended or revisited instead of being re-raised indefinitely. The source pairs this with a related discipline earlier in the follow-up: pull the open questions and assumptions raised in the session into a separate list, share them, and assign responsibility for chasing specific items.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 137-138. Practitioner routine, presented as one person's approach rather than as a method.
confounders: assuming every collected item must be acted on
recording the decision but not the reason, which is the half the source emphasises
conflating declined items with the open-questions list, which is a different artifact for a different purpose

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 125-126 (Ch. 5, sidebar 'The Facade of Authority' — Brad Nunnally)
qa_items.question: A facilitator asks a room of senior stakeholders to close their laptops and is refused. What does the sidebar in this book say that reveals, and what does it prescribe instead of personal authority?
qa_items.answer: It reveals that the facilitator never had authority to lose. Brad Nunnally's sidebar argues that taking the facilitator role confers no real authority — it is "only as strong as your personality and overall social presence", and "the true owners of the room are the participants of the session". In his own account, a wisecrack acknowledging he had no authority ended any prospect of compliance, and the design studio that followed produced shallow rounds of critique and no group consensus on direction or priority. What he prescribes instead is to become a group leader rather than an authority figure, and to vest authority in external artifacts: an outline and agenda shared in advance, which establish "a social contract between you, the facilitator, and the group of participants"; and a timetable reviewed with the group at the start, which "allows time to be the authority in the room, which you the facilitator are simply enforcing." The general form is that the more external artifacts you can use as sources of authority, the easier the conversation is to manage.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 125-126, a signed sidebar by Brad Nunnally — a different practitioner's assertion carried inside this book. The evidence is a single recounted session, and the causal chain from the laptop exchange to the absent consensus is the narrator's own reading.
confounders: attributing it to Connor and Irizarry, whose own chapter says it is the facilitator's job to see the rules are adhered to
concluding the fix is a more assertive facilitator, which is what the sidebar argues against
reading the agenda as an organisational convenience rather than as a transfer of authority away from the person

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 130-131 (Ch. 5, 'Adding Simple Structures: Round Robin and Quotas')
qa_items.question: Describe Round Robin and Quotas as this source defines them, and state the cost it attaches to both and the advice that follows from that cost.
qa_items.answer: Round Robin is the facilitator going around the room in a specific, repeatable order, calling on and collecting feedback from each participant — which removes the question of who speaks first, reinforces that everyone should participate, and gives people predictability about when their turn comes. Quotas set a number of things each participant should bring, often two that are not working and one that is, with the formula varied to see what works. The cost the source attaches is social rather than analytical: some groups find these structures annoying because they seem too basic, or, as the authors have heard, "too grade-school". The advice that follows is to hold them in reserve — wait until a team clearly has difficulty getting a critique started before proposing them — and to note that Round Robin can be run without announcing it, kept by the facilitator as a private structure. They also advise against using Round Robin for a whole session, since it does not fit a natural flow, though it works at the end to catch what was not said.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 130-131. Practitioner technique with a stated cost; no evidence is offered that either structure changes what is said, only that it gets a stalled group talking.
confounders: adopting them as defaults for every session, which the source advises against
assuming the cost is that the feedback gets worse; the stated cost is that participants resent the format
reading Quotas as a rule that criticism must outnumber praise — the formula is meant to be varied

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 132-133 (Ch. 5, 'Putting on the Thinking Hats (Lens-Based Analysis)')
qa_items.question: What is the constraint this source adds to lens-based analysis that makes it a focusing device rather than a role-play exercise? What does it say teams may do beyond de Bono's six hats?
qa_items.answer: The constraint is simultaneity: when using the Six Thinking Hats, team members all wear the same colour hat at the same time. That is what keeps everyone analysing the design through the same lens and keeps the conversation focused — if each person picked their own, the technique would just relabel the fragmentation it is supposed to cure. Beyond de Bono's six, the source says teams can devise their own lenses to fit their context, and gives the example of using each persona as a lens: analysing the design for a particular scenario in the context of one persona's needs, expectations and behaviours before moving on to another. The method itself is Edward de Bono's and is credited to him; the same-lens constraint and the own-lenses suggestion are how this source puts it to work.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 132-133. The Six Thinking Hats method is attributed by the source to Edward de Bono and his book of that name; the framing here is the authors'.
confounders: assigning different hats to different people, which is the common misuse and the opposite of what the source says
assuming the six hats are the source's own contribution
treating the red hat as an invitation to preferential critique — in de Bono's scheme as the source describes it, it is a bounded slot for feelings, hunches, fears, likes and dislikes

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 117 (Ch. 5, 'Who Should We Include?') and printed p. 78 (Ch. 4, 'Start Small')
qa_items.question: How many people does this source say can hold a single critique conversation, what is its reasoning about numbers generally, and what does it say to do when you must exceed the limit?
qa_items.answer: About six. The source's framing is to think about the maximum number who can carry on a single conversation without it splintering into side discussions, and in its experience that is around six. The general reasoning about numbers is stated in Chapter 4: the number of people involved has a direct effect both on how much effort it takes to manage the conversation and on each participant's ability to follow along, which is why the source advises introducing critique with small groups — maybe just pairs — and growing from there as people become comfortable. If you are required to have more people, the source does not say you cannot critique; it says it is likely to take a bit more active facilitation, or the session may need to be broken into smaller groups. On who to include, it advises looking beyond the design team — developers, marketing, business analysts, product managers, subject-matter experts, project managers, executives — and notes that subject-matter experts need no design background, since understanding the need being designed for is what makes their input valuable.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 117 for the number and the attendee advice, p. 78 for the start-small reasoning. "About six" is a practitioner estimate of when a conversation splinters, not a measured threshold.
confounders: treating six as a hard cap rather than as the point where a single conversation stops holding
restricting critique to designers, which the source spends both chapters arguing against
assuming subject-matter experts need design literacy to contribute

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 148-149 (Ch. 6, 'Using Laddering to Expand on Feedback')
qa_items.question: Laddering is repeated "Why?". What makes it a test rather than an interrogation in this source's hands — and what constraint does it place on how the whys are worded?
qa_items.answer: That it has two possible terminations and the source treats both as successes. Either the questioning uncovers what the person is trying to communicate in a way that ties back to the objectives of the product, or it leads them to realise that the feedback rests on their personal preference and motivations rather than the objectives — "and therefore it should be left alone and the conversation can move on." A procedure that can return either answer is a test; one that can only extract agreement is not. The wording constraint the source treats as decisive is that a bare "Why?" can be seen or interpreted as aggressive or accusatory, and that the sense grows significantly stronger with repetition — so the whys should be worded "in a way that is more akin to an invite for the individual to continue sharing." The source's own worked chain runs from "I think we should use less blue" to a differentiation objective: almost all the competitors' sites are some shade of blue.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 148-149, borrowed from design research and related by the source to the "5 Whys". The authors concede that discerning motivations "isn't easy"; no case where laddering fails is shown.
confounders: assuming the goal is to make the person retract the feedback
reading the preference outcome as a failure of the technique rather than as one of its two results
treating the wording caution as a courtesy; the source says the aggressive reading compounds with each repetition

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 159-161 (Ch. 6, 'Dealing with Reactive Feedback')
qa_items.question: Someone reacts to your work with "This is horrible." Give the order of the two questioning steps this source prescribes, why that order, and the stopping rule it gives for when to abandon the attempt.
qa_items.answer: First get specific: ask which aspects of the design are not working. Only then ask the whys and hows — why those aspects are terrible, and how that relates to the objectives of the design. The order matters for a reason the source states: making the reaction specific tells you which parts of the design the person is responding to, which lets you either focus the rest of the conversation on those parts or discover that they are reacting to something outside what you wanted feedback on, and steer them back. Asking "why" before knowing "about what" has nothing to attach to. The stopping rule is explicit: if someone is nonresponsive to your attempts at clarification, or gets no less difficult as the conversation progresses, that is a sign you will not make progress and it is not worth following up. Thank them, move on to another topic or another person, and take note of how they interacted so you know what to expect — in some cases collecting their feedback another way, and where the person is not part of the project, excluding them from future critiques.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 159-161. Practitioner procedure with a stated rationale for the ordering. The source also advises considering the source of the feedback: someone with a history of being a problem whose comments can be ignored, probably should be.
confounders: asking 'why do you say that?' first, which the source's ordering puts second
assuming the reaction must be salvaged; the source explicitly permits abandoning the attempt
confusing the stopping rule with giving up on the person — the source suggests changing how their feedback is collected, not always exclusion

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 104-107 (Ch. 4, 'The Challenges Design Reviews Pose to Critique'), restated printed p. 179 (Appendix A, 'Confusing Critique with Review')
qa_items.question: A team says it already critiques, because it holds a design review at the end of every phase. Give the three characteristics by which this source identifies a design review, and the four reasons it says a review is a poor host for critique. What does it recommend — and what does it not recommend?
qa_items.answer: A design review is generally held toward the end of the design phase; it includes a goal of collecting approval from someone so effort can shift to a new focus; and where approval is not captured it focuses on identifying the changes needed to obtain it later. The four reasons it hosts critique badly: its intended outcome is approval rather than iteration; the feedback it collects therefore arrives as a list of what must change — "It isn't ready yet, but if you do these things and show it to us again, we'll give you the OK" — which is directive feedback by construction; the attendees are largely there to ensure their own interests survive into the final design rather than to compare it to its objectives, and the group is usually too large for a coherent conversation, Adam having once been in one with more than seventy people, most by phone; and the timing is set by the project plan, so it is both too late to use the feedback and disjointed from when the team actually needs analysis. What the source recommends is to critique regularly in the run-up so the review can serve its own purpose as a focused forum for approval, plus mitigations — take a lead role, recap the objectives at the start, use the difficult-people techniques. What it does not recommend is abolishing reviews; it says for some organisations collecting sign-off is essential, and its mitigations are damage limitation, not a conversion.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 104-107, with the Appendix A restatement at p. 179 and the "Do not rely on design reviews for critique" instruction at p. 107. Practitioner argument with a stated mechanism; the seventy-person review is a single recollection.
confounders: assuming the source wants design reviews eliminated
reading the difference as one of formality or attendee seniority rather than of intended output
assuming applying the critique techniques inside a review turns it into a critique; the source presents them as improving the feedback collected, not as changing what the meeting is

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 84-87 (Ch. 4, 'When Should You Critique?' — Early critique, Later critique, Finding the sweet spot)
qa_items.question: This source bounds when critique is worth holding by two conditions rather than by a schedule. State both bounds and what each is a condition on. What is its position on the familiar "20 percent to 80 percent baked" shorthand?
qa_items.answer: The opening bound is communicability: critique is premature until the maker has enough clarity about the idea to explain it to someone else — before that, "as soon as the first person asked us to clarify things, all we would be able to answer with is 'I don't know'." The authors are careful that this does not require every detail to be settled; unanswered questions at that stage are expected. The closing bound is actionability: at the point where something must be let go so it can be produced, feedback can still be collected but cannot be used until the work comes round again. Between them is what the authors call the sweet spot, defined by immediacy — the designer can walk away, think about the insights, and begin iterating right away. On the percentage shorthand their position is explicit: such labels can be useful for talking about timing but "still have the possibility of being taken a bit too literally for our comfort", and the durations depend on the scale of the problem, the idea, the team and the process — "in some cases, you'll get to that 20 percent mark very fast, maybe a matter of minutes or even seconds." They prefer understanding the two conditions and using judgement.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 84-87. The source explicitly refuses numeric boundaries — "we can't say that the first point comes exactly two days after the idea begins to form". It also concedes critique after the closing bound is still possible and worth doing; the claim is about immediacy of use.
confounders: adopting 20-80 as the source's rule, when the source names it in order to qualify it
assuming the opening bound requires a finished or detailed artifact
reading the closing bound as a claim that late critique is worthless rather than not immediately usable

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 94-96 (Ch. 4, 'Building Better Brainstorms')
qa_items.question: A workshop is meant to produce lots of ideas and then pick one, and it reliably produces four. What does this source say is happening, what structure does it prescribe, and at exactly which point does it place critique — and why there?
qa_items.answer: Critical thinking is happening when it should not be — the source calls it "the nemesis of creative or generative thinking" — and it suppresses ideas in two distinct ways. Participants who are analysing the ideas already proposed are not producing new ones; and participants who are producing ideas analyse them prematurely, decide they are not worth mentioning, and keep them to themselves. A third obstruction is that people are pushed into discussion before they have formed any view of the problem themselves. The prescribed structure divides the time into a divergent phase, whose activities minimise the chance to think critically — usually via a time limit and a challenge, such as sketching six to eight ideas in five minutes — and a convergent phase that compares, contrasts, consolidates and eliminates. Critique goes inside the second phase, before any vote. The reason is stated: voting participants otherwise use criteria that vary and may have little to do with the project's goals, whereas running critique first "primes the pump" so that ideas are kept or eliminated on their strength against the agreed objectives, and consensus about which ideas are strongest is often visible before the vote is taken.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 94-96. The authors report the typical brainstorm pattern as their repeated observation — "we can't say that we've often seen it work out that way" — with no count of sessions or ideas.
confounders: placing critique after the vote, as a check on the winner
placing critique in the divergent phase to raise idea quality, which is the failure being diagnosed
assuming the source rejects brainstorming; it calls having many ideas 'a worthy and righteous goal' and objects to how brainstorms are run

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 102-103 (Ch. 4, 'When Not to Use Design Studio')
qa_items.question: Half your team has framed the problem; the rest have not seen the framing. Someone proposes running a generate-and-critique workshop tomorrow. Using this source's stated conditions, what happens if you proceed, and what does it say you should have done?
qa_items.answer: The source names this as one of the specific conditions under which not to run the activity, and describes two ways it goes wrong. Either the group becomes mired in debating what the framing should be instead of generating ideas — an important discussion, the authors say, but one that should have happened earlier, and its arrival at the kickoff means the group is not ready — or you get people sketching without an agreed framing, in which case they generate ideas from their own individual opinion of what the problem is, and the critique rounds inside the workshop then break down "because people are analyzing and judging the value of ideas on different sets of criteria." That is the same foundation failure the book diagnoses everywhere else, appearing inside a workshop. What you should have done is hold the framing conversation beforehand. The source's other stated conditions are: the problem not being adequately framed at all; a concept already existing that the team cannot or will not stray from; and participants unwilling to take part — where it advises trying, but not forcing.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 102-103. Written about one named methodology (Design Studio, credited to architecture and art-school studio teaching and to Todd Zaki Warfel's adaptation); the reasons given are about framing, agreement, latitude and willingness rather than about the method.
confounders: running the session and treating the framing debate as valuable use of the time
assuming the fix is a better facilitator
concluding these conditions are peculiar to Design Studio — the mechanism given for the second condition is the general foundation failure

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 91-92 (Ch. 4, 'What Should You Critique?'), with the reflexive case at printed p. 18 (Ch. 1)
qa_items.question: Your team has just written a set of design principles. Can they be critiqued, and if so against what? Use this source's claim about what does and does not change between different things being critiqued.
qa_items.answer: Yes. The source's claim is that the framework does not change no matter what is being critiqued — what are the objectives, what elements relate to them, are those elements effective, why or why not — and that what changes is the set of objectives the thing is analysed against. For design principles the yardstick is the best practices for making design principles, and the source names two of them: a good principle should help you eliminate more ideas than you pursue, and it should be specific, avoiding overly subjective and ambiguous terms like "fun". The reflexive move is stated explicitly in both places: any artifact made toward an objective is critiquable, including personas, scenarios, journey maps, and the tools, methodologies and processes a team uses — "Critique. All. The. Things." The source adds two refinements: some product objectives are pertinent to one artifact and not another, since a colour palette may or may not bear on a goal of increasing authenticated visits; and different aspects of a design carry their own objectives, usually as principles and best practices specific to interaction or visual design.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 91-92 and p. 18. The invariance is asserted rather than demonstrated across artifact types; the critique of design principles against best practices for principles is the only worked case the source gives.
confounders: assuming critique applies only to visual artifacts — wireframes, comps, prototypes
concluding a different framework is needed for non-visual artifacts, which is what the source denies
using the product's business goals as the yardstick for the principles, when the source's yardstick here is the best practices for writing principles

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 153-154 (Ch. 6, 'The sandwich method')
qa_items.question: What position do these authors take on the feedback sandwich, and what exactly do they keep from it? Give their three objections.
qa_items.answer: They describe it — positive, negative, positive — state the rationale offered for it, and then decline it while keeping the practice underneath. Their three objections: in practice the positive comments are superficial or vague, about a quality unrelated to what is being discussed or about no real strength at all, and most people see through them, so the opening praise "does little more than signal that something bad is coming"; because more cognitive energy and attention goes to processing negative situations than positive ones, the initial positives are forgotten as soon as the negative arrives; and for some people the whole method feels manipulative. What they keep is the balance: discussing strengths and weaknesses matters, and starting on a positive note can help set tone. Their condition is the operative part — the positive comments must be about real strengths, aspects thought about critically and believed effective and important to the objectives, "not just things we came up with at the spur of the moment to make a weakness we want to point out easier to handle." Their summary instruction: "Don't worry about the 'sandwich'. Be honest with the recipient. Balance the conversation."
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 153-154. The authors refer to "research that it doesn't work" without citing any; no reference, note or bibliography for it appears anywhere in the book, and the asymmetric-processing claim is likewise uncited. The position is theirs, argued, not measured.
confounders: reading the rejection as 'do not say positive things', which inverts the authors' own instruction
treating the cited research as established because the authors invoke it — they name no source
conflating this with their separate argument for discussing strengths (pp. 29-30), which rests on reuse and on preventing silent regression, not on softening criticism

qa_items.source_title: Adam Connor and Aaron Irizarry, Discussing Design: Improving Communication and Collaboration through Critique (O'Reilly, 2015)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 29-30 (Ch. 2, 'Talk about strengths'), reinforced printed p. 178 (Appendix A, 'Focusing on What Isn't Working')
qa_items.question: Give the two reasons this source offers for discussing what works, neither of which is about making criticism easier to hear. Which of the two is a claim about what happens across iterations?
qa_items.answer: The first is reuse: when the team talks about aspects that are working, the designer can examine those areas and abstract the concept or element behind them, then use it to strengthen other areas that are working less well. The authors tie this to their view that design proceeds by deconstructing and abstracting ideas and recombining them. The second is the one about iterations: with the understanding that the designer will iterate after a critique, an aspect that seemed effective but was never discussed carries no reason for the team not to change it, so it can be lost in the next revision without anyone noticing it was load-bearing — the authors pose it as the situation of arriving at the next critique to find a previously strong aspect has been changed and is no longer as effective. Both are stated explicitly as being separate from the common argument that positives make critical feedback easier to take, which the authors treat elsewhere and largely reject.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 29-30, reinforced in Appendix A where the suggested structure is two things working and two causing concern. The regression argument is put as a rhetorical question rather than as a reported occurrence, and "we spend the vast majority of time talking about what isn't working" is asserted with no count.
confounders: giving the morale answer, which is the argument the authors are distinguishing themselves from
assuming the reuse argument is about reusing components rather than about abstracting why something worked
missing that the regression claim depends on iteration actually following the critique

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: Part 4 Graphics, part introduction, converted-PDF page 72
qa_items.question: Freeman opens his Graphics part by making a distinction about what a photograph actually contains. What is it, and what does it imply about who supplies the lines and shapes?
qa_items.answer: He says that strictly speaking graphics are the province of artwork and illustration, and that a photograph contains edges, contrast and whatever associations the eye and mind make up. The lines and shapes are therefore not in the photograph; they are what we think we see, completed by the viewer out of those edges. His practical conclusion is that graphics depend on the photographer to find and exploit — they are not given by the subject — and that by no means all photographs have them, which he says is part of their appeal when they do appear. He defines a graphic photograph as one in which lines and shapes play a strong part, often stronger than the subject.
qa_items.support: Part 4 introduction, converted-PDF page 72. The distinction between artwork and photography and the definition of a graphic photograph are both stated there.
confounders: treating lines and shapes as objective features present in the scene, which is the position Freeman explicitly separates himself from
assuming a graphic photograph means a highly designed or posed one, when his criterion is only that lines and shapes outrank the subject
confusing this with the design-education sense of 'graphic', which is about deliberate mark-making

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: CLOSE, converted-PDF page 110
qa_items.question: Freeman is careful to distinguish "close" from "close-up". What is the difference in his terms, and what common assumption about equipment does he remove?
qa_items.answer: Close-up, he says, is to do with magnification of small things. Close is a sense of being right up against the subject, shooting from nearer than most people would consider normal and possibly nearer than feels comfortable. The assumption he removes is that close means a wide-angle lens: he says close viewpoints do not always mean wide-angle lenses, and his own example was shot at close to normal, 48mm, with tight framing doing the work instead. He also separates the practical reasons for being close — no room to stand back, obstructions such as telegraph lines forcing an architectural photographer nearer — from the expressive one, and only the expressive one carries his claim about a personal and emotional connection.
qa_items.support: CLOSE, converted-PDF page 110. The close/close-up distinction, the 48mm figure and the separation of practical from expressive reasons are all stated there.
confounders: the widespread assumption that a close viewpoint requires a wide-angle lens, which he contradicts with his own focal length
reading 'close' as macro or detail work, which is exactly the confusion he is guarding against
assuming the emotional connection comes from the lens rather than from the physical distance and the subject's eye level

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: COUNTER FOCUS, converted-PDF page 131
qa_items.question: What does Freeman mean by "counter-focus", and what does he say about the status of the term?
qa_items.answer: Counter-focus is tilting the lens back against a scene that lies tilting forward — the reverse of the ordinary forward tilt, which is used to lay the plane of sharp focus along a subject. Reversed, with the aperture wide open, he says it gives the most extreme selective focus possible. He flags the term as his own coinage, saying explicitly that it is just his term for it, and he notes that using the movements this way is the exact opposite of how these cameras were designed to be used. His own example is a scriptorium desk shot with a standard lens tilted right back and, on a 4x5-inch studio camera, the film back tilted far forward as well, so that only a few letters and a hand are sharp.
qa_items.support: COUNTER FOCUS, converted-PDF page 131, with the geometry set out in TILT, converted-PDF page 128. The coinage disclaimer and the design-intent remark are both in the counter-focus text.
confounders: assuming this is established terminology, when Freeman says it is his own word
confusing it with the 'miniature faking' or tilt-shift look, which is a different aim from his — his purpose is to isolate a few letters, not to make a scene look like a model
supposing extreme selective focus is only an aperture matter, when the tilt is what makes it extreme here

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: RICH, converted-PDF page 158, and CONTRAST, converted-PDF page 171
qa_items.question: Describe the three axes of Freeman's colour cylinder and state where he locates "rich" and where he locates the strongest colour contrasts.
qa_items.answer: Hue runs radially, like spokes of a wheel. Saturation runs from the centre outward, grey at the centre and intense at the rim. Brightness runs from black at the top to white at the bottom. Rich he locates close to the outer rim at a medium-dark level — he cuts away the upper section of the solid so the reader can see in to that level. The strongest colour contrasts are between opposite wedges of the hue circle: orange against blue, red against green, yellow against violet, which are also the complementary pairs. His stated point about contrast is that what counts as different for perception is the hue alone, not dark against light and not grey against saturated.
qa_items.support: RICH, converted-PDF page 158 for the three axes and the position of rich; CONTRAST, converted-PDF page 171 for opposite wedges and the hue-only claim.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: NEAR-FAR, converted-PDF page 177
qa_items.question: Freeman attributes the term "near-far" to Ansel Adams. What are its requirements as he states them, and what does he say does NOT qualify?
qa_items.answer: It requires a very close foreground subject and another subject in the background, both impeccably sharp, and a meaningful relationship between them. What does not qualify is his own phrase — just slapping a rock in the foreground and a mountain behind. The two elements must compare in some way, either graphically or in meaning, or both. He adds a practical consequence: it is a wide-angle effect, so tiny adjustments to the camera position make a big difference to how the near and far elements register against each other. In his cormorant picture the whole result rests on exactly where the bird's head and neck fall against the edge of the boat and the man.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: COMPOSITE, converted-PDF page 197
qa_items.question: What does Freeman say distinguishes the Chinese "mountain-water" scroll from the European painting tradition, and what method does he report for building one?
qa_items.answer: He names two differences. Long and vertical is not part of the European painting canon. And the Chinese approach is to express the essence of the landscape rather than an image of what can be seen. The method he reports is to combine elements from the landscape in general and stack them vertically, almost always leading to an upper peak. Attempting it photographically in the Nujiang gorge, he began with a shot of a footbridge and built upward from images taken within an hour or two's drive up and down the gorge, including a large rock window high above the valley. He accepts that the combined view is impossible and claims that, like a mountain-water painting, it shows more of the essence of the gorge than a single image could.
qa_items.support: COMPOSITE, converted-PDF page 197. This is a photographer's summary of another tradition, offered without sources, and should be treated as his understanding of the form.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: DIAGONALS, converted-PDF page 79
qa_items.question: In the St Peter's picture Freeman credits the energy of the frame to something more specific than "diagonals are dynamic". What is the actual mechanism he names, and what does his own counterfactual concede?
qa_items.answer: The mechanism is opposition, not diagonality. He points out that the diagonals in that frame are entirely a creation of camera angle and lens, and that rotating the camera about its viewing axis turns every vertical in the building into a diagonal running counter to the already-diagonal shafts of sunlight. It is that counter-running of two diagonal sets he credits with the energy. His counterfactual is honest about the cost: had the camera been levelled, the shafts of light would have been longer, but the picture would have been less dynamic and more rigidly architectural. Something is given up as well as gained.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: TRIANGLES, converted-PDF pages 84 and 86
qa_items.question: Freeman says any three prominent points are read as a triangle. What single change turns that flat reading into a depth reading, and why does he say it works?
qa_items.answer: Making the three elements differ in size while they still look alike. He says that if there is a difference in size the eye puts them into perspective — literally — so the arrangement stops reading as a flat triangle and starts reading as recession. The reason is that similarity of kind licenses the assumption that the objects are really the same size, so any difference in apparent size can only be distance. His demonstration is three Mao badges shown first at matching sizes and then at graded sizes. His caption states the condition explicitly: if the objects look similar but vary in size, it suggests depth and perspective.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: TUNNEL, converted-PDF page 106
qa_items.question: Freeman treats lens vignetting as a compositional device. What mechanism does he give, and what conflict does he name between that use and the technical defaults?
qa_items.answer: Vignetting is a darkening away from the centre, and because our eyes tend to look toward brighter areas it concentrates attention toward the centre. He is explicit that the effect on attention is separate from and more interesting than the effect on brightness. The conflict he names is that lens manufacturers consider vignetting an optical fault and engineer their lenses to minimise it, and that processing programs carry lens-correction modules that remove it by default — so using it means turning the correction off or lessening it rather than accepting it as automatic. He concedes the position is a taste one against an engineering consensus: some of us, he says, actually like it.
