qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: MOVING IN, converted-PDF page 148
qa_items.question: Why does Freeman say a walking figure looks most natural on the side of the frame it entered from rather than in the centre?
qa_items.answer: Because the viewer extrapolates the motion. The figure is obviously moving, so we assume the movement will continue and project it forward in our minds — we sense the figure as being a little further into the frame than it actually is. Placing it back toward its entry edge therefore makes the perceived position land where a centred figure would only appear to be. He describes the figure as adding a vector to the image. He then hedges the rule in the same paragraph: this kind of placement is not compulsory, just natural.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: STACKING, converted-PDF page 181
qa_items.question: In the Grand Canyon picture, what actually converts the landscape into a stack of flat planes? Name the conditions Freeman lists and say which one carries the mechanism.
qa_items.answer: He lists three. A long telephoto, 400mm, whose compression makes the successive rocky spurs seem almost equal in size. A viewpoint high enough to see over each spur. And summer haze with backlighting. The last one carries the mechanism: the haze and backlighting hide the detail inside each plane and so make them two-dimensional, and his caption puts it plainly — lacking detail because of the haze, each outcrop appears as a two-dimensional cut-out. Depth is then read from which flat shape sits in front of which, rather than from any modelling within them. That is the reverse of the usual account: the depth is produced by taking information away.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: COLOR-WASH BACKGROUND, converted-PDF page 123
qa_items.question: What is Freeman doing with the abalone shell behind the quartz crystal, and what is the general permission he draws from it?
qa_items.answer: He is using defocus to strip an object of its identity and keep only its hue. The crystal is colourless but refracts, so he placed a polished abalone shell several inches behind it and shot at a fairly wide aperture — just enough to keep most of the crystal sharp. At that distance and blur the shell is made completely abstract and unrecognisable for what it was, present only as iridescent blue and green which the crystal's facets then refract. The general permission he states is that there are times when colour will enliven an image and times when it matters less what those colours actually represent in real life.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: SELECTIVE, converted-PDF page 121
qa_items.question: Freeman claims the sharp-to-blurred gradient is a purely photographic phenomenon. What is his argument, and what practical conclusion does he draw from it?
qa_items.answer: His argument is about ordinary vision: normal human eyesight does not experience optical blur. We see things at the periphery of vision as indistinct, but not as blurred. Because the gradient does not occur in direct experience, it reads as a photographic statement rather than as the viewer's own inattention, and he says this is what gives such images their visual appeal. The practical conclusions are two. What is not in focus is every bit as important as what is. And since the eye cannot help drifting toward whatever is sharp, the choice of exactly what to focus on is critical — the sharp point is a pointing device. He also sets aside the quality of the blur, telling the reader to forget bokeh, which he glosses as the subjective quality rather than the objective quantity.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: TILT, converted-PDF page 128
qa_items.question: State the Scheimpflug relationship as Freeman uses it, and say what shape the depth of field takes once the lens is tilted.
qa_items.answer: In an ordinary camera the lens plane and the sensor plane are fixed parallel, so changing focus only moves the sharp zone nearer or farther and the depth of field runs near to far. Tilting the lens tilts the lens plane, and under the Scheimpflug Principle the point where the lens plane meets the sensor plane is also where the plane of sharp focus must meet — so the sharp plane swings away with the tilt. The resulting depth of field is wedge-shaped rather than slab-shaped, opening out as it recedes. His reason for wanting this is that what needs to be sharp is often not perpendicular to the sensor — objects on a table, a flat landscape.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: EYELINES, converted-PDF page 154
qa_items.question: What is Freeman's account of why an eyeline works, and what does he say happens when two eyelines converge?
qa_items.answer: His account is curiosity: if we see someone looking intently at something, we want to see what it is and our eyes follow the gaze; and if the person suddenly looks up and away, he calls that irresistible — we can hardly help following the line of sight with our own eyes. When two individuals look at each other and the two eyelines converge, that point becomes almost magnetically the centre of attention. He adds an amplifier, half in jest: the effect is multiplied if someone is intently focusing a camera, because that suggests the subject really is worth looking at.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: WIDE-ANGLE IMMERSIVE, converted-PDF page 135, and TELEPHOTO COOLNESS, converted-PDF page 138
qa_items.question: Freeman sets the wide-angle and the telephoto against each other as an opposed pair. What is each one's effect on the viewer's position, and does he rank them?
qa_items.answer: The wide angle used from close, inside a busy scene, produces what cinematography calls subjective camera — the camera is you — projecting the audience into the scene so they feel they are there rather than standing back observing. The telephoto used from across the street produces the opposite: a fly on the wall, an objective observer, quietly watching at leisure. He does not rank them. He calls the choice a matter of mood and personal taste, tells the reader not to pay attention if someone criticises them for being too shy to get close, and in the same passage rejects the blunt "just get closer". He also names an optical contributor to the cool version: at that distance depth of field covers everything, so the whole scene appears to lie on a similar plane.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: HORIZONTAL LINES, converted-PDF page 73
qa_items.question: In the Yosemite Falls picture Freeman accepts a specific loss to buy a specific gain. What is the exchange, and why did the composition force it?
qa_items.answer: He needed the silhouetted branches in the foreground and the distant falls to be equally sharp, because the effect depends on the branches reading as a flat overlay on the scene beyond rather than as a separate near object. That meant plenty of depth of field, so he stopped down to ƒ/32, which in that light gave 1/5 second — and he says plainly that he accepted some softness in the falling water as the price. The only moving thing in the frame is the thing that paid. He states the trade as a fact of the picture he made, not as a general exposure rule, and he does not claim the softness was desirable.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: PASTEL, converted-PDF page 161, and MUTED, converted-PDF page 163
qa_items.question: Pastel and muted are adjacent cases in Freeman's colour part and are easily confused. On his own colour solid, what is the difference?
qa_items.answer: They move along different axes. Pastel is a move down the brightness axis to a lower, brighter, whiter level — he slides that section of the cylinder out to show the pale hues. He is explicit that the result is more about brighter than about less saturated: in his foggy Pennsylvania farm the grey wooden building is unsaturated, but the browns and greens still keep their colourfulness. Muted is the saturation move, inward from the rim, which he illustrates by drawing each main colour expanded back out to full saturation to show how much the soft grey light took away. He also gives a diagnostic for pastel: an overall pastel scene keeps its character by not containing black.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: DISTANT, converted-PDF page 113, and COMPRESSING, converted-PDF page 179
qa_items.question: Freeman gives two ways of relating a near element to a far one across a large gap, and they work in opposite directions. Compare them.
qa_items.answer: Showing distance keeps the scale difference and makes the interval legible: a slightly raised viewpoint so the ground is visible continuously from foreground to subject, aerial perspective, and in his Big Bend frame a sky of towering clouds standing over the mountains. The viewer can measure the gap. Compression does the reverse — a very long lens from nearly end-on destroys the scale difference, so pedestrians along a bridge appear nearly the same size as each other, and figures on the far bank of the river appear nearly the same size as those on the bridge. That equalisation is what makes their relationship part of the composition. The cue that supports the first is the one the second removes.

qa_items.source_locator: STREAKING, converted-PDF page 146
qa_items.question: Freeman makes an asymmetry claim about two kinds of photographic unsharpness. What is it, and how confident is the claim?
qa_items.answer: He says motion blur is one kind of photographic fuzziness that is thoroughly accepted by viewers and almost never rejected as some kind of mistake — and that the same cannot be said about out of focus. It is a claim about audience convention rather than about optics, and he offers no evidence for it. It also sits awkwardly beside his selective-focus case, where he argues that optical blur is read as a deliberate photographic statement because ordinary vision never produces it. He is similarly unwilling to give a rule for how much blur: asked whether there is a best shutter speed, he answers no, it is a matter of taste and of the balance you want between clear information and impression.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: PRECISION, converted-PDF page 108
qa_items.question: Where does Freeman rank exact alignment among the things going on in a frame, and what changes that ranking?
qa_items.answer: He ranks it low. Most of the time, he says, there are more important things going on in front of the camera than exact alignments — things like expression, action and gesture. What changes the ranking is a particular kind of subject rather than a decision by the photographer: his word is "inevitably". A gate in a wall with an identical gateway directly beyond it can only be shot from the exact centre line, because from an angle the gateway skews and from any head-on position that shows the second gateway even a slight misalignment reads as sloppy. Nested or repeated identical geometry gives the viewer a perfect reference, so the error becomes directly visible instead of merely felt.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: DEEP, converted-PDF page 117, and LAYERING, converted-PDF page 183
qa_items.question: Freeman argues for maximum sharpness in one case and declines available sharpness in another. What are the two, and what does the pair show about how he treats the control?
qa_items.answer: In DEEP he places the camera as close as the depth of field at minimum aperture will just cover, and sets the focus plane slightly nearer than the middle of the range so it reaches both ends. In LAYERING he says he could have brought more of the mirror-mosaic pillar into focus, with a smaller aperture or with focus blending, and states plainly that this would have spoilt the merged overlaps of sky and stupas. He does not treat sharpness as a quantity to maximise but as a distribution to place — where in the frame the viewer is permitted to see clearly. That is why he can argue for ƒ/32 in one case and against a smaller aperture in another without contradicting himself.

qa_items.source_locator: SILHOUETTE, converted-PDF page 188
qa_items.question: What technical capability does Freeman set his silhouette case against, and what general principle does he draw from the opposition?
qa_items.answer: He sets it against shadow recovery. Advanced digital processing makes it possible to open up shadows and recover detail, which he grants is valuable for some images, but he says it has created a kind of obsession among some photographers for revealing everything in an image. Against that he states a general principle: sometimes you need to hold things back from the viewer in order to make the photograph more interesting. The silhouette is offered as one clear case where shadow detail is not wanted, since the picture relies entirely on two separated planes and on outline, and underexposure is what delivers it along with a rich saturated background.

qa_items.source_locator: RHYTHM, converted-PDF pages 89 and 90
qa_items.question: Freeman tried two treatments of the same row of memorial arches. Which failed, which worked, and what did he say made the difference?
qa_items.answer: The higher, more distant viewpoint — the one he calls part of the usual procedure — failed; he describes the result as uninspired. What worked was the opposite, taken the next morning: a closer viewpoint with a wide-angle lens, from lower, making use of the slight fog. His stated reason is that two kinds of perspective then combine, scale perspective from the wide lens and aerial perspective from the fog, and together they make a solid progression into the distance rather than a flat inventory of similar objects. The two frames also differ in weather, light and time of day, so viewpoint is not the only variable that changed.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: PATTERN & FIELD, converted-PDF pages 91 and 92
qa_items.question: You have photographed a market stall piled with identical brass pots. The heap fills most of the frame, but the outermost pots sit complete inside the frame with a strip of table visible beyond them. On Freeman's account of field images, what has gone wrong and what is the fix?
qa_items.answer: The image will read as a finite heap of pots rather than as a field. Freeman calls it essential for a field image to frame so that the elements run off at all the edges, and gives the reason: this alone suggests that they go on and on. Elements severed by the frame edge are read as continuing past it, so the visible mass is taken as a sample of a larger one. The fix is framing, not arrangement — he says of his own LED lamps that he did not touch a thing to arrange them. Move in or crop so that pots are cut at every edge and no complete outermost element or surrounding table survives. He would add a prior question: the pattern also needs some surprise or curious element, or sheer weight of content, or it is not worth the frame at all.

qa_items.source_locator: MOVING IN, converted-PDF page 148, and MOVING OUT, converted-PDF page 150
qa_items.question: A colleague shows you a street frame in which a cyclist is riding out of the right-hand edge, and says it breaks the rule about leaving space in front of a moving subject. Using Freeman, what would you need to look at before agreeing?
qa_items.answer: You would look at whether the setting itself carries a direction. Freeman states the entry-side rule and then reverses it in the very next case, and the reversal is conditional. In his Torquay frame the lit façades of the harbour front give a clear impression of facing right toward an out-of-frame setting sun, so the whole scene is already directed that way and the girl walking out completes that direction rather than fighting it. If the cyclist's frame has such a vector — light, receding architecture, other elements oriented the same way — the departure reads as completion. If it does not, the criticism stands. Note also that Freeman hedges the original rule in the same paragraph he states it: not compulsory, just natural.

qa_items.source_locator: SPOT, converted-PDF page 170
qa_items.question: A picture editor says a frame works because of a small red figure against a grey background. What single check does Freeman demonstrate for settling that, and what does his own result look like?
qa_items.answer: Convert the frame to greyscale and look again. He shows exactly this on the facing page of his own picture and says the point is lost — the composition needs the spot colour. In his greyscale version the woman does not merely weaken; she becomes very hard to find at all against the weir behind her. The check is cheap, repeatable on any frame, and settles the specific claim being made rather than a general one about colour. Two cautions from the same case: he ran it on one picture to settle one argument, and a frame that survives desaturation is not thereby a worse colour photograph. He gives no threshold for how much loss counts.

qa_items.source_locator: MOMENT, converted-PDF pages 152 and 153
qa_items.question: You are photographing a row of brightly painted shopfronts and waiting for a passer-by to bring the scene to life. Following Freeman's method, what do you decide before anyone arrives, and what is the constraint that makes those decisions narrow?
qa_items.answer: You decide, in advance, one or two specific gaps within the composition where you would like to catch a figure. The constraint that makes them narrow is his hard rule for this kind of scene: you cannot afford to let the figure cross over any graphic line. In a strongly graphic setting the divisions are already load-bearing, so a figure overlapping one damages the structure instead of adding to it, and only the intervals between divisions are usable. In his beach-cabin frame he had three anticipated positions and timed the shot for the central one, catching the girl exactly in a white space; he says most of the other frames were unsuccessful because of poor positioning, and that the windows of opportunity were very narrow. He also concedes the limit of the method — you can expect how a figure will move through the frame, but it is rarely completely certain.

qa_items.question: You are asked to photograph a nineteenth-century lighthouse together with its tropical island setting, and every attempt from sea level either loses the setting or buries the lighthouse in foreground. What was Freeman's answer to exactly this brief?
qa_items.answer: He climbed the lighthouse and shot down from its own top, so that the lighthouse is the subject of the picture without appearing in it — represented by its shadow, for which he waited until later in the day so the shadow would be longer. He arrives at this through a general observation: what is often missing from a high vantage point is any evidence of the viewpoint itself, and there are times when including it adds to the scene. His sea-level attempts, which he shows, are the workaround that fitted the lighthouse against a variety of foregrounds and failed to combine both elements. He is candid that the appeal of the high viewpoint is partly an illusion — commanding, putting us in charge — and that you may not always want evidence of the viewpoint interfering with the view.

qa_items.source_locator: CURVES, converted-PDF pages 82 and 83
qa_items.question: Someone claims a photograph is structured by a strong diagonal mass running from the lower left to the upper right. What test does Freeman's own illustration method suggest for settling that, and what are its limits?
qa_items.answer: Redraw the frame as three or four flat tonal masses, with all texture and detail removed, and ask the question again. If the claimed line or shape survives that reduction it was in the image; if it disappears it was in the description. Freeman does this in his cattle-camp case, where the reduction leaves only the bull's outline and the horn curves, and it is what carries his claim that the curved outline defines the corner so strongly that it almost separates. The limits are real. He never proposes it as a test — he performs it as an illustration — and he does not use it consistently, illustrating several shape cases with arrows over the unmodified photograph instead. His reductions are also hand-drawn, so they already encode his reading and cannot falsify it. Reading it as a diagnostic is an extrapolation, not his claim.

qa_items.source_locator: FREEZING, converted-PDF pages 142 and 143
qa_items.question: In the Kerala fisherman picture, what was the fast shutter speed actually spent on, and what does Freeman say happens to the frame without it?
qa_items.answer: Not on the man. He says the straining movements of the fisherman's body were not the issue and that a modest shutter speed would have dealt with them. The 1/500 second was spent on the spurt of sand at his feet, which catches the eye because it is sharp and slightly unexpected, and which Freeman says makes the shot. His caption states the effect directly: the spurt, simply by being crisp and airborne, draws the eye down to the man's feet — and without it the immediate focus of attention is the torso. So a small frozen detail relocates the attention of the whole frame. He is measured about the size of the gain: at a slower speed the image would still have worked to an extent, but without that extra finesse.

qa_items.source_locator: DISTANT, converted-PDF page 113
qa_items.question: A landscape frame taken with a 300mm lens shows a distant range of hills filling the upper half and nothing else. The photographer complains that it does not feel far away. Using Freeman's account, what is missing and what would you look for instead?
qa_items.answer: What is missing is the evidence of the interval. Freeman separates being far away from a subject from showing distance: a telephoto deals with the first by bringing the subject closer in the frame and letting it be seen in detail, but that can leave nothing for the viewer to measure the gap against. What supplies distance is a set of visual clues — ground visible continuously from the foreground all the way to the subject, a viewpoint raised enough to let that ground be seen, aerial perspective, and in his Big Bend frame a sky of towering clouds that shows distance by standing over the mountains. He is explicit that this does not depend much on the lens: he qualifies himself by noting that some telephoto shots do carry strong distance, where the viewpoint is high enough to see mountains arranged one behind another with haze at work.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: SHIFT, converted-PDF pages 133 and 134
qa_items.question: You are photographing a tall church from street level and the walls lean inward. Set out Freeman's optical solution, its prerequisite, and how he handles the obvious objection.
qa_items.answer: The leaning comes from tilting the camera up to take in the building. His solution is not to tilt at all: aim straight, keep the camera level, and then shift the lens upward to bring the whole building into view. The prerequisite is a lens that projects an image circle larger than the sensor — ordinarily a waste of optics, and the reason a shift or perspective-control lens is a special item. His own diagram is honest about the intermediate state: levelling first cuts off the top of the church and shows unnecessary foreground, and the shift is what restores the view. The obvious objection is that this can be corrected in software, and he raises it himself, then answers it on preference rather than on result — "isn't it better to do it for real on the spot?" That is a practitioner opinion and should not be reported as a finding about which method produces the better picture.

qa_items.source_locator: TRIANGLES, converted-PDF page 84
qa_items.question: A reviewer notes approvingly that a portrait "forms a strong implied triangle". On Freeman's own account of implied triangles, how much does that observation establish?
qa_items.answer: Very little on its own. Freeman says implied triangles are the most frequent shapes in imagery simply because they happen with any three prominent points — even three badges thrown down connect in the eye. If a triangle is almost always present, noticing one is close to uninformative. He supplies the filter himself in the same case: a shape is worth the shot only where it is in some way unexpected or unpredictable, and he then widens that to photography in general — we like to see what we cannot predict, not what is already obvious. So the useful question is not whether a triangle is there but whether this one is surprising. His own example is a momentary triangle made by a cloth as a bather prepares to wrap it, which he says he was not quite expecting. Note that he never defines unpredictability or gives a test for it.

qa_items.source_locator: MUTED, converted-PDF page 163
qa_items.question: Two reviewers look at the same restrained colour photograph. One calls it muted, the other calls it drab. What does Freeman say resolves the disagreement?
qa_items.answer: Nothing in the picture. He asks the question himself and answers that the difference does not lie in the actual colour scheme but in our own value judgement: if you are in the mood for colour pizzazz, then it is drab; if you feel like restraint, it is muted. He supplies the reason the category exists at all in the same passage — rich colours give plenty to react to and for exactly that reason quickly become too much for comfort, so visual excitement works best as part of a balanced diet. This is the sharpest epistemic statement in his colour part and it undercuts the rest of it: a named colour quality with no image-side definition cannot be detected in a frame, only reported by a viewer.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: FOUR-SQUARE, converted-PDF pages 95 and 96
qa_items.question: A documentary series is shot entirely head-on and squared up, and the photographer says this makes it more objective. How would Freeman respond, and what would he grant?
qa_items.answer: He would call the belief a delusion, and he uses that word. His position is that the treatment certainly looks as if you are approaching the subject head-on and without fancy dramatic angles, which is why it has become the treatment of choice for documenting things, people and places — but the look of objectivity is itself a compositional effect, not a property of the method. What he would grant is that the treatment is genuinely useful and that many serious photographers have used it, naming Sander, Strand and the Bechers. He would also grant a purely practical virtue with nothing to do with meaning: magazine picture editors and art directors like it for covers, because the horizontal and vertical alignments take headlines, mastheads and other typography very well.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: FOUR-SQUARE, converted-PDF page 95, and PRECISION, converted-PDF page 108
qa_items.question: A portrait is intended as a squared-up frontal document but the subject sits at a slight angle to the camera. Following Freeman, is that a defect, and does it matter which case you are in?
qa_items.answer: It matters a great deal which case you are in, and in the four-square case it is a change of meaning rather than a defect. His caption is precise: even a slight angle to the subject becomes more casual, less deliberate. Nothing is broken; the picture now says something different from what was intended, which is a different kind of problem from a fault. In the precision case the verdict is harsher, and for a structural reason: where two identical forms are nested one behind the other the viewer has a perfect reference for alignment, so a small error is directly visible and, in his word, sloppy. The general rule under both is his ranking — most of the time there are more important things going on in front of the camera than exact alignments, such as expression, action and gesture — so alignment only becomes decisive when the subject makes it so.

qa_items.source_locator: LOOKING THROUGH, converted-PDF pages 104 and 105
qa_items.question: An art director asks for a photograph that makes the viewer feel what it is like to walk down through a forest and come upon a village. What did Freeman actually do, and what convention did it break?
qa_items.answer: He deliberately put unfocused tree trunks in the foreground, so that the viewer knows they are walking toward the edge of a forested slope and about to enter the village. The convention it breaks is that a viewpoint means a good view — clear, unobstructed, looking out over a worthwhile scene, of the kind that authorities signpost as scenic overlooks. He treats that convention as true and normal, citing Ansel Adams writing at length about one Yosemite vista he returned to many times, and offers the obstruction as an alternative rather than a correction. His own summary of the result is modest and worth preserving: not a neat view, but more personal, and perhaps with more of a sense of place. The brief was for a feeling, and the answer was to break the clear view.

qa_items.question: Putting a blurred colour wash behind a subject and putting one in front of it look like symmetrical options. Freeman says they are not. What is the asymmetry?
qa_items.answer: The background version is comparatively easy: choose an aperture wide enough to blur the far element while keeping the subject sharp, and in his still life he simply placed the colour source — a polished abalone shell — a few inches behind. The foreground version requires a different and, in his words, not natural shooting technique. You have to shoot through gaps or around the edges of a colourful subject close to the camera while focusing on something distant, and you have to keep the blurred foreground colours dominant, which is not what the camera or the situation wants. He shot his through the lettering on a food vendor's glass case at ƒ/2.8 on a 200mm and reports a lot of moving around to get the right amount of blur, which depends on how close the camera is to the lettering. The background case is also a constructed still life and the foreground case is found, so they are not equally repeatable.

qa_items.source_locator: ACTION COINCIDES, converted-PDF page 190
qa_items.question: You have a crowded street scene that refuses to cohere. What three routes out does Freeman name, and how reliable does he say the third one is?
qa_items.answer: He names camera angle, light, and the way the action unfolds. He puts the third last and immediately withdraws confidence from it: "Rely may be the wrong word, because things often don't work out, and you end up with just a busy scene." His own instance is a South Indian temple where a statue of the bull Nandin stood near a live cow. He waited and tried several things — people coming, praying, going — and calls all those shots mediocre. Then, briefly, the cow looked up at the statue just as one man reached down to touch its feet and another reached up to touch the statue. The actions were all separately motivated and simply came together, which he says brought some order out of chaos. He does not claim the coincidence was made; he claims it was waited for.

qa_items.answer: What licenses it, in his text, is the strength of the hue: red is the most insistent and eye-catching of all colours, so the figure can be placed way off near a corner and the image still works. The frame was widened by a pan-and-stitch precisely because more of the same greyish background lay sideways, and he says the balance between a small strong colour and a large grey background works better that way. His middle diagram goes further than that. It plots progressively less colourful versions of the figure at positions progressively nearer the centre, which draws placement latitude as a function of chromatic strength rather than stating it for one colour. Reading it as a scale is ours, not his; his text claims only that red allowed a corner placement.

qa_items.question: A picture editor asks you to assess whether a single photograph "has a colour theme". On Freeman's definition, what is wrong with the request?
qa_items.answer: The unit is wrong. He defines a colour theme as something that covers a number of images and that works well for a picture story because it holds them together and gives them a sense of unity. It is a property of a set, not of a frame, so a single photograph cannot pass or fail the test. Two further points from the same case. It need not be intentional — he says you could simply select it from what you already shot, and in his own Akha assignment he only realised after a couple of weeks that the community lived within a certain range of colours. And the everyday vocabulary is legitimate: he notes that words like ochre and brick are understood by everyone better than hue-saturation-brightness descriptions, while still denoting a tight zone of the colour solid.

qa_items.question: You photograph a family dinner squared up down the length of a long table and a viewer says it references a famous painting. Freeman anticipates this exact situation. What is his position?
qa_items.answer: That the association operates whether or not you intended it. He says the Last Supper has become so iconic that almost any squared-up image of a long table with people sitting at it, talking, evokes some association at least — and he states plainly that his own picture is neither a reference to it nor an imitation of it. It is simply lunch among friends; the symmetrical arrangement and the light made him want to shoot it as the conversation became animated. The practical consequence is that the arrangement imports a reading you cannot switch off, so the choice is to accept it or to change the arrangement. One qualification worth keeping: the association is culturally specific and he states it as though universal — it holds for viewers formed by a particular pictorial tradition.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: VERTICAL LINES, converted-PDF pages 76 and 77
qa_items.question: You are processing a facade shot in which the vertical planking should dominate, and your instinct is to even out the tonal range. What did Freeman do instead, and what else did he remove?
qa_items.answer: The opposite. He says he was far from wanting to balance tones and actively wanted strong contrast so that the vertical lines would dominate, and he processed for contrast accordingly. The reason is that contrast is what separates a line from its surroundings sufficiently for the eye to read it as a line rather than as a boundary between two similar tones. He then removed everything competing: he cropped to eliminate anything that would distract from the verticals — naming a window at the left and lit grass below — and shaved the frame at top and bottom. He also offers, conditionally rather than as a recommendation, a further step: if you do not mind altering the geometry in post-production, straightening the roof ridge from diagonal to horizontal would allow an even tighter crop. Note that the picture did not begin as an image about verticals; he was photographing the architecture and redirected when the low sun caught the planking.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: CIRCLES, converted-PDF pages 87 and 88
qa_items.question: How does Freeman rate implied circles against ready-made ones, and what does his own case show about how he found the picture?
qa_items.answer: He rates implied circles as much more interesting than complete ready-made ones such as a clock face, while conceding they do not happen as often as implied triangles. His case is built on a hub and spokes: nuns seated round a mixing bowl, with the bowl as the focus and the arms forming spokes to the wheel, and with heads and robes making a stack of overlapping concentric circles that repeat each other in different ways. The finding matters as much as the structure. He says exploring alternative camera positions is standard procedure; a balcony overview was the natural first move; and the picture came from moving on — closer, overhead, and onto a longer lens. He shows the sequence of shots leading up to it. Both the interest rating and the frequency comparison are impressions, not arguments.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: OVERHEAD, converted-PDF page 99
qa_items.question: A famous monument has been photographed from every ground-level angle for a century. What is Freeman's compositional argument for going overhead, as distinct from the ordinary appeal of height?
qa_items.answer: The compositional argument is that overhead gives a plan view, and a plan view often holds out the possibility of a shape of some kind — in his Stonehenge frame, a broken circle of grey stone sitting on a field of green. From directly above the arrangement of elements on the ground is presented without recession, so the arrangement itself becomes the visible form. He separates this cleanly from the ordinary appeal, which he puts down to privilege and unavailability: overhead is tempting because it is easy to imagine and usually difficult to reach, and it is a view not available to most people, which alone suggests a different image. He also frames the whole exercise as a response to saturation — the search for visual surprise becomes all the more pressing when a subject is well known and already thoroughly photographed. The condition is that the subject's meaning has to survive being reduced to a two-dimensional arrangement.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: LOW, converted-PDF page 101
qa_items.question: A street scene has an expanse of dull pavement in front of the subject. Freeman gives two independent reasons for dropping the camera. What are they, and how well supported is each?
qa_items.answer: The first is subtractive and is a geometric consequence: kneeling rather than standing takes in less of the foreground, and he names sidewalk and street as the things being removed. The second is additive — a low position injects angles, and with them, he says, a little drama and presence. In his own horse-caravan case he adds a third reason that is neither: from ground level more of the horses showed against a white wall, which is about separation rather than about angle. The three are not equally supported. Removing foreground follows directly from the geometry; the separation against the wall is demonstrated in the picture; drama and presence are asserted. Worth noting that the case was fully pre-planned — site chosen for a curved whitewashed wall, time to prepare, subject expected to walk past — so it is a set-up, not a reaction.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: IMPOSSIBLY DEEP, converted-PDF page 119, and DEEP, converted-PDF page 117
qa_items.question: Freeman states a hard physical limit on depth of field. Where does it bite hardest, and what does he say the photographer can and cannot do about it optically?
qa_items.answer: It bites hardest in close-up: the laws of physics set limits for any particular lens, and the closer you get to macro the less depth of field you can expect. He is blunt that beyond a point front-to-back sharpness cannot be had by normal means — his own still life is not even an extreme close-up and there is no way to get it with a normal camera lens. Optically, what the photographer can do is stated in the deep case: choose a wider angle, which gives a better chance of everything being pin-sharp at a small aperture; place the camera as close as the depth of field at minimum aperture will just cover; and set the focus plane slightly nearer than the middle of the range, which his diagram puts about a third of the way in. Beyond that his answer is a software one, focus stacking, which this extraction does not treat as compositional knowledge.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: TILT, converted-PDF page 128, with the book's own introduction, converted-PDF page 10
qa_items.question: What does Freeman say about the sufficiency of his own words, and where in Parts 4-10 does he say it about a specific case?
qa_items.answer: His introduction states the book's premise as words to a necessary minimum, with visuals carrying the story — he says that in explaining a point about composition or colour it would often have been simpler to bypass words entirely and rely on a purely visual explanation. In Parts 4-10 he says it about one case in particular. Of tilt he writes that it is fairly easy to use once you have the equipment but becomes difficult to describe in words, so he will let the illustrations tell the story. This matters for anyone working from the text alone: the author has declared in advance that his words are deliberately insufficient, so a text-only reading of this book is known to be partial before it begins.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: Part 9 Juxtaposing, part introduction, converted-PDF page 174
qa_items.question: A frame places a billboard model behind a tired commuter, implying a comment neither person intended. A colleague calls this dishonest. What is Freeman's position on the implied connection in a juxtaposition?
qa_items.answer: He would not call it dishonest, and his position is unusually explicit. Setting one thing against another implies that together they equal something else — and he says that often, and maybe even usually, the two do not in reality have a connection, which does not prevent the photographer from making a point. He then says the technique is totally open to abuse, and calls that good, because the openness is what admits the whole range of ideas from silly to thoughtful and from clarifying a situation to complicating it. He also names who sees the connection: in his own case the participants are unaware, and only the photographer can see or suggest the link, through where they stand and the framing and the lens. A reader looking to this source for an ethical constraint on juxtaposition will not find one.
qa_items.support: Part 9 introduction, converted-PDF page 174, with the unaware-participants case on converted-PDF page 175.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: Part 9 Juxtaposing, part introduction, converted-PDF page 174
qa_items.question: Freeman says juxtaposition adds two kinds of depth and then ranks them. What are they and which outranks which?
qa_items.answer: Depth of idea and depth of graphic form — often just one of them, and sometimes, when the photographer is lucky or working harder, both together. Idea outranks form, and he states the ordering directly: you can make graphic forms coincide, and that strengthens the case, but ultimately it is still all about idea. Form is reinforcement, not the substance. Two honest caveats: the ordering is asserted rather than argued, and his own analysis of the case that follows is entirely formal — two juxtapositions, real telephone boxes against a painted one, and real people against painted people.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: COMPRESSING, converted-PDF page 179
qa_items.question: Freeman opens one case with a remark about where he put it in the book. What is the remark, and why does it matter for anyone reading the book's structure as a taxonomy?
qa_items.answer: He opens the compression case by saying he could as easily have put it in the Optics chapter, because it is very much a feature of using a telephoto lens. That is an explicit admission that his ten part headings are organisational rather than principled. It matters because several claims sit under one heading and belong equally under another — compression under juxtaposing and optics, the coinciding-actions case under juxtaposing and motion, the tunnel case under viewpoint and optics — so no inference should be drawn from where a case appears. He makes the admission once, about one case; reading it as a general statement about all ten parts is an extrapolation, though the straddling cases support it.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: COLLAGE, converted-PDF page 194
qa_items.question: You are assembling seven photographs into a single grid image and it reads as a contact sheet rather than as one picture. What two conditions does Freeman name for a collage cohering?
qa_items.answer: First, the edges must fit. The images are defined and usually separated by their edges, left clear and straight, but by positioning them so that certain edges fit neatly against others they can be blended in an almost seamless way — the viewer understands that they are separate and at the same time they appear to make a whole. Second, the selection must share a premise. He says it is equally understood that the images have something in common, which is why they are grouped together. His own case is seven archive photographs of London windows, each of which already contains two layers because the glass reflects a scene beyond it, and most of which work because the reflected view is sunlit — layered images layered together. A contact-sheet reading usually means one of the two conditions is missing rather than that the layout needs adjusting.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: Part 10 Combining, part introduction, converted-PDF page 193, and COMPOSITE, converted-PDF page 197
qa_items.question: How does Freeman frame the argument about manipulated photographs, and does he settle it?
qa_items.answer: He frames it around intent rather than technique. The basic question he poses is whether the photographer is trying to fool people into believing the image has not been manipulated; and then, even if fooling is the aim, whether the intention is pure or impure — pure meaning art, impure meaning making money or delivering the image you originally failed to get in one shot. He does not settle it. He says you could go on forever with this debate and that it is not likely to be rewarding, and he moves on to the technique. He does introduce one working distinction: the images in his part are all declared composites, in that they do not pretend to be single unadulterated photographs — "except one, possibly" — and he describes one of his own as dodgier on the ethics front because it sets out to fool the viewer, though with the aim of entertaining and exploring. He also notes that compositing predates digital tools, having done one entirely in camera in 1990.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: GRAPHIC COMPOSITE, converted-PDF page 200
qa_items.question: You are shooting fifty photographs of the same product category for one book and every frame is starting to look alike. What reasoning does Freeman offer, and what is the observation unit of the argument?
qa_items.answer: He offers the same problem and his answer to it. Every picture in one of his books was a bowl of noodles, and he says that just as no one wants to eat noodles continuously, we also need a varied visual diet. There are only so many ways to photograph noodle dishes and still show all the ingredients, and it turns out top-down is very efficient, so he varied the setting instead and did one image in a consistently graphic, deliberately illustrative way — a bowl surrounded by the extended mitred joints of a saké box, with fading views making rests for the chopsticks and spoon. The observation unit is the body of work, not the frame. The argument has no meaning applied to any single picture; it is a statement about what a sequence of pictures does to a reader.

qa_items.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
qa_items.source_locator: SEQUENCE, converted-PDF page 204, and STEPPED ACTION, converted-PDF page 195
qa_items.question: Freeman gives two ways of putting duration into a single still image. What are they, and what precondition does the merged version require?
qa_items.answer: The first, in the sequence case, is to slice a movement into frames and either stack them in a strip — which he calls the uncomplicated way — or, with more effort, turn the entire sequence into one image. The precondition for the merged version is spatial: the set of frames must have been shot rapidly enough that consecutive frames overlap, which is what lets them be positioned into a continuous single picture. His example is a hawk-eagle taking off, panned left to right, six frames positioned together, with the irregularities showing it was handheld. The second, in the stepped-action case, is to lock the camera on a tripod, shoot many frames of a repeated action, and bring several positions of the same hands into one frame — reaching for something of the jerky, sped-up flavour a cinematographer would get by undercranking. He notes that the result covers 144 seconds, so it is, in his words, a still snapshot of a possible movie sequence.
qa_items.support: SEQUENCE, converted-PDF page 204, for the overlap precondition and the strip alternative; STEPPED ACTION, converted-PDF page 195, for the locked-camera version and the undercranking reference. The layer-stack procedure he describes is a software step and is not extracted here.

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "Forcing a focus" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: State Godin's mechanism for why narrowing the audience improves the work. The answer is not that a smaller audience is easier to reach — what is it?
qa_items.answer: The mechanism runs through the artefact, not the audience. Pursuing mass means aiming at the centre of the curve, which requires you to offend no one and satisfy everyone, and those are constraints on the thing you make: they force compromises and generalisations, and produce work that is average. Narrowing removes the constraints. With a small, specific audience you can go to their extremes, take a position where you alone are the perfect answer, and overwhelm their wants with attention — producing a change profound enough that people cannot help but talk about it. So the size question is asked as a floor, not a target: what is the minimum number of people you would need to influence for the effort to be worth it.
qa_items.support: Forcing a focus: the relentless pursuit of mass will make you boring, because mass means average, requires you to offend no one and satisfy everyone, and leads to compromises and generalisations; begin instead with the smallest viable market; find a corner of the market that can't wait for your attention and go to their extremes.
confounders: the efficiency reading — that a small audience is cheaper to reach, which is not his argument

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "Specific is a kind of bravery" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: Godin says naming a specific audience takes bravery. Bravery against what? Give his mechanism, not the sentiment.
qa_items.answer: Against being shown to have failed. His argument is that a specific audience makes the work accountable — it matched or it did not, it spread or it did not — whereas an unspecified audience cannot be contradicted by any outcome, so "everyone" functions as a place to hide. He names the comfort explicitly: you will never be able to serve everyone, which is comforting, since you are less likely to be disappointed when it does not happen. The claim is therefore about falsifiability, not about ambition. Note that this is a claim about practitioners' motives, made from his observation of the people he teaches and no other evidence.
qa_items.support: Specific is a kind of bravery: specific means accountable — it worked or it didn't, it matched or it didn't, it spread or it didn't; are you hiding behind everyone or anyone; you'll never be able to serve everyone, which is comforting.
confounders: reading the bravery as commercial risk-taking rather than as exposure to judgement
assuming he means courage to turn down revenue

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "Shun the nonbelievers!" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: A campaign is widened to a general audience and the work gets progressively blander over three rounds of feedback. What does Godin say happened, and where does he say the mechanism operates?
qa_items.answer: Seeking the largest possible audience guarantees mass rejection — the chorus of no becomes deafening, and the feedback arrives direct, personal and specific. Under that pressure the natural response is to sand off the edges and fit in, and to fit in more than anyone else. His point about location matters: the mechanism operates through the maker, not the audience. Nothing about the audience changed; the maker averaged the work in response to rejection from people it was never for. Since the edges were what made it fit its intended audience, more reach destroyed the thing that was working. His instruction is to resist, on the ground that the rejection carries no information: it is not for them.
qa_items.support: Shun the nonbelievers: when we seek to serve the largest possible audience, that audience will turn us down and the chorus of no will become deafening; in the face of so much rejection it's easy to sand off the edges and fit in, fit in all the way, fit in more than anyone else; resist, it's not for them.
confounders: attributing the blandness to committee process or client timidity rather than to the reach decision
concluding all negative response should be ignored; Godin separately distinguishes feedback from advice
assuming the audience changed; his mechanism is that the maker did

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "It's not for you" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: Godin argues that saying "it's not for you" is an act of respect. Set out the argument, and give the case in his own book that shows what it costs.
qa_items.answer: The argument has two parts. Refusing to pursue someone respects them: you are not wasting their time, pandering to them, or insisting they change their beliefs, and "I made this for you, not for the other folks" and "it's not for you" are two sides of one coin. And the alternative is unavailable anyway — every bestselling book has one-star reviews, and it is impossible to create work that both matters and pleases everyone. The cost shows in his restaurant case: a group that eliminated tipping had to accept that diners who enjoyed the status of leaving a large tip could no longer get it, and the honest formulation is "it's not for you, sorry". So the choice is not how to avoid disappointing people; it is which people to disappoint.
qa_items.support: It's not for you: shows the ability to respect someone enough that you're not going to waste their time, pander to them, or insist that they change their beliefs; it's impossible to create work that both matters and pleases everyone. No tipping at USHG: some diners find joy in the status of leaving a big tip and the group can no longer offer that thrill.
confounders: reading exclusion as a marketing tactic for creating exclusivity rather than as an unavoidable consequence stated plainly
assuming the excluded group is unimportant; in his case they were paying customers with a preference he removed

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "The comedian's dilemma" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: A piece of work fails badly in front of an audience. Godin says there are two candidate causes. What are they, what does he supply to tell them apart, and why does that matter?
qa_items.answer: The two are: the work is not as good as it needs to be, or you failed to be clear about who it was for in the first place. His illustration is a skilled comedian bombing in front of a tour group that does not speak his language — total failure, no information about the material. What he supplies to tell them apart is nothing: in his own story the answer is discovered by accident after the show. It matters because the two diagnoses license opposite responses. Read as a quality failure you rewrite the work; read as an audience failure you keep the work and change who sees it. Acting before the diagnosis is made risks destroying work that was fine.
qa_items.support: The comedian's dilemma: the comic brings his best material and no one laughs; then he discovers the audience is a tour group and no one understands English; it's entirely possible that your work isn't as good as it needs to be, but it's also possible that you failed to be clear about who it was for in the first place.
confounders: assuming Godin provides a test; naming the branch is all he does
defaulting to the quality diagnosis, which is what the symptom superficially suggests
treating this as licence to dismiss all criticism as audience mismatch

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 "Not Mass, Not Spam, Not Shameful . . .", section "The lock and the key" (spine 8)
qa_items.question: What ordering constraint does Godin place on the work, what is his argument for it, and where in his own book does it sit uncomfortably?
qa_items.answer: The constraint is that the audience is chosen before the artefact is built: it makes no sense to make a key and then look for a lock, so find the lock and fashion the key. His argument is asymmetry of difficulty — it is easier to make products and services for the customers you seek to serve than to find customers for the products and services you already made. Where it sits uncomfortably is his own account of what audiences can tell you: he says the crowd did not invent the Model T, the smartphone or rap, and that people are intimately aware of their wants but terrible at inventing ways to address them. So the audience is chosen first but not consulted first, and he does not reconcile the two.
qa_items.support: The lock and the key: it doesn't make any sense to make a key and then run around looking for a lock to open; it's easier to make products and services for the customers you seek to serve than to find customers for your products and services. Ch. 7: the crowd didn't invent the Model T, the smartphone, or rap; people are terrible at inventing new ways to address their wants.

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", sections "What change are you trying to make?" and "The simple marketing promise" (spine 11), with "A Simple Marketing Worksheet" (spine 32)
qa_items.question: You are handed a brief that names a deliverable and a deadline. Applying Godin's method, what two things must be settled before anything is produced, and what are the two ways he says the second one gets answered badly?
qa_items.answer: Who is it for, and what is it for — the second in its strong form, what change are you trying to make. He treats these as generative rather than descriptive: once you are clear who it is for, the answer shifts the product you make, the story you tell and where you tell it, so a brief that starts from a deliverable has already skipped the decisions. The two bad answers he names are specific. First, the grandiose one — a change that has never been done by anyone with your resources — which he says is both a heavy burden and a convenient excuse when things go badly. Second, the reverse-engineered one, constructed backwards from what you were already going to make and loaded with buzzwords. His three-sentence template forces the answers: my product is for people who believe ___; I will focus on people who want ___; I promise that engaging with what I make will help you get ___.
qa_items.support: What change are you trying to make: Stumble 1, the grandiose change that has never been done — a heavy burden and a convenient excuse; Stumble 2, reverse-engineering a change to match what you were already selling, loaded with buzzwords. Who's it for has the ability to shift the product you make, the story you tell, and where you tell it. The three-sentence promise template.

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "Worldviews and personas" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: What grouping rule does Godin substitute for demographics, what does he admit about it, and what tension does he leave unresolved?
qa_items.answer: Group people by what they dream of, believe and want rather than by what they look like — psychographics rather than demographics — and treat the group as sharing a worldview, the lens, assumptions and biases through which they see. What he admits is that this is deliberate distortion: "yes, we're typecasting — willfully exaggerating people's attitudes and beliefs in order to serve them better". The unresolved tension is that he also writes, in the same passage, that everyone deserves to be treated as an individual, with dignity and respect for their choices. He states both and moves on. The payoff he claims is predictive — with evidence about someone's worldview you can make pretty good assumptions about how they will respond — asserted with no accuracy claim and no failed prediction anywhere in the book.
qa_items.support: Worldviews and personas: begin by choosing people based on what they dream of, believe and want, not based on what they look like; use psychographics instead of demographics; a worldview is the shortcut, the lens each of us uses; everyone deserves to be treated as an individual; yes, we're typecasting — willfully exaggerating people's attitudes and beliefs in order to serve them better.
confounders: treating his named personas as a taxonomy rather than as illustrative caricatures
assuming psychographics means observed behavioural data; his unit is the story people tell themselves

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "Worldviews and personas" (spine 11)
qa_items.question: Godin's retail failure case: an incoming chief executive ended a chain's constant discounting because he could not imagine a quality store behaving that way. What does Godin say the customers were actually buying, and how strong is this as evidence?
qa_items.answer: They were not enduring the discounts, they were playing a game that made them feel like they were winning — so removing the discounts removed the product. The executive's decision was made from his own worldview as a luxury buyer, and it abandoned the store's true fans: people who loved the sport of bargain hunting. Godin reports sales falling by more than fifty per cent. As evidence it is weak and should be labelled: a single retrospective case, no controls, a figure reported without a source, a causal attribution to worldview mismatch in a decision with many other moving parts, and a US department-store episode of the early 2010s in a retail environment that no longer exists in that form.
qa_items.support: Worldviews and personas: Johnson took that action based on his worldview, on his bias about how to shop; as a result sales plummeted by more than 50 per cent; he abandoned the true fans, people who loved the sport of bargain hunting, people whose worldviews differed from his; Penney's customers were playing a game, one that made them feel like they were winning.
confounders: treating the fifty-per-cent figure as evidence for the mechanism rather than as a reported outcome
reading the lesson as 'don't remove discounts' rather than 'don't decide from your own worldview'

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", sections "Empathy is at the heart of marketing" and "A million-dollar bargain" (spine 12)
qa_items.question: Godin's empathy principle has a clause at the end that changes what it demands. State the principle with that clause, and give his strongest formulation of the consequence.
qa_items.answer: The principle is that the people you seek to serve do not believe what you believe, do not know what you know and do not want what you want — and the clause is: they probably never will. That turns empathy from a stage on the way to persuasion into a standing constraint. You are not modelling them in order to bring them round; you are modelling them because they are not coming round. His strongest consequence inverts the usual ethics: if you are unwilling to have empathy for the narrative of the person you seek to serve, you are stealing — withholding a valuable option from someone who would have benefited. His supporting case is a fundraiser who cannot ask for a large donation because she cannot imagine making one, when the donation was never for her.
qa_items.support: Empathy is at the heart of marketing: people don't believe what you believe, don't know what you know, don't want what you want; they probably never will (Ch. 2 executive summary). A million-dollar bargain: if you're unwilling to have empathy for the narrative of the person you seek to serve, you're stealing.
confounders: reading empathy as a step toward eventually converting them, which the 'never will' clause rules out
reading 'you're stealing' as the claim rather than as the rhetoric on top of it

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 "Marketing Changes People Through Stories, Connections, and Experience", case study "VisionSpring—Selling glasses to people who need them" (spine 10)
qa_items.question: In Godin's glasses case, the offer was reframed from a purchase to a decision about handing something back. What is his explanation for why that mattered, and what is the honest status of the result he reports?
qa_items.answer: His explanation is about risk capacity, not about loss aversion in general. Shopping is a risk — you spend time and money on something that might be great — and it is enjoyable only to people for whom being wrong is not costly, because being wrong does not cost them dinner or a medical check-up. For an audience without that margin, the same offer reads as a threat rather than as fun. He draws the general rule that his own narrative about how to buy glasses is not better or worse, only his, and that insisting on it when it is not working is arrogance. The status of the result: he reports that removing the choice doubled the proportion who bought. That is an outcome claimed without controls — one afternoon, one village, one observer, no comparison group, no counts beyond "about a third" and "doubled" — and the risk-capacity explanation is his interpretation afterwards, not a tested hypothesis. It is not a rate and should not be used as one.
qa_items.support: VisionSpring case: about a third of those who needed and could afford glasses bought them; the offer was changed to "here are your new glasses, pay three dollars or give them back"; desire for gain versus avoidance of loss; to go shopping is to take a risk, and we're able to take that risk because being wrong isn't fatal; my narrative is simply my narrative.
confounders: generalising it as 'loss aversion beats gain framing', which drops the risk-capacity condition that makes it his argument
citing the doubling as a measured effect size
assuming the finding transfers, when the point of the case is that the marketer's assumptions do not

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", section "The marketing of dog food" (spine 12)
qa_items.question: Why does Godin use dog food rather than a human product to make his point about performance and appeal, and what is the general claim it is there to support?
qa_items.answer: Because it separates the two parties cleanly and unarguably: he has never seen a dog buy dog food. The premium ingredients and rising prices are for the owners — for how buying it makes them feel, the satisfaction of caring for an animal, the status of a luxury purchase — and we have no idea whether dogs enjoy the expensive kind, because we are not dogs. The general claim is that there is almost always a disconnect between performance and appeal, and that the engineer's choice of the best price-performance combination is rarely the market's choice. So a marketer trying to sell more dog food by making food that tastes better has taken on the wrong problem; the formula is food that owners want to buy.
qa_items.support: The marketing of dog food: I've never seen a dog buy dog food; dog food is for dog owners, for the way it makes them feel; there's almost always a disconnect between performance and appeal; the engineer's choice of the best price/performance combination is rarely the market's choice.
confounders: reading it as a claim about pet marketing rather than as an argument about buyer and user coming apart
assuming the point is that customers are irrational; his point is that the valuer is not the one you assumed

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", sections "Thinking about better" and "Better isn't up to you" (spine 12)
qa_items.question: Godin denies that "better" is transitive. What is his mechanism, and what does he explicitly exempt from the relativism?
qa_items.answer: His mechanism is about memory. Nobody can hold two hundred and fifty motorcycles or nineteen thousand drink combinations in mind, so we remember the best one — and "best" is always best-for- me on the dimension I happen to care about. Memory holds one slot per person per dimension, not one ranking per category, so the same category has a different winner in each head. Price orders cleanly and carries no claim about quality: a more expensive handbag is more expensive, which is one of many things someone might care about. What he exempts is competence. Quality in the sense of meeting specification is required but no longer sufficient — and if you cannot deliver it, he says the book is no help to you. The relativism is about appeal, not about whether the thing works.
qa_items.support: Thinking about better: linear comparisons don't make sense; an expensive bag is not therefore better. Better isn't up to you: we remember the best one; best for what; best for us. Ch. 6: quality, the quality of meeting specifications, is required but no longer sufficient.
confounders: extending the relativism to whether the product works, which he explicitly excludes
reading it as 'all preferences are equally valid' rather than as a claim about how memory stores options

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", sections "Positioning as a service" and "Choose your axes, choose your future" (spine 12)
qa_items.question: Set out Godin's XY positioning method, and state the trade-off he attaches to the choice of axes — including what he says happens to the customer in the wrong case.
qa_items.answer: Draw two axes, each an attribute people care about; plot every available alternative on them; and take a position at an extreme rather than in the middle. The trade-off is in choosing which attributes. It is tempting to pick the ones most people care about, and it is hard work to claim an edge nobody wants — but picking the popular axes puts you in a crowded quadrant, and without the magic of advertising you cannot grow there. What happens to the customer is the specific part: he does not know what to do, so he does nothing. Inaction, not a random pick. The alternative is to build your own quadrant from two overlooked axes and be the clear and obvious choice on them. Note the method organises a decision it does not make — Godin prints two dozen candidate axes and says you know your space better than he does.
qa_items.support: Positioning as a service: draw a simple XY grid; for each axis choose something that people care about; this involves going to extremes. Choose your axes: if you pick the popular one you'll be choosing a crowded quadrant and without the magic of advertising it's very difficult to grow there; your customer doesn't know what to do, so he does nothing; the alternative is to build your own quadrant.
confounders: assuming a crowded quadrant means losing share; his claim is that the customer stalls entirely
treating the axis list as prescriptive; it is a prompt
confusing this with mid-century positioning, which he says invented differentiating claims and no longer holds up

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 "In Search of Better", section "Positioning as a service" (spine 12), with Ch. 6 "Beyond Commodities", section "But your story is a hook" (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Godin's music-teacher example: one teacher claims rigour and competition results, another claims the whole student and refuses competitions. What does he say this costs the first teacher, and what general rule is the example there to demonstrate?
qa_items.answer: It costs him his freedom of action. Having claimed rigour, he now has to actually be more rigorous and professional than other teachers, has to make the difficult decision of expelling students who are not serious enough, and has to persevere until his students really do win competitions. The general rule is that a position is an obligation: once you claim a story you are on the hook to deliver, and Godin contrasts this with merely offering an alternative, which he calls the low-risk path — take it or leave it. He also adds two modern conditions on the claims themselves: they must be true and continually doubled down on in all your actions, and they must be generous, existing as a service to the customer. And he notes, without softening it, that this is not a teacher he would have wanted himself — which is the "it's not for you" principle applied to his own example.
qa_items.support: Positioning as a service: the teacher who chooses rigour and competition results now has his work cut out — he has to be more rigorous, to expel students who aren't serious, and to persevere so they actually win; is this the teacher I wish I'd had? Absolutely not. It's not for me. But your story is a hook: once you claim a story you're on the hook to deliver.
confounders: reading positioning as a communications choice with no operational consequence
assuming Godin endorses the rigorous teacher; he explicitly says it is not for him

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 "Price Is a Story", sections "Cheap is another way to say scared" and "Trust and risk, trust and expense" (spine 23)
qa_items.question: Godin argues against competing on price, and one of his claims runs against intuition. What are the two claims, and what exemption does he allow?
qa_items.answer: The first is that cheapness promises no change: when you are the cheapest you are promising the same, but cheaper — which removes the only thing he says a marketer has to offer — and that the race to the bottom is tempting because nothing is easier to sell than cheaper, requiring no calculation or thought from the buyer. The counter-intuitive one is that lowering your price does not make you more trusted, it does the opposite: where a transaction is risky or expensive, people construct a story that justifies their commitment, and that story carries trust with it — which is why high-end restaurants and hotels survive bad reviews. The exemption is genuine efficiency: unless you have found an extraordinary new way to deliver, racing to be cheapest means you are not investing sufficiently in change. He is objecting to cheapness as a position, not to a real cost advantage. He also notes, without embarrassment, that every confidence trickster relies on the trust mechanism — which is reason enough to hold it loosely.
qa_items.support: Cheap is another way to say scared: unless you've found an extraordinary new way to deliver, racing to be cheapest means you're not investing in change; when you're the cheapest you're promising the same, but cheaper; low price is the last refuge of a marketer who has run out of generous ideas.
