Trust and risk: when people are heavily invested they often make up a story to justify their commitment, and that story carries trust; lowering your price does the opposite.
confounders: missing the efficiency exemption and reading it as a blanket rule against low prices
treating the trust-from-cost mechanism as established; it is cognitive-dissonance reasoning with no citation

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 "Trust and Tension Create Forward Motion", section "How the status quo got that way" (spine 17)
qa_items.question: "The status quo doesn't shift because you're right." Reconstruct Godin's full argument, including the chain he states in Chapter Nine.
qa_items.answer: The status quo exists for a reason and is good at resisting insurgents. If truth alone were sufficient we would have changed long ago; if a better idea or a simpler solution or a more efficient procedure were sufficient, the change would have happened a year or a decade or a century ago. It shifts because the culture changes, and the engine of culture is status. The chain behind this is stated in Chapter Nine: behaviour is driven by the desire to fit in — do people like me do things like this — and by the perception of status, both of those forces push us to stay as we are, and therefore it takes tension to change them. That is why a correct argument does nothing: it addresses neither driver.
qa_items.support: How the status quo got that way: they're good at resisting insurgents; if all it took was the truth we would have changed long ago; it shifts because the culture changes, and the engine of culture is status. Ch. 9: changing our behaviour is driven by our desire to fit in and our perception of our status; since both push us to stay as we are, it takes tension to change them.
confounders: reading it as advice to argue better or to simplify the message
treating status as one factor among several; Godin makes it the engine

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 "People Like Us Do Things Like This", sections "People like us (do things like this)" and "Which us?" (spine 16)
qa_items.question: Godin's phrase is "people like us do things like this". What is the loop he describes, what does he say the marketer's first job is, and what does he say is the wrong way to do it?
qa_items.answer: The loop is: normalisation creates culture, culture drives our choices, and those choices lead to more normalisation — with the individual choice made in answer to one question, do people like me do things like this. He adds that even outliers are aligning, with the behaviour of outliers. The marketer's first job is simple and he states it as such: define "us". The more specific, the more connected and the tighter the "us", the better. The wrong way is to define it by outcome — "the people who give are people like us" — which he says is backwards. And the scope claim matters: we cannot change "the culture", only "a culture", our little pocket of the world, which is why he treats the smallest viable market as the unit that maximises the chance of changing anything at all.
qa_items.support: People like us: from the first day we can remember, our actions are primarily driven by "do people like me do things like this?"; normalization creates culture, and culture drives our choices, which leads to more normalization; we can't change the culture, but each of us can change a culture. Which us?: the first job is to define "us"; the right answer is not "the people who give are people like us" — that's backwards.
confounders: treating it as a slogan about social proof rather than as a self-reinforcing loop with a defining step
defining the group by who already buys, which is the backwards definition he rejects

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 "Status, Dominance, and Affiliation", section "Six things about status" (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Godin lists six properties of status. Give them, and say which one most often trips up a marketer who assumes what everyone wants.
qa_items.answer: Status is always relative — there is no absolute scale and no highest number. It is in the eye of the beholder, so someone can be low status to outsiders and high status in their own narrative, both true at once. Status attended to is the status that matters; it is only relevant when the person engaged with cares about it. It has inertia: we are more likely to work to maintain our status, high or low, than to change it. It is learned, though a cohort can shift the perception quickly. And shame is the status killer, which is why shame is used as a lever — it works. The one that trips people up is inertia, together with the correction Godin draws from it: it is a mistake to believe everyone wants higher status, and equally a mistake to believe no one wants lower. Some people will fight to keep the role they have. All six are assertions in a numbered list, unsourced and untested.
qa_items.support: Six things about status: always relative; in the eyes of the beholder; status attended to is the status that matters; has inertia; is learned; shame is the status killer. Plus: it's a mistake to believe that everyone wants to make their status higher — in fact, few people do.
confounders: assuming a status offer is always an upgrade offer
treating the six as findings rather than as a practitioner's working list

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 "Status, Dominance, and Affiliation", sections "Affiliation and dominion are different ways to measure status" and "Affiliation or dominance is up to the customer, not you" (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Two audiences respond to completely different status signals. Distinguish Godin's two measures, give the questions each asks, and say why the pair is not a segmentation.
qa_items.answer: Dominion is vertical — above or below. Its questions are: who has more power; this is mine, not yours; I did this myself; my side dominating your side. Affiliation is horizontal — who is standing next to me. Its questions are: who knows you; who trusts you; have you made things better; where do you stand within the tribe. They also behave differently under abundance: affiliation admires the network effect, since more affiliation benefits everyone affiliated, while dominion is scarcity-bound because someone must be below. The reason it is not a segmentation is that Godin says the same person switches by situation — his example is a twelve-year-old who cares about nothing but beating the opposition on the field and cares a lot about who sits next to him on the bus. It describes a moment, not a personality. And the priority is stated: which measure applies is the customer's, not yours.
qa_items.support: Affiliation and dominion: the affiliation questions (who knows you, who trusts you, where do you stand within the tribe) against the dominion ones (this is mine not yours, who has more power); dominion is vertical, affiliation horizontal; affiliation admires the network effect, abundance is welcome; the ball-field child who cares only about winning but also about who sits next to him; the way you see the world isn't nearly as important as the worldview of those you seek to serve.
confounders: using it as a persona split, when Godin makes it situational
assuming affiliation is the good one; he presents both as legitimate measures
projecting your own measure onto the audience, the error he names explicitly

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 "Trust and Tension Create Forward Motion", section "Tension is not the same as fear" (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Godin distinguishes tension from fear. State the distinction and its mechanism, then say why the test he offers is unsatisfactory.
qa_items.answer: Fear is a dream killer: it puts people into suspended animation, holding their breath, paralysed and unable to move forward, and fear alone will not produce change. Tension is different in kind — it is the promise that we can get through that fear to the other side, the state of "this might work versus this might not work", and the state of being aware you do not yet know something. He calls it the hallmark of a great educational experience and says all effective education creates it. The mechanism is that both are discomfort and they differ in whether a route out is visible: where forward motion is available the discomfort is a reason to move, and where it is not, the same discomfort immobilises. The test is unsatisfactory because it is the maker's own feeling — if you feel like you are coercing, manipulating or frightening people, you are probably doing it wrong — which gives the person on the receiving end no criterion at all. Several of his own approved cases sit close to the line he is drawing.
qa_items.support: Tension is not the same as fear: if you feel like you're coercing people, manipulating them or causing them to be afraid, you're probably doing it wrong; fear's a dream killer, it puts people into suspended animation; there might be fear, but tension is the promise that we can get through that fear to the other side; tension is the hallmark of a great educational experience.
confounders: treating tension and fear as points on one scale rather than as different states
accepting the maker's-feeling test as an operational criterion
the modern default of reading any manufactured urgency as illegitimate; Godin defends manufactured tension and rejects only fear

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 "Trust and Tension Create Forward Motion", sections "What are you breaking?" and "Marketers create tension, and forward motion relieves that tension" (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Godin says launching anything breaks something. What does he mean, and how does that connect to his claim that the tension is manufactured?
qa_items.answer: The very existence of an alternative causes something else to stop being true. The second hotel in a town means the first is no longer the only one; an exclusive party makes the uninvited into outsiders; a fancier casino makes last year's satisfied visitor ask whether he is the sort of person who goes somewhere this run-down. So a new offering does not merely add an option — it degrades the standing of what people already chose, and that degradation is the tension. The connection to manufacture is that Godin is unusually direct about it: none of these feelings existed before a marketer showed up with something that caused them; if there were no new album you would not feel left out for not having heard it. We intentionally create these gaps, these little canyons of tension people find themselves leaping over. His diagnostic is a question to the maker: when you arrive with your solution, do you also create tension — because if you do not, the status quo is likely to survive.
qa_items.support: What are you breaking?: the very existence of an alternative causes something else to no longer be true; when you host an exclusive party, the people who aren't invited become outsiders; this is what tension feels like, the tension of being left behind. Marketers create tension: none of those feelings existed before a marketer showed up with something that caused them; we intentionally create these gaps.
confounders: reading the tension as pre-existing demand that the offering satisfies
assuming 'breaking something' means damaging a competitor commercially rather than changing what a choice says about the person who made it

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 "Trust and Tension Create Forward Motion", section "Pattern match/pattern interrupt" (spine 17)
qa_items.question: You are launching into a category where every buyer already has an established routine. What does Godin say you are up against, and what timing rule does he derive from it?
qa_items.answer: A pattern interrupt. Where a pattern exists, the routine has to be undone before any forward motion is possible, and the default answer to that request is no — because the pattern is established, time is precious and risk is feared. His mechanism is that undoing a pattern requires the person to accept their previous choice was wrong, which is a status cost on top of the switching cost. The timing rule follows: market to people who do not have a pattern yet. When life interferes — a new parent, someone recently engaged, someone who has just moved — there is nothing to match, so it is all interrupt and you do not have to persuade anyone that their old choices were mistakes. The same logic makes a brand-new platform the best time to launch an app on it. He also notes the institutional mirror: a purchasing manager has been taught that matching the pattern is how you keep a steady job with no surprises.
qa_items.support: Pattern match/pattern interrupt: a pattern interrupt requires some sort of jolt and most of the time the answer is no, because the patterns are established, time is precious and risk is feared; when life interferes, new patterns are established, which is why it's profitable to market to new dads, engaged women and people who have recently moved; when you market to someone who doesn't have a pattern yet, you don't have to persuade them their old choices were mistakes.
confounders: answering with message strategy when his answer is about timing and audience state
assuming a better offer overcomes an established pattern; the pattern must be undone first

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 13 "Semiotics, Symbols, and Vernacular", sections "What does this remind you of?" and "Why is Nigerian spam so sloppy?" (spine 20)
qa_items.question: Godin argues that badly spelled advance-fee scam mail is not incompetent. What is his reading, and what general claim about form does it illustrate?
qa_items.answer: His reading is that the errors are a filter. The mail is sending a signal to people who are skeptical, careful and well-informed: go away. Putting anyone else into the process wastes the sender's time, and they would rather lose you at the beginning than invest in you and lose you at the end. The general claim is that form acts before content does. Busy people scan rather than study, and while scanning they ask what this reminds them of — and the answer decides whether they are the audience and whether the maker is credible, before any argument is considered. So the vernacular of a category — typefaces, photo styles, copy — is a membership signal: you are not people like us if you do not talk the way we expect you to. Note this is an inference about the senders' intent, not a reported finding about their strategy.
qa_items.support: Why is Nigerian spam so sloppy?: because it's not for you; they're sending a signal to people who are skeptical, careful and well-informed: go away; they'd rather lose you at the beginning than invest in you and lose you at the end. What does this remind you of?: we scan instead of study; we want to know if it's for us, and if you're the real deal.
confounders: reading the sloppiness as low effort or poor language skills
treating semiotics as decoration on top of the message rather than as the thing read first

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 13 "Semiotics, Symbols, and Vernacular", sections "The flag is not for everyone" and "The same and the different" (spine 20)
qa_items.question: You need a piece of work to read as new without reading as untrustworthy. What two-part instruction does Godin give, and what paradox does he say sits underneath it?
qa_items.answer: Send a signal that feels like a sign we already trust, then change it enough to let us know it is new and that it is yours. He explains why the first half is not laziness: most car ads look alike because the sameness signals that this is a car worth considering, a safe alternative for a large purchase, and most big-company logos resemble each other because the designers are trying to remind you of a solid company. The paradox is that to make change you have to go first, hanging over one edge or another, but that innovation reminds some people of a past thing that went wrong — so you begin with the audience that tolerates the resemblance, because it is the only audience that will give a new thing a chance. He adds that not flying a flag is as intentional as flying one, and that pretending your features are so good nothing else matters is the foolish move.
qa_items.support: The flag is not for everyone: send a signal that feels like a sign we already trust, then change it enough to let us know that it's new, and that it's yours; there's a paradox — to make change we need to go first, but that innovation reminds some people of a past event that went wrong. The same and the different: most car ads look the same because the sameness signals a safe alternative; a good designer offers you the chance to fit in.
confounders: reading category conventions as unimaginative rather than as a trust signal Godin defends
maximising distinctiveness, when his instruction is resemblance first and variation second

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 14 "Treat Different People Differently", section "In search of the neophiliacs" (spine 21)
qa_items.question: Godin says you should not spend a minute on people who are satisfied with what they have. Is that a judgement about those people? Give his actual reason.
qa_items.answer: No — it is a resource argument. If someone is satisfied with what they have, you are unlikely to have the time or the money to reach out and make them dissatisfied enough to become interested, so the minute is wasted for both of you, which is why he calls the restraint humility rather than dismissal. The people worth beginning with are the neophiliacs, who are addicted to the new, thrilled by discovery and forgiving of missteps while the thrill lasts. His stark version is that the only people you can serve are the curious, the dissatisfied or the bored — everyone else can opt out and refuse to pay attention. And the exclusion is temporary in principle: it's not for them, not right now; with persistence you may reach them later, horizontally, person to person.
qa_items.support: In search of the neophiliacs: good marketers have the humility to understand that you shouldn't waste a minute on anyone who isn't on the left part of the curve; if someone is satisfied with what they have, you're unlikely to have the time or money to cause them to become dissatisfied; it's not for them, not right now; with persistence you'll get to them, perhaps, horizontally.
confounders: reading it as writing those people off permanently
assuming a big enough budget solves it; his claim is about what dissatisfaction costs to manufacture

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 19 "The Funnel", sections "Bridging the chasm" and "Where's your bridge?" (spine 26)
qa_items.question: Why does Godin deny that early adopters will carry your idea to the mass market, and what does he say the bridge actually is?
qa_items.answer: Because the two groups want opposite things. The mass market wants something that works and is safe — a pattern match, not a pattern interrupt — and takes "people like us do things like this" very seriously; so satisfying the early adopters may require annoying the masses, and the very thing the innovation did, breaking things, is what the mass market does not want to happen. The bridge is structural rather than persuasive: an idea that works better when others also use it gives the early adopter a selfish reason to recruit, because their own life improves when their network joins. He reduces the design question to two: what will I tell my friends, and why will I tell them. And the negative is stated flatly — it is never the case that people tell their friends because you want them to, asked them to, or worked hard.
qa_items.support: Bridging the chasm: the intuitive answer is that early adopters bring your idea to the masses, but often that's not what happens; the mass market wants something that works, something safe, a pattern match not a pattern interrupt; in order to satisfy the early adopters you may just need to annoy the masses. Where's your bridge?: the bridge lies in network effects; what will I tell my friends, why will I tell them.
confounders: assuming enthusiasm or advocacy carries the idea across; his bridge is self-interest
treating the chasm as a marketing-spend problem rather than as a conflict of wants

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 19 "The Funnel", section "You might not find the bridge" (spine 26)
qa_items.question: Godin tells one failure story against himself. What did his project achieve, what did it lack, and which two lessons does he draw?
qa_items.answer: The project — pages profiling products, with a share of the resulting commission going to a charity — achieved trial: thousands of pages were built. What it lacked was whales. Fewer than six people built more than a dozen pages or promoted them much. His diagnosis is that the tension dissipated too quickly, people felt they had no good reason to return after a single visit, and a typical page sold nothing in a month, so the dynamic that would have turned early users into connected ambassadors never formed. The two lessons he draws are that they did not tell a story about status, and that they were not nearly specific enough about who the first customers would be, what they might have wanted, believed and said. He adds that four months was a naïve amount of time in which to create an overnight success.
qa_items.support: You might not find the bridge: we kept at it for months but we failed; we got trial, thousands of pages were built, but we failed to find any whales; the tension dissipated too quickly, people felt they had no good reason to return; we didn't do enough to tell a story about status, and we weren't nearly specific enough about who our first customers would be.
confounders: attributing the failure to the offer's economics rather than to the absence of a reason to return
reading trial as evidence the mechanism was working

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 17 "Permission and Remarkability in a Virtuous Cycle", sections "Transform your project by being remarkable" and "Designing for evangelism" (spine 24)
qa_items.question: A team asks how to make an asset that people will share. Give Godin's two constraints, and say why they rule out most of what is usually attempted.
qa_items.answer: First, the verdict is not yours. Whether something is remarkable is decided by the user: if they remark on it, it is remarkable — so remarkability can be observed but never claimed. Second, the motive belongs to the teller. People spread the word when it benefits them, because talking about your thing is a way of talking about themselves — look how good my taste is, look how good I am at spotting important ideas — and never because it matters to you, because you asked, or because you worked hard. Together these rule out the usual attempts: adding a share prompt, appealing to the importance of the cause, and the stunt, which Godin says comes from a place of selfishness and warns is not the same thing as remarkable. What is left is designing the reason to tell into the product or service itself, which is why he says effective marketers are also in charge of the customer's experience.
qa_items.support: Transform your project by being remarkable: whether something is remarkable isn't up to you, the creator; if they remark on it, then it's remarkable; you must do it with intent, building it deep into the product or service. Designing for evangelism: people aren't going to spread the word because it's important to you; they'll only do it because it's important to them.
confounders: reaching for a share incentive or a call to action, which addresses neither constraint
assuming being talked about proves the mechanism worked; Godin notes criticism also spreads, as a signal to shun you
treating 'if they remark on it, it's remarkable' as a test rather than as the circular definition it is

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 17 "Permission and Remarkability in a Virtuous Cycle", sections "Permission is anticipated, personal, and relevant" and "Earn your own permission and own it" (spine 24)
qa_items.question: Godin defines permission and then gives a test that disqualifies most of what is called permission. State both, and give the two consequences he draws.
qa_items.answer: The definition: the privilege of delivering anticipated, personal and relevant messages to people who want to get them. The test: if you stopped showing up, would people be concerned and ask where you went. He is explicit that real permission is not presumed or legalistic — having somebody's address, their failure to complain, or a clause in a privacy policy is none of it. The two consequences. First, the promise made in exchange is binding until both sides agree to change it: a launch, the end of a quarter or a campaign does not create a right to break the deal you made. Second, an audience assembled on a platform is not an asset you own — you do not have permission to contact those people, the platform does, which makes you a sharecropper on someone else's land.
qa_items.support: Permission is anticipated, personal, and relevant: real permission is different from presumed or legalistic permission; if you stop showing up, people are concerned, they ask where you went; the promise is the promise until both sides agree to change it. Earn your own permission: it's not your land, you don't have permission to contact people, they do.
confounders: equating permission with consent under a privacy policy, which he explicitly excludes
counting followers on a platform as an owned permission asset

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 "Reaching the Right People", section "Frequency" (spine 22)
qa_items.question: A team wants to change its campaign because everyone internally is sick of it. What does Godin say is happening, what is his memory claim, and what stopping rule does he actually supply?
qa_items.answer: They are inside the dip — the gap between when the maker gets bored and when the audience gets the message — and changing now forfeits the trust that frequency was building. His memory claim is that people do not remember what they read, hear or see; they remember what they rehearse, the things seen again and again, and the market has been trained to associate frequency with trust, because the familiar is normal and the normal is trusted. The stopping rule he supplies is a quoted maxim: do not change your ads when you are tired of them, or when your employees are, or when your friends are — change them when your accountant is tired of them. That is a heuristic with no criterion in it, and it cannot distinguish persistence from stubbornness. He generalises the point well beyond advertising: people give a talk a few times and move on, or raise money and spend it fast, hitting the wall just before the good part.
qa_items.support: Frequency: people don't remember what they read, hear or see — we remember what we rehearse; the market has been trained to associate frequency with trust; there's a very real dip, a gap between when we get bored and when people get the message; don't change your ads when you're tired of them, change them when your accountant is tired of them.
confounders: treating internal boredom as evidence of audience wear-out
reading the accountant maxim as an actual decision criterion
confusing this with a claim about creative quality; his claim is about repetition and trust

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 "Reaching the Right People", sections "Brand marketing makes magic; direct marketing makes the phone ring", "A simple guide to online direct marketing" and "A simple guide to brand marketing" (spine 22)
qa_items.question: Godin says two paragraphs of his book should have paid for it. What is the separation they make, what opposite disciplines follow, and what does he say the real danger is?
qa_items.answer: Direct marketing is action-oriented and is measured; brand marketing is culturally oriented and cannot be measured. The disciplines that follow are opposites, and he states both as instructions. For direct: measure everything — what attention costs, what a click costs, what an order costs — and if you cannot measure it, it does not count. For brand: be patient, refuse to measure, engage with the culture, focus and above all be consistent — and if you cannot afford to be consistent and patient, do not buy brand advertising at all. The danger he names is neither discipline done badly but the confusion of the two, which is what makes a shift to a measured environment destroy a business built on unmeasurable brand advertising. He adds the gate: if you cannot see the funnel, do not buy the ads, and if you can see it and it costs too much, fix the funnel first. And the narrowing rule still applies — you cannot afford to build a brand for everyone, so be specific.
qa_items.support: Brand marketing makes magic: direct marketing is action oriented and measured, brand marketing is culturally oriented and can't be measured; the danger is in being confused; if you're buying direct ads measure everything, if you're buying brand ads be patient and refuse to measure; if you can't afford to be consistent and patient, don't pay for brand marketing ads. Ch. 19: if you can't see the funnel, don't buy the ads.
confounders: trying to measure brand advertising, which he treats as the characteristic error
assuming digital measurement is always an improvement; his case is a business destroyed by the shift
treating attribution as the issue; his separation is about what the spending is for

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 19 "The Funnel", section "The truth about your funnel" (spine 26)
qa_items.question: Godin gives the direct-response funnel a careful treatment and then undercuts it. What is the undercut, and what does he say builds the brands that matter?
qa_items.answer: The undercut is that the lifetime value of a new customer rarely exceeds the cost of the advertising needed to acquire one. People are distrustful, the web is cluttered, and the ads rarely have enough power to pay for themselves, so a self-running funnel of income is rare however carefully it is built. What builds the brands that matter, in his account, is everything after the first click: they are primed by advertising but built by good marketing — they grow because users evangelise to their friends, because they keep offering more value to the communities they serve, and because they find groups that coalesce around the change they produce. His warning is that attempts to build a perpetual motion machine of profit almost always end in bitterness, because they require you to push too hard and too fast to do anything that lasts.
qa_items.support: The truth about your funnel: it's not going to be a magical fountain of results; the lifetime value of a new customer rarely exceeds the cost of running the ads necessary to get one; most brands that matter are primed by advertising but built by good marketing; attempts to build a perpetual motion machine of profit almost always end with bitterness.
confounders: reading the funnel arithmetic as his recommendation rather than as a control he then qualifies
assuming better optimisation closes the gap; his claim is that the economics usually do not work

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market" (spine 11) against Ch. 19 "The Funnel", section "Bridging the chasm" (spine 26)
qa_items.question: Godin tells you to serve the smallest viable market and also that the mass market wants the opposite of what those people want. Reconcile the two, and say what he does not resolve.
qa_items.answer: They are consecutive stages, not competing strategies. The smallest viable market is where you begin, because a defined audience permits the extremity that makes the work worth remarking on and because it maximises the chance of changing a culture — one pocket of the world rather than the culture. The chasm is the cost of having begun there: satisfying that group may require annoying the mass market, whose wants are opposite. The bridge between the two is not persuasion, and it is not the early adopters' enthusiasm; it is a network effect that gives the early adopter a selfish reason to recruit. What he does not resolve is what to do when the offering has no network effect — his own counter-example is a chocolate you like, which does not improve your life if others eat it. For those categories he names no bridge, and the sequence simply stops.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4: the smallest viable market is the focus that leads to your growth; Ch. 9: it maximises your chances of changing a culture. Ch. 19: the mass market wants something that works, safe, a pattern match; in order to satisfy the early adopters, you may just need to annoy the masses; the bridge lies in network effects; there's no reason to talk about a new kind of chocolate you like, it doesn't make your life better if others eat it.
confounders: treating the two as a contradiction rather than as stages
assuming the narrow audience simply grows into the mass market; Godin explicitly denies the glide
assuming every offering has a bridge available

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 "The Smallest Viable Market", section "Forcing a focus" (spine 11), with Ch. 8 "More of the Who", section "What would Jerry do?" (spine 15)
qa_items.question: A client wants the widest possible reach and cites their competitors' audience numbers. Using Godin's argument, what do you tell them — and what is the weakest part of your own case?
qa_items.answer: That the reach target is a constraint on the work, not a measure of it: aiming at the centre of the curve requires offending no one and satisfying everyone, which forces the compromises and generalisations that make work boring, and boring audiences are static and are not looking for you. The alternative is to ask the floor question — the minimum number of people we would need to influence for this to be worth doing — and then spend everything on making the work extreme enough for them to talk about. The weakest part of the case is the evidence. Every example Godin offers is a survivor: a restaurant that became famous, a band that grossed hundreds of millions, a lobbying organisation with millions of members. Projects that narrowed and simply stayed small are absent from the book and cannot appear in it, so the promise that focus leads to growth is supported by cases selected on the outcome it predicts.
qa_items.support: Forcing a focus: mass means average and requires you to offend no one and satisfy everyone; what's the minimum number of people you would need to influence to make it worth the effort; the smallest viable market is the focus that leads to your growth. Ch. 7: the marketplace of people who are happy with boring is static, they aren't looking for better. Ch. 8: the survivor cases.
confounders: arguing from efficiency or budget, which is not his case
presenting the survivor examples as evidence for the growth claim
dropping 'viable' and arguing for the smallest audience rather than the smallest sufficient one

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 "More of the Who: Seeking the Smallest Viable Market", section "Why don't people choose you?" (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Godin sets an exercise for the people who buy from a competitor even though they know you exist. What is the exercise, what sentence must be completed, and what is it for?
qa_items.answer: The exercise is to ask why those people are right — not why they are misinformed, and not what would change their minds. He is explicit that the tempting move is to denigrate their judgement, question their values and assume they are ill-informed, selfish or wrongheaded, and the exercise is to put that aside. The sentence to complete is: "For people who want what you want (___) and believe what you believe (___), your choice of ___ is exactly correct." It is for stretching the empathy muscle: people make perfectly rational decisions based on what they see, believe and want, so completing the sentence forces you to reconstruct the worldview under which the competitor is the right answer. His cooking-class illustration makes the point that both parties can be right at once — the student who substitutes an ingredient cares more about the story than about matching a taste profile, and the chef for whom the memory of the dish is everything reads substitution as disrespect for his work.
qa_items.support: Why don't people choose you?: those people who don't buy from you, who happily buy from a competitor even if they know you exist — why are they right?; it's tempting to denigrate their judgement and assume they're ill-informed, selfish or wrongheaded; find the empathy to fill in this sentence; people are quite likely to make perfectly rational decisions based on what they see, what they believe, and what they want.
confounders: reframing the exercise as identifying objections to overcome, which reverses its purpose
treating the competitor's customers as a segment to be won rather than as people for whom your offering is not the answer
assuming Godin means they are right about the product; he means right given what they want and believe

qa_items.source_title: Seth Godin, This Is Marketing: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 21 "Some Case Studies Using the Method", section "Getting the boss to say yes" (spine 28)
qa_items.question: You need internal approval for a project. Godin says marketing to one person is not different in kind. Apply his method: what are you modelling, and what three moves does he say will not work?
qa_items.answer: You are modelling the same things you would model for any audience. She is not eager to change her worldview; she sees things through the lens of her experience, not yours; she is aware of who the people like us are and what they think; and she wants what helps her achieve her goals, which probably include status, safety and respect. So the work is to see the status roles, decode whether she is measuring dominion or affiliation, and use trust to earn enrollment — turning her from a customer into a student, step by step. The three moves he says will not work: going to her with what you want; leading on price, features or false urgency; and asking for authority without offering responsibility.
qa_items.support: Getting the boss to say yes: it's one thing to market to the world and it feels different to market to one person, except it's not, not really; your boss is probably not eager to change her worldview, she sees things through the lens of her experience, she wants what helps her achieve her goals, which probably include status, safety and respect; if you go to her with what you want, with a focus on price or features or false urgency, it's unlikely to lead to the answer you seek; if you ask for authority without offering responsibility, that too is unlikely.
confounders: building a business case on features and cost, which is the first move he rules out
assuming internal persuasion is a different discipline requiring different tools
leading with urgency, which he names as the false version

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, "About the ABCDs of effective video ads", section "Benefits"; Think with Google, "Understanding the ABCDs of effective creative on YouTube", section "Crafting a successful ad"; Google for Business resources, "ABCDs of effective video ads", headline statistic callouts and footnote
qa_items.question: Google states the same ABCD effectiveness result on three of its own pages. How does the phrasing differ between them, and why does the difference matter?
qa_items.answer: Three different strengths for one finding. Google Ads Help says the ABCDs "Deliver as much as a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution" — an upper bound. Think with Google says "On average, the ABCDs deliver a 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17% lift in long-term brand contribution" — a central tendency. The Google for Business resources article prints the two numbers as bare callouts with no qualifier at all, above a page-footer line reading "Actual results will vary by advertiser". An upper bound and an average are different statistics, and a reader who meets one page will draw a different expectation from a reader who meets another. Nothing on any of the three pages resolves which is right, and this bank does not resolve it either.
qa_items.support: The three phrasings are verbatim from the three pages named in the locator. The source offers no reconciliation and the underlying study is not published on any of them.
confounders: assuming Google's own pages must state the same finding identically, and reporting only one phrasing
reading 'as much as' as the average, which is the more flattering error and the more common one
confusing this with an IPA-style databank figure of the kind Binet and Field report, which comes with a published methodology appendix
assuming the bare callouts on the resources article carry the 'on average' qualifier from elsewhere

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google for Business resources, "ABCDs of effective video ads", footnote to the headline statistics; Google Ads Help, section "Benefits", asterisked source note; Think with Google, "Sources (1)"
qa_items.question: What study are the 30% and 17% figures attributed to, and which of the three pages tells you the sample size?
qa_items.answer: All three attribute them to a Google/Kantar study called "The Short & the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness", global, dated April 2021 — but only the Google for Business resources article gives a sample, "n=11,000 ads". Google Ads Help cites the same study, publisher, scope and month with no sample size. Think with Google cites it as "Google/Kantar Link AI, Global, The Short and the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness, 2021", naming Kantar's Link AI, dropping the month and giving no sample size. The study itself is not linked or published on any of the pages.
qa_items.support: The three footnotes differ as described. n=11,000 ads appears only in the resources article's footnote.
confounders: attributing the sample size to the Google Ads Help page, which is the page most often cited but does not give it
assuming n=11,000 refers to people surveyed rather than ads
conflating this Kantar study with the separate Ipsos collaboration described on Think with Google, which has no stated sample

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Benefits" and its source note; Think with Google, "Understanding the ABCDs of effective creative on YouTube", opening paragraph
qa_items.question: A colleague cites the 30% lift as independently verified evidence that the ABCDs work. On the source's own presentation, what can honestly be said about that figure and what cannot?
qa_items.answer: It is a reported measurement result, so it is more than an assertion — but it is reported by the company that sells advertising on the platform the research validates, from a study named but not published on any of the three pages. No method, comparison baseline, market coverage or dispersion is given, and neither "short-term sales likelihood" nor "long-term brand contribution" is defined. The independent-reviewer language on the Think with Google page (Ipsos as research partner, Nielsen and Kantar as two independent reviewers) is stated about how the framework was arrived at, not offered as verification of these two numbers. And the figure is claimed for the ABCDs as a set: the source never decomposes it by principle. Third- party involvement moderates the publisher's interest here; it does not remove it.
qa_items.support: Ads Help "Benefits" carries the figure and the source note; the Ipsos/Nielsen/Kantar sentence is on Think with Google and describes the derivation of the principles, not an audit of the lift figures.
confounders: reading 'two independent reviewers' as an independent audit of the 30%/17% figures
treating a named study as a published one
attributing part of the lift to a single principle, which the source never does

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Think with Google, "Understanding the ABCDs of effective creative on YouTube", section "B = Branding: Brand early, often, and richly"
qa_items.question: The source states that "YouTube is almost entirely a sound-on experience". What is the scope of that claim, and what would it be wrong to conclude from it?
qa_items.answer: It is a claim about how one named platform was being watched, made once, on the Think with Google page dated April 2022, and offered as the reason to exploit the multisensory nature of the medium. It is not a claim about short-form or feed video in general, and it points the opposite way from the sound-off default that other feed surfaces are usually designed against. No measurement, figure or study is attached to it. Neither of the other two pages states it, even though guidelines on both — reinforcing branding with audio, supercharging the CTA with voice-over, supporting the story with audio — depend on it being true. Viewing behaviour changes, so a claim of this kind is true of a period, and the source names no period beyond its own date.
qa_items.support: The sentence appears once, under Branding on the Think with Google page. The audio-dependent guidelines appear on the other two pages without the premise being restated.
confounders: the widely repeated claim that most social video is watched on mute, which is about other surfaces and points the other way
generalising the claim to all vertical or short-form video
assuming the Google Ads Help article states it, since that is where most of the audio guidelines live
treating it as a measured finding; the source gives no number for it

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Think with Google, section "B = Branding"; Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", rows "Attention", "Branding" and "Direction"; Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Awareness: Get noticed"
qa_items.question: You are adapting an ad built to this guidance for a feed placement that autoplays muted. Which of the source's guidelines lose their premise, and what does the source itself say about that situation?
qa_items.answer: Every audio-dependent guideline loses its premise, because the premise is the source's assertion that YouTube is almost entirely sound-on. That is: "Reinforce with audio" / "See and say" (an audio brand mention enhancing the on-screen brand visual), "Supercharge CTAs with audio" (voice-over reinforcing the on-screen CTA), the audio half of "Support the story with audio and supers", the audio component of the Attention principle's immersive opening, and the awareness row's "Pump up the volume by using audio to get viewers to pay attention". As to what to do instead, the source says nothing at all. It addresses YouTube, asserts sound-on there, and offers no sound-off variant, no fallback and no acknowledgement that other surfaces behave differently. Anything filled in here comes from outside this source.
qa_items.support: The five audio-dependent guidelines are at the locators given; the sound-on premise is stated only on Think with Google. No page addresses a muted surface.
confounders: importing standard muted-feed practice (burn-in captions, text-first storytelling) and attributing it to this source
assuming the source's 'supers' guidance is a sound-off provision; it is stated as reinforcement, not as substitution
assuming the objective table has a sound-off row; it has four rows, all objectives

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", the "Principle" column of all four rows
qa_items.question: Give the source's own one-line statement of each of the four ABCD principles, as printed in the core table.
qa_items.answer: Attention — "Hook and sustain attention with an immersive story." Branding — "Brand early, often, and richly." Connection — "Help people think or feel something." Direction — "Ask them to take action." Two details are easy to lose. Attention asks for two things, hooking and sustaining, not one. And Branding's three adverbs are three separate dimensions: when the brand first appears, how often it recurs, and how many different kinds of branding element carry it.
qa_items.support: The four principle statements are printed verbatim in the "Principle" column of the core ABCDs table.
confounders: expanding Direction as 'drive conversions', which is a category the source does not use here
reading Branding as a frequency instruction only, dropping 'richly'
reading Attention as being about the opening alone, dropping 'sustain'

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs" (all four rows); Google for Business resources, "ABCDs of effective video ads", sections "A – Attention" through "D – Direction"
qa_items.question: The Google Ads Help table and the Google for Business resources article both enumerate the core ABCD techniques. Where do the two lists differ?
qa_items.answer: In naming and in one item of substance. Four techniques carry different names on the two pages: "Support the story with audio and supers" against "Emphasize key points"; "Reinforce with audio" against "See and say"; "Engage" against "Be engaging"; and "Supercharge CTAs with audio" against "Boost CTAs with audio". The substantive difference is in Branding: Google Ads Help carries a third guideline, "Draw on all your branding assets", that the resources article's Branding section does not have — it names only two. So the Ads Help table lists eleven techniques (3 Attention, 3 Branding, 3 Connection, 2 Direction) and the resources article lists ten (3, 2, 3, 2). Anyone retrieving on one page's label alone will miss the other page.
qa_items.support: Counted directly off the two pages' sub-headings. The naming differences are verbatim.
confounders: assuming the two lists are identical because both are Google-published
treating 'See and say' and 'Reinforce with audio' as two different techniques rather than one under two names
assuming each principle carries three techniques; Direction carries two on both pages

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Awareness: Get noticed"
qa_items.question: For an awareness objective, what does the source's objective table prescribe for each of the four principles?
qa_items.answer: Attention: "Pump up the volume by using audio to get viewers to pay attention". Branding: "Put your brand front and center". Connection carries two instructions in one cell — "Make the people core to the story" and "Be different, yet simple". Direction: "Apply core principles", meaning no objective-specific treatment. The awareness row is the only one in which Direction takes no special instruction.
qa_items.support: Read from the awareness row of the four-column objective table on the Google Ads Help page.
confounders: expecting a stronger or softer CTA instruction for awareness; the source gives none
assuming attention for awareness is won visually; the source's instruction here is specifically audio
assigning 'Be different, yet simple' to Direction; both it and 'Make the people core to the story' sit in the Connection cell

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", all four table rows
qa_items.question: In the objective table, three cells read "Apply core principles". Which principle is left at core under which objective, and what does that pattern tell you about the framework?
qa_items.answer: Direction is left at core under awareness. Attention is left at core under both consideration and action. The full-funnel row has no such cell — all four principles carry an objective-specific instruction there. The pattern matters because it shows the objective table varies emphasis and never varies membership: no principle is dropped for any objective, and where an objective calls for no special treatment the cell says to apply the core guidance rather than being left empty. That is the strongest textual evidence that the source treats the four as jointly applied rather than as a menu.
qa_items.support: Read off the four-row, four-column table; the "Apply core principles" cells are in the Direction column of the awareness row and the Attention column of the consideration and action rows.
confounders: assuming action campaigns downweight Branding; the action row carries the table's strongest branding instruction, 'Make the product the ad'
assuming awareness campaigns drop Direction entirely rather than leaving it at core
assuming full funnel is a blend of the other three rows rather than four instructions of its own

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Awareness: Get noticed"; section "Core ABCDs", rows "Attention", "Branding" and "Connection"
qa_items.question: A 20-second ad for a new energy drink opens on a silent slow-motion product beauty shot, brings the logo up only at the very end, shows no people at all, and closes on a "Buy now" end card. The brief is an awareness campaign. Judged strictly by this source, what is wrong with it — and what is not?
qa_items.answer: Three of the four awareness instructions are missed. Attention for awareness is to be won with audio ("Pump up the volume by using audio to get viewers to pay attention") and the opening is silent. Branding is to be "front and center" and the brand arrives last, which also fails the core guideline to show up early and throughout. Connection is to "Make the people core to the story", and there are no people, which also fails the core guideline to humanise the story. What is not wrong on this source's terms is the end card: awareness is the one row where Direction is left at "Apply core principles", and the core guidance asks only that a CTA be present and intentionally chosen for a specific objective. The source gives no basis for calling the ask misplaced or over-strong here, and asserting one would go beyond it.
qa_items.support: Awareness row: audio-led attention, brand front and centre, people core to the story, Direction at core. Core rows supply the early-and-throughout and humanise guidelines.
confounders: criticising the 'Buy now' CTA as wrong for awareness — a reasonable marketing instinct that this source does not support
citing 'Jump in' against the slow-motion opening; the source's pacing guidance is about reaching the story's point, and a beauty shot is not judged on speed alone
assuming a product-led ad satisfies Branding; the source's awareness instruction is about the brand being front and centre, and its Branding guidance asks for variety of asset

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Action: Present an enticing call-to-action with the right context"; section "Core ABCDs", row "Direction"
qa_items.question: A performance team wants to put the call to action in the first two seconds of an action-objective ad, to catch viewers who skip. What does this source's own guidance say about that placement?
qa_items.answer: It says the opposite, and it is the source's only placement instruction anywhere. The action row's Direction cell reads "Present the ask after the context is set", and the objective's own statement is "Present an enticing call-to-action with the right context" — so on this source's account the context precedes the ask for exactly this objective. Two qualifications belong in the answer. The core Direction guidance says nothing about placement at all, so there is no general end-of-ad rule here to appeal to either. And the full-funnel row goes a third way — "Use CTAs throughout your ad, and be more direct as you go" — but that is a different objective, and it does not license a front-loaded ask on an action brief.
qa_items.support: The action row's Direction cell and the objective's own description both order context before the ask; the core Direction row contains no placement guidance.
confounders: asserting a general 'CTA at the end' rule; the core guidance names no placement
borrowing the full-funnel row's 'CTAs throughout' to justify a front-loaded ask on an action brief
importing the skippable-ad convention of front-loading everything, which this source does not discuss

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", Direction column of all four table rows
qa_items.question: How does the source vary how directly the ad asks, across its four marketing objectives?
qa_items.answer: Awareness: nothing objective-specific — "Apply core principles". Consideration: "Plant the seed of urgency", the softest of the asks. Action: "Present the ask after the context is set", which is an ordering instruction rather than a wording one. Full funnel: "Use CTAs throughout your ad, and be more direct as you go", the only instruction that both distributes the ask and escalates it. Those four cells are the entirety of the source's guidance on how directness should vary with objective; it offers no CTA taxonomy and no wording guidance beyond "say what you'd like viewers to do".
qa_items.support: Direction column, four rows of the objective table, plus the core Direction guideline "Include a call to action (CTA)".
confounders: supplying a hierarchy of CTA verbs; the source gives none
assuming the action row asks for the most insistent CTA — its instruction is about ordering, and full funnel is the row that escalates
assuming awareness gets a soft CTA instruction; it gets none

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Think with Google, "Understanding the ABCDs of effective creative on YouTube", section "Crafting a successful ad"
qa_items.question: Does the source claim the ABCDs will help you arrive at a good creative idea?
qa_items.answer: No, and it says so outright: "The ABCD principles are not a formula for generating creative ideas." They are execution guidance, applied once the concept exists — the source's own worked example starts at an already-approved concept and enters at the storyboard. Its argument for caring about execution at all is a third party's: it says research from NCSolutions shows creative, concept through execution, is the leading driver of campaign effectiveness and ROI, and concludes that execution matters as much as the idea. Note that this boundary appears on the Think with Google page only; a reader who arrives at the Google Ads Help article or the resources article never meets it.
qa_items.support: The disclaimer and the NCSolutions attribution are both in the "Crafting a successful ad" section of the Think with Google page.
confounders: treating the four principles as a concept-generation checklist, which is what the framework's shape invites
attributing the NCSolutions claim to the Google/Kantar ABCDs study; they are separate and differently sourced
assuming the disclaimer appears in the Google Ads Help article

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Branding", guideline "Reinforce with audio"; Google for Business resources, section "B – Branding", sub-heading "See and say"
qa_items.question: What exactly does the source claim about audio brand mentions, and is it an additive claim or an interactive one?
qa_items.answer: Interactive. The claim is that "Audio brand mentions enhance onscreen brand visuals' performance" — the spoken mention raises the performance of the visual it accompanies, rather than contributing a separate increment of its own. That is why the instruction is to pair the two ("see and say") rather than to choose between them. It is a performance claim with nothing attached: no figure, no measure, no study at this level, and the headline lift the pages carry is stated for the ABCDs as a set and never decomposed by principle. The claim also presupposes the audio is heard, which the source asserts for YouTube and for nothing else.
qa_items.support: The verb is "enhance ... performance", applied to the on-screen visual. No quantity is given at either locator.
confounders: reading it as 'audio branding also works', which is the additive reading and loses the interaction
attaching part of the 30% lift to this technique; the source never decomposes the figure
assuming a mechanism is given; the source states the effect and not the cause

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Attention", guideline "Keep visuals bright and high-contrast"; Google for Business resources, section "A – Attention"; Google Ads Help, article introduction
qa_items.question: The source gives a reason for keeping visuals bright and high-contrast. What is the reason, and what does the guidance not supply?
qa_items.answer: The reason is device coverage: "Ensure visuals are optimized for all devices", and the source's own illustration reduces that to holding visual engagement on small screens. What it does not supply is any measurable target — no contrast ratio, no luminance figure, no reference screen and no viewing distance. The article instead points readers to a separate page for video specs and safe zones. So the guidance is a direction, not a specification, and any threshold used to check an ad against it is the implementer's rather than the source's.
qa_items.support: The device-coverage rationale is printed with the guideline; the introduction defers specs and safe zones to a separate article.
confounders: supplying a WCAG-style contrast ratio, which this source neither gives nor references
reading the guidance as being about legibility of on-screen text; the source scopes it to visuals and devices, and states no legibility rationale for supers
assuming the specs page is part of this guidance; it is a separate linked article

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Attention"; Google for Business resources, section "A – Attention"; Think with Google, section "A = Attention: Hook the viewer"
qa_items.question: The source's Attention principle asks for two distinct things. What are they, and what means does it name for achieving them?
qa_items.answer: Hooking attention and sustaining it — "Hook and sustain attention with an immersive story" — so an arresting opening that then loses the viewer does not satisfy the principle. The means named for both is audio and visuals together: "Drop viewers in from the start and immerse them with audio and visuals that pique their interest." The audio half is the one part of Attention for which the source gives a mechanism: music, voice-over and sound effects are said to create a rich, sensory experience that helps people pay attention. What it never gives is a duration — no page names a number of seconds for "the start".
qa_items.support: The principle statement is in the core table; the immersion instruction and the audio mechanism are on the resources article and Think with Google respectively.
confounders: reading Attention as being about the opening only, which drops 'sustain'
supplying a first-five-seconds rule; the only five-second figure in the source describes one illustrative ad's brand introduction
treating the hook as a visual problem; the source's stated mechanism here is the audio

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Connection", guideline "Focus the message"; Think with Google, section "C = Connection: Help people think or feel something"
qa_items.question: Under which of the four principles does the source file the fault of doing too much in an ad, and what does that filing imply?
qa_items.answer: Under Connection — not Attention and not Direction. Google Ads Help lists "Focus the message: Avoid doing too much in your ad. Keep messaging and language focused and simple" as a Connection guideline. Think with Google is more explicit about why it sits there: it states the instruction as a brake on the Connection instructions immediately preceding it — lean into humour and surprise, "But avoid doing too much in your ad. Focus the message as you make your connection." So on the source's arrangement an overloaded ad is one that fails to connect, and the focus instruction is the stated limit on how far the engagement devices may be pushed. The source quantifies neither side: no message count, and no test for when an ad is doing too much.
qa_items.support: "Focus the message" is in the Connection row of the core table; the "But avoid doing too much" construction is in the Connection section of the Think with Google page.
confounders: filing message overload under Attention, which is where a clutter or competing-elements framing would put it
treating 'Focus the message' and 'Avoid competing elements' as one instruction; they sit under different principles
assuming the source sets a message count

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Connection", guideline "Focus the message", and row "Attention", guideline "Support the story with audio and supers"; row "Attention", guideline "Jump in"
qa_items.question: An ad packs three separate product benefits into fifteen seconds, each with its own voice-over line and its own super, over fast cutting. Which named faults does this source say it hits, under which principles — and which element of the description does the source not object to?
qa_items.answer: Two named faults, under two different principles. "Doing too much" under Connection, from "Focus the message: Avoid doing too much in your ad. Keep messaging and language focused and simple." And "competing elements" under Attention, from "Support the story with audio and supers: Reinforce your message with audio and text. Avoid competing elements." — three voice-over lines and three supers carrying three different messages are not reinforcing one message. The fast cutting is the element the source does not object to: engaging pacing is what it asks for under "Jump in". Neither fault is quantified anywhere — no message count, and no test for when two elements compete rather than reinforce — so the diagnosis is directional and the threshold would be the implementer's.
qa_items.support: Both faults are named at the locators given; "engaging pacing" is part of the Jump in guideline.
confounders: condemning the fast cutting, which the source's own Attention guidance encourages
filing both faults under one principle
supplying a 'one message per ad' rule as if the source stated it

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Branding" (all three guidelines); Think with Google, section "B = Branding: Brand early, often, and richly"
qa_items.question: An ad carries no brand presence at all until a five-second logo lockup at the end. Which parts of the source's Branding guidance does that miss?
qa_items.answer: All three of them. "Show up early and throughout" — the brand neither appears at the start nor maintains a presence. "Reinforce with audio" — no spoken brand mention accompanies the on-screen visual, so the see-and-say pairing is absent. "Draw on all your branding assets" — one asset type where the source names six (product shots, pack shots, in-situ branding, graphic elements, voice-overs, musical treatments) and asks for a variety fitted to the message and objective. Mapped to the principle's own three adverbs, the ad fails early, fails often and fails richly. It is worth adding that the source quantifies none of the three, so the judgement is about kind rather than degree.
qa_items.support: The three Branding guidelines are in the core table; the six-item asset list is on the Think with Google page.
confounders: treating an end lockup as satisfying Branding because the brand is present somewhere
assuming 'richly' means a bigger or longer logo rather than more kinds of branding element
assuming the source sets a required time for the first brand appearance; the five-second figure in the source describes one illustrative ad

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Consideration: Show users how your product fits into their lives"
qa_items.question: A brief asks to show existing customers how the product fits into their day and to leave them wanting it soon, without pushing for a purchase now. Which of the source's objective rows is that, and what does the row prescribe?
qa_items.answer: Consideration — the source's own statement of the objective is "Show users how your product fits into their lives", which is the brief almost word for word. The row prescribes: Attention — apply core principles, no objective-specific treatment; Branding — "Hero the product"; Connection — two instructions in one cell, "Show how it works" and "Be relatable"; Direction — "Plant the seed of urgency", which is exactly the soft ask the brief calls for. confounders: choosing the action row because the brief mentions wanting the product
assuming Attention gets a special instruction here; the row leaves it at core
assigning 'Be relatable' to Branding; both it and 'Show how it works' sit in the Connection cell

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Full funnel: Maximize effectiveness by incorporating all objectives"; section "Core ABCDs", row "Direction"
qa_items.question: The full-funnel row says something about calls to action that appears nowhere in the core guidance. What is it, and does it contradict the core guidance?
qa_items.answer: It says "Use CTAs throughout your ad, and be more direct as you go" — plural asks, distributed across the ad, escalating in directness. Nothing in the core Direction guidance says that, or anything else about count or placement: the core row asks only for an explicit, intentionally chosen CTA reinforced by voice-over. So there is no contradiction with what the core guidance actually states — but it does cut against the common reading of it as one ask at the end, and that reading is not supported anywhere in the source. Two further points: the full-funnel row is the only one where all four principles carry an objective-specific instruction, and it exists only in the Google Ads Help table — the Think with Google page names three objectives and not this one.
qa_items.support: The full-funnel Direction cell against the core Direction row, which names neither count nor placement; the Think with Google objectives paragraph names only awareness, consideration and action.
confounders: asserting the core guidance requires a single end-of-ad CTA, which it does not say
assuming full funnel is a documented blend of the other three rows
