qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Think with Google, "Understanding the ABCDs of effective creative on YouTube", opening paragraph
qa_items.question: On the source's own account, how were the ABCDs arrived at, and what does that method not establish?
qa_items.answer: The source says the question of what ads that drive results on YouTube have in common "inspired a collaboration with Ipsos, and the involvement of two independent reviewers, Nielsen and Kantar", and that what emerged is a set of principles "demonstrated across video ads that worked effectively for brands". As described, that is selection on the outcome: the principles were read off ads that already worked. The source reports no comparison against ads that did not work, no sample size for this exercise, no market coverage, no selection rule, and no statement of what the two reviewers reviewed or what they concluded. So the account establishes that the principles are common among successful ads as the publisher selected them; it does not establish that they caused the success, and it is a separate exercise from the Kantar study the lift figures come from.
qa_items.support: The whole account is one paragraph on the Think with Google page. The n=11,000 sample sits on a different page and is attached to the Kantar effectiveness study.
confounders: importing the n=11,000 sample into this derivation account; the source does not say they are the same exercise
reading 'independent reviewers' as peer review or as an audit of the effectiveness figures
treating a set of common features of successful ads as a causal finding

qa_items.source_title: Google, "ABCDs of effective video ads" — Google Ads Help, Google for Business resources and Think with Google (retrieved 30 August 2026)
qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Attention", guideline "Jump in"; Google for Business resources, section "B – Branding", sub-heading "Show up early and throughout"
qa_items.question: You are asked to build an automated check for the source's "Jump in" guideline. Why can it not be run on individual frames, and what does the source fail to give you?
qa_items.answer: Because what "Jump in" describes is a property of a span, not of a still: how quickly the ad reaches the heart of its story, and whether the pacing and framing across the opening draw the viewer in. No single frame carries any of that, so the unit of observation has to be the opening sequence at least. What the source fails to give you is every number the check would need — no target time to the heart of the story, no definition of what the heart of the story is, and no reference point for "faster", which is comparative with nothing to compare to. The only figure anywhere nearby is a five-second mention in an illustrative caption about when one ad introduced its brand, which is a different guideline and is not stated as a rule. A check built from this can be directional; any threshold in it is the implementer's.
qa_items.support: "Jump in" names pacing and framing over the opening and gives no duration; the five-second figure belongs to the Weekendesk caption under "Show up early and throughout".
confounders: borrowing the five-second figure as a Jump in threshold; it belongs to a different guideline and to one example
treating tight framing as a per-frame property that makes the check frame-level — the guideline is about the opening's effect, not a single composition
assuming the source's video specs page supplies a timing rule; it covers specs and safe zones

qa_items.answer: Almost all of them. "The start" and "early" carry no number of seconds. "Often" carries no count. "Richly" carries no minimum number of asset types. "Faster" has no reference point. qa_items.source_locator: Google Ads Help, section "Core ABCDs", row "Connection", guideline "Humanize the story"; section "ABCDs by marketing objectives", table row "Action: Present an enticing call-to-action with the right context"
qa_items.question: Two teams building an action-objective ad both cite this source: one to justify a cast-led human story, the other to justify cutting the people entirely and shooting the product. Which of them has the source right?
qa_items.answer: Both are quoting it accurately, and the source does not settle it. The core Connection guideline says "Humanize the story: Feature people to help you tell a better product story and relate to your consumer.", which supports the first team. The action row's Branding cell says "Make the product the ad" — the strongest branding instruction in the whole table — and its Connection cell says "Be exact and tangible", not "feature people", which supports the second. qa_items.question: A planner wants to argue that adding a spoken brand mention on its own will deliver most of the 30% short-term sales lift. Can this source support that argument?
qa_items.answer: No, on three counts. The lift figures are stated for "the ABCDs" as a set on all three pages and are never decomposed by principle, still less by individual technique, so no share of the 30% can be assigned to anything. The source's only claim about audio brand mentions is qualitative — that they enhance the on-screen brand visual's performance — with no figure attached at all. And the set-level number itself is unstable across the publisher's own pages, appearing as an upper bound on one and as an average on another, so it will not carry a per-campaign expectation even before anyone tries to split it.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 1-2 (Chapter One, 'Early Influences', opening argument); restated printed p. 172 (Chapter Sixteen)
qa_items.question: Hopkins opens the book by separating two things that are both ordinarily called failure in advertising. What is the distinction, which of the two does he call inexcusable, and what reason does he give?
qa_items.answer: An ordinary failure is a small venture that does not respond. He treats that as expected, cheap and informative — every venture in its initial stage is only a way of feeling the public pulse. A disaster is a large and costly commitment made before any response has been observed, and that he calls rashness: needless and inexcusable. The reason he gives is not that practitioners are careless but that no amount of experience guides a man correctly in even the majority of cases, so being wrong is normal and only incaution is culpable. He restates it later as an operating rule: never involve the advertiser to any large extent before a profit is sure. He offers no figure anywhere for how often a small test misleads.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 1-2, the book's opening pages, where advertising disasters are attributed to rashness; the decision rule is restated at printed p. 172. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism, no supporting figures.
confounders: the modern fail-fast reading, in which failure itself is the teacher; Hopkins's point is about the size of the commitment, not about the value of failing
reading it as general caution about advertising, when he is prescribing small ventures rather than fewer ones
treating it as a claim that tests are reliable; he claims the opposite about judgement and says nothing about test reliability

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 175-177 (Chapter Seventeen, 'Scientific Advertising', opening)
qa_items.question: Hopkins states directly where his principles came from. Summarise the evidence base he claims, and then state what the book itself actually exhibits of it.
qa_items.answer: He claims thirty-six years of traced advertising, campaigns on some hundreds of different lines, and comparison by keyed returns of thousands of pieces of copy on some lines, always facing records on cost and result. He adds that mail order gives the most exact basis but that most advertising can be conducted so as to give an approximate guide. What the book exhibits is very much less: no dataset, protocol, sample size, date range, product list or result table appears anywhere in it. A handful of figures across roughly half a dozen campaigns is the whole of the displayed evidence. The claimed corpus is asserted; it is not shown.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 175-176, where the thirty-six years, hundreds of lines and thousands of pieces of copy are stated. The absence of exhibited evidence is an extraction observation about the book as a whole, not a claim by the source.
confounders: treating the claimed corpus as though it were published data; it is a recollection stated in one paragraph
assuming keyed returns imply a controlled comparison — he describes ranking advertisements one by one, with nothing held constant
confusing this book with Scientific Advertising (1923), which is the book he says the phrase attached to; that book is not reproduced here

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 175-176 (Chapter Seventeen, on why he distrusts most advertising theories)
qa_items.question: Hopkins gives an explicit rule for refusing evidence: why does he say most advertising theories deserve little respect, and what alternative explanations does he name for a commercial success whose returns were never traced?
qa_items.answer: He says most theories are unproved and rest on limited experience and exceptional conditions, and that some lines appear to succeed on methods every traced return proves impossible. His named alternatives are that the line may have succeeded in spite of its advertising; that unadvertised lines become successful because people discover a wanted quality; that dealers may have been induced to feature it; or that the name itself tells an appealing story. He names gum and a breakfast cereal as name-driven cases with almost no story to tell, and adds the sharpest move in the passage: the very men who succeeded with one such name failed again and again with others, which is a disconfirmation test applied to the rival explanation. His conclusion is that conclusions drawn from untraced successes lead others astray.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 175-176. Argued position with named cases, no figures.
confounders: reading it as a claim that untraced advertising does not work, rather than that it carries no information about what worked
the modern attribution framing of incrementality; Hopkins's argument is about overdetermination of the outcome, not about a control group
assuming he exempts himself; he does not address whether his own untraced narratives fall under the rule

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 175-176 (Chapter Seventeen), applied against the campaign narratives throughout
qa_items.question: Apply Hopkins's own refusal rule to Hopkins. A reader takes the Schlitz, Van Camp and Palmolive chapters as proof of the principles they illustrate. On the source's own stated criterion, what is wrong with that, and what defence does the book leave open?
qa_items.answer: On his own criterion the narratives do not qualify. He says safe principles are evolved only by those who know with reasonable exactness what the advertising does and who compare results on many lines with thousands of pieces of copy — and nearly every campaign he recounts is an outcome asserted decades later with no control, no comparison and usually no figure. By his rule those accounts illustrate the principles rather than establishing them. The defence the book leaves open is the one he implies at printed pp. 175-176: the principles came from the traced work, and the narratives are exposition. That defence is available but unverifiable here, because the book never exhibits the traced work. He nowhere applies the rule to himself.
qa_items.support: The refusal rule is at printed pp. 175-176; the campaign narratives run through Chapters Seven to Fifteen. The reflexive application is an extraction observation using the source's own stated criterion, not a claim the source makes.
confounders: treating the book's confidence of tone as evidence quality
dismissing the principles as false; the point is that these accounts do not test them, not that they are wrong
assuming the keyed Pepsodent work at printed pp. 153-156 supplies the missing data; that passage reports the loop existed, not what it returned

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 150 and 156 (Chapters Thirteen and Fourteen, the two statements of the rule against relying on judgement)
qa_items.question: Hopkins states his most general methodological rule twice, and supports it with a concession about himself. What is the rule, what is the concession, and what is wrong with the ratio he offers alongside it?
qa_items.answer: The rule is that none of us can afford to rely on judgement or experience: new problems require new experience, undertakings must be tested in the most exact way possible, and mistakes must be learned and corrected. The concession is the strongest support he gives it — he had spent nearly thirty years in advertising and learned from hundreds of campaigns when he himself prepared a Pepsodent series he says would have wrecked the business in three months. The ratio he offers beside it, that perhaps one guess in fifty is right while fifty tests in fifty tell you what to do and avoid, is rhetoric: no derivation is given, and the second half is false as literally stated, since a test can also mislead. He also does not apply the rule uniformly — he repriced the Quaker puffed-grain line on conviction rather than test.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 150 (one time in fifty; fifty times in fifty) and printed p. 156 (none of us can afford to rely on judgment or experience, after the near-fatal series). The repricing decision is at printed pp. 143-144.
confounders: treating the fifty-in-fifty figure as an empirical result rather than a rhetorical flourish
reading it as a claim that experience is worthless; he claims experience does not transfer to a new problem, which is narrower
assuming he applied the rule consistently; the pricing decision at printed pp. 143-144 is his own counter-example

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 92-94 (Chapter Eight, 'My Liquozone Experience')
qa_items.question: The Liquozone account is the one place in the book where a measurement, a waiting period and the same measure at national scale are all stated. Give the figures, and say why the thirty-day wait is the load-bearing part of the procedure.
qa_items.answer: In a dozen small Illinois test cities, inquiries for the free bottle cost 18 cents each. He then waited thirty days deliberately, and found sales averaged 90 cents per inquirer; claims under the money-back guaranty came to less than 2 per cent of sales. Rolled out nationally the following year, the campaign produced over 1,500,000 requests at an average cost of 18 cents — the same figure — with an average sale of 91 cents per request. He reports first-year net profits of $1,800,000. The wait is load-bearing because the free bottle only produces a countable inquiry; the revenue per inquirer does not exist until the response has had time to convert, so reading the ratio early would have measured the offer and not the business. Note this is a single unreplicated instance, reported from memory two decades later, on a product whose advertising he elsewhere disowns as a class.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 92-94, where the 18-cent inquiry cost, the thirty-day wait, the 90-cent and 91-cent sale figures, the sub-2-per-cent claim rate and the 1,500,000 requests are all stated. The repudiation of medicine advertising as a class is at printed pp. 73-75.
confounders: treating the test-to-scale agreement as a controlled result; nothing tells us what a different plan would have returned
confusing the 18-cent inquiry cost with the 25-cent free-sample figure quoted for puffed grains at printed p. 147
reading the sub-2-per-cent guaranty claim rate as a general rate for money-back offers; it is one product, one year, on a remedy whose effect a buyer could not judge

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 153-156 (Chapter Fourteen, 'Pepsodent', the keyed reporting loop)
qa_items.question: Describe the reporting loop Hopkins ran on Pepsodent, and state precisely what he claims it bought him. Be careful to state the claim he actually makes rather than the stronger one.
qa_items.answer: Every advertisement carried a keyed coupon; hundreds of advertisements were tried; results came back to him week by week, and each report arrived with the headline that had produced it, so the appeal and its response stayed attached. The claim he actually makes is about the cost of being wrong, not about finding the right answer: one series he had himself prepared would, he says, have wrecked the business in three months, he caught it by the coupon within about a week, and reversed strategy at once. So the loop caps the price of a wrong theory at roughly a week of spending. He adds that competitors who fell down did so because they were wedded to a theory and did not check results quickly enough. He never says what was wrong with the series, never quotes it, and gives no figures from the loop.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 153-156. The wrecking series and the one-week detection are stated at printed p. 155; the competitor diagnosis at printed p. 156. Outcome claimed, no figures given.
confounders: the stronger claim that the loop finds the winning appeal; his stated benefit is bounding the loss
reading hundreds of freely varying advertisements read on weekly returns as a controlled test; nothing separates a headline effect from a week, a season or a medium
assuming the loop catches every kind of failure — his own Mitchell case at printed pp. 119-120 is a campaign with excellent response and a ruinous outcome

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 153-156 (Pepsodent loop) read against printed pp. 119-120 (Chapter Ten, the Mitchell campaign)
qa_items.question: A team runs Hopkins's weekly keyed loop faithfully and every reading is excellent — coupon response is high and rising. On the source's own evidence, what class of failure would this loop not see, and which case in the book demonstrates it?
qa_items.answer: The loop measures response to the advertising, so it cannot see a failure that occurs after the purchase. The case is the automobile campaign at printed pp. 119-120, which he calls the most successful automobile advertising he ever did and which destroyed the client: inquiries ran at a rate he says he never saw matched and sales started at an amazing rate, but the car had been skimped in every detail, hundreds came back, and the larger the sales the worse the ruin. His own formulation is that the note played was too high for the product available. His other criterion is where the check belongs — the repeat-sale test at printed p. 135, which asks whether repeat business paid for the advertising before the bills fell due. He does not connect the two, and nowhere draws the conclusion that response volume is not evidence of a successful campaign.
qa_items.support: The loop is at printed pp. 153-156; the Mitchell collapse at printed pp. 119-120; the repeat-sale criterion at printed p. 135 and printed p. 155. The observation that he never joins them is an extraction observation.
confounders: assuming a high response rate is what Hopkins means by a campaign paying; his stated criterion is repeat sales inside the billing period
attributing the Mitchell failure to the advertising; he attributes it to the product and to the height of the claim
reading this as a general warning about vanity metrics; the specific mechanism he describes is that each additional sale converts into an additional damaged reputation

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 135 (Chapter Twelve, Palmolive at Benton Harbor) and printed p. 155 (Chapter Fourteen, the first Pepsodent test city)
qa_items.question: What does Hopkins treat as the signal that a tested campaign may be scaled? State the criterion in his terms and say what makes it a stricter test than an inquiry count.
qa_items.answer: The criterion is a cash-cycle test: repeat sales in the test town must pay for the advertising before the advertising bills fall due. He reports it met at Benton Harbor for Palmolive, in the first Pepsodent test city on $1,000 which came back with a profit before the bills were due, and on Liquozone where profit on sales more than paid the advertising before the bills fell due; in each case that was the signal to raise capital and scale. It is stricter than an inquiry count because a first purchase measures the advertising and a second measures the product, so requiring repeat revenue inside the credit period tests both the appeal and the article. He calls the question of what users do after they try the product the most vital factor in advertising. He reports the criterion met in every campaign he scaled and no case where it failed, which is what survivorship would predict.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 135 for the most-vital-factor statement and the Benton Harbor repeat sales; printed p. 155 for the $1,000 Pepsodent test city. He flags the Palmolive figures as possibly inexact and dating from 1911.
confounders: reading it as payback or ROI in the modern sense; the deadline is the advertising credit period, an artefact of how his bills were settled
confusing it with the coupon-response loop, which is a copy-selection device and not a scaling gate
assuming the criterion is generally available; it only exists for goods repurchased fast enough to clear a billing cycle

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 133-137 (Chapter Twelve, Benton Harbor) and printed p. 154 (Chapter Fourteen, the 52-countries claim)
qa_items.question: The whole of Hopkins's test-then-scale method rests on one assumption about transfer. State it in his terms, state the strongest form he gives it, and name the internal evidence against it.
qa_items.answer: The assumption is that a result obtained in one small market transfers: human nature over the country is about alike, and the appeal that won in Benton Harbor won from coast to coast. The strongest form is international — he says Pepsodent was sold in 52 countries and advertised in 17 languages and that in each the appeal proved equally effective, with no comparative figures offered. The internal evidence against it is his own: he records certain evaporated-milk brands holding certain markets for years regardless of advertising, for no reason he can find but familiarity; and his own doctrine that a campaign's key-note must be drawn from the current local preoccupation sits badly with one appeal working equally in seventeen languages. The deepest problem is structural — only successful transfers are reported, and a book written by the man who chose which tests to scale cannot tell us how often a local success failed to generalise.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 133-137 for the Benton Harbor test and the human-nature claim; printed p. 154 for the 52 countries and 17 languages; printed p. 103 for the evaporated-milk observation; printed pp. 120-121 for the key-note doctrine. He himself flags the 1911 figures as possibly inexact.
confounders: treating test-to-scale agreement on Liquozone as evidence for the general transfer claim; it is one product
reading the 17-languages claim as a measured finding; no figure accompanies it
assuming the survivorship problem is one he acknowledges; he does not raise it anywhere

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 149-150 (Chapter Thirteen, Two-minute Oats and Quick Quaker Oats)
qa_items.question: Hopkins tested two reformulations of the same product and got opposite results. Describe the principle he draws, and identify the procedural difference between the two tests that he does not remark on.
qa_items.answer: The principle is that a product change must be judged by the existing users who would have to accept it. Two-minute Oats was thought so obviously right that most people involved wanted to adopt it without testing; he insisted on trying it in a few towns with a free package and a letter asking users their opinion, and the verdict went against him — the flavour differed from oatmeal as they knew it, and although new users would probably have preferred it there were too few of them to matter. A later version cooking in three to five minutes, with no unique flavour, was opposed by most of the directors precisely because the first had failed; he insisted on another test, and some 90 per cent of users voted for it. The difference he does not remark on is procedural: in the second test he bought the first package rather than giving it, and told every user he did not care which they preferred. Both moves are ones he elsewhere says change behaviour, so the two tests are not the same procedure and their results are not cleanly comparable.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 149-150. The free package and the letter for Two-minute Oats; the bought package, the disclaimer of preference and the 90 per cent figure for Quick Quaker. The 90 per cent has no denominator, method, geography or date beyond a few towns. The free-versus-bought distinction is his own doctrine at printed pp. 133-134.
confounders: concluding that faster cooking was the variable; his stated variable is the flavour familiar to existing users
reading the second test as a replication of the first; the offer and the framing both changed
assuming the directors were wrong to hesitate; his own account is that they were reasoning from the first result, which was real

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 158-159 (Chapter Fifteen, the five-dollar mail-order article)
qa_items.question: Give the cost-per-reply figures in Hopkins's clearest documented comparison, and state what conclusion he draws from it. His conclusion is not the one most readers take.
qa_items.answer: An advertiser selling a five-dollar article by mail had replies costing 85 cents and sales about $2.50, and was becoming unprofitable. Hopkins's agency prepared an advertisement the advertiser rejected as too unattractive; a rival agency's larger, more alluring advertisement was run instead and produced replies at $14.20 each on a five-dollar article. The advertiser then ran the rejected one and replies cost 42 cents, a level he says held for years on some 250,000 replies a year. The conclusion he draws is not about layout. It is about decision-making: advertisers without a trace on cost judge advertisements by appearance, and they lose on the same scale as this man did. Appearance is the only signal available to a decider with no cost trace, so in the absence of measurement the selection criterion is systematically wrong rather than merely noisy.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 158-159, where the 85-cent, $14.20 and 42-cent figures and the 250,000 replies a year are stated. Neither advertisement is described beyond attractive and unattractive; no dates, media, offer or seasonality are given, and Hopkins was a party to the comparison.
confounders: reading it as a rule that plain layouts outperform attractive ones; his rule is that appearance is not the signal to decide on
treating the 34-fold spread as a clean copy effect; nothing rules out media, offer or season, none of which is reported
confusing cost per reply with cost per sale; both are given and they are different figures

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 157 (Chapter Fifteen, why he kept doing mail-order work)
qa_items.question: Hopkins says he did mail-order advertising throughout his career against his own financial interest. What are his two distinct reasons, and what is the logical form of the second?
qa_items.answer: The first reason is calibration of the practitioner: the work is educational, keeps one on his mettle and fixes one's viewpoint on cost and result, so a man who keeps doing it cannot drift into judging work by appearance. The second is a reason for imitating surviving mail-order advertisements: they are known to be profitable, else they would not continue, and they are usually the residue of many traced experiments, so they represent the best method yet found for that line. The logical form of the second is a survivorship argument, used deliberately as a selection filter. It is used correctly here — but it inherits the conclusions of experiments run on other products in other conditions, and he states elsewhere that methods succeeding in one line cannot be applied to another.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 157. The qualification that methods do not transfer between lines is at printed p. 176. He concedes in the same passage that the work seldom ran to large amounts and was not worth the effort from a writer's standpoint.
confounders: reading it as advice to run mail-order campaigns; the stated benefit is to the practitioner's judgement, not to the client
missing that the second reason is survivorship reasoning, which he does not name as such
assuming what transfers is settled; his own statement at printed p. 176 that methods do not transfer between lines cuts against the copying

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 6 (Chapter One) and printed p. 174 (Chapter Sixteen, closing paragraph)
qa_items.question: Hopkins draws an explicit boundary around the market he claims to understand. State it, name the products he says he would expect to fail on, and say what he concedes about the field he excludes himself from.
qa_items.answer: He limits himself to ordinary wage-earning purchasers — what he calls the common people — and says he does not know the reactions of the rich. He names Rolls-Royce, Tiffany and a Steinway piano as lines he would expect to fail on. What he concedes is important: the exclusive-appeal field, which he typifies by Cadillac advertising, is a real and ably occupied field, and people of small incomes can well be excluded from it. So this is a statement about the limits of his own contact, not a claim that exclusive-appeal advertising does not work. It is the single most important boundary condition on the whole book: nearly every other principle in it was derived inside this scope, and he nowhere claims any of them holds outside it. The surrounding passages carry 1920s American class framing — simple folks, plebeian, the vast majority — which is his own framing of his audience and not a taxonomy of buyers.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 6 for the naming of Rolls-Royce, Tiffany and Steinway; printed p. 174 for the Cadillac concession and the confinement of his appeals to the common people. Explicit source statement, culturally bounded.
confounders: reading it as a claim that luxury advertising fails; he says the opposite, that the field is ably occupied
treating his principles as unrestricted because he states them without qualification elsewhere; this passage is the qualification
taking his class vocabulary as an analytical segmentation rather than as period framing

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 73-75 (Chapter Seven, 'Medical Advertising', opening pages)
qa_items.question: Before recounting the medicine campaigns that made his reputation, Hopkins states a reversal. What exactly does he repudiate, what does he not repudiate, and what reason does he give?
qa_items.answer: He repudiates the class of product. He says he no longer approves of medicine advertising, has not advertised a medicine except for simple ailments for seventeen years or more, would not do so under any circumstances, and is refusing an appropriation of $900,000 to advertise one as he writes. His reason is external to advertising technique: medical science advanced, doctors turned away from drugs, and it came to be understood that an ailing person needs a diagnosis rather than the quelling of symptoms. What he does not repudiate is the practitioners — he still defends the medicine-makers as high-minded and believes they did more good than harm, even though the good came largely through mental impressions — and he does not withdraw a single technique. The guaranty, the free first bottle, the keyed return and the test-city method all come out of these campaigns and are urged on the reader elsewhere without qualification. He asks the reader to remember that what he describes happened many years earlier and accorded with the practices of that time. This is recorded as his 1927 position and as historical record, not as guidance.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 73-75. The $900,000 refusal, the seventeen-year abstention and the separation of how advertising works from what ought to be advertised are all stated there. Ethically dated material, recorded as the source's own position.
confounders: reading the repudiation as extending to the methods; it does not, and the book keeps recommending them
reading it as a full retraction; he continues to defend the makers in the same passage

assuming the methodological point he makes about these campaigns — that nothing but the advertising could sell the goods, so profit and loss attached to the advertising alone — is an ethical defence; it is an argument about measurement

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 182-183 (Chapter Seventeen, on art and colour in advertising)
qa_items.question: On expensive art and colour printing, Hopkins does something he does almost nowhere else in the book. What is it, and what exactly does he say the state of the evidence is?
qa_items.answer: He marks the question as unresolved instead of settling it. He reports advertisers paying $1,500 to $4,000 per drawing, says no test he knows proves such expense profitable, and says he knows of no case where coloured pictures paid better than black-and-white; he notes people use colour more and more but rarely on traced advertising, and that when a great advertising journal appealed for proofs that colour advertising paid, no actual proof came to his attention. He then concedes he is prepared to believe colour may prove profitable on some lines, naming fruits and desserts, calls it a question for further experiment, and doubts the results could ever be applied to all lines. His own explanation — that fine art work, like fine language, simply makes buyers wary — he offers explicitly as his idea, not as a finding. This is the clearest place in the book where he separates what he has proved from what he believes.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 182-183, where the $1,500-$4,000 range, the absence of proof, the fruits-and-desserts concession and the phrase marking it a question for further experiment all appear. Absence of proof within one practitioner's traced work is weak evidence of absence, which is in effect why he leaves it open.
confounders: reading it as a finding that colour does not pay; he says he has no proof either way and expects exceptions
carrying the conclusion to any later medium; colour reproduction cost and quality in the 1920s are what the argument is about
conflating this with his firmer rule in the same chapter that pictures must have selling value and none be used for decoration — that one he does assert

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 204 (Chapter Nineteen, 'Some Things Personal')
qa_items.question: Hopkins closes with a scope claim about his own book that has two halves in tension. State both halves, and say what the tension costs the strong reading.
qa_items.answer: The first half is concessive: the tempo of American life is changing, fads, fancies and desires change like a kaleidoscope, certain styles in advertising are changing, and every campaign has always required a different key-note because imitators never succeed. The second half is the assertion: human nature does not change, and the principles set down in the book are as enduring as the Alps. He does not reconcile them. If every campaign needs a key-note drawn from the current public preoccupation, then a large part of what the book teaches is contingent, and the enduring residue is smaller than the Alps claim implies. A great deal of the content is plainly period-bound in any case: coupon redemption at independent retailers, one-cent letters to dealers, 8-point reading matter, $10 per word, publisher-paid commissions, untargetable circulation, and door-to-door canvassing. The claim is recorded as a 1927 position by one American practitioner working in one market and one class, not as a finding.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 204, where both halves appear within a few sentences. The key-note doctrine he is in tension with is at printed pp. 120-121. The list of period-bound mechanics is an extraction observation across the book.
confounders: quoting the Alps sentence without the concession that precedes it
treating the research analogy he draws to medical research as evidence of a protocol; no protocol, dataset or replication appears in the book
assuming he means the specific tactics endure; his claim is about principles, and he says the tactics must change every campaign

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 189 and 192-193 (Chapter Eighteen, 'My Great Mistake')
qa_items.question: Chapter Eighteen is titled 'My Great Mistake'. What was the mistake, and why does that matter for reading the book as an account of advertising failure?
qa_items.answer: The mistake is not an advertising error at all. It is that he stayed as an employee. Bissell told him the day before Christmas that he was too good a man to work for him and should start out for himself; Hopkins says his Scotch conservatism led him to stay, that he married soon after, and that he thus tied himself to a lifetime of service as an employee. He adds that he watched coworkers found their own companies on lines he had taught them, and that had he invested merely his commissions in the enterprises he fostered the amount would run into many millions. It matters because the chapter with the most confessional title in the book contains no admission of an advertising mistake — his regret is about who captured the value he created. The book's actual admitted campaign failure is elsewhere, at printed pp. 147-148, where he calls the Quaker Oats habit-change campaign one of the greatest mistakes of his life.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 189 for the Bissell advice and the decision to stay; printed pp. 192-193 for the commissions calculation and the switch to working for himself. The Quaker Oats admission is at printed p. 147.
confounders: expecting a campaign post-mortem from the chapter title; the chapter is about career structure
reading it as a claim about advertising risk; the risk asymmetry he describes is between practitioner and owner
treating the many-millions estimate as a computation; it is a retrospective figuring with no working shown

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 154 (Chapter Fourteen, why featuring the free offer divided results by four)
qa_items.question: Hopkins reports that the same device helped in one category and hurt badly in another. Give both results, his explanation, and — the part usually got wrong — what he actually changed in response.
qa_items.answer: On food products the word free was appealing and multiplied the readers of his advertisements. On a hygiene product, featuring a free offer at the top of the advertisement divided results by four. His explanation is about the role the advertiser appears to occupy: professing to offer benefits of vast importance, a featured giveaway made them traders simply seeking to sell rather than scientists seeking to benefit, and so discredited the very factors that brought converts. What he changed was placement, not the offer. The sample stayed free; the free offer was moved out of the position of chief appeal, so the apparent object of the advertisement was to prove at the advertiser's own cost what the product could do. Reading this as a rule against free samples reverses him. He also stresses that such things are not easy to discover and that he found it only through keyed coupons.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 154. Divided our results by four is a single reported ratio with no absolute figures, no denominator and no statement of what else differed between versions. The altruistic framing he substituted is described at printed p. 153.
confounders: concluding that free offers do not work in hygiene categories; the sample remained free
generalising the divide-by-four ratio; it is one comparison on one product with no denominator
assuming he presents this as a limit on his own generalisations; he presents it as a discovery about psychology, though it is the book's strongest evidence that his rules are category-conditional

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 147 (Chapter Thirteen, the cost of charging for a sample)
qa_items.question: Hopkins gives his sharpest arithmetic warning about charging for a trial. State the figures, and the companion finding he attaches about half-price and free-with-purchase offers.
qa_items.answer: Inquiries for free samples may cost about 25 cents each; ask ten cents for the same sample and the inquiries may cost $1.25 or more. So to gain that ten cents you may lose a dollar, and start only a fifth as many users for the money you spend. He calls economy on this point one of the greatest follies in advertising, and states the rule as: remember you are the seller, make trial easy for the people you have interested, and do not ask them to pay for your efforts to sell them. The companion finding is that tens of millions of advertisements offering one puffed grain free with the purchase of the other were ineffective, because such an offer is simply a price reduction — and it is just as hard to sell at half price as at full price to people who are not converted. The figures are given as illustrative magnitudes, in the form may cost and may be, not as the result of a specific dated test.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 147 for the 25-cent, ten-cent and $1.25 figures and the one-fifth claim; printed p. 146 for the free-with-purchase finding and the half-price reasoning.
confounders: treating 25 cents and $1.25 as measured results; they are stated as magnitudes that may obtain
extending the finding to price promotion generally; his stated mechanism is that price is not the obstacle for an unconverted buyer
reading it as contradicting his earned-sample rule at printed p. 146; the reconcilable form is that effort in attention may be demanded and effort in money may not

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 146 (Chapter Thirteen, why promiscuous puffed-grain sampling was stopped)
qa_items.question: Hopkins distinguishes two practices both called sampling and says one is nearly worthless. Draw the distinction as he draws it, and give the four specific objections he raises to the bad one.
qa_items.answer: The distinction is whether the recipient did anything to get the sample. Distributing samples to people who did not ask — house to house, cast on the doorstep, handed out at large — he calls a very bad plan; he reports distributing millions of puffed-grain samples this way and winning few users, then stopping. His objections are that the product has no prestige and the giving itself cheapens it; that the stores are not stocked when the sample is used; that grocers are offended by free distribution of goods they sell; and that the samples are like waifs, arriving with no reason to be wanted. The good form is sampling into an interest the advertising has already created: the reader must read the story to know the sample exists, cut the coupon and present it at a grocery, and finds the product in stock. His rule is to give samples only to people who take some action to acquire them because of an interest created — give the product an atmosphere, otherwise it will never make a lasting impression.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 146. The promiscuous-sampling failure is reported without figures and sits in the same passage as a separate failure about medium choice, so the two causes are not separated.
confounders: treating the effort required as a purchase; his other rule at printed p. 147 is that charging anything collapses response
reading this as a claim about sample quality or the product; his mechanism is entirely about how the sample was obtained
assuming the grocer objection is incidental; retail stocking is load-bearing in his account, since the sampled user must be able to buy

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 133-134 (Chapter Twelve, the two-stage Palmolive introduction)
qa_items.question: Describe the two-stage introduction plan Hopkins says he originated for Palmolive, and explain why he insists that we will buy is a better headline than a free offer.
qa_items.answer: Stage one runs two or three advertisements carrying the product story, each with a boxed announcement above it that in a few days the advertiser will buy a cake of the product for any woman who applies. He claims this announcement multiplies the readership of the story advertisements, because a woman told that something is to be bought for her wants to know what it is. Stage two, once sufficient desire exists, is a full page carrying a coupon redeemable at any store, with the dealer authorised to hand over the goods and charge the advertiser the retail price. He says the plan produces, in about two weeks, both a general understanding of the product and thousands of users. His argument for we will buy over free is that paying the dealer full retail shows supreme confidence that the article will please, whereas a free offer cheapens the product and creates resistance to paying later for what was first received as a gift. He never supports this with a traced comparison of the two headlines anywhere in the book.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 133-134, where the boxed pre-announcement, the coupon page and the we-will-buy versus free argument are set out. The superiority claim is argued psychologically, not measured.
confounders: reading it as a rule against the word free; at printed p. 154 he reports free multiplying readers on food products
collapsing the two stages into one; the delay between announcement and coupon is what he says builds the desire
assuming the retail-redemption mechanic has a modern equivalent; it is a physical mechanic of independent retailers and paper coupons

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 92-95 (Chapter Eight, the successive guaranty forms) read with printed p. 85 (Chapter Seven, the guaranteed shoe fit)
qa_items.question: Hopkins built risk transfer into successively stronger forms. Trace the escalation, state his general finding about people who are trusted, and name his own counter-case.
qa_items.answer: The escalation runs: a druggist-signed money-back warrant on a remedy; then a warrant covering a five-dollar lot of six bottles, so that a single-bottle purchase was underwritten by it; then paying outright for the buyer's first fifty-cent bottle and warranting the six that followed. His formulation is that asking a person to take a chance on you means a fight, while offering to take a chance on him makes the way easy, and that he analysed his propositions until he was sure the buyer had the best end of the bargain. His general finding is that very few people cheat a seller who offers a square deal — try to hedge or protect yourself and human nature likes to circumvent you — and that he has been robbed often but at roughly a tenth of what enforcing a safe proposition would have cost. His own counter-case is the Racine Club shoe scheme, where he guaranteed a fit and the returns absorbed most of the profit. So the cost of risk transfer depends on how often the product actually disappoints.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 92-95 for the escalating guaranty forms and the under-2-per-cent claim rate on Liquozone; printed p. 85 for the guaranteed shoe fit. The strongest applications are on patent medicines whose advertising he elsewhere disowns.
confounders: generalising the sub-2-per-cent claim rate; it is one product in one year on a remedy whose efficacy a buyer could not judge
assuming a guarantee is a contract the buyer intends to use; his account is that it functions as a statement of the seller's confidence
separating the mechanism from its evidence too cleanly; the evidence comes from campaigns he repudiates as a class

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 76 (Chapter Seven, the neighbourhood druggist's signature on the guaranty)
qa_items.question: Hopkins claims a guarantee's force comes from something other than its terms. What, and what second effect does he report that does not follow from the terms at all?
qa_items.answer: It comes from who signs it. He observes that many an advertiser a thousand miles away offered to guarantee results, but the guarantors were strangers, so the promise carried no weight — redress from a stranger is not a real option to the buyer. His move was to have the neighbourhood druggist, to whom people actually paid their money, sign the guaranty. The second effect is the interesting one: the guarantee was written against a six-bottle, five-dollar purchase, few users ever bought that amount, and it nonetheless gave them confidence in every single-bottle purchase. That does not follow from the terms — it follows only if the guarantee is being read as a statement of the seller's confidence rather than as a contract. He reports the plan worked on a cough remedy and then on two further remedies and secured most of the trade, with no figure for this mechanism in isolation.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 76. Outcome reported as enormous, with no figures for the guarantor effect alone; the one claim-rate figure in the book belongs to the later Liquozone campaign, which combined the guarantee with a free first bottle. Bounded to a retail structure of independent neighbourhood druggists with standing local reputations.
confounders: reading it as a rule about guarantee terms — coverage, duration, conditions — which is exactly what he says does not matter
treating it as third-party endorsement in the modern sense; his mechanism is that redress must be locally collectible
assuming the scope effect is a mistake by buyers; he reports it as the mechanism working

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 163-165 (Chapter Fifteen, the mail-order catalogue and the sales manager's card)
qa_items.question: A category where four competitors present near-identical offers at the moment of choice. Give Hopkins's unit economics for it, where he placed his intervention, and the one design rule he puts on the intervention itself.
qa_items.answer: His economics: inducing a woman to write for a catalogue cost about 25 cents, the colour catalogue at least 35 cents, so about 60 cents was invested per inquirer; she typically wrote to three or four advertisers, so about $2.40 was being spent across the field to produce an average sale of around $10, and which catalogue she ordered from turned largely on chance or fancy. He placed his intervention at the ordering moment rather than at the inquiry: every inquirer received a personal card from the sales manager, worded differently for new and returning customers, instructing that her order be referred to him personally so he could include a present. The design rule is that the gift was deliberately not described, because curiosity makes a stronger appeal than description — describe a gift and some decide they want it while more decide they do not, whereas everybody wants a secret gift. He adds a strict condition: the gift must not disappoint and must be something every recipient wants. The result is reported only as sales per catalogue enormously increased, with no figure — conspicuous in a passage where he gives precise unit economics for everything else.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 163-165, where the 25-cent, 35-cent, 60-cent, $2.40 and $10 figures appear, along with the card wording, the undescribed gift and the condition on it. The outcome is qualitative.
confounders: placing the intervention at the inquiry stage, which is where the competitive spending already was and where he says it is wasted
describing the gift, which is precisely the move he says loses more people than it wins
treating the enormous increase as a measured result; it is the one unquantified outcome in a heavily quantified passage

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 106 (Chapter Nine, the unnamed present) and printed p. 164 (Chapter Fifteen)
qa_items.question: Hopkins names curiosity as the strongest activating factor he knows and derives a specific rule from it. State the rule and the selection argument behind it, and give the condition he attaches.
qa_items.answer: The rule is that an undisclosed reward outperforms a described one. His argument is about selection rather than about excitement: describe a gift and some will decide they want it while more will decide they do not, whereas everybody wants a secret gift — description gives the reader enough information to refuse, and withholding it removes the ground for refusal. He applies the same logic to campaign concepts, citing foods shot from guns, grains pictured at eight times normal size, and a pamphlet about convict-cut Indian wood hauled to the Ganges by elephants, all built to make the reader want to see the thing. His condition is hard: the undisclosed gift must not disappoint, must be something every recipient wants, and should be somewhat better than expected; and the offer should be handled quietly rather than blazoned. No comparative figure for described versus undisclosed rewards appears anywhere in the book.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 106 for the wrapped unlabelled presents in grocers' windows and the curiosity claim; printed p. 164 for the undescribed gift on the sales manager's card. He also states in the same material a period belief that curiosity is especially strong with women, which is 1920s framing and is not extracted here as a claim about buyers.
confounders: reading it as a general endorsement of mystery or teasing; his mechanism is specifically about removing grounds for refusal
ignoring the disappointment condition, without which the device damages the seller on delivery
assuming a measured comparison supports it; there is none in the book

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 77-78 (Chapter Seven, the conditions for entering an occupied field)
qa_items.question: State Hopkins's entry condition for a new advertiser, including the softening clause that makes it far easier to satisfy than it first appears.
qa_items.answer: Before committing, one must know the competition, know what others offer, know what people want, and be able to outbid the field in some way — on qualities, on service, or on terms. Crying a name or a brand does not satisfy the condition, and until one feels sure the advantages are strongly on his side it is folly to risk a battle. He adds a second constraint: never pay the cost of acquiring customers without seeing how they will be kept. The softening clause is that, failing a real advantage, one may create a seeming advantage by citing facts which others fail to cite. That makes the condition satisfiable by communication alone, and it is the clause his Schlitz and Van Camp campaigns actually run on. He gives no method for judging in advance whether an available claim is exceptional enough; his operational answer is elsewhere — run a cheap local test and read the repeat sales.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 77-78. The seeming-advantage clause is stated there in his own terms; the commonplace-facts method it licenses is at printed pp. 79-82, and the repeat-sale test at printed p. 135.
confounders: reading the condition as requiring a genuine product advantage; the seeming-advantage clause explicitly does not
treating it as a differentiation doctrine; his own account is that the article need not be unique and may embody no advantage at all
omitting the retention constraint, which is half the rule

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 185-186 (Chapter Seventeen, things too costly to attempt)
qa_items.question: Hopkins names two conditions that disqualify a product from advertising regardless of how good the campaign would be. State both, and say which of the two is an artefact of his era's media and which is not.
qa_items.answer: The first is narrow incidence: an ointment, a germicide, a treatment for asthma or hay fever, a rub for rheumatism appeal to a small percentage, and the cost of reaching them in mediums of universal circulation is excessive — it cannot come back for decades. The second is a long repeat cycle: there are products every home should have, on convincing reasons, where a single purchase lasts months or years, so the cost of securing a customer exceeds the first-sale profit and further profits are so long deferred that advertiser and advertising man are discouraged before the tide can turn. The first is an artefact of media economics — circulation was bought whole and a narrow product paid for everyone it could not sell — and must not be carried forward as a general property of narrow products. The second is not media-dependent; it is plain unit economics and holds wherever acquisition cost must be recovered from purchases. He says the world is full of such things and that he has seen many men of great ability discouraged by them.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 185-186. He names the excessive cost of reaching a small percentage through universal-circulation mediums, and the repeat-sales-too-far-apart condition, in adjacent paragraphs. The separation of which condition is era-bound is an extraction observation.
confounders: carrying the narrow-incidence rule forward as though reach were still untargetable
reading the long-cycle condition as solved by his auxiliary-products structure at printed p. 197; he never connects the two
treating this as advice about campaign quality; his point is that these products are ruled out before any campaign is designed

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 191-192 (Chapter Eighteen, why he specialised on repeat-purchase goods)
qa_items.question: Hopkins states the rule that governed which products he took on at all. State it, and explain what it does to the reported success rate in this book.
qa_items.answer: He specialised on proprietaries and foods — products people buy over and over — because the whole profit on a one-sale article must be made on that sale, which caps what may be spent to obtain it, whereas a product in daily consumption permits almost unlimited acquisition spending. His stated ideal is products that appeal to nearly every home and must be advertised forever, giving the example of foods mothers teach their children to use. He reports accepting a premium costing more than the profit on the six purchases required to earn it, because those six purchases made the brand familiar and the user then asked for it by name. What it does to the book is create a survivorship effect he built deliberately: his reported success rate is conditioned on a selection rule that excluded the hardest cases in advance. He also concedes the counter-case — a carpet sweeper lasting ten years at about a dollar of profit, which he says nobody has found an ordinary way to advertise profitably.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 191-192. Hardly a limit is rhetorical — the real limit is discounted lifetime value, which he computes nowhere, and his own screen at printed pp. 185-186 is exactly where that arithmetic bites.
confounders: reading hardly a limit literally; he gives no ceiling and computes no lifetime value
treating the selection rule as separate from his results; it is the reason the results look as they do
confusing this with the repeat-sale scaling test at printed p. 135; that is a gate on a campaign, this is a gate on which products to take

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 193-195 (Chapter Eighteen, the cosmetic line he prepared and abandoned)
qa_items.question: Hopkins prepared a complete cosmetic line and then decided to abandon it. What was present, what was missing, and what does his own word for the missing thing tell you about his screen?
qa_items.answer: Present were market size and a finished product: he had learned that American women spent $700,000,000 a year on cosmetics, more than on all other advertised lines combined, and he had prepared the line. Missing was what he calls a theory. The field was overcrowded, leading dealers held thousands of kinds, scores of new makers solicited them weekly, no line dominated, and a converted buyer arriving at a store faced a dozen demonstrators pushing something else. He sent men to Paris and Vienna to find something unique, some claim that would give him an advantage, and they found none — so he decided to abandon the line. His word for the missing element tells you the screen is not about the product's merit or the market's size: it is about whether a specific proposition exists around which an appeal can be built, and in the absence of one he treats abandonment as correct even after the goods exist. The venture resumed only when a proposition appeared, and the theory he eventually adopted was a person rather than a product property.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 193-195, where the $700,000,000 figure, the overcrowding, the Paris and Vienna search and the abandonment decision appear, followed by the account of the theory he found. He held an ownership interest in the resulting business and reports its performance as proprietor.
confounders: reading market size as the entry signal; it is present in this case and he abandons anyway
assuming a theory means a product differentiator; the one he adopted was a named person
taking the recovery as the lesson; the abandonment decision is the transferable part, and he spends more space on the recovery

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 131-132 (Chapter Twelve, the agency advisory board)
qa_items.question: Hopkins reports refusing most of the propositions brought to his agency. Give the ratio, the observation he attaches about who hesitates, and the reason he states for the agency's refusing posture — which is not the reason a reader expects.
qa_items.answer: Of several hundred men with dubious prospects who came to the agency's standing advisory board of some sixteen experienced men, open without obligation, nineteen in twenty were advised not to proceed. His attached observation is that the men who hesitated over their own propositions were the large advertisers with most at stake, and that this is generally so. The reason he gives for the posture is frankly self-interested rather than protective: failures and disasters damage advertising as a whole and therefore damage the agency, while one conspicuous success encourages many new ventures. Two limits: nineteen in twenty is a ratio over a self-selected population — men with dubious prospects who walked in — and not a base rate for propositions generally; and nothing tells us how the refused propositions actually fared.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 131-132. The refusal criteria are not stated in this passage; they have to be assembled from his screening rules scattered elsewhere, principally printed pp. 77-78 and 185-186.
confounders: reading nineteen in twenty as a failure rate for advertising propositions in general
assuming the stated motive is client protection; he gives a reputational-externality argument for the agency
expecting the criteria to be in this passage; they are not, which is why the ratio alone teaches nothing

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 103 (Chapter Nine, the evaporated-milk advice)
qa_items.question: Hopkins advised a client against advertising a standard product on a superiority basis. What is his stated reason, what did he do instead, and where does this sit against his own commonplace-facts doctrine?
qa_items.answer: His reason is that one cannot establish or claim an advantage on natural or standard products — evaporated milk was made to government requirements — and he names eggs, butter, lard, flour and oatmeal as the same case, saying many millions have been wasted trying to tie people to a brand of a staple. His diagnosis of the category was that dominance there was not produced by advertising at all: certain brands held certain markets for years against every effort to displace them, and the only apparent reason was familiarity. So instead of arguing superiority he set out to manufacture familiarity. Where it sits is awkwardly: his commonplace-facts doctrine at printed pp. 79-82 was applied to beer and to canned beans, both arguably standard products. He does not draw the line, and the practical difference appears to be whether the production process is unfamiliar enough to the public to be worth publishing. Note also that the advice was not taken as stated — the campaign ran on the familiarity basis instead, so the rule itself was never tested.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 103, where the standard-product argument, the eggs-and-butter list and the familiarity diagnosis appear. The tension with printed pp. 79-82 is an extraction observation; the source does not remark on it.
confounders: resolving the tension in his favour by assuming beer and beans are not standard products; he never draws that line
treating familiarity as brand-building in the modern sense; his claim is narrower, that recognition is the operative variable where argument is unavailable
reading the rule as tested; the campaign that ran was the alternative

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 79-82 (Chapter Seven, the Schlitz brewery visit and the purity campaign)
qa_items.question: Hopkins built a famous campaign out of facts that were true of every competitor. Describe the mechanism, and state the precondition without which it does not work.
qa_items.answer: Going through the brewery he found filtered-air cooling rooms, wood-pulp filters, pumps and pipes cleaned twice daily, bottles cleaned four times, a 4,000-foot artesian well beside Lake Michigan, six-month ageing, and a mother yeast cell developed through 1,200 experiments — and was told by the brewers that none of it was worth saying because all good brewers did it. He published it, and says he thereby gave the word purity a meaning that rival claims of Pure did not have. The mechanism is a communication asymmetry, not a product advantage: a category-wide claim word carries no information and is discounted, whereas the same claim supported by concrete process facts is believed; and because the facts are unfamiliar to the public though ordinary in the trade, the first to publish them is taken to own them and a later claimant appears to be imitating. He is explicit that the article need not be unique and may embody no advantage at all. The precondition is that no rival has already told the story. The outcome — fifth place to neck-and-neck with first in a very few months — is asserted with no figure, date or source, some thirty years after the fact, and no other cause is examined.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 79-82 for the brewery facts, the brewers' dismissal and the purity claim; the same method is reported for Van Camp beans at printed pp. 98-103, where every process fact told was standard canning practice.
confounders: reading it as a product-differentiation strategy; he insists the product need not differ at all
assuming being first is optional; the whole effect rests on nobody having said it yet
treating the Schlitz outcome as evidence for the mechanism; it is an uncontrolled recollection decades later

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 81-82 (Chapter Seven, the brewers on their own processes) with printed pp. 124-125 (Chapter Eleven)
qa_items.question: You interview a manufacturer and he says a detail of his process is too ordinary to mention because every competent maker does it. Separately, he volunteers at length the thing he is proudest of. On Hopkins's account, what should you conclude about each, and why?
qa_items.answer: His diagnostic runs in both directions. The fact the maker dismisses as commonplace is the cue that it may be the campaign, because his dismissal is caused by familiarity and familiarity is exactly what the buyer lacks — he is too close to his product, sees only the ordinary in his own methods, and does not realise the world at large might marvel at them. The thing he volunteers is what he takes pride in, and Hopkins's repeated finding is that this is usually of no interest to the buyer: makers talk construction because construction is what interests them. The Goodyear case is the paired example — the company promoted a construction name while the two results it produced went unmentioned. Two limits Hopkins does not supply: a fact being unfamiliar does not make it interesting, and he offers no test for which commonplace facts are worth telling short of running the campaign. The discipline that keeps the cue from licensing any process fact at all is his own procedure elsewhere — find out what buyers say they want first, then get figures on those things.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 81-82 for the brewers' dismissal and the maker's blindness to his own methods; printed pp. 124-125 for the construction-versus-result case; the wants-first procedure is at printed pp. 140-142.
confounders: inverting the cue and treating the maker's enthusiasm as the signal, which is what he says produces bad copy
assuming any dismissed fact will do; unfamiliar is not the same as interesting, and he gives no filter
reading it as a research method; it is a cue observed during an interview, and the actual method he prescribes is buyer interviews first

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 124-125 (Chapter Eleven, the straight-side tire renamed)
qa_items.question: A manufacturer's advertising is built on a construction feature the trade is proud of. Hopkins faced exactly this on Goodyear. What did he do, and what is the general move?
qa_items.answer: He had seen the straight-side tire advertised repeatedly without ever learning what it meant. On asking, he found the construction produced two results: the tire would not rim-cut, and it held ten per cent more air size for size. He renamed the product for the result and headed every advertisement with those results. The general move is to convert a construction fact into a result claim, and Hopkins treats that conversion as often being the whole campaign. His stated reason is that the buyer is not a mechanic and cannot evaluate construction, so a construction claim carries her no value, whereas the same fact expressed as an outcome is immediately valuable — results are what people are after and they care not how you get them. His strongest counter-case is in the same book: for Palmolive Shaving Cream he published laboratory process figures as the campaign, and his reconciliation is that those figures answered wants buyers had stated. The ten-per-cent figure is the manufacturer's own; he records no independent verification.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 124-125. The same point is made earlier against broom action, patent dumping devices and cyco bearings on carpet sweepers, at printed pp. 40-41.
confounders: assuming technical detail is always wrong; the Palmolive shaving-cream campaign at printed pp. 140-142 is built entirely on laboratory figures
reading the rename as branding; the name was made to carry the result claim, which is a copy decision in his account
treating the ten-per-cent oversize claim as verified; it is the client's figure

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 184-185 (Chapter Seventeen, on superlatives and definite figures)
qa_items.question: Hopkins claims superlatives are worse than useless. Give his two-part argument, the credibility condition it depends on, and the tungsten-lamp illustration.
qa_items.answer: Part one: a superlative such as the best in the world makes no impression whatever, because it is the expected claim — the reader may not blame you for exaggeration, but you lose much of his respect. Part two is the damage: he naturally minimises whatever else you say, so the superlative discounts the rest of the advertisement. Definite figures behave in the opposite way. Such definite statements are either facts or lies, and people do not expect that reputable concerns will lie, so the figures are accepted at par. His illustration: say a lamp gives more light than other lamps and people are mildly impressed; say it gives three and a half times the light of carbon lamps and they realise you have made actual comparisons. The condition the whole argument rests on is institutional and era-specific, and he states it twice — readers know you cannot, in the better mediums, deliberately mislead them. Note the mechanism rewards whoever quantifies first rather than whoever is better: he says plainly that rivals could probably meet the same shaving-cream specifications.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 184-185. The tungsten figure, the either-facts-or-lies formulation and the better-mediums condition are all stated there; the shaving-cream concession is at printed pp. 140-142 and the three-per-cent margin case at printed p. 166.
confounders: reading it as a claim that specificity is persuasive in itself; his mechanism runs through checkability and legal exposure
dropping the better-mediums condition, which is a fact about 1920s publishing and not a general property of figures
assuming a definite figure implies superiority; he says the device rewards quantifying first, not being better

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 165-166 (Chapter Fifteen, the three per cent net profit)
qa_items.question: Six mail-order competitors were all guaranteeing lowest prices. Hopkins was asked for a more impressive claim. What did he do, why did he say the existing guarantees were worthless, and what can a reader actually check about his answer?
qa_items.answer: All six blazoned low-price claims and published guarantees to undersell any other price, with money back to anyone who found a better bargain. His diagnosis is that in a chorus of that kind all are on the same plane and all are as ineffective as though they made no claims at all. He looked up his client's figures, found the average profit for years past had been less than three per cent, advertised that profit, and promised not to exceed it — the argument being that prices quoted on a three per cent profit must be close to minimum and could not be materially decreased, so those quotations were accepted as bottom prices despite everyone else's guarantees. What a reader can actually check is nothing: a margin is not verifiable by a buyer, the figure came from the client's own historical accounts, and no independent verification is reported. So the device works, on his own account, because definite figures are believed rather than because this one was confirmable.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 165-166. The chorus-of-bargains diagnosis, the three per cent figure and the undertaking not to exceed it are stated there; the general credibility argument is at printed pp. 184-185.
confounders: treating the margin claim as more verifiable than a lowest-price guarantee; it is less so
reading the guarantees as failing because they were untrue; his argument is that identical claims cancel
assuming a competitor could not copy the move; nothing in his account prevents it

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 177-178 (Chapter Seventeen) and printed pp. 99-100 (Chapter Nine)
qa_items.question: Hopkins names two specific phrases-and-postures he says kill advertisements. Name both families, quote the short phrases he gives for the first, and state the single mechanism that condemns both.
qa_items.answer: The first family is brand insistence: insist on this brand, avoid imitations, look out for substitution — to which he adds buy my brand, mine is the original, be sure to get the genuine. He says such appeals have no good effect and indicate a motive with which buyers cannot sympathise, and that he has seen many an advertisement killed by a single unfortunate phrase of this kind. The second family is institutional boasting: about the plant, the output, the age of the firm, anything more interesting to you than to your prospect. Boasting is repulsive, he says, and he identifies it as the recurring reason he lost large accounts. The single mechanism is that both make the advertiser's own interest the visible content of the appeal. Every such phrase is in substance a request to transfer money from a competitor for the advertiser's benefit — a grocer would not say come to my store rather than the next store, he offers an advantage.
