His estimate that nine-tenths of advertising money is lost to selfish purposes openly displayed is rhetorical, with no computation given, and he elsewhere concedes that name-crying may sometimes pay to an extent.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 177 for the insist-on-this-brand phrases and the killed-by-a-single-phrase claim; printed p. 178 for do not boast and boasting is repulsive; printed pp. 99-100 for the buy-my-brand diagnosis and the account-loss dynamic.
confounders: reading these as tone problems; his mechanism is about whose interest is visible
assuming brand insistence fails because of wording; he says the motive is what buyers detect
taking nine-tenths as a measurement

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 66-70 (Chapter Six, 'Personal Salesmanship') and printed p. 177 (Chapter Seventeen)
qa_items.question: A manufacturer wants copy that asks people to buy his product, states where it is stocked and quotes the price. On Hopkins's doctrine, what is wrong with all three, what does he substitute, and what does he concede about the substitution?
qa_items.answer: All three make the seller's interest the content of the appeal, and his position is that no selfish appeal produces a reading or an action. He says he never asks people to buy, rarely says the goods are stocked by dealers, and seldom quotes a price. What he substitutes is service: the appeal must consist of something useful offered to the reader, with the seller's gain left unmentioned. His own worked case is selling shortening to bakers at above the market price, which six salesmen had failed to do at all, by never discussing the product — he offered each baker a printed pie card for his shops, or a signed railcar advertising the baker's own pies for nine hundred miles, on condition that he order the shortening. What he concedes is that the appearance is engineered: the advertisements sound altruistic and the advantage to himself was covered up in his efforts to please. This is a persuasion technique presented as such, not an ethical claim. He also concedes a hard failure condition located in the client rather than in the method — he could not make it work at Swift and Company, which refused to give anything away, and says he knows of no advertising success made by a packing house.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 66-70 for the Cotosuet pie cards and railcar cases and the covered-up advantage; printed p. 177 for from start to finish offer service. The Swift failure is his own counter-case; the six-salesmen comparison is not a controlled one, since they were selling at a price the trade had already refused.
confounders: reading the doctrine as an ethical commitment; he states plainly that the altruistic appearance is constructed
assuming service means customer service; in his cases it is a concrete useful thing given to the buyer
generalising the Cotosuet result; his own Swift case shows the method failing on a client's refusal to give anything

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 177 (Chapter Seventeen, brilliant writing has no place in advertising) and printed p. 22 (Chapter Two)
qa_items.question: A team is pleased that readers call their advertisement beautiful and admire the writing. What does Hopkins say that reaction indicates, and what is the mechanism he proposes?
qa_items.answer: He treats admiration as evidence against the advertisement. His claims are that brilliant writing has no place in advertising, that a unique style takes attention from the subject, that any apparent effort to sell creates corresponding resistance, and that persuasive ability arouses the fear of over-influence. His prescription follows: be natural and simple, keep the language inconspicuous, use the shortest words possible, never try to show off — in fishing for buyers, as in fishing for bass, one should not reveal the hook. The mechanism is signalling: visible skill signals intent to persuade, and a buyer who detects intent to persuade discounts the content, exactly as a buyer becomes wary of an over-dressed salesman. Two limits worth stating. He scopes the claim to his own audience of ordinary purchasers spending their own money, and he offers no traced comparison anywhere of a plain against a stylish text where only style differed — the nearest evidence, the mail-order cost-per-reply case, varies size, type, decoration and copy together.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 177 for the four claims and the fishing image; printed p. 22 for the earlier statement that style is a handicap and that education and literary style hinder this work. The claim shades into his stated personal hostility to formal education at printed pp. 7-8.
confounders: reading it as advice to write badly; he prescribes plainness, not incompetence
treating the mail-order 42-cent case at printed pp. 158-159 as isolating style; several variables move together there
carrying the claim outside the audience he scopes it to at printed p. 6

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 152-153 and printed p. 185 (Chapters Fourteen and Seventeen, on prevention and negative appeals)
qa_items.question: A hygiene brand proposes a campaign showing the consequences of neglect in order to frighten people into buying. State Hopkins's objection in two parts — one psychological, one economic — and the exception he grants.
qa_items.answer: The psychological part: people will do little to prevent troubles they do not have, because they do not cross bridges in advance; they are seeking happiness, safety, beauty and content, not avoiding hypothetical harms. He couples this with an absolute rule against negative presentation — never advertise negatively, do not picture or feature ills, show the happier results — and reports that every illustration he used showed attractive people and good teeth. The economic part is the sharper half and is usually missed: people will do anything to cure troubles which exist, but legitimate advertising has little scope there, because those who have met the misfortune form in most lines a percentage too small to consider. So the exception is real — fear works where the trouble already exists — and it is ruled out by audience size, not by psychology. His evidence is that scores tried to scare people into using a dentifrice and none succeeded so far as he knows, which is an absence of success in his own recall rather than a comparison.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 152-153 for the prevention-versus-cure reasoning and the resolution to advertise the tooth paste as a creator of beauty; printed p. 185 for never advertise negatively and the too-small-a-percentage statement.
confounders: stating the rule as fear never works; he says it works where the trouble exists and is uneconomic there
reading the beauty appeal as a creative choice; he reports verifying by keyed returns that beauty was the appeal that drew
treating the claim as measured; it rests on his not knowing of a successful fear campaign

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 151-153 (Chapter Fourteen, the film and the beauty appeal)
qa_items.question: Hopkins initially refused the Pepsodent proposition. What changed his mind, and what is the device he used, stated generally?
qa_items.answer: He refused because it was a technical proposition and he did not see a way to educate the laity in technical tooth-paste theories. He then read book after book by dental authorities and in the middle of one found a reference to the mucin plaques on teeth, which he afterwards called the film. The device, stated generally, is to name a concrete obstacle and attach a wanted outcome to removing it: rather than teaching the buyer a theory, give her a single named thing standing between her and something she wants — here, beauty — and let the product be the removal of it. He then verified by keyed returns that beauty was the appeal that drew. Two things to keep in view. The obstacle was renamed by the advertiser, from a term of art to a coined word, so the device includes constructing the category in which the product wins. And he held a stock option in the enterprise and reports making a million dollars on it, which bears on how his retrospective account of his own foresight should be read.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 151-152 for the initial refusal, the option on a block of stock, the reading and the film; printed p. 153 for beauty as the chief appeal learned from the coupon reports.
confounders: reading it as consumer education; he explicitly rejected educating the laity in the theory
treating film as a technical term he adopted; it is a word he coined for one
reading his initial scepticism as modesty; it is a useful record of how uncertain the decision was in advance

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 140-142 (Chapter Twelve, Palmolive Shaving Cream)
qa_items.question: Hopkins entered a category of loyal users with a product he says had no real advantage. Give his two-step procedure, say why the order of the two steps matters, and state what he concedes about the resulting advantage.
qa_items.answer: Step one: send research men to interview men by the hundreds and record what they say they most desire in the product. Step two: take those stated wants to the chemist and require measured figures on each of them for your own product. The resulting claims were lather multiplied 250 times, fifteen per cent of water absorbed by the beard within one minute making the hairs wax-like for cutting, and lather holding its fulness ten minutes on the face. The order matters because interviewing establishes which attributes buyers will attend to, so measurement effort is spent only where it will be credited and the figures answer questions buyers were already asking; reversed, you get measured facts nobody asked for. What he concedes is decisive: rivals could probably meet the same specifications, and he has no idea that one maker far excels others in the line — the advantage came from being first to give figures on results. One wrinkle in his own procedure: the chemist volunteered a further factor buyers had not named, so the method as described also permits adding wants buyers never expressed.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 140-142. Interviews reported with no sample definition, method, geography or date beyond men by the hundreds; the outcome of domination in eighteen months is explicitly reported as hearsay — he says he is told it happened.
confounders: reading it as product development; nothing about the product changed
reversing the steps into measure-then-message, which is the failure mode the procedure is designed against
treating the eighteen-month domination as a reported result; he marks it as something he was told

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 98-103 (Chapter Nine, the Van Camp investigation)
qa_items.question: Every advertiser in a category is arguing against the other brands. Hopkins investigated and concluded they were all fighting over the wrong thing. What did he find, what did he do, and what is the general principle?
qa_items.answer: He found that 94 per cent of housewives baked their own pork and beans, so only 6 per cent were amenable to any canned-bean argument — and every advertiser in the field was crying buy my brand at that six per cent. His move was to change the opponent: he could not bake better beans than his rivals, but he could bake better beans than any woman at home, so the campaign attacked the home practice on its specific weaknesses — sixteen hours of cooking, crisped beans on top and mushy beans below, fermentation, poor digestibility. The general principle is that advertising can only win a buyer away from whatever she is doing instead, so where the dominant alternative is a household practice rather than a rival product, arguments aimed at rival products address a small minority and leave the real contest untouched. Two cautions. The 94 per cent figure is reported without method, sample, geography or date, attributed to investigators he sent out. And this sits in direct tension with his later Quaker Oats conclusion that habits cannot be changed profitably in paid print — a contradiction he never addresses.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 98-103 for the 94 per cent finding, the attack on home baking and the restaurant distribution used as evidence to women. The contradiction is with printed pp. 147-148.
confounders: reading it as competitive positioning against brands, which is exactly the framing he rejects
assuming the 94 per cent is a measured statistic; no method is reported
resolving the contradiction with the habit-change chapter by assuming he changed his mind; he presents both as lessons and never reconciles them

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 147-148 (Chapter Thirteen, the Quaker Oats educational campaign)
qa_items.question: Hopkins calls the Quaker Oats campaign one of the greatest mistakes of his life. What was the reasoning that led him into it, why did it fail on his account, and what is the sweeping conclusion he draws — including the part of it that is narrower than he admits?
qa_items.answer: The reasoning was share arithmetic: the company controlled a large percentage of the oatmeal business, so increasing total consumption of oatmeal would bring it most of the benefit. He employed hundreds of men to gather data and ran an educational campaign to create new users. He says it was far-reaching and effective as far as it went and did not pay, because no new user would repay the cost of his conversion in his lifetime. The sweeping conclusion: no one can profitably change habits in paid print; new habits are created by general education and largely by writers who occupy free space; if it cannot be done on a large scale it certainly cannot be done on a small one; every line and every word directed to that end is waste; the advertiser comes in after the habit is changed and says which method is right. The narrower truth is in his own diagnosis of this case: everybody already knew the value of oatmeal, so those not using it had a reason hard to overcome. That is a specific feature of this category, not a general law, and the conclusion drawn from it is much wider than the case supports. He offers a second costing — converting a person to the tooth brush at some $25 a convert — as his own figuring, with no derivation.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 147-148. The one-line structural argument he does not make explicit but which follows from his text is that one advertiser bears the whole cost of conversion while every competitor shares the benefit.
confounders: reading it as a claim that category growth never pays, when his own diagnosis rests on oatmeal already being universally known
treating the $25 conversion cost as measured
missing that it contradicts the Van Camp account at printed pp. 98-103, where he claims to have moved women off home baking

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 98-103 (Van Camp) read against printed pp. 147-148 (Quaker Oats)
qa_items.question: Hopkins reports moving housewives off home baking and also concludes that habits cannot be changed profitably in paid print. Both are his own accounts, both are asserted as lessons. State the distinction that could reconcile them, and be clear about whose distinction it is.
qa_items.answer: The distinction that could reconcile them is that Van Camp substituted a purchase for a task the housewife was already performing — she already wanted baked beans and the change was who did the baking — whereas the Quaker campaign tried to make people who did not eat oatmeal start eating it, which is adoption of a practice rather than substitution of a supplier for one. On that reading, converting existing demand is cheap and creating demand is not. It must be stated plainly that this distinction is not Hopkins's. He never addresses the contradiction, never qualifies either conclusion by reference to the other, and states both in the strong form. A reader who attributes the reconciliation to the source is putting words in his mouth; what the source actually provides is two opposed lessons drawn from two of his own campaigns.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 98-103 and printed pp. 147-148. The contradiction is an extraction observation; the proposed distinction is the extractor's, offered as the available reconciliation and marked as such.
confounders: attributing the substitution-versus-adoption distinction to Hopkins
assuming the later chapter supersedes the earlier one; the book presents both as standing lessons
resolving it by chronology; he does not date the two conclusions against each other

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 120-121 (Chapter Ten, choosing the key-note) and printed p. 149 (Chapter Thirteen, calories)
qa_items.question: Hopkins treats the choice of a campaign's central note as a decision about something other than the product. About what, and give two of his own examples with the period condition each depended on.
qa_items.answer: About what the public is currently preoccupied with. He says one can never strike the right chord until he knows the trend of popular opinion, that one must know what buyers are thinking about and coming to want, and that he re-educated himself in current conditions after years away from a category because the situation changes like a kaleidoscope. Examples: he chose efficiency as the key-note for a car in a period when efficiency was a general business preoccupation; he chose engineering in a period when cars broke down and buyers valued engineering above everything; and on Quaker Oats during the war, when meat substitution was urged and calorie counting had become a fad, he presented cost per thousand calories at about a tenth the cost of meat and reports sales doubled. Each depends on its moment, and he says so. Two cautions: the doubling coincides with wartime meat scarcity and a national campaign for meat substitutes, and he claims the presentation as the cause; and his most successful key-note choice by his own account destroyed the client, so matching the preoccupation is necessary and plainly not sufficient.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 120-121 for the trend-of-popular-opinion argument and the efficiency choice; printed p. 149 for the calorie presentation and the doubling claim. The destroyed client is at printed pp. 119-120.
confounders: deriving the key-note from the product, which is the move he argues against
reading the calorie doubling as isolated from wartime conditions
treating a well-chosen key-note as sufficient; his Mitchell case is the counter-example in the same chapter

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 119-120 (Chapter Ten, the efficiency campaign that ruined its client)
qa_items.question: Hopkins reports a campaign he calls the most successful automobile advertising he ever did, which ended in the client's destruction. Trace the mechanism, and state the governance conclusion he does not draw.
qa_items.answer: The key-note was efficiency, chosen because efficiency was a general preoccupation and the firm had a genuine efficiency expert and an efficient plant. Inquiries ran at a rate he says he never saw matched, sales started at an amazing rate, the company was recapitalised — and the car had been skimped in every detail. Hundreds came back, every car sold damaged the name, the bad reputation spread so widely that recovery proved impossible, and his own formulation is that the larger the sales the worse became the ruin. The mechanism is that advertising accelerates trial, so where the product fails on trial each additional sale converts into an additional damaged reputation, and the rate of destruction rises with the effectiveness of the advertising rather than falling. His own phrase is that they played too high a note for the product they had to sell. The governance conclusion he does not draw, anywhere he discusses how success should be judged, is that inquiry volume and early sales are not evidence of a successful campaign. The account is qualitative throughout, in a chapter where he elsewhere gives figures freely.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 119-120. No figures are given for this campaign. The observation that he does not generalise it into a rule about judging campaigns is an extraction observation.
confounders: diagnosing it as a copy failure; the copy worked, which is the point
reading too high a note as exaggeration in the claims; his account is that the claim was true of the plant and false of the car
assuming he draws the measurement lesson; he presents it as an accepted lesson about products, not about how to read response

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 116-117 (Chapter Ten, the trend of the crowd)
qa_items.question: Hopkins names one device the single most effective thing he ever found in advertising. Which, on what reasoning, and what does every case he reports have in common that limits the claim?
qa_items.answer: The trend of the crowd — the observable direction of other buyers. His reasoning is that people cannot judge values and know they cannot, so they accept the verdict of the majority; it is hard for them to analyse reasons and worth, so they follow the crowd. He built whole campaigns on it: a car sold on the story of demand outrunning a bankrupt factory until production moved into tents; a tire brand whose growth in demand was featured in pictures and type until it seemed the whole motor world was turning to it; a car sold on multiplying sales and the production economies they permitted. He adds a variant for categories where ordinary buyers cannot measure — cite the choices of commercial users who do measure, since the ordinary buyer knows fleet operators do not choose on guesswork. What every case has in common is a brand that was already growing. The device requires a real trend to point at, so on his own evidence it amplifies momentum rather than creating it, and he does not distinguish it from a claim that the crowd is right. He also concedes that the figures in the Overland story may not be accurate and that he tells it from memory.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 116-117. The commercial-user variant appears in the tire material at printed pp. 123-130. He hedges the Overland figures explicitly.
confounders: reading it as social proof that can be manufactured; every case he gives has an underlying real trend
assuming he claims the crowd judges well; his claim is that buyers substitute the crowd's verdict for a judgement they cannot make
treating the commercial-user variant as third-party testing; it is borrowed judgement from buyers who do measure

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 125 (Chapter Eleven, after rivals adopted the same tire construction)
qa_items.question: Hopkins's most successful differentiation campaign forced every rival to copy the feature. What happened next, what did he do, and what does his successor argument require that makes it unavailable to most advertisers?
qa_items.answer: Within two or three years the advantage the campaign had been built on no longer existed, because the campaign itself had forced all rivals to that type of tire and Goodyear could no longer claim it. His response had three parts: he gradually reduced the coined product name, promoted the house name in its place, and shifted the argument to a different and, he says, more impressive talking point — the demonstrable growth of demand. He reports the same pattern in sampling, where rivals adopted the coupon plan and a new mechanism had to be invented, and states generally that few who dominate a field have any exclusive advantage and there are few advertised products which cannot be imitated. What the successor argument requires is a visible lead in demand, which is available only to a brand that is already winning. He offers no successor at all for a brand whose differentiator expires while it is behind. The two-or-three-year timing is one observation in one category in one period and he does not offer it as a general figure.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 125. The general statement that few who dominate have any exclusive advantage is at printed p. 82.
confounders: reading the retreat to the house name as brand-building strategy; in his account it is what remains when the claim expires
treating two or three years as a rule of thumb he endorses
assuming the demand-trend successor is generally available; it is available only to the leader

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 125-126 (Chapter Eleven, on names that tell a story)
qa_items.question: Why does Hopkins treat naming as a principal creative decision rather than a labelling step, and what does he concede about names that succeeded without one?
qa_items.answer: Because the name is the part always displayed — in every advertisement and on every package — so a name that states the claim forms an advertisement in itself and delivers the claim at every exposure, including exposures where nothing else is read. He says coining the right name is often the major step in good advertising and that no doubt such names often double the results of expenditures, which is offered as no doubt and carries no measurement. His cases: a tire named from the result its construction produced; an anti-skid tread named for the usage he wanted to establish, all wheels and all weathers, which he says became the custom largely through that influence; a cereal renamed so that two products could be advertised as a pair; a car reframed as a numbered model signed by its designer as a farewell creation. What he concedes is substantial: some products succeeded on fortunate names with almost no story to tell, and the very men who succeeded with one such name failed repeatedly with others — cases from which, he says, no principle can be drawn. He also concedes that a name built on a differentiator inherits that differentiator's expiry.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 125-126 for the name-tells-a-story argument and the doubling estimate; printed p. 176 for the fortunate-name concession and the repeated failures of the same men.
confounders: treating the doubling claim as measured
reading the fortunate-name cases as supporting naming generally; he cites them as cases yielding no transferable principle
assuming a claim-carrying name is permanent; he retired one himself when the claim expired

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 110-111 (Chapter Ten) and printed p. 145 (Chapter Thirteen, Professor Anderson)
qa_items.question: Hopkins says he attached a named individual to a product wherever possible. Give his stated reasons, the three uses he reports, and the thing he says openly about where such names come from.
qa_items.answer: His reasons: personalities appeal while soulless corporations do not; make a man famous and you make his creation famous; it is far easier to make a man famous than an institution; and an individual's name is usually better than a coined name and far better than a trade mark. His uses: featuring an unknown chief engineer by name, which he says gave a mid-priced car a distinction against a better-known and handsomer rival at the same price; making a designer sign the advertisements, borrowing his existing reputation; and writing an entire selling book in the name and voice of an independent practical chicken raiser who cared more for serving than for selling, producing a catalogue unlike the five or six identical ones the prospect had requested. He also established the inventor of puffed grains as the personality on that campaign. What he says openly is that the device is constructive — such names are often created for the purpose, as in theatre, film and authorship, and he wrote a book in another man's name on facts that man supplied. The strongest case he reports is a single uncontrolled comparison in which price, reputation and appearance all differed as well.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 110-111 for the personality doctrine and the engineer and designer cases; printed p. 145 for the establishment of Professor Anderson on puffed grains. His largest later use of it was a business in which he held equity.
confounders: reading it as spokesperson endorsement; his claim is that advertising makes the person prominent and the name then becomes an exclusive asset
assuming the person must already be famous; he says such names are often created for the purpose
treating the Chalmers-against-Cadillac comparison as isolating the device

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 99 (Chapter Nine, 'Try Our Rivals, Too')
qa_items.question: Faced with substitution once imitators arrived, rival advertisers insisted on their own brands. Hopkins did the opposite. What did he do, what is his stated reading of why it worked, and what does the move presuppose?
qa_items.answer: He came out with headlines urging readers to buy the named competing brands and compare them with his own. His stated reading is that the willingness to invite comparison is itself the evidence: if we were certain enough of our advantage to invite such comparisons, people were certain enough to buy. So the operative effect is the buyer's inference from a costly signal — directing a buyer to a rival is expensive to fake — rather than the comparison itself. He reports the rivals' brand insistence fell on deaf ears. What it presupposes is a genuine advantage, or at least a strongly held claim; and here his own account of the category cuts against him, since he says the product was materially like its rivals and that in a blind serving of half a dozen brands nobody present could identify it. No response figures are given; the outcome is reported only as the appeal winning over others.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 99 for the Try Our Rivals headlines and the certainty argument; printed p. 101 for the blind serving in which the brand could not be identified.
confounders: reading it as comparative advertising in the modern sense; he is not claiming the comparison will be won on merit
assuming the advantage must be real; his own account suggests it was not, which is the interesting part
treating the rivals' failure as evidence for his mechanism; neither side's returns are reported

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 160-161 (Chapter Fifteen, the women's garment credit business)
qa_items.question: Hopkins set up a mail-order business on terms identical to a competitor next door and says he drove that competitor out. Since the terms were the same, what changed, and what is the general principle?
qa_items.answer: Everything about how accepting the offer would feel. He gave the business a woman's name, selected a capable middle-aged woman and pictured her in every advertisement, had her sign them, and made the appeal from one woman to another. The advertisements never mentioned instalments; they dealt with credit, appealed to young women who wished to appear at their best, and pointed out what that meant in a woman's career. Six months to pay was presented as an accommodation extended between equals — made to resemble the thirty-day store credit that richer women received — rather than as a concession to need. His formulation is that the offer was flattering, not humiliating, and that cold commercialism could not compete with the atmosphere created. The general principle is that where an offer implies something about the buyer's circumstances, the framing decides whether accepting it is degrading or flattering; borrowing the framing of a higher-status arrangement lets the buyer accept without admitting need. The outcome is asserted with no figures and no date, and he was selling a second line into the same customer base at the same time.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 160-161. Culturally bounded: the appeal, the class comparison and the woman-to-woman device belong to American commerce and gender conventions of the 1910s and are recorded as the source's own framing.
confounders: attributing the result to better terms; the terms were identical by his own statement
reading it as tone of voice; the specific move is borrowing a higher-status arrangement's frame
treating the competitor's closure as demonstrated causation; no figures or dates are given

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 173-174 (Chapter Sixteen, the reason is rarely economy)
qa_items.question: A brand aimed at buyers of limited means proposes to lead on how much money the product saves them. State Hopkins's objection, his substitute, and the character of the evidence he offers.
qa_items.answer: His objection is that the reason for a purchase is rarely economy, and that where economy is a necessity most people like to defy it: suggest a thing because it is economical and you arouse opposition, you hurt their pride. A price appeal classifies the buyer, and buyers who must economise experience that classification as an injury. His substitute is to direct the appeal to those who do not consider cost, so that the buyer who must economise can include herself without accepting the classification — she demands what the best people use. His evidence is his own observation of the gardeners, their families and the village folk near his country home, whom he presents as typifying the ninety-five per cent who are his customers; and a cosmetics experience in which a low price on perfume did not appeal to the girl who should have economised. That is a convenience sample chosen and interpreted by him and presented as authoritative. The passage is heavily bounded by 1920s American assumptions about class, pride and gender, and is recorded as his framing, not as a finding about buyers.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 173-174. He states in the same passage that he does not consult managers and boards of directors and submits campaigns to the simple folks around him instead.
confounders: reading it as a rule against price mechanics; he used coupons, free bottles and a published margin extensively
treating the country-place observations as research
generalising it beyond the socially visible goods and the 1920s American context he draws it from

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 19-21 (Chapter Two) and printed p. 174 (Chapter Sixteen)
qa_items.question: Hopkins says the people deciding a campaign are systematically the wrong judges of it. State his mechanism, the remedy he prescribes, and the weakness in the remedy.
qa_items.answer: The mechanism is structural rather than a failure of intelligence: preferences are formed by surroundings and the prosperous mingle with the prosperous, so the further a decider has moved from ordinary purchasers the less his own reaction predicts theirs. His formulations are that we must never judge humanity by ourselves, that he knows nothing more ridiculous than grey-haired boards of directors deciding what housewives want, and that where men insisted on judging the world by themselves, four times in five they failed. His remedy is to submit the question to ordinary members of the buying public rather than to managers and boards — he says he does not consult managers and directors because their viewpoint is nearly always distorted, and submits campaigns to the simple folk around his country place. The weakness is that his own alternative is a convenience sample he chose, living on his own property, presented as authoritative; and the four-times-in-five figure is asserted with no basis, sample or definition of failure. He also concedes that people who judged the world by themselves sometimes succeeded.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 19-21 for the childhood origin — a book he was certain everyone wanted, refused by the town mayor on moral grounds and then sold seven times over in one business office — and the four-times-in-five claim; printed p. 174 for the remedy.
confounders: reading it as an argument for consumer research; his remedy is asking the people around him, not a designed study
treating four times in five as a measurement
assuming he exempts his own judgement; the whole passage is offered as why his judgement was better, which is the same structure he criticises

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 42-44 (Chapter Four, the Christmas display racks and the twelve woods)
qa_items.question: A manufacturer needs independent retailers to stock a slow-moving item and to give it window display. He has no sales force and refuses to concede margin. Hopkins faced exactly this at Bissell. What form did he give the offer, what did he require in return, and what does he say the form itself accomplished?
qa_items.answer: He offered the dealer something the dealer wanted — a display rack and show cards for Christmas, and later a run of sweepers built in twelve distinguished woods, twelve to the dozen — and he offered it free but explicitly not as a gift: as a reward, and as a privilege the dealer had to apply for. In return he required a signed agreement that the dealer would display the goods on the furnished rack with the furnished cards until sold, and would enclose his pamphlets in every package leaving the store for three weeks. Scarcity was stated into the offer — the twelve woods would never be offered again. His account of why the form works is that it made the dealer solicit him: he appeared as a benefactor rather than a salesman, and he never asked for a purchase, which he calls useless. The figures he reports are dealer-side only: about five thousand letters brought a thousand orders, and the whole stock of 250,000 sweepers cleared in three weeks. He reports no consumer-sales measurement for the twelve-woods run at all.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 42-44. The privilege-not-inducement formulation, the signed display agreement, the 5,000 letters and 1,000 orders, and the three-week clearance of 250,000 sweepers are all stated there. Practitioner assertion with reported order figures and no consumer-side measurement.
confounders: the modern trade-promotion default — a discount, a rebate, or free goods with the order; Hopkins is specifically avoiding a margin concession and says so at pp. 129-130 and pp. 195-196
reading it as a merchandising giveaway; the conditional signed agreement is the load-bearing part, not the free rack
assuming the 1,000 orders measure consumer demand; they measure dealer response to a letter
confusing it with the pre-announced coupon plan of pp. 103-105, which forces stocking through consumer demand rather than through a privilege offered to the dealer

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 40-41 (Chapter Four, the Powers pamphlet for the Bissell Carpet Sweeper Company)
qa_items.question: A client must choose between a pamphlet by the most celebrated copywriter of the day and one by an unknown who has spent years inside the trade. On Hopkins's account of this exact episode, what was wrong with the celebrated writer's work — and, applying Hopkins's own evidence rule, what does the outcome of the episode actually establish?
qa_items.answer: His objection is not to the writing. He grants that the man was at the height of his fame and remembers the opening line. The objection is that the writer knew nothing about carpet sweepers, had given no study to the trade situation, knew none of the company's problems, and had never spent a moment on a woman's possible wish for a sweeper — so there was not one word in the pamphlet that would lead a woman to buy. General craft did not substitute for knowledge of the specific buying situation. Applying his own refusal rule from pp. 175-176, the outcome establishes much less than it appears to. What is reported is that the company decided against the famous writer, that the writer sued for his fee, and that the company fought and won the suit on Hopkins's pamphlet. That is an internal preference and a court result. No keyed comparison of the two pamphlets selling sweepers is reported, and by the standard Hopkins states elsewhere — an untraced success is not evidence about the advertising that accompanied it — this case is an anecdote in favour of his rule, not a test of it.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 40-41 for the episode and for the "not one word which will lead women to buy" objection; printed pp. 175-176 for the refusal rule applied back against it. The pamphlet comparison was decided by the client and by a lawsuit, not by traced returns.
confounders: reading it as an argument against hiring good writers; his argument is about what the writer investigated, not about ability
treating the lawsuit outcome as evidence that the pamphlet sold better
the modern brief-versus-craft framing, in which the fix is a better brief; Hopkins's fix is the writer doing the investigation himself
confusing it with his separate claim at pp. 22 and 177 that literary style is itself a handicap — a different objection with a different mechanism

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 79 (Chapter Seven, the Montgomery Ward sewing-machine inquiry)
qa_items.question: A mail-order house receives an enquiry about one specific product and its standing practice is to mail the general catalogue to every enquirer alike. Hopkins changed exactly this at Montgomery Ward. What did he substitute, what second element did he add, and what is the general principle he draws?
qa_items.answer: He argued that a woman who writes in about a sewing-machine has that and nothing else on her mind, and should be treated like a prospect who had walked into a store. So the general catalogue was replaced by a special sewing-machine catalogue showing every style and price. The second element was social proof made local and checkable: each enquirer was also sent the names of everyone in her own vicinity who had bought one of their sewing-machines, and was asked to go and see the machines and talk to their owners. The principle he draws is that in a wide-reaching campaign we are too apt to regard people in the mass and broadcast seed hoping some part takes root, which he calls too wasteful ever to bring a profit; we must get down to individuals and treat people in advertising as we treat them in person, centring on the desires the person actually expressed. He reports no figures for the change.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 79, the Montgomery Ward passage he handled through the J. L. Stack agency. The special catalogue, the names of nearby owners, and the "get down to the units" formulation are all stated there. Asserted as a valuable principle learned; no result is reported.
confounders: the modern personalisation/segmentation reading; his unit is the single expressed desire in a single letter, and his tool is a different catalogue plus a list of neighbours
reading the neighbour list as a testimonial device supplied by the seller; he sends her to talk to them unmediated
assuming the change was measured; nothing is reported beyond his advocacy of it
confusing it with the trend-of-the-crowd argument at pp. 116-117, which works on an anonymous mass verdict rather than on named local owners

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 101-102 (Chapter Nine, the blind tasting at the Van Camp factory) read against printed p. 103 (the evaporated-milk refusal)
qa_items.question: A client's product cannot be told from its rivals in a blind comparison, and he concludes that advertising cannot help him. Hopkins met this literally — in the Van Camp factory a half-dozen brands were served and nobody present could pick out Van Camp's. What did he do, and where does he say this move stops working?
qa_items.answer: He did not look for a superiority claim. He told the ordinary facts of good canning practice that no competitor had bothered to state: beans grown on particular soils, vine-ripened Livingston Stone tomatoes, every lot analysed, steam ovens baking for hours at 245 degrees, boiling in soft water so the skins would not toughen, sealing so flavour could not escape. He says plainly that this was the same story any rival could have told, and that the others thought it too commonplace to tell. The claim is not that the product is better; it is that the article first allied with those facts comes to typify them. The boundary is on the facing page. When Van Camp went into evaporated milk, Hopkins advised against advertising it, because it is a standard product made to government requirements — no advantage can be established or claimed on a natural or standard product, and he lists eggs, butter, lard and flour as the same case. So the move applies where practice varies and is untold, not where the product is standardised by specification and there is nothing left to tell.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 101-102 for the indistinguishable brands and the list of commonplace facts he told; printed p. 103 for the refusal on evaporated milk and the eggs/butter/lard/flour comparison. The Van Camp campaign outcome is asserted as an enormous success with a price premium; no traced figures for it are given anywhere in the chapter.
confounders: the modern positioning default of finding or manufacturing a differentiator; Hopkins is explicitly conceding parity and claiming the untold fact instead
reading it as permission to imply superiority from a parity fact; he says the story is one any rival could tell
assuming the Schlitz and Van Camp move is universal; p. 103 is his own stated exception and he acted on it against his own billings
confusing 'standard product' with 'commodity category' — his test is a specification others must also meet, not merely a crowded market

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 103-105 (Chapter Nine, the Van Camp's Milk coupon page in New York)
qa_items.question: A brand has almost no shelf presence in a city dominated by a rival, and no budget for salesmen to call on grocers. Apply Hopkins's Van Camp's Milk plan: what is the sequence, what makes the grocer stock, and what did he report it cost and return?
qa_items.answer: The sequence is announce, then redeem. For three weeks he announced in the newspapers that a coupon good at any store for a ten-cent can would appear, and told housewives what to expect from the milk. In parallel he mailed proofs of those advertisements to grocers, telling them every one of their customers would receive a coupon. The grocer's own arithmetic does the stocking: each coupon is a ten-cent sale that goes to a competitor if he cannot fill it — the manufacturer pays the grocer his retail price on redemption, so the grocer takes his normal profit and carries no risk. Then the coupon ran on a single Sunday page. In New York he reports 97 per cent distribution secured within three weeks, largely by letter; 1,460,000 coupons presented from that one page; $146,000 paid out to grocers to redeem them; a total enterprise cost of $175,000 including the advertising; and the cost returned with a profit in under nine months. These are his own retrospective figures, unaudited, and he warns in a neighbouring chapter that his memory of dates and sums may be at fault.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 103-105. The three-week pre-announcement to consumers and to grocers, the 97 per cent distribution figure, the 1,460,000 coupons, the $146,000 redemption, the $175,000 total and the under-nine-months payback are all stated there. Era-bound: paper coupons redeemed at independent grocers, general-circulation newspapers, no targeting.
confounders: the modern digital-coupon or trade-listing analogy; the whole mechanism depends on the grocer physically fearing a lost ten-cent sale to the shop next door
treating the 1,460,000 coupons as 1,460,000 converted users; he claims homes trying the milk in a single day, and the repeat question is answered separately at p. 135
confusing it with promiscuous house-to-house sampling, which he attacks on the very next page as cheapening the product and offending grocers
assuming the figures were audited; they are his recollection two decades later

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 117-118 (Chapter Ten, on the desire for a change) with printed p. 183 (Chapter Seventeen)
qa_items.question: A campaign is still producing, but the client, the account team and the writer are all tired of it and want something new. Apply Hopkins: whose fatigue is this, what does he say about the reader, and what is the one condition under which he would change?
qa_items.answer: He treats the fatigue as belonging to the wrong people. Continuous advertising along one line grows monotonous to the advertiser, who feels the public reads his story as often as he does, and it bores the man who writes it; both come to long for a change. The reader, on his account, reads the story once, as he reads a news item, and Hopkins says he knows of no reason why the reader should read it again — which is also why he insists every advertisement must carry the complete case rather than deferring anything to a later insertion. His default is therefore to keep a course that is working: there may be another way to success, even greater success, but the chances are against it, and the best way found to sell a product to thousands is probably the best way to sell other thousands. The condition he states for changing is not boredom and not elapsed time: he hesitates to drop a profitable method until he has found and proved a better one by some local tests. He offers no figure anywhere for how long a campaign keeps working.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 117-118 for the monotony argument, the read-once claim and the local-test condition; printed p. 183 for the complete-story consequence. Practitioner assertion; no wear-out data of any kind is reported.
confounders: modern creative-wear-out and frequency-decay findings, which describe an audience effect Hopkins denies exists in his medium
reading him as forbidding change; his rule is to change only against a locally tested alternative
his own aside on the same pages that he personally lost interest once a campaign was on a clear course — a remark about his temperament, not a rule
generalising the read-once premise past 1920s general-circulation print, where a given reader met one insertion in one issue

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 126-127 (Chapter Eleven, naming the stocking dealers in the Goodyear newspaper campaign)
qa_items.question: Dealers in a category buy hand-to-mouth and will not hold stock. Hopkins solved this on Goodyear with a device that used no salesmen and no discount. What was it, what was the qualifying condition, and what does he say makes it compound?
qa_items.answer: He ran a large local newspaper campaign and offered to name, in every advertisement, every dealer who stocked. The qualifying condition was a minimum stock — he states $250 — so the dealer had to buy in before he could appear. He reports inducing some 30,000 dealers to stock Goodyear tires on that basis within a few months, and says the campaign did much to change the whole complexion of the tire business. The compounding mechanism he gives is peer visibility rather than economics: no dealer likes to see his rivals named in a big campaign with his own name omitted, so the more dealers who join, the easier it becomes to get the rest. He claims to have secured almost universal distribution on new products this way more than once, and calls the plan an almost irresistible inducement to stock. No cost-per-dealer or sell-through figure is given.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 126-127. The $250 minimum, the ~30,000 dealers, the omitted-name mechanism and the "few plans are more effective" assessment are stated there. Outcome claimed, no traced figures. Era-bound: local newspapers with space enough to print a long list of dealer names.
confounders: reading it as co-operative advertising, in which the dealer pays a share; here the manufacturer pays and the dealer's price of entry is holding stock
the modern retailer-locator or store-finder analogy, which is a service to the shopper rather than a lever on the dealer
confusing it with the pre-announced coupon plan at pp. 103-105, which works through consumer demand the grocer cannot afford to miss
assuming a margin concession is involved; the whole point at pp. 129-130 is that he refuses to pay the trade

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 129-130 (Chapter Eleven) restated at printed pp. 195-196 (Chapter Eighteen)
qa_items.question: A launch plan has two halves: a consumer campaign, and a sales force selling jobbers and retailers with free goods and extra margin to secure listings. Hopkins states a doctrine that rules on this directly. What is the doctrine, what failure does he describe, and what does he say he actually did across his own accounts?
qa_items.answer: The doctrine is that one cannot afford to sell anything twice: selling margins are not sufficient to accommodate both consumer demand and bought trade distribution, so an advertiser must choose. If a line can be sold by interesting dealers, let the dealer sell; but if you are going to do the selling for him, he can be paid no more than a distributor's profit. The failure he describes is doubled selling expense — the advertiser wins the consumer, which is expense enough, then gives his profits away in free goods and inducements to jobbers and dealers who thereupon become mere order-takers and supply a demand they did not create. He adds two reasons the concession never ends: whatever margin you offer, somebody will bid higher, and jobbers and retailers have their own brands, on which he says they make four times as much, so they have no interest in giving you a hold. In Chapter Eighteen he restates it with numbers on the trade's side — the wholesaler wanting some 20 per cent and charging you his cost of competing, the retailer demanding a dozen free in ten — and reports that most lines he advertised never employed a salesman at all. It is a doctrine he repeats and illustrates; he reports no comparison of the two routes run side by side.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 129-130 for the choose-one doctrine and the doubled-expense failure; printed pp. 195-196 for the restatement, the 20 per cent jobber margin, the dozen-free-in-ten demand and the never-employed-a-salesman claim. Repeated within the source; asserted, not measured.
confounders: the modern omnichannel default in which trade investment and consumer demand are complements to be balanced
reading it as advice to skip retail; he wants the retailer to stock, but pulled in by consumer demand rather than paid in
confusing it with his approval of the dealer-privilege offer at pp. 42-44 and the dealer-naming plan at pp. 126-127 — both give the dealer something he wants without giving him margin
treating the 20 per cent and dozen-free-in-ten as market data; they are his characterisation of the trade's demands

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 133-134 (Chapter Twelve, the Benton Harbor introduction of Palmolive) with printed p. 154 (Chapter Fourteen)
qa_items.question: The same coupon offer can be headlined two ways: the advertiser will buy a cake of the soap for every woman who applies, or a ten-cent cake is free. Chapter Twelve argues for one of these. Which, what mechanism does Hopkins give, and what later page in the book complicates it?
qa_items.answer: He argues for the buying frame — he states outright that "We Will Buy" is a much better headline than a ten-cent cake free. His mechanism is about what each frame signals and what it costs later. Offering to buy the article for her at the dealer's own price shows supreme confidence that the article will please, and it is more impressive because the advertiser is paying what she would pay; a free offer cheapens the product, and there is a resistance to afterwards paying for something that first arrived as a gift. He adds a distribution effect: the coupon is as good as a dime, women will not throw it away, and if one dealer will not redeem it another will, so proofs mailed to dealers obtain general distribution without salesmen. The complication is on p. 154. On food products the word free multiplied the readers of his advertisements; on a hygiene product, featuring the same free offer at the top divided results by four, because the woman did not want her interest in that class of product read as an admission about herself. So the frame's effect is not a constant. He gives no split-test figures for the "We Will Buy" headline itself.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 133-134 for the two-stage plan, the "We Will Buy" preference and the cheapening argument; printed p. 154 for the food-versus-hygiene reversal. The headline preference is asserted psychologically; the reversal is the one place he reports a magnitude. OCR note: the losing headline is set in damaged display type on printed p. 134 and reads as garbage in both the working text and a fresh pdftotext pass; "ten-cent cake free" is the reading the surrounding argument requires, and it is given here as a paraphrase rather than as a quotation. "We Will Buy" itself is clean in the scan.
confounders: the modern promotional default that free maximises trial, which is what p. 154 shows failing in one category and working in another
reading the buying frame as a discount mechanic; the consumer pays nothing either way, and only the framing and the dealer's settlement differ
confusing this with his separate rule at pp. 146-147 that charging even ten cents for a sample multiplies acquisition cost
treating 'We Will Buy' as tested; the Benton Harbor result at p. 135 tests the whole introduction, not the headline pair

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 143-144 (Chapter Thirteen, the repricing of Puffed Rice and Wheat Berries)
qa_items.question: Two products are in decline, their makers are convinced they cannot succeed, and there is no money for a campaign. Hopkins's first act on this exact brief was not a creative one. What was it, how does the arithmetic work, and what did he assert rather than establish?
qa_items.answer: His first act was to raise the prices. Puffed Rice went from ten cents to fifteen and Wheat Berries from seven cents to ten — renamed Puffed Wheat so the two could be advertised together — and he states that this added an average of $1.25 per case to the billing price. That increment was the advertising appropriation: the fund to develop new users came out of the price rather than out of the client's existing margin, on a line the client had already written off. What he asserts rather than establishes is the demand side. He says he was sure the extra price would not reduce the sale in view of the advertising effort, and reports no test of the price change on its own, no before-and-after unit figures, and no attempt to separate the price effect from the campaign effect. He is also candid on the following pages that the same campaign then wasted large sums in newspapers, so the appropriation he created was partly spent on a medium he later proved could not pay for this line.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 143-144 for the two price rises, the renaming and the $1.25 per case; printed pp. 145-146 for the newspaper waste that followed. Outcome claimed for the campaign as a whole; the price decision itself is asserted with no isolating test.
confounders: modern price-elasticity reasoning, which would want the demand response measured; Hopkins states his confidence and moves on
reading it as premium positioning; the stated purpose of the increase is to fund the advertising, and the appeals he then built were curiosity and the puffing process, not price
assuming the price rise was validated by the campaign's success; the two were changed together and he separates them nowhere
confusing it with his rule at pp. 173-174 that an economy appeal offends the buyers who most need to economise — a different argument about what copy may say

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 145-146 (Chapter Thirteen, why puffed grains left newspapers for magazines)
qa_items.question: A medium offers the widest reach in the market at the lowest cost per thousand, and the product is priced above what most of that audience can pay. Hopkins made this mistake in the open. What was it, what is the criterion he substitutes for reach, and what limits the transfer of this rule?
qa_items.answer: He spent large sums on newspaper advertising for the puffed grains, and states the reason it could not pay: newspapers reach all the people, while this expensive food line appealed only to the classes, so nine in ten of those he reached could not afford the product. They finally proved that magazine advertising was their only possibility. The criterion he substitutes is not audience size or cost per reader but the proportion of the audience that can afford the product — waste is measured against affordability, not against reach. He states the same idea as a screen in Chapter Seventeen, where things that appeal to one per cent are ruled out because the cost of reaching them in mediums of universal circulation is excessive and cannot come back for decades. The transfer is limited by his own era: in 1920s American print the only instrument of selection available to him was the choice of vehicle, so the whole rule is a statement about buying a publication whose readership happens to match a price point. He describes no other targeting mechanism because he had none.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 145-146 for the newspaper waste, the nine-in-ten figure and the move to magazines; printed pp. 185-186 for the same reasoning stated as a general cost screen. The nine-in-ten is his characterisation, not a measured readership figure.
confounders: the modern targeting default, in which a broad vehicle is made narrow by audience selection; Hopkins's only lever is which publication he buys
reading it as a rule against newspapers; he calls newspapers the cheapest distribution available for an offer at p. 77, on a differently priced line
treating cost per thousand as the thing he is optimising; his objection survives a cheap newspaper because the wasted nine-tenths cannot buy at any price
assuming the class/mass split is a market measurement; it is a 1920s social categorisation stated as one

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 146 (Chapter Thirteen, the free Puffed Wheat with every Puffed Rice)
qa_items.question: A team proposes driving trial by giving one product free with the purchase of its sister product. Hopkins ran precisely this offer across tens of millions of advertisements. What was the result, what does he say such an offer actually is, and what did he substitute for it?
qa_items.answer: He reports that the offer was ineffective — and generalises, saying such offers always are — because it amounts simply to a price reduction. His argument is that it is just as hard to sell at half price as at full price to people who have not been converted, so a coupon good for half the price is a small inducement; all those millions of advertisements brought few new users. What he substituted was a coupon good at any grocery store for a full package of Puffed Wheat or Puffed Rice, published in magazines. The difference he draws is not the discount depth but who ends up holding the coupon: the reader met the story first, and if she cut the coupon out it was because the story had interested her, so the sample went only to people whose interest had already been created and who then found in the package what they had been led to look for. This sits with his rule on the same page that a sample must be earned by an act of interest and never cast on the doorstep. He gives no response figures for either version.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 146. The ineffective free-with-purchase offer, the "simply a price reduction" reading, the half-price/full-price argument and the full-package magazine coupon are all stated there. Outcome claimed for both; no traced numbers reported at this point in the chapter.
confounders: the modern promotional default that bundling and BOGO drive trial cheaply
reading it as a general objection to discounting; his objection is that a discount does no persuading, not that a lower price never sells

confusing it with his separate finding at pp. 146-147 that charging ten cents for a sample can push the cost of an inquiry from about 25 cents to $1.25 or more — that one has figures, this one does not
assuming the full-package coupon worked because it was more generous; on his account it worked because the story came first and the coupon selected for interest

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 178-179 (Chapter Seventeen, on the climax and getting action)
qa_items.question: An advertisement carries a strong argument, is read attentively, and ends. Hopkins names a specific loss that occurs at exactly this point. What is it, what device does he prescribe, and what does he claim as evidence for the device?
qa_items.answer: The loss is the half-made convert. His picture of the moment is precise: the reader has paused because the subject or the headline caught her, and in a moment she will be interested again in her reading and will usually forget you — so many an advertiser loses most of his half-made converts to procrastination, which he says one cannot afford. The climax must therefore inspire immediate action in those already interested. His usual device is the coupon, and his account of why it works is physical rather than economic: people do not put the magazine aside, they clip the coupon as a reminder of something they have decided to do — a woman lays it on her desk, a man slips it into his vest pocket — and on some convenient occasion it turns up and is sent in, giving the advertiser a chance to follow up. He names other action devices: week sales, retail offers good for a certain day or hour, and limited offers of every sort. As evidence he says countless tests have proved coupons multiply returns, and that he has seen mail-order houses run catalogue advertisements with and without coupons where the difference in returns was enormous. He gives no numbers, no lines and no dates for any of it.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 178-179. The half-made convert, the clipping behaviour, the week sales and limited offers, and the claim that countless tests proved coupons multiply returns are all stated there. Measurement asserted, magnitude withheld — the characteristic evidence pattern of this source.
confounders: the modern call-to-action or conversion-rate framing, which treats the device as an interface element rather than as a physical token the reader carries away
reading the coupon here as a sampling or discount mechanism; on these pages its whole function is to defeat delay and open a follow-up
assuming the enormous difference is a reported figure; he describes tests he has seen and states no result
confusing urgency devices with his warning at pp. 152-153 against appeals to fear, which is about what the argument may say rather than about how it closes

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 179-180 (Chapter Seventeen, on frivolity and on competing with the reading matter)
qa_items.question: An agency presents a comic campaign that will be widely enjoyed, laid out to read like the magazine's own editorial pages. Hopkins objects to both halves, on two different grounds. Give each objection, the exception he grants, and the kind of evidence he offers.
qa_items.answer: Against the humour his ground is what money means to the reader. Spending money is serious business; money represents life and work and is highly respected; to most people spending in one direction means skimping in another, so the choice is a serious one and people want full value. Appeal for money in a lightsome way, he says, and you will never get it — people do not buy from clowns. He grants one exception explicitly: this does not apply to amusement advertising. Against the editorial disguise his ground is different and is about selection, not tone. You may win attention that way but not valuable attention, because most of the people attracted by amusement have no interest in your subject; the advertising columns and the reading matter have separate purposes, you cannot fool people by a resemblance, and any product worth advertising is, rightly presented, more interesting to an interested reader than a story. His evidence is weak by his own standards. He names "Sunny Jim" and "Spotless Town" as campaigns that proved his point and says many others are long forgotten, then rests on a challenge — nobody can cite a permanent success built on frivolity. That is an invitation to produce a counter-example, not a traced comparison, and it is the form of argument he refuses to accept from others at pp. 175-176.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 179-180 for both objections, the amusement-advertising exception, the two named campaigns and the no-permanent-success challenge; printed pp. 175-176 for the evidence standard he applies to others. Argued and asserted; no traced returns are offered on either point.
confounders: the modern view that entertainment buys attention and attention is the scarce good — which is close to the position he is attacking, and which he answers on the quality of the attention rather than its quantity
collapsing the two objections into one; the humour argument is about the seriousness of spending, the editorial-mimicry argument is about attracting uninterested readers
forgetting the amusement-advertising exception, which he states in the same breath
treating the two named campaigns as evidence; they are cited as known failures without figures

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 181-182 (Chapter Seventeen, on type size and on capitals)
qa_items.question: A designer argues for large display type and all-capital headlines so the advertisement will command attention. Hopkins answers both. What are his two arguments, and on what basis does he make them — which is not the basis a modern reader will assume?
qa_items.answer: On size he argues from habit and from cost. Ordinary reading of the period was done in 8-point type; most mail-order advertisers, presenting something more interesting than ordinary reading matter, had gone down to 6-point. The easiest type to read, he says, is the ordinary, because anything unusual presents difficulties; advertisers use big type because they are trying to demand attention rather than induce it; and anyone who traces results can quickly prove that oversize type does not pay, because doubling the space you need doubles your cost. His summary is that if the story is interesting people will read it in their accustomed type, and if it is not they will not read it in any size. On capitals he argues from habit alone: all our reading is done in upper-and-lower case, so lines set in capitals have to be studied out — a detriment always, though he concedes it may not be a severe one. The basis is what readers are accustomed to, plus space economy, and not legibility as a measurable property of the letterforms. He runs no vision experiment, cites no study, and the point sizes he names are the reading conventions of 1920s American print rather than thresholds.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 181-182. The 8-point ordinary reading, the 6-point mail-order convention, the demand-versus-induce framing, the doubling of cost with space, and the all-caps habituation argument are all stated there. Argued from habit and cost; the claim that traced results prove it is asserted without figures.
confounders: modern legibility research and accessibility minimums, which reason from vision and prescribe larger sizes — the opposite conclusion from a different premise
reading the 6-point and 8-point values as recommended settings rather than as the reading conventions of his period
assuming his objection to capitals is about shouting or tone; it is about the reader having to study out an unaccustomed form
treating 'anyone who traces results can quickly prove it' as a reported test

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 183 (Chapter Seventeen, that advertisements should tell the full story)
qa_items.question: A campaign is planned as a sequence: the first advertisement raises the problem, the second gives the proof, the third closes. Hopkins rules this out. What is his premise, what does he require instead, and how does he decide what goes in?
qa_items.answer: His premise is that people do not read advertisements in series. The advertiser who attracts a reader today may not get her attention again for months, so nothing can be deferred to a later insertion: when you get a reading, present all your arguments, because you will not get another chance to convince her and she will not read a second advertisement of yours if the first failed to offer something she wanted. What he requires instead is that every appeal that has proved important appear in every advertisement, since some buy for one reason and some for another, and an omitted appeal simply fails to reach the readers it would have convinced. The selection is not a matter of taste: appeals are tested by being featured as headlines, and he keeps the facts that bring a great deal of interest and drops the ones that bring little or none. He accepts the consequence openly on the following pages — completeness means similarity, so good advertisements on a line cannot vary greatly, and the real difference between them lies in the headline.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 183 for the no-series premise, the every-appeal-in-every-advertisement rule and the headline method of selecting appeals; printed p. 187 for the completeness-means-similarity consequence. Argued from a premise about reading behaviour that he asserts rather than measures.
confounders: modern sequenced messaging and funnel-stage creative, which presume a reachable individual across insertions — the thing his premise denies
reading it as an argument for long copy as such; the length is a consequence of including every proved appeal, not a target
assuming the appeal set is fixed by judgement; he says it is settled by featuring claims in headlines and watching the interest each brings
confusing it with the monotony passage at pp. 117-118, which answers why repetition does not tire the reader — a related but distinct claim

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 186-187 (Chapter Seventeen, on headlines)
qa_items.question: A campaign is underperforming and the team proposes rewriting the body copy. On Hopkins's account, where is the leverage, what magnitudes does he claim for it, and what does he not supply?
qa_items.answer: The leverage is the headline, and he puts it there for a structural reason: because every advertisement must be complete, good advertisements on a line cannot vary greatly, so the great difference lies in the headline. Its function is selection rather than persuasion — it salutes the people you want to reach, like a bell-boy in a hotel calling for Mr. Jones, or like the heading on a news article that lets a reader pick, out of far more than he has time for, the few things he will read. The magnitudes he claims are large: again and again, he says, he has multiplied the results of an advertisement by eight or ten through a simple change of headline, and one sort of headline may appeal to 25 per cent of prospects where another appeals to 50 per cent. He states the method that establishes this — keyed tests comparing one headline against another — and says anyone can quickly prove it with keyed returns. What he does not supply is any of the evidence: no campaign, no line, no date, no volume of returns, and never the losing headline against the winning one. The multiples are recalled, not shown.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 186-187. The bell-boy and news-heading images, the eight-or-ten multiplication, the 25-versus-50-per-cent contrast and the keyed-test method are all stated there. This is the clearest instance in the book of measurement asserted with the result withheld.
confounders: modern headline-testing practice, which would report the pair, the sample and the interval; Hopkins reports only the multiple
reading the headline as the persuasive element; on his account it selects the audience and the complete body carries the case
treating eight-or-ten and 25-versus-50 as findings rather than as recollections offered without cases
assuming he therefore rates body copy unimportant; he requires it to be complete, and says the similarity between good advertisements is why the headline is where the variance lives

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 170-172 (Chapter Sixteen, the three interests and the economics of a test campaign)
qa_items.question: A client with money to spend asks why his agency insists on a small test first. Hopkins answers this from his own books rather than from principle. Reconstruct his arithmetic, and state what it implies about whose interest the small-test rule also serves.
