qa_items.answer: His figures are these. A valuable new client arrives with an opportunity that consists of a test campaign costing under $5,000, on which the agency commission is $750. Developing that test rarely costs under $20,000 if a competent man is employed, because the men in charge may spend weeks reading and researching. So the advertiser usually gets his money back whatever the outcome, while the real stake is the agency's: failure means the advertiser loses a trifle and the agency loses much, and success may mean millions to the advertiser but only 15 per cent commission to the agency, and only for as long as the advertiser's goodwill lasts. He draws the conclusion himself — he feels no obligation to an advertiser who permits him to make a test, because the speculation is his. The implication he does not hide is that the rule is doubly motivated. Keeping the advertiser's exposure small until a profit is sure protects the advertiser from a loss he would denounce advertising for, and it also protects the agency's development investment and its relationship. He ranks the three interests in the same passage in an order most readers find surprising: the publisher first, because the publisher pays the commission; the agency second; and the advertiser last, while conceding that everything depends on the advertiser's attitude.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 170-172. The under-$5,000 test, the $750 commission, the $20,000 development cost, the 15 per cent commission, the "mine is the speculation" conclusion and the publisher-first ordering are all stated there. His own accounting of his own trade, offered as such.
confounders: reading the small-test rule as purely an evidence discipline; he states its commercial logic himself on these pages
assuming the client bears the risk of a test, which is the modern default and the reverse of his arithmetic
treating the publisher-first ordering as a claim about who matters most; he ranks by who pays the commission and says the advertiser's success is what everything depends on
generalising the 15 per cent publisher-paid commission structure past its era; it is the pre-fee agency economics of the period

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 161-162 (Chapter Fifteen, the reciprocal credit letters between the garment house and the house-furnishing house)
qa_items.question: Two mail-order businesses each hold a list of customers who have paid their instalments as agreed, in different product lines. Hopkins built a mechanism on exactly this. What was it, why does he say the offer was almost irresistible, and what should a reader note about how it works?
qa_items.answer: Each house wrote to the other's good payers. The president of the house-furnishing concern told the garment company's customers that he had met the proprietress, that she had said they were valued customers who had paid as agreed, and that he was therefore opening a like account: here is our catalogue, disregard the terms in it that ask for payment in advance, order what you want, send no money at all, begin paying in a month if the goods satisfy you. The garment seller then wrote the mirror-image letter to the house-furnishing customers. His account of the force is social rather than financial. These women had ordered clothing on credit wondering whether they would even receive it and could hardly believe strangers would trust them; a flattering offer of that kind, he says, makes any woman who receives it try to find some way to use it. He reports extending it to a third business in men's clothing and says that by making a customer in one line a buyer of another they multiplied ordinary results, so that nobody on a single line could compete. Two things a reader should note: he reports no figures for the loop, and the whole mechanism runs on one business disclosing a named customer's payment record to another, with no consent step described anywhere — a 1920s mail-order practice recorded here as historical fact, not as a recommendation.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 161-162, following the garment business he set up at pp. 160-161. The paraphrased letters, the "could hardly believe strangers would trust them" reading, the men's-clothing extension and the multiplied-results claim are stated there. Outcome claimed; no figures.
confounders: modern cross-sell or lookalike-audience framing, which treats the shared list as data rather than as a personal introduction between two named proprietors
reading the flattery as the offer of credit itself; on his account it is being vouched for by name that does the work
assuming any consent or privacy consideration is present in the source; none is mentioned, and its absence is part of the historical record

confusing it with the framing lesson at pp. 160-161, where identical terms were made flattering rather than humiliating — that item is about how one offer is worded, this one about how two businesses feed each other

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 190-191 (Chapter Eighteen, 'My Great Mistake', why the man who builds an account loses it)
qa_items.question: An agency built a client from nothing; the business is now large and the client is being told that ordinary work would keep it going. Diagnose this with Chapter Eighteen: what is the structural dynamic, and what does Hopkins say is the only remedy available to the agency side?
qa_items.answer: He describes it as near-inevitable and in stages. At the start the advertising does nine-tenths of the work while the trade-mark owner ventures little or nothing — it is not hard to make a breakfast food, a tooth paste, a soap or a cleanser, most advertisers employ others to make them, salesmen can aid but little. If the test fails the advertising man is the main loser, having spent his time and talent; if it succeeds he takes a commission on the expenditure while the profits go to others, and being anonymous he does not even get the credit. Then the business acquires momentum, and a time comes when even mediocre advertising will keep it going upward — advertising which, he says pointedly, could never have started it. Meanwhile the advertising man clings to the methods he established and fears to change, which Hopkins says is in fact usually right, since the best way to win new customers is usually the way that won millions. But the work becomes monotonous to the men who read every advertisement, and they come to want something new. So the man who builds a big account is pretty sure to lose it sooner or later. The only remedy he offers is not defensive: to keep up his volume and his earnings he must always be starting new ventures.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 190-191. The nine-tenths claim, the asymmetry of loss and gain, the momentum stage where mediocre advertising suffices, the clinging-and-monotony sequence and the always-starting- new-ventures remedy are all stated there. His own career pattern generalised into a dynamic; no cases outside his own are cited.
confounders: reading the boredom as market wear-out; at pp. 117-118 he insists the reader is not tired, only the men who read every advertisement are
the modern account-management framing in which the fix is deeper client relationships; his stated fix is a pipeline of new ventures
treating 'even mediocre advertising will keep it going' as a claim that advertising stops mattering; his point is that maintaining and starting are different problems
assuming this is offered as the great mistake of the title; the mistake is his own decision at p. 189 to stay an employee rather than start out for himself

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 197 (Chapter Eighteen, the Edna Wallace Hopper line of twenty-three products)
qa_items.question: A line's advertised item cannot recover its acquisition cost, and the finance side wants it stopped. Hopkins reports running a business on exactly that footing. What is the structure, what figures does he give, and what should be said about their standing as evidence?
qa_items.answer: The structure is that the first sale is not required to pay. His cosmetic line ran to twenty-three products, each a formula attributed to Miss Hopper, and his claim is that a woman who tries one wants to try the rest — the converts to Miss Hopper are converts to her line. The figures he gives are an average of $1.78 per sale on that line, against 50 cents for a tooth paste, 35 cents for a shaving cream and 10 cents for a soap. He then states the point plainly: the profit on what they sell from the advertising would never pay its cost, but one thing sells another, and the whole profit comes in auxiliaries — which he says is so in many lines. It is the same economics he states as a selection rule at pp. 191-192, where he specialised in products bought over and over because the whole profit on a one-sale article must be made on that sale. On their standing: these are unaudited figures for his own young business, given in the year he wrote the book, by an owner with an interest in the account, and he concedes on the same page that some of his new enterprises will fail. They are a description of how he set the venture up, not a demonstration that it worked.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 197 for the twenty-three products, the $1.78 average and the 50/35/10-cent comparisons, and for the auxiliaries conclusion; printed pp. 191-192 for the same logic as a selection rule. Self-reported figures for his own current business.
confounders: modern lifetime-value or loss-leader framing, which would want retention and repeat-rate data; he offers an average order value and an assertion about cross-buying
reading the $1.78 as a measured lift; it is the line's average sale compared with single-product categories, not a before-and-after
assuming the auxiliaries logic licenses any unprofitable acquisition; at pp. 185-186 he rules out whole categories precisely because repeat sales are too far apart
treating his ownership of the business as incidental to the claim

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 197-198 (Chapter Eighteen, closing pages) with printed p. 189
qa_items.question: A young practitioner reads Chapter Eighteen and concludes that the book's advice is to stop working for others and own the enterprises you build. Hopkins addresses this directly. What does he actually say, and what makes his own case a poor template?
qa_items.answer: He withdraws the recommendation in the same breath as the account. Having described starting his own ventures, he says plainly that this is not, as he well realises, good advice to the majority: the average man should work under direction, success depends on many qualities of which he has but few, and his own adventure was made only after decades of working in co-operation. He closes by telling readers to deduce what suggestion and direction they can, saying he has tried to point out the ways to success in advertising, that those ways lead in many directions, and that each must decide what is best. What makes his case a poor template is the position he was in when he took it. He was already wealthy and famous, with the Pepsodent holding behind him — $13,000 put in, some $200,000 taken in dividends, the stock sold for $500,000 — and a career of commissions that reached $185,000 in a year. He also states that his failures now cost him a trifle and would have cost the same had he failed for someone else, which is a claim available only to someone who can absorb them. And the regret at p. 189 is about a refused opportunity at twenty-one, framed by his own account as a shortage of courage rather than of equipment.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 197-198 for the explicit withdrawal, the failures-cost-a-trifle remark and the closing instruction to each reader; printed p. 193 for the Pepsodent figures; printed p. 168 for the $185,000 year; printed p. 189 for the Bissell conversation. Source position, stated by the source about its own advice.
confounders: the modern founder-versus-employee reading, which the book's title invites and which its closing pages decline
treating the Pepsodent return as evidence that the strategy generalises; it is one holding in a company he himself built the advertising for
assuming 'my great mistake' names the account-loss dynamic; it names his decision at twenty-one to stay employed
reading the closing hedge as modesty; it is a stated limit on the applicability of his own example, and belongs in the answer

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 64-69 (Chapter Six, 'Personal Salesmanship', the Cotosuet calls on New England bakers)
qa_items.question: A product is identical to a cheaper rival, the price premium is essential to profit, and the sales force reports the premium cannot be held. Hopkins was sent to prove otherwise. What did he actually sell, what is the general form he draws from it, and what did he refuse to claim afterwards?
qa_items.answer: He did not sell the product. He arrived at the largest bakery with the proof of a street-car card picturing an ideal pie, set it up fifty feet away, explained what it had cost and how it was printed, and asked the baker — a pie expert — to criticise it, which turned the man from a reluctant buyer into an adviser defending his own verdict. Then he offered a card like it for every store selling that baker's pies, carrying a line that only Swift's Cotosuet was used in the shortening, at 250 cards per carload ordered. He repeated it down the New England cities, and for a baker who could not have the card he offered signs on both sides of two railway cars announcing Mansfield's pies for nine hundred miles. He reports selling more Cotosuet in a week than six salesmen had sold in six weeks, with no complaint about price. The general form he draws is that the appeal must consist of a service useful to the buyer with the seller's own advantage covered up — the average salesman's plea, buy mine and not the other fellow's, is a selfish appeal to selfish people and meets resistance. What he refused was to teach it: asked by Mr. Swift to train the other men, he said it cannot be taught, and says in 1927 that he is still of that opinion. Two things a reader should hold onto: the week-against-six-weeks comparison is his own recollection with no records behind it, and the boxcar sign is precisely the vanity advertising — keeping your name before the people — that he condemns everywhere else, which he half-concedes on the page.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 64-69. The pie card and its critique, the 250-cards-per-carload offer, the boxcar signs at Springfield, the week-versus-six-weeks claim, the service-not-selfishness formulation and the "it cannot be taught" reply are all stated there. Anecdotal, with an outcome claimed and no records.
confounders: reading it as a co-operative-advertising or point-of-sale programme; on his account the card is the whole sale and the shortening goes with it
the modern value-add or partnership framing, which would state the mutual benefit openly; Hopkins requires his own advantage to be covered up
treating the six-salesmen comparison as a controlled result
missing that the Mansfield boxcar sign is name-spreading of the kind he calls folly elsewhere, sold to a customer who wanted it

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, My Life in Advertising (Harper & Brothers, 1927)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 17-18 (Chapter Two, the silver polish sold door to door) with printed pp. 146-147 (Chapter Thirteen)
qa_items.question: A client refuses to fund samples on two grounds — they cost too much, and the same people will keep asking for them. Hopkins names both objections and answers them. What is his answer, what comparison is it built on, and what three conditions elsewhere in the book restrict it?
qa_items.answer: His answer is that persuasion alone is vastly more expensive: a good article is its own best salesman, and selling without samples, in print or in person, is uphill work. The comparison it rests on is a childhood one. Selling his mother's silver polish house to house, he sold about one woman in ten by talking the polish at the door, and nearly all of them when he could get into the pantry and demonstrate it. He generalises from street fakers, who never tried to sell without showing in some dramatic way what the product would do, and says advertisers would not dream of sending a salesman out without samples yet spend fortunes urging people to buy without seeing or testing. Three conditions elsewhere restrict it. The sample must be earned by some act of interest — promiscuous distribution on the doorstep gives the product no prestige and he calls it a very bad plan (pp. 134, 146). It must not be charged for: free-sample inquiries may cost about 25 cents each, and asking ten cents can push an inquiry past $1.25, so the ten cents recovered can cost a dollar (pp. 146-147). And the free framing is not universal — on a hygiene product, featuring it at the top divided results by four (p. 154). The one-in-ten figure is a recollection of his own boyhood selling, not a controlled comparison.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 17-18 for the silver-polish comparison, the two objections he names and the street fakers; printed pp. 134 and 146 for the earned-sample condition; printed pp. 146-147 for the cost-of-charging figures; printed p. 154 for the category reversal. The pantry comparison is anecdotal; the 25-cent and $1.25 figures are among the few he states.
confounders: the modern free-trial default, which treats sampling as unconditionally good; three of his four conditions are restrictions on it
reading the one-in-ten versus nearly-all as a measured conversion rate
assuming cost is his answer to the cost objection; his answer is that the alternative costs more, which he asserts rather than prices
confusing the repeaters objection with his own separate warning that a sample given to someone with no created interest is wasted regardless of who asks

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 25-26 (Chapter 8, 'Tell Your Full Story')
qa_items.question: Hopkins forbids running a case across successive advertisements. What is the mechanism he gives, and why does it make the prohibition follow rather than being a matter of taste?
qa_items.answer: His mechanism is that the decision, not the exposure, is the scarce event: in one reading of an advertisement a person decides for or against the proposition, and that verdict then operates against ever reading it again. People do not read successive advertisements on one line any more than they read a news item twice. So an argument withheld from the reading that happens is an argument the reader will never meet, and serials, he says, almost never connect. The prohibition follows from the mechanism: if there is only one reading, splitting the case guarantees part of it is never delivered.
qa_items.support: p.25: "In one reading of an advertisement one decides for or against a proposition. And that operates against a second reading." p.25 on serials: "There is no greater folly. Those serials almost never connect."
confounders: That serials fail through weak recall between issues — a memory argument. Hopkins's argument is that the second reading does not happen at all.
That the objection is to length or to frequency. It is to splitting the case.
The modern default that repeated exposure across a sequence builds the argument cumulatively.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 26 (Chapter 8, 'Tell Your Full Story')
qa_items.question: A client wants a section of every advertisement to thank existing customers and reassure them about a recent formula change. On Hopkins's chapter 8 position, what should be done, and what is the one concession he allows?
qa_items.answer: On his position the section should not run in the body copy at all. He holds that people using the product will not read the advertising for it — they have already read and decided — so every line addressed to them is space wasted, and he says he would rather assume the reader is always an unconverted prospect. His single concession is that something aimed at present users may be said in a HEADLINE, because a headline reaches people who do not read the advertisement. Note this is a 1923 position about periodical readership, argued from the cost of paid space at a time when an advertiser had no way to address existing and prospective customers separately, and he offers no readership measurement for it.
qa_items.support: p.26: "In every ad consider only new customers. People using your product are not going to read your ads." "So never waste one line of your space to say something to present users, unless you can say it in headlines." "Bear in mind always that you address an unconverted prospect."
confounders: That he forbids speaking to users entirely — the headline exception is explicit and easy to drop.
The modern default that retention communication is a separate and valuable job.
That his objection is about tone or relevance rather than about the cost of paid space.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 25 (Chapter 8, 'Tell Your Full Story')
qa_items.question: Hopkins says the best advertisers learn their appealing claims by comparing headline results. What do they then do with the claims that did not win, and why does this not contradict testing?
qa_items.answer: They keep them. The winners of the headline comparisons are not run alone; claims that prove important enough are added to a standing list, and all of them then appear in every advertisement thereafter. His reason is that different facts convince different people, so a claim that loses a headline comparison can still be the fact that converts a share of readers once they are reading. The headline test measures pulling power; the standing list preserves converting power. He gives no threshold for "important enough", which is the decision the procedure actually turns on.
qa_items.support: p.25: "They learn their appealing claims by tests—by comparing results from various headlines. Gradually they accumulate a list of claims important enough to use. All those claims appear in every ad thereafter." "One fact appeals to some, one to another."
confounders: That testing selects a single winning claim to run — the standard read of Hopkins as an optimiser.
That the losing claims are discarded and re-tested later.
Confusing this with running several appeals as several parallel advertisements; here they are co-resident in one.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 26 (Chapter 8, 'Tell Your Full Story')
qa_items.question: Does Hopkins prescribe long copy? State his actual rule and the boundary he puts on it.
qa_items.answer: No. He explicitly says there is no fixed rule on brevity — one sentence may tell a complete story on a line like chewing gum, or on an article like Cream of Wheat. What he prescribes is COMPLETENESS, not length: whether long or short, the story should be reasonably complete. The length follows from what completeness requires for that product, which is why a car, as a lifetime investment involving an important expenditure, will absorb columns while chewing gum will not.
qa_items.support: p.26: "There is no fixed rule on this subject of brevity. One sentence may tell a complete story on a line like chewing gum... But, whether long or short, an advertising story should be reasonably complete."
confounders: The very common summary of Hopkins as an advocate of long copy per se.
That the rule scales with media space bought rather than with what the purchase decision requires.
That 'complete' means comprehensive about the product; he means complete as a case for the sale.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 26 (Chapter 8, 'Tell Your Full Story')
qa_items.question: In the Marmon anecdote, what does Hopkins say the famous expensive cars did wrong, and what does the anecdote actually demonstrate on the evidence he supplies?
qa_items.answer: He reports a man inclined toward a Rolls-Royce who also considered a Pierce-Arrow and a Locomobile, but found their advertisements very short and offering no information — their makers evidently thinking it undignified to argue comparative merits. The Marmon told a complete story, the man read columns and books about it, and bought a Marmon. On the evidence supplied it demonstrates nothing: it is one unnamed buyer, recounted second-hand, with no sales figure and no test. It also undercuts itself, since the same man is described as never sorry and yet as later learning facts about a car at nearly three times the price that would have sold him that car.
qa_items.support: p.26, the Marmon passage: the short advertisements of the famous cars "offered no information"; the Marmon "told a complete story"; the buyer "afterwards learned facts about another car at nearly three times the price which would have sold him that car had he known them."
confounders: Reading the anecdote as evidence rather than illustration.
That the criticism is of the cars' prestige positioning; his criticism is of the information withheld.
That Hopkins reports the Marmon's sales; he reports one man's purchase.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 27 (Chapter 8, 'Tell Your Full Story')
qa_items.question: A colleague justifies a proposed layout by pointing to a well-known campaign that uses it. What is Hopkins's chapter 8 rule about that argument, and what weakness does the rule have when applied to his own book?
qa_items.answer: His rule disqualifies the argument outright: never be guided in any way by advertisements that are untraced, never be led in new paths by the blind, and take the opinion and the verdict of nobody who knows nothing about his returns. His reasoning is that an advertiser who cannot see his returns cannot have learned anything from them, so his practice records only his preferences. The weakness is that the rule applied consistently disqualifies the book: his own returns are equally unavailable to the reader, and he supports the observation that "brief ads are never keyed" and "every traced ad tells a complete story" with no sample, no count and no advertisement reproduced anywhere in the volume.
qa_items.support: p.27: "Never be guided in any way by ads which are untraced... Never be led in new paths by the blind... Take the opinion of nobody, the verdict of nobody, who knows nothing about his returns." "Note that brief ads are never keyed."
confounders: That he objects to imitation generally; he objects to imitating the unmeasured specifically.
That the rule is about creative originality rather than about evidence admissibility.
Missing the self-application: readers routinely take the rule as authority for the book rather than as a standard the book fails.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 28 (Chapter 9, 'Art in Advertising')
qa_items.question: Hopkins says pictures in advertising are very expensive. Expensive in what, on his accounting, and what test does that cost imply?
qa_items.answer: Expensive in SPACE, not merely in the cost of the artwork — and he says from one-third to one-half of an advertising campaign is often staked on the power of the pictures. Because the picture is bought with paid space, its cost is the selling argument that space would have carried otherwise, which gives him a single admission test: use a picture only when it forms a better selling argument than the same amount of space set in type. This is arithmetic over 1923 print economics — space priced by area, with a page of type a live alternative to a page of picture — and he offers no source for the one-third-to-one-half figure.
qa_items.support: p.28: "Pictures in advertising are very expensive. Not in the cost of good art work alone, but in the cost of space. From one-third to one-half of an advertising campaign is often staked on the power of the pictures." "Use them only when they form a better selling argument than the same amount of space set in type."
confounders: That the expense he means is illustration fees — he explicitly rules that out as the main cost.
That the test is a quality standard ('is this a good picture'); it is a comparison against an alternative use of the space.
Treating this as a general claim about images rather than an arithmetic over a specific cost structure.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 28-29 (Chapter 9, 'Art in Advertising')
qa_items.question: Chapter 9 is often quoted as hostile to pictures. Where does Hopkins say pictures DO pay, and what is the common structure of those cases?
qa_items.answer: He names apparel, correspondence schools and beauty articles, and the common structure is that the picture depicts the condition the buyer wants to reach rather than the article for sale. Arrow Collars and clothing advertising picture not only the collar but men whom others envy in surroundings others covet, so the picture subtly suggests the article will aid a man to those desired positions; correspondence schools picture men in high positions or taking upward steps; beauty articles picture beautiful women, admired and attractive. He also names Puffed Grains, where pictures of the grains themselves beat every figure drawing tried because they awake curiosity. The picture pays when it is an argument made pictorially — which is exactly what lets it beat type.
qa_items.support: pp.28-29: "picturing men whom others envy, in surroundings which others covet. The pictures subtly suggest that these articles of apparel will aid men to those desired positions." p.29 on Puffed Grains: "the pictures of the grains were found to be most effective. They awake curiosity."
confounders: The widespread reading of Hopkins as simply anti-illustration.
That he favours product photography generally — Puffed Grains is a stated case, not the general rule, and he sets aside 'the lines where the article itself should be pictured'.
That the mechanism is attention; he says the mechanism is implied argument.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 29 (Chapter 9, 'Art in Advertising')
qa_items.question: A designer proposes a striking, unexpected image on the ground that it will make the advertisement impossible to ignore. Give Hopkins's two separate objections.
qa_items.answer: First, an attention objection: a picture that is eccentric or unique takes attention from the subject, and since the main appeal lies in the headline, overshadowing the headline kills it — "Don't, to gain general and useless attention, sacrifice the attention that you want." Second, a respect objection: treating the subject lightly or attempting frivolity lowers regard for the advertiser and the article, because people do not patronise a clown; his figures are the man who gains attention by wearing a fool's cap and the salesman in conspicuous clothes, whom the sane and thrifty majority despise. He supplies no comparison of an eccentric and a plain treatment for either objection, and this is squarely a period position at odds with much later practice that buys attention deliberately.
qa_items.support: p.29: "a picture which is eccentric or unique takes attention from your subject... Your main appeal lies in your headline. Over-shadow that and you kill it." "People do not patronize a clown." "Don't be like a salesman who wears conspicuous clothes."
confounders: Collapsing the two objections into one; the attention argument and the respect argument are separable and only one concerns the headline.
That he objects to distinctiveness as such — chapter 17 says the opposite about manner and tone.
The modern default that attention is the scarce resource and worth buying with surprise.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 30 (Chapter 9, 'Art in Advertising')
qa_items.question: What is Hopkins's verdict on colour, what exception does he state, and what makes the exception work?
qa_items.answer: His verdict is that colour does not generally pay better than black and white, "according to the evidence we have gathered to date" — one of the few explicit provisionality hedges in the book. His exception is lines whose appeal is the appearance of the product itself: certain food dishes look far better in colours, and tests on lines like oranges and desserts are said to show colour paying. What makes it work is that colour "comes close to placing the products on actual exhibition" — it does selling work no other treatment can do. Colour used to amuse or to gain attention falls back under his general rule: it may attract many times as many people yet secure a hearing from no more of the people wanted. The verdict is a judgement on a 1923 colour-printing premium he never states, so it is a cost finding rather than a claim about colour perception.
qa_items.support: p.30: "Do color pictures pay better than black and white? Not generally, according to the evidence we have gathered to date. Yet there are exceptions... Color comes close to placing the products on actual exhibition."
confounders: Reading the verdict as a claim about colour and attention rather than about a price premium.
That the exception is 'food' as a category; his stated principle is exhibition of appearance, which is why oranges and desserts qualify.
Dropping the hedge 'to date', which is the source scoping its own finding.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 28 and 30 (Chapter 9, 'Art in Advertising')
qa_items.question: Chapter 9 contains an unresolved contradiction about how much art matters. State both halves and say what the source does about it.
qa_items.answer: The chapter opens by calling art in advertising "a study of paramount importance", with one-third to one-half of a campaign often staked on the pictures. It closes by ruling the whole class of art questions minor: "these are minor questions. They are mere economies, not largely affecting the results of a campaign" — because some decisions cut results in two while others multiply them, and one man may do business in a shed and another in a palace without it mattering. The source does nothing about it; the two positions sit two pages apart and are never reconciled. A reconciliation is available — that the stake is in the SPACE, which is a basic decision, while execution quality is a minor one — but Hopkins does not state it.
qa_items.support: p.28: "So art in advertising is a study of paramount importance." p.30: "But these are minor questions. They are mere economies, not largely affecting the results of a campaign."
confounders: Resolving the contradiction on Hopkins's behalf and attributing the resolution to him.
That he means art matters less than copy; his contrast is between minor economies and basic principles generally.
Quoting only one half, which is how the chapter is usually cited in either direction.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 29-30 (Chapter 9, 'Art in Advertising')
qa_items.question: On fine versus ordinary art work, and on whether a picture may be repeated, what does Hopkins actually conclude?
qa_items.answer: On fine versus ordinary art he declines to decide. He gives both cases — some advertisers pay up to $2,000 per drawing on the reasoning that the space is expensive and the art small by comparison; others hold that art judges are too small a percentage to consider and bring their ideas out well at a fraction of the cost, mail order advertisers generally being in this class — and concludes only that good art pays as well as mediocre and that preparation cost is very small beside insertion cost. On repetition he offers a probability rather than a finding: repetition is probably an economy, because the advertiser is always after new customers who are unlikely to remember a picture used before, and if they do remember it repetition does not detract. Note that the repetition answer is derived from his new-customers-only premise, not from any test.
qa_items.support: p.29-30: "Some advertisers pay up to $2,000 per drawing... The question is one of small moment. Certainly good art pays as well as mediocre." "The probability is that repetition is an economy. We are after new customers always."
confounders: Supplying a verdict he explicitly withholds.
That he condemns expensive art work; he says good art pays as well as mediocre and calls the question small.
Treating the repetition answer as a tested finding rather than a deduction from the new-customers premise.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 31 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly')
qa_items.question: What figure does Hopkins report for the cost of converting someone to the tooth-brush habit, what two reasons does he give for it, and what is missing from the report?
qa_items.answer: He reports that tests he knows of have indicated the cost of such converts may run from $20 to $25 each. His two reasons are the difficulty of the change itself, and the fact that much of the advertising goes to people already converted. What is missing is everything that would let anyone check it: no product, no advertiser, no date, no method, no sample size, and no definition of what counts as a convert. It is a reported number without a reported study — and it is one of only a handful of places in chapters 8-21 where he says what a measurement returned rather than that a measurement was made.
qa_items.support: p.31: "Tests which we know of have indicated that the cost of such converts may run from $20 to $25 each. Not only because of the difficulty, but because much of the advertising goes to people already converted."
confounders: Attributing the figure to Pepsodent or another named brand; the maker is unnamed.
Treating $20-$25 as a cost per customer for the product rather than per habit convert.
Missing the second reason — wasted reach on the already-converted — which is half the arithmetic.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 31-32 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly')
qa_items.question: An advertiser accepts that educating the market to a new habit is unaffordable as a campaign, so proposes devoting a quarter of each advertisement's space to it instead. What does Hopkins say?
qa_items.answer: He calls it the same folly on a smaller scale and says it is not good business. His rule is that what cannot be done profitably on a large scale cannot be done on a small scale: the cost per convert does not fall with reduced commitment, only the number of converts does, so a fractional budget buys a fraction of an already unaffordable result. He notes there are many advertisers who know facts like these and concede them, would not think of devoting a whole campaign to such an object, and then devote a share of their space to it anyway. His own example of doing it right is the dentifrice maker who learned the convert cost by test and thereafter devoted not one line to the tooth-brush habit.
qa_items.support: pp.31-32: "What cannot be done on a large scale profitably cannot be done on a small scale." "Yet they devote a share of their space to that object. That is only the same folly on a smaller scale. It is not good business."
confounders: That a smaller commitment is a reasonable compromise — the intuitive answer and the one he names as the error.
That the objection is about focus or message clarity rather than about unit economics.
Confusing this with his separate point that co-operative advertising by many growers CAN build category demand.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 32 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly')
qa_items.question: Hopkins says no single orange or raisin grower could increase consumption of those fruits. What is the mechanism, and what exception does he name?
qa_items.answer: The mechanism is that demand created attaches to the category rather than to the brand that paid for it, so the spender funds the whole benefit and captures only his share — the cost, he says, might be a thousand times one grower's share of the returns, and a maker educating people to a habit finds the new business shared by his rivals. His exception is co-operation: thousands of growers combined have done it on those and many other lines, and he calls this one of the great possibilities of advertising development, adding that the general consumption of scores of foods can be profitably increased if it is done through wide co-operation. The alternative he recommends for a single advertiser is to watch a popular trend developing and offer at the right time to satisfy the want already created, as was done on yeasts and antiseptics.
qa_items.support: p.32: "The cost might be a thousand times his share of the returns. But thousands of growers combined have done it on those and many other lines." "But it must be done through wide co-operation." "watch the development of a popular trend... Then at the right time offer to satisfy those desires."
confounders: That he holds category demand cannot be built — he says it can, just not by one advertiser.
That the trend-riding advice is about timing a launch; it is about not funding the want.
Treating 'a thousand times his share' as a measured ratio; it is a rhetorical magnitude.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 32 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly')
qa_items.question: A product could be sold to half the homes in the country. On Hopkins's chapter 10 reasoning, why might that still be a project to refuse?
qa_items.answer: Because breadth of appeal and revenue per customer are independent, and only revenue pays. His case is a Dakin-fluid germicide: it might be sold to half the homes in the country, but consumption would be very small, a small bottle might last for years, customers might cost $1.50 each, and the revenue per customer might not repay the cost of getting in ten years. Acquisition cost is roughly fixed per customer regardless of how much that customer then buys, so a low-consumption product cannot amortise it however wide its potential market. He adds two reference figures for the cost side — mail order sales on single articles rarely cost less than $2.50 each, and it is reasonable to suppose dealer sales on like articles cost approximately as much — and notes these facts must be considered on any one-sale article. The germicide figures are explicitly hypothetical.
qa_items.support: p.32: "the consumption would be very small. A small bottle might last for years. Customers might cost $1.50 each. And the revenue per customer might not in ten years repay the cost of getting." "Mail order sales on single articles, however popular, rarely cost less than $2.50 each."
confounders: That wide appeal makes a product a good advertising candidate — the intuitive answer he is attacking.
Reading the $1.50 and $2.50 figures as measurements; the first is hypothetical and the second is asserted without a source.
Confusing this with his separate reach argument about the percentage of readers a claim can address.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 32-33 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly')
qa_items.question: What is Hopkins's position on prevention as an appeal, and what evidence does he give?
qa_items.answer: His position is that prevention is not a popular subject however much it should be: people will do much to cure a trouble and little to prevent one. He applies it to a tooth paste that both prevents decay and beautifies the teeth, saying tests will probably show the beauty appeal many times as strong, and reports that the most successful tooth paste advertiser never features tooth troubles in his headlines because tests have proved them unappealing. His evidence is: "This has been proved by many disappointments", naming no disappointment, and "Tests have proved them unappealing", reporting no test, no advertiser and no margin. Measurement is asserted and the result is withheld in both places.
qa_items.support: p.32: "People will do much to cure a trouble, but people in general will do little to prevent it. This has been proved by many disappointments." p.33: "The most successful tooth paste advertiser never features tooth troubles in his headlines. Tests have proved them unappealing."
confounders: Treating the claim as demonstrated because he uses the word 'proved' twice.
That the prevention weakness is about credibility rather than about motive to act now.
Naming the tooth paste advertiser; Hopkins does not.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 33 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly')
qa_items.question: Hopkins makes two DIFFERENT arguments against featuring a narrow claim. Separate them, and say which one he leaves unexplained.
qa_items.answer: The first is reach arithmetic: a claim reaching one in a hundred requires covering a hundred useless readers to get one, so the cost of results might be twenty times as high as for an article appealing to one in five — an excess he says would probably mean disaster. The second is an interference claim of a different kind entirely: for a soap that cures eczema and also improves the complexion, "to even mention the eczema claims might destroy the beauty claim". The first is a cost calculation and follows from bought circulation. The second says the narrow claim damages the broad one by being present, not by displacing it — and he gives no mechanism for it at all, hedges it with "might", and reports no comparison. They also imply different repairs: choose the bigger claim, versus remove the smaller one even where the space is free.
qa_items.support: p.33: "he would need to cover a hundred useless readers to reach the one he wants. His cost of results might be twenty times as high..." and "The eczema claim may appeal to one in a hundred while the beauty claims would appeal to nearly all. To even mention the eczema claims might destroy the beauty claim."
confounders: Merging the two into one 'pick the bigger claim' rule, which loses the interference claim entirely.
Assuming a mechanism for the interference — audience self-selection, or category association — that Hopkins does not give.
Treating the one-in-a-hundred and one-in-five figures as measured; they are figures inside a stated hypothetical.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 33 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly')
qa_items.question: A claim appeals to about a quarter of your possible customers — not enough to lead on. On Hopkins's rule, what happens to it?
qa_items.answer: It is not dropped. He says a claim popular enough to influence a certain number of people — say one-fourth of your possible customers — may be featured to advantage in a certain PERCENTAGE of headlines, and should probably be included in EVERY advertisement. So the claim earns a share of headline slots and a permanent place in the body copy. He immediately adds that these are not things to guess at and should be decided by actual knowledge, usually by traced returns. The one-fourth threshold is offered casually and is not derived from anything; the structure of the rule is the reusable part.
qa_items.support: p.33: "say one-fourth of your possible customers. Such a claim may be featured to advantage in a certain percentage of headlines. It should probably be included in every advertisement. But those are not things to guess at."
confounders: Dropping the claim because it cannot lead — the intuitive optimiser's answer.
Featuring it in every headline rather than a share of them.
Treating one-fourth as a threshold he established rather than an illustrative figure.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 34 (Chapter 11, 'Information')
qa_items.question: What single fact did Hopkins say reframed a caffeine-free coffee, and what problem did it solve?
qa_items.answer: The problem was that caffeine-free coffee had been advertised for years and people regarded it like near-beer — a diminished version of the real thing. The fact, found in one scientific article out of a thousand he read, was that caffeine stimulation comes two hours after drinking, so the immediate bracing effect people seek from coffee does not come from the caffeine at all. Removing caffeine therefore removes neither the kick nor the taste, since caffeine is tasteless and odourless. The physiological claim is his 1923 statement of the science and is recorded here as his claim, not as verified fact; what is being learned from the passage is the method of hunting for a fact that dissolves a misperception, not the fact itself.
qa_items.support: p.34: "It was the fact that caffeine stimulation comes two hours after drinking. So the immediate bracing effects which people seek from coffee do not come from the caffeine. Removing caffeine does not remove the kick." "People regarded it like near-beer."
confounders: Taking the caffeine pharmacology as established fact rather than as the source's 1923 claim.
That the fact was a product improvement; it was a fact about the existing product.
That the campaign argued the health benefit of removing caffeine — his angle is that nothing desirable is lost.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 35 (Chapter 11, 'Information')
qa_items.question: In the pork and beans case, what did the canvass find and how did it change the campaign's task?
qa_items.answer: A canvass of some thousands of homes found that only 4 per cent of people used any canned pork and beans and 96 per cent baked their beans at home. All previous pork and bean advertising had been based on "Buy my brand", which could address only that 4 per cent. The task was therefore not to sell a particular brand but to win people away from home-baked beans. Hopkins says the resulting advertising, which without that knowledge must have failed, proved a great success. The canvass half is a genuine reported measurement with numbers; the outcome half is asserted with no figure, no advertiser and no period, and "must have failed" is a counterfactual he cannot test.
qa_items.support: p.35: "That canvass showed that only 4 per cent of the people used any canned pork and beans. Ninety-six per cent baked their beans at home... The right appeal was to win the people away from home-baked beans."
confounders: That the finding refined the brand message; it replaced the competitive frame entirely.
Treating 'proved a great success' as reported evidence on a par with the 4/96 split.
Missing that the recommended campaign is precisely the household-habit change chapter 10 prices out of reach — a tension Hopkins never addresses.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 35 (Chapter 11, 'Information')
qa_items.question: Hopkins lists three quantities that must be learned before a campaign. Name them with the decision each protects.
qa_items.answer: What a user spends a year, because otherwise it is unknown whether users are worth the cost of getting. Total consumption, because otherwise the advertiser may overspend. And the percentage of readers to whom the product appeals — often gathered by class, because the percentage may differ on farms and in cities — because the cost of advertising largely depends on the percentage of waste circulation. The third is the one he treats as dominant, and it is arithmetic over 1923 media buying, where circulation was bought whole and paid for whether or not it contained prospects.
qa_items.support: p.35: "We must learn what a user spends a year, else we shall not know if users are worth the cost of getting. We must learn the total consumption, else we may overspend. We must learn the percentage of readers to whom our product appeals... The cost of advertising largely depends on the percentage of waste circulation."
confounders: Reciting the quantities without the decision each protects, which is where the value is.
Treating the class breakdown as optional; he specifies it because the percentage varies.

Missing that this third quantity sits in tension with chapter 15's claim that small-scale averages always hold. Hopkins never raises the tension; a reader could reconcile it by assuming the test towns are average, which he never says either.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 35-36 (Chapter 11, 'Information')
qa_items.question: Hopkins describes two different verification controls in chapter 11. What failure does each one catch, and why does he need both?
qa_items.answer: The first tests the advertiser's own assertions: chemists are employed to prove or disprove doubtful claims, because a true claim will be a big factor while an untrue one may prove a boomerang and may bar the advertising from good mediums — and he notes it is remarkable how often a maker proves wrong about assertions he has made for years. The second guards the writer's reasoning rather than the client's facts: in every line involving scientific details a censor is appointed, because a well-informed ad-writer may still draw wrong inferences from correct facts, so an authority passes on every advertisement. He needs both because they catch different failures — a false premise, and a false inference from a true premise — and testing the premise does nothing about the second.
qa_items.support: p.35: "Often chemists are employed to prove or disprove doubtful claims... If untrue, it may prove a boomerang. And it may bar our ads from good mediums." p.36: "The ad-writer, however well-informed, may draw wrong inferences from facts. So an authority passes on every advertisement."
confounders: Treating the censor as a legal or compliance review; his stated concern is inference from facts.
Collapsing both into 'fact-checking', which loses the distinction the passage exists to make.
Reading the motive as ethical; his stated reasons are persuasive force, boomerang risk and medium admissibility.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 36 (Chapter 11, 'Information')
qa_items.question: You have a claim that is true but vague — a drink has "a large food value". What does Hopkins do about it, and what uncomfortable feature does the procedure have?
qa_items.answer: He commissions a measurement to make the claim exact, then restates the figure against something familiar: the drink goes to a laboratory, the answer is 425 calories per pint, and that is expressed as one pint equal to six eggs in calories of nutriment — which he says makes a great impression. His principle is that impressive claims are made far more impressive by making them exact, so experiments are often made to get the actual figures. The uncomfortable feature, which he does not address, is that the measurement is undertaken because the copy needs a number rather than to find out whether the claim is true — a different activity from the verification he describes a paragraph earlier, and he places the two side by side without distinguishing them.
qa_items.support: p.36: "Impressive claims are made far more impressive by making them exact. So many experiments are often made to get the actual figures... its food value is 425 calories per pint. One pint is equal to six eggs in calories of nutriment."
confounders: Stopping at 'be specific' and missing that he manufactures the specificity by commissioning it.
Missing the second step — the familiar comparison — without which the raw figure is unusable.
Assuming the measurement was a verification; the passage frames it as a copy requirement.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 37-38 (Chapter 12, 'Strategy')
qa_items.question: Hopkins treats price as having more than one regime. Set out the three he describes and what determines which applies.
qa_items.answer: Volume: the greatest profits are made on great volume at small profit — Campbell's Soups, Palmolive Soap, Karo Syrup, Ford cars — and a price that appeals only to, say, 10 per cent multiplies the cost of selling. Low consumption: on some lines high price is unimportant but high profit is essential, because sale per customer is small; a buyer hardly cares what he pays for a corn remedy because he uses little, so the maker must have a large margin. Judgement: on other lines a higher price is itself an inducement, because the line is judged largely by price and a product costing more than the ordinary is considered above the ordinary. What determines the regime is how much the customer consumes and whether he has any way to judge the product other than by price — though Hopkins never states a test for placing a new product, which is the decision the passage is about.
qa_items.support: p.38: "the greatest profits are made on great volume at small profit... A price which appeals only to—say 10 per cent—multiplies the cost of selling." "The maker must have a large margin because of small consumption." "A product which costs more than the ordinary is considered above the ordinary."
confounders: Reducing him to 'low price wins volume', which is only the first regime.
Treating the price-as-quality-signal point as the same as his chapter 6 claim that people judge value by stated price; here it is a pricing decision, not a copy effect.
Assuming he supplies a rule for classifying a new product; he does not.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 38 (Chapter 12, 'Strategy')
qa_items.question: What does Hopkins say makes a competitive field almost impregnable, and how much does the diagnosis actually help?
qa_items.answer: The near-impregnable fields are, he says, usually lines that created a new habit or custom and which typify that custom with consumers — so the incumbent's name is how buyers think of the behaviour itself — combined with the volume and profit to make a tremendous fight. It helps less than it looks. He immediately concedes such fields are constantly invaded, and the two routes he allows — some convincing advantage, or very superior salesmanship-in-print — are what any challenger would attempt anyway. He names no field as impregnable and no invasion as successful. The diagnosis identifies difficulty; it does not discriminate between actions.
qa_items.support: p.38: "They are usually lines which created a new habit or custom and which typify that custom with consumers... Such fields are being constantly invaded. But it is done through some convincing advantage, or through very superior salesmanship-in-print."
confounders: Reading the diagnosis as actionable strategy; the qualification empties most of it.
That scale alone makes a field impregnable — he specifies habit creation and typification as the mechanism.
Confusing this with the new shaving soap case, which he places in a lesser tier.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 38 (Chapter 12, 'Strategy')
qa_items.question: A manufacturer says frankly that his product is good but much like every rival's, and that he has nothing exclusive to offer. Quote Hopkins's answer precisely — including the word that makes it uncomfortable.
qa_items.answer: He answers that there is nearly always something impressive which others have not told, that it must be discovered, and — in his own words — "We must have a SEEMING advantage." The word is "seeming", and it should not be softened into "differentiator": the chapter does not require the advantage to be real, only to be perceived. His justification is that people don't quit habits without reason, so a switching campaign supplying no reason cannot work whatever the product's quality. He gives no case in this chapter, and the claim that something untold nearly always exists is unfalsifiable as stated, since failing to find one is always attributable to insufficient search.
qa_items.support: p.38: "However, there is nearly always something impressive which others have not told. We must discover it. We must have a seeming advantage. People don't quit habits without reason."
confounders: Paraphrasing 'seeming advantage' as 'genuine differentiation', which reverses the source.
Attributing to him a claim that the product must actually be improved.
Confusing this with his chapter 7 process-fact tactic, which is the execution rather than the strategic premise.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 39 (Chapter 12, 'Strategy')
qa_items.question: Why does Hopkins hold up Vaseline, and what does the case rest on evidentially?
qa_items.answer: Vaseline established a new demand and then almost monopolised that demand through wisdom at the start — the name. To have called it some brand of petroleum jelly, he says, might have made a difference of millions in results, because a pioneer's demand attaches to whatever name the market can use for the thing, and if that name is available to everyone the competitors inherit demand the pioneer funded. He sets Royal Baking Powder, Toasted Corn Flakes and Horlick's Malted Milk against it as pioneers who left the way open to perpetual substitution. Evidentially it rests on nothing testable: every case is selected on its outcome and read backwards, the "difference of millions" is an untestable counterfactual, and the chapter contains no case where an exclusive name failed or a generic one succeeded.
qa_items.support: p.39: "Vaseline is an example. That product established a new demand, then almost monopolized that demand through wisdom at the start. To have called it some brand of petroleum jelly might have made a difference of millions in results."
confounders: Treating the Vaseline case as evidence rather than as retrospective explanation.
That the lesson is about trademark law; his argument is about which demand the name captures.
Confusing this with his chapter 6 tactic of inviting comparison, which is a copy response to substitution rather than a structural one.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 41 (Chapter 13, 'Use of Samples')
qa_items.question: A client wants to charge ten cents for the sample to filter out non-serious enquirers. What does Hopkins say it costs, and what is his reasoning about half-price offers?
qa_items.answer: He says getting that dime may cost them from 40 cents to $1 — that is, it may add that much to the cost of each reply — and it also forfeits the word "Free" in the advertisement, which he holds generally more than pays for the samples on its own. Three in four will refuse to pay, he says, perhaps nine in ten. On half-price constructions — "You buy one package, we will buy the other", or a coupon good for part of the purchase price — his position is that any keyed returns will clearly prove such offers do not pay, because before a prospect is converted it is approximately as hard to get half price for the article as to get the full price. The barrier is the act of paying, not the amount: an unconverted prospect has no basis for valuing the article, so any price is a full-price decision to him.
qa_items.support: p.41: "Getting that dime may cost them from 40 cents to $1... Three in four will refuse to pay—perhaps nine in ten." "Before a prospect is converted, it is approximately as hard to get half price for your article as to get the full price for it."
confounders: The intuitive qualification argument — that a small charge filters for intent — which is what he is refuting.
That half price is a reasonable middle course; he places it in the same class as full price.
Confusing this with his separate chapter 6 point that the MAKER should buy the sample at retail rather than give away his own stock.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 42 (Chapter 13, 'Use of Samples')
qa_items.question: Hopkins reports the same advertisement producing inquiries at two very different costs. Give the figures and the explanation, and say why this passage is evidentially stronger than most of the book.
qa_items.answer: On a line then before him, sample inquiries obtained by mail averaged 70 cents each, and the same advertisement brought inquiries at 18 to 22 cents each when the coupons were presented at a local store; he adds that often four times as many will present a coupon at a store as will mail it. On another line, where three routes were offered — write, telephone, or call at a store — 70 per cent of inquiries came by telephone. His explanation is friction, not motivation: most people write few letters, writing is an effort, they may have no stamps in the house, and most will pay carfare to get a sample rather than two cents postage. It is stronger than most of the book because it holds the advertisement constant — "the same ad" — varies one factor, and reports a returned cost on both arms. It is still one unnamed line, with no market, period, volume, or statement of whether the arms ran simultaneously.
qa_items.support: p.42: "sample inquiries obtained by mail average 70 cents each. The same ad brings inquiries at from 18 cents to 22 cents each when the coupons are presented at a local store." "Seventy per cent of the inquiries came by telephone."
confounders: Attributing the difference to the copy or the offer rather than to the response route.
Reading the 70-per-cent telephone figure as a cost finding; it is a distribution of choices.
Generalising a 1923 finding about stamps, telephones and carfare into a claim about response friction in any other setting.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 43 (Chapter 13, 'Use of Samples')
qa_items.question: Hopkins says samples should be free. He also condemns handing them out. Reconcile the two and state the gate he specifies.
qa_items.answer: Free to the prospect is not the same as freely distributed. His gate has three conditions, stated as three sentences: give samples to interested people only; only to people who exhibit that interest by some effort; and only to people to whom you have told your story. The reason is that the product sells itself only inside a mental impression and atmosphere the advertising has placed around it — first create an atmosphere of respect, a desire, an expectation, and then the sample will usually confirm the qualities claimed. Samples distributed to homes "like waifs on the doorsteps" probably never pay: many never reach the housewife, and where they do there is no predilection for them and the product is cheapened. Store demonstrations are put in the same class.
qa_items.support: p.43: "Give samples to interested people only. Give them only to people who exhibit that interest by some effort. Give them only to people to whom you have told your story." "Samples distributed to homes, like waifs on the doorsteps, probably never pay."
confounders: Reading 'free' as 'widely distributed' — the confusion the gate exists to prevent.
Giving two conditions instead of three; the 'told your story' condition is the one most often dropped.
Assuming he reports the cost of doorstep sampling; he concedes it has not been traced.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 42 (Chapter 13, 'Use of Samples')
qa_items.question: Sample abuse worries a client: people taking several, children collecting coupons, dealers buying up newspapers. Give Hopkins's four measures and the finding that governs how far to go.
qa_items.answer: Declared limits: say to the woman "Only one sample to a home" and few will try for more, since the few who cheat are not generally people who would buy — the loss is samples, not purchasers. Declared eligibility: say "adults only" in the coupon, and children will not present such coupons and will rarely mail them. And two structural precautions against bulk exploitation of a full-package coupon: do not announce the date of such offers, and insert them in Sunday papers, which are not so easily bought up. The governing finding is that he checked repeaters in certain territories for a time and found the loss much less than the cost of checking — so verification is priced against the loss it prevents, and where the loss is smaller than the check, the check is the more expensive error. He adds that repeaters form a small percentage and should simply be figured into cost.
qa_items.support: p.42: "Say to the woman, 'Only one sample to a home'..." "Then say in your coupon 'adults only.'" "We do not announce the date of such offers. And we insert them in Sunday papers." "we have checked up on repeaters. And we found the loss much less than the cost of checking." "But repeaters form a small percentage. Figure it in your cost." All five sit on printed p.42.
confounders: Proposing enforcement rather than declaration — the intuitive answer he prices out.
Missing the cost-of-control finding, which is the only measured thing in the passage.
Treating 'repeaters form a small percentage' as a reported rate; the rate is never given.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 43 (Chapter 13, 'Use of Samples')
qa_items.question: A sampling budget looks extravagant — it costs more than the media. What two things does Hopkins say to do about the disagreement?
qa_items.answer: First, change the measure. Samples sometimes seem to double advertising cost and often cost more than the advertising, but he holds that rightly used they almost invariably form the cheapest way to get customers, because cost per customer is the only way to gauge advertising — any measure short of it can move in the opposite direction to the result. Second, look at who is arguing and then stop arguing: the arguments against samples are usually biased and may come from advertising agents who like to see all the advertising money spent in print, and such arguments should be answered by tests — try some towns with them, some without them. Note that he prescribes the test and reports no result from one, for any line; and that the same conflict-of-interest logic applies to a practitioner author recommending his own methods, which he does not note.
qa_items.support: p.43: "Samples sometimes seem to double advertising cost... Yet, rightly used, they almost invariably form the cheapest way to get customers." "The arguments against samples are usually biased... Answer such arguments by tests. Try some towns with them, some without them."
confounders: Giving only the cost-per-customer half and missing the paired-town procedure.
Treating 'almost invariably' as a reported finding; no town comparison is reported anywhere.
Reading the bias observation as an argument about samples rather than about the arguer.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 44 (Chapter 14, 'Getting Distribution')
qa_items.question: Magazine advertising suits the product best. Why does Hopkins nevertheless say to start local, and what is his stated scope limit on the advice?
qa_items.answer: Because distribution is a precondition rather than a consequence: national advertising is unthinkable without it, and a venture cannot be profitable if nine in ten of the converts fail to find the goods. So distribution is built town by town with local advertising first, even where magazine advertising is best adapted to the article, and the campaign converts to national afterwards. His scope limit is explicit and stated twice: this chapter deals with articles of wide appeal and repeated sales, like foods or proprietary articles, and other lines require different methods too numerous to discuss in a book like that one.
qa_items.support: p.44: "A venture cannot be profitable if nine in ten of the converts fail to find the goods." "We usually start with local advertising, even though magazine advertising is best adapted to the article." "We shall deal here with articles of wide appeal and repeated sales, like foods or proprietary articles."
confounders: Reading the local-first rule as a budget-phasing or risk-management principle rather than a supply precondition.
Generalising past his stated scope to considered or infrequent purchases.
Confusing town-by-town rollout with his chapter 1 town-by-town measurement method — same words, different purpose.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 45-46 (Chapter 14, 'Getting Distribution')
qa_items.question: Describe the pre-announced coupon mechanism and say exactly why a dealer stocks under it.
qa_items.answer: A coupon good at any store for a full-size package is placed in the advertising, and before it appears a proof of that advertisement is mailed to dealers — in the national version with the list of magazines to be used and their circulations. Each dealer is shown that many of his customers are bound to present that coupon, and that each coupon means a cash sale at full profit. He stocks because refusing has a visible cost to him: no average dealer will let those customers go elsewhere. What makes it work rather than a promise of advertising is that it converts a future promise into an itemised forecast of paying customers arriving at his counter — evidence rather than persuasion. Hopkins claims makers have sometimes attained reasonable national distribution in one week this way, without a single salesman, naming Palmolive Soap and Puffed Grains — with no dates, dealer counts or costs, and no case where the method failed.
qa_items.support: p.45: "Mail to dealers proofs of the ad which will contain the coupon... Each coupon means a cash sale at full profit. No average dealer will let those customers go elsewhere." "In this way, in one week sometimes, makers attain a reasonable national distribution." p.46 carries the salesman claim: "many advertisers get national distribution without employing a single salesman."
confounders: That the dealer is persuaded by the promise of advertising support — the thing he says dealers no longer believe.
Omitting the pre-announcement, which is the whole mechanism; the coupon alone is not the device.
Treating Palmolive and Puffed Grains as evidence; they are outcome-selected names with no figures.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 45-46 (Chapter 14, 'Getting Distribution')
qa_items.question: Half a newspaper's circulation goes to towns where you have no distribution. Those readers write in for a sample. What does Hopkins say to do, and what failure is he avoiding?
qa_items.answer: Invite them to write — otherwise that half of the circulation is wasted — but do NOT mail them the sample. Send the samples to a store near the inquirer and refer him there. The failure he is avoiding is the convert who cannot be supplied: mailing the sample may make a convert with no route to purchase, and the full cost of the conversion has then been paid with none of the revenue collectable. Routing it through a shop also does the second job, since the store that supplies the sample will usually supply the demand that follows. Note this is a 1923 physical-fulfilment device that depends on retailers accepting consignment samples, and no measurement of it is reported.
qa_items.support: pp.45-46: "Say in your coupon that outside people should write you for a sample. When they write, do not mail the sample. Send the samples to a local store, and refer inquirers to that store... Mailing a sample may make a convert who cannot be supplied."
confounders: Mailing the sample, which is the direct and obvious fulfilment and the specific error named.
Suppressing the offer to outside towns, which wastes the circulation he is trying to recover.
Reading the point as customer-experience rather than as demand routed into a stocking decision.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 48 (Chapter 15, 'Test Campaigns')
qa_items.question: Set out Hopkins's test campaign procedure exactly as he specifies it: scale, how users are started, and the sequence of questions it answers.
qa_items.answer: Scale: four or five towns. Starting method: a sample offer or a free package, used to get users started quickly. The first measure is the cost per customer started.
