Then he waits, and the remaining questions come in a fixed sequence — do the users buy those samples; if they do, will they continue; how much will they buy; and how long does it take for the profit to return the cost of selling. He puts the cost of such a test at $3,000 to $5,000 and argues the real cost is less because some sales are made even on an unpopular product and nearly every test will in time bring back its entire cost. The payback answer is what determines financing: on some products the cost returns before the bills are due, meaning the product can be advertised without investment; on another it may take three months, and the advertiser must finance accordingly when he spreads out.
qa_items.support: p.48: "Perhaps we try out our project in four or five towns. We may use a sample offer or a free package to get users started quickly. We learn in this way the cost per customer started. Then we wait and see if users buy those samples. If they do, will they continue? How much will they buy? How long does it take for the profit to return our cost of selling?" "A test like this may cost $3,000 to $5,000."
confounders: Adding a control or comparison town; the procedure as he describes it has no comparison arm.
Reading $3,000-$5,000 as something a test returned; it is what a test costs.
Assuming a duration for the test itself — he gives payback periods, never a test length.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 47-48 (Chapter 15, 'Test Campaigns')
qa_items.question: What is the inferential premise that makes the test campaign decision-useful, how strongly does Hopkins state it, and what does he offer in support?
qa_items.answer: The premise is that averages established on a small scale always hold. He states it without any qualification: from what a thousand customers cost we know almost exactly what a million will cost; from what they buy, what a million will buy; before spreading out we prove the undertaking absolutely safe; an advertiser who branches out knows to a certainty just what his results will be; and there are today no advertising disasters piloted by men who know. In support he offers nothing. No mechanism is given for why a four-or-five-town average should generalise, no conditions are named, and not one paired figure — predicted from a test, observed at scale — appears anywhere. The strongest statement in his measurement doctrine is the one he supports least, and the last claim is unfalsifiable as constructed, since any disaster shows the pilot did not know.
qa_items.support: p.47: "When we learn what a thousand customers cost, we know almost exactly what a million will cost... We establish averages on a small scale, and those averages always hold... So there are today no advertising disasters piloted by men who know."
confounders: Assuming the chapter validates the extrapolation somewhere later; it does not.
Reading the 91 per cent or 75 per cent figures as support for this claim; neither is an extrapolation checked against a national result.

Missing that it sits in tension with his own chapter 11 instruction to gather appeal percentages by class because they differ on farms and in cities. He never raises the tension and never says which towns count as average.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 48-49 (Chapter 15, 'Test Campaigns')
qa_items.question: Chapter 15 reports a 91 per cent result. What exactly was measured, and is it a test-campaign return?
qa_items.answer: It is a vote on a product form, not an advertising return. A large food advertiser and all his advisers were certain a product would be more popular in another form and were willing to act without consulting consumers. A test was run instead — an advertisement in a few towns with a coupon good at any store for a package of the new-style product, followed by writing to the users — and they were almost unanimous in disapproval. When a further variant was proposed, he submitted it to a few thousand women the same way and 91 per cent voted for it. Each test cost about $1,000. So the number is a survey result from self-selected coupon redeemers, and it is not cost per customer, repeat rate, purchase volume or payback — none of which chapter 15 reports for any product. The first test's result is given only qualitatively, with no figure to set against the 91 per cent.
qa_items.support: p.49: "he submitted the question to a few thousand women in a similar way and 91 per cent voted for it... These tests cost about $1,000 each. The first one saved him a very costly mistake."
confounders: Reading 91 per cent as an advertising response or sales result.
Treating 'saved him a very costly mistake' as established; it assumes the disapproval was correct, which the test cannot show.
Assuming the respondents were a representative sample; they were people who redeemed a coupon.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 49 (Chapter 15, 'Test Campaigns')
qa_items.question: Your current campaign is working and you do not want to risk it, but you think a better approach exists. What arrangement does Hopkins describe, and what is wrong with the 75 per cent figure he attaches to it?
qa_items.answer: Run the new methods as tests alongside the campaign rather than in place of it, so better methods can be sought constantly without interrupting plans already proved out. He reports doing this for one food advertiser over five years, trying more than fifty separate plans, finding an improvement every little while, and ending with a best plan that reduced the cost of selling by 75 per cent — four times more effective than the best plan used before. What is wrong with the figure is that it is the winner of fifty attempts reported as if it were the effect of the method: he gives no distribution of outcomes across the fifty, and a 75 per cent reduction accumulated over five years against a baseline that was itself the best of an earlier search cannot be attributed to the final plan alone. The advertiser, product, plans and absolute costs are all unnamed. The durable content is the structure — the proved plan keeps running while the candidate is tested beside it — not the number.
qa_items.support: p.49: "we use test campaigns to try out new methods on advertising already successful... without interrupting plans already proved out. In five years for one food advertiser we tried out over fifty separate plans... It reduced our cost of selling by 75 per cent."
confounders: Quoting the 75 per cent as a demonstrated effect size for a testing programme.
That the improvement came from one change; he describes fifty attempts over five years.
Missing the champion/challenger structure, which is the part that does not depend on the figure.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 49 (Chapter 15, 'Test Campaigns')
qa_items.question: Hopkins proposes settling a claim of superior advertising skill by test. Describe the arrangement and the two problems with it that he does not raise.
qa_items.answer: The challenger takes a few towns without interfering with the general campaign, and his results are compared with the general results; the advertiser makes no commitment, which he likens to telling a salesman to go out for a week and prove. He adds that a large percentage of all the advertising then being done would change hands if the method were applied. Two problems he does not raise. First, the comparison is not clean: a few towns worked by a motivated challenger against the general results of a national campaign differ in market, scale, attention and effort as well as in skill, and nothing is held constant. Second, the prediction is in the direct commercial interest of his own agency — a conflict of the exact kind he warns about in chapter 13 when he says arguments against samples may come from agents who want the money spent in print.
qa_items.support: p.49: "The new agent may take a few towns, without interfering with the general campaign. Then compare his results with the general results and prove his greater skill... A large percentage of all the advertising done would change hands if this method were applied."
confounders: Accepting the design as a controlled comparison because it uses the word 'test'.
Treating the change-hands prediction as a finding.
Missing the parallel with his own chapter 13 warning about biased advisers.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 47-50 (Chapter 15, 'Test Campaigns')
qa_items.question: Chapter 15 is the book's chapter on measurement. Does it report what any test campaign returned?
qa_items.answer: No. It specifies the procedure fully and reports no test campaign's returns at all — not one cost per customer started, repeat rate, purchase volume or payback period for any product in any town. The only dollar figures in it are the cost of RUNNING a test ($3,000 to $5,000 for a town test, about $1,000 for a coupon question), not anything a test brought back. The two numbers it does report belong to side-uses of the apparatus: 91 per cent, a vote on a product form, and 75 per cent, the cost reduction of the best of fifty plans over five years. The claim on which everything rests — that small-scale averages always hold — is stated as an absolute and supported by nothing. So the chapter supplies a well-specified METHOD and almost no reported OUTPUT.
qa_items.support: p.48: cost of a test given as $3,000-$5,000; p.49: tests "cost about $1,000 each"; the reported outcomes at p.49 are a 91 per cent product-form vote and a 75 per cent cost reduction from a five-year programme. No cost per customer started, repeat rate, volume or payback is reported anywhere in pp.47-50.
confounders: Assuming the book's most-quoted chapter must contain its evidence.
Counting the 91 per cent or 75 per cent as test-campaign returns; neither is.
Treating the detailed procedure as evidence — specificity of method is not reporting of result.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 51-52 (Chapter 16, 'Leaning on Dealers')
qa_items.question: A window display measurably lifts sales at the shop that runs it. On Hopkins's argument, what has been measured, and what measurement would settle it?
qa_items.answer: What has been measured is redistribution, not gain. A window display acting as a reminder may bring one dealer a lion's share of the trade and yet not increase total sales at all; dealer effort, if made, does not usually increase total sales but merely swings trade from one store to another. The advertiser has no interest in centring trade at any particular store. What would settle it is a comparison at the town level: try one town in one way, one in another, and compare TOTAL sales in those towns — which is the only measure that distinguishes a gain from a reallocation. He predicts that in many lines such tests will show costly displays to be worthless and says a growing number of experienced advertisers spend no money on displays, but reports no such test and names no line.
qa_items.support: pp.51-52: "A window display, acting as a reminder, may bring to one dealer a lion's share of the trade. Yet it may not increase your total sales at all." "Try one town in one way, one in another. Compare total sales in those towns."
confounders: Accepting the shop-level lift as evidence — the intuitive reading and the one he attacks.
That his objection is to the expense of displays rather than to the level at which they are measured.
Treating 'such tests will show' as a report of tests run.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 51 (Chapter 16, 'Leaning on Dealers')
qa_items.question: What does Hopkins claim about a sale made on a dealer's recommendation rather than by advertising, and how well supported is it?
qa_items.answer: He claims a sale without a convert does not count for much on most lines: sales made by conviction — by advertising — are likely to bring permanent customers, while people who buy through casual recommendations do not often stick, because next time someone else gives other advice. The mechanism is that a recommendation transfers no reason to the buyer, so nothing in him resists the next recommendation. It is supported by nothing whatever: no retention comparison between advertising-acquired and dealer-recommended customers is reported and no rate is given for either. It is also the justification for moving money from the trade into consumer advertising, which is the same direction the rest of the chapter argues in and, in a practitioner author's book, worth noticing.
qa_items.support: p.51: "On most lines, making a sale without making a convert does not count for much. Sales made by conviction—by advertising—are likely to bring permanent customers. People who buy through casual recommendations do not often stick."
confounders: Treating it as an established retention finding rather than an unevidenced assertion.
Dropping his own scope limit, 'on most lines'.
Reading it as a claim about word of mouth generally; his case is a shopkeeper's recommendation at the counter.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 53 (Chapter 17, 'Individuality')
qa_items.question: Chapter 9 rules out eccentricity; chapter 17 requires standing out. How does Hopkins hold both, and what selection rule does he give?
qa_items.answer: He distinguishes two kinds of uniqueness: one that belittles and arouses resentment, and one that is refreshing, that enhances, and that we welcome and remember. Being eccentric or abnormal is not a distinction to covet; doing admirable things in a different way is. So the requirement is distinctiveness in manner and tone rather than in appearance or subject treatment. His selection rule is fit to audience: each advertiser is given an individuality best suited to the people he addresses — rugged and honest in a line where rugged honesty counts, a good fellow where choice is a matter of favour, an authority in other lines. He gives no way to classify a candidate persona in advance as refreshing rather than belittling, which is the decision the chapter exists to support, and he attaches no line, product or result to any of the three castings.
qa_items.support: p.53: "There is uniqueness which belittles and arouses resentment. There is refreshing uniqueness which enhances." "He is given an individuality best suited to the people he addresses. One man appears rugged and honest in a line where rugged honesty counts."
confounders: Reading chapters 9 and 17 as contradicting; the distinction is between kinds of distinctiveness and between appearance and manner.
That the persona expresses the client; he says it is selected to fit the audience.
Assuming he supplies an operational test for the two kinds of uniqueness; he does not.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 53-54 (Chapter 17, 'Individuality')
qa_items.question: A new writer takes over a long-running account and wants to refresh the tone. What does Hopkins require of him, on what grounds, and what exception exists?
qa_items.answer: He requires the writer to get into the spirit the advertiser has adopted before writing anything — to play a part as an actor plays it — and to never change the tone. Two grounds. Recognition: people know an advertiser by looks and mannerisms, not by name alone, so appearing different every meeting never builds confidence, and a change in characteristics would compel the advertising's best friends to get acquainted all over. Concealment: the appeals must not seem created, studied or artificial, but must seem to come from the heart, and the same heart always. The exception is stated in a subordinate clause and easily missed — a complete change is allowed where a wrong tack forces it. The constancy rule applies to a PROVED individuality, and his warrant for it is only that what won so many is "probably" the best way to win others.
qa_items.support: pp.53-54: "Before a man writes a new ad on that line, he gets into the spirit adopted by the advertiser. He plays a part as an actor plays it." "They must seem to come from the heart, and the same heart always, save where a wrong tack forces a complete change."
confounders: Stating the rule as absolute and missing the wrong-tack exception.
Justifying constancy by brand-recall arguments Hopkins does not make; his grounds are acquaintance and concealment of effort.
Missing the tension with his own account of the persona as constructed, coached and signed — which he presents as compatible with seeming to come from the heart.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 55 (Chapter 18, 'Negative Advertising')
qa_items.question: Hopkins claims a positive advertisement outpulls a negative one four to one. State the claim exactly as he makes it, including what he attaches to it.
qa_items.answer: He says: compare the results of two advertisements, one negative and one positive, one presenting the dark side and one the bright, one warning and the other inviting — "You will find that the positive ad outpulls the other four to one, IF YOU HAVE OUR EXPERIENCE." The conditional is his and it is routinely dropped in quotation. He reports no comparison at all: no product, no pair of advertisements, no returns. It is an outcome claimed on records he does not show, explicitly conditioned on the reader's records resembling his. Note also that the figure is attached only to the framing claim, not to his separate claims that attacking rivals is bad policy or that assuming compliance outperforms implying neglect.
qa_items.support: p.55: "Compare the results of two ads, one negative, one positive... You will find that the positive ad outpulls the other four to one, if you have our experience."
confounders: Quoting 'four to one' as a measured result — the standard citation of this passage.
Extending the figure to the whole chapter's doctrine rather than the one claim it is attached to.
Reading the prohibition on attacking rivals as evidenced by the four-to-one claim; it rests on policy and on 1923 medium acceptance rules.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 55-56 (Chapter 18, 'Negative Advertising')
qa_items.question: You are advertising a wrinkle treatment. On Hopkins's rule, what goes in the picture, what goes in the call to action, and what exception does he allow?
qa_items.answer: The picture shows the face as it will appear, not the wrinkles you propose to remove — his reason being that your customers know all about the wrinkles already; picture what others wish to be, not what they may be now, and envied people rather than the envious. The call to action assumes compliance: "Send now for this sample", not "Why do you neglect this offer?", because the second suggests that people are neglecting, and the reader should be invited to follow the crowd. Tell people what to do, not what to avoid. His one exception is historical and grudging: the "before and after taking" advertisements, which he calls follies of the past that never had a place save with the afflicted.
qa_items.support: p.55: "Don't show the wrinkles you propose to remove, but the face as it will appear. Your customers know all about the wrinkles." "Assume that people will do what you ask." p.56: "The 'Before and after taking' ads are follies of the past. They never had a place save with the afflicted."
confounders: Showing the problem to establish relevance — the standard before/after construction he rejects.
Missing the call-to-action half; the rule covers the instruction as well as the image.
Treating the afflicted exception as a general licence for problem-first advertising.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 57 (Chapter 19, 'Letter Writing')
qa_items.question: Describe the letter test Hopkins reports, including its two possible outcomes. How does its specification compare with the test campaign of chapter 15?
qa_items.answer: Before sending five million letters, the publisher puts a few thousand to test: he may try twenty-five letters, each with a thousand prospects, and learns what results will cost. Two outcomes are provided for, and the first is the notable one — the plan may be abandoned altogether because it appears unprofitable; only otherwise is the letter that pays best the one he uses. Its specification is TIGHTER than chapter 15's own procedure: it states arm count and cell size, which chapter 15 never does, and it can kill the programme as well as rank the candidates. What it still omits is randomisation, simultaneity and list comparability — and, like everything else in the span, any reported result: no cost per result, no winning margin, no letters.
qa_items.support: p.57: "Before the publisher sends out five million letters he puts a few thousands to test. He may try twenty-five letters, each with a thousand prospects. He learns what results will cost. Perhaps the plan is abandoned because it appears unprofitable."
confounders: Assuming chapter 15 is the book's most precise test description; this one is.
Missing the abandonment branch, which is what makes it a go/no-go design and not merely a ranking.
Reading twenty-five thousand pieces as a validated sample size rather than as one publisher's reported practice.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 58 (Chapter 19, 'Letter Writing')
qa_items.question: What does Hopkins say about fine stationery, and how far does he take the claim?
qa_items.answer: Further than "it does not help". His first claim is neutral: experience generally shows a two-cent letter gets no more attention than a one-cent letter and fine stationery no more than poor, because the whole appeal lies in the matter. His second is stronger — it has been FOUND that fine stationery and pamphlets LESSEN the effect, because they indicate an effort to sell on other lines than merit, which he says has the same effect in letters as in advertisements. So visible expenditure on the vehicle actively reduces response by making the effort to sell apparent. His evidence is "experience generally shows" and "it has been found": no test, no comparison, no return, with the harder of the two claims asserted in the passive voice. The artefacts are 1923 postage classes, stationery grades and mailed pamphlets.
qa_items.support: p.58: "a two-cent letter gets no more attention than a one-cent letter. Fine stationery no more than poor stationery. The whole appeal lies in the matter." "It has been found that fine stationery and pamphlets lessen the effect. They indicate an effort to sell on other lines than merit."
confounders: Stopping at the neutral claim and missing that he says it actively reduces response.
Reading the mechanism as perceived cheapness or trustworthiness; his mechanism is visible selling effort read as a substitute for merit.
Treating it as an evidenced production finding; it is asserted twice in the passive voice.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 58-59 (Chapter 19, 'Letter Writing')
qa_items.question: Someone sends for your sample after an advertisement about durability. Your follow-up letter is drafted around price. What is Hopkins's objection, and what does he add about timing?
qa_items.answer: His objection is that you are discarding the only information the inquiry gave you. A letter to an inquirer is like a salesman going to an interested prospect: you know what created that interest, so follow it up along THAT line and not on some different argument — complete the impression already created, and don't undertake another on a guess. On timing, he says people are naturally dilatory, they postpone, and a postponed action is too often forgotten, so something should be done to get immediate action: offer an inducement for it, or tell what delay may cost, and note how many successful selling letters place a limit on an offer expiring on a certain date purely to force a prompt decision. You can afford to pay for prompt action rather than lose by delay. He adds that the specific device rarely transfers between two lines even though the principles are universal.
qa_items.support: p.58: "You know what created that interest. Then follow it up along that line, not on some different argument. Complete the impression already created. Don't undertake another on a guess." "Note how many successful selling letters place a limit on an offer."
confounders: Broadening the follow-up to cover more benefits, which is the natural instinct and the error he names.
Reading the dated limit as artificial scarcity for its own sake; his stated purpose is overcoming delay.
Assuming a device that worked on one line can be reused on another — he says the reverse.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 60 (Chapter 20, 'A Name That Helps')
qa_items.question: Why does Hopkins argue about names in terms of space rather than in terms of memorability?
qa_items.answer: Because he treats the name as an item of purchased display. The name is usually prominently displayed, so to justify the space it occupies it should aid the advertising — and a name like Cream of Wheat, May Breath or Dutch Cleanser is almost a complete advertisement in itself, obtained in space that was going to be spent regardless. The failure he names is general: a vast amount of space is wasted displaying names and pictures which tell no selling story. It is the same argument he makes about pictures in chapter 9 — an element that occupies paid display must outperform what else that display could carry — applied to a different element, though he does not draw the parallel himself. He adds that the service of the product, not the name, is the important thing.
qa_items.support: p.60: "The name is usually prominently displayed. To justify the space it occupies, it should aid the advertising." "A vast amount of space is wasted in displaying names and pictures which tell no selling story."
confounders: Framing his argument as being about recall or distinctiveness, which is the modern default.
Missing that his examples are outcome-selected, and that he supplies successful non-descriptive names a paragraph later.
Reading 'the service of the product, not the name, is the important thing' as an argument for generic names.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 60-61 (Chapter 20, 'A Name That Helps')
qa_items.question: You must choose between a descriptive name, a meaningless coined name, and an ingredient name. Set out the trade-off as Hopkins does, including the patent complication.
qa_items.answer: Descriptive: protectable while still describing the product, so the display is valuable and the name sells in space spent anyway. Meaningless coined — Kodak, Karo, Mazda, Vaseline, Postum: also protectable, and long-continued advertising may give it a meaning, at which point it becomes very valuable, but the great majority never attain that status, so such names do not aid the advertising and it is very doubtful whether they justify display. Ingredient names — Syrup of Figs, Tar Soap, Palmolive Soap: may dominate a market if the price is reasonable, but they invite substitution and are naturally classified with other products having like ingredients, so the price must remain in that class. The patent complication is separate and severe: on a patented product the right to a name expires with the patent — Castoria, Aspirin, Shredded Wheat Biscuit became common property — which he says often makes a patent an undesirable protection. And where a product must be called by a common name, the best auxiliary is a man's name, better than a coined one because it shows some man is proud of his creation.
qa_items.support: pp.60-61: "Such names do not aid the advertising. It is very doubtful if they justify display." "They invite substitution... so the price must remain in that class." "the right to a name expires with the patent." "the best auxiliary name is a man's name."
confounders: Reading him as simply preferring descriptive names; he sets out a real trade-off with exclusivity.
Missing the price-class consequence of an ingredient name, which is the sharpest point in the chapter.
Treating the patent reasoning as legal fact; it is his 1923 understanding, recorded as his claim.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 62-63 (Chapter 21, 'Good Business')
qa_items.question: An advertiser of many years spends $700,000 a year and says he does not know whether his advertising is worth anything. What does Hopkins propose, what does the proposal measure, and what is his diagnosis of how the situation arose?
qa_items.answer: He proposes ending an advertisement with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes in that he read the advertisement through, predicting that the scarcity of replies will amaze the advertiser — he claims he could prove the advertising utterly unprofitable in one week. What it measures is READING, not selling, which is a narrower question than the one asked, and he does not distinguish them. His diagnosis is default attribution: advertising is taken as prima facie evidence that the man who pays believes in it, so he takes it like a secret tonic others have endorsed, and if the business thrives the tonic gets the credit while otherwise the failure is put down to fate. His contrast is the big store, where every line is charged to the proper department and every inch must justify its cost the next day. Note that he predicts the result in the same sentence as the proposal and reports no run of it.
qa_items.support: p.62: the $700,000 advertiser. The five-dollar proposal straddles the page break — "End an ad with an offer to pay" closes p.62 and "five dollars to anyone who writes you that he read the ad through. The scarcity of replies will amaze you." opens p.63. p.63: "So he takes it like some secret tonic which others have endorsed. If the business thrives, the tonic gets the credit."
confounders: Treating the five-dollar test as something he reports running; it is a proposal with a predicted result.
Assuming the instrument answers the profitability question; it measures readership only.
Missing the default-attribution diagnosis, which is the durable part and explains why the situation persists.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 33 and 35 (Chapter 10, 'Things Too Costly'; Chapter 11, 'Information')
qa_items.question: An inventor brings you a remedy for a condition he suffers from and is certain it is a great advertising possibility. Walk through what Hopkins would do before agreeing, and what would make him refuse.
qa_items.answer: First, find out how many readers have the condition, because he says plainly that he has no statistics on it — a canvass is the instrument, and chapter 11 lists the reachable percentage as one of the quantities that must be learned before space is bought, gathered by class because it may differ on farms and in cities. Then do the arithmetic: if the condition affects one in a hundred, the advertiser must cover a hundred useless readers to reach one, and his cost of results might run twenty times as high as for an article appealing to one in five — an excess Hopkins says would probably mean disaster, because the cost of advertising largely depends on the percentage of waste circulation. He would refuse on that arithmetic, not on the merit of the remedy, and he notes that the inventor's own certainty is exactly the input the procedure exists to override. He also warns that every new advertiser should seek wise advice and that no one with the interests of advertising at heart will advise a dubious venture.
qa_items.support: p.33: "We have no statistics on this subject... A canvass might show it to be one in a hundred... His cost of results might be twenty times as high as on another article which appeals to one in five." p.35: "We must learn the percentage of readers to whom our product appeals... The cost of advertising largely depends on the percentage of waste circulation."
confounders: Judging the project on the strength of the product or of the inventor's conviction.
Proposing a smaller test budget as a compromise, which chapter 10 calls the same folly on a smaller scale.
Treating the one-in-a-hundred figure as an established prevalence; Hopkins states he does not know it.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 38 (Chapter 12, 'Strategy')
qa_items.question: A maker wants to price a small remedy low to widen its market, reasoning that volume is where the profit is. On Hopkins's chapter 12 reasoning, when is that right and when is it wrong?
qa_items.answer: It is right in the volume regime — he does say the greatest profits are made on great volume at small profit, and that a price appealing only to, say, 10 per cent multiplies the cost of selling. But he places small remedies in a different regime. Where sale per customer is small, high price is unimportant and high PROFIT is essential: a buyer hardly cares what he pays for a corn remedy because he uses little, so the maker must have a large margin precisely because consumption is small. Widening the market at a low margin does not help when each customer buys once or twice — which is the same variable, consumption per customer, that governs chapter 10's feasibility test. So the reasoning is wrong here, and Hopkins would want to know which regime the line is in first. He never states a test for placing a new product in a regime, which is the weakness of the framework.
qa_items.support: p.38: "the greatest profits are made on great volume at small profit... A price which appeals only to—say 10 per cent—multiplies the cost of selling. But on other lines high price is unimportant. High profit is essential... One hardly cares what he pays for a corn remedy because he uses little."
confounders: Applying the volume rule universally, which is how Hopkins is usually summarised on price.
Confusing the low-consumption regime with the judged-by-price regime, where a higher price is an inducement for a different reason.
Reading this as his chapter 6 claim that people judge value by stated price; that is a copy effect, this is a margin decision.

qa_items.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 28-29 (Chapter 9, 'Art in Advertising')
qa_items.question: A layout devotes half a page to a lifestyle photograph of people enjoying the product. Apply Hopkins's chapter 9 test, and say what evidence he would accept as settling it.
qa_items.answer: The test is not whether the photograph is good but whether it forms a better selling argument than that same half-page set in type — because the picture is bought with space, and its cost is the argument the space would otherwise have carried. A lifestyle photograph can pass, but only on a specific condition: it must depict the condition the buyer covets, so that it implies the product is a route to it, as with men others envy in surroundings others covet. A photograph that merely interests, decorates or attracts fails, since he holds that advertisements are not written to interest, please or amuse. As for what would settle it, he is explicit that generalities cannot well be applied to art, that each line must be studied by itself, and that the only way to know is by compared results — with the further instruction that where no principles exist for a line, the advertiser should work out his own by tests.
qa_items.support: p.28: "Use them only when they form a better selling argument than the same amount of space set in type." "Ads are not written to interest, please or amuse." p.29: "Generalities cannot well be applied to art... Each line must be studied by itself." "The only way to know, as is with most other questions, is by compared results."
confounders: Judging the photograph on craft quality, which he calls a question of small moment.
Assuming he would reject a lifestyle image outright; his apparel and beauty cases are exactly that.
Offering engagement or attention evidence; his stated criterion is compared selling results.

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Introduction: 'Two Kinds of Error', the four shooting teams and the back of the target (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Noise and bias are both components of error in this book's scheme. State what distinguishes them, and then state the asymmetry in what it takes to MEASURE each.
qa_items.answer: Bias is systematic deviation — errors mostly in one direction, so the deviation is predictable and invites a causal explanation. Noise is scatter: judgements that should have been identical are spread out, with no direction and usually no available explanation. The measurement asymmetry follows from that. Measuring bias requires knowing the true value, because bias is defined as the average distance from it. Measuring noise requires only several judgements of the same case by people aiming at the same thing; the spread IS the measurement. The book's image is looking at the back of the target: the bull's-eye is invisible, so you cannot tell which team is closer to it, but you can see at a glance which team is scattered. This is why noise is tractable in the many professional domains where the right answer is unknown, unknowable, or arrives too late to matter.
qa_items.support: The book's own framing device, introduced as an illustrative metaphor rather than a study. The condition it names for the measurement to be licensed is that all the judges were aiming at the same target.
confounders: reading 'bias' as social discrimination — the book uses it in the statistical sense of average error and warns separately against that reading
assuming you need to know the right answer before you can say anything about a set of judgements
treating noise as a small residual once bias is removed; the book's whole argument is that it is frequently the larger term

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'A Noisy System', section 'A Lottery That Creates Noise'; Ch. 6 'The Analysis of Noise', 'Some Judges Are Severe: Level Noise'; Ch. 7 'Occasion Noise', 'The Second Lottery'
qa_items.question: Give the book's three components of system noise in its own terms, say what each one is a property of, and state which of the three the book reports as smallest.
qa_items.answer: System noise is unwanted variability in judgements that should ideally be identical. It decomposes into level noise and pattern noise, and pattern noise decomposes again into stable pattern noise and occasion noise. Level noise is variability in the average level of different judges' judgements — some are across-the-board more severe or more generous, which the book says behaves like a personality trait and has nothing to do with the case in front of them. Pattern noise is variability in how a given judge responds to particular cases over and above their general severity; the technical name is the judge-by-case interaction. Occasion noise is variability in the same person's judgements of the same case on different occasions. The book states that in every case it reviewed where the share could be measured, occasion noise was the SMALLEST contributor — you are less consistent with yourself than you think, but still more similar to yourself last week than to a colleague today.
qa_items.support: The taxonomy is the book's own and is stated as three nested sum-of-squares equations. The claim that occasion noise is smallest is explicitly presented as a review of a limited set of cases, not a law.
confounders: treating occasion noise as a sibling of pattern noise rather than as its transient component
assuming occasion noise is the biggest problem because it is the most vivid — mood, weather, hunger
confusing level noise with bias: level noise is variability BETWEEN judges' averages, bias is the distance of the average from truth

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'A Noisy System', section 'Noise Audits Reveal System Noise'; procedure in Appendix A 'How to Conduct a Noise Audit'
qa_items.question: What, exactly, is a noise audit? Name the design requirements the book puts on it, and say what an audit does and does not tell you.
qa_items.answer: It is an experiment in which several interchangeable professionals independently judge the same cases, real or constructed, without being told that the variability of their answers is what is being studied. The spread of the answers is the measurement. The design requirements the book names: the judges must be genuinely interchangeable — the test is that if one were unavailable another would be assigned and expected to reach a similar judgement; each judge should handle several cases, because the level-versus-pattern split is only recoverable from a multi-case design; the task should be completable from written information and answerable numerically; participants work at the same time, physically separated, and do not communicate. What it tells you is how much your people disagree, and in what proportions. What it does NOT tell you is who is right. The book is explicit that no one in its insurance audit could say how much error there was, because no one knew the right premium for any case.
qa_items.support: The book's own audit at an insurance company, plus the procedural guide in Appendix A. The audit is the authors' own study; the numbers it produced are from one company.
confounders: assuming an audit measures accuracy — it measures disagreement, and the book keeps these strictly apart
thinking one case per judge is enough; that design cannot separate level noise from pattern noise
confusing an audit with test-retest reliability, which measures one person against themselves

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Matters of Judgment', opening argument on bounded disagreement
qa_items.question: The book says a "matter of judgment" is defined by an expectation of bounded disagreement. What lies on either side of that space, and what does the book say about how the bound is set?
qa_items.answer: On one side are matters of fact or computation, where reasonable people are expected to agree perfectly and disagreement is not admissible. On the other are matters of taste or opinion, where unresolved disagreement is entirely acceptable and the concept of noise does not apply. Judgement occupies the space between: people may differ, but not by much, and they act as though there were an invisible bull's-eye whether or not one exists. On the bound itself the book gives no procedure — it says explicitly that how much disagreement is acceptable "is itself a judgment call" and depends on the difficulty of the problem. What it offers instead is a boundary marker at the extremes: judges who differ widely on an ordinary fraud sentence will still concur that a one-dollar fine and a life sentence are both unreasonable, and wine judges who disagree about medals are often unanimous in contempt for the rejects. Agreement on absurdity marks the edges without fixing any point inside.
qa_items.support: The book's own conceptual framing. The wine and sentencing illustrations are used to locate the boundary, not to measure it.
confounders: reading 'bounded disagreement' as a numeric tolerance the book supplies — it does not
assuming that because reasonable people may differ, any amount of difference is acceptable
treating the fact that colleagues agree an outlier is absurd as evidence that they agree on ordinary cases — the book identifies this as a source of the illusion of agreement

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Matters of Judgment', section 'What Judgment Aims to Achieve: The Internal Signal'; Ch. 11 'Objective Ignorance', opening section
qa_items.question: Define the internal signal of judgment completion, and explain why the book treats it as misleading rather than merely uninformative.
qa_items.answer: It is the feeling that a judgement fits the evidence coherently, which is what tells a judge the judgement is finished. The book stresses that it is self-administered and unrelated to any outside information — which is why making a judgement about a fictitious person feels exactly like making one about a real one, and why an unverifiable judgement still feels complete. It is misleading, not merely uninformative, because of how it is construed: the emotional experience "the evidence feels right" masquerades as rational confidence in validity, "I know, even if I don't know why." The book adds that the coherence producing the signal is often manufactured, "bolstered by hiding or ignoring pieces of evidence that don't fit", so confidence needs only a coherent story and no attractive alternative in mind — both achievable by suppression rather than by being right.
qa_items.support: The internal signal is the authors' proposed construct, offered as an interpretation of the managerial-intuition literature. It is not a measured quantity, and the definition of intuition it builds on is a third party's review.
confounders: treating confidence as weak evidence of accuracy rather than as evidence of nothing about accuracy
assuming the book wants intuition eliminated — its position is that intuition should be delayed, not banned
reading the signal as a property of experts only; the book presents it as universal

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 18 'Better Judges for Better Judgments', section 'Experts and Respect-Experts'
qa_items.question: What is a respect-expert in this book's terms, and what warning does the book attach to the category?
qa_items.answer: A respect-expert is someone whose expertise cannot be checked against outcomes, so the confidence placed in them rests entirely on the regard of their peers. The book insists the term is not meant to be disrespectful — many professors, scholars and consultants are in this position, and it is a fact of life in domains like underwriting, sentencing, wine tasting and essay grading rather than a criticism. The warning is that the traits producing respect are not the traits producing accuracy. Respect-experts command trust through shared professional doctrine, experience, and the ability to construct a coherent story with confidence — and the book notes that confident people carry extra weight in a group whether or not the confidence is warranted. It also flags the trap: high general ability improves your ability to convince others as well as your judgement, so in the absence of reality feedback it manufactures respect-experts. "Medieval astrologers must have been among the highest-GMA people of their time."
qa_items.support: The book's own coinage and argument. The supporting material on general mental ability and cognitive style is third-party research the book reports.
confounders: reading 'respect-expert' as a slur for a fake expert — the book explicitly rejects that reading
assuming shared professional training produces agreement on cases; the book says doctrine eliminates some possibilities without specifying a positive answer, so trained professionals drift apart
treating verifiability as a property of the person rather than of the domain

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'A Noisy System', section 'The Illusion of Agreement'
qa_items.question: Colleagues who disagree substantially can work together for years without noticing. Give the book's account of why — both the psychological half and the organisational half.
qa_items.answer: Psychologically, the book invokes naive realism: we hold one interpretation of a situation at a time, experience it as simply true, and invest little effort in generating plausible alternatives — from which it is one small step to assuming others see it as we do. Because we never imagine the alternative reading, we never expect the disagreement. Organisationally, three things reinforce the illusion. Shared doctrine and vocabulary create constant apparent agreement while never specifying a positive answer to any particular case, so drift between colleagues is invisible. Confidence is built by agreeing with your own past self, not by ever checking agreement with others — the book quotes an underwriter who discussed three-quarters of cases with a supervisor as a novice and none as a veteran, growing confident by exercising judgement rather than testing it. And post-mortems examine only judgements far outside the norm, which everyone finds easy to condemn; that easy consensus about bad judgements can even reinforce the illusion, because the real lesson — that people disagree about ordinary, broadly acceptable cases — never surfaces.
qa_items.support: The book's own diagnosis, following its own insurance audit and its polling of executives whose median expected difference was 10% against a measured 55%. Naive realism is third-party work it invokes; the admissions-office anecdote was related to the authors by a colleague.
confounders: attributing the invisibility to bad faith or conflict avoidance alone — the book gives conflict avoidance as one contributing mechanism among several
assuming that professionals who share training and rules therefore reach similar conclusions
thinking experience corrects the illusion; the book argues experience deepens it

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'A Noisy System', section 'Unwanted Variability Versus Wanted Diversity'; closing paragraphs
qa_items.question: "Random errors cancel out, so noise doesn't matter." Reconstruct the book's answer, and be precise about the condition under which cancellation actually would occur.
qa_items.answer: Cancellation requires averaging multiple judgements OF THE SAME CASE. That is exactly what an operating system does not do. A noisy system makes single judgements of different cases: one underwriter prices one policy, one adjuster handles one claim, one judge sentences one defendant. So one overpriced contract and one underpriced contract are not an average that comes out right — they are two costly errors, one losing business and the other losing money. The book's sentence is "In noisy systems, errors do not cancel out. They add up." It concedes the cancellation property itself is real and says it is precisely what noise-reduction strategies exploit: averaging several independent judgements of the same case does reduce noise, which is why aggregation is one of its recommended remedies. The error in the objection is applying a property of repeated measurement to a process that never repeats a measurement.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument, illustrated with its insurance material and with sentencing. It grants the underlying statistical property and disputes only its applicability to operating systems.
confounders: conceding the point for evaluative judgements because there is no true value — the book's fairness argument applies there too: two felons who both deserve five years getting three and seven is not justice on average
confusing the wisdom of crowds, which averages many judgements of one case, with a system, which makes one judgement of many cases
assuming the objection is simply wrong; the book's position is that the property is real but misapplied

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Patterns', sections 'Problems: Hard and Easy' and 'The Personality Analogy'
qa_items.question: Why, on this book's account, do some judgement problems produce far more disagreement than others? Give the mechanism, not just the observation.
qa_items.answer: The driver is whether the cues in the case point the same way. Where they cohere — as in the description of Bill, where every detail supports the same stereotype — fast intuitive thinking makes sense of the evidence easily and most people converge on the same answer. Where the cues conflict, there is more than one defensible way to construct a coherent story, so different people select different pieces of evidence as the core of their narrative and reach different conclusions, each of which feels coherent to its owner. The book states the rule bluntly: "if there is more than one way to see anything, people will vary in how they see it." It locates the variability at three points in the judgement process — selective attention and recall over the available cues, informal (not formal) integration of them into an impression, and conversion of that impression into a value on a scale. Cue conflict pulls the first two apart. This is where pattern noise comes from, and it is why the book says complex problems are noisier than simple ones.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument, demonstrated with two cases it wrote itself — the Gambardi CEO problem, where estimates from 115 MBA students ranged from 10 to 95, and the extended Julie description. Both were designed to be difficult; they illustrate rather than test the claim.
confounders: attributing the difference to how much information is available rather than to whether it coheres
assuming coherent cases produce accurate judgements — the Bill case produces agreement AND a shared logical error
treating this as a claim about task difficulty in general; the book's variable is specifically cue conflict

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 13 'Heuristics, Biases, and Noise', section 'Psychological Biases Cause Noise'
qa_items.question: The book argues that a psychological bias does not necessarily produce a statistical bias. Explain the mechanism, and give the two conditions under which the same bias produces noise instead.
qa_items.answer: A psychological bias is a mechanism; whether it shows up as bias or as noise in a set of judgements depends on how uniformly it operates. If everyone is pulled the same way by the same amount, the errors are shared and the result is statistical bias — the book's example is Bill the jazz-playing accountant, where nearly everyone makes the same substitution and the same logical error, producing no noise at all. The two conditions that convert the same mechanism into noise are: individual differences in the bias, and context-dependence in its trigger. Half of hiring managers biased against women and half in their favour produce no overall bias and a great many wrong hires. "Is there climate change?" answered by "do I trust the people who say so?" gives a different answer per person depending on their social circle. And where the order in which evidence arrives varies haphazardly from case to case, excessive coherence converts that arbitrary order into system noise.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument. Its striking supporting instance — that training designed to reduce forecasters' biases in fact improved their scores mainly by reducing noise — comes from the BIN analysis by Satopää, Tetlock, Mellers and Salikhov, not from the authors.
confounders: assuming 'bias' in the psychological sense implies a directional error in the aggregate
treating noise and bias as competing explanations rather than as two possible expressions of one mechanism
concluding that anti-bias training is pointless — the book reports it worked, just not through the channel intended

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How Groups Amplify Noise', section 'Cascades'
qa_items.question: Walk through the book's ten-person hiring meeting and explain how a cascade makes noise ACROSS similar groups, not merely error within one.
qa_items.answer: Arthur speaks first and favours Thomas. Barbara is unsure, trusts Arthur, and agrees. Charles privately thinks Julie is the better candidate but goes along — not out of cowardice, the book is careful to say, but because he is a respectful listener who assumes Arthur and Barbara have grounds. David, lacking strong reason to think the first three are wrong, follows too. By the time Erica, Frank and George speak, the consensus is self-sustaining, and the private information Charles and David held was never shared. The noise point is counterfactual: had Barbara spoken first and favoured Sam, or had Arthur felt slightly differently and preferred Julie, the group would plausibly have landed there instead — not because the candidate was better but because that is how the cascade would have run. So very similar groups reach very different conclusions, which is variability, not just error. The book adds that cascading is often individually rational, which is what makes it hard to stop, and that the same pattern arises from social pressure alone with no learning at all.
qa_items.support: The hiring example is the book's own illustration, which it calls highly artificial. The supporting measurements are all third-party: Salganik and colleagues' parallel music-download worlds, Macy and colleagues on political positions, and Muchnik and colleagues, where a single artificial early up-vote raised a comment's mean rating by 25% five months later.
confounders: reading cascade participants as cowards or conformists — the book's point is that deference can be reasonable
treating a cascade as producing a wrong answer; its signature is that the answer is arbitrary, which is a different complaint
assuming a large group is safer than a small one; the book says the effect can be more dramatic in small ones

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How Groups Amplify Noise', section 'Group Polarization'
qa_items.question: The book compares "statistical juries" with deliberating juries. Describe the comparison, what it found, and the two mechanisms offered for the result.
qa_items.answer: In the authors' own experiments, 899 participants first made independent judgements of case vignettes on scales of outrage, punitive intent and dollars. Millions of virtual six-person "statistical juries" were then assembled by computer, with the median of the six independent judgements taken as the verdict. These were markedly less noisy — the book calls that "a mechanical effect of statistical aggregation". A follow-up with more than three thousand jury-eligible citizens forming more than five hundred real six-person juries deliberating on the same cases found the deliberating juries were far NOISIER than the statistical ones. They were also more extreme in whichever direction their median member already leaned, and 27% chose an award as high as or higher than their most severe member. The two mechanisms: informational — a group leaning one way hears mostly arguments for that way — and reputational — members who care about standing shift toward the dominant tendency. The book adds that group dynamics amplify whatever level, pattern and occasion noise the individuals brought in, notably through whoever speaks first.
qa_items.support: The authors' own studies, using mock jurors and constructed product-liability vignettes rather than real trials. The finding is about noise and about polarisation; because punitive damages have no true value, no claim is made that deliberating juries were less accurate.
confounders: concluding that discussion is always harmful — the book reports the opposite result for the Good Judgment Project's teaming intervention and leaves the two standing
reading the result as being about jury competence rather than about what deliberation does to variability
assuming polarisation means groups become more severe; the book found shifts toward greater leniency too, in the direction the median member already leaned

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Judgments and Models', section 'Goldberg: The Model of You Beats You'
qa_items.question: A simple linear model of your own past judgements outperforms you at predicting outcomes. A model can only subtract information, never add it. Reconcile these two facts using the book's argument.
qa_items.answer: The model subtracts exactly two things, and one of them is worth more than the other. It drops the complex, case-specific rules you apply — the intuition that a perfect 10 on communication deserves a bigger boost than the gap between 7 and 6, or that a well-rounded candidate beats a spiky one with the same average. And it drops your pattern noise and occasion noise: the arbitrary reactions to particular cases and the influence of your momentary state, which are not correlated with anything and behave as random. Losing the subtlety costs accuracy only to the extent the subtlety is valid; losing the noise always improves it. The book's finding is that the second gain reliably exceeds the first: "You may believe that you are subtler, more insightful, and more nuanced than the linear caricature of your thinking. But in fact, you are mostly noisier." It adds why valid subtlety pays so little: complex rules apply only under rarely-observed conditions, and measurement error at both ends drowns their advantage before it can show up.
qa_items.support: Goldberg's model-of-the-judge research and its replications, all third-party. One early replication found the model beat the participant for every one of ninety-eight participants predicting student GPAs. The book reports the average correlation between a model of a judge and that judge's actual judgements as about .80.
confounders: concluding that human subtlety is always worthless — the book says some subtleties are valid and simply do not pay enough
assuming this shows models are highly accurate; the book insists elsewhere that models are consistently better than people but not much better
reading it as an argument to replace judges, which the book explicitly declines to make

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 14 'The Matching Operation', section 'Noise in Matching: Limitations of Absolute Judgment'
qa_items.question: Explain why the book expects a twenty-point rating scale to be noisier than a five-point one, and what it recommends instead of simply reducing the number of points.
qa_items.answer: The constraint is on absolute judgement. People can reliably assign items to roughly seven categories on an intensity scale — the book cites the classic "magical number seven, plus or minus two" — and beyond that they start making errors, such as putting A in a higher category than B when a head-to-head comparison would rank B higher. Strikingly, the limit barely moves when the range of the stimuli widens. Any scale finer than that resolution therefore manufactures disagreement that has nothing to do with the thing being judged. The book's recommendation is not merely a coarser scale but a change of operation: comparison is not subject to the same limit, so people can rank items they cannot reliably label. The recipe is to sort into about five categories first, then rank within each — "you probably know whether you prefer Joe's Pizza to Fred's Burgers … even if you assigned them to the same category." It concedes the cost: comparative procedures are more effortful and slower.
qa_items.support: The magical-number-seven result is a 1956 third-party classic about lines, tones and brightness. Its extension to professional rating tasks is the authors' argument rather than a demonstration on professional work.
confounders: assuming the fix is a coarser absolute scale; the book's fix is to change from labelling to comparing
believing the limit widens with the range of the material, which the book says it does not
reading this as endorsing forced ranking — the book rejects the forcing while endorsing the ranking

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 'Scales', sections 'Dollars and Anchors' and 'An Unfortunate Conclusion'
qa_items.question: In the punitive-damages study, dollar awards were 94% noise. Replacing each juror's awards with their rank cut that to 49%. Explain what that transformation reveals and why the finding is a problem for real courtrooms specifically.
qa_items.answer: It reveals that the jurors agreed about the relative severity of the cases all along and disagreed only about the absolute numbers. The dollar scale is a ratio scale — meaningful zero, unbounded top — and Stevens's finding is that such a scale is tied down by a single anchor, with both the judgements and their standard deviation scaling proportionally with whatever anchor is supplied. Given no anchor, each juror invents one on the first case and then judges everything else consistently against it. So the absolute values are arbitrary while the ordering is not; converting to ranks strips out all the judge-level differences mechanically, because the 1-to-10 distribution of ranks is the same for everyone. The problem for real courtrooms is that the remedy is unavailable there. Jurors in the study judged ten cases, which is what made ranking possible. A real jury sees one case, and American law explicitly prohibits telling them the size of awards in other cases. The book calls the assumption behind that rule "psychological nonsense — it assumes an ability that humans do not have."
qa_items.support: The authors' own study (Kahneman, Schkade and Sunstein), 899 mock jurors on constructed vignettes. The percentages rest on an assumption the book flags as possibly wrong: that the average of individual judgements is the unbiased just value and every deviation from it is error. Stevens's ratio-scale work is third-party.
confounders: concluding that jurors were incompetent — the study shows their punitive intentions were largely shared and the scale hid them
assuming the fix is better instructions to jurors rather than an anchor case
generalising the 94% figure to professional judgement; the book calls punitive damages an extreme case and says professional judgements are rarely expressed on scales this ambiguous

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 20 'Sequencing Information in Forensic Science', sections 'The Forensic Confirmation Bias' and 'Sequencing Information'
qa_items.question: The book reports that biasing context changed not only fingerprint examiners' conclusions but what they saw. Explain the finding and why it matters for the design of any remedy.
qa_items.answer: In work by Dror and colleagues, examiners shown a latent print alongside a target exemplar recorded significantly fewer details — minutiae — than examiners shown the latent print alone. A later independent study confirmed it and added that how this happens "is not obvious". So context does not merely tilt the interpretation of a fixed perception; it changes the perception. That matters for remedy design because it rules out the intuitive fix. If bias operated only on interpretation, you could ask an expert to set the context aside and judge the evidence on its merits. If it operates on what gets perceived in the first place, the only reliable intervention is at the input: withhold the biasing information until the judgement that must not depend on it has been recorded. That is why the book's remedy is sequencing — reveal information gradually, document the judgement at each step, and record any later change of mind and its reasons — rather than instruction or awareness training.
qa_items.support: All third-party: Itiel Dror and colleagues, with independent replication. The book reports the effects as modest in absolute terms — four of twenty-four decisions changed in one study, about one decision in ten in an FBI re-test of seventy-two examiners — with most changes to or from "inconclusive" and none producing false identifications.
confounders: assuming awareness of the risk is protective; the book reports 71% of forensic scientists surveyed thought bias was a concern for their field and only 26% thought it affected their own judgements
reading the finding as being about incompetence rather than about an ordinary cognitive process
treating fingerprinting as a special case; the book's point is that if the most objective-seeming forensic discipline is susceptible, others are too

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'The Valley of the Normal', sections 'Understanding in the Valley of the Normal' and 'Inside and Outside'; Ch. 17 'The Sources of Noise', 'Noise Is Statistical'
qa_items.question: Why does the book say noise is invisible while bias is easy to see? Give the cognitive mechanism, not the sociology.
qa_items.answer: Because our default mode of understanding is causal and noise is inherently statistical. Most events fall in what the book calls the valley of the normal — neither actively expected nor especially surprising. When one occurs, memory is searched for a candidate cause, and the search almost always succeeds because causes can be drawn from an unlimited reservoir of facts and beliefs; the same news flow explains a market rise and a market fall. Because the explanation arrives only after the outcome is known, the outcome feels like it could have been anticipated, and the story leaves no room for the possibility that it could easily have gone otherwise. Applied to judgement errors, that habit finds a bias every time — motive, incompetence, overconfidence — and never finds noise, because noise cannot appear in a single case at all. It becomes visible only when an ensemble is examined statistically, and statistical thinking is effortful and must be learned. The book's line: "Causally, noise is nowhere; statistically, it is everywhere."
qa_items.support: The book's own argument. Its supporting evidence about the ceiling on prediction — the Fragile Families common-task challenge, where 160 teams predicted eviction at a correlation of .22 — is third-party work it reports.
confounders: attributing the invisibility to organisations preferring not to look; the book gives that as a separate, additional reason
assuming causal thinking is simply a defect — the book says it avoids unnecessary effort while retaining vigilance for genuinely abnormal events
confusing this with hindsight bias alone; the book's claim is broader, about how understanding itself works

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Matters of Judgment', sections 'Evaluative Judgments' and "What's Wrong with Noise"
qa_items.question: Noise is a problem in both predictive and evaluative judgements, but for different reasons. Give both reasons, and say what follows for a system whose judgements are largely evaluative.
qa_items.answer: In predictive judgement, disagreement is evidence of error: the judgements aim at a true value, so two different answers cannot both be right. In evaluative judgement there is no true value to be wrong about, and the complaint is different — fairness and credibility. People affected by an evaluation expect it to reflect the values of the system, not of whichever individual was assigned; when identical cases get different outcomes, the assignment has become a lottery. The book's phrase is "System noise is inconsistency, and inconsistency damages the credibility of the system," and its example is deliberately mundane: one customer with a defective laptop reimbursed and another given an apology. What follows for a largely evaluative system is that the book's quantitative apparatus does not apply — it says explicitly that the error equation does not cover evaluative judgements, error costs there are rarely symmetric, and there is no reason to think they are proportional to the square of the deviation. The fairness and consistency argument survives; the arithmetic does not.
qa_items.support: The book's own distinction and its own stated boundary on the error equation. It concedes the boundary is fuzzy and that practitioners feel, act and justify themselves identically on both sides.
confounders: assuming noise matters less where there is no true value; the book argues the fairness complaint is if anything sharper there
importing the mean-squared-error reasoning into evaluative settings, which the book rules out by name
treating a decision as purely one or the other; the book says most consequential decisions contain both, with predictive judgements as inputs and evaluative ones resolving the trade-offs

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 19 'Debiasing and Decision Hygiene', sections 'A Limitation of Debiasing' and 'Noise Reduction: Decision Hygiene'
qa_items.question: Compare debiasing with decision hygiene as the book presents them. What does each assume, and what situation makes debiasing the wrong tool?
qa_items.answer: Debiasing — whether ex post correction, nudging, or training — targets a specific bias which it assumes is present and directional. It works where the general direction of error is known and shows up as a clear statistical bias; the planning fallacy is the book's example of a finding robust enough to warrant it. Decision hygiene assumes nothing about which error is present: like handwashing, it adopts techniques that prevent an unspecified range of errors without your ever knowing which one you avoided. Debiasing is the wrong tool when the direction of error is not known in advance — which is exactly the noise case, where the effect of psychological biases varies unpredictably between judges. The book's worked illustration is a project team you assume is overconfident: the leader may have been burned before and be over-conservative; the team may have anchored on an analogous project; or, anticipating your buffer, it may have made its estimate more bullish to pre-empt you. In any situation of some complexity, multiple biases may be conspiring or offsetting with unpredictable net effect. Hygiene's cost is that its victory is invisible: you never learn which error it prevented.
qa_items.support: The book's own framework. It also proposes a middle option it says has not been systematically explored — a designated decision observer detecting biases in real time with a checklist — and reports only encouraging results from informal, small-scale efforts.
confounders: assuming decision hygiene is a form of debiasing; the book keeps them distinct by what they assume
reading the decision observer as an established technique — the book explicitly says it is not aware of any systematic exploration of it
believing hygiene is superior in general; the book says debiasing is useful where the error direction genuinely is known

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 23 'Defining the Scale in Performance Ratings', sections 'In Praise of Relative Judgments' and 'Rank but Do Not Force'
qa_items.question: The book endorses ranking and rejects forced ranking. Set out both halves of that position precisely.
qa_items.answer: The endorsement: rankings are less noisy than ratings, and they attack both components. You are less likely to be inconsistent comparing two people than grading each separately, which reduces pattern noise; and rankings eliminate level noise mechanically, because a lenient ranker and a tough ranker use the same ranks even though their average ratings would differ. The rejection is of the forcing, not the ranking — "the fatal flaw of forced ranking is not the 'ranking,' but the 'forced.'" Two specific objections. First, confusing relative with absolute performance: it is impossible for 98% of people to be in the top 20%, but it is perfectly possible for all of them to meet expectations defined in advance in absolute terms, and the book notes you would not sneer at NASA if every astronaut on a successful mission fully met expectations. Second, a mandated distribution assumes the population distribution reproduces in each small group, which it does not — pick ten people from several thousand and the chance that exactly two fall in the top 20% is about 30%. Forcing a differentiated distribution on an undifferentiated reality increases error rather than reducing it.
