qa_items.support: The book's own analysis, drawing on performance-appraisal research it reports. The related finding that relative judgements are less noisy than absolute ones is demonstrated in the authors' own punitive-damages study.
confounders: reading the critique of forced ranking as a critique of ranking, which is the common objection the book explicitly sets aside
assuming relative scales are always right; the book says they suit an organisation only if it actually cares about relative performance, as with a fixed promotion quota
believing rating inflation proves standards are too low — the book allows that most employees may genuinely meet high expectations

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 28 'Rules or Standards?', sections 'A Framework' and 'The Return of the Repressed'
qa_items.question: On what two factors does the book's choice between rules and standards turn, and what failure mode does it warn about when an institution shifts to firm rules?
qa_items.answer: The two factors are the costs of decisions and the costs of errors. Standards make every decision expensive, because whoever applies them must do the work of giving open-ended terms content — deciding what counts as "unreasonably fast" or "feasible". Rules make each decision cheap but make writing the rule expensive, sometimes prohibitively; that is why legal systems and companies resort to words like reasonable and prudent in the first place. On the error side there is no general winner: a perfect rule produces no errors but rules are rarely perfect, while a standard applied by trustworthy agents practising decision hygiene may produce few. The book collapses this into a question about trust: "Principals need to impose rules when they have reason to distrust their agents." The failure mode is that rules producing terrible results in particular cases get quietly ignored — jury nullification, prosecutors declining to bring a third felony charge, employees disregarding rules that seem stupid. Discretion is driven underground, "there will be noise, but no one will hear it." Hence the instruction to monitor rules and treat reappearing noise as a clue that they need revising.
qa_items.support: The book's own framework, illustrated with legal and corporate examples including a social media company's public standards against its non-public implementation rules. Analytical, not empirical.
confounders: assuming rules always reduce noise; the book notes fact-finding under a rule is itself judgement and can be noisy
treating the choice as binary — the book says they are a continuum and can be mixed, a rule constraining the pool and a standard choosing within it
overlooking the reason for standards that has nothing to do with quality: where a group is divided or lacks information, a standard may be the only thing agreeable at all

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 17 'The Sources of Noise', section 'Sizing the Components'
qa_items.question: Why does the book say that findings about professional variability drawn from ordinary operating records understate the problem "by at least a factor of two"?
qa_items.answer: Because operating records can only show level noise. Where cases are assigned to professionals more or less at random, the differing averages — patent examiners with different propensities to grant, case officers with different propensities to place children in foster care, judges with different grant rates — become visible across enough cases without any special study. Pattern noise cannot appear this way at all, because it is an interaction between a judge and a case, and recovering it requires several judges to have judged the SAME case, which normal operations never arrange. Since the book's assembled evidence suggests pattern noise is generally the larger component, the component an organisation can see is the smaller one, and any finding based on operating data alone understates the total. The book is careful to hedge the sizing claim itself: it calls the conclusion tentative, says it required "some triangulation", warns against overgeneralising from a limited selection of examples, and names an exception — asylum-judge variability, which it expects is due more to level noise.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument. The mix it rests on is split by origin: the 20%-level/80%-pattern split at the insurance company and the punitive-damages pattern shares are the authors' own studies; the 208-judge sentencing analysis, the bail-judge analysis and the patent and child-protection findings are third parties'.
confounders: assuming a random-assignment analysis of operating data is a substitute for an audit
importing the factor of two as a general constant rather than as a consequence of a hedged sizing claim
forgetting the precondition: without approximately random assignment, differences in average outcome may reflect the caseload rather than the person

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'Objective Ignorance', sections 'Poor Judges and Barely Better Models' and 'The Denial of Ignorance'
qa_items.question: Distinguish objective ignorance from noise, and explain why the book insists that a small improvement in predictive accuracy is nevertheless worth having.
qa_items.answer: Objective ignorance is a property of the TASK — intractable uncertainty about what cannot be known, plus imperfect information about what could be known but is not. It sets a ceiling on achievable accuracy that no improvement in judges can lift. Noise is a property of a SET OF JUDGEMENTS and is reducible below that ceiling. Confusing them produces the executive's fatalism the book records: if human judges achieve a correlation of .28 with performance and mechanical prediction achieves .44, both are far from perfect, so why bother? The book's answer is that the same executives routinely make significant changes to capture smaller gains, and that "none of them would buy a lottery ticket that had a 59% chance of winning if they could buy, for the same price, one with a 65% chance." It then names why the price is not in fact the same: intuitive judgement comes with the internal signal, an emotional reward that a mechanical process offering no claim of high validity cannot match. So the resistance is not about the arithmetic. It is about giving up the feeling of knowing.
qa_items.support: The ceiling evidence is entirely third-party — Tetlock's expert political judgement work, the Fragile Families challenge, the personnel-selection reviews, the Mullainathan and Obermeyer heart-attack model. The argument about why the improvement is refused is the authors'.
confounders: treating a low ceiling as a licence to tolerate noise; the ceiling caps accuracy, not agreement
assuming objective ignorance is the same as the judge being poorly informed — the book includes what cannot be known by anyone
reading the resistance to formal methods as irrational; the book's account is that the internal signal is a genuine reward being given up

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 21 'Selection and Aggregation in Forecasting', section 'Where Selection and Aggregation Work'
qa_items.question: The book says the average of a noisy group can be more accurate than the average of a unanimous one. Explain the reasoning, and what it implies about how to assemble a panel.
qa_items.answer: Because the validity of pooled judgements rises faster when the individual judgements are uncorrelated with each other than when they are redundant. The book draws the analogy with assembling a battery of predictive tests using multiple regression: the first test chosen is the most valid, but the second is not necessarily the next most valid — it is the one that adds the most predictive power by being valid AND non-redundant. A personality test correlating .30 with performance but uncorrelated with aptitude may beat a second aptitude test correlating .45. Applied to a panel: pick the best judge first, then prefer a moderately valid judge who brings a new skill over a more valid one who duplicates the first. Such a team will show relatively high pattern noise, because its members will differ case by case — and that is the point, not a defect. The book's example of complementarity is four witnesses to a crime who saw it from four different angles: the requirement is that they are kept from influencing one another, and the bonus is that they saw different things.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument, built on standard regression reasoning. The empirical support for selection and aggregation comes from the Good Judgment Project, third-party work.
confounders: concluding that pattern noise is desirable in general; the book's claim is narrowly about a panel whose judgements will be aggregated, not about individuals judging alone
assuming diversity substitutes for independence — the book states aggregation reduces noise only if judgements are truly independent, regardless of diversity
reading unanimity as a quality signal, which is what the book is arguing against

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Occasion Noise', section 'One Is a Crowd'
qa_items.question: You cannot get a second opinion from anyone else. What does the book say you can do instead, how much of the benefit does it deliver, and what should you do with the two answers?
qa_items.answer: Make the same judgement yourself a second time to create what the research calls the crowd within. The book reports three variants and their sizes, all as fractions of the value of a genuine second opinion. Simply answering again immediately gets you about one tenth. Letting time pass first — Vul and Pashler used three weeks — raises it to about one third; this is the book's rationale for "sleep on it, and think again in the morning." Herzog and Hertwig's dialectical bootstrapping, where you assume your first estimate was off, list reasons it might have been, ask what those imply about the direction of the error, and then make a deliberately different second estimate, gets about one half immediately. What to do with the two answers: unless you have very strong reasons to weight one more heavily, average them. The book's larger point is that the first answer was never the sum of your knowledge — it was one point drawn from an internal distribution of answers your mind could have produced.
qa_items.support: Third-party research: Vul and Pashler on the crowd within, Herzog and Hertwig on dialectical bootstrapping. The gains are modest and the book reports them as such.
confounders: assuming the inner crowd approaches the value of a real second opinion — at best it is about half, and only with deliberate effort
taking the second estimate as a correction of the first rather than averaging them
expecting a benefit from an immediate re-answer without either delay or the dialectical instruction

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'A Noisy System', section 'The Illusion of Agreement'; Ch. 8 'How Groups Amplify Noise', 'Cascades'
qa_items.question: A review board of six people has signed off unanimously on every one of the last forty submissions, with high stated confidence. A manager reads this as evidence that the review criteria are clear and well applied. Using this book's material only, give the two readings the manager has not considered and say what would distinguish them.
qa_items.answer: First reading: contagion rather than agreement. If the six express views in sequence and can see each other, an informational or social-pressure cascade will produce unanimity regardless of what the members privately think, and the book stresses that observers systematically underestimate how much of an apparent consensus is people following predecessors. Group polarisation compounds it, since discussion also produces greater confidence and unity. Second reading: the illusion of agreement. If the board's records simply never contained a mechanism capable of surfacing disagreement, the absence of recorded disagreement is not evidence of its absence — the book's insurance underwriters worked alongside one another for years without discovering that they differed by a median of 55%. What distinguishes them from real agreement is the same thing in both cases: collect each member's judgement independently and before any discussion, on the same submissions. If the pre-discussion spread is small, the manager's reading survives. If it is large, the unanimity was manufactured. The book adds that unanimity should be treated with more suspicion than a split, not less.
qa_items.support: Combines the illusion of agreement (the authors' own insurance audit and executive polling) with the cascade and polarisation material (their own jury studies plus third-party work by Salganik, Macy and Muchnik). The remedy — record judgements before discussion — is the book's own stated procedure.
confounders: treating high stated confidence as corroboration; the book's whole argument on the internal signal is that confidence is not evidence of accuracy
proposing to interview the board members about whether they really agreed — a self-report that the illusion of agreement predicts will be reassuring and wrong
concluding the board should be disbanded; the book's move is to measure first, and it says nothing about whether this board is accurate

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 20 'Sequencing Information in Forensic Science', section 'The Forensic Confirmation Bias'
qa_items.question: A quality process routes every item flagged as failing to a second reviewer for confirmation, and the second reviewer is shown the first reviewer's verdict and reasoning. Management treats agreement between the two as strong evidence. Diagnose this using the book, and state the minimal change.
qa_items.answer: The second review is not an independent observation, so the agreement carries almost none of the weight management is putting on it. This is precisely the flaw the book identifies in the ACE-V verification step in fingerprint work: because the verifier knows the first examiner concluded an identification, "the verification step therefore does not provide the benefit normally expected from the aggregation of independent judgments, because verifications are not, in fact, independent." The book's Mayfield case shows how far it can run — three FBI experts concurred on an erroneous identification, the later investigation found that once the first examiner erred "the subsequent examinations were tainted", and even an independent expert appointed for the defence agreed. Two further defects here. Only failures are double-checked, so the process is structurally incapable of catching a wrongly-passed item. And routing on the flag itself supplies the biasing context. The minimal change is the book's: the second reviewer should not be aware of the first judgement. Withholding the verdict and the reasoning costs nothing and restores the independence the aggregation assumes.
qa_items.support: Directly parallels the book's forensic case: Dror and colleagues' work on the forensic confirmation bias, plus the official investigation of the Mayfield error. Third-party evidence throughout; the procedural recommendation is the book's own.
confounders: assuming a second opinion is valuable regardless of what the reviewer was told
proposing to instruct the second reviewer to ignore the first verdict; the book's finding that context changes what is perceived makes instruction an unreliable remedy
treating this as a problem of reviewer independence in the organisational sense — seniority, reporting lines — rather than of informational independence

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 23 'Defining the Scale in Performance Ratings', section 'What's Next?'; Ch. 15 'Scales', 'Noisy Scales'
qa_items.question: A team's rubric asks reviewers to rate outputs from 1 to 10 on "overall quality", with 10 labelled "outstanding" and 1 "unacceptable". Reviewers disagree constantly. Using only this book, name the three separate defects in that rubric and the repair for each.
qa_items.answer: First, the scale is too fine for absolute judgement. People reliably discriminate about seven categories, and a ten-point absolute scale manufactures disagreement that has nothing to do with the outputs. Repair: fewer points, or better, convert to a comparison — sort into a small number of categories and rank within each. Second, the anchors are ambiguous words. "Outstanding" and "unacceptable" are interpreted differently by different people, so two reviewers who agree entirely about an output can record different numbers; the book identifies scale ambiguity as a source of level noise, and its punitive-damages study showed noise tracking scale specificity rather than content. Repair: anchor the scale in concrete reference cases known to everyone — a case scale — installed by having reviewers practise on shared examples and see how their ratings compare, which is frame-of-reference training. Third, "overall quality" is a single aggregate judgement, so the halo effect has nothing to work against. Repair: decompose into named dimensions and score each separately; the book is explicit that ranking on an ill-defined aggregate would not reduce halo at all.
qa_items.support: Combines three of the book's strands: the limits of absolute judgement (third-party classic), scale ambiguity (the authors' own punitive-damages study), and structuring against the halo effect (personnel-selection research the book reports). All remedies are the book's own.
confounders: fixing only the wording of the anchors, which the book says behaviourally anchored scales alone do not suffice to do
adding more dimensions to the rubric — the book warns that overengineered questionnaires make halo worse and exhaust raters
mandating a distribution across the ten points, which is the forcing the book rejects

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Appendix A 'How to Conduct a Noise Audit', sections 'Construction of Case Materials', 'Prelaunch Meeting with Executives', 'Administration of the Study'
qa_items.question: You have been asked to run a noise audit on a team of eight reviewers and you expect the result to be unwelcome. Following the book's Appendix A, list the design choices that protect the audit from being dismissed, and say what each one blocks.
qa_items.answer: Build the cases with subject-matter experts from inside the team, so the most likely critics are the authors — this blocks dismissal of the finding as an outsider's artefact. Apply the book's acceptance test to the materials before running anything: if we find high disagreement on these simulated cases, will people here accept that there is disagreement in real work? "The noise audit is only worth carrying out if the answer is a clear yes." Hold a pre-launch meeting where leadership states, on the record, what difference it expects between two randomly chosen reviewers and what difference would be unacceptable, and document the answers — this blocks the result being reinterpreted afterwards as normal. Obtain a commitment to accept the results whatever they are; without it, do not proceed. Do not use the words "noise" or "noisy" to participants, especially about people — call it a decision-making study. Guarantee individual anonymity, hiring an outside firm to anonymise if necessary. Include every qualified reviewer, not a sample. Run everyone at the same time, physically separated and not communicating — this blocks the contamination that would destroy the independence the measurement depends on. Administer the reasoning questionnaire only after all cases are done.
qa_items.support: Appendix A, the book's own procedural guide, generalised from the authors' two audits — federal sentencing and the insurance company. It is a practitioner's protocol; the book offers no comparison of audits run with and without these precautions.
confounders: sampling a few reviewers to save time, which the book rules out for credibility
telling participants the study is about consistency, which invites them to manage their answers
collecting the executives' expectations after the results are in, which is exactly what the pre-launch documentation exists to prevent

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'The Analysis of Noise', 'Judges Differ: Pattern Noise'; Ch. 17 'The Sources of Noise', 'Sizing the Components'
qa_items.question: An organisation discovers two of its five reviewers are systematically harsher than the rest and equalises their averages through calibration training. It declares the consistency problem solved. What has it actually fixed, what has it not touched, and what design would have revealed the rest?
qa_items.answer: It has fixed level noise — the differences in reviewers' across-the-board severity — which is genuinely worth fixing and which the book says organisations can sometimes see without an audit, provided cases are assigned roughly at random. What it has not touched is pattern noise: the variability in how each reviewer responds to particular items over and above their general severity. Two reviewers with identical averages can still rank the same set of items differently, because each has an idiosyncratic sensitivity to particular features and combinations of features. On the book's assembled evidence that is generally the larger component, which is why it says that "attaining only this objective would leave most of the problem of system noise without a solution." Equalising averages can even conceal the residual by making the summary statistics look healthy. The design that would have revealed the rest is a multi-case, multi-judge audit: several reviewers judging the SAME items, which is the only way an interaction between a reviewer and an item becomes recoverable, and which ordinary operations never arrange.
qa_items.support: The book's own decomposition. The sizing claim it rests on is explicitly hedged by the book as tentative, from a limited selection of examples, with asylum adjudication named as an exception where level noise probably dominates.
confounders: assuming equalised averages imply equalised judgements — the book's central point about the two components
importing a specific ratio of pattern to level noise, which the book declines to generalise
concluding that calibration training was worthless; the book says reducing level noise remains a worthwhile objective

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 'Noiseless Rules', section 'More Complexity: Toward Machine Learning'; Ch. 25, 'The Decision Meeting'
qa_items.question: A reviewer wants to overturn a rule-based recommendation. Apply the book's test, and say what should happen in each of the two possible outcomes.
qa_items.answer: The test is a question about information, not about strength of feeling: does the reviewer hold decisive information that the rule could not take into account? If yes, that is a broken leg — the reference is Meehl's example of a model predicting who will go to the cinema tonight and someone who knows a particular person just broke a leg — and the override is right; the private fact is decisive and outside the model's inputs. If no, and the reviewer simply disagrees having seen the same predictors the rule used, then what they are applying is a personal pattern, which the book says is "highly likely to be invalid", and overriding "is likely to make the prediction less accurate." The reviewer should refrain. The book's own phrasing for the challenge is "You disagree with the model's forecast. I get it. But is there a broken leg here, or do you just dislike the prediction?" It keeps a place for the override at the end of a structured process precisely so that unanticipated decisive factors can still be caught — but the licence is the private information, not the disagreement.
qa_items.support: The broken-leg principle is Meehl's example, presented by the book as a decision rule. The book supplies no evidence about how often overrides that pass the test actually improve outcomes.
confounders: treating a strongly-held professional intuition as sufficient grounds; the test asks specifically for information the rule lacked
concluding that overrides should be forbidden, which is not the book's position

assuming a model that has been wrong before earns a general licence to override — the book notes people abandon algorithms as soon as they see a mistake, and calls the expectation of perfection the problem

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 24 'Structure in Hiring', section 'Improving Personnel Selection Through Structure'
qa_items.question: A team already has a list of four criteria every reviewer is supposed to consider, and its judgements are still noisy. Using the book's three principles of structured judgement, explain why the list alone was never going to be enough, and what has to be added.
qa_items.answer: The list gives you decomposition and nothing else, and the book is explicit that decomposition is one of three necessary parts. Its remark about interviewers applies directly: "most recruiters conducting traditional interviews also know the four or five things they look for in a candidate. The problem is that, in the conduct of the interview, they do not evaluate these elements separately. Each assessment influences the others, which makes each assessment very noisy." What has to be added is independence and delay. Independence: evidence for each criterion must be gathered and SCORED separately, one at a time, with the score recorded before moving to the next — otherwise the halo effect keeps the ratings within a narrow band and the four criteria are really one judgement wearing four labels. Delay: the holistic verdict is not banned but is forbidden until every criterion has been scored, so the final intuition is anchored on the recorded assessments rather than on a first impression. The book adds a fourth thing worth doing first — investing in the problem definition, so that the criteria are specific enough to score rather than a vague wish list.
qa_items.support: The book's three principles — decomposition, independence, delayed holistic judgement — illustrated with a technology company's hiring process. The supporting validity figures for structured versus unstructured interviews are from the personnel-selection literature, not the authors' work.
confounders: adding more criteria, which the book warns makes the halo effect worse and exhausts raters
banning intuition from the final decision — the book's prescription is to delay it, not exclude it
assuming written criteria imply independent assessment; the book's point is precisely that they do not

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 25 'The Mediating Assessments Protocol', sections 'The Decision Meeting' and 'What the Protocol Changes'
qa_items.question: A committee runs the mediating assessments protocol and the resulting profile is uneven — some assessments strongly positive, others weak. A member argues the analysis must be flawed because a good option should look good on everything. How does the book answer this?
qa_items.answer: The unevenness is the expected result of doing it correctly, not evidence of a flaw. The book has its CEO character notice exactly this on reading the report: because the assessments were kept independent of one another, they did not paint a simple, all-systems-go picture. "When excessive coherence is kept in check, reality is not as coherent as most board presentations make it seem." A conventional report looks uniform because each section is written in the light of the conclusion the team is already reaching — which is the contamination the protocol exists to prevent. The book then treats the discrepancies as the point: "These discrepancies between assessments will raise questions and trigger discussions. That's just what we need to have a good debate… The diverse results will not make the decision easier, for sure—but they will make it better." The instruction to the analysts reinforces it: include all relevant factual information in each chapter, and "if there is information that seems inconsistent or even contradictory with the main rating, don't sweep anything under the rug."
qa_items.support: The book's own protocol, illustrated with a stylised composite of real cases rather than a reported study. No measured effect on decision quality is offered.
confounders: treating a coherent, uniformly favourable analysis as a sign of quality — the book treats it as a symptom of contamination
resolving the unevenness by averaging the assessment ratings, which the book's protocol explicitly declines to do at the final step
assuming the protocol is meant to make decisions easier or faster; the book claims better, not easier

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 14 'The Matching Operation', 'The Bias of Matching Predictions'; Appendix C 'Correcting Predictions'
qa_items.question: A reviewer sees an exceptionally strong first submission from a new supplier and predicts that supplier will be in the top tier within a year. Apply the book's four-step correction and say what determines how far the prediction should move.
qa_items.answer: Step one: keep the intuitive guess. It is not worthless — it is the prediction that would be correct if the evidence were perfectly predictive, so write it down. Step two: find the outside-view value — what you would predict knowing nothing about this supplier at all, which is the average outcome for the reference class of new suppliers. Step three, the hard one: estimate the diagnostic value of the evidence you actually have, expressed as a correlation with the outcome. The book warns this will almost always be a back-of-the-envelope estimate, and supplies calibration: correlations above .50 are very rare in the social sciences and many meaningful ones sit around .20. Step four: move from the outside-view value toward your intuitive guess by that proportion. So what determines the distance is solely the predictive value of the evidence — one strong submission, not the strength of the impression it made. The book's parallel case is an interview so impressive it suggests $1m of first-year sales against a $500k mean; at a generous r = .40 the corrected estimate is $700k. It also warns what you are accepting: corrected predictions never bet on outliers, so in hindsight they will produce some highly visible misses.
qa_items.support: Appendix C, the book's own procedure. The correlation benchmarks come from reviews of the social science literature that the book reports.
confounders: discarding the intuitive guess entirely, which the book says would waste real information
adjusting by how confident the reviewer feels rather than by the diagnostic value of the evidence
assuming that because corrected predictions sometimes miss spectacularly they are worse — the book argues the opposite error, predicting outliers stay outliers, is far more frequent

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Singular Decisions', sections 'Noise in Singular Decisions' and 'Controlling Noise in Singular Decisions'
qa_items.question: A team faces a one-off decision with no precedent and argues that noise-reduction procedures are irrelevant because there is nothing to be consistent with. Give the book's reply, and be honest about what kind of argument it is.
qa_items.answer: The book's reply is that unmeasurability is a property of the observation, not of the process. Its image is the shooting range run in reverse: watching only the first shooter tells you nothing about the team's scatter, but the unsteady hand that produces the scatter is present in that first shot too. Every factor that produces disagreement among judges of recurrent cases is still operating — a different but equally competent team, with different backgrounds, or the same team in a different mood, or with the facts presented in a slightly different order, could plausibly have concluded otherwise. So "we cannot measure noise in a singular decision, but if we think counterfactually, we know for sure that noise is there," and the practical rule is that "a singular decision is a recurrent decision that happens only once" — the same hygiene applies. Honestly: this is an argument from counterfactual reasoning, not a measurement, and the book says so. Nothing in it establishes HOW MUCH noise a singular decision carries, and the book concedes the prescription is more counterintuitive than it looks, since the instinct with a one-of-a-kind decision is to treat it as one of a kind.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument. Its COVID-19 cross-country illustration is offered as a demonstration of the counterfactual — variation that would have been invisible had the epidemic struck one country — not as evidence about any particular decision.
confounders: accepting the objection because noise is defined as variability and there is no variability to see
assuming the book claims to have measured noise in singular decisions
treating singular and recurrent as a clean category distinction; the book says there is a continuum, with a fourth house purchase shading into a recurrent decision

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Matters of Judgment', section 'How Judgment Is Evaluated: The Outcome and the Process'
qa_items.question: A reviewer's assessment turned out to be wrong on one item, and a colleague's lucky guess turned out right. Management wants to act on this. Apply the book's position on evaluating judgement.
qa_items.answer: The book's position is that the two ways of evaluating a judgement — against its outcome, and by the quality of the process — can reach different conclusions in any single case, and that the process is the right target. Its own illustration is exactly this pair: "A skilled and careful forecaster using the best possible tools and techniques will often miss the correct number… Meanwhile, in a single quarter, a dart-throwing chimpanzee will sometimes be right." One outcome does not reveal whether the process that produced it was sound. The book gives two ways to assess the process instead: how it performs across an ensemble of similar cases, and whether it conforms to the principles of logic and probability. It also supplies a specific test to apply to whatever explanation management reaches for: a bias counts as an explanation only if it could have been predicted in advance or detected in real time, or if it yields a prediction about future cases. "In that case they failed, so they must have been overconfident" is, in the book's words, completely vacuous — it feels like understanding and predicts nothing. The book does concede this is not standard practice; professionals are usually evaluated against outcomes.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument on process versus outcome, plus its test for what counts as a bias explanation, from the chapter on the sources of noise.
confounders: concluding outcomes should be ignored entirely; the book's rule is about a SINGLE case, and it endorses evaluating a process across an ensemble of outcomes
accepting a post-hoc bias label as an explanation of the miss
treating the lucky right answer as evidence for the colleague's method

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 21 'Selection and Aggregation in Forecasting', section 'Improving Forecasts'
qa_items.question: You want to halve the disagreement in a scored set by averaging more independent assessors. How many do you need, what exactly does that buy, and what does it not touch?
qa_items.answer: Four. Averaging divides noise by the square root of the number of judgements averaged, so four judgements halve it; a hundred cut it by 90% and four hundred by 95%, essentially eliminating it. What it buys is a reduction in the noise term only. What it does not touch is bias: the book states plainly that "averaging does nothing to reduce bias", so its effect on total error depends on the proportions of bias and noise present, and this is why the wisdom of crowds works best where the judgements are independent and therefore less likely to contain shared errors. Two practical qualifications the book adds. The arithmetic assumes genuine independence — assessors who have seen each other's answers are not supplying the sample size the formula assumes. And returns diminish in practice sooner than the arithmetic suggests: it reports a company that cut its interviews from twenty-five to four on finding that additional interviews added almost no predictive validity beyond the first four.
qa_items.support: The square-root relation is standard statistics, stated by the book. The diminishing-returns example is a company's own reported review, and the wisdom-of-crowds material is third-party.
confounders: expecting averaging to improve accuracy when all the assessors share the same misconception — it will produce a precise, unanimous wrong answer
counting non-independent assessments toward the four
assuming more assessors is always proportionally better; the book records real diminishing returns and a cost

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Occasion Noise', sections 'Measuring Occasion Noise' and 'Sizing Occasion Noise'
qa_items.question: You want to measure how much a single reviewer's own judgements vary across occasions. Design the test according to the book, and name the trap that makes the naive version useless.
qa_items.answer: The trap is recognition. When people form a considered opinion they associate it with the reasons that justify it, and if presented with the same problem again and recognising it, they will reproduce the earlier answer both to save effort and to remain consistent. So a within-session retest, or any retest on memorable material, systematically understates occasion noise; the book notes that reviews of studies where experts judged twice in the same session unsurprisingly found they agreed with themselves. The design must therefore make the repeat unrecognisable. The book's examples all do this: wine judges in a blind re-tasting scored only 18% of the same wines identically; fingerprint examiners were shown pairs they had already seen but weeks or months later and without being told; software experts were re-asked about tasks they had already estimated, again after an interval and without being told. Some examiners consented in advance to being tested unannounced at any point over five years, and the exercise was embedded in routine casework so they did not know they were being studied. The book also names an indirect route where a large sample of past decisions exists: check statistically whether irrelevant occasion-specific factors — time of day, weather, the sequence of preceding cases — moved the decisions.
qa_items.support: Third-party studies throughout — the US wine competition re-tasting, Dror and colleagues on fingerprints, software estimation research, and the econometric analyses of asylum sequencing and opioid prescribing. The authors report no occasion-noise measurement of their own.
confounders: re-testing in the same session, or on material distinctive enough to be recognised
telling participants the second pass is a consistency check
expecting occasion noise to be the dominant component; the book reports it as the smallest wherever the share could be measured

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 13 'Heuristics, Biases, and Noise', 'Substitution'; Ch. 15 'Scales', 'The Outrage Hypothesis'
qa_items.question: Reviewers are asked "how likely is this to succeed with the audience?" and their answers correlate almost perfectly with how much they personally liked the item. Diagnose this with the book, and say what evidence would confirm the diagnosis.
qa_items.answer: The diagnosis is substitution: an easier question is being answered in place of the hard one, without the reviewers noticing. The book's structurally identical case is the outrage hypothesis — asked how much a defendant should be punished, ordinary people answer the easy question "how angry am I?", and across twenty-eight scenarios the mean outrage ratings correlated 0.98 with mean punitive intent. The consequence is not merely relabelling: substitution guarantees error, because the evidence gets weights appropriate to the substituted question rather than the one asked. The confirming evidence is a misweighting test, which is how the book confirms psychological bias where no true value exists — show that a factor which SHOULD matter to the real question does not move the answers, or that one which should not does. The book ran exactly this: harm suffered barely moved outrage ratings (4.24 for severe versus 4.19 for mild) but did move punitive intent (4.93 versus 4.65) and doubled the median award, revealing which question each scale was really answering. The analogue here is to vary something that should affect audience outcome but not personal taste, and see whether the answers move.
qa_items.support: The authors' own punitive-damages study for the outrage result and the harm manipulation; the general substitution mechanism is from the heuristics-and-biases programme the book reviews. The 0.98 figure is between MEAN ratings of scenarios, not between individuals.
confounders: reading the near-perfect correlation as evidence that liking is a valid predictor of audience success
treating substitution as dishonesty — the book stresses the participants were unaware they were assigning weights at all
concluding that the reviewers agree; the outrage study showed agreement on averages coexisting with very large case-by-case disagreement

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 19 'Debiasing and Decision Hygiene', section 'The Decision Observer'; Appendix B 'A Checklist for a Decision Observer'
qa_items.question: Set up a decision observer for a recurring review meeting. What does the book say the role requires, what tool does it use, and what does the book warn will make it fail?
qa_items.answer: The role is someone who watches the group in real time and uses a checklist to diagnose whether familiar biases are pushing the judgement away from the best available one — as opposed to correcting a bias afterwards or preventing a specific one beforehand. It rests on the observation that people recognise biases more easily in others than in themselves, the bias blind spot. The tool is a bias checklist, which the book says should be customised rather than generic, and should focus on the most frequent and consequential biases rather than attempting to be exhaustive; its Appendix B example follows the chronology of a discussion, asking about substitution, whether the outside view was used, diversity of views, prejudgments and premature closure, availability, anchoring, nonregressive prediction, and the planning fallacy. The failures the book warns about: it does not work if the ultimate decision makers are not committed to fighting biases, and the decision makers must be the ones who initiate the role and support it. "We certainly do not recommend that you make yourself a self-appointed decision observer. You will neither win friends nor influence people." It also names a structural cost of one variant — a bias-buster inside the team becomes a devil's advocate and "may quickly run out of political capital."
qa_items.support: The book's own proposal, which it explicitly flags as not systematically explored: it reports encouraging results only from informal, small-scale efforts and says it is not aware of any study of the approach or of the trade-offs among ways to deploy it.
confounders: treating the decision observer as an established, evidenced technique
assuming the observer should be a neutral outsider by default — the book lists three options with different trade-offs, including a supervisor and an outside facilitator
confusing this with decision hygiene; the book places the observer under debiasing, because it targets identifiable directional errors

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 25 'The Mediating Assessments Protocol', section 'The Decision Meeting'
qa_items.question: Describe estimate-talk-estimate as the book's CEO character runs it, and explain which specific problem each of the three phases addresses.
qa_items.answer: Phase one: after a brief factual summary of one assessment, every participant records their own rating privately — in the book's staging, on a phone app — and the distribution is projected without identifying anyone. "This is not a vote. We are just taking the temperature of the room on each topic." This addresses cascades and social influence: by capturing each independent opinion BEFORE anyone speaks, it removes the possibility that early speakers set the room, and it makes the true extent of disagreement visible instead of letting it be talked away. Phase two: discussion, concentrated where the first round revealed opposing views rather than where it revealed consensus, with both sides required to speak and to argue with facts, nuance and humility. This addresses the loss of private information that a cascade causes — the reasons people hold different views get shared. Phase three: a second private rating, whose average is the consensus. This captures whatever was genuinely learned in the discussion while keeping the aggregation mechanical rather than letting the loudest voice or a drift toward apparent unanimity settle it. The whole sequence is repeated per assessment, before any discussion of the overall decision.
qa_items.support: The book's own protocol, illustrated with a stylised composite case. Estimate-talk-estimate is described as a single-meeting form of the Delphi method, which is third-party.
confounders: treating the first round as a vote or a decision rather than as a measurement of spread
spending equal time on assessments that produced immediate consensus
letting the discussion produce the conclusion directly, without the second independent round

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 22 'Guidelines in Medicine', the Apgar discussion
qa_items.question: Using the book's account of why the Apgar score reduces noise, list the three things a guideline does, and say which of them a checklist of criteria alone would NOT give you.
qa_items.answer: Three things. It focuses the judge on a fixed set of predictors known to matter, so attention cannot wander to unimportant cues or skip important ones depending on the day or the mood. It specifies how each cue is to be evaluated, which makes each sub-judgement simple enough that "practitioners with even a modest degree of training are unlikely to disagree a great deal" — in the Apgar score only heart rate is strictly numerical and the other four components still involve judgement, but each is easy. And it specifies how to combine the components mechanically, removing the judge's discretion over the weights, which human clinicians would otherwise differ on. A bare checklist of criteria gives you only the first. It does not tell a reviewer how to assess each criterion, so each sub-judgement stays as noisy as it was; and it does not fix the weights, so two reviewers agreeing on every component can still disagree on the conclusion. The book's summary of the mechanism is exactly these three: "A focus on the relevant predictors, simplification of the predictive model, and mechanical aggregation—all of these reduce noise." It also stresses what a guideline is not: unlike a rule, it does not eliminate judgement, and disagreement on each component remains possible.
qa_items.support: Third-party medical instruments — Apgar, Centor, BI-RADS — reported by the book, with the mechanism supplied by the authors' own analysis in terms of simple prediction models.
confounders: assuming a guideline removes judgement; the book insists it decomposes it instead
believing the naming of criteria is the load-bearing part, when the book's mechanism puts equal weight on the assessment rules and the fixed weights
expecting the same benefit where the criteria are open-ended — the book's psychiatric case is the counter-example

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'A Noisy System', section 'Unwanted Variability Versus Wanted Diversity'
qa_items.question: Where does the concept of noise NOT apply, on the book's own account, and what test separates the cases?
qa_items.answer: Two places. Matters of preference or taste: ten critics rating a film, ten tasters rating a wine, ten readers on a novel — the book says diversity of tastes is welcome and entirely expected, and "no one would want to live in a world in which everyone has exactly the same likes and dislikes." And competitive settings, where the best judgement will be rewarded: several teams attacking a problem from different angles, several traders pricing a stock, the analyst who calls a recession no one else saw. There, variation is the raw material selection works on, and suppressing it would destroy the mechanism. The test is whether the variation is subsequently SELECTED ON. In a competitive setting variation is only the first phase; a second phase pits the results against one another and the best wins. In a system there is no second phase — one judgement is made on the organisation's behalf and acted on, so the variation is never selected, only suffered. Hence "System noise is a problem of systems, which are organisations, not markets." The book adds that the boundary is crossable in one direction: a producer's personal liking is welcome diversity as taste and a major mistake if it stands in for a professional judgement about an audience.
qa_items.support: The book's own scoping argument. It gives clear cases at each end and explicitly leaves the middle to judgement, supplying no test for deciding which side a given task falls on.
confounders: assuming any disagreement among reviewers is noise
reading 'markets versus organisations' as being about the sector rather than about whether a second selection phase exists
expecting the book to supply a decision procedure for the middle of the range, which it does not

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Measuring Error', sections 'The Error Equations' and 'The Cost of Noise'
qa_items.question: The book's error equation says bias and noise contribute equally to overall error. Give the exact class of judgements it applies to, and the counter-cases the book uses to mark the boundary.
qa_items.answer: It applies to purely predictive judgements — forecasts and estimates that aim to approach a true value — scored by mean squared error. MSE is the two-hundred-year-old standard for scientific measurement; it yields the sample mean as the best estimate, treats positive and negative errors equally, and penalises large errors disproportionately. The book states the boundary itself: "The error equation does not apply to evaluative judgments." Its counter-cases show why. A lift's maximum load: underestimating is costly, overestimating is catastrophic, and squared error is beside the point. When to leave for a train: being one minute late and five minutes late cost you the same thing, the train. Insurance pricing, where the costs of the two directions of error are different in kind. In all of these the error costs are asymmetric and there is no reason to think they are proportional to the square of the deviation. The book also concedes that MSE conflicts with common intuition — people care about near-misses and are insensitive to the difference between two large errors, which it calls "almost the mirror image of what they should be".
qa_items.support: The book's own statement of its scope. The worked illustration in which halving bias and halving noise produce identical reductions is a constructed, deliberately smooth example, not a measurement.
confounders: applying the equal-contribution result to acceptance or grading decisions, which are evaluative
reading MSE as a description of what error actually costs; the book says it does not reflect the real, often asymmetric costs of judgement errors
assuming that because MSE is standard it is uncontroversial — the book records its clash with intuition

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Measuring Error', 'The Error Equations'; Ch. 26 'The Costs of Noise Reduction'
qa_items.question: The book says reducing noise is worthwhile regardless of what you know about bias. State the argument, then state the three qualifications the book itself attaches to it.
qa_items.answer: The argument: because bias and noise are independent terms entering the error equation with equal weight, you do not need to know how biased a set of predictive judgements is before deciding whether reducing their noise is worth it. Waiting to discover the bias first — the intuitively sensible course — is wrong. The book adds a presentational warning: halving noise while bias stands makes the judgements more uniformly wrong and makes the bias impossible to miss, which can look like deterioration and is not, since the relevant measure of bias is the average error, not the imbalance of positive and negative errors. The three qualifications. First, the priority does shift: "reducing noise would be less of a priority if bias were much larger than noise." Second, noise-reduction procedures help only "as long as they do not increase bias to a larger extent" — and the book's own later chapters give cases where a blunt instrument does exactly that. Third, this is a mathematical argument about a scoring rule, inheriting the equation's boundary: it does not extend to evaluative judgements, and the book presents no study showing that organisations which reduced noise first did better.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument from the error equation, with the qualifications stated in its own words. The illustration is constructed rather than measured.
confounders: reading 'always useful' without the condition that the procedure must not increase bias more
concluding that a set of judgements that became more uniformly wrong has got worse
extending the argument to evaluative judgements, which the equation does not cover

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Part VI 'Optimal Noise', introduction listing the seven objections
qa_items.question: The book raises seven objections to noise reduction against itself. List them, and state the single structural reply it gives to nearly all of them.
qa_items.answer: One: reducing noise can be expensive and might not be worth the trouble, or even be feasible. Two: the strategies used can introduce errors of their own, including systematic bias. Three: dignity — people want an individualised hearing and a real person with the power to act, and noise may be its price. Four: noise leaves room for moral and political values to evolve, where a noise-free system might freeze existing values. Five: clear rules that remove noise create clear edges that people can game, so a little vagueness may prevent wrongdoing. Six: unpredictable penalties may deter better than certain ones. Seven: people do not want to be treated as cogs, and some strategies squelch creativity and morale. The structural reply is that these are objections to particular INSTRUMENTS — nearly always firm rules — and not to noise reduction as such: "whether an objection is convincing depends on the particular noise-reduction strategy to which it is meant to apply. You might, for example, object to rigid guidelines while also agreeing that aggregation of independent judgments is a good idea." Hence the reply to a crude instrument is a better instrument, not tolerated noise. The book states it presents the objections as sympathetically as it can and by no means endorses them as reasons to reject the goal.
qa_items.support: The book's own enumeration and its own stated stance. Chapters 26 to 28 work through the seven.
confounders: reading the catalogue as concessions the book accepts
assuming an objection that defeats one strategy defeats the programme
missing that the book concedes real force to some of them, particularly cost and demoralisation

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 26 'The Costs of Noise Reduction', opening section and 'Less Noise, More Mistakes?'
qa_items.question: Give the book's own worked example of a case where noise reduction may not be worth doing, and then state the condition under which it says the cost objection stops being a good reason.
qa_items.answer: The example is a high school teacher grading twenty-five essays a week at fifteen minutes each. The grading is probably noisy and therefore unfair, and several remedies are available: a colleague reading every paper too, more time per essay, structuring the assessment, reading each essay more than once and in different orders, a detailed grading guideline used as a checklist, or grading at the same time of day to reduce occasion noise. The book's judgement is that if the teacher's own judgements are pretty accurate and not terribly noisy, it might be sensible to do none of these — it might not be worth the bother. It then makes the stakes explicit: the same limit should be different when the essays are ninth-graders' or senior theses with university admission on the line. The condition under which the objection fails is measurement. The comparison of benefits with costs "is one reason noise audits are so important. In many situations, the audits reveal that noise is producing outrageous levels of unfairness, very high costs, or both. If so, the cost of noise reduction is hardly a good reason not to make the effort." The book's sharper formulation elsewhere: without an audit, invoking the difficulty of reducing noise "is nothing but an excuse not to measure it."
qa_items.support: The book's own worked example and its own concession that "the belief that it is too expensive to reduce noise is not always wrong". It calls for a disciplined analysis without specifying one.
confounders: treating the book as claiming noise should always be reduced
reading the cost objection as settled by the stakes alone, without measuring the noise
assuming the book supplies a cost-benefit procedure; it does not

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 26 'The Costs of Noise Reduction', section 'Noiseless, Biased Algorithms'
qa_items.question: The book argues that consistency can make bias worse, not better. Reconstruct that argument, and give the one structural advantage it claims for a rule-based process over human judges.
qa_items.answer: A noise-free process applies the same treatment every time. If that treatment embeds a directional error, the error is applied every time too — so "since they eliminate noise, they could be more reliably biased than human judges." The book names two routes by which this happens without anyone intending it: predictors that correlate with a protected characteristic even when the characteristic itself is not used, such as height and weight with gender or location with race; and training data that already encodes the problem, as with predictive policing built on records reflecting the overpolicing of particular neighbourhoods, or a hiring model trained on past promotion decisions, which will replicate every bias in them. The parallel case for a simple rule is a content filter removing all posts containing certain words: less noisy, and taking down many posts that should stay. The one structural advantage claimed is auditability — not fairness. "The fact that this question can be raised at all, however, is a distinct advantage." A rule can be inspected for inadmissible inputs and tested for objectionable discrimination; "it is much harder to subject individual human beings, whose judgments are often opaque, to the same kind of scrutiny." The book is careful to say algorithms CAN outperform humans on accuracy and discrimination together, not that they will.
qa_items.support: The book's own argument. The favourable results it cites — a bail algorithm jailing 41% fewer people of colour at constant crime rate, a résumé screener selecting a more diverse pool — are third-party studies, and it records the opposing literature without adjudicating it.
confounders: concluding the book opposes rules or algorithms; its stated conclusion is that a crude instrument calls for a better one
assuming that excluding a protected characteristic from the inputs prevents discrimination
reading the auditability point as a claim that rule-based processes are fairer

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 27 'Dignity', opening section and 'Creativity, Morale, and Fresh Ideas'
qa_items.question: Two of the book's objections concern people rather than accuracy: dignity and morale. State each, and state precisely how far the book concedes them.
qa_items.answer: Dignity: people want to be treated as individuals, to have a real human being consider their particular circumstances with power to act, and they may regard noise as a price worth paying for it. The book treats this as a genuine value with deep moral foundations in politics, law, theology and literature, and quotes Portia on mercy. Morale: people in positions of authority do not like having discretion taken away, may feel diminished, constrained and even humiliated, and a noisy system may be good for morale — not because it is noisy but because it lets people decide as they see fit; it may also leave room for new ideas. The concessions are precise and limited. On dignity: "We are not saying that the interest in individualized treatment does not matter. But there is a high price to pay if such treatment leads to all sorts of terrible consequences, including palpable unfairness." On morale: "Demoralization is itself a cost and leads to other costs, such as poor performance." In both cases the book's escape is the same — most strategies do not run into the objection at all. Three decision makers rather than one still give an individualised hearing; guidelines leave discretion; structuring complex judgements leaves room for fresh ideas. Only rigid rules bite. Its closing position is that "most of the efforts to defend noise aren't convincing."
qa_items.support: The book's own objections chapter. The dignity argument is legal, literary and philosophical; no evidence is offered about how much people actually value individualised hearings or what they would trade for them.
confounders: reading the concessions as acceptance of the objections
assuming the objections apply to all noise-reduction strategies equally
missing that the book grants the morale objection real force while still rejecting it as a defence of noise

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 22 'Guidelines in Medicine', section 'The Depressing Case of Psychiatry'
qa_items.question: Guidelines are one of the book's noise-reduction strategies, and psychiatry is its own worst case for them. What does that case show about the limits of the strategy?
qa_items.answer: It shows that a guideline reduces noise only to the extent that its components can actually be assessed consistently, because the mechanism is decomposition into easier sub-judgements. Psychiatry has pursued noise reduction since at least the 1940s; early studies found agreement between two psychiatrists on the kind of illness present around 50 to 57% of the time. Successive revisions of the diagnostic manual introduced explicit criteria and did help, but the book reports that noise remained high, that field trials for the 2013 edition found "minimal agreement" — highly trained specialists agreeing that a patient has depression between 4 and 15% of the time — and that on some field trials that edition made things worse, with some diagnoses "so unreliable as to appear useless in clinical practice." The book's explanation is exactly the mechanism's precondition: "the diagnostic criteria of some disorders are still vague and difficult to operationalize… to the extent that such criteria are relatively open-ended, noise remains likely." It reports the proposed remedies — clarifying criteria, reference definitions of symptoms and severity, structured interviews — and declines to predict whether they will work. Notably, it also concedes that the explanations for the noise are themselves contested.
qa_items.support: Third-party psychiatric reliability research from 1964 onwards, including the field trials, reported by the book. It presents this as a genuine negative case rather than explaining it away, while maintaining that guidelines have been highly successful in medicine generally.
confounders: generalising from psychiatry to guidelines in general, which the book explicitly refuses to do
assuming more detailed criteria always reduce noise; one revision appears to have increased it
reading the failure as being about psychiatrists rather than about the operationalisability of the criteria

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Patterns', section 'Pattern Noise: Stable or Transient'
qa_items.question: The book concedes that pattern noise is not always error. Give the two cases it names, and say what would be needed to tell them apart.
qa_items.answer: First, a judge who is genuinely more accurate than the others. "Imagine a single forecaster with crystal-ball powers that no one knows about (including herself). Her accuracy would make her deviate in many cases from the average forecast. In the absence of outcome data, these deviations would be regarded as pattern errors." The book's blunt statement: "When judgments are unverifiable, superior accuracy will look like pattern noise." Second, systematic differences in what people are good at. Where a coach, a physician and a psychologist each evaluate the same athletes on the aspects they know best, "pattern noise is better described as variability in what people know than as error." What would tell them apart is outcome data — the ability to check who was right — which is precisely what these settings lack. The book adds a consequence for the second case: variability in skills is simply noise when professionals decide alone, but becomes a potential asset when judgements are aggregated across complementary specialists, because they cover different aspects and complement one another. The defect and the asset are the same measurement; what changes is whether the judgements are pooled.
qa_items.support: The book's own concession, stated in its own words in the chapter that develops pattern noise.
confounders: treating all pattern noise as error, which is the book's usual but not universal framing
assuming the two cases can be distinguished by examining the reasoning rather than the outcomes
concluding that complementary skills make pattern noise harmless; the book says this holds only once the judgements are aggregated

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Review and Conclusion 'Taking Noise Seriously', section 'How to Reduce Noise (and Bias, Too)', first principle
qa_items.question: "The goal of judgment is accuracy, not individual expression." State what this principle rests on, and the boundary the book draws around it.
qa_items.answer: It rests on the book's finding about where noise comes from: stable pattern noise is the largest component of system noise, and it is a direct consequence of individual differences — judgement personalities that lead different people to form different views of the same problem. So the uniqueness that makes a person interesting is the same thing that makes a judgement system noisy, and the book accepts this conclusion "will be as unpopular as it is inescapable: judgment is not the place to express your individuality." Its operational form is perspectival: when you expect others to agree with you, "you should also consider what other competent judges would think if they were in your place." The boundary is explicit and generous. "To be clear, personal values, individuality, and creativity are needed, even essential, in many phases of thinking and decision making, including the choice of goals, the formulation of novel ways to approach a problem, and the generation of options." The principle bites only at the moment of judging between options. Two honest caveats: the finding it rests on is one the book itself marks as tentative, and the book concedes elsewhere that removing discretion can leave people feeling diminished, which is a real cost.
qa_items.support: The book's own first principle of decision hygiene, grounded on its tentative sizing conclusion about stable pattern noise.
confounders: extending the principle to idea generation or problem framing, which the book explicitly protects
treating the sizing finding it rests on as established rather than as the book's own hedged conclusion
reading it as a claim that individuality is undesirable in professionals generally

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 28 'Rules or Standards?', section 'A Framework'; 'Bosses, Controlling Subordinates'
qa_items.question: An organisation currently instructs reviewers to "use your judgement, applying our quality bar", and is considering replacing that with a specific list of disqualifying conditions. Apply the book's two-factor framework, and name the one thing it says should be monitored afterwards.
qa_items.answer: Factor one, the cost of decisions. The current instruction is a standard, so every reviewer must do the work of giving "quality bar" content on every item, which is burdensome and — the book adds — will be noisy. A rule makes each decision cheap. But the book insists on the offsetting cost: someone has to decide what the rule IS, and producing a good rule can be hard and sometimes prohibitively costly, which is exactly why organisations reach for words like reasonable and appropriate in the first place. Factor two, the cost of errors, where the book says there is no general winner. A rule is error-free only if it is perfect, and rules rarely are; a standard applied by knowledgeable, reliable agents practising decision hygiene may produce few errors. It collapses this into trust: "Principals need to impose rules when they have reason to distrust their agents." Volume matters too — where many similar decisions must be made, the book says there are real advantages to moving toward rules. The thing to monitor afterwards is whether the rule is actually being followed. The book warns that rules producing bad results in particular cases get quietly ignored, driving discretion underground, where "there will be noise, but no one will hear it" — and that reappearing noise is the clue that the rule needs revising.
qa_items.support: The book's own framework, illustrated with legal and corporate cases including a social media company's public standards against its non-public implementation rules. The framework is analytical, not empirical.
confounders: treating the choice as all-or-nothing; the book says they mix, e.g. a rule constraining the pool and a standard choosing within it
assuming a rule ends the noise, when fact-finding under it is itself judgement
adopting the rule for its cheapness without counting the cost of writing an accurate one

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 13 'Heuristics, Biases, and Noise', base-rate discussion; Review and Conclusion, 'Think statistically, and take the outside view of the case'
qa_items.question: A reviewer is asked to predict whether a particular submission will meet its target. They begin by studying the submission in detail. Using the book, say what they have skipped, why skipping it produces noise as well as error, and what taking the outside view would concretely involve.
qa_items.answer: They have skipped the base rate — how often submissions of this kind meet that target — and gone straight to the specifics. The book's parallel is the Gambardi CEO case: almost no reader thinks to ask what proportion of incoming CEOs are still in the job after two years, though a few minutes' research gives about 15% annual turnover and hence roughly a 72% two-year survival rate. Skipping it produces error, through base-rate neglect, and it produces NOISE as well, because when people apply their unique experience to a unique reading of a case, the result is pattern noise; judges who share a reference class are less noisy. Concretely, taking the outside view means defining a reference class of comparable submissions, finding the rate in that class, anchoring on it, and only then adjusting for the specifics of this one — and the adjustment should be proportional to how predictive the specifics actually are, which the book's correction procedure makes explicit. Two honest points. The base rate is a starting point, not the answer; the specifics do move it. And defining a defensible reference class is itself work — the book's own example has analysts having to determine which past transactions count as comparable enough.
qa_items.support: The book's own material on base-rate neglect and the outside view, plus its enumerated decision hygiene principle. It concedes the authors themselves missed the base-rate reading of their own Gambardi case for weeks.
confounders: treating the outside view as a substitute for examining the case rather than as the anchor to adjust from
assuming the reference class is obvious; the book treats defining it as a distinct task
reading this as an accuracy fix only — the noise-reduction rationale is that a shared reference class replaces private associations

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 18 'Better Judges for Better Judgments', section 'Cognitive Style'; Ch. 21 'Perpetual Beta'
qa_items.question: You can choose who joins a review panel but cannot test candidates formally. What does the book suggest you look for, what does it warn against, and what does it report about the alternatives it tested?
qa_items.answer: Look for the sort of people who actively search for new information that could contradict their prior beliefs, who are methodical in integrating it, and who are willing — even eager — to change their minds as a result. That is the book's description of actively open-minded thinking, and it is the one cognitive-style measure it reports as predicting forecasting performance. The warning is against the obvious proxy. High general ability improves both judgement and the ability to convince others, so in the absence of reality feedback it produces respect-experts rather than accurate ones — "Medieval astrologers must have been among the highest-GMA people of their time." The book also cautions against the confident, decisive personality: people trust leaders who seem to know immediately what is right, but "if the goal is to reduce error, it is better for leaders (and others) to remain open to counterarguments and to know that they might be wrong. If they end up being decisive, it is at the end of a process, not at the start." On alternatives tested: the need-for-cognition scale did NOT reliably predict forecasting performance, and did not predict who would work harder to seek information. The book records that negative result rather than glossing it.
qa_items.support: Third-party research throughout — Baron's actively open-minded thinking scale, the cognitive reflection test, the need-for-cognition scale, Haran, Ritov and Mellers' negative result, and Tetlock's superforecaster work. The book does not claim to have tested any of them.
confounders: selecting for intelligence alone, which the book says is necessary but produces convincing respect-experts as readily as accurate judges
assuming all cognitive-style measures work; the book reports one of them failing to predict
selecting for decisiveness and confidence, which the book identifies as the traits that earn trust without earning accuracy
