qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Occasion Noise', 'Sources of Occasion Noise'; Ch. 20, closing section on sequencing as a safeguard against occasion noise
qa_items.question: A team wants to eliminate occasion noise from its review process by controlling the reviewers' working conditions. Using the book, say how far that can get them and what it recommends instead.
qa_items.answer: Some way, but not all the way, and the book is explicit about the ceiling. Known triggers can be dampened: mood, which changes both what you notice and how you think — people in a good mood rely more on first impressions and are more receptive to unfounded claims; stress and fatigue, with physicians significantly more likely to prescribe opioids at the end of a long day; the weather; and the sequence of preceding cases, where asylum judges were 19% less likely to grant asylum after two approvals. But the book reports a tightly controlled memory study in which alertness, sleep, time of day, practice, within-session position and material difficulty together explained only 11% of the within-person variation. The residual had no identifiable external cause, and the researchers attributed it to "the efficiency of endogenous neural processes". The book's conclusion is that this "should give pause to anyone who thinks occasion noise can be eliminated." What it recommends instead is to shield judgements from the most obvious triggers rather than chase all of them: sequence the information so that an early impression cannot organise everything after it, and where you can, revisit a judgement at a different time, when the triggers of occasion noise will be different.
qa_items.support: Third-party studies throughout — Forgas on mood, the opioid-prescribing and asylum-sequencing analyses, and Kahana and colleagues' memory study. The authors report no occasion-noise measurement of their own.
confounders: assuming occasion noise is fully controllable given a tidy enough environment
prioritising occasion noise over the between-person components; the book reports it as the smallest wherever the share could be measured
treating mood as affecting only what is noticed, when the book's point is that it also changes how you think

qa_items.source_title: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark, 2021)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 23 'Defining the Scale in Performance Ratings', 'A Problem Long Recognized but Not Solved'; Ch. 26 'The Costs of Noise Reduction'
qa_items.question: A team proposes fixing rater disagreement by expanding its review form from six questions to thirty-two, and adding more raters. Using the book, give three reasons this may make things worse.
qa_items.answer: First, halo. The book says the proliferation of dimensions is pernicious as well as useless, because "the halo effect implies that supposedly separate dimensions will in fact not be treated separately. A strong positive or negative rating on one of the first questions will tend to pull answers to subsequent questions in the same direction." Its cited horror case is a system with forty-six ratings on eleven dimensions per rater and ratee. Second, rater capacity. "It would take a superhuman rater to recall and process accurate, relevant facts about numerous people being evaluated on so many dimensions," and the explosion in demands on time-constrained raters "cannot be expected to improve the quality of the information they supply." Third, cost against benefit. The book puts this case directly in the noise-reduction-costs frame: "In this case, the reduction of noise may not be worth the cost." Its example of where that lands is a firm calculating it spent two million hours a year on evaluations. What the book would do instead is not more questions but better scales: make the dimensions few and specific, anchor them in concrete reference cases, train raters to use the scale consistently, and score each dimension separately — the length of the form is not the lever.
qa_items.support: The book's own analysis of 360-degree feedback systems, drawing on performance-appraisal research it reports. The forty-six-rating example is cited from that literature, not measured by the authors.
confounders: assuming more dimensions means more structure — the book's structuring principle requires independent SCORING, not more questions
assuming more raters always helps; the book records diminishing returns and a real cost
treating the problem as insufficient detail rather than as ambiguous scales and contaminated dimensions

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces'
qa_items.question: The book coins the term "complex surface". What does it mean by it, and what makes such a surface require a divided treatment rather than simply more light?
qa_items.answer: A complex surface is the authors' term for a single surface that requires both diffuse and direct reflection to be defined properly. Their example is glossy wood: only direct reflection can tell the viewer the wood is glossy, and only diffuse reflection can reveal the colour and grain beneath the gloss. The treatment must be divided because the two cannot occupy the same area of the surface — a region showing the direct reflection of the source is showing the source, not the wood. So they lit a polished wooden box with a source large enough to fill the entire family of angles and then blocked part of it with a gobo, so one part of the lid carries the gloss and the other shows the colour and grain. They note that the diffusely lit region is the only place the wood's true colour is clearly apparent.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, 'Complex Surfaces': the definition is given verbatim, and the gobo arrangement and its result are described and shown in the wooden-box figures.
confounders: reading 'complex' as meaning geometrically complicated or many-faceted, rather than needing two reflection types
assuming the answer is a larger or softer light, when the source's answer is a large light partly blocked
confusing it with a mixed-material scene, where two different objects need different treatment; this is one surface

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Bright-field Lighting' and 'Dark-field Lighting'
qa_items.question: Define bright-field and dark-field lighting as this book defines them, in terms of the family of angles rather than in terms of the resulting picture.
qa_items.answer: Both are defined by what occupies the two extreme limits of the family of angles that acts on a glass edge — the points the book labels L. Bright-field lighting requires that there be NO light at those limits, so the edge stays dark, and the glass must therefore be shown against a bright background; the authors also call it the dark-on-light approach. Dark-field lighting requires that light come from those limits and from nowhere else, so the edge is bright, and the glass must be shown against a dark background; the light-on-dark approach. The two are the same geometric fact read in opposite directions, which is why the authors call them two attractive opposites.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Two Attractive Opposites' onward. The L-limits framing is the source's own; the two step sequences give the practical form.
confounders: defining them only by the resulting picture — dark glass on white, light glass on black — which misses that both are statements about where light may be
assuming dark-field means less light overall; it uses one very large source
supposing the whole family of angles matters, when the source says only its extreme limits do

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'A Glossy Background'
qa_items.question: What does this book mean by "invisible light", and what makes the light invisible?
qa_items.answer: Invisible light is the authors' name for lighting a subject by bouncing light off a glossy surface that sits inside the subject's family of angles while its own family of angles excludes the camera. Their worked case is a metal box on glossy black acrylic: the family of angles for the box's front face falls on the acrylic, so the acrylic is the only possible source for that face, and although the acrylic is too black to reflect diffusely it is glossy enough to reflect directly. A light placed under the camera bounces off the acrylic into the metal, which reflects it onward to the camera. The light is invisible because the camera lies outside the acrylic's own family of angles, so it cannot see the acrylic doing the lighting. The source for the box is in the scene and cannot be seen to be one.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'A Glossy Background', where the term is introduced and the geometry stated. The result is shown in the accompanying photograph of the box on black acrylic.
confounders: thinking the light is hidden behind something; it is fully in the frame and simply outside the camera's view of the reflecting surface
confusing it with the transparent-glass support, where light passes through rather than bouncing off
assuming a black surface cannot light anything, which is the intuition the source sets up in order to break

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'Adding Depth to the Background'
qa_items.question: What does the book mean by "falloff", where does it recommend putting it, and what is it for?
qa_items.answer: As the authors use the term, falloff means a transition in the scene from light to dark — deliberate uneven illumination of the background. It can occur in any area of the picture, and they say photographers most commonly place it at the top, both because it looks good there and because that is the easiest place to put it without interfering with the lighting of the primary subject. Its purpose is depth: a difference in tonal value between the foreground and background is another visual clue suggesting depth, and it separates the subject from the background. They produced it simply by aiming the light more toward the camera so less of it fell on the seamless paper at the back of the set, and they add a gobo over the lens because aiming the light that way risks serious camera flare.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'Adding Depth to the Background', where the term is defined and the method given.
confounders: confusing this with light falloff in the inverse-square sense, a property of the source rather than a compositional choice
assuming it needs a second light; the source produced it by re-aiming the existing one
forgetting the flare consequence, which is why the source pairs it with a gobo

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Black Magic'
qa_items.question: "Black magic" in this book is not a figure of speech. What is it, and how is its hardness controlled?
qa_items.answer: Black magic is anything added to a lighting set-up solely to place a black reflection in a metal surface. Its uses are practical: a black reflection in an edge helps differentiate that edge from the background, and reflected across the centre of a slightly irregular surface it adds dimension. It usually means a gobo, and its hardness is set by which side of the diffusion sheet the gobo sits on. Between the diffusion sheet and the subject, it makes a hard black reflection. Behind the sheet, away from the subject, it makes a softly graduated one, and the farther back it goes the softer it becomes. Where the source is an opaque reflector rather than a diffusion sheet a gobo cannot graduate, and the authors substitute a soft-edged stripe of black spray paint across the reflector.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Black Magic', in the 'Other Resources' group, which gives the purpose, the gobo placement rule and the painted-stripe alternative.
confounders: assuming black magic means removing light, when its purpose is to place a specific dark shape
reversing the gobo rule — near the subject is hard, not soft
confusing it with a black card used as negative fill on a diffuse subject, which works by subtraction rather than by reflection

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', section 'Subject and Background' (white-on-white half)
qa_items.question: The book gives a rare numeric window for the separation between a white subject and a white background. What is it, and what fails on each side of it?
qa_items.answer: For its own remaining white-on-white examples the book keeps the background between half a stop and one stop brighter than the greys at the edges of the primary subject. Below half a stop, part of the subject may disappear against the background. Above one stop, flare may scatter enough light inside the camera to cost contrast in the subject. The window is stated for the source's examples rather than as a universal, so it is a reference point rather than a threshold, and it sits inside a larger claim: technically it does not matter whether subject or background is the darker, but psychologically it matters a great deal, because the viewer only accepts the scene as white-on-white if the BACKGROUND is the white one.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Subject and Background' in the white-on-white half: the window and both failure modes are stated in one paragraph, immediately after the white-on-white versus white-on-gray comparison.
confounders: reading it as a lighting ratio for the subject rather than a subject-to-background difference; the book explicitly refuses to publish lighting ratios
assuming more separation is always safer, when the upper bound is a real flare limit
measuring against the subject's overall tone rather than the greys at its edges

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Set Up a Large Light Source'
qa_items.question: Dark-field lighting appears in the plan diagram to need light at only two points. Why is that wrong, and what does the book substitute?
qa_items.answer: The two-point appearance is what the authors call a representational defect caused by drawing in two dimensions. In three dimensions the same reasoning demands more: a source above and behind to keep the rim bright, and on a stemmed glass yet another to illuminate the underside of the bowl. That is four large sources for one small glass, which they call unwieldy at best. They replace all of them with a single source large enough to illuminate the top, bottom and sides at once, and say its exact size is not critical — any size between ten and twenty-five times the diameter of the subject works well. It is a rare instance of a book that argues through diagrams warning the reader against one of its own.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Set Up a Large Light Source', where the defect is named and the ten-to-twenty-five-times band given.
confounders: taking the two-light reading literally and building a two-strip set-up, which lights only a point on each side
treating the size band as a precise requirement; the source says the exact size is not critical
assuming the large source must also be bright, when its job is angular coverage

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', sidebar 'Do Lenses Affect Perspective Distortion?'
qa_items.question: Photographers commonly say a wide lens introduces distortion. What does this book say instead, and how did it demonstrate the point?
qa_items.answer: The authors say it is the camera's position that determines perspective distortion, not the lens mounted on it. To prove it they made every frame of their chessboard comparison with the SAME wide-angle lens and simply moved the camera, enlarging the more distant frames so all three matched in subject size; the convergence of the board's parallel lines still varies with camera distance alone. Had they used a longer lens for the distant shots they would not have needed to enlarge, and the shape of the board would have been the same. Focal length matters only in that it lets a chosen viewpoint fill the sensor: a short lens permits a close viewpoint that produces distortion, a long one permits a distant viewpoint that minimises it. They allow that extremely wide-angle and inferior lenses may produce other kinds of distortion — but not perspective distortion.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, the sidebar 'Do Lenses Affect Perspective Distortion?', which describes the controlled comparison and the conclusion.
confounders: the common belief the source is correcting: that wide lenses stretch subjects
over-generalising to 'lenses cause no distortion at all', which the source explicitly does not claim
missing why this matters in a lighting book — viewpoint also sets the family of angles

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', sections 'Using Diffuse Reflection and Shadow to Reveal Texture' and 'Capitalizing on Direct Reflections'
qa_items.question: A raking light reveals the texture of a light-blue sponge beautifully and destroys the texture of a black leather notebook. Explain the mechanism, and give the book's remedy for the leather.
qa_items.answer: Texture is read as a tonal difference between two faces of each texture particle. Raking light creates that difference by shadowing one face and relying on diffuse reflection to light the other. The sponge is light-toned and strongly diffuse, so both halves are present. The leather is black, and a black subject by definition produces little diffuse reflection, so the shadow side survives and the diffuse highlight side does not — there is no difference left to read. The authors are explicit that the failure is caused by the subject, not by the technique. Their remedy is to switch the surface to the reflection channel it actually has: a large source above the subject, big enough to fill the whole family of angles, so the leather is rendered by direct reflection instead. They note this is the exact opposite arrangement on both variables — direction and size — and say the earlier theory taken alone would call it the worst possible way to light the leather. The texture highlight moves from near black to middle grey with the same light falling on the subject and no exposure increase.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, the sponge sequence and then 'Capitalizing on Direct Reflections'. The source states that the amount of light falling on the leather is the same in both leather frames, which is what rules out an exposure explanation.
confounders: answering 'increase the exposure', which the source explicitly refuses on two stated grounds
assuming the leather needs an even harder or more raking light — more of the failing treatment
attributing the difference to colour rather than to the diffuse-reflection channel that colour implies

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light'
qa_items.question: Moving a soft box closer to a metal spatula on a white ground brightens the background and leaves the metal exactly as bright as it was. Why?
qa_items.answer: Because two different laws are acting on the two surfaces from the same lamp. The background is lit by diffuse reflection, whose brightness follows the inverse square law, so it rises as the light comes closer. The metal is lit by direct reflection, whose brightness equals that of the source regardless of how far away the source is, so it does not change at all. The consequence is a near-independent control over the relative brightness of metal and background from a single light — the authors call it nearly infinite control and immediately hedge it, because the range is bounded by how much of the family of angles the source still covers as it recedes.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light', with its matched pair of spatula photographs at two light distances. The two underlying laws are chapter-3 material, already live Canon; what this chapter contributes is running them against each other in one scene.
confounders: assuming the metal must brighten too, since more light is falling on the whole set
attributing the effect to the light becoming effectively larger, which is a separate consequence of moving it
thinking the metal's constancy is an exposure artefact rather than a property of direct reflection

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light', the two-camera comparison
qa_items.question: Two cameras frame a metal subject identically, one close with a short lens and one far with a long one. The incident light is the same in both. Why is the background brighter in one of them, and which?
qa_items.answer: Brighter in the distant, long-lens arrangement — and the reason is the lens's indirect effect on the effective size of the light. A distant viewpoint produces a narrow family of angles, so the soft box is much larger than the family and can be moved a long way without the metal changing; that freedom lets the light be brought close, which brightens the background. A close viewpoint produces a wide family that the same soft box only just fills, so the light cannot be moved back without the edges of the metal going black, and the light must stay where it is. With the metal exposed identically in both, the background therefore comes out brighter in the distant arrangement and darker in the close one despite identical incident light. The authors say this surprises even highly experienced photographers, and they recommend a longer lens and a more distant viewpoint whenever the subject is bright metal and the camera position is free.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light', the A/B camera diagram and the recommendation that follows it.
confounders: assuming the lens changes the light directly, rather than through the width of the family of angles
getting the direction backwards — a wide lens close in feels like it should give more freedom, not less
forgetting the chapter-5 coupling: the viewpoint that frees the light also fixes the perspective

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Finding the Family of Angles'
qa_items.question: Describe the test-light procedure for locating the family of angles, and state the inversion the book says will make hot spots easy to find afterwards.
qa_items.answer: Hang a white target where you think the family will be — larger than you think you need, and the less sure you are, the larger. Put a narrow-beam test light exactly at the lens position, removing the camera if necessary. Aim it at the point on the metal nearest the camera; where the reflected beam lands on the target is the near limit of the family, and you mark it with removable tape. Aim it at the farthest point for the far limit, and mark as many additional points as the subject's shape requires. The procedure works because light paths are reversible: a beam sent from the camera's position and reflected by the subject traces exactly the path a source would need to occupy. The inversion to remember is that the point reflecting in the metal edge at the BOTTOM of the image corresponds to the limit marked at the TOP of the test surface, and vice versa.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Finding the Family of Angles', the four numbered steps. The authors also record a reader's suggestion of a laser pointer as the test light and endorse it untested, writing that it should work well.
confounders: putting the test light where the main light will go, rather than at the camera
forgetting the top/bottom inversion, which is what makes the marked area interpretable
assuming the marked family must be filled exactly; the source says a source or gobo that exactly fits is almost never needed

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Position the Subject and Focus the Camera'
qa_items.question: Moving a glass closer to the camera improves its edge definition. The book insists this is not because bigger detail is easier to see. What is the actual reason?
qa_items.answer: It is because moving the subject toward the camera also moves it AWAY from the lighted background, and the closer a subject is to a lit background the more of that background falls inside the family of angles that acts on the glass edge. Light from those angles is exactly what obscures the edge, so increasing the subject-to-background distance reduces the light reaching the edge and the outline sharpens. The authors state the wrong explanation explicitly in order to reject it, which is worth noting: the observable effect and the plausible reason for it are different things here.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Position the Subject and Focus the Camera' in the bright-field sequence, repeated in the dark-field one.
confounders: the rejected explanation — larger detail is easier to see — which the source names and dismisses
attributing it to depth of field or focus, which the source addresses separately and says is negligible
thinking a larger background would help; the source says that is exactly what destroys the edge

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'A Transparent Background'
qa_items.question: A metal box stands on a sheet of clear glass. A polarizing filter on the lens turns the glass black and leaves the metal untouched. What makes the filter able to discriminate?
qa_items.answer: The two surfaces polarize differently. Most of the direct reflection from glass viewed at that angle is polarized, so a lens polarizer can extinguish it. Direct reflection from metal is never polarized unless the light source itself is polarized, so the same filter passes it and the metal is unaffected. The filter is not selecting by object or by brightness; it is selecting by a physical property the two materials do not share. The book is careful about the boundary elsewhere: the same trick fails for a black subject on glass, because much of a black subject's direct reflection is likely to be polarized too, so the filter that clears the table would probably blacken the subject as well.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'A Transparent Background', with the before-and-after photographs; the withdrawal for black subjects is in ch. 9, 'Keeping the Subject Away from the Background'. The conductor-versus-insulator guideline behind it is chapter-3 material and already live Canon.
confounders: assuming a polarizer reduces all reflections, which is the general belief the source contradicts
attributing the discrimination to the angle rather than to the material class
generalising the trick to any dark support, which the book explicitly blocks

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Using a Tent', the closing paragraph on tent size
qa_items.question: Building a bigger tent to move the camera farther from a mirrored sphere feels like it should shrink the camera's reflection. The book says the extra work is always wasted. Why?
qa_items.answer: Because the camera is the one reflection whose size cannot be reduced by moving it away. Moving the camera back does shrink its reflection — and shrinks the image of the subject by the same factor, so a longer lens is needed to restore the framing, and that enlarges the camera's reflection back to its original size. The ratio of the camera's reflection to the subject is constant. The authors state the intuition, grant that it is intuitive, and then close it off; they are equally candid that the tent itself does not solve the problem, since the dark camera hole and the tent seams reflect in the subject and must be retouched. Its real value, they say, is that it makes the retouching easier.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Using a Tent', final paragraphs. The tent photograph shows the reflected camera hole as small dark marks on the ornaments.
confounders: the intuition the source is refuting: distance shrinks reflections
assuming a tent removes all reflections; it removes the studio and substitutes its own hole and seams
confusing this with flat metal, where a shift lens really can take the camera out of the family of angles

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 'Traveling Light', sections 'Do the Colors Mix?' and 'The Remedies'
qa_items.question: Why can a single white-balance or global colour correction fix a scene lit by fluorescent light plus ceiling-bounced flash, but not the same room with the flash aimed at the subject?
qa_items.answer: Because of where the two colours meet. Bounced flash mixes with the fluorescent light before either reaches the scene, so the whole frame is lit by one new balance: the error is uniform, and a single global transform can remove it. Direct flash lights the foreground subject while the fluorescents light the rest, so different regions carry different errors, and whatever correction is right for one is wrong for the other — a compromise value leaves nothing in the scene right. The book calls these mixed and unmixed colour. Its remedy for the unmixed case is counter-intuitive: gel the sources so they match EACH OTHER as closely as possible, aiming for a single colour and not necessarily the correct one, and then let a global correction fix the whole scene. Its example is a light-green gel on the flash to approximate the overhead fluorescents.
qa_items.support: Ch. 10, 'Do the Colors Mix?' for the distinction and 'Correcting Unmixed Colors' for the remedy. The authors also flag a case that is easy to miss: a flash-cast shadow on a wall filled in by fluorescent light, which renders yellow-green.
confounders: assuming a better white balance or a more capable camera resolves the unmixed case; the source says none can
gelling the flash to be 'correct' rather than to match the ambient, which is the opposite of the advice
treating local retouching as the first answer; the source calls it tedious and a last resort

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Liquid as a Lens'
qa_items.question: A wine glass is photographed against a background that exactly fills the camera's frame, and the studio appears as a dark surround inside the bowl of the glass. What has happened, and why is the obvious fix barred?
qa_items.answer: A round transparent container filled with liquid is optically a lens, and it sees a wider field than the camera does. A background large enough to fill the camera's field of view is therefore not large enough to fill the field of view seen through the liquid, so the white rectangle in the centre of the glass is the background and the dark area around it is the rest of the studio. The obvious fix — a larger background, or one moved closer to increase its effective size — is barred because a background larger than the field of view extends into the family of angles acting on the glass edge and sacrifices the edge definition the whole chapter exists to protect. The book's remedy is to move the CAMERA closer and, if necessary, fit a shorter lens to hold the image size, so the existing background fills the area seen through the liquid. The stated cost is increased perspective distortion, visible as a deeper ellipse at the rim, which may or may not be acceptable in a given scene.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Liquid as a Lens', with the before-and-after wine-glass pair; the bar on enlarging the background comes from 'Position the Camera' earlier in the chapter.
confounders: enlarging or approaching the background, which is the natural move and the one the source rules out
assuming the dark surround is a vignetting or exposure problem
forgetting that the remedy costs perspective, which the source states plainly

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', sections 'The Distance of Light' and 'Doing the Impossible'
qa_items.question: The book says even illumination and glare-free illumination can be mutually exclusive goals on a flat subject. Set out the tension and the one solution it says always works — including why that solution is unusable at its limit.
qa_items.answer: The closer the source is to the camera axis, the more directly it lights the subject and the more even the illumination; the farther to the side it is, the less likely it is to fall inside the family of angles that produces direct reflection. So the two goals pull in opposite directions. A shallow side angle avoids the glare and overlights the near edge, and a second light on the far side does not fix it — you get two overexposed edges with a dark centre. Moving the light toward the camera evens the illumination and is likely to put it inside the family, which the authors call the worse problem. The only solution that always works is to move the light farther away: in theory a light at infinite distance produces exactly equal diffuse reflection at every point of the surface even at the most shallow angle. It is unusable at the limit because a light at an infinite distance is also likely to be infinitely dim. The practical answer is a compromise distance — far enough for acceptably even illumination, close enough for acceptable exposure times. The authors say they could give formulas and that the reader would not use them, and prescribe judging by eye and checking with a meter.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, 'The Distance of Light' and the opening of 'Doing the Impossible', where the mutual exclusivity is stated and the working-space consequence spelled out in two bullets.
confounders: adding a second light as the fix, which the source shows produces two hot edges rather than one
treating the infinite-distance case as the answer rather than as the limit that shows the direction
assuming a bigger softbox resolves it; the conflict is about position and distance, not softness

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'Fill Light', the silver-versus-white reflector discussion
qa_items.question: In a cramped tabletop set, when will a white fill card put more light on the subject than a silver one, and when is a silver card guaranteed to give a hard fill regardless of how big it is?
qa_items.answer: A silver card reflects directly, so it behaves as a mirror and has its own limited family of angles; its aim is critical, and in a crowded arrangement the only position available may be one from which it reflects no light to the subject at all. A white card reflects mostly diffusely, so its angle is much less critical, and from some positions it will therefore deliver more light than a silver one despite reflecting less overall. On hardness, a silver card produces a mirror image of the main light and inherits that light's size: a large silver card is a soft fill only if the main light is large, and if the main light is small the silver card is a hard fill regardless of its own size. A white reflector is the only reflector that can provide soft fill light from a small main light.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'Fill Light'. The reasoning is the family-of-angles idea applied to something that is not the subject — the reflector itself.
confounders: ranking the two by reflectance alone, so silver always wins
assuming a large reflector is always a soft source, which is only true for the diffuse case
forgetting the source's separate warning that fill bounced from a coloured background can colour a pale subject

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'The Glossy Box' compared with Ch. 6 'Metal Boxes'
qa_items.question: A glossy wooden box and a polished metal box present the same two families of angles from the same camera position. Why does the book spend a whole section removing direct reflection from one and go straight to creating it on the other?
qa_items.answer: Because the two surfaces have different channels available. A glossy non-metallic box that is not black produces both diffuse and direct reflection, and the direct reflection obscures the diffuse one that carries the wood's colour and grain — so the authors work through a ladder of remedies to suppress it. A polished metal box produces only direct reflection, and without it the box records as black; since they usually want metal to read bright, the job is to fill each family of angles rather than to vacate any. The book states the point explicitly: the theory is identical to that applied in the earlier picture, and the difference in material makes them likely to apply it the opposite way. It is the same author team inverting its own prescription because the surface class changed — not a contradiction and not a disagreement between sources.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'The Glossy Box'; Ch. 6, 'Metal Boxes', where the cross-reference and the inversion are both stated.
confounders: treating the two as inconsistent advice from one book
assuming the difference is about gloss level rather than about whether a diffuse channel exists
carrying the polarizer step across: it is a late resort for the glossy box and nearly useless on metal

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'Try a Polarizer'
qa_items.question: Chapter 4 offers a polarizer among the first remedies for competing surfaces; chapter 5 demotes it to a next-to-last resort for a glossy box. What optical reason do the authors give, and how should the apparent inconsistency be recorded?
qa_items.answer: The reason is that a glossy box usually carries polarized reflection on more than one side, and the reflection from one side is likely to be polarized perpendicular to the polarization of the other. So as the lens polarizer eliminates one polarized reflection it effectively increases another — the filter trades rather than solves. The authors therefore work through the geometric remedies first, so that whatever direct reflection remains is the single hardest case, and only then spend the polarizer on it. The apparent inconsistency should be recorded as the same authors qualifying their own earlier statement within a stated scope: the earlier advice was for competing flat surfaces in copy work, the later ordering is for a box with mutually perpendicular faces, and the source names the difference. It is not cross-source disagreement and must not be presented as two sources conflicting.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'Try a Polarizer', which states both the perpendicular-polarization reason and the ordering, and refers back to the previous chapter's advice.
confounders: reading it as the book contradicting itself
presenting it as a disagreement between two sources, which it is not — one author team, one work
assuming the polarizer is simply weak, rather than that it redistributes among faces

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', sidebar 'Using Light-polarizing Filters'
qa_items.question: Cross-polarizing the lights and the lens rescues an otherwise impossible copy job. The book still calls it a solution to avoid whenever possible. List the costs it actually names.
qa_items.answer: Five. First, exposure: two perfect polarizers should cost two stops in theory, but real ones carry a lot of neutral density, so the actual reduction is likely to be four to six stops — and worse in non-copy work, where diffusion material absorbs more still. Second, the consequences of those lost stops: the resulting aperture may be too wide to hold adequate depth of field, or the exposure long enough that subject or camera movement becomes hard to avoid. Third, heat: polarizing filters are damaged by it, so they must be kept off incandescent lights at a tested distance, and photographers using strobes leave them off until they are ready to shoot and turn the modelling lights off first. Fourth, a minor effect on colour balance. Fifth, the opportunity cost the authors state directly: understanding and controlling the size and angle of the source makes polarizing the source unnecessary in most situations, and some photographers go for years without needing it.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, the sidebar 'Using Light-polarizing Filters', which enumerates the drawbacks; the authors say they deliberately conceived the impossible copy problem as one of the rare cases where it is the only solution.
confounders: quoting the theoretical two stops as the working figure
treating it as a general glare cure rather than a rare last resort
missing the heat hazard, which the source treats as a practical safety matter with a test procedure

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', sections 'The Size of the Light' and 'Light on the Side'
qa_items.question: The book says a hard shadow often shows more depth than a soft one at the same grey. Does it conclude that hard lights are better, and what does it prescribe instead?
qa_items.answer: No. It states the observation — two shadows recording as the same grey are not equally visible, and the harder-edged one is more visible, which is why a hard shadow often increases the illusion of depth — and then immediately blocks the inference. A shadow that is too hard can be so visible that it competes with the primary subject. The authors say explicitly that they cannot offer firm rules about what size light is always best, and they leave the trade-off itself as the thing to reason with. Their worked answer for a tabletop subject is not to soften the shadow away but to MOVE it: the least distracting place is directly under and in front of the subject, which means the light goes above and slightly behind, and only then do they substitute a soft box to make the relocated shadow unobtrusive. Softening it out of existence entirely is rejected, because the shadow proves the subject is sitting on the table rather than floating above it.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'The Size of the Light' for the visibility claim, 'Light on the Side' and 'Light above the Subject' for the relocation and the grounding argument.
confounders: concluding hard light is better for product work because it shows more depth
softening the shadow to nothing, which loses the contact cue
assuming the source ranks light sizes; it explicitly declines to

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Photograph the Metal at an Angle' and 'Retouch the Reflection'
qa_items.question: Two of the four remedies for a camera reflecting in flat metal are not lighting solutions at all. Compare them on the terms the book uses.
qa_items.answer: Shooting the metal at an angle and correcting the geometry afterwards always results in some quality loss, and it requires composing with generous extra space because the trapezoidal projection has to be cropped to a rectangle; the authors call it a bad remedy that may be better than no remedy, to keep in mind if circumstances force it. Retouching the reflection out — shooting straight on, letting the camera reflect, and removing it afterwards — loses no image quality at all, and they say that for some subjects, especially large ones, it is so much easier than any lighting solution that it should not be forgotten. Their comparison is explicitly economic rather than optical: spending half a day lighting instead of half an hour at a computer makes no sense. They flag that it is not a lighting solution and decline to discuss it in detail, but they do not discourage it.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Keeping the Metal Square', the third and fourth sub-sections.
confounders: assuming a lighting book will always prefer the lighting answer
conflating the two: one loses quality, the other explicitly does not
reading the view-camera solution as equivalent; the source calls that the best solution and these the fallbacks

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'White-on-White' and 'Lighting Black-on-Black Scenes'
qa_items.question: Both extremes are described as mirror images of each other. On the availability of direct reflection they are not symmetrical in the obvious way. Explain what actually differs.
qa_items.answer: The asymmetry is in visibility, not in production. White-on-white scenes generally have as much direct reflection as any other scene; white subjects do not produce less of it. What happens is that their diffuse reflection is bright enough to overpower it, so the camera cannot see much direct reflection and manipulating it accomplishes little — which is why the white case is deprived of one of the book's favourite tools. Black subjects likewise do not produce any MORE direct reflection than others; theirs is simply more visible because it faces less competition from diffuse reflection. So the black case gets the tool back, and the authors' rule of thumb follows: light black-on-black as if it were metal, regardless of the actual material — find the family of angles and fill it.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, the opening of 'White-on-White' and the corresponding paragraphs of 'Lighting Black-on-Black Scenes'. The underlying mechanism — that visibility of the direct component is set by its ratio to the diffuse one — is chapter-3 material and already live Canon.
confounders: the natural but wrong reading: white things reflect diffusely, black things reflect directly
assuming the two cases are handled by inverting the same technique
forgetting the practical consequence, which is that the black case can borrow the metal chapter wholesale

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Defining the Surface of Glassware' and 'Position the Light'
qa_items.question: Compare a small bright highlight and a large dim one on the surface of a glass. What does the book say each does for the viewer, and what sets the difference in practice?
qa_items.answer: They do opposite jobs. The tiny bright spots are distracting at the least and meaningless at best: they are too small and too bright to tell the viewer anything about surface detail or texture. A large highlight informs — it serves the constructive purpose of saying how the glass surface looks and feels. In practice the difference is set by how much of the relevant family of angles is filled with light, and, with a diffusion sheet, by the distance from the lamp head to the sheet: close in, only the centre of the sheet lights and the highlight is small and bright; pulled back, the whole sheet lights and reflects as a larger highlight. The authors add that the larger highlight should usually be kept dimmer, because a brightly lit whole sheet reflects as an obvious hard-edged rectangle that advertises a studio light and costs the scene its reality — and that strips of black tape on the sheet can make the reflection read as a window instead.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Defining the Surface of Glassware', including the two matched highlight frames and the taped diffusion sheet.
confounders: assuming brighter highlights read as more premium or more glossy
attributing the difference to the size of the source alone, ignoring the lamp-to-diffuser distance
missing that the source deliberately makes the large highlight dimmer, not brighter

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'How Much Tonal Variation is Ideal?'
qa_items.question: Why does the book say a simple cube can be lit with a black shadow and a white highlight while a product package usually cannot, and what does it refuse to give you?
qa_items.answer: Because of where the detail is. A simple cube with no important detail on any of its sides can take the full range — the shadow can go black and the highlight white. A package that has to sell a product may have important detail on all three visible sides, and detail in either extreme would be lost, so the highlight must be only slightly brighter and the shadow only slightly darker than the third side. The depth clue is deliberately weakened in exchange for legibility. What the authors refuse to give is a number: they say they never specify lighting ratios in the book because the decision has to be based on the specific subject as well as personal taste. Their stated ideal — a highlight side, a shadow side and a side between — is offered as a standard for evaluating whatever lighting exists, not as a requirement good lighting must meet.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'How Much Tonal Variation is Ideal?', which states both the refusal and the package case in the same short section.
confounders: supplying a ratio anyway; the source's position is that it will not
treating the highlight/shadow/mid ideal as a rule rather than as an evaluation standard
assuming the package needs MORE contrast to look three-dimensional, which inverts the advice

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'What Is a "Normal" Exposure for Metal?'
qa_items.question: A brightly lit metal spatula sits on white paper. A grey-card reading gives a good exposure for the paper and ruins the metal; exposing for the metal renders the paper dark grey. What does the book say to do, and what does it say NOT to do?
qa_items.answer: It says there is no normal exposure that works for both, and that if the metal and the white paper are both important the scene has to be relit. What not to do is look for an exposure compromise: the general rule of placing the middle greys accurately and letting the extremes fall where they may fails whenever the important subject is much brighter than an 18% grey card, because a near-pure direct reflection records at about the brightness of the source rather than at a reflectance of the illuminated scene. When the metal alone matters, the method is a spot reading on the metal opened two to three stops beyond the indicated value — the meter would place it at 18% grey and it should be brighter, and how much brighter is a creative decision. The relight the authors have in mind is their "elegant compromise": light filling the family of angles to make the metal bright, plus light from other angles producing diffuse reflection from the background.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'What Is a "Normal" Exposure for Metal?' and 'The Elegant Compromise'. The advertisement needing legible black type on the paper is the source's own example of the conflict.
confounders: splitting the difference in exposure, which the source says cannot work
using an incident or grey-card reading, which the source says is fine only when the metal is DARK
treating the two-to-three-stop figure as a technical constant rather than a creative range

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Shoot the Picture' in the dark-field sequence
qa_items.question: The edge highlights in a dark-field glass shot are far too small for an ordinary meter. What proxy does the book use, and why does it then insist on a bracket?
qa_items.answer: The proxy is the light source itself. Because a pure direct reflection is as bright as the source that produces it, the reflections may be too small to read but the large source is not: place the meter close enough to read the source alone, read the EDGE of the source because that is the part illuminating the glass, and open two stops to place it near white rather than at the meter's assumed 18% grey. The bracket is required because that exposure is only correct if the highlight on the glass is a perfect un-polarized direct reflection, and in practice there is no realistic chance of it being both. So the authors treat that value as a theoretical starting point and try one, two and three stops more. They also note that a correct instrument would be a spot meter of much less than one degree, that few photographers own one, and that bracketing with a conventional meter is an acceptably close approximation — an explicit substitution of procedure for instrument.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, the 'Shoot the Picture' step of the dark-field sequence. The source-brightness fact and the dimming of polarized reflection are both chapter-3 material and already live Canon.
confounders: metering the background, which is the bright-field procedure, not this one
treating the two-stop opening as the final answer rather than the start of a bracket
trying to lighten a dark-field background by increasing exposure, which the source says overexposes the subject

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Dulling Spray'; Ch. 5, section 'Use Dulling Spray'
qa_items.question: Dulling spray is the last rung of two separate remedy ladders in this book. What does it physically do, what does it cost, and how do the authors' warning and their own practice compare?
qa_items.answer: It creates a matte surface that increases diffuse reflection and decreases direct reflection, which buys a little freedom to light without strictly obeying the limits of the family of angles. The costs are stated plainly. Metal with dulling spray on it no longer looks brightly polished and may not even look like metal. On a glossy box it can reduce the sharpness of the very detail it was applied to preserve, and if that detail is fine type the loss of sharpness may be worse than the loss of contrast it was curing. And the chemistry may not agree with the subject, so a small and hopefully insignificant area must be tested first. The authors add that heavy-handed use reveals rather than conceals an inability to light metal well — and immediately admit that all three of them keep dulling spray handy in their studios. Their prescription is to light as well as possible first and then add a little, only to an overly bright highlight or a disappearing edge, keeping as much gleam as possible.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Dulling Spray', and the parallel treatment at the end of the glossy-box ladder in ch. 5.
confounders: treating it as a general anti-glare tool rather than a last resort
missing that it changes what the material looks like it IS, not only how bright it is
reading the authors' warning as a prohibition; they concede they use it

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'Using a Translucent White Background' and 'Using a Mirror Background'
qa_items.question: Compare a translucent white background and a mirror background for a white-on-white subject, on the two things the book says each costs or gives.
qa_items.answer: A translucent background lit from behind decouples subject and background entirely — with a reasonably opaque subject the background can be taken to any brightness without affecting the subject — and it costs the ground shadow, because light from beneath erases any hint of one. The authors then turn that cost into an advantage: because the shadow is now independent of the subject's lighting, it can be manufactured by tracing a pleasing test-light shadow onto paper, cutting it out and gluing the cut-out under the panel. A mirror is the easiest white background of all, because it reflects almost nothing but direct reflection and those reflections are much brighter than any diffuse white; a light large enough to fill the whole background's family of angles usually produces shadows soft enough that no fill is needed, and it is one of the few arrangements where the background reflects fill light under the subject. Its costs are that the light must show no texture, since it will be sharply reflected, that the subject's own reflection may be confusing depending on crop and shape, and that no ground shadow is obtainable at all.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Using a Translucent White Background' and 'Using a Mirror Background', with the flower photographed on each.
confounders: assuming the mirror produces a shadow the way any table would
treating both as simply 'brighter backgrounds' rather than as different reflection mechanisms
forgetting the mirror's requirement that the source itself be featureless

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Minimizing the Horizon'
qa_items.question: Why does the book say the table under a piece of glassware is an optical problem and not just a compositional one, and what does it rank as the options?
qa_items.answer: Because an opaque table blocks light that is essential for edge definition — light that has to reach the lower edges of the subject from below and behind — which a transparent one passes as if the table did not exist. The usual compositional cures fight the requirement that the background barely fill the image area, so a bigger table or a taller sweep is not available. The options, in order of how completely they remove the horizon: a transparent glass or acrylic table, which the authors say resembles a nonexistent table more closely than anything else; a mirror, whose reflected background softens the tonal step and which can light glass surfaces almost as well as a transparent table, at the cost of a visible but less obtrusive horizon; and, where the horizon must go entirely, a paper strip taped to a large diffusion panel and cut to fit the field of view exactly, which they say costs no lighting quality. For either transparent surface they add a variation: mist it with water to disrupt and camouflage the subject's reflection.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Minimizing the Horizon', including the explicit statement that an opaque table blocks light essential for edge definition.
confounders: treating the horizon purely as a composition problem to be cropped or swept away
using white or silver reflectors on a dark table, which the source says is less effective because one light serves both
assuming a mirror removes the horizon; the source says it reduces it

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Metal Boxes' and 'A Light Background'
qa_items.question: A brief calls for a metal tin standing on a dark surface, shot so all three of its faces show. The tin's front face keeps going black and its bottom edge dissolves into the table. Using this book's reasoning, what is happening and what is its easiest answer?
qa_items.answer: Each visible face of the tin has its own family of angles, and they face different directions. The family defined by the FRONT face falls on the table where the tin stands, so the table is the light source for that face whether or not the photographer wants it to be — and a dark table is a source that emits almost nothing, so the front face has nothing to reflect and records black. The bottom edge dissolves for the related reason: a near-pure direct reflector records at about the brightness of what it reflects, and where the tin's lower face and the surface it stands on reach the same brightness there is no tonal boundary left for the camera to record. No reflector card fixes this without appearing in the frame, because the family it must occupy is inside the picture; the authors say brightly polished metal boxes almost always exhibit the problem. Their easiest answer is a light-toned background: the background itself becomes the light source for much of the visible metal, and much of the work is done as soon as the tin is placed on it. The one requirement they stress is that the background must be large enough to fill the family of angles the metal reflects, not merely the area the camera sees.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Metal Boxes' for the three-families problem and the table-as-source consequence; 'A Light Background' for the remedy and the fill-the-family-not-the-frame requirement; 'Other Resources' for the disappearing-edge mechanism. Shown in the pair of gift-box photographs on dark and light grounds.
confounders: adding a front fill light, which either fails to enter the family or appears in the shot
raising the exposure, which cannot help a surface with no diffuse channel
sizing the background to the frame rather than to the family of angles

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Keeping True Color' and 'Liquid as a Lens'
qa_items.question: A client wants a chilled amber lager against a textured slate-blue backdrop. The first frames show a dark, murky brown drink. Diagnose it in the book's terms and describe the fix it prescribes, step by step.
qa_items.answer: The diagnosis is the book's stated rule that a liquid in a transparent container always takes on some of the colour and texture of its background: the mottled mid-toned backdrop is showing through the beer, and the drink is reading dark and unappealing as a result. The fix is a secondary background — a white or silver card sitting immediately behind the glass, lit separately, shaped so it fills as much of the area behind the liquid as possible without extending far enough to be visible past the edges of the glass. The authors build it in five steps: place the card behind the subject on a flexible wire taped to the table, not yet fixed; remove the camera and put a test light in its place, so the subject casts its shadow on the card; outline that shadow, take the card away and cut it out; reposition the cut-out, restore the camera, and check through the lens that no edge of the card is visible; then add a light that illuminates only the cut-out. They note that some photographers prefer a foil coloured like the liquid — gold for beer — rather than white or silver.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Keeping True Color', including the five numbered steps and the before-and-after beer photographs. The two-sided size constraint is what makes the tracing step necessary.
confounders: changing the backdrop, which the client has specified
colour-grading the beer afterwards, which the source does not offer here and which would not restore the transmitted texture
using a card larger than the glass, which the source's constraint explicitly forbids

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Secondary Opaque Subjects'
qa_items.question: A labelled glass bottle has to look premium and its label has to be legible. The lighting that gives the bottle its describing highlight puts a sheen across the paper. Work through the book's options and say which it rules out and why.
qa_items.answer: The conflict is real and the book states it: most of a paper's reflection is diffuse but some is direct, so the light producing the direct reflection on the glass is also likely to obscure the label. Two remedies work. Move the offending light higher, so the label's direct reflection goes downward instead of toward the lens. Or, where good highlight placement forbids moving the light, interpose a small opaque card blocking exactly the angles that produce direct reflection on the label — and its size is critical: a gobo extending beyond the label's own family of angles will itself reflect in the glass. A polarizing filter is the third option and the book rules it out in most cases: much of the desirable highlight on the glass is usually polarized already, so a polarizer that eliminates the label's reflection is also likely to interfere with the light the glass needs. Underneath all three sits the prior question the authors insist comes first — which of the two is the principal subject — and they say that cannot be settled on a technical basis at all.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Secondary Opaque Subjects' for the three options and the gobo size constraint; 'Recognizing the Principal Subject' for the prior decision.
confounders: reaching for the polarizer first, which is the intuitive move and the one the source blocks here
oversizing the gobo, which converts a label fix into a black reflection in the glass
treating this as a legibility defect rather than as a scene lit for the wrong principal subject

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Keeping the Metal Bright', 'Keeping the Metal Dark' and 'The Elegant Compromise'
qa_items.question: You are handed a brushed-steel flask and told it should read as a light mid-grey, sitting on a background that reads near-white, in one frame. Using only what this book gives you, how do you get both?
qa_items.answer: Treat the two surfaces as reading different parts of the same source. The flask, being close to a pure direct reflector, responds only to whatever lies inside its family of angles; the background responds to the whole source through diffuse reflection. So one large soft source can serve both: the portion of it covering the family sets the flask's tone, and the whole of it sets the background's. Having more of the source inside the family makes the metal brighter; a source large enough that little of it falls inside makes the background brighter instead. Then use distance as the second control, since the background follows the inverse square law and the metal's direct reflection does not — moving the light closer lifts the background toward white while the flask holds its tone exactly. The book's phrase for this is the elegant compromise, and the claim worth taking from it is that the metal's tone is placeable at any step between black and white independently of the rest of the scene. The bound to watch is the lens: from a close viewpoint the family is wide and the source may only just fill it, in which case the light cannot be moved without the flask's edges going black.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'The Elegant Compromise' for the single-soft-box arrangement, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light' for both the distance control and the lens bound. The matched spatula frames show the tonal independence directly.
confounders: using two lights and balancing their power, which works but misses that one large source already gives the control
expecting the metal to brighten when the light comes closer
ignoring the lens constraint, which is what makes the control fail from a close viewpoint

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'The Best of Both Worlds'
qa_items.question: A photographer puts a set of glassware inside a white tent to get rid of the studio reflections, and the glass loses its outline entirely. Explain the failure using the book's own account, and say what it prescribes for a frame that genuinely needs both fields.
qa_items.answer: The tent removed the extraneous reflections and removed the edges with them. The part of the tent the camera saw became a light background, while the rest of the tent lit the glass — which is the light-on-light combination, and the one arrangement that cannot define an edge, because edge definition requires a tonal difference between the edge and the ground immediately behind it. The book attributes most failures in photographing glass to using bright field and dark field simultaneously, deliberately or naively, and it names this specific case. Where a picture genuinely needs both, the prescription is not to blend them but to keep them separate: divide the scene mentally, assign one region to bright field and the other to dark field. Wherever the two remain distinct the glass is well defined; only the transition area mixes them, and there can be a noticeable loss there, so the transition should be kept small. Note also that the tent is the remedy the same book recommends for round metal — right subject, wrong subject.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'The Best of Both Worlds', which reports the tent failure and gives the divide-the-scene prescription; Ch. 6, 'Using a Tent', for the contrasting recommendation.
confounders: adding a light to 'bring back' the edges, which is the light-on-light problem again
assuming the tent was too bright or too dim; the failure is structural, not a level
carrying a metal solution to glass because both are direct reflectors

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', sections 'The Angle of Light' and 'The Success and Failure of the General Rule'
qa_items.question: A photographer copies a small painting with lights at 45 degrees and gets a clean result; the same 45-degree set-up on a large canvas in a narrow gallery produces a hot spot. Nothing about the angle changed. What did?
qa_items.answer: Two distances. The book's correction to the 45-degree copy rule is that an angle stated to the CENTRE of a subject does not fix the angles to its edges, and that whether a light falls inside the family of angles depends on both the light-to-subject distance and the camera-to-subject distance. Two lights both at 45 degrees to the centre of the same subject can differ: the nearer one is inside the family and puts a hot spot on the surface, the farther one is outside it and lights the surface cleanly. Separately, working close to a large canvas with a wide lens enlarges the family of angles substantially and shrinks the range of acceptable lighting angles, so the light has to go much farther to the side than it did before. The authors add why the rule usually survives in practice anyway: photographers tend to move lights back for an unrelated reason, to get even illumination, and that incidentally takes them outside the family.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, 'The Angle of Light' for the wide-lens case and 'The Success and Failure of the General Rule' for the two-lights-at-45-degrees comparison.
confounders: assuming the angle rule is simply wrong; the source says it usually works and explains why
blaming the lens rather than the viewpoint the lens permitted
moving the light closer to even out the illumination, which is exactly the move that puts it in the family

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', section 'Subject and Background' (both halves)
qa_items.question: A packshot of a white ceramic diffuser on white shows clean separation and good detail, and the art director says it reads as "product on grey" rather than white-on-white. Nothing is technically wrong. What does this book say has happened, and what is the fix?
qa_items.answer: The lighting has put the extreme on the wrong element. Technically it does not matter which of the subject and background is the slightly darker — either way the tonal distinction is preserved and the shape is legible. Psychologically it matters a great deal: the brain is less willing to accept a grey background than a white one, so a scene lit to render the background white and the subject light grey reads as white-on-white, while the same scene relit so the subject is white and the background light grey reads as white-on-gray. The authors demonstrate exactly this with two frames of the same bust and say the second is not a bad picture, only not a white-on-white one. The fix is to relight so the BACKGROUND carries the extreme and the subject sits just inside it — for their examples, between half a stop and one stop darker at its edges. The same asymmetry holds in reverse at the dark end: a dark-grey subject on a black ground reads as black-on-black, a black subject on a dark-grey ground does not.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Subject and Background' in the white-on-white half, with the two bust frames, and the parallel passage in the black-on-black half with the crow.
confounders: brightening everything, which loses the separation the frame currently has
treating it as a colour-temperature or white-balance issue
assuming the subject should be the whitest thing in a white-on-white picture

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'Using an Opaque Black Background' and 'Using a Glossy Black Surface'
qa_items.question: A matte black cosmetics compact has to be photographed on black, keeping detail in the product and a truly black ground. Black seamless paper is on hand. Walk through what this book says will happen and what to do.
qa_items.answer: Black paper is one of the worst common choices, and the authors discuss it first only because it is usually the one available. The paper directly under the subject receives as much illumination as the subject, and since the compact has to be rendered dark grey rather than black to hold detail, the paper under it cannot be black either. A spotlight would keep the background darker but is ruled out, because producing direct reflection on the subject — which is how a black subject is rendered at all — requires a large source. Two things follow. First, replace the paper with a material producing less diffuse reflection than the subject: black velvet, at the same exposure, records far darker than the paper. Second, light the compact as if it were metal — find the family of angles and fill it. Velvet has two stated limits: a few subjects are so black that even velvet is not blacker, and the subject's edges may merge with its own shadow. For those edges the book offers glossy black acrylic and invisible light, at the cost that the overhead source then fills the acrylic's own family and the ground stops being black; the clean alternative is distance, putting the subject far enough from the background that lighting one does not touch the other.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Lighting Black-on-Black Scenes' through 'Keeping the Subject Away from the Background', with the paper-versus-velvet pair at identical exposure.
confounders: underexposing to darken the ground, which takes the subject's detail with it
using a spot or snoot to hold the background down, which the source rules out because the subject needs a large source
reaching for the glass support and polarizer that worked for metal, which the source withdraws for black subjects

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'A Transparent Background'; Ch. 9 'The Extremes', section 'Keeping the Subject Away from the Background'
qa_items.question: The transparent-glass support with a lens polarizer works beautifully under a metal box. A photographer tries it under a black lacquered box and the subject goes dead. Why, and what does that tell you about when the trick is available?
qa_items.answer: The trick depends on the two surfaces polarizing DIFFERENTLY. Under metal it works because most of the direct reflection from the glass at that angle is polarized while direct reflection from metal is never polarized unless the light source itself is polarized — so the filter extinguishes the support's reflection and passes the subject's. A black lacquered box is an insulator, and much of a black subject's direct reflection is likely to be polarized too, so the filter cannot discriminate: whatever orientation clears the table also darkens the subject, and since the subject is being rendered by direct reflection in the first place, killing it kills the subject. The general rule the case teaches is that a polarizer discriminates between two surfaces only where those surfaces differ in polarization — so the availability of the trick is a question about the two MATERIALS, not about the geometry. The book withdraws it explicitly in the extremes chapter, which is the same authors qualifying their own earlier prescription rather than a disagreement between sources.
