qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'A Transparent Background', for the working case; Ch. 9, 'Keeping the Subject Away from the Background', for the explicit withdrawal. The conductor-versus-insulator guideline is chapter-3 material and already live Canon.
confounders: rotating the polarizer harder, as if the failure were a matter of angle
concluding polarizers do not work on dark subjects at all, which over-generalises
reading the withdrawal as an inconsistency in the book

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Stopping Flare'; Ch. 9, section 'In Any Case, Keep the Background Small'
qa_items.question: A set of dark-field glass frames comes back looking flat and slightly milky, with no visible streak or fogged corner anywhere. Is flare a plausible cause on this book's account, and what would you do?
qa_items.answer: Yes, and the absence of visible streaking is not evidence against it. The book calls the basic dark-field arrangement probably the worst flare-producing arrangement one could encounter, because the very thing that makes it work — a large source surrounding a small dark background — puts non-imaging light just outside the field of view on all four sides at once. It states that even where the flare is not bad enough to produce visible fogging or streaking, the general degradation from all sides accumulates, and at best produces a picture with low contrast. The same invisible-uniform failure is named again in the extremes chapter for large white backgrounds. The remedy is a gobo that blocks non-imaging light from all four sides of the field of view — four cardboard blades, or a single board with a rectangular hole, clamped to a stand in front of the camera — positioned by the book's own trick of looking into the front of the lens and moving the card until the offending source is no longer reflected there, then pulling back slightly.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Stopping Flare'; the gobo-positioning trick is from the ch. 5 sidebar 'Managing Flare'; the parallel white-background case is in ch. 9.
confounders: ruling out flare because nothing is visibly streaked, which is the specific error the source warns against
raising contrast in post, which treats the symptom
gobo-ing only the top, which is standard practice and inadequate here

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'Light the Subject from Above' and 'Use a Gobo Above the Subject'
qa_items.question: A white-on-white packshot lit from above has good separation at the sides of the subject and has lost the top of it entirely into the background. What does the book prescribe, and how is the prescription tuned?
qa_items.answer: Lighting from above puts the front of the subject slightly in shadow and fully illuminates the tabletop, which is what gives the good side separation — and it also fully illuminates the top of the subject, which is why the top has gone. The prescription is a gobo above the subject, casting just enough shadow on its top to bring that area down to a brightness similar to the front. The authors say this step is almost always necessary. It is tuned by two coupled controls: the closer the gobo is to the subject the harder its shadow becomes, and the farther away the softer but also the lighter. So start with a gobo about the size of the offending highlight, hold it in your hand while experimenting, and move it until the edge of its shadow blends with the edge of the highlight you are concealing. If the shadow blends but is too dark, cut the gobo smaller; if it becomes too light as you move away, use a larger one. They recommend a medium-sized main light from the start precisely to keep this adjustment available — too small and the gobo's shadow cannot be made soft enough, too large and it cannot be made hard enough to shade effectively.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Using an Opaque White Background', the two steps and the tuning paragraphs, with the before-and-after bust frames.
confounders: moving the main light instead, which restores the top and loses the side separation
getting the distance rule backwards — closer is harder, not softer
using a very large or very small main light, either of which removes the gobo's adjustment range

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', section 'Use a Gobo Above the Subject', the shallow-subject case
qa_items.question: Where does the gobo-above technique stop working, and what does the book offer instead?
qa_items.answer: It fails on very shallow subjects. The gobo works by shading the top of the subject more than the background behind it, and it can do that because the background is farther from the gobo than the subject is, so the gobo's shadow arrives on the background softer and often imperceptibly. On a tall enough subject there may be no perceptible shadow on the background at all. In the extreme case the authors name — a white business card on a white table — it is impossible to put a shadow on the card without shading the background equally, because the two are at effectively the same distance. In those situations they say the answer is one of the other backgrounds discussed later in the chapter, a translucent white background or a mirror, both of which decouple the lighting of subject and background entirely; or, failing that, masking or retouching after the photograph is made.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Use a Gobo Above the Subject', final paragraph, and the sections on the translucent and mirror backgrounds that follow.
confounders: trying a smaller or harder gobo, which cannot separate two coplanar surfaces
assuming the technique fails because the subject is small rather than because it is flat
forgetting that the source explicitly permits retouching as the fallback here

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', section 'Using a Translucent White Background', the manufactured-shadow procedure
qa_items.question: A backlit translucent panel gives perfect subject-to-background separation for a pale product and leaves it apparently floating, with no ground shadow at all. The book turns this into an advantage. How?
qa_items.answer: Because the shadow can now be controlled completely independently of the lighting of the subject. The procedure: turn off every light intended for the actual exposure; set up a test light purely to cast a pleasing shadow, without caring whether that light would be any good for the subject; slide a sheet of opaque or semi-opaque paper under the subject to act as a custom gobo, and trace the shadow pattern onto it in pencil; remove the paper and cut the pattern out; glue the cut-out under the translucent background; turn the test light off and light the subject in any manner you please. The shadow in the finished frame was not cast by the light illuminating the subject, and the authors say it certainly looks as though it was. This is the same tracing device they use twice elsewhere in the book — for the family of angles with a test light at the lens, and for the cut secondary background behind a glass of liquid.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Using a Translucent White Background', which gives the step sequence and cross-references its own earlier uses of the tracing method.
confounders: adding a second light to cast a real shadow, which would also fall on the backlit panel
assuming the test light must be a good light for the subject; the source says explicitly it need not be
confusing this with a mirror background, where no ground shadow is obtainable at all

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Keeping the Metal Dark'
qa_items.question: A brief calls for a steel component to read almost black in a soft, evenly lit scene. Simply putting the light near the camera does keep the metal dark and the authors reject the result. What is wrong with it, and what do they build instead?
qa_items.answer: What is wrong is not the metal's tone but the shadows: the position of the soft shadows that arrangement produces does nothing to delineate the shape of the object, so the component reads dark and formless. The arrangement they build instead uses the marked family of angles directly. Assume the white target used to find the family was much larger than the minimum needed to fill it. Back the light up so it illuminates that entire diffusion sheet as evenly as possible, then attach a gobo cut to barely fill the family of angles. Every point of the sheet except the family lights the scene, so the light is large and soft while the metal stays black. Two practical notes: the white test target must be removed if it is not being used as the source, because left in place it would reflect the general illumination and act as an additional light; and the technique fails with an opaque white reflector card, because the light illuminating the card also illuminates the gobo, which then behaves more like a reflector than a blocker even if it is black — though the authors concede that hybrid might be the most pleasing compromise of all.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Keeping the Metal Dark', including the removal of the test surface and the reflector-card failure condition.
confounders: keeping the light near the camera and accepting the shadowless result
leaving the white finding-target in place, which quietly re-lights the metal
using a front-lit reflector card with a black gobo, which the source says does not work as a blocker

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Round Metal' and its three remedies
qa_items.question: A polished sphere has to be photographed and the camera keeps appearing dead in the middle of it. Rank the book's three remedies and say what each actually achieves.
qa_items.answer: First the constraint: the family of angles for round metal is practically the whole environment including the camera, the camera's reflection always falls exactly at the centre of the subject where it is most noticeable, and there are no view-camera tricks to move it out. So all three remedies are mitigations. Camouflage means any desirable clutter that makes the unwanted reflection less obvious — an irregular surface where the reflection can fall between the cracks, or additional subjects appropriate to the scene whose reflections break it up; the authors describe using ribbon and greenery this way on a department store catalogue cover. Keeping the light off the camera works because a camera in the dark cannot see itself reflected: confine the lighting to the subject, work farther away with a longer lens so less stray light falls on the camera, or cover it with black cloth or a black card with a hole — though that only works in a studio large enough that the surrounding walls do not reflect. A tent makes the environment and the source the same white enclosure, and the authors are candid that by itself it does not solve the problem: the dark camera hole and the tent seams reflect in the subject and must be retouched. Its value is that it makes the retouching easier.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Round Metal' through 'Using a Tent', with the untented and tented ornament photographs.
confounders: expecting one of the three to remove the reflection outright; none does
building a larger tent to shrink the camera's reflection, which the source shows is always wasted
assuming a black-covered camera works anywhere; the source restricts it to a large studio

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces'; Ch. 5, 'The Glossy Box'
qa_items.question: A lacquered wooden gift box has to show both its high-gloss finish and the grain and colour of the wood beneath. Using this book, how do you get both in one frame, and where does the same book warn you the approach can go wrong?
qa_items.answer: Treat it as a complex surface — one that needs both diffuse and direct reflection — and divide the surface rather than compromising across it. The authors' method is to position a source large enough to fill the entire family of angles required to produce direct reflection over the whole lid, so the gloss is available everywhere, and then block part of that source with a gobo so one region of the lid produces only diffuse reflection. In their frame the direct reflection sits camera-left and shows the gloss, and the diffusely lit camera-right region shows the grain and the true colour — and they note that the diffuse region is the only place the true colour of the wood is clearly apparent. The warning comes from the glossy-box section of the next chapter: on a three-dimensional box each visible face has its own family of angles facing a different direction, so the same large source that gives a pleasing gloss on the lid may put direct reflection on the sides too, and the ladder of geometric remedies — darker background, light toward the camera, camera height, falloff, black card on the tabletop, tipping the box, longer lens — exists for exactly that.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, 'Complex Surfaces', for the divided-surface method; Ch. 5, 'The Glossy Box', for the multi-face complication and the ordered remedies.
confounders: using a medium source everywhere and accepting a partial gloss, which shows neither property well
removing the direct reflection entirely to save the grain, which loses the finish
assuming the lid solution transfers unchanged to the sides, which face different directions

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces', the closing figure
qa_items.question: The book says adding a three-dimensional object to a glossy flat surface both improves the picture and makes the lighting easier. Why does it help, and why does the chapter drop the idea immediately?
qa_items.answer: It helps because the object's reflection in the surface is unambiguous evidence of gloss in a way that a featureless bright area is not: the reflection of a pair of eyeglasses in a polished lid tells the viewer the wood is glossy, and the authors say adding a secondary subject reveals the surface better than they are likely to render it alone. It makes the lighting easier for the same reason — the proof of the finish no longer has to be carried entirely by the shaped highlight. The chapter drops it because it had committed at the outset to two-dimensional and nearly two-dimensional subjects, and the authors say they cannot pursue the approach far without breaking that promise; three-dimensional subjects are the next chapter's business. So the claim is stated and demonstrated but deliberately not developed.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, 'Complex Surfaces', final paragraphs, with the eyeglasses-on-the-box frame.
confounders: reading the secondary object as a composition device rather than as evidence about the surface
assuming the book recommends it generally; it raises it and sets it aside for structural reasons
confusing it with camouflage on round metal, which hides an unwanted reflection rather than supplying a wanted one

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'Making Portraits', section 'Eyeglasses'
qa_items.question: A portrait sitter wears large eyeglasses and the main light reflects in them. The photographer's instinct is to raise the light. What does this book say about that, and what does it call the only solution that always works?
qa_items.answer: Raising the light might clear the reflection, but the authors say that depending on the size and shape of the glasses, by the time it is high enough it might fill the eye with shadow — so it is not reliable. The only solution that always works, in their words, is to change from short lighting to broad lighting, moving the main light to the same side as the visible ear. It works because that position puts the main light outside the family of angles that the eyeglass lenses define, which is the same reasoning the book applies to any mirror-like surface. Two corollaries follow. The size of that family scales with the diameter of the eyeglass lenses, so the problem is worse with big glasses. And with small lenses a smaller main light can sometimes preserve short lighting, because a smaller source is easier to position entirely outside the family.
qa_items.support: Ch. 8, 'Eyeglasses'. Broad and short lighting are named in the preceding section by the position of the main light relative to the sitter's visible ear.
confounders: raising the light, which the source says can fill the eye with shadow
treating broad-versus-short purely as a stylistic preference; here it is an optical necessity
cross-polarizing the light and lens, which the source blocks for portraits on separate grounds

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'Making Portraits', sections 'Eyeglasses' and 'Dark Skin'
qa_items.question: A still-life photographer moving to portraits proposes cross-polarizing the main light and the lens to eliminate eyeglass glare once and for all. What does the book say goes wrong, and what does the same fact about skin let you do elsewhere?
qa_items.answer: Human skin itself produces a small amount of direct reflection, and eliminating all direct reflection in the highlights of a portrait may give the skin a lifeless appearance — so the technique that rescues an impossible copy job is blocked here, because it removes something the picture needs. The same fact is a resource in the other direction. Because direct reflection is most visible on a dark surface, a dark complexion is best rendered not by opening the aperture — which would ruin any light-toned subject in the same frame, the book's example being a bride's white dress — but by increasing the direct reflection from the skin. That means a much larger source: a human head is roughly spherical, so the family of angles producing a large direct reflection on it is itself large, and the authors are explicit that a slight increase in light size offers almost no improvement while the larger the light the better the result. The aperture may still need opening a little, but not much.
qa_items.support: Ch. 8, the closing paragraphs of 'Eyeglasses' and the section 'Dark Skin'. The mechanism — that direct reflection shows most where diffuse reflection is weak — is chapter-3 material and already live Canon.
confounders: carrying the copy-work cross-polarization technique into portraits unchanged
increasing exposure for dark skin, which the source shows fails as soon as anything light is in frame
enlarging the light a little, which the source says achieves almost nothing on a roughly spherical subject

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'Overexposure', 'Underexposure' and 'Exposing White-on-White Scenes'
qa_items.question: "Shoot it bright and pull it down later" is offered as a safe habit for a white-on-white packshot. On this book's account, is it safe, and what does it prescribe instead?
qa_items.answer: It is not safe, and the reason is that compression at the extremes is not recoverable. Increased exposure relieves shadow compression and makes highlight compression much worse; darkening the frame afterwards restores the overall tonality without restoring any distinction among the highlights, and the authors show that the corrected version still offers little additional separation between highlight tones. A white-on-white scene is already recorded on the least favourable part of the curve, so brightening it pushes exactly the tones that matter further into the compressed region. Their prescription is the opposite: reduce exposure by up to two and a half stops, which in practice means metering the white subject and using the reading WITHOUT the routine two-and-a-half-stop white correction, so the subject sits on the straighter part of the curve and away from the shoulder — then lift it in reproduction. They give two reasons: the reduced exposure reserves more choices for later, and the sensor's response is not perfectly linear either. The one warning attached is a secondary black subject in the same scene, which will then lack shadow detail.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, 'Overexposure' and 'Underexposure' for the unrecoverability, 'Exposing White-on-White Scenes' for the prescription and its caveat.
confounders: the modern habit of exposing to the right, which is the specific move this passage argues against for this scene type
assuming Raw removes the problem; the source says the straightened curve looks flat and the compression is reintroduced deliberately
applying the reduced exposure to a scene containing an important black element

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'The Extremes', sections 'Exposing White-on-White Scenes' and 'Exposing Black-on-Black Scenes'
qa_items.question: The book gives the same magnitude — up to two and a half stops — for both extremes, in opposite directions. Are the reasons the same, and what single condition breaks both shortcuts?
qa_items.answer: The magnitude matches and the reasons only partly do. Both shifts move the scene toward the middle of the curve, where the least detail is lost, and both are undone afterwards in reproduction. The white-on-white reduction is justified by the curve's shoulder and by reserving choices for later. The black-on-black increase has an additional and different ground: digital noise in the shadow steps, which may be unnoticeable in a normal scene but is apparent in a black-on-black one — and the authors say that because of noise they are more likely actually to use the full extreme at the dark end. The condition that breaks both shortcuts is the same: a secondary subject at the opposite extreme. Reduced exposure leaves an important black subject without shadow detail; increased exposure overexposes any light-grey secondary subject. Whether it matters is explicitly a psychological judgement about that subject's importance and size, not a technical one, and the authors say it is entirely reasonable to expose two technically identical scenes differently on that basis.
qa_items.support: Ch. 9, the two exposing sections. The noise ground is stated as depending on camera quality and as present to some extent in all cameras at the time of writing.
confounders: treating the two as a symmetric rule with one reason
assuming the noise argument applies equally at the highlight end
reading the secondary-subject test as a measurement rather than a judgement of importance

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Capitalizing on Diffuse Reflections'
qa_items.question: The book says diffuse reflection tells you very little about what a surface is made of. What test does it offer, and what carries the material information instead?
qa_items.answer: The test is a thought experiment about the book's own page: had it been printed on smooth leather or glossy plastic instead of paper, the diffuse reflection would still look about the same. What diffuse reflection does carry is how black or how white a subject is — the page's blacks and whites come from areas producing a great deal of diffuse reflection, the paper, and areas producing little, the ink — and, because diffuse reflection can reflect frequencies selectively, most of the colour information; the authors say a page printed with magenta ink on blue paper would announce itself through its diffuse reflection. What carries the material identity is the direct reflection: you could tell the difference in material by it. This is why copy work, which wants the colours and values of the original rather than the surface it sits on, is the case where only diffuse reflection is wanted.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, 'Capitalizing on Diffuse Reflections', where the leather-and-plastic test and the copy-work consequence are both stated.
confounders: assuming texture and material are the same question; texture can be shown by shadow, material by finish
attributing colour to direct reflection, which is a mirror image of the source and carries the source's colour
treating this as a claim about physics rather than about what each channel tells a viewer

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'Photographing Cylinders: Increasing Tonal Variation'
qa_items.question: A cylindrical aerosol can lit evenly reads as a flat shape. What does this book say cylinders need that boxes do not, and what does its remedy cost?
qa_items.answer: Cylinders usually need a brighter highlight side or a darker shadow side than boxes do. The reason is that a box supplies abrupt tonal steps at its edges while a curved surface supplies only a gradient, so the shadows blend so gradually into the highlights that the dimensional distinction is lost and the subject reads flat. The remedy is to build more tonal variation into the scene, and the authors' method is subtractive as much as additive: a light source on one side of the subject and a black card on the other. The cost is that placing the main light to one side puts the subject's shadow on the table beside it — and shadows are least likely to become strong compositional elements when they fall at the bottom of the picture, under the subject. So when they do put the main light to the side of a cylindrical subject they usually use a large source, which softens that shadow and makes it less likely to compete.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'Photographing Cylinders: Increasing Tonal Variation', including the black-card method and the resulting shadow problem.
confounders: adding fill on the dark side, which reduces the very variation the cylinder needs
using a small hard light to increase contrast, which worsens the cast-shadow problem
assuming the black card adds nothing because it emits nothing; its job is to subtract

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', sidebar 'Managing Flare'
qa_items.question: You need a gobo in front of the lens but the source is soft, so its shadow is too diffuse to see, and at full aperture the gobo itself is too unsharp to spot if it intrudes. What trick does the book give?
qa_items.answer: Use the lens itself as the detector. The glass lens reflects like a mirror, so with the camera on a tripod you can look into the front of the lens and see the reflection of any light source likely to cause flare. Move the gobo in front of the lens just far enough that the source is no longer reflected there, then pull the gobo back slightly for safety. A gobo in that position eliminates almost all flare without extending into the image. The trick works because the set of sources the lens surface can see is exactly the set that can produce camera flare, so occluding them in that reflection occludes them at the lens. The authors set it up by first stating both difficulties — a hard source lets you place the gobo by its shadow, a soft one does not, and shallow depth of field at the composing aperture hides an intruding card.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, the sidebar 'Managing Flare', which distinguishes lens flare from camera flare and gives this positioning method for the latter.
confounders: stopping down to check, which changes the framing conditions you were trying to judge
using a lens hood, which the source says often does not extend far enough forward to help
positioning by the gobo's own shadow, which is exactly what fails under a soft source

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 'Traveling Light', section 'Correcting Mixed Colors', the caution on highlights
qa_items.question: A frame with a visible lamp in it is colour-corrected globally and the lamp's highlight comes out tinted. What has happened on this book's account, and what does it prescribe?
qa_items.answer: An area bright enough — a light source in the frame, or the mirror reflection of one — records as a white highlight regardless of the colour of the light that produced it, because it has clipped and carries no chromatic information of its own. When a correction is then applied to fix the rest of the scene, those highlights have nothing to shift and instead take on the colour of the correction. The book says the problem can be dealt with but requires more than the straightforward colour adjustment most people know how to do, that only first-rate printers have prepress departments able to handle it, and that it is a topic too far from photographic lighting to cover. Its own prescription is therefore preventive: either correct the colour while shooting the picture, or compose it so that it does not contain any troublesome highlights. As a diagnostic, the pattern is worth keeping — a tinted specular highlight matching a correction applied elsewhere is evidence of the correction rather than of the original lighting.
qa_items.support: Ch. 10, 'Correcting Mixed Colors', the caution that follows the account of why mixed colour is easy to fix.
confounders: assuming the tint reveals the true colour of the source
correcting the highlight separately as the first move; the source calls it beyond straightforward adjustment
reading it as an artefact of the display or the printer rather than of the correction itself

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 'Traveling Light', section 'Filtering Daylight'
qa_items.question: An interior is lit by tungsten photographic lights and by daylight through a window. Two gelling strategies both match the colours. Which does the book prefer, and on what ground that has nothing to do with colour?
qa_items.answer: It prefers gelling the window. Blue gels on the photographic lights, shot at a daylight balance, would match the colours — but the photographic lights are probably weaker than the sun already, and filtering them absorbs light where it can least be spared. Orange theatrical gel on the OUTSIDE of the window, shot at a tungsten balance, achieves the same colour match and also better balances the intensity of the two sources, because the loss is now imposed on the stronger one. The general point the authors make first is the one still photographers overlook: a window is a light source and can be filtered like any other, which motion picture and video photographers do routinely.
qa_items.support: Ch. 10, 'Filtering Daylight', which sets out both strategies and the intensity argument for choosing between them.
confounders: choosing on colour accuracy alone, where the two strategies are equivalent
gelling the lamps because they are the controllable elements
raising ISO or opening up instead, which does not address the ratio between the two sources

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'Light above the Subject'; Ch. 9, 'Using a Mirror Background'
qa_items.question: Two arrangements in this book leave a subject with no ground shadow at all. Why does the book treat that as a serious loss, and which of the two offers no way back?
qa_items.answer: Because the shadow carries information the picture cannot do without: it proves the subject is sitting on a surface rather than floating above it, and the relationship of the subject to the background is an essential part of the depth message. That is why the book relocates a competing shadow instead of softening it out of existence — the only way to stop it drawing the eye would be to soften it so much that it would not exist at all, and then the brain has no way of knowing where the subject is. The two shadowless arrangements in the extremes chapter differ. A translucent white background lit from behind erases the shadow, but the loss is recoverable and in fact becomes an advantage: the shadow can be manufactured by tracing a test light's cast shadow, cutting it out and gluing it under the panel. A mirror background offers no way back — the authors say plainly that there is no way to obtain a ground shadow with that set-up, and that if the shadow is necessary for the subject, some other arrangement will be better.
qa_items.support: Ch. 5, 'Light on the Side' and 'Light above the Subject' for why the shadow must be kept; Ch. 9, 'Using a Translucent White Background' and 'Using a Mirror Background' for the two shadowless cases.
confounders: treating the ground shadow as decorative
assuming the manufactured-shadow trick can be applied to the mirror background too
softening a competing shadow to nothing, which is the move the source rejects

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', opening argument
qa_items.question: The book opens the surface chapters with a claim about human vision rather than about light. What is it, what does the book decline to explain, and why does it matter to a photographer?
qa_items.answer: The claim is that the brain edits a live scene and cannot edit a picture of one to the same degree. Every surface produces some mixture of the three reflection types, but a person standing in the room is not conscious of all of it: the brain suppresses reflection that is distracting or trivial and promotes whatever is needed to comprehend the scene, so the psychological image differs from the optical one. That editing does not survive into a photograph, which is why photographers discover defects in their images that they could not see at all when carefully examining the original scene. The authors explicitly decline to explain WHY pictures reveal what the scene conceals — they call it a question for another book, note that psychologists have not completely explained it, and say movement is part of it but not all. It matters because it sets the photographer's job: to perform consciously, at the set, the editing that an observer of the scene performs unconsciously.
qa_items.support: Ch. 4, the chapter opening, before 'Photographer as an Editor'. The claim is asserted from practitioner experience of spotting defects in images, not from a study the source cites.
confounders: reading it as a claim about camera limitations rather than about perception
assuming the source explains the mechanism; it deliberately does not
treating checking the scene carefully as sufficient, which is exactly what the source says fails

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Keeping the Metal Bright'; and 'Flat Metal'
qa_items.question: A large fill light is added well outside the family of angles to lift a polished steel subject that is reading too dark. Nothing happens. Why, and what does that fact buy you elsewhere in the scene?
qa_items.answer: Because polished metal produces almost no diffuse reflection, light coming from any angle other than inside the family of angles has practically no effect on it, regardless of how bright the light is or how long the exposure. The family is a hard boundary rather than a matter of degree. What that buys is the cleanest separation of controls in the book: everything outside the family acts only on the rest of the scene, so the metal's tone can be set entirely by what occupies the family while the background is set independently. It also produces a practical trap the authors flag: the large white target used to FIND the family must be removed before shooting dark metal, because left in place it reflects the general illumination and quietly becomes an additional source inside the family.
qa_items.support: Ch. 6, 'Keeping the Metal Bright' for the statement about off-family light, 'Keeping the Metal Dark' for the test-surface warning. The spatula photographed from outside the family records as solid black on white paper.
confounders: adding more power, which the source says makes no difference
lengthening the exposure, which the source names explicitly as also making no difference
assuming a dulling-sprayed or brushed surface behaves the same way; adding diffuse reflection is exactly what breaks this

qa_items.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Recognizing the Principal Subject'
qa_items.question: The glass chapter ends by refusing to say when to use bright field and when to use dark field. What reason does it give, and what does it claim the chapter was actually for?
qa_items.answer: It refuses because the nature of the subject determines the best lighting, and deciding which subject is more important is the first step in lighting any scene containing both glass and non-glass — a decision the authors say cannot be made on a purely technical basis. They put it bluntly: they might light two identical scenes differently depending on the intended picture caption, on who is paying the bill, or on personal whim. As for what the chapter was for, they say seeing how light behaves matters more than the mere ability to make a routine glassware shot look professional, and that they devote a whole chapter to glass because generations of photographers have found it one of the classic subjects that helps us learn to see. The methods are a vehicle; the editorial decision that selects between them belongs to the photographer and the client.
qa_items.support: Ch. 7, 'Recognizing the Principal Subject', the closing section of the chapter.
confounders: expecting a decision rule the source explicitly declines to give
reading 'personal whim' as carelessness rather than as the authors' point that the choice is not technical
assuming the technical material is therefore optional; the source's claim is that the physics constrains without deciding

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Headlines' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy states that five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy, and then immediately draws a much stronger conclusion from it. What is that conclusion, and what step is hidden inside it?
qa_items.answer: His conclusion is that unless the headline sells the product, ninety per cent of the money has been wasted. The hidden step is a move from a readership ratio to a spending ratio: the five-to- one figure is about how many people read two parts of an advertisement, and the ninety per cent is a claim about wasted expenditure, which requires the further assumption that readership of the headline is what the money buys. He also derives from the same ratio that the brand name must appear in the headline, since eighty per cent of readers never reach the body copy and would otherwise never learn what is being advertised.
qa_items.support: Chapter 7 opens by naming its evidence base — factor analyses commissioned from Gallup and Robinson, the Starch Readership Service, direct-response test results and the author's own observation — then gives the five-times figure and the ninety per cent conclusion in adjacent sentences. The readership figure is a reported measurement; the ninety per cent is his inference, not a measured waste.
confounders: reading the ninety per cent as a measured finding rather than as an inference from the readership ratio
assuming the claim is about attention span; it is about the fall-off between two elements of one advertisement
confusing this with the chapter-2 doctrine that advertising must sell rather than please — that is a different claim, about the criterion, not about where readership sits

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Headlines', the Starch and retail-study passage (spine 13)
qa_items.question: On headline length Ogilvy reports two findings that point opposite ways and then refuses to choose between them. State both findings, and name the reconciliation that is available in his own text but which he does not make.
qa_items.answer: Starch reports that headlines of more than ten words get less readership than short headlines; a study of retail advertisements found that ten-word headlines sell more merchandise than short ones. His stated conclusion is that a long headline is fine if you need one and a short one is fine too. The reconciliation he does not make is that the two studies measure different quantities — readership in the first, merchandise sold in the second — so both can be true at once, and the practical question becomes which quantity you are buying. Elsewhere in the same chapter a caption states flatly that long headlines sell more merchandise than short ones, which is stronger than his running text allows.
qa_items.support: Both findings are quoted from named sources in the Headlines section with his own one-sentence conclusion. Neither carries a sample or date. The readership-versus-sales distinction is present in his wording and absent from his reasoning.
confounders: concluding that Ogilvy favours long headlines; his running text explicitly declines to favour either
treating the two findings as a contradiction that one of them must lose; they measure different outcomes
importing the modern default that shorter is always better, which neither study supports

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Headlines', the passage on tricky headlines (spine 13)
qa_items.question: A team defends a punning headline as memorable and rewarding to decode. On Ogilvy's stated reasoning, what is wrong with the defence, and what is the specific property of the reading situation his objection rests on?
qa_items.answer: His objection is not that puns are in poor taste but that the headline is not read in isolation. He states that in the average newspaper a headline competes with three hundred and fifty others and that readers travel fast through that jungle, so anything requiring a second pass loses the reader before the reward arrives. Obscurity is therefore a failure of speed inside a competitive scan. His instruction is that the headline should telegraph what you want to say. The property the argument rests on is the density of competing headlines on a 1983 newspaper page, which is a fact about that medium at that time rather than a general law.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a mechanism, in the Headlines section. No measurement of the penalty is offered; the three-hundred-and-fifty figure describes the newspaper page of his period.
confounders: arguing that Ogilvy dislikes wit as such; his objection is about decoding time in a competitive scan
generalising the density figure to any medium; he states it for the newspaper page of his era
confusing this with his separate finding that 'blind' headlines run about twenty per cent below average in recall — that is about naming the product, not about obscurity of phrasing

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Illustrations', item 5 of 15 (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy holds that photographs beat drawings on readership, believability and memory, and then names a condition under which he found the reverse. What is the condition, what case does he give, and what does the reversal tell you about why photographs win in the first place?
qa_items.answer: The condition is reproduction quality: photographs reproduce so badly in some newspapers that a line drawing gives a more lifelike picture. His case is that scratch-board drawings sold more shoes for one retail client than photographs did. The reversal tells you the advantage of a photograph is realism rather than the medium itself, so the advantage survives only as far as the printing preserves it — where reproduction destroys the realism, a drawing that keeps its form wins. This is one of the few boundary conditions in the book that names a physical circumstance and reports a case where the general rule flipped.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with an explicit exception and one reported counter-case, in the illustrations list. The general claim is reported from unnamed research; the exception is his own observation. The Come to Britain case in the same item reports readership tripling, which is a measurement, and tourism tripling, which is attributed with nothing else excluded.
confounders: treating the exception as a preference for illustration style; it is a claim about the printing process
reading the tripled tourism as evidence for the photograph rule; only the readership figure is a measurement
assuming the rule concerns aesthetic realism rather than believability under degraded reproduction

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Body copy', the opening question (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Asked whether anybody reads body copy, Ogilvy refuses a yes or no and decomposes the question. Into what, and why does the decomposition change what a low readership figure means about the advertisement?
qa_items.answer: He decomposes it into two determinants: how many people are interested in that kind of product, and how many were enticed into the advertisement by its illustration and headline. Only the second is inside the advertiser's control. The consequence is that a low body-copy readership figure is not by itself evidence that the advertisement is bad, because the same craft applied in a low-interest category returns a smaller number. He puts average magazine body-copy readership at about five per cent and argues that five per cent of a large circulation is still an enormous number of people.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a reported average readership figure, in the Body copy section. The category examples are given in the gendered terms of his period. The five per cent average and the circulation arithmetic describe magazines of 1983.
confounders: reading it as 'nobody reads body copy, so keep it short' — which is the position he is refusing
assuming category interest can be raised by the advertisement; he places it outside the advertisement's control
treating the five per cent as a target rather than as an average he uses to argue about absolute numbers

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Body copy', the passage on analogies (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy advises avoiding analogies in copy. His Rembrandt example describes a failure sharper than mere confusion. What exactly goes wrong, and which other failure in the book has the same shape?
qa_items.answer: In his example an advertisement compares the product to a Rembrandt portrait and readers come away thinking the painting is what is for sale. The failure is not that the comparison is missed but that the borrowed vehicle displaces the product as the subject of the advertisement. His general statement is that readers do not complete the equation. The same shape appears in his account of celebrity testimonials, where the viewer remembers the celebrity and forgets the product, and again in his warning that a named competitor in a comparative commercial can end up being taken for its hero. In all three a more vivid borrowed element takes the memory the product needed.
qa_items.support: Attributed to Gallup with no study, sample or rate of misunderstanding supplied — a finding asserted with its result withheld. The parallel to the celebrity and competitor cases is drawn from Ogilvy's own statements in chapters 7, 8 and 12; he does not connect them himself.
confounders: reading the advice as a stylistic preference for plain language
assuming the failure is that the analogy is too difficult; his claim is that the vehicle is remembered instead
treating the Gallup attribution as a citation; no study, sample or result is given

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Short copy or long?' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy lists nine long-copy successes with response counts and market-share reversals. Why does none of the nine actually support his long-copy claim, and which single sentence in the section is doing the real evidential work?
qa_items.answer: None of the nine supports the claim because each reports what one long-copy advertisement achieved with no short-copy version of the same offer to compare against, so copy length is not separated from everything else about the advertisement; and the nine were selected because they succeeded. The sentence carrying the weight is his statement that in direct-response split-run tests long copy invariably outsells short copy, because a split run is the one design in the book that holds the offer constant and varies the copy. He supplies no test, no margin, no product and no source for it — the measurement is asserted and the result withheld.
qa_items.support: Nine cases with outcomes, plus one sentence citing split-run evidence without any of its particulars. He also names his own two failures with long copy, a popular-priced cigar and a premium-priced whiskey, without analysing either.
confounders: counting the response totals as evidence of the length effect; a single-arm result cannot isolate it
assuming the split-run claim is documented somewhere in the chapter; it is not
treating his two failures as the boundary condition; he names the products and never states the condition

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Short copy or long?', the two claims about the block of copy (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy makes two further claims about long copy and marks them very differently. Identify both, say how he marks each, and explain why they pull against each other.
qa_items.answer: The first is that advertisements with long copy convey the impression that you have something important to say, whether or not people read the copy — and he flags this himself as a belief held without any research to support him. The second is a condition: if you want long copy read you had better write it well, and in particular the first paragraph must be a grabber. They pull against each other because if part of the effect comes from the copy being seen rather than read, then the quality of the writing matters less than the second claim demands. He does not notice the tension.
qa_items.support: Both claims are in the same short passage. The first is explicitly disclaimed by the author as unsupported; the second is asserted with a counter-example of a limp opening sentence from a resort advertisement.
confounders: treating the importance-signal claim as one of his research findings; he says the opposite
reading the grabber rule as being about the headline; it concerns the first paragraph of body copy
assuming he resolves the tension — he does not raise it

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Layouts', the scanning-order passage (spine 13)
qa_items.question: You are handed a print layout with the headline set across the top, a photograph beneath it and copy below that. State Ogilvy's objection, the figure he attaches to it, and the reason he gives for why the order matters.
qa_items.answer: His objection is that readers look first at the illustration, then the headline, then the copy, and scan from top to bottom, so putting the headline above the illustration asks people to scan against their habit. The elements should run illustration, headline, copy down the page. He reports that headlines below the illustration are read by ten per cent more people on average, notes that ten per cent of a large circulation is a very large number, and observes that fifty-nine per cent of magazine advertisements nonetheless put the headline above. The reason is habit rather than aesthetics: the page should match the movement the eye already makes.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with a reported readership difference and a reported violation rate, neither given a sample or a source. The claimed scanning order itself is asserted rather than demonstrated in the text.
confounders: justifying the rule by visual balance or composition; his ground is a claimed scanning habit
assuming the fifty-nine per cent violation rate proves art directors are wrong; it is equally consistent with their weighing something he does not measure
confusing the rule with his separate instruction never to superimpose a headline on the illustration

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Layouts', the news-magazine format passage (spine 13)
qa_items.question: What does Ogilvy claim the conventional graphics of advertising communicate to a reader before a word is read, and what does he propose in their place?
qa_items.answer: He claims the inherited graphic conventions of advertising telegraph to the reader that this is only an advertisement and can be skipped, and reports that roughly six times as many people read the average article as the average advertisement while very few advertisements are read by more than one reader in twenty. His proposal is to adopt editorial graphics instead: copy given priority over illustration, serif type, three columns of thirty-five to forty-five characters, a caption under every photograph, drop-initials, and black type on white. His instruction is to pretend you are an editor. The whole argument depends on a specific historical relationship between editorial and advertising conventions in the print of his period.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a reported article-to-advertisement readership ratio, no source given. The six-element list is his description of the format shared by named news magazines in five countries.
confounders: reading it as a preference for restraint or good taste; his claim is about a learned signal that triggers skipping
carrying the specific format list into any later medium; it describes printed magazines of 1983
confusing 'looks like editorial' with disguising the advertiser — he wants the graphics, and separately jokes about the required 'advertisement' slug

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Layouts' and Ch. 11 'The secrets of success in business-to-business advertising', section 'Print' (spine 13 and spine 17)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy gives the caption a special status among the elements of a print advertisement. What is the claim, what must a caption contain, and what internal inconsistency does the book carry on this point?
qa_items.answer: The claim is that more people read the caption under an illustration than read the body copy, from which he concludes that no illustration should ever run without a caption and that the caption should carry the brand name and the promise — in the business chapter he calls the best captions mini-advertisements in themselves. The inconsistency is in the multiplier: the print chapter says four times as many people read captions as read body copy, and the business-to-business chapter says twice as many. Neither figure carries a source, and he never notices the discrepancy.
qa_items.support: Two statements in two chapters, both reported as readership findings without sample or source, with different multipliers. The instruction about what a caption should contain is identical in both.
confounders: assuming the caption is a courtesy label; he treats it as a second selling element
picking one of the two multipliers as the correct one; the book supports neither over the other
confusing the caption rule with the drop-initial and cross-head devices, which raise readership of copy already entered

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Layouts' and the chapter's closing footnote on spreads (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy tells you to swear off two-page spreads, then corrects himself in a footnote. What does the correction say, and why is the corrected version more useful than the rule it qualifies?
qa_items.answer: The rule is that a spread costs twice a single page and seldom returns twice the readership or twice the coupons, so swearing off spreads buys twice as many insertions. The footnote, which he introduces by calling the rule one of his own over-simplifications, reports that Starch finds spreads average twenty-eight per cent higher rating than single pages, that for financial advertisers spreads average one hundred and fifty per cent more readership, and that advertisements for low-interest products benefit more from big space than those for high-interest products. The corrected version is more useful because it supplies the variable — the reader's prior interest in the category — that decides when the size premium is worth paying, instead of a blanket prohibition.
qa_items.support: Rule in the running text; qualification in his own footnote, citing two different named sources measuring different populations. He states the low-interest generalisation but does not reconcile the two figures.
confounders: keeping the rule and discarding the footnote; he flags the rule himself as an over-simplification
reading the financial-advertiser figure as an industry quirk rather than as an instance of the low-interest generalisation
confusing readership gain with order gain — the direct-response chapter states the spread question in orders, where he again says spreads seldom double them

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Typography – the eye is a creature of habit' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy's typography advice runs off one organising principle. Name it, derive two of his specific rules from it, and state the limit he himself places on the whole subject.
qa_items.answer: The principle is that the eye is a creature of habit: what is easy to read is what people are accustomed to reading. From it he derives that capitals retard reading, since they have no ascenders or descenders to help word recognition and tend to be read letter by letter, and that copy should be set about forty characters wide, the measure people are used to in newspapers; the same principle gives him familiar faces such as Century, Caslon, Baskerville and Jenson, and his line that the drama belongs in what you say, not in the typeface. The limit he states himself is that no reader ever bought a product because of the typeface, but an advertisement nobody can read cannot sell — you cannot save souls in an empty church. Typography is a necessary condition, not a cause.
qa_items.support: Stated principle with derived rules. Tinker is cited by name and institution without a study or date; the serif preference is supported by a novelist's opinion. The familiarity argument is explicitly relative to what readers of that period had been trained on.
confounders: treating the typeface list as an aesthetic canon rather than as a claim about reader familiarity
reading 'you can't save souls in an empty church' as a claim that typography sells; it says the opposite
assuming the familiarity claim is about letterforms; it is about trained habit, and moves with the habit

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Typography', the reverse-type passage, with Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', section 'Direct response advertising in magazines and television' (spine 13 and spine 18)
qa_items.question: Reverse type is the rule Ogilvy repeats most often. What is the one comparison he reports for it, and what two exceptions does he allow — and what do the exceptions have in common?
qa_items.answer: The comparison is a charity that had been running advertisements in reverse — white type on black — and, on his suggestion, tested black type on white; he reports it raised twice as much money. The two exceptions, given in the direct-response chapter, are theatre programmes, which people read in the dark by holding them up against the light coming from the stage, and slides projected onto a screen. What they share is that the page is not the light source: in both, the surface is backlit or projected rather than reflecting, which reverses the legibility. These are the only boundary conditions he gives for a typography rule anywhere in the book.
qa_items.support: A reported before-and-after comparison with a result supplied, and two exceptions stated in a later chapter. The shared property — the page not being the light source — is implicit in his own descriptions of both exceptions.
confounders: treating reverse type as a matter of taste; he reports a fund-raising difference
generalising the exceptions to any bright display without noticing that his stated reason is the direction of the light
assuming the charity comparison was controlled — it is a before-and-after on one organisation with no other cause excluded

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', sections 'Posters' and 'Subway cards' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy treats posters and subway cards very differently as evidential cases. Set the two side by side, and say what the subway case shows about how he thinks format should be chosen.
qa_items.answer: On posters he states there has been little or no research, offers what little is known — make it a visual scandal, deliver the promise pictorially as well as in words, largest possible type, brand name visible at a distance, strong pure colours, never more than three elements — and closes by asking the reader to tell him if they know more. On subway cards he reasons from a measured property of the medium instead: the average New York rider is exposed to the card for twenty-one minutes and eighty-five per cent of passengers carry nothing else to read, so the card can carry a long message, and he warns explicitly against designing one like a billboard with five or six words. The subway case shows he thinks format should follow from exposure duration and the presence of competing reading matter, not from the physical resemblance of one out-of-home surface to another. Both figures describe the New York subway of his period.
qa_items.support: Poster guidance explicitly marked by the author as unsupported by research, with an invitation to correct him. Subway guidance derived from two reported audience measurements. He states the exposure-duration reasoning for this case only.
confounders: carrying the twenty-one-minute reasoning into any other medium; he applies it to one transit system in one era
treating the three-element poster rule as evidence-based; he says the opposite
assuming out-of-home is one category with one set of rules — the contrast is his point

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Illustrations', item 10 of 15, and the Rinso caption (spine 13)
qa_items.question: A creative team argues for an illustration subject on the ground that everyone on the team finds it fascinating. Ogilvy has a specific answer to this, drawn from his own failure. What is it?
qa_items.answer: He states as a rule that a subject interesting you will not necessarily interest consumers, and supports it with his own mistake: as a former chef he assumed everyone found chefs interesting, used them in an advertisement, and got miserable readership among the intended audience. He reports a colleague at a food company having independently observed the same reaction. The point is that the writer's own interest is not evidence about the audience's, and he treats his own enthusiasm as the thing that misled him. The passage is written in the terms of his period, with housewives named as the target audience for the food products in question.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with one reported failure of his own and one colleague's agreement. No measurement of the readership deficit is given. It is his clearest self-correction in the print chapter and cuts against his habit of asserting from taste elsewhere in it.
confounders: reading it as advice to be unimaginative or to avoid personal taste altogether
confusing it with his story-appeal rule, which is about arousing the reader's curiosity — this item says your judgement of what is curious is not self-validating
treating the housewife framing as a finding about who buys food; it is the assumption of his era

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Warning' following 'Illustrations' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Immediately after fifteen confident rules about illustration, Ogilvy prints a short section headed Warning. What does it say, and why does it sit awkwardly with the fifteen rules?
qa_items.answer: It says that the illustrations in advertisements are often misunderstood, and gives a pilot-study case in which a photograph of a luxurious hotel foyer in a cigarette advertisement was taken by one respondent for a hospital ward for cancer patients. It sits awkwardly because all fifteen preceding rules assume the illustration is read as intended: story appeal, before-and-after, package-as-subject and the rest are claims about what a correctly understood picture does. He prints the warning and revises none of them. Note that the example inverts the meaning rather than blurring it.
qa_items.support: A pilot study and a single respondent, reported by a named former partner. No rate of misunderstanding is given for print, unlike the television chapter, which does supply one.
confounders: assuming he quantifies print misunderstanding; the measured figure in the book is for television
reading the warning as an argument for captions; he makes the caption case separately, in the layout section
treating a single respondent as a finding rather than as the illustration of a possibility

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', chapter opening before 'Above average' (spine 14)
qa_items.question: Before making a single craft claim, the television chapter states which measure it will use. What is it, what is the argument for it, and what does adopting it do to the rest of the book?
qa_items.answer: The measure is change in brand preference, taken from factor analyses he commissions, and the argument for it is that people who register such a change after seeing a commercial subsequently buy the product three times more than people who do not. He rejects recall on the ground that some commercials scoring high on recall score low on brand preference and that there appears to be no correlation between recall and purchasing. What this does to the rest of the book is awkward: several central claims in his print chapter are recall claims — the twenty-two per cent news effect, the twenty-eight per cent quotation-mark effect, the twenty per cent penalty on blind headlines — and he never reconciles the two positions.
qa_items.support: Stated measure with a reported multiple linking preference change to later purchase; no study, sample or date given. He also concedes at the chapter's opening that his television experience is more limited than his print experience and that the chapter rests mostly on research and on watching other people's commercials.
confounders: assuming he rejects all pre-testing; he rejects one measure and prefers another
treating the three-times multiple as showing the commercial caused the purchase; it links a measured attitude change to later behaviour
missing that the same book argues from recall figures elsewhere

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Above average', item 1 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: On humour in commercials Ogilvy reverses a position he had held for years. State the reversal precisely, and say why the caveat he attaches makes it much less usable than it first appears.
qa_items.answer: He had held, with Hopkins, that people do not buy from clowns, and says he believes this was true in Hopkins's day and until recently; the latest wave of factor analysis, he says, reveals that humour can now sell. The caveat is that very few writers can write funny commercials which are funny, and anyone who is not one of them should not try. That caveat does most of the work, because a technique whose success depends on a rare individual capability is not usable guidance for most readers. Note also that he dates the change rather than explaining it: he says humour can NOW sell, implying audiences changed rather than that the earlier measurement was wrong, and he does not say which.
qa_items.support: Stated reversal attributed to a wave of factor analysis with no result, sample or date supplied — measurement asserted, result withheld — followed by his own execution caveat.
confounders: reading it as a general endorsement of funny advertising
assuming he explains why the finding changed; he only dates it
confusing the humour reversal with his position on emotion, which he says researchers have not found a way to quantify at all

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Above average', items 2, 5, 6 and 8 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy's list of formats that test above average on brand preference is dominated by formats agency people dislike. Name them, and say what he takes the pattern to show.
qa_items.answer: Slice of life, in which one character argues with another about a product in a roughly realistic setting and the doubter is converted; problem-solution, which shows a familiar problem and the product solving it; talking heads, a pitchman extolling the product, which he says are particularly appropriate for announcing new products; and reason-why commercials, which he reports as slightly above average. Copywriters detest slices of life as corny and over-used, and agency people find talking heads non-creative. The pattern he takes from it is the gap between what the trade enjoys making and what moves the measure — the same argument he makes in the abstract in his chapter on the cult of creativity, stated here with named formats.
qa_items.support: Four formats reported as above average with no numbers, no average and no sample. The new-product claim for talking heads rests on a single instance, a German cigarette brand said to be the only successful launch among more than a hundred.
confounders: reading 'above average' as a measured effect size; the distribution is never given
assuming these formats are recommended for every objective — his direct-response chapter uses problem-solution differently, over two minutes and with several benefits
treating the German cigarette case as evidence for the general claim rather than as one instance

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Above average', item 3 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: You are casting a testimonial commercial and have found a genuine loyal customer who happens to be an excellent, polished speaker. What does Ogilvy say about that, and what device does he recommend for producing conviction?
qa_items.answer: He tells you to avoid users who would give so polished a performance that viewers would think they were professional actors, on the stated ground that the more amateurish the performance, the more credible it is. The device he recommends is to have the interviewer pretend to find fault with the product so that the loyal user rises to its defence, which he says produces far more conviction than simply asking what the user thinks — and he prefers filming users who do not know they are being filmed. The mechanism is that credibility comes from the speaker appearing not to be performing for the advertiser, and both clumsiness and spontaneous defence are signals of that.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with a reproduced hidden-camera script and one supporting case — a French campaign whose elderly heroine became recognised by three in four people, with the product reported to have moved from fourth to second in sales. The recognition figure is measured; the rank change is attributed with nothing else excluded.
confounders: assuming production polish always helps; his claim runs the other way for this specific format
reading it as an argument for using real people generally, missing the defensive-response device
confusing this with his position on expert testimony, which works through standing rather than through amateurism

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Above average', item 4 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: A client wants a demonstration commercial that names the competing brand and shows it losing. What does Ogilvy report about that, and what does he say the risk actually is?
qa_items.answer: He reports that his agency's studies found commercials naming competing brands less believable and more confusing than commercials that do not, and names a specific risk: viewers tend to come away with the impression that the brand you disparage is the hero of your commercial. So the danger is not merely wasted attention but transferred credit. He notes the practice was illegal in Germany and encouraged by the United States government as consumer information, which is a regulatory position of 1983. His enthusiasm for demonstration itself is undiminished — he wants demonstrations, and insists they need not be dull.
qa_items.support: Studies by his own agency cited without design, sample, date or effect size, with the failure mode stated as a tendency. The business-to-business chapter states the opposite emphasis, urging demonstrations that compare performance with competitors', and he does not reconcile the two.
confounders: concluding he opposes comparative demonstration in general; his business chapter recommends comparison
reading the risk as legal rather than perceptual
assuming the finding is about believability alone, missing the hero-transfer claim

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Above average', item 10 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: Emotion is the one item on Ogilvy's above-average list that fails his own chapter's evidential standard. How does he handle that, and what two constraints does he attach?
qa_items.answer: He states the failure openly: researchers have not yet found a way to quantify the effectiveness of emotion, and his position is a belief formed from watching commercials — that nostalgia, charm and even sentimentality can be enormously effective, and that emotion can be as effective as any rational appeal, particularly where there is nothing unique to say about the product. The two constraints are that consumers need a rational excuse to justify an emotional decision, so one should always be included, and that emotion should not be attempted by anyone who cannot deliver it. He also quotes a partner's warning that both clients and agency people overrate how much the rational benefits of their product matter to the consumer.
