qa_items.support: Explicitly unquantified and marked as belief by the author, inside a chapter organised around a measure. The rational-excuse claim is asserted with no evidence at all and is a claim about the structure of a purchase decision rather than about a commercial.
confounders: treating the emotion claim as one of his measured findings
reading the rational excuse as the persuader; he casts it as the justification the buyer needs afterwards
assuming the scope is general — he raises it particularly for products with nothing unique to say

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Below average', item 2 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: Of the three formats Ogilvy reports as below average on brand preference, one carries evidence much closer to a controlled comparison than anything else in the chapter. Which, what is the evidence, and what boundary does he place on the finding?
qa_items.answer: Cartoons. He reports a fabric-softener case in which two commercials were made, one live action and one cartoon: the cartoon had no effect on the downward sales trend and the live-action version reversed it. That is a same-product pair with opposite outcomes on the same trend, which is closer to a controlled comparison than the rest of the chapter — though he gives no sample, no market and no magnitude, and the two commercials differed in more than technique. The boundary he states is audience age: cartoons can sell things to children and are below average in selling to grown-ups, holding the viewer less well than live action.
qa_items.support: A reported two-arm case with directions supplied for both arms, plus a stated audience boundary. The other two below-average formats, celebrity testimonials and musical vignettes, carry no comparison of this kind.
confounders: extending the cartoon finding to children, which he explicitly exempts
treating the pair as a clean experiment; only the technique is named as differing, and no magnitudes are given
choosing celebrity testimonials as the best-evidenced item — that one rests on his account of why viewers discount them

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Body copy', with Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Below average' item 1, and Ch. 12, section 'Direct response advertising in magazines and television' (spine 13, 14, 18)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy states the celebrity-testimonial problem three times in three chapters with three different framings. Give the three, and state the single exception that survives in all of them.
qa_items.answer: In print he says celebrity testimonials get high recall scores but readers remember the celebrity and forget the product, and assume the celebrity was bought, which he says is usually the case. On television he says they are below average at changing brand preference, viewers guess the celebrity has been bought and are right, and he lists the fees of the period to show what is being paid for. In direct response he says simply not to use them. The exception that survives everywhere is relevant expertise: expert testimony persuades — his print example is an ex-burglar testifying that he could never crack a particular safe — and the direct-response chapter states it most precisely as recognised authorities only, such as a champion golfer on golf clubs. The celebrity case is also the example he uses to argue that recall and persuasion come apart.
qa_items.support: Three statements in three chapters, none with a study attached. His own worst-remembered instance is his own: paying a famous public figure to endorse a margarine, which he calls not one of his proudest memories.
confounders: assuming fame is the variable; his stated mechanism is inferred payment destroying disinterest, plus memory attaching to the more memorable object
treating the expert exception as celebrity endorsement with a better-chosen celebrity
missing that celebrity commercials are his standing demonstration that high recall can coexist with low persuasion

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Sixteen tips', items 1 and 2 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy treats getting the brand remembered as work that has to be done deliberately rather than as a by-product of a good commercial. What is the failure he says is the default, and what does he prescribe?
qa_items.answer: The default failure is that a shocking percentage of viewers remember the commercial and forget the name of the product, and all too often attribute the commercial to a competing brand — which is worse than forgetting, because the advertising then works for the rival. His prescription is to use the name within the first ten seconds and to play games with it, such as spelling it out; he reports a commercial that repeated the brand name twenty times without irritating anyone, and says that for a new product you have to teach people its name on television. He also reports that commercials ending by showing the package change brand preference more effectively than those that do not, and notes that many copywriters think it crass to belabour the name.
qa_items.support: The shocking percentage is never given and the research demonstrating it is not identified — measurement asserted, result withheld. The package finding is stated without numbers. The same practice appears in his account of Procter & Gamble, where the name is reported to appear in the first ten seconds and about three times thereafter.
confounders: reading it as a claim that repetition is inherently persuasive; the claim is about attribution
assuming a memorable commercial is a memorably branded one — his point is that these come apart
treating misattribution as equivalent to forgetting

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Sixteen tips', item 5 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: A director defends a slow, atmospheric opening on the ground that it sets up a strong payoff twenty seconds in. Give Ogilvy's answer in his own terms, including the asymmetry he names.
qa_items.answer: His answer is open with the fire: with thirty seconds available, grabbing attention in the first frame with a visual surprise gives a better chance of holding the viewer, and commercials get screened out because they open with something dull. The asymmetry he names is that the maker knows great things are about to happen and the viewer does not — and the viewer will never find out, because she has left the room. So an opening judged by what it sets up rather than by what it shows loses the audience that would have received the payoff. His literal instruction is that when you advertise fire extinguishers, you open with the fire. All of this is stated for the thirty-second commercial in the broadcast environment of 1983.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a mechanism and no measurement. The thirty-second length and the surrounding exposure figures — thirty thousand commercials a year, a set on six hours a day — are facts about American television households of the period.
confounders: reading it as a rule about pacing throughout the commercial rather than about the first frame
carrying the rule forward to any later medium; it is stated for broadcast television of 1983
confusing it with his separate instruction to use the brand name inside the first ten seconds — both make claims on the same opening

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Sixteen tips', items 6, 7, 8 and 9 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: Set out Ogilvy's four findings about the sound layer of a commercial, and say which one he reports as a genuine null result.
qa_items.answer: Voice-over holds the audience less well than actors talking on camera, and he reports a manufacturer who made two commercials identical except for this and found the on-camera version sold more. Supers — the promise set in type over the picture while the soundtrack speaks it — pay, but the words must be exactly the same as the spoken words, because any divergence confuses the viewer. Sound effects, such as sausages sizzling, can make a positive difference; he instances a commercial built round the sound of coffee percolating that ran five years. The null result is background music: research shows it is neither a positive nor a negative factor, doing no harm and no measurable good. Jingles, separately, are below average at changing brand preference and should never go on air until people who have not read the script can make out the words.
qa_items.support: The voice-over comparison is the closest thing to a controlled pair in the chapter — two commercials identical except for one variable, tested, direction reported — though the magnitude, product and method are not given. The music null is stated as a null, which is unusual in this book. His argument against background music is rhetorical rather than evidential.
confounders: assuming music is discouraged because it hurts; he reports it as inert
conflating jingles with background music; he treats them as separate findings with different verdicts
treating the supers rule as being about emphasis rather than about exact correspondence with the spoken words

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Sixteen tips', item 15 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: What did the 1979 miscomprehension study Ogilvy cites actually find, and what makes its floor more consequential than its ceiling?
qa_items.answer: A study of twenty-five typical television commercials found that all of them were miscomprehended, some by as many as forty per cent of viewers and none by fewer than nineteen per cent. The floor matters more than the ceiling because it says the failure is universal rather than occasional: there was no commercial in the sample that everyone understood, so miscomprehension is a baseline condition of the medium rather than a defect of bad work. His stated remedy is to make commercials crystal clear, and he adds that he cannot understand more than half the commercials he sees. Having reported it, he revises none of his sixteen tips in the light of it.
qa_items.support: A named academic study of 1979 with its result supplied, cited in a single tip. This is the measured counterpart of the unquantified warning about misunderstood illustrations in his print chapter.
confounders: remembering the forty per cent and forgetting the nineteen per cent floor, which is the load-bearing number
reading it as a finding about badly made commercials; every commercial in the sample failed
assuming he adjusts his craft advice afterwards; he does not

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Radio – the Cinderella medium' (spine 14)
qa_items.question: How does Ogilvy describe the evidential position of radio in 1983, and how does he mark the advice he nevertheless gives?
qa_items.answer: He says there is no research to measure the efficacy of radio commercials, so nobody knows what works. He then offers four factors from a pilot study he commissioned — identify the brand early, identify it often, promise the listener a benefit early, repeat it often — and reports that ninety commercials in a hundred do none of these. Everything beyond that he marks explicitly as opinion and nothing more: surprise them, arouse curiosity, wake them up, then talk to them as one human being to another. He closes by noting that in some developing countries radio still reached more people than television and that nobody knew what worked there either, asking whether it was not time somebody found out.
qa_items.support: Explicit statement that the evidence does not exist, with the author marking his own advice as opinion. This and the poster section are the two places in the book where he says plainly that he is guessing.
confounders: treating the four pilot-study factors as established findings; they come from one pilot study
assuming his confidence is uniform across media — radio and posters are where he concedes ignorance
reading the ninety-in-a-hundred figure as a measured audit rather than as his characterisation

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Advertising corporations', the passage listing nineteen corporate slogans (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy prints nineteen real corporate slogans in a list. What test is the list designed to apply, and what does he say such lines cost the advertisement even when nobody objects to them?
qa_items.answer: The test is interchangeability: he observes that all of them are interchangeable, that any company could use any of them, and therefore that they identify nobody and cannot differentiate. The cost he names is twofold — they generally sit at the foot of the advertisement where nobody reads them, and by cluttering the layout they reduce readership of the copy. So a line that does no persuading still takes something away. The transferable part is the test itself: ask whether a competitor could sign the same line.
qa_items.support: An observation about nineteen reproduced slogans, stated as an observation rather than as a rule. The readership cost is asserted without measurement.
confounders: reading the objection as being about vagueness of language rather than about non-identification
assuming the harm is only that the line is ignored; he claims it also depresses readership of the copy
treating it as advice against slogans in general — his positive case is a campaign whose sponsor he recognises without reading a word

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Advertising corporations', the passage on short-lived campaigns and the Container Corporation caption (spine 15)
qa_items.question: A corporate campaign is up for review after eighteen months with no agreed measure of success. Using Ogilvy's account of why such campaigns fail, what would you say about the review itself — and what does his own reversal of judgement on one campaign add?
qa_items.answer: On his account the campaign was already set up to fail: he says most corporate campaigns are short-lived because they do not start with any clear objective and because research is not used to track their progress, so they are aborted before they could achieve anything measurable — while the companies he names as successes had run for forty-five, sixty-two and seventy-five years. The review therefore has no basis for a verdict, and the fault is in the setup rather than in the work. His prescribed remedy for the budget question is to analyse the task: what will it cost to achieve a specific goal among a specific audience. His own reversal adds caution about short-horizon aesthetic judgement: he denounced one campaign as an exercise in pretension and, forty-five years later, judged it one of the best corporate campaigns ever run, saying he recognises its sponsor without reading the copy — like recognising a man who dresses unlike other men.
qa_items.support: Stated diagnosis with named long-running campaigns, plus his own recorded change of judgement. The chapter also reports a study of 731 corporations finding an average two per cent positive influence on share price — an average across firms whose advertising differed in every respect, which attributes nothing to any property of the advertising.
confounders: reading the long-running examples as proof that duration causes success
using the two per cent share-price figure as evidence for a particular campaign
treating his change of mind as evidence about the campaign rather than as a caution about early aesthetic verdicts

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 'How to advertise foreign travel', the passages on choosing subjects and on converting dreams (spine 16)
qa_items.question: A tourist board wants its campaign to feature its country's new industrial achievements. Ogilvy faced exactly this and gives both a rule and a warning. What are they?
qa_items.answer: The rule is to illustrate what is unique to the country, because people do not travel half way round the world to see things they can see at home — do not advertise ski resorts to the Swiss or American food to the French. Research told him American tourists wanted history and tradition in Britain, so that is what he featured. The warning is the consequence: he was attacked in the British press for projecting a country living in the past and asked why he had not shown a progressive industrial society, and his answer was that research had shown American tourists had no desire to see such things. He reports the same conflict twice more, with a government directing that only economically depressed areas be featured and with a senator's home state being written into a campaign. Research-led travel advertising is routinely unacceptable to a government client, because the client wants the country it wishes to be rather than the one visitors want to see.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with three reported instances of the political conflict. He treats the conflict as an occupational hazard rather than as a reason to abandon the research. The reported tourism increases are attributed to the campaigns with nothing else excluded.
confounders: assuming the rule is to show famous landmarks; the rule is uniqueness relative to the visitor's home
treating the client conflict as a failure of persuasion rather than as a structural difference of objective
reading the tourism outcomes as measurements; only the research on what visitors wanted is reported as measured

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 10 'How to advertise foreign travel', the passage beginning 'People dream about visiting foreign countries' (spine 16)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy says travel advertising has a job different from creating desire. What is it, and what does he say the advertisement must therefore contain?
qa_items.answer: He says people already dream about visiting foreign countries, so the job of the advertising is to convert the dream into action. What it must contain is mouth-watering photographs combined with specific how-to-do-it information — you show an ancient college and tell the reader what it costs to go and see it — and for little-known countries a great deal of it: in one two-page newspaper advertisement he reports telling readers what to wear, the weather to expect, the language, the food, the costs, every mortal thing. The reasoning is that the missing ingredient is not desire but the specific knowledge that closes the gap between wanting and booking; he adds that fear, as well as cost, obstructs travel and should be allayed.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a mechanism and a named campaign example. The list of American fears about foreign countries that he reports research finding is recorded in the terms of his period and is a report of 1983 attitudes, not guidance.
confounders: reading it as a general preference for informative copy; the argument is specific to a category where desire pre-exists
assuming the photographs do the work; he insists on the pairing with practical detail
confusing dream-to-action with the brand-image argument of chapter 2, which is about personality rather than about closing a specific gap

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'The secrets of success in business-to-business advertising', section 'Print' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: A software company wants its advertising to lead on how large the company is. Ogilvy reports exactly this case. What happened, and what general rule does he draw?
qa_items.answer: Research found the supplier's customers were not interested in size at all; they were looking for responsiveness, support, service and a good product. The general rule he draws is that what you promise must be important to your customer rather than to you, and that the promise must be specific — percentages, time elapsed, dollars saved rather than generalities, because you are talking to engineers. The reasoning is that a professional buyer evaluates against criteria he already holds, so a claim outside those criteria carries no weight however true it is, and a quantified claim can be checked against them.
qa_items.support: One reported research finding with its result supplied, generalised into a rule. The chapter states it draws heavily on research conducted by one business publisher, which is a party with an interest in businesses advertising in business publications.
confounders: reading it as advice against ever mentioning company scale; the finding is about one customer set's criteria
assuming specificity is about credibility alone; here it is about checkability against a buyer's existing criteria
missing that a substantial part of this chapter's evidence base comes from an interested party

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'The secrets of success in business-to-business advertising', section 'Print', the passage on babies, beagles and bosoms (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy names a specific failure that comes from a copywriter projecting his own boredom onto the reader. Describe it, and state the two conclusions he draws from the same premise.
qa_items.answer: The failure is that, assuming the reader will find the product as boring as they do, copywriters try to inveigle him in with irrelevant attractive imagery — his phrase is pictures of babies, beagles and bosoms. He rejects it because the specialist buyer is more interested in the product than in anything else in the world, and says to play it straight. From the same premise he draws two conclusions: that copy of more than three hundred and fifty words attracts more readers than short copy in these publications, and that although body copy is read by no more than ten per cent of a publication's readers, that ten per cent are the prospects, so what is said to them decides the advertisement. Where prior interest is high and constant, the advertisement's job is information rather than seduction.
qa_items.support: Stated failure with a mechanism, plus reported readership figures for business publications of 1983 sourced from one publisher's research. The phrase quoted is Ogilvy's own and carries the register of his period.
confounders: generalising 'play it straight' to consumer categories where he argues the opposite about curiosity and story appeal
reading the ten per cent as a weakness; he treats it as pre-qualified
assuming the length rule is about the medium; his reason is the reader's prior interest

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'The secrets of success in business-to-business advertising', sections 'How to stimulate inquiries' and 'Analyse your inquiries' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Your boss asks what tangible results the trade advertising is producing. Ogilvy anticipates the question and gives three ways to answer it. What are they, and which does he say does most?
qa_items.answer: Survey a sample of inquirers to find whether they intend to buy, are waiting for a salesman, or are simply keeping the product in mind. Question the salespeople who followed the inquiries up: did the inquiry lead to a sale, was it a new prospect, how did the salesman rate it. And relate inquiries to the media that produced them, which he says lets you fine-tune media selection — he reports one manufacturer cutting his budget by a quarter this way. He says the second does most in one specific sense: the discovery of a single major sale resulting from an inquiry can do more than anything else to demonstrate the value of the advertising.
qa_items.support: Three stated methods with one reported budget outcome. This is the second measurable branch in the book alongside direct response, and he builds the same argument: where the response is attributable, the practice can be corrected.
confounders: treating inquiry volume as the answer; he asks what the inquiries turned into
assuming the media analysis is about buying more; his reported outcome is a smaller budget
confusing this with brand tracking, which measures attitudes rather than attributable responses

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'The secrets of success in business-to-business advertising', section 'Print', the buying-influences passage (spine 17)
qa_items.question: What function does Ogilvy assign to business advertising, and what is his argument for it — given that he concedes an advertisement can seldom close a sale?
qa_items.answer: Its function is to pave the way for salesmen by pre-selling the product and attracting leads. His argument is coverage rather than persuasion: industrial companies have an average of four buying influences, the sales force is unlikely to know all four, and sixty per cent of specifiers — the people who set the specifications that must be met — read advertisements to learn what is on the market. Advertising's contribution is therefore access to the decision-makers the sales force cannot reach. He supports it with the cost comparison of his period between a salesman's call, a letter, a telephone call and reaching a prospect through advertising.
qa_items.support: Reported figures from one publisher's research, given with results. The cost figures, the four buying influences and the specifier percentage are 1983 data.
confounders: reading it as a claim that advertising is more persuasive than a salesman; the argument is about reach
carrying the cost ratios forward; they describe 1983 selling costs
assuming the specifier is the buyer — his separate point is that top management and specifiers may need different campaigns

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', the passage beginning 'Advertisers who distribute their products in the normal way' (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Why, on Ogilvy's own account, is direct mail testable when general advertising is not — and what does the answer say about where the advantage actually lies?
qa_items.answer: Because advertisers distributing through wholesalers and retailers have great difficulty isolating the results of their advertising from the other factors in the marketing mix, while direct-mail advertisers can measure the results of a mailing to the dollar. The advantage therefore lies in the distribution channel, not in the format: a closed loop between the piece sent and the order received removes the confound that defeats measurement elsewhere. This extends his chapter-2 argument that where direct response and general advertising diverge the measured party is likelier to be right, by supplying the reason the measurement is possible at all.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a mechanism. He also notes in the same chapter that direct mail is where the swindlers are found and reports one and a half million consumer complaints in 1980 — the branch he treats as his evidence base is also the one he says attracts fraud.
confounders: attributing the testability to the mail format rather than to attributable response
assuming the conclusion transfers to any advertising that can be counted; his condition is that the order comes back to the advertiser
treating this as a new claim rather than as the reason behind his chapter-2 position

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', the passage on choosing which variables to test (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy says everything in a mailing can be tested and then immediately says you cannot test it all. Explain the constraint, how he says practitioners resolve it, and the circularity in his resolution.
qa_items.answer: The constraint is that only one variable can be tested at a time, so tests are serial and test capacity is finite; you therefore have to choose which variables to test. Experienced practitioners, he says, always test certain variables and seldom test those experience has taught them make little difference — and after the positioning of the product he names pricing, terms of payment, premiums and the format of the mailing as the most important. The circularity is that experience decides what gets tested while testing is what produces experience; he does not remark on it. It is nonetheless the most honest statement about measurement in the book, because it concedes that measurement is rationed.
qa_items.support: Stated constraint with a stated priority order, asserted from practice. No evidence is given that these four variables move results more than others. The same serial limit appears in his research chapter, where a split run can test only two headlines at a time.
confounders: reading the priority list as a finding rather than as practitioner convention
assuming multivariate testing is dismissed on principle; he states a practical serial limit of his period
missing that the same limit constrains his preferred split-run method for choosing a promise

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', the passages on terms of payment and on the Moscow Olympic coins (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy reports two direct-mail tests whose results contradict the obvious expectation. Give both with their numbers where he supplies them, and say why these two items carry more evidential weight than most of the book.
qa_items.answer: A magazine tested three subscription terms; the cheapest and shortest cut the price by forty per cent and generated thirty-five per cent more net revenue than the alternatives — he introduces it by inviting the reader to guess which won. And a coin collection sold better in its complete form when the mailing offered only the cheapest part of it, the silver coins, than when the mailing offered the complete collection itself. They carry more weight than most of the book because in both cases the test, its conditions and its numerical or directional result are all reported together, rather than a result being claimed for a campaign after the fact. He offers no mechanism for either and draws no rule beyond the instruction to test.
qa_items.support: Two reported tests with conditions and results supplied, each a single test in a single category. He presents them as illustrations of why testing is necessary rather than as findings that transfer.
confounders: generalising the price result into a rule that lower prices raise revenue
reading the coin result as a rule about partial offers rather than as one surprising outcome
assuming he explains either result; he does not attempt a mechanism

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', the passage on premiums and terms (spine 18)
qa_items.question: A mailing with a sweepstake entry is beating the control on response rate by a wide margin. What would Ogilvy have you consider before adopting it, and what is the mechanism behind his warning?
qa_items.answer: He would have you consider who the extra responses are coming from. Sweepstakes, premiums, free offers and low prices build up initial response, but the customer attracted by these devices is not always the customer who turns into a long-term buyer; asking full price with cash on order reduces the number who respond and may turn up more customers likely to stay with you over the years. The mechanism is that the device which lowers the barrier also changes who crosses it, so response rate and customer quality are moved by the same lever in opposite directions. His only resolution is that only testing will tell — which here means testing against a longer-horizon outcome than response.
qa_items.support: Stated trade-off with a mechanism, hedged throughout with 'not always' and 'may', so he is describing a risk rather than a measured effect. No figures are given for either side. It is the sharpest statement in the book that the measurable quantity and the wanted quantity can diverge, and it comes from the branch he treats as authoritative because it is measurable.
confounders: treating response rate as the outcome, which is exactly the substitution he is warning about
reading it as advice against premiums; he recommends testing them and says to offer one when margin allows
assuming he quantifies the quality difference; he does not

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', the passages on the control and on making an expensive control cheaper (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Once a mailing is profitable, Ogilvy says it becomes the control. Testing then proceeds in two directions — name both, and say which one practitioners are likelier to neglect and why it matters.
qa_items.answer: Upward: add a premium, an expiration date, enclosures such as a personalised letter from the president — they cost money, and he says that if they increase profit there is no reason to worry. Downward: test a smaller piece, drop the personalisation, print the brochure in two colours instead of four, or drop the brochure altogether, because an expensive control can sometimes be made cheaper without reducing orders — less can be more. The downward direction is the neglected one, because it produces no new creative work and asks whether existing spend is earning anything. It matters because the criterion is profit rather than response, so removing cost and adding response are equally valid experiments.
qa_items.support: Both directions stated, the downward one marked as an expectation to be tested rather than as a finding — 'you may be in for a pleasant surprise'. The profit-rather-than-response criterion is explicit in his phrasing about premiums.
confounders: optimising response rather than profit, which makes the downward tests look like losses
assuming the control should be replaced whenever a variant wins on any measure
reading his carrier-pigeon anecdote as evidence for novelty; it reports one sale with no comparison

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', section 'Direct response advertising in magazines and television', the coupon passage (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy says readers of a response advertisement do something that general advertising does not plan for. What is it, and what does he conclude the coupon must therefore be?
qa_items.answer: Readers often skip from the headline straight to the coupon, to find out what the offer is. The coupon is therefore a second entry point rather than a mechanism at the end of a linear read, so he concludes it must be a miniature advertisement in its own right — complete with the brand name, the promise and a small photograph of the product. He adds that many readers tell themselves they will mail the coupon later and never do, citing a survey that twice as much response is lost that way as is received, and names four holding devices: limited edition, limited supply, last time at this price, special price for promptness.
qa_items.support: Stated reading behaviour with a design consequence, plus a cited survey whose ratio is given without source. This modifies the linear scan order — illustration, headline, copy — that his print chapter derives its layout rule from.
confounders: keeping the coupon as a bare form because the copy above it already sells
assuming the scan-order rule from the print chapter applies unchanged where there is a coupon
reading the four urgency lines as general copy advice rather than as devices against a specific measured loss

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', section 'Television' (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy's direct-response television advice contradicts a rule he praises elsewhere in the same book, and he flags the contradiction himself. What is it, and what reconciliation is available that he does not state?
qa_items.answer: He says the demonstrations in a direct-response commercial should promise not one benefit but several, and adds in parentheses that this runs counter to the Procter & Gamble formula — the single-benefit rule he admires in his chapter on competing with that company. The reconciliation available but not stated is that the two rules serve different objectives: a commercial that must complete a sale in one exposure has to carry enough reasons to close it, while a campaign building a brand over years is trying to own one association. He also sets a length floor from the same reasoning — his most experienced colleague has almost never seen a commercial shorter than two minutes produce profitable sales, and twenty seconds must go to ordering information alone.
qa_items.support: The conflict is marked by the author in his own parenthesis and left unresolved. The two-minute floor is attributed to one colleague's experience rather than to a test; the twenty seconds of ordering information is a requirement of 1983 telephone and mail ordering.
confounders: concluding that Ogilvy abandons the single-benefit rule; he states both and marks the clash
carrying the two-minute floor into any other objective or era
assuming the several-benefits rule is about richness of content rather than about closing a sale in one exposure

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', section 'Television', the passage on programme quality (spine 18)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy reports that the better the programme a direct-response commercial appears in, the fewer sales it makes. What is his explanation, and what does he conclude about buying media on audience size?
qa_items.answer: His explanation is that a bored viewer will pick up the telephone and a riveted one will not: when viewers are bored by an old film they are more likely to order than when they are gripped by a popular drama. The act being asked for competes with the programme for the same moment, so attention to the programme is a cost rather than a benefit. His conclusion is blunt — there is no correlation between the size of your audience and the number of orders you receive — and his colleague buys time by counting the orders received each time a station broadcasts a commercial and eliminating the stations and dayparts that do not pay. Reach is the wrong currency where the response is an action taken during the exposure.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a mechanism; no data are given for the no-correlation claim, which is stated as a thing to remember. The dayparts, months and programme titles named are those of 1983 American television.
confounders: generalising the finding to brand advertising, where the response is not an act performed during the exposure
reading it as an argument for cheap inventory rather than for a different buying currency
carrying the specific dayparts and months forward as recommendations

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Direct mail, my first love and secret weapon', section 'Where to advertise' (spine 18)
qa_items.question: On repeated insertion Ogilvy says something in this chapter that sits against what he says in chapter 2 about repeating a winner. State both, and say precisely why this is not a disagreement between sources.
qa_items.answer: In chapter 2 he reports research showing readership does not decline across at least four repetitions in the same magazine, argues the audience is a moving parade rather than a standing army, and advises repeating a good advertisement until it stops selling. Here he says that when you advertise repeatedly in the same magazine response rates almost always drop, and that the number of profitable insertions differs by publication — some support six a year, others twelve. This is not a disagreement between sources because it is one author in one book, and the two statements are about different measures: readership in the first case, orders in the second. He never sets them side by side, so the reconciliation is available and unmade. Treating it as two sources conflicting would be a mistake about what the evidence is.
qa_items.support: Chapter 2 is live Canon and is not re-extracted here; the comparison is stated because the later chapter qualifies it. Neither statement carries a study, and the decay claim is given as practitioner experience.
confounders: presenting the two as evidence that the field disagrees about wear-out; both are Ogilvy
assuming one statement supersedes the other; they concern different measures
confusing response decay with creative wear-out as measured by attitude tracking, which he discusses separately in the research chapter

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 13 'Advertising for good causes', section 'Raising money' (spine 19)
qa_items.question: A charity plans to judge its advertising by the contributions that arrive in reply. Ogilvy warns against exactly this. What is the warning, and what does he say the advertising is actually for?
qa_items.answer: His warning is that it is rare for any advertisement, however powerful, to bring in enough direct contributions to pay for the cost of the space — so contributions returned by post measure the campaign at the wrong place. What advertising can do is sensitise the market, making it easier to raise money by more personal methods of solicitation, since it is difficult to persuade people to give to a charity they know nothing about. The advertisement is not the transaction; it creates the knowledge that makes a later personal ask possible. His own case describes a campaign whose advertisements produced only modest cash in the mail and whose function was to prepare the ground.
qa_items.support: Stated warning with a mechanism, and a reported case in which the campaign's function is described as sensitising rather than collecting. The chapter's behaviour outcomes elsewhere — teenage drinking falling, cancer clinic check-ups tripling — are attributed with nothing else excluded.
confounders: keeping the response measure because it is the only attributable one; his point is that it is attributable and wrong
reading it as pessimism about cause advertising; he reports substantial effects, measured at a different place
confusing the sensitising claim with brand-image building, which is about personality rather than about enabling a later ask

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 13 'Advertising for good causes', section 'Teenage alcoholism in Norway' (spine 19)
qa_items.question: A public-health campaign aimed at teenagers records the highest readership ever measured in its market and the behaviour does not shift. Ogilvy reports a campaign that faced this. What was done, and what should you be careful not to claim about the outcome?
qa_items.answer: The campaign began by addressing fourteen to sixteen year olds directly, with headlines quoting their own words, and recorded the highest readership ever measured in that country. It was then modified to address parents instead, explaining why children drink and the risks they run — a change of audience inside the same objective, rather than a change of message or craft. More than seventy per cent of parents are reported to have read those advertisements, and he reports that drinking among teenagers decreased for the first time in many years. What you should be careful not to claim is that the campaign caused the decrease: the readership figures are measurements and the behaviour change is attributed with nothing else excluded and no comparison group.
qa_items.support: Two waves of a real campaign with readership measured and reported for both, and an uncontrolled behaviour outcome. The audience switch is the reusable move and Ogilvy does not draw it out as a principle; he reports it as what happened next.
confounders: concluding the first wave failed; he reports record readership for it
treating the behaviour change as demonstrated by the campaign
reading the fix as better creative work rather than as a change in who is addressed

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 14 'Competing with Procter & Gamble', the passages on discipline, sampling and product superiority (spine 20)
qa_items.question: In Ogilvy's account of the most formidable advertiser in his categories, where does advertising sit in the sequence — and what has to be true before it is expected to work at all?
qa_items.answer: Advertising sits last. On the account he reports, superior product performance is the key and no amount of ingenious advertising can save a brand in which the consumer perceives no real benefit. Superiority is verified by blind in-home tests, so that it is apparent to the consumer rather than only to the maker. Then massive home-delivered sampling puts the product in hands, on the stated ground that the other elements of the mix become fully productive only once satisfied customers have had firsthand experience. Only then is advertising expected to do its work. Testing is patient to the point of six years for one regional expansion, and of the three products that went national without at least six months in test market, two failed.
qa_items.support: Reported at second hand, from a partner's study of a competitor, with its key statements quoted from that company's own chairmen — parties with an interest in a flattering account. Budget figures and market shares are those of 1983.
confounders: reading it as an argument for spending more on advertising; the sequence puts product and trial first
assuming blind testing is about advertising claims; it is about whether the advantage is perceptible at all
treating the chairmen's statements as independent evidence

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 14 'Competing with Procter & Gamble', the passage on the Achilles' heel (spine 20)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy admires an advertiser's consistency at length and then names it as their weakness. Explain the double reading, and say what it qualifies in his own earlier doctrine.
qa_items.answer: He reports strategies unchanged for thirty years with executions continually retested, campaigns running ten years or more, and never changing a successful strategy — and then says their Achilles heel is their consistency: they are always predictable, and it helps to win battles when you can anticipate the enemy's strategy. Consistency is what allows a strategy to be validated and re-used, and the same property makes the next move inferable by a competitor; the advantage and the vulnerability are one fact seen from two sides. This qualifies his chapter-2 doctrine that advertising should project the same image year after year, which names only the internal forces that erode consistency and no external cost of holding it. It is the same author adding a cost to his own earlier claim.
qa_items.support: Both halves stated in the same chapter, the first at length and the second in two sentences. Chapter 2 is live Canon and is not re-extracted here; the qualification is noted because the later chapter supplies it.
confounders: reading the Achilles heel remark as a general argument against consistency
treating this as a disagreement with chapter 2 rather than as Ogilvy adding a cost to his own rule
assuming the predictability cost falls on the advertiser's audience; it falls to a competitor who can anticipate them

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', miracle 13 (spine 21)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy points at one sentence in the book and tells the reader to read it again. Which sentence, and what is weak about the way he supports it?
qa_items.answer: The sentence is that advertising which promises no benefit to the consumer does not sell, yet the majority of campaigns contain no promise whatever. What is weak is the support on both halves. The claim that most campaigns contain no promise is an assertion with no count behind it. And the one measurement he offers nearby — a Starch report that headlines promising a benefit are read by an average of four times more people — measures readership, while the sentence he emphasises is about selling. He also says the selection of the promise is the most valuable contribution research can make to advertising.
qa_items.support: His own designation of the sentence as the most important in the book, with a parenthetical instruction to read it again, alongside one readership measurement whose result is supplied.
confounders: treating the four-times readership figure as evidence about selling
reading the majority claim as an audit finding
confusing the promise claim with the chapter-2 big-idea doctrine; a promise is a benefit stated, not an idea

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', miracle 13, the passage on uniqueness (spine 21)
qa_items.question: A promise scores highest on persuasion in your test. Ogilvy says that is not enough. What is the second criterion, what are his two examples of the failure, and what is awkward about the criterion in a chapter about measurement?
qa_items.answer: The second criterion is uniqueness: the promise must be not only persuasive but also unique. His examples are a coffee promise of making a perfect cup every time, which may score highest on persuasion and is not unique, and a soap promise of getting you clean, which may win the test without being distinctive enough to make the cash register ring. What is awkward is that he supplies no method for measuring uniqueness in a chapter organised around what can be measured — the rating method he describes does ask consumers to rate promises for uniqueness as well as importance, but he prefers the split run, which returns only which of two promises drew more response. He also notes what happens when the winning promise is already in use by a competitor, and offers no remedy.
qa_items.support: Stated second criterion with two worked failures. The interview method he describes does collect a uniqueness rating; his preferred method does not, and he does not remark on the gap.
confounders: picking the highest-scoring promise, which is precisely the failure he describes
reading uniqueness as novelty of phrasing rather than as distinctiveness of the claim in the category
assuming a split run can settle uniqueness; it settles which of two draws more response

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', miracle 13, the split-run passage (spine 21)
qa_items.question: You have five candidate promises and want to choose between them the way Ogilvy prefers. Describe his method, its stated merit, its stated limit, and the substitution inside it that he does not remark on.
qa_items.answer: Write two advertisements differing in the headline promise, offer a free sample at the end of the copy, and run them so that half the circulation gets one headline and half the other; the headline drawing more applications wins. Its merit, in his words, is that it tests promises in the context of advertisements rather than in the unreal context of an interview. Its limit is that only two headlines can be tested at a time, so five candidates require several successive runs. The substitution he does not remark on is that the measured response is an application for a free sample, which is a proxy for buying rather than buying itself — the method that escapes the artificiality of the interview introduces an artificiality of its own in the outcome measured.
qa_items.support: Method, merit and limit all stated by the author in one passage; the technique is attributed to a named inventor without a date or reference. The proxy outcome is visible in his description and is not commented on.
confounders: assuming several promises can be compared in one run
treating sample requests as purchases
preferring the interview rating method because it handles more options — he explicitly prefers the split run and says why

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', miracle 16, the four lettered shortcomings (spine 21)
qa_items.question: Give Ogilvy's four objections to recall testing, and say which is a mechanism rather than an absence of evidence.
qa_items.answer: First, nobody has demonstrated a relationship between recall and sales. Second, some commercials scoring about average on recall score below average on changing brand preference, with celebrity commercials the standing case of high recall and low persuasion. Third, it is too easy for the copywriter to cheat, and he quotes a colleague saying that when he wants a high recall score all he has to do is show a gorilla in a jock strap. Fourth, he doubts recall tests even measure recall, believing they measure the viewer's ability to articulate what is recalled, which is a very different thing. The third is the mechanism: it explains how the number can be moved by something unrelated to the product, whereas the first two report an absence of relationship and the fourth is marked as his belief.
qa_items.support: Four objections stated and lettered by the author. The gaming objection rests on a colleague's remark rather than on a demonstration; the fourth is explicitly his belief. The same book states several central print findings in recall terms and never reconciles this.
confounders: treating all four as equally strong
concluding he opposes pre-testing; he prefers a different measure
missing that his own print chapter argues from recall figures

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', miracle 16, the wear-out passage (spine 21)
qa_items.question: A tracked campaign's attitude scores are still positive but have stopped climbing. What does Ogilvy's wear-out case say you should do, and what is the signal you are actually reading?
qa_items.answer: His case is a five-year campaign built on one theme whose tracking studies recorded increasingly favourable attitudes to the product; when attitudes finally stopped improving, the advertising was changed to a different technique and the upward trend resumed. So the signal you read is the flattening of the series, not a fall in it — the decision to change is made on the rate of improvement rather than on the level. This gives an operational form to his chapter-2 instruction to repeat a winner until it stops selling and to measure at regular intervals: the stopping point is where the tracked series stops improving.
qa_items.support: One reported case with the direction of the series given at each stage. It reports attitudes rather than sales, and the resumption after the change is attributed to the change with nothing else excluded.
confounders: waiting for scores to decline, which on his account is too late
reading the case as evidence about the specific replacement technique rather than about the timing signal
treating the attitude series as a sales measure

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', section 'Pitfalls of research', the glass-and-can case (spine 21)
qa_items.question: A food manufacturer sends households samples of the same product in glass jars and in cans, then asks two weeks later which tasted better. A majority say the glass. What did the study actually measure, and what general failure does Ogilvy use it to illustrate?
qa_items.answer: It measured the container, not the taste. The product was identical in both, so the taste verdict could only have come from the packaging — as he puts it, without knowing it they were voting for glass. The general failure he illustrates is that respondents answer a question other than the one asked, either because an uncontrolled difference is present and gets attributed to the thing being asked about, or because the wording lets them avoid an admission — his other case being a question about whether people had read a famous best-seller, which produced inflated agreement until it was reworded to ask whether they planned to read it. In each case the measurement is valid and about the wrong variable.
qa_items.support: A reported test with its design and result supplied, in a section the author heads Pitfalls of research. It is the clearest instance in the book of a confound reported as a confound.
confounders: concluding that glass packaging improves taste perception in general, which would be a finding rather than the warning he is giving
treating the reworded best-seller question as a trick rather than as removing the pressure to misreport
assuming the pitfall is dishonest respondents; his cases are about the instrument

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', the closing passage after miracle 18, and section 'Size of sample' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: After eighteen claimed uses of research, Ogilvy names two questions research cannot answer, and scopes sample size to the question. Give both, and say why the two unanswerable questions are awkward for his position.
qa_items.answer: The two are which campaign will make the biggest contribution to your brand over a period of years, where he says you still have to rely on judgement, and what price to charge for the product. On sample size he says surveys can produce reliable results with amazingly small samples — twenty people suffice to learn whether a word is understood — but that looking for trends over time requires larger samples and rigidly constant sample composition and question wording. The two unanswerable questions are awkward because they are the two with the longest horizons and the largest consequences, and he states them without treating that as a problem for the position he has been arguing. The first repeats a limit he had already stated in chapter 2, that research cannot predict the cumulative value of an idea.
qa_items.support: Both limits stated by the author at the close of the chapter that praises research, with the sample-size guidance explicitly scoped to the type of question.
confounders: taking the twenty-respondent figure as a general sample-size claim; he scopes it to a narrow class of question
assuming pricing is answerable by asking consumers what they would pay
reading the long-run limit as new; it restates a chapter-2 position inside the research chapter

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 '18 Miracles of research', section 'Where I come out' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy admits one specific misuse of research and states one specific benefit he claims from it that runs against the usual objection. What are they?
qa_items.answer: The misuse is that agencies and clients use research to prove they are right — as a drunkard uses a lamppost, not for illumination but for support. The benefit that runs against the usual objection, that research inhibits creativity, is that research has repeatedly given him ideas he would not otherwise have used: he names the eyepatch in the Hathaway campaign, and reports that his partners told him he was mad to want tourism headlines written in French until research found French headlines outperformed English ones. His stated position is that ideas so wild nobody in his senses would dare use them have survived because research found they worked. He notes the wider obstacle himself: anyone can be trained to conduct surveys, but getting people to use the results requires salesmanship of a high order.
qa_items.support: His own summary of where he stands, with two reported instances of research licensing rather than restricting an idea, and one named misuse. The instances are his own successes, reported by him.
confounders: reading his position as research constraining creative choice, which is the objection he is answering
assuming the lamppost line is aimed at clients only; he names agencies too
treating the French-headline case as a general finding about foreign-language headlines

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'What little I know about marketing', section 'Repertory of brands' (spine 22)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy reports a set of findings about how consumers hold brands that bounds what advertising can be expected to do. State the findings and the conclusion he draws about where money should go.
qa_items.answer: Consumers do not buy one brand in a category but keep a repertory of four or five and move among them; buying is steady and habitual rather than dynamic; a brand is almost never admitted to a repertory after its first year on the market; and consumers mostly ignore advertising for brands they are not already using. The conclusion is that the only thing post-launch advertising can be expected to do is make present users buy this brand more often than the others in their repertory — which makes launch advertising a matter of life and death, to be funded with every penny available, now or never. He introduces the conclusion conditionally, with 'if this is true'.
qa_items.support: Findings attributed to two named academics and quoted from their publications, without study design, category coverage or dates. It is the strongest boundary condition in the book on what advertising can do, it is not the author's own work, and he states it and then goes on writing about persuasion elsewhere without carrying it through.
confounders: reading advertising's job as conversion of non-users, which these findings deny for post-launch spend
treating the repertory finding as Ogilvy's own research
missing the conditional framing — he reports a position he thinks important rather than one he vouches for

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'What little I know about marketing', section 'Promotions' (spine 22)
qa_items.question: A brand manager proposes shifting budget from advertising to price promotion because the promotion produces a visible sales spike. Give Ogilvy's answer, including the two authorities he quotes.
qa_items.answer: He answers that in the long run the manufacturer who dedicates his advertising to building the most sharply defined image for his product gets the largest share of the market, and that the one who ends up in trouble is the short-sighted opportunist who siphons his advertising money into short-term promotions. He quotes a former food-company president, who invented a technique for measuring consumer purchases, saying that sales are a function of product value and advertising and that promotions cannot produce more than a temporary kink in the sales curve; and a researcher saying that a cut-price offer can induce people to try a brand but they return to their habitual brands as if nothing had happened. He adds that price-off deals are habit-forming, and that he is not against all promotion — he would not launch a detergent without sampling.
qa_items.support: Two quoted authorities and his own position, none accompanied by a study, a sample or a date. The 1981 spending and coupon figures he gives are context for his complaint, not evidence for the claim.
confounders: reading him as opposed to promotion in general; he names sampling at launch as an exception he would not skip
treating the spike as a disproof of his claim; his claim is about what happens afterwards
assuming the argument is about margin rather than about whether the trial converts to habit

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'What little I know about marketing', section 'Pricing is guesswork', with Ch. 15, section 'Pitfalls of research' (spine 22 and spine 21)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy states that a higher price makes a product more desirable and also reports a study finding price and quality almost uncorrelated. Are these in conflict, and what does the pair actually establish?
qa_items.answer: They are not in conflict. The first is about what a price signals to a buyer; the second, a study relating the prices of six hundred and seventy-nine food brands to their quality and finding the correlation almost zero, is about what a price tracks in the products. Together they establish that price is read as evidence of quality while carrying almost no information about it. His research chapter supplies the signal working in a controlled setting: identical cheeses offered at two prices, and the dearer selling faster. He states all three and never draws the conclusion, and he separately says pricing decisions are in almost every case guesswork.
qa_items.support: A named study with its author, institution, sample size and result supplied — one of the better-documented citations in the book, though its quality measure is not described — alongside a reported price experiment with its result, and his own assertion about desirability.
confounders: treating the two as a contradiction that one side must lose
concluding that raising a price improves the product's standing without limit
assuming Ogilvy states the reconciliation; he sets the pieces down separately

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 17 'Is America still top nation?', section 'The N.I.H. Syndrome' (spine 23)
qa_items.question: A local office insists a campaign built elsewhere will not work in their market. Ogilvy has a procedure for this dispute. What is it, and what does the procedure assume about the argument being had?
qa_items.answer: Test the international campaign in each country, use it locally only where the results are positive, and modify it to fit the local culture even then. The procedure assumes the argument contains two things that need separating: a real question — does this work here, which he says often carries some weight — and a motive that no amount of argument will settle, the Not Invented Here syndrome, since a campaign invented elsewhere threatens local self-respect. Testing answers the real question and leaves the motive nothing to attach to. He reports that campaigns performing well in one market more often than not performed equally well elsewhere, with a campaign successful in thirty-four countries as his instance.
qa_items.support: Stated procedure with a named mechanism. The transfer claim is asserted with three success cases, no failure cases and no base rate. The surrounding chapter contains extended national characterisations of advertising and audiences that reflect 1983 attitudes and the author's position as a visitor, and are not treated here as guidance about any market.
confounders: resolving the dispute by ruling on whether the market is genuinely different
reading the transfer claim as established; it rests on selected successes
dropping the modification step — he requires local adaptation even after a positive test

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 18 'Lasker, Resor, Rubicam, Burnett, Hopkins and Bernbach', the section on Claude Hopkins (spine 24)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy records one of his predecessor's conclusions as disproved by later research. Which, what replaced it, and why does the correction matter beyond the specific claim?
qa_items.answer: The disproved conclusion is that an advertisement should consider only new customers, because people already using your product are not going to read your advertisements. Ogilvy states flatly that users of a product read its advertisements more than non-users. It matters beyond the specific claim because it inverts who advertising reaches, and because it agrees with the repertory findings he reports in his marketing chapter — that consumers mostly ignore advertising for brands they are not already using. Two independent lines in the same book point the same way, and he does not connect them.
qa_items.support: Stated as an established fact — 'we now know' — without naming the later research, its sample or its date. The convergence with the repertory findings is drawn from Ogilvy's own two statements; he makes neither connection himself.
confounders: assuming the correction means advertising cannot recruit at all; it says users read more, not that non-users never do
treating 'we now know' as a citation
reading the correction as a rejection of the older practitioner's method; Ogilvy calls him an uncompromising practitioner of the experimental method in the same passage

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 18 'Lasker, Resor, Rubicam, Burnett, Hopkins and Bernbach', the section on Claude Hopkins, the quoted criticism (spine 24)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy quotes a criticism of his most admired predecessor's writing. What is it, and why is it uncomfortable when applied to this book?
qa_items.answer: The criticism, quoted from another researcher, is that he did not always indicate the boundaries between direct findings from experimentation and conclusions arrived at by general observation and reasoning. It is uncomfortable applied to this book because that is exactly its own habit: measured findings with numbers, results asserted without their measurements, and craft rules held from taste appear in the same numbered lists in the same confident voice, so a reader cannot tell from the presentation which is which. Ogilvy records the fault in a predecessor and does not apply it to himself.
qa_items.support: A quoted criticism that Ogilvy endorses in passing. The application to his own book is an extractor observation about the form of chapters 7 and 8, not a statement he makes.
confounders: reading it as Ogilvy criticising the predecessor's conclusions rather than his marking of them
assuming Ogilvy accepts the criticism for his own writing
treating the criticism as being about honesty; it is about the boundary between two kinds of claim

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 19 'What's wrong with advertising?', sections 'Can advertising sell bad products?' and 'Not enough information' (spine 25)
qa_items.question: Answering the charge that advertising sells inferior products, Ogilvy concedes it — with one word. What is the concession, what bounds it, and what condition does the bound require that he does not state?
qa_items.answer: He concedes it can — once. The bound is repeat purchase: the consumer perceives the product is inferior and never buys it again, which causes grave financial loss to the manufacturer, whose profits come from repeat purchases. From this he concludes that the best way to increase sales is to improve the product. The condition he does not state is that the product must be bought often enough for the buyer to learn; the bound does not hold for something bought once in a lifetime, and he asserts it without that qualification.
qa_items.support: Stated concession and bound, with the repeat-purchase mechanism given. The unstated frequency condition is an extractor observation. His supporting counter-cases are his own successful factual campaigns, reported by him with sales attributed and no unsuccessful case reported.
confounders: reading the concession as a denial that advertising can sell an inferior product
generalising the bound to any purchase without noticing it needs repetition
confusing the argument with a claim about honesty; his mechanism is the buyer's own experience

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 19 'What's wrong with advertising?', section 'Not enough information' (spine 25)
qa_items.question: A whole category's advertising is full of slogans and show business and short on facts. Ogilvy diagnoses one such category from its content alone. What does he conclude, and what makes the diagnostic move transferable — and what makes it weak?
qa_items.answer: After six months of reading car advertisements while replacing his own car he found only fatuous slogans and flatulent generalities, and concluded that the advertising is not aimed at consumers at all: its purpose is to win an ovation when projected on the screen at dealer conventions, because show-business commercials have that effect and sober factual ones do not. The transferable move is to ask who the work appears designed to please, on the reasoning that where advertising is approved by an audience other than the buyer, its content drifts towards what that audience applauds. What makes it weak is that it is an inference from content to intended audience, with no evidence offered about how those advertisements were actually approved.
qa_items.support: A diagnosis from content with a stated mechanism and no evidence about the approval process. His contrasting cases are his own factual campaigns, with sales increases attributed and no unsuccessful factual campaign reported.
confounders: reading it as a general preference for factual copy; the diagnostic point is about whose approval shaped the work
treating the inference as established rather than as an inference from content
assuming he demonstrates that factual car advertising would sell better; his evidence is his own campaigns in other categories

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Overture', the passage beginning 'I am sometimes attacked for imposing rules' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy denies that he imposes rules. What does he say he is doing instead, what form does he give for delivering a finding, and where does the book itself fail his own description?
qa_items.answer: He says he hates rules and that all he does is report on how consumers react to different stimuli. The form he gives is a question put to the person doing the work: telling a copywriter that research shows commercials with celebrities are below average at persuading people to buy and asking whether he is sure he wants one, or telling an art director that research suggests black type on white will be read by more people than white on black — a hint, he says, but scarcely a rule. The book fails the description in two ways: the same chapter states his findings without hedge and dismisses those who disagree as idiots and noisy lunatics, and elsewhere the findings, the asserted results and the craft rules held from taste are presented in one voice, so a reader cannot tell which is which.
qa_items.support: His own statement of intent with two worked speech acts. The failure noted is an extractor observation about the register of the same chapter and of chapters 7 and 8, not a statement he makes. He also declares that the book contains nothing about media, cable television or advertising in Japan, because he writes only about what he knows from his own experience.
confounders: reading the disclaimer as false modesty; the two speech acts he gives are specific and workable
assuming his rules are all soft in practice; he states most of them flatly
confusing this with his chapter-2 attack on the cult of creativity, which is about the criterion for a good advertisement rather than about how findings should be delivered

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Jobs in advertising – and how to get them', section 'Researchers', the fourth of nine complaints (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Ogilvy names a concrete mechanism by which advertising research fails to accumulate. What is it, and what does it add to the chapter-2 complaint that the field refuses to learn its own rudiments?
