qa_items.answer: Reports are read, sometimes acted on and filed; within about two years the researcher, the account executive, the copywriter and the brand manager have all moved to other jobs, and even if somebody remembers the research was done, nobody can find it — so the wheel is reinvented year after year. What it adds to the chapter-2 complaint is a cause. Chapter 2 attributes the failure to a wilful refusal to learn the rudiments of the craft; here the same author supplies a mechanical explanation — no retrieval system plus personnel turnover fast enough that institutional memory goes with the people. It is one author extending his own earlier claim, not a second source disagreeing with it.
qa_items.support: Stated as the fourth of nine complaints about agency research departments, alongside slowness, methodological disagreement and a perfectionism that refuses projects which would produce actionable results. The two-year turnover figure is asserted from experience without a count.
confounders: reading it as a complaint about researchers' competence rather than about retention of findings
presenting it as a correction of chapter 2 rather than as an extension of it
assuming a retrieval system is the whole answer; he names turnover as the other half

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'Overture', the passage beginning 'When I set up shop on Madison Avenue in 1949' (spine 7)
qa_items.question: Writing in 1983 about the previous three decades, what single change does Ogilvy call major, and why should his claim about everything else be treated carefully?
qa_items.answer: The only change he calls major is that television emerged as the most potent medium for selling most products. Everything else, he says, has had its significance exaggerated by commentators looking for trendy labels, and he names two supposed novelties that were not new: brand image, which he popularised in 1953 and which a predecessor had described twenty years earlier, and the Creative Revolution of the 1950s, which he says could equally be ascribed to agencies of the 1930s. The claim should be treated carefully because he is the person whose techniques are said to have survived, which is an interest in the conclusion; because it is a statement about what was true up to 1983, made from inside that moment; and because he raises the alternative reading himself — that old age disqualifies him — and answers it in his own favour.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with two named examples of exaggerated novelty. His supporting argument is that what consumers respond to — value for money, beauty, nutrition, relief from suffering, social status — had not changed.
confounders: treating the durability claim as evidence that the techniques still hold after 1983; it is a claim about the period up to that year
reading the two examples as historical trivia rather than as his argument against novelty claims generally
missing that he is an interested party in the conclusion

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Layouts', the news-magazine format list (spine 13)
qa_items.question: A magazine spread is proposed with a full-bleed photograph, a sans-serif headline reversed out of it, one column of copy running the full page width and no captions. Working only from what Ogilvy states in the layout and typography sections, list what he would change and give his reason for each.
qa_items.answer: Five changes, each with its own stated reason. Move the headline off the illustration and beneath it: readers look first at the illustration, then the headline, then the copy, and he reports headlines below the illustration read by ten per cent more people. Set the headline in lower case rather than reversed out: reverse is almost impossible to read and capitals retard reading because they lack ascenders and descenders. Set the copy in a serif face: readers are accustomed to serifs in books, magazines and newspapers, and the eye is a creature of habit. Break the single full-width column into columns of roughly thirty-five to forty-five characters: people are used to about forty characters in newspapers, and a measure too wide is illegible. Add a caption under the photograph carrying the brand name and the promise: more people read captions than read body copy, so an uncaptioned illustration wastes the best-read position on the page. Every reason turns on what readers of his period had been trained by editorial print to expect.
qa_items.support: All five prescriptions are stated in the Layouts and Typography sections, each with a reason and most with a reported readership figure whose source is not given. The claims are bound to the print conventions and reader habits of 1983.
confounders: justifying any of the changes on aesthetic grounds; every reason he gives is about a trained reading habit
keeping the reversed headline on the argument that it is more striking, which he answers with a fund-raising comparison
treating the caption as optional decoration rather than as the second-best-read element

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Typography', the ten numbered devices, with 'Short copy or long?' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: You have nine hundred words of copy that the client will not cut. Set out what Ogilvy would do to the setting of it, and name the one thing he says has to be true before any of it helps.
qa_items.answer: Put a two-line subhead between the headline and the body to heighten the appetite for what follows. Start the body with a drop-initial, which he reports raises readership by an average of thirteen per cent. Hold the opening paragraph to a maximum of eleven words. Insert a cross-head after two or three inches and thereafter throughout, making some of them interrogative to excite curiosity about the next run, since cross-heads keep the reader marching forward. Set key paragraphs in bold or italic, use bullets or marginal marks, and number unrelated facts. Set at about eleven point — five is too small, fourteen too big — and lead the paragraphs, which he reports worth an average twelve per cent more readership. The thing that has to be true first is the writing: he warns that long copy will only be read if written well, and in particular that the first paragraph must be a grabber. Typography cannot make unread copy sell — you cannot save souls in an empty church.
qa_items.support: Ten numbered devices in the Typography section, two carrying reported percentage gains without sample or source, plus the grabber condition stated in the long-copy section. Point sizes describe print of his period.
confounders: treating the typographic devices as a substitute for a weak opening; he states the opposite order
carrying the point sizes forward as absolutes; they describe print at a stated reading distance
assuming these devices raise entry into the advertisement; most of them raise continuation once the reader has started

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'How to make TV commercials that sell', section 'Sixteen tips', items 1, 5 and 9 (spine 14)
qa_items.question: A thirty-second script opens on eight seconds of wordless atmosphere, names the brand at twenty-two seconds, and carries a super whose wording paraphrases the voice-over. Give Ogilvy's three objections and say which two of his rules are competing for the same seconds.
qa_items.answer: First, the opening: he says open with the fire — grab attention in the first frame with a visual surprise, because people screen out commercials that open with something dull and the viewer does not know a payoff is coming. Second, the brand: he says use the name within the first ten seconds, because a shocking percentage of viewers remember the commercial and forget the product, and often attribute it to a competitor. Third, the super: it must carry exactly the same words as the soundtrack, because any divergence confuses the viewer — a paraphrase is the failure he names. The two rules competing for the same seconds are the visual surprise and the brand name: both make a claim on the opening ten seconds, and he never says how to spend them when the surprise and the name cannot be the same thing.
qa_items.support: Three stated tips, none carrying a measurement; the brand-attribution figure is asserted with its result withheld. The competition between the two opening rules is an extractor observation, not something Ogilvy raises. All of it is stated for the thirty-second commercial of 1983.
confounders: defending the slow open as building anticipation, which is the exact position his asymmetry argument answers
treating the super as reinforcement in spirit rather than word for word
assuming Ogilvy resolves the conflict between the surprise and the brand name; he states both and leaves it

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', sections 'Posters' and 'Subway cards' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: You are handed one brief covering a roadside poster and a transit card inside a train carriage, and asked to run the same execution on both. Using only what Ogilvy states, say what you would do and how confident you could be in each half.
qa_items.answer: You would not run the same execution. For the poster he prescribes a visual scandal, the promise delivered pictorially as well as in words, the largest possible type, a brand name visible at a distance and no more than three elements. For the transit card he prescribes the opposite of that compression: he warns explicitly against designing a subway card like a billboard with five or six words, because the average rider was exposed to the card for twenty-one minutes and eighty-five per cent of passengers carried nothing else to read, so a long message can be read — he reports writing seventy-six words for one. Confidence differs sharply. The transit prescription follows from two reported audience measurements; the poster prescription he marks himself as resting on little or no research, closing the section by asking the reader to tell him if they know more. Both figures describe one transit system in one era.
qa_items.support: Two adjacent sections with opposite evidential standing, one explicitly disclaimed by the author and one derived from reported exposure measurements for the New York subway of the period.
confounders: treating out-of-home as one medium with one rule, which is what the contrast is there to block
carrying the twenty-one-minute reasoning to any other placement without checking exposure duration and competing reading matter
reading the three-element poster rule as evidence-based

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising', section 'Body copy', the price passage (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Two advertisements are in front of you: one for a packaged soap, one for a refrigerator. Neither carries a price. Ogilvy's rule on price is not the same for both. What does he say, and what is the mechanism?
qa_items.answer: His general instruction is always to try to include the price, and the mechanism is that a missing price leaves a question the reader cannot resolve and will not ask, so he abandons the item — his analogy is the necklace in a jeweller's window that goes unconsidered because the price is not shown and the passer-by is too shy to go in and ask. He then scopes it himself: he does not think it matters with packaged goods, and says it matters a lot with products that cost real money, like cars and refrigerators. So the omission is a real fault in the refrigerator advertisement and by his own judgement close to immaterial in the soap advertisement. He notes the structural obstacle of his period — manufacturers cannot dictate prices to retailers, so they often cannot state one — and says this reduces the selling power of their advertisements.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with an explicit category boundary marked by the author's own hedge, 'I don't think', and no measurement separating the two categories. The obstacle he names is a fact about the trade of his era.
confounders: applying the rule uniformly; he scopes it himself by purchase size
reading the mechanism as price transparency or fairness rather than as an unresolved question the reader will not pursue
assuming he supports the category boundary with evidence; he marks it as his own belief

qa_items.source_title: David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (London: Pan Books and Orbis, 1983; Vintage Books edition, 1985)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'The secrets of success in business-to-business advertising', sections 'Print' and 'Analyse your inquiries' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: A campaign for industrial valves is proposed with an arresting lifestyle image, a short headline, forty words of copy and a logo. Using Ogilvy's business-to-business chapter, say what is wrong with it and what you would need to add before anyone could tell whether it worked.
qa_items.answer: Three things are wrong on his account. The lifestyle image is the failure he names as babies, beagles and bosoms — the copywriter assuming the reader finds the product as boring as he does, when the buyer of a specialist industrial product is more interested in that product than in anything else in the world; play it straight. Forty words is far too short: he says copy of more than three hundred and fifty words attracts more readers in these publications, and that although body copy is read by no more than ten per cent of readers, that ten per cent are the prospects. And the promise is missing — the headline should promise a benefit or deliver news, and the promise must be specific in percentages, time elapsed or dollars saved, because you are talking to engineers. Before anyone could tell whether it worked you would need the response mechanism and the analysis around it: a toll-free number, a business reply card and a coupon, the address and number repeated at the close of the copy because the journal is read by about three people besides the subscriber and the first cuts the coupon out, then a survey of inquirers, questions to the salespeople who followed them up, and inquiries related back to the media that produced them.
qa_items.support: All prescriptions stated in the chapter, drawing heavily on research from one business publisher — a party with an interest in businesses advertising in business publications. The readership figures, the three-extra-readers figure and the response mechanics describe printed trade journals of 1983.
confounders: defending the lifestyle image as standing out in a dull category, which is the reasoning he names as the mistake
measuring the campaign by readership alone when the chapter's whole argument is that inquiry can be traced to a sale
carrying the passed-along-copy argument forward; it is a physical fact about a printed journal

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. xi-xii (Introduction, the passage beginning 'Some managers believe that brands possess unique identities')
qa_items.question: Ries and Ries reject the whole vocabulary of brand architecture — flanker brands, megabrands, subbrands, model names. What test do they apply to reach that conclusion, and what definition of a brand do they put in its place?
qa_items.answer: Their test is conversational: they ask the reader to imagine a customer saying to a friend "what do you think of this new flanker brand?" and answering "not much, I stick with megabrands or subbrands". Since nobody talks or thinks that way, they conclude the distinctions have no existence in the only place they regard as real — the prospect's mind — and that on paper there is no difference between a company name, a product name and a brand name. In their place they put a definition with no hierarchy in it at all: a brand name is a word in the mind, specifically a proper noun, and any and every proper noun is a brand. That deliberately extends beyond registered trademarks to places (Philadelphia the cheese and the city, Patagonia the clothing and the region) and to people. They separately insist a brand name on a package is not the same thing as a brand name in a mind, since the same shopper may buy milk and bread as commodities and beer and cigarettes by brand on one trip.
qa_items.support: The authors' own definition and the argument they use to reach it, printed pp. xi-xii. The entire support is the observation that customers do not say the words; no evidence is offered that customers cannot hold hierarchical structures.
confounders: reading this as a claim that brand architecture never affects behaviour; their argument is narrower — the vocabulary is not spoken, so they treat it as an internal fiction
the modern brand-equity tradition, which treats a brand as a bundle of associations, awareness and perceived quality; that is not this definition
assuming they mean the legal trademark; they explicitly say brands are not limited to the 2.5 million registered US trademarks

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. ix-x (Introduction, 'the difference between selling and branding')
qa_items.question: The Introduction says you could sell a hundred-dollar Rolex and sell millions of them. Why do the authors treat that as an argument against doing it, and what general distinction is the example carrying?
qa_items.answer: Because they separate selling from branding and hold that the two can point in opposite directions. Selling millions of cheap Rolexes would increase sales of Rolex watches in the short term and, they say, ultimately kill the expensive Rolex brand — a cheap Rolex destroys what the name means. The general distinction is that conventional marketing strategies, specifically expansion and line extension, can increase sales in the short term while in the long run undermining the power of the brand and decreasing sales. Behind it sits their claim that successful branding rests on singularity, which is also why they say no brand can have universal appeal: broadening the base, widening the appeal and extending the line are the same forces that increase share and undermine the brand.
qa_items.support: The authors' framing of the book's central trade-off, printed pp. ix-x. Practitioner assertion. No time horizon is specified anywhere for when the reversal is supposed to occur, and no case is measured.
confounders: reading it as an argument about product quality; the objection is to what a cheap Rolex does to the name, not to the watch
the price-tiering practice of running a premium line and an accessible line under separate sub-labels, which is the very move the book's Law of Subbrands condemns
assuming they deny the short-term sales gain; they concede it explicitly and locate the whole disagreement in the later half of the curve

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. xiv-xv (Introduction, the dotcom failure list) and p. xiv ('all the laws of branding apply equally to the Internet')
qa_items.question: A colleague says the book proves its case because it can explain every dotcom failure. Using only what the Introduction actually does, explain why that is not a strength, and identify the one thing the book never supplies that would be needed to test any of its laws.
qa_items.answer: The Introduction assigns each named failure to the violation of a specific numbered law — the retailer dotcoms to the Law of Either/Or, the common-name dotcoms to the Law of the Common Name, the give-it-away sites to the Law of Advertising — and assigns the successes to "good branding". Because a law can be found for any outcome after that outcome is known, no case in the book is capable of counting against a law; the explanatory success is a property of the method, not evidence for the laws. The missing thing is a base rate. The reader is never told how many focused brands were launched, how many extensions were launched, or what proportion of each survived, so the frequency with which following or breaking a law is followed by success cannot be assessed at all. Note that the same passage also asserts the laws apply equally to the Internet and the real world, which removes the last place an exception could have been located.
qa_items.support: The Introduction's own method, printed pp. xiv-xv. The observation that this makes the laws untestable is the extractor's, recorded as such in sk_r22_0004 and PROVENANCE.md §6; the material it rests on is entirely the authors' own text.
confounders: concluding the laws are therefore false; nothing here shows that, only that this book supplies no test of them
treating the volume of examples as evidence — the book has many cases and no comparison group, which is a different thing
assuming the authors would disagree; they do concede elsewhere that nothing in branding is absolute (printed p. 101), but they never withdraw the post-hoc attribution

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 3, 6-7 (Ch. 1, 'The Law of Expansion')
qa_items.question: State the Law of Expansion in the authors' own terms, and then explain the distinction they draw in the same chapter that stops market-share numbers from settling the question either way.
qa_items.answer: The law is "the power of a brand is inversely proportional to its scope" — put the name on everything and the name loses its power. The distinction is between a brand's power and its sales. Sales, they say, are a function not only of a brand's power but of the strength or weakness of its competition, so if the competition is weak or non-existent you can often increase sales by weakening your brand, that is by extending it. A share gain following an extension therefore demonstrates only the weakness of the competitor, on their account. Their worked instance is Diet Coke: Coca-Cola had nothing to lose because Pepsi had already line-extended into Diet Pepsi. The practical consequence is that neither a rise nor a fall in share can settle whether the law held in a given case.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 3 for the law, pp. 6-7 for the power/sales distinction and the Diet Coke case. The authors state the distinction themselves; the observation that it makes the law hard to disconfirm is the extractor's (sk_r22_0007).
confounders: reading 'inversely proportional' as a quantity; nothing is computed anywhere in the book, and the phrase is rhetorical
assuming the American Express and Levi's share falls prove the law — they are two-number pairs with no comparison group, and the authors' own distinction says share cannot prove it
the portfolio-theory reading that more SKUs capture more shelf and more occasions, which is the position the chapter is arguing against

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 5-6 (Ch. 1, the teeter-totter passage)
qa_items.question: A car company argues that its parent name is a megabrand and its model names are the brands beneath it. What is the authors' specific objection to that structure, and what image do they use to make it?
qa_items.answer: Their objection is that people assign exactly one name to each product, and they choose the name that best captures its essence — sometimes the parent name, sometimes the model name, sometimes a nickname — and are not consistent about which. The hierarchy therefore does not survive contact with a customer. Their image is a teeter-totter: thousands of tiny ones in the consumer's mind, and like real ones both sides cannot be up at once. On the Chevrolet/Lumina teeter-totter the Chevrolet side is up, so the owner says "I drive a Chevrolet"; on the Chevrolet/Corvette one the Corvette side is up, so the owner says "I drive a Vette". Which end rises is not the marketer's choice. They add that customers want brands that are narrow in scope and distinguishable by a single word, the shorter the better.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 5-6. The mechanism is the authors' own image; the supporting dialogue is invented by them, and no observation of actual customers is reported anywhere in the passage.
confounders: assuming they say hierarchies confuse people; their claim is stronger and stranger — the hierarchy simply collapses to one name, and the marketer does not control which
the house-of-brands / branded-house distinction from later brand-architecture literature, which is not the frame here
reading the Corvette case as an exception to the law; the authors use it as an illustration of the teeter-totter, not as a licensed extension

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 10 (Ch. 2, 'The Law of Contraction', the five-step pattern)
qa_items.question: Give the five steps the authors say most retail category killers follow, in their order. Then identify the tension that steps 2 and 5 create with step 1 — a tension the book does not address.
qa_items.answer: Narrow the focus; stock in depth; buy cheap; sell cheap; dominate the category. The authors chain them causally: narrowing permits depth, depth permits buying power, buying power permits low prices at maintained margin, and the result is domination, which they call the ultimate objective of any branding programme. The tension is that steps 2 and 5 are both expansions. Step 2 widens assortment inside the narrowed category — a Toys "R" Us store carrying ten thousand toys against a department store's three thousand — and step 5 enlarges the brand's share of it, with Microsoft at 95 per cent, Intel at 80 and Coca-Cola at 70 cited approvingly on the following page. So the brand contracts what it is about while expanding what it carries and how much of the category it takes, and the book never says where narrowing stops and depth begins. The domination figures also sit against the roughly 50 per cent ceiling the same authors state twice later.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 10 for the five steps and the Toys "R" Us figures, pp. 10-11 for the domination percentages. The steps are the authors'; identifying the tension is the extractor's reading, recorded in sk_r22_0010 and scs_r22_001 and checkable against those pages.
confounders: resolving the tension by saying narrowing applies to category and depth to assortment — that is a plausible reading, but the authors do not make it and supply no boundary
assuming steps 3 and 4 are supported by figures; no retail economics of any kind appear in the chapter
treating the pattern as descriptive of all retail; the authors restrict it to 'most retail category killers'

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 11-12 (Ch. 2, the passage beginning 'let's say that you want to be rich')
qa_items.question: A founder wants to imitate the market leader in her category and points out that the leader has just launched into three adjacent categories. Apply the authors' diagnostic from Chapter 2 to her reasoning, and state the correction they would make.
qa_items.answer: They would say she is observing at the wrong point in the leader's history. Their diagnostic is that people look at currently successful companies, see them expanding, and infer that expansion causes success — inverting the order, since the expansion is a consequence of success and not its cause. Their analogy is personal wealth: buying an expensive house, a Rolls-Royce and a Rolex will not make you rich and is likely to make you poor, because those are things rich people do after becoming rich. The correction is to look at what the leader did before it led. Their cases are Domino's, Little Caesars and Papa John's, each of which sold a wider menu at the outset — Papa John's sold cheesesteaks, submarines, fried mushrooms, fried zucchini, salads and onion rings alongside pizza — and each of which narrowed. Note the analogy cuts against the book's own method too, since its evidence is overwhelmingly companies observed after success.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 11-12. An argument by analogy; the authors do not establish that their example companies' early behaviour was in fact narrowing rather than something else.
confounders: the competitive-benchmarking default of studying what leaders currently do, which is exactly the error the passage names
concluding that a leader's expansion is always a mistake; the chapter's claim here is only about what a follower should imitate
reading the wealth analogy as evidence; it is an analogy, and the chapter offers nothing else

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 11 (Ch. 2, the parenthesis on Starbucks) with pp. 8, 13 (Starbucks as an exemplar)
qa_items.question: Starbucks is one of the book's showcase cases for the Law of Contraction and again for the Law of Publicity. What does the same book note about Starbucks in passing, and why does that note matter to a reader assessing the Law of Contraction?
qa_items.answer: In the middle of arguing that marketers wrongly copy what successful companies currently do, the authors note parenthetically that Starbucks "currently is busy getting into everything from ice cream to bottled drinks to tea". By their own Law of Expansion that is a brand widening its scope, and the note appears in the very chapter in which Starbucks stands as the demonstration of narrowing. The authors do not treat it as bearing on the law and do not return to it. It matters because the book's central case is presented in a snapshot: the narrowing is credited for the success, and the subsequent broadening — which on the book's own account should weaken the brand — is mentioned and dropped. A reader has no way to tell from this text whether contraction or something else produced the outcome being celebrated.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 11 for the parenthesis; pp. 8-9 and 13 for Starbucks as exemplar of contraction and of publicity. The observation that the parenthesis undercuts the exemplar is the extractor's, recorded as a caveat on sk_r22_0009.
confounders: answering with what happened to Starbucks afterwards — that is outside this copy and this bank deliberately records nothing about it
assuming the authors retract the example; they do not, and the parenthesis is not presented as a qualification
reading this as the book conceding an exception; it is an unremarked inconsistency, not a stated exception like the Law of Change

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 13-16 (Ch. 3, 'The Law of Publicity') and p. 19 (Ch. 4)
qa_items.question: The Law of Publicity and the Law of Advertising appear to contradict each other. Explain how the authors reconcile them, including the specific sentence that states the relation and the reason they give for the transition.
qa_items.answer: They are not alternatives but phases of one sequence, and the reconciling sentence is "first publicity, then advertising is the general rule" (printed p. 19). The distinction underneath it is between brand building and brand maintenance: advertising will generally not get a new brand off the ground, but a hefty budget may be needed to maintain an established one. The transition is caused, on their account, by publicity potential being finite and consumed in two phases — first the introduction of the new category, then the rise of the company that pioneered it. Once both stories have been told there is no news story left, so advertising takes over. Their illustration is Xerox: hundreds of articles on the 914 copier and the new category, then hundreds on the rise of the company from the ashes of Haloid, and after that nothing left to report.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 13-14 for the building/maintenance split, pp. 18-19 for the two phases and the sequence sentence. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism; no measurement of either channel appears anywhere in the book.
confounders: treating this as an integrated-communications point about channel mix; the authors' claim is a hard sequence with a stated cause, not a blend
assuming publicity is recommended because it is cheaper; their stated reason is credibility — what others say outweighs what you say
reading 'brands are born, not made' as being about product quality; it is about coverage potential

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 18-19, 21 (Ch. 4, 'The Law of Advertising')
qa_items.question: How do the authors tell a market leader to think about its advertising budget, and what do they say the budget actually buys? Quote the analogy they use.
qa_items.answer: They tell leaders not to think of advertising as an investment that will pay dividends but as insurance protecting against losses caused by competitive attack. Their analogy is a national defence budget: "your advertising budget is like a country's defense budget" — the tanks, planes and missiles buy nothing, they only keep the country from being overrun. What the money buys, on their account, is a raised price of admission: heavy spending forces any challenger to spend heavily too, which they say many competitors cannot afford and those who can will not bother, settling instead for crumbs. They go further and concede that advertising may not pay for itself, adding that if you are the leader it will at least make your competitor pay through the nose for the privilege of competing with you.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 18-19 and 21. This is a practitioner position stated without any return figure; no calculation of advertising's effect appears anywhere in the book.
confounders: the effectiveness tradition's treatment of advertising as an investment with a measurable return and an optimal share of voice — this passage is the direct opposite of that position, and the book supplies no measurement on either side
assuming they recommend cutting advertising; they recommend massive spending, but for deterrence rather than return
reading it as advice for challengers; it is explicitly advice for leaders, and the chapter says advertising will not build a fledgling brand

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 19-21 (Ch. 4, 'what should a brand leader advertise?')
qa_items.question: The authors say a leader should advertise its leadership rather than its superiority. Set out the loop they describe, and explain why they say leadership claims are nevertheless rare.
qa_items.answer: The loop: everyone believes the better product wins in the marketplace; most people want the better product, so most people buy the leading brand; buying it keeps it the leader; and its leadership sustains the perception that it is better. The claims land differently for that reason — "our product is better" gets the response "that's what they all say", while "our product is the leader" gets "it must be better". Leadership is the one premise a prospect will accept on the advertiser's word, because it is a fact about the market rather than a claim about the product. Such claims are rare, they say, because companies do consumer research and customers insist they would never buy a brand just because it leads, going out of their way to deny it and saying instead that they buy it because it is better. The authors treat the stated reason as unreliable and the circle as real; they also root the whole inference in an American belief that the better product always wins.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 19-21. The consumer's inner responses are supplied by the authors as invented dialogue, and no test of the two claim types against each other is reported.
confounders: treating this as social-proof psychology with an evidence base; the passage cites none
assuming the research finding refutes them; the argument is constructed so that a customer denial confirms the position, which means survey evidence cannot count against it
reading 'leadership' as category leadership only; the neighbouring chapter shows the authors will define a category narrowly enough to make the claim true

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 14 (Ch. 3, the Miller Regular case)
qa_items.question: Miller spent $50 million launching a beer called Miller Regular and the brand failed. The authors use this case to carry two separate claims at once. Name both, and explain why that weakens the case as evidence for either.
qa_items.answer: The first claim is that advertising cannot build a new brand — fifty million dollars produced almost no perceptions among beer drinkers and very little sales, and they add that better, fresher creative work would not have built it either. The second is that a line-extended name has no publicity potential: there is, they say, no publicity potential in a regular beer with a line-extended name like Miller. The case cannot discriminate between the two, because both conditions held simultaneously in it. If the failure was caused by the name, it says nothing about advertising's power to build brands with good names; if it was caused by the spending being on the wrong channel, it says nothing about line-extended names. The book presents no case that separates them, and no brand that advertised heavily at launch and succeeded is examined anywhere in the chapter.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 14. The two claims are the authors'; the observation that the single case cannot separate them is the extractor's, recorded as a caveat on sk_r22_0012.
confounders: accepting the case as evidence for the Law of Publicity because the numbers are large; the size of the spend does not create a comparison group
assuming the authors acknowledge the confound; they do not, and they use the case for both purposes on the same page
supposing a third cause is offered — the chapter considers no alternative explanation for the failure at all

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 14-15 (Ch. 3, 'the best way to generate publicity is by being first')
qa_items.question: A client has a genuinely better version of an existing product and wants a publicity campaign built on that superiority. What would this book tell them to do instead, and what is the stated reason?
qa_items.answer: It would tell them to stop announcing a product and announce a category. The authors' rule is that the best way to generate publicity is by being first — the first brand in a new category — and the reason they give is about what news organisations want: the media want to talk about what is new, what is first and what is hot, not what is better. "Better" is not a story because every brand claims it; "first" is a story because it can only be told once. So the client's superiority is, in this frame, unusable as a publicity asset, and the move is to define a category narrow enough that the product is first into it, and then launch on that. Their own consulting case is Lotus Notes, positioned as "the first successful groupware product" with the emphasis on the category word, which they say the press took up while Lotus's own advertising ignored the idea.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 14-15 for the rule and its stated reason, p. 17 for the Lotus Notes case. The supporting material is a list of twenty-one brands the authors say were first in their category — all of them successes, with no first-but-failed brand anywhere in the chapter.
confounders: recommending a comparative campaign, which is what the passage is arguing against
assuming 'first' means first to exist; the authors mean first into a category as the brand defines it, and the neighbouring chapter shows they will define categories narrowly to achieve that
treating the list of firsts as evidence that being first causes success; every brand on it succeeded, which is how it was assembled

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 26 (Ch. 5, 'The Law of the Word', the sacrifice passage)
qa_items.question: What argument do the authors give for why a brand cannot own more than one word, and what is the problem with the two quantities they compare?
qa_items.answer: They give a capacity argument. The average adult knows the meanings of perhaps fifty thousand words, while about two and a half million trademarks are registered in the United States, and from that they conclude it is a physical impossibility for most brands to go beyond a single word — a limit they say could only be lifted if science replaced brain tissue with silicon chips. The practical instruction that follows is sacrifice: discard the laundry list of attributes and keep one that nobody else already owns in the category. The problem is that the two figures are not comparable quantities. One is an individual person's vocabulary; the other is a national register of legal marks, the overwhelming majority of which no individual will ever encounter. Nothing follows from their ratio about how many attributes a mind can attach to a name, and no cognitive evidence of any kind is cited in the chapter.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 26. The argument is the authors'; the objection to the comparison is the extractor's, recorded as a caveat on sk_r22_0018.
confounders: reading it as an application of cognitive load or memory research; no such research is cited and the chapter has no account of memory beyond the assertion
assuming 'physical impossibility' is meant loosely; the authors state it as a physical limit and reach for silicon to escape it
supposing the one-word rule is about slogans; it is about a single attribute a brand owns in a category

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 24 (Ch. 5, 'you can't become generic by overtaking the leader')
qa_items.question: A challenger brand outsells the category leader and its marketing director expects the brand name to become the generic term for the category. What boundary condition do the authors state, and what test do they give for whether a brand has actually got there?
qa_items.answer: The boundary is absolute in their statement of it: you cannot become generic by overtaking the leader. A brand can own the category word only by having been the first brand and having established the category, and they say Pepsi would not become generic for cola even if it outsold Coke — noting that it once did outsell it in the supermarket distribution channel. Their test for whether a brand has the generic position is ordinary speech: people asking for a Xerox copy, a Q-Tip, Reynolds Wrap, Scotch tape, or asking someone to hand them a Kleenex while looking at a box of Scott tissue. The remedy they offer a brand that was not first is not to push harder on volume but to create a new category by narrowing the focus, and own the word there instead.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 24 for the boundary and the speech test, pp. 24-25 for the narrowing remedy and the Federal Express illustration. No mechanism is given for why priority rather than usage fixes the generic term; the rule is stated and illustrated.
confounders: the trademark-law worry about genericide, which is a different concern — the authors treat generic status as an asset, not a risk
assuming heavy advertising can buy the position; the chapter's whole point is that it cannot be bought after the fact
confusing owning the category word with owning an attribute word — the authors treat Kleenex (category) and Prego's 'thick' (attribute) as two different routes

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 26-28 (Ch. 5, 'what works is not expanding the brand, but expanding the market')
qa_items.question: A brand owns a single narrow word and the board demands growth. What do the authors offer as the alternative to broadening the brand, and what mechanism do they say makes it work?
qa_items.answer: Expand the market rather than the brand: grow demand for the narrow thing the brand already owns instead of attaching the name to adjacent things. Their mechanism is that the brand's narrowness is itself what makes the category desirable. Because Federal Express stood only for overnight delivery, a package arriving by it signalled that the contents were important — "hey, this package must be important because it came via Federal Express" — and that made overnight the in thing among executives, which grew the whole category. Mercedes is their second case: it built the market for expensive cars by pricing at about twice a comparable Cadillac and giving buyers an engineering claim as the excuse to buy one. Their closing instruction is to stop asking what percentage of an existing market the brand can take and ask instead how large a market it can create by narrowing and owning a word.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 26-28. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism. The counterfactual — that FedEx would have grown more by staying narrow — cannot be checked against anything in the book, and no market size before or after is given in any of the four "what was the market before X?" passages.
confounders: reading 'expand the market' as reaching more buyer segments with a broader offer, which is the opposite of the recommendation
assuming the authors think FedEx's expansion damaged the company; they say explicitly it hurts the brand and may not hurt the company, so long as no competitor narrows against it
treating category expansion and brand expansion as the same thing — the whole passage rests on separating them

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 27 (Ch. 5, the two-part prestige procedure)
qa_items.question: The authors say a brand cannot simply claim prestige. Give their two-part procedure for building a prestige position, and the reason they give for the second part.
qa_items.answer: First, make the product or service more expensive than the competition. Second, find a code word for prestige. The reason for the second part is a social one: the connotations of prestige work in brand building but the word itself does not, because it is not that people are not dying to own prestige brands — they just hate to admit it. The code word supplies a defensible reason for a purchase actually made on another one. Their case is Mercedes-Benz, priced at about twice a comparable Cadillac, with "engineered like no other car in the world" as the code; the price itself does work too, since the buyer infers that a car costing twice as much must be better. They note the same structure did for Mercedes what "overnight" did for Federal Express: it expanded the market by giving the owner an excuse to buy.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 27. Practitioner assertion; the claim about what buyers will and will not admit is stated, not measured. The authors themselves record on the following page that Mercedes has since moved into cheaper cars and is not the largest-selling luxury car in America.
confounders: assuming high price alone is the recommendation; the code word is the half the authors say is hard
reading the code word as a euphemism for quality; it is a substitute justification, and the passage is explicit that the real motive is social
treating this as a general pricing rule; it is specific to prestige as the target attribute

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 29-31 (Ch. 6, 'The Law of Credentials')
qa_items.question: What do the authors mean by credentials, what problem do credentials solve, and what do they say happens to benefit claims that lack them?
qa_items.answer: Credentials are the collateral a brand puts up to guarantee its own performance — most often a claim to authenticity or to leadership. The problem they solve is disbelief: customers are suspicious and discount most product claims, so a brand needs one claim that takes precedence over the others and makes them believable. Where the credentials are right, they say, the prospect will believe almost anything else the brand says. Benefit claims without credentials fall into an undifferentiated mass — tastes great, saves money, whitens teeth, bigger, smaller, lighter, faster, cheaper — which prospects meet with "that's what they all say" and generally ignore. Structure the same benefits around a credential and they carry much more weight: if Act claims to cut your paperwork in half you tend to believe it, because Act is the largest-selling contact software.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 29-31. The universal form of the claim — "the crucial ingredient in the success of any brand" — is demonstrated by one advertising line and two of the authors' own client cases, reported by them with the figures they chose to report.
confounders: confusing credentials with proof; the authors' credential is a market fact like leadership, not evidence about performance
assuming credentials mean testimonials or certifications; neither appears in the chapter
reading 'authenticity' in the later sense of brand origin storytelling; here it means the claim to be the real thing as against imitators

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 31-33 (Ch. 6, the Datastream case and 'never forget leadership')
qa_items.question: A company leads a market that is currently tiny and its board wants to drop leadership messaging and sell the benefits of the category instead. Apply the authors' position, including what they say about the sophisticated customers such a strategy will lose.
qa_items.answer: They would keep the leadership claim and reject the board's reasoning, which they state and dismiss in the chapter: the market is small, nobody cares that we lead, forget leadership and concentrate on selling the category's benefits. Their answer is never to forget leadership no matter how small the market, because a leadership position is hard to lose once held and because new prospects in a young category have no experience of it and gravitate to the leading brand — and one should never assume people know which brand leads. Their case is Datastream, which held 32 per cent of a very, very small maintenance-software market, promoted itself as the leader in all its literature, and still dominated once the market grew. On the sophisticated customers: they say that as a category matures the more adventurous buyers go out of their way not to buy the leader, and the instruction is blunt — write them off, you cannot appeal to everybody.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 31-33. The durability claim rests on "a widely publicized study of twenty-five leading brands . . . in the year 1923" with no author, title or method given — a third-party figure reported second-hand, not a measurement made by this book.
confounders: the category-education strategy of selling the category first in a new market, which is what the board proposes and what Chapter 8 recommends for a leader — the two chapters point differently here and the book does not reconcile them
assuming the small market makes the credential dishonest; the authors treat a true claim about a tiny market as fully usable, and say elsewhere they invented categories to create such claims
reading 'write them off' as segmentation advice; it is a refusal to chase a segment, which is the opposite

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 35 (Ch. 7, 'The Law of Quality', the Consumer Reports passage)
qa_items.question: What is the strongest piece of evidence the authors offer for the claim that measured quality does not track market success, and what exactly is wrong with it as evidence?
qa_items.answer: It is a Consumer Reports ranking of sixteen small cars, from which they report that the number-one brand in quality was twelfth in sales, the number two was ninth, and the number three was last. Around it sits their methodological statement in full: "years of observation have led us to this conclusion". What is wrong with the ranking as evidence is that the ranking is undated and unnamed beyond "recent"; the source of the sales ranking is not given; only three of the sixteen ranked brands are reported, and they are precisely the three that make the point; and no statistic of any kind is computed — the word "correlation" is used but nothing is calculated. It is the closest thing to a measurement in the whole book and it is still a selected illustration rather than a test. The blind taste test comparing Coke and Pepsi, cited on the previous page, is reported without any citation at all.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 34-35. This lane examined the passage specifically as a candidate for `empirical_within_source` and rejected it for the reasons above; see PROVENANCE.md §7.
confounders: treating three reported pairs as a correlation; three points selected to make a point are not a sample
assuming the underlying claim is thereby false — it may well be right, and the objection here is only that this book supplies no test of it
reading 'years of observation' as fieldwork; no method, sample or data set is named anywhere

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 35-38 (Ch. 7, 'to build a quality brand you need to narrow the focus')
qa_items.question: If measured quality does not build a brand, what three components do the authors say do build a quality perception, and what do they say about the order in which price should be decided?
qa_items.answer: A narrow focus, a better name and a higher price. Narrowing makes the brand a specialist and a specialist is perceived to know more — their analogy is the cardiologist against the general practitioner, and they add that from a marketing point of view it does not matter whether the perception is true. A better name wins where other factors are equal, and they say being a specialist and having a better name go together, since expanding a brand destroys your ability to choose a powerful name. High price is treated as a benefit to the customer rather than a cost, because it lets an affluent buyer take psychic satisfaction from public consumption — the Rolex wearer is not buying punctuality. On order: they invert the conventional sequence. Instead of building quality and pricing to match, deliberately start with a higher price and then ask what can be put into the brand to justify it — a bigger and heavier watch, an oversized driver, a fatter pen, more butterfat, longer ageing.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 35-38. The authors qualify their own advice on the same page: they say they always advise clients to build as much quality into their brands as they can afford, so this is a claim about what builds the brand, not a licence to build a worse product.
confounders: reading this as advice to skimp on the product; the authors explicitly say the opposite in the same passage
the value-pricing default of matching price to delivered quality — 'quality is job 1' is the position the chapter names and rejects
assuming the price-first inversion is offered generally; it is offered for a sea of similar products at similar prices

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 36-37 (Ch. 7, the omnibus-brand passage)
qa_items.question: Very large diversified companies are the obvious objection to the Law of Expansion. How do the authors handle that objection, and what does their handling of it cost them?
qa_items.answer: They separate size from brand strength and say omnibus or mile-wide brands are weak, not strong: they look strong because they are well known and have been in business for decades, but where such a brand succeeds it is because its competitors are equally broad. Their formulation is that when two weak brands compete the winner is a weak brand that happens to be less weak than its rival, and their test of real strength is what happens when a broad brand meets a specialist — General Electric losing about $300 million in mainframes against IBM, and selling its appliance business to another omnibus brand. What it costs them is disconfirmability. This is the third use in the book of the same move: a counter-example is re-described as a case of weak competition rather than counted, and the book offers no way to establish independently that a set of competitors is weak, so no successful broad brand can ever count against the law.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 36-37. The two GE cases are selected failures; GE's successful businesses are not examined. The observation about disconfirmability is the extractor's, recorded on sk_r22_0026, and the same move appears at printed p. 7 (Diet Coke) and p. 66 (Vaseline Intensive Care).
confounders: accepting the two GE failures as a test; they are two cases chosen from a company with many businesses
assuming the authors deny the sales and profits of these companies; they concede them explicitly and relocate the disagreement to what 'strong' means
concluding that broad brands must therefore be strong — the passage establishes nothing either way, which is the point

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 39-42 (Ch. 8, 'The Law of the Category')
qa_items.question: Chapter 8 says a leading brand should promote the category rather than the brand. Set out the two things the authors say must be done at once when building a brand in a category that does not yet exist, and the reason they give for preferring category promotion.
qa_items.answer: Launch the brand so as to create the perception that it is the first, the leader, the pioneer or the original — they say one of those words should invariably be used — and at the same time promote the new category. The reason for preferring the category is a claim about what customers care about: customers do not really care about new brands, they care about new categories. They do not care about Domino's, they care about whether the pizza arrives in thirty minutes; not about Callaway, but about whether an oversize driver will cut strokes; not about Prince, but about whether an oversize racquet improves their game. Promoting the brand alone is easier, they concede, but not as effective. The money should go behind the concept so the concept takes off and pulls the brand with it, and while that happens the brand name becomes the category word.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 39-42. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism; the five "what was the market for X before Y? Almost nothing" passages carry no figures at all.
confounders: reading it as category-development advertising in the usual sense; the authors want the pioneer's own budget spent on the category, not a trade body's
assuming the advice applies to a follower; it is for the pioneer and the leader of a young category
the Apple Newton case is used both as a category-naming failure and as a product failure, and the chapter does not separate them

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 42-43 (Ch. 8, 'the rightful share of a leading brand is never more than 50 percent')
qa_items.question: A brand that created a category watches its share fall from 100 per cent to 70 as competitors arrive, and its leadership wants to fight them off. What does Chapter 8 tell it to do instead, and what number does the chapter attach to its expectations?
qa_items.answer: It tells the leader to stop fighting competitive brands and start fighting competitive categories — take the bus and leave the driving to us, take your meals home and leave the cooking to us. Falling share in a growing category is treated as normal, and the number attached is that a leading brand's rightful share is never more than 50 per cent: there is always room for a second brand and a train of lesser ones. Beyond that, competition is said to help the pioneer, because rival brands stimulate consumer interest in the category even while the leader's share declines, so the smaller share is a share of something larger. Their counter-example is Polaroid, which forced Kodak out of instant photography and won a few million in court while removing a competitor that they say could have greatly expanded the market.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 42-43. The 50 per cent figure is asserted here and again at p. 60 as "our research indicates", with no research reported. It conflicts with the 95, 80 and 70 per cent domination figures the same authors cite approvingly at pp. 10-11, and the book does not address the conflict.
confounders: the defend-share reflex the passage is written against, which is the conventional answer
assuming the 50 per cent ceiling is established; it rests on an unreported claim to research and contradicts the book's own domination figures
the Polaroid case is a counterfactual — that Kodak would have grown the market — and cannot be checked

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 44-45 (Ch. 9, 'The Law of the Name')
qa_items.question: What do the authors say a brand needs in the short term as against the long term, and what is the argument that gets them from one to the other?
qa_items.answer: In the short term a brand needs a unique idea or concept: it needs to be first in a new category and to own a word in the mind. In the long term the unique idea disappears and all that is left is the difference between your name and your competitors' names — or rather the perception of those names. The argument connecting the two is erosion by imitation. Xerox was the first plain-paper copier and in the beginning you could sell one by showing the difference between a Xerox copy and an ordinary copy; today all copiers are plain-paper copiers, so the technical asymmetry is gone. What remains is the name, which competitors cannot copy, and that is why they say the most important branding decision anyone makes is what to call the product, and that the most valuable asset of the Xerox Corporation is the Xerox name itself.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 44-45. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism. "In the long run" is never defined, and the valuation of the Xerox name is an assertion rather than a calculation.
confounders: reading it as a claim that product quality does not matter at all; the same authors advise building as much quality as you can afford (p. 38)
assuming the erosion argument applies immediately; it is explicitly a claim about the long run, with no time constant supplied
confusing this with brand-equity valuation, which is a different apparatus and absent from the book

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 46-48 (Ch. 9, the East Asia passage)
qa_items.question: Chapter 9 ends with the claim that East Asia does not have a banking, financial, monetary or political problem but a branding problem. What figures are offered for it, and what would a careful reader need before accepting the inference?
qa_items.answer: The figures are a comparison of top-hundred company results in a recent unnamed year: US sales of $3.2 trillion against Japan's $2.6 trillion, but average profits of 6.2 per cent of sales in the US against 0.8 per cent in Japan, with Korea's sixty-three largest companies posting a combined net loss of 0.4 per cent. Around them sit counts of how many of the hundred largest Japanese companies market under one name — sixteen under Mitsubishi, eight each under Matsushita and Mitsui — and Hyundai's "chips to ships" range. A careful reader would need a great deal more: the source and date of the figures, which are given for neither; some consideration of accounting conventions, capital structure, cross-shareholding, exchange rates, the 1997-98 financial crisis, or any of the other differences between the economies, none of which the chapter mentions; and some reason to prefer brand architecture over all of them as the explanation. The chapter offers a single-cause reading of a two-number comparison.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 46-48. Third-party figures reported without source or date; the closing sentence is polemical restatement. Recorded in sk_r22_0030 as an example of how far the authors extend the Law of Expansion, not as something the book supports.
confounders: accepting the profit gap as evidence because the numbers are specific; specificity is not provenance
assuming the extraction endorses the conglomerate-naming criticism; it records the claim and its support, and the support is a two-number comparison
answering with what happened to these groups later; that is outside this copy

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 51 (Ch. 10, 'management measures results with the wrong end of the ruler')
qa_items.question: The authors say one reason 90 per cent of new brands are line extensions is a measurement error. State the error precisely, name the second cost they say goes unmeasured, and give the question they use to expose it.
qa_items.answer: The error is that management measures only the success of the extension and never measures the erosion of the core brand — the ledger records the new item's sales and not what the new item took from the old one. The second unmeasured cost is opportunity: the new separate brand that could have been launched instead was not, so its foregone value never appears anywhere. The exposing question is about source of volume. When Coors was planning Coors Light they asked an executive where the business would come from and were told it would be taken from Budweiser and Miller; Budweiser said the same about Miller and Coors when planning Bud Light, and Miller said the same about the other two. The authors' reply is that the Coors Light drinker is more likely to come from Coors, the Bud Light drinker from Budweiser and the Miller Lite drinker from Miller High Life — and they note the three regular brands all declined substantially after the three lights launched.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 51-52. The beer inference has no comparison group and no other cause considered, and the authors themselves acknowledge on p. 52 that the market genuinely shifted from regular to light beer — which they call "really two markets".
confounders: treating incrementality analysis as what the authors mean; they describe the error, not a method, and offer no measurement technique
assuming the decline of the regular brands proves cannibalisation; a real demand shift is conceded in the same passage and is not separated from it
reading the 90 per cent figure as evidence that extensions fail; it says only how common they are, and is cited without source

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 53-55 (Ch. 10, the Bayer Select case and 'let sleeping brands lie')
qa_items.question: A brand team proposes a "reduced-sugar" version of the company's flagship product under the same name. Apply the authors' specific objection to extensions named by a subtracted attribute, and give the pre-launch test they prescribe.
qa_items.answer: Their objection is that such an extension argues against its own parent. Names built on light, clear, healthy, fat-free or free-of-something tell the customer that the regular product has the defect the new one removes — a reduced-sugar version says the flagship is loaded with sugar, and the assertion comes from the manufacturer, which is the one source the customer has no reason to disbelieve on that point. They run the same reading across Heinz Light ketchup, Hellmann's Light, Campbell's Healthy Request and Crystal Pepsi. Their case is Bayer Select: a company launching five "aspirin-free" products under the name of an aspirin brand, which they gloss as asking why anyone should buy Bayer aspirin when the manufacturer says its aspirin-free products are better. The prescribed test is to ask, before launch, what customers of the current brand will think when they see the extension on the shelf. If the answer is that they will conclude something bad about the product they already buy, do not launch it; let sleeping brands lie.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 54-55. The Bayer figures — a $116 million programme, $26 million of first-year sales in a $2.5 billion market, regular Bayer falling about 10 per cent a year — are reported without source, and the authors themselves say the aspirin decline predated the launch, so the case cannot separate the two causes.
confounders: the health-portfolio default of meeting a real dietary demand under the trusted name, which is the move the passage forbids
assuming the objection is about dilution generally; this is a narrower and more specific failure mode about what the name asserts
reading the Bayer numbers as proof; the parent brand was already declining for reasons the authors state themselves

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 55 (Ch. 10, closing rule) with pp. 77-82 (Ch. 15, 'The Law of Siblings')
qa_items.question: Chapter 10 forbids putting your name on a new thing and Chapter 15 licenses launching a second brand. State the rule that connects them, and the single criterion that separates the licensed move from the forbidden one.
qa_items.answer: The connecting rule closes Chapter 10, and both of its branches begin the same way: if the market is moving out from under you, stay where you are and launch a second brand; if it is not, stay where you are and continue building your brand. Following the market with the existing name is not among the options. Chapter 15 then opens by conceding that the laws seem to suggest concentrating everything on a single brand, agreeing that this is true, and licensing a second, third and fourth. The criterion separating the two moves is whether the existing name is asked to carry new meaning. A line extension attaches the old name to the new thing; a sibling is a genuinely separate name — DeWalt rather than Black & Decker Pro, L'eggs rather than Hanes II, Olive Garden rather than an Italian Red Lobster. Note the authors give no test for whether a market shift is real, which is the judgement the whole rule turns on.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 55 for the two-branch rule, pp. 77-81 for the concession and the sibling cases. The separating criterion is stated by this lane, not by the authors, who argue case by case; it is recorded as an extractor reading in scs_r22_003.
confounders: assuming any second brand is licensed; Chapter 15 attaches six conditions, including that a sibling be launched only when it can create a new category
treating a subbrand as the middle ground; Chapter 14 condemns exactly that, and the criterion above is what separates it from a sibling
expecting a test for a real market shift; the book supplies none, and the rule cannot be applied without one

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 56-59 (Ch. 11, 'The Law of Fellowship')
qa_items.question: Why do the authors say a dominant brand should welcome competitors rather than merely tolerate them? Give the three mechanisms in the chapter.
qa_items.answer: First, attention: competition increases the noise level in a category, makes customers more conscious of it and raises consumption per head — the best thing that happened to Coca-Cola, on their reading, was Pepsi-Cola, and they call it ironic that Coke fought Pepsi over the use of "cola" and fortunate that it lost. Second, comparison: choice is itself read by customers as a benefit, and where there is none they become suspicious — maybe the category has flaws, maybe the price is too high; who wants to buy a brand with nothing to compare it against? Third, focus preservation: two competing brands can each stay narrow and powerful while between them covering a market neither could cover alone, their example being one brand appealing to older customers and one to younger. They see the same effect geographically, in the clustering of used-car dealers, garment and diamond districts, and forty music theatres in a town of under four thousand people.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 56-59. Practitioner assertion with three stated mechanisms; the clustering examples are descriptions of existing agglomerations offered as illustration, not evidence.
confounders: assuming this is about antitrust or market structure; it is advice to a dominant brand about its own posture
reading the office-superstore example as showing competition helps everyone; the independents in the same passage fell from about ten thousand to three thousand
the Law of Advertising in the same book tells a leader to smother competitors and make them pay through the nose (p. 21); the two laws conflict and the book does not reconcile them

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 57-58 (Ch. 11, the wine passage)
qa_items.question: Where do the authors bound their own Law of Fellowship, and what is the weakest link in the case they use to bound it?
qa_items.answer: They bound it at the point where choice becomes confusion: customers can have too much choice, and the more brands, flavours and varieties, the more confusion in the category and the lower the consumption per head. They name two major brands per category as apparently ideal and give five paired examples. Their case for the failure mode is wine — more than a thousand wineries and five thousand brands in California alone, an annual magazine ranking some twenty-four thousand individual wines, and no major brand having emerged. The weakest link is the inference they draw from American consumption being a tenth of France's, a ninth of Italy's and under a third of Germany's. That comparison is cited without source and is used to make brand structure the cause of low consumption, with no consideration of drinking culture, licensing, taxation, price, climate or history — any of which a reader would reach for first. The five ideal pairs are also the five categories that fit.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 57-58. Third-party consumption figures with no source; the causal reading is the authors' and the objection to it is the extractor's, recorded on sk_r22_0035. The authors' own forecast that someone will one day build a worldwide wine brand is recorded as a forecast.
confounders: accepting the consumption comparison as support; it establishes a difference, not a cause
reading 'two brands is ideal' as a finding; it is an observation about five categories the authors chose
assuming this bound weakens the Law of Fellowship's core claim; the authors present it as a limit, not a retraction

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 60 (Ch. 11, 'our research indicates') with pp. 10-11 (Ch. 2, the domination figures)
qa_items.question: The book states a ceiling on a dominant brand's market share and elsewhere cites shares well above it approvingly. Set out both, and say what the reader is left with.
qa_items.answer: At printed p. 60 the authors say no brand can own an entire market absent a government-sanctioned monopoly, and that "our research indicates that 50 percent is about the upper limit", illustrated with Federal Express at 45 per cent of domestic overnight delivery and Coca-Cola at 50 per cent of domestic cola; above that level, they say, a company must launch separate brands. At pp. 10-11 the fifth step of the category-killer pattern is "dominate the category", named as the ultimate objective of any branding programme, and illustrated with Microsoft at 95 per cent of desktop operating systems, Intel at 80 per cent of microprocessors and Coca-Cola at 70 per cent of the world cola market. The two passages cannot both be operative as stated, and Coca-Cola carries two different figures without comment. The reader is left with an unreconciled conflict and no criterion for which passage governs — and with the fact that the ceiling's only support is an appeal to unreported research.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 60 and pp. 10-11. Both passages are the authors'. The identification of the conflict is the extractor's, recorded in scs_r22_001's conflict list and in sk_r22_0036, and is checkable against those two pages.
confounders: reconciling them by domestic versus worldwide scope — the Coca-Cola figures do differ that way, but the Microsoft and Intel figures are worldwide and still exceed the stated ceiling
treating 'our research indicates' as a citation; no method, sample or categories are given anywhere
assuming one figure must be a misprint; both are stated in argument and used to support opposite instructions

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 63, 65-66 (Ch. 12, 'The Law of the Generic')
