qa_items.question: What is the authors' mechanism for why a generic brand name cannot differentiate, and what does it imply about how naming decisions are usually made?
qa_items.answer: Their mechanism is that the mind deals in sounds rather than letters. Most brand communication happens verbally — they claim the average person spends nine times as long listening to radio and television as reading print — and even the printed word is processed through the sound it generates, so a reader cannot hear the difference between "general" and "General". Capitalising a common word therefore does not make it a proper noun in a mind. What it implies about practice is the chapter's sharpest point: the naming process is usually conducted visually, with logotypes set in type, mounted on foamcore and passed round a boardroom, which is exactly the wrong sense for a decision that will be settled by ear. The same mechanism is their explanation for why line extensions fare poorly, since an extension typically pairs a brand name with a generic descriptor and the descriptor cannot create a separate identity — "Michelob Light" being heard as "Michelob light", a watered-down version of the regular beer.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 63 and 65-66. The nine-to-one listening ratio is cited without source and concerns media time, not name processing. The historical objection — that General Electric and its peers succeeded — is handled by asserting they succeeded in spite of their names because they were first.
confounders: assuming this is about descriptive versus suggestive marks in trademark practice; the concern here is retrieval from memory, not registrability
reading the Vaseline Intensive Care case as a counter-example the authors accept; they concede it and explain it as customers happening to treat the descriptor as a name
supposing the historical successes are counted against the law; they are reassigned to priority, so neither outcome can disconfirm it

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 64-65 (Ch. 12, 'take a regular word and use it out of context')
qa_items.question: A start-up in office supplies has shortlisted three names: General Office Products, Staples, and Supply Systems Inc. Apply the authors' two constructive naming procedures to explain which they would choose and why the other two fail.
qa_items.answer: They would choose Staples. It is their own worked example of the first procedure — take a regular word and use it out of context so that it connotes the brand's primary attribute — and they point to the double entendre as making it particularly powerful: buy your office staples from Staples. The other two are the failure the chapter is about: common descriptive words that cannot separate the brand from anything, because the mind hears "general office products" and "supply systems" as descriptions no matter how they are capitalised, and every competitor can use the same words. The second procedure they offer is truncation — cutting a generic phrase down to something short and distinctive, as Intelligent Chip Company becomes Intel, with the point that all computers have intelligent chips inside but only some have Intel inside. Their warning case is the company that dropped McAfee, the only real name it owned, for Network Associates, and then spent $10 million including a Super Bowl spot trying to make two generics register.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 64-65. The procedures are illustrated only with names that succeeded; no failed displacement or truncation appears, and the chapter gives no way to tell in advance which ordinary word will work.
confounders: choosing a descriptive name for search or clarity reasons, which is the modern default and the chapter's target
assuming an invented name is always best; the authors reserve invention for genuinely revolutionary products unlikely to be copied soon
reading the procedures as rules that can be applied in advance; they describe successful outcomes and specify no test

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 68-71 (Ch. 13, 'The Law of the Company')
qa_items.question: The authors say brands are brands and companies are companies, then recommend using the company name as the brand name. Explain how both positions sit together, and give the two-question test they offer.
qa_items.answer: The separation is about whose point of view governs: a company is the organisation that produces a brand and is not the brand, but customers are brand-oriented while managers, being employees, are company-oriented, so the brand name should almost always take precedence. The recommendation follows from that rather than contradicting it — unless there are compelling reasons otherwise, the cleanest arrangement is for company and brand to be one name, so that the question has one answer: what is a Coca-Cola, a Zippo, a WD-40? Cola, windproof lighter, lubricating spray. Their test is a pair of questions: what is the name of the brand, and what is the name of the stuff inside the packaging? Both had better be the same or you have big problems. They push the identification hard — the liquid itself is Coca-Cola, not a cola made by a company — which is why they say a company that understood branding could never have introduced New Coke. They add a symptom: when customers feel they must say both names together, there is usually a branding problem, normally because a generic word was used as the brand name.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 67-71. Practitioner assertion; the Microsoft Excel and Microsoft Word contrast is an argument about what the authors say customers say, with no observation reported.
confounders: assuming the advice is safe for any company; it holds only where the company makes one thing, which is the condition the Law of Expansion imposes — the authors do not state the dependency and Chapter 9 gives the opposite advice for a company that makes many things
reading it as an endorsement of corporate branding as usually practised; the chapter's preference is for the brand name to dominate and the company name to sit in small type
confusing the recommendation with the house-of-brands approach it contrasts, where the maker is relegated to tiny type

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 73-74, 76 (Ch. 14, 'The Law of Subbrands')
qa_items.question: A budget hotel chain proposes a premium sub-line under its existing name. Apply the authors' diagnostic test, then state what they say about who gets to decide whether the new name is a brand.
qa_items.answer: The test is to render the demand the sub-line serves as a sentence a customer would actually say. Did anybody ever walk into a Holiday Inn and ask the clerk "don't you have a more expensive hotel I can stay at?" If no one would say it, the subbrand answers a demand that does not exist, and the customer's reasoning runs the other way: if I am forking out the big bucks, I want to stay with a top hotel brand — why spend all that money and still stay at a Holiday Inn? Their case reports customer research at Holiday Inn Crowne Plaza returning exactly that — a nice hotel, but a little expensive for a Holiday Inn — after which the parent name was cut. On who decides: not the company. What the manufacturer sees as a brand the customer sees as a model, and what the manufacturer sees as a megabrand the customer sees as a brand; customers do not understand the megabrand concept at all, and you cannot apply your own branding system to a market that sees things differently.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 73-74 and 76. The customer research is the company's own, reported second-hand by the authors with no method. The chapter also records Marquis by Waterford as "a big success" and disposes of it by predicting future erosion rather than by evidence.
confounders: the endorser-brand strategy of using the parent for reassurance while the sub-line carries the positioning, which is the practice the chapter is written against
assuming the authors forbid multiple models under one brand; they explicitly allow it, provided the models do not detract from the singular idea that sets the brand apart
treating the Waterford success as an exception the authors accept; they concede it and predict it will erode the parent line

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 81-82 (Ch. 15, the six principles)
qa_items.question: Give the six principles the authors set for a family of sibling brands, and explain the one about names — including the phrase they use for getting it wrong.
qa_items.answer: Focus on a common product area. Select a single attribute to segment, price being the most common. Set up rigid distinctions among the brands, which price makes easiest because numbers can be attached to each. Create different, not similar, brand names. Launch a new sibling only when you can create a new category — never to fill a hole in the line or to block a competitor. Keep control of the family at the highest level. On names: the instruction is that you do not want to create a family of brands, you want to create a family of different brands, and the phrase for getting it wrong is that alliteration is the curse of a sibling family. Their example is Chevrolet's Cavalier, Camaro, Corsica, Caprice and Corvette, which they say are too similar to function as brands. The fifth principle is the one they call most often violated, and they name four Coca-Cola launches — Mr Pibb, Fruitopia, Mello Yello and Surge — each made to block a rival rather than to create a category.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 81-82. Practitioner assertion; the four Coca-Cola blocking launches are all reported as having gone nowhere, which is consistent with the principle and is again a set selected after the outcome was known.
confounders: assuming a family look is desirable, which is standard practice and the opposite of principle four
reading principle six as a call for decentralisation; the authors say a sibling strategy needs more top-management supervision, not less, and blame decentralisation for General Motors
supposing any of the six is a test for when to launch; only the fifth constrains timing, and it constrains the reason rather than the moment

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 80-81 (Ch. 15, the General Motors passage)
qa_items.question: The authors say General Motors' five brands were once instantly identifiable and later were not. What mechanism do they name for the decay, and what management conclusion do they draw from it?
qa_items.answer: The mechanism is sibling rivalry: a pattern of corporate behaviour in which each brand copies the best features of its sibling competitors, so that a portfolio of distinct brands converges. They pair it with a second cause — control over the brands was lifted and each division allowed to set its own course, after which each division broadened the scope of its own brand, producing expensive Chevrolets, cheap Cadillacs and general confusion. Their summary is that all General Motors cars ended up with fins. The management conclusion runs directly against the common belief they quote, that a sibling strategy works best in a decentralised organisation: a sibling strategy requires more top-management supervision, not less, because the urgent long-term need is to maintain the separation between brands and human instincts work in the opposite direction.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 80-81. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism; no other cause of the convergence — platform sharing, cost structure, regulation — is considered anywhere in the passage.
confounders: attributing the convergence to manufacturing economics, which is a plausible account the chapter never addresses
assuming decentralisation is recommended for brand portfolios generally; this passage is the argument against it
reading 'fins' literally; it is their shorthand for every brand acquiring every other brand's features

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 83-84 (Ch. 16, 'The Law of Shape', the typography passage)
qa_items.question: Why do the authors put legibility above expressive character in a logotype? Give the cycle they describe, and say what they concede about typographic mood.
qa_items.answer: Because they hold the trade is not worth making. The cycle: to get an average prospect to notice the mood of a logotype you have to exaggerate the characteristics of the typography, and when you do that you lose the logotype's legibility — and an illegible logotype has little or no meaning in the consumer's mind, not because of the face but because the prospect cannot read the words and therefore cannot remember the name. Hence legibility is the most important consideration in selecting a typeface. What they concede is that perceptual differences are real: sans serif faces look modern and serif faces old-fashioned, bold looks masculine and light feminine. Their point is that these differences only become obvious through exaggeration — they ask whether you would really set a brand name in black-letter Gothic to look established, and answer that few prospects could then read it. They also say customers are only dimly aware of typeface differences, paraphrasing David Ogilvy to the effect that no one ever declined to buy a detergent over the choice of Futura Demibold.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 83-84. The argument is the authors' own with a stated cycle; no legibility measurement is cited, and the chapter's only external authority is a paraphrase of Ogilvy.
confounders: assuming they say typography carries no meaning; they concede specific perceptual associations and rank them below readability
reading this as an accessibility argument; the concern here is recall of a name, not readability for readers with impairments, and no criterion or threshold is given
the brand-expression default of choosing a face to express brand attributes, which is the practice the chapter is arguing against

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 84-85 (Ch. 16, the Nike and Shell/Mobil passages)
qa_items.question: What is the authors' position on the visual trademark as against the name, and what specific disadvantage do they identify in a wordless mark?
qa_items.answer: They hold the trademark is overrated and that the meaning lies in the word, not the visual symbol: it is the Nike name that gives meaning to the Swoosh, and the Swoosh does not give much meaning to the Nike brand. A symbol can come to represent a name after long association through a kind of rebus effect, but the name still carries the power, and the advantages of using the symbol alone are slim and situational — visibility at a distance, use on clothing where a name would look too commercial. Their specific disadvantage concerns succession: comparing Shell's wordless mark with Mobil's wordmark, they ask how people growing up and entering the market will learn that the yellow symbol means Shell, especially if they do not know Shell is a brand of petrol. They add that the elaborate crests, shields and coats of arms produced by design shops are for the most part wasted, and that only a handful of simple symbols work — if history has not already given you one, it is probably too late to make one.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 84-85. Practitioner assertion. Note that in the copy inspected the argument is carried entirely by prose: no illustration survives in this file's text layer, so a reader cannot see any of the marks being discussed.
confounders: assuming they recommend abandoning symbols; they say a symbol may work, and question only what is gained by using it alone
reading this as an argument about design quality; their objection is that a symbol acquires meaning from the name rather than supplying it
treating the Nike example as evidence; the passage notes hundreds of millions a year for over a decade were spent linking the two, and then asks what the advantage is

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 87-88 (Ch. 17, 'The Law of Color', the Maxion tractor case)
qa_items.question: A new entrant in a category where the leader owns the category's natural colour asks which colour to take. Apply the authors' rule, and state the trade they say you should accept.
qa_items.answer: Take the colour opposite the major competitor's, not the one symbolic of the category — the leader has first choice, and the leader normally takes the symbolic colour. Their own worked case is a Brazilian tractor brand they named Maxion. John Deere, the leading tractor brand, had green, the colour of grass and agriculture; the second brand had red; so they made Maxion blue. The trade they say to accept is stated plainly: is blue a good colour for a farm tractor? No — but it is more important to create a separate brand identity than to use the right symbolic colour. They run the same logic through car rental (Hertz yellow, so Avis red, National green) and hold up Pepsi as the counter-case, having taken red and blue together and so struggled for decades against a world that seems awash in Coca-Cola red. They add that whatever colour is chosen must be held consistently over years, which is their reading of the Tiffany box.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 87-89. The rule and the trade are the authors'; the chapter's physiological justification — wavelengths focusing behind or in front of the retina — is offered without a source and does not support the cultural colour meanings the chapter derives from it. The associations listed are Western conventions.
confounders: choosing the category-symbolic colour for recognisability, which is the move the passage explicitly rejects for a non-leader
assuming the leader's rule and the follower's rule are the same; the chapter separates them, and only the leader is told to take the symbolic colour
reading the red/blue physiology as established; it is asserted, and the emotional readings drawn from it are conventions rather than consequences of optics

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 89 (Ch. 17, the Miller and Tiffany comparison)
qa_items.question: The authors connect the Law of Color to the Law of Extensions through a single comparison. What is the comparison, and what does it claim?
qa_items.answer: They compare Miller with Tiffany. Miller's line extensions each need to be told apart from one another, so the brand uses an array of colour combinations, and in the process it loses the chance to differentiate its core brand from Budweiser, its key competitor — one of the many problems the authors attribute to those extensions is that they destroy the brand's colour identity. Tiffany, by contrast, holds a single colour and holds it even at Christmas when every other brand and retailer turns to red and green, which they say makes it more noticeable under the tree rather than less. The claim they draw is a wager about recall: you have probably seen many more Miller cans than Tiffany boxes, but they would bet you know the hue of a Tiffany box and are not quite sure about Miller's. The connection is that a colour is an asset only if it is both differentiated and held, and line extension destroys both conditions at once.
qa_items.support: Printed p. 89. The recall wager is rhetorical — no test of it is reported — and the claim that extensions destroyed Miller's colour identity is asserted rather than demonstrated.
confounders: reading exposure frequency as the driver of colour recall, which is the assumption the wager is set up against
assuming the point is about luxury versus mass brands; the argument is about consistency and differentiation, not price tier
supposing the Tiffany case shows a single colour is always best; the same chapter allows multiple colours where the object is physical stand-out, as with FedEx's orange and purple

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 91 (Ch. 18, 'The Law of Borders', the two ironclad beliefs)
qa_items.question: Chapter 18 opens with two beliefs the authors say most of their clients hold. Name both, explain why the pair produces line extension, and give the authors' alternative resolution.
qa_items.answer: The beliefs are that the brand's market share cannot be substantially increased in its home country, and that the company needs to grow. Together they close off the obvious route and leave only one apparent exit: extend the brand into other categories, which the clients defend by saying it may be dangerous but it is the only way to grow. The authors say that reasoning falls victim to the first law of branding, the Law of Expansion. Their resolution satisfies both beliefs without breaking it: keep the brand's narrow focus in its home country, and go global. Growth comes from more geography rather than from more categories, and nothing about what the brand means has to change. Heineken is their case — the leading brewery in a country of fifteen million becoming the second-largest brewery in the world by going global.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 91-92. The belief pair is quoted by the authors from their own consulting practice. Practitioner assertion; no comparison of the two growth routes is offered anywhere.
confounders: assuming they think home-market share genuinely is capped; they argue elsewhere that the market itself can be expanded, which is a third route (printed p. 26)
reading 'no barriers to global branding' as being about trade; the same chapter lists duties, tariffs, quotas and inspections, and the claim is about mental barriers
supposing the route is generally available — the authors say plainly that not every brewery can do what Heineken did

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 92-94 (Ch. 18, the Heineken passage and 'there is no such thing as a global brand with a global perception')
qa_items.question: What two conditions do the authors set for a successful global brand, and why does their own leading example undercut the sufficiency of those conditions?
qa_items.answer: Be first, and have a product that fits the perceptions of its country of origin. Country perception is treated as inescapable — every brand, like every person, is from somewhere, whatever the place of manufacture, and its name and connotations fix where. Coca-Cola bottled in Mexico is still, in their phrase, a gringo brand. Their example undercuts sufficiency because they explain Heineken's success by three separate strokes of luck rather than by the two conditions. Beer is associated with Germany rather than Holland, but Holland is close to Germany geographically and ethnically so many drinkers take Heineken for German — the company has even distributed coasters printed in Germany. Its main German rival on world markets, Beck's, is saddled with an English-sounding name. And the largest-selling German beer, Warsteiner, begins with a syllable that they say will not travel. If three accidents were needed on top of the two conditions, the conditions were not sufficient, and the chapter does not draw that conclusion.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 92-94. The three strokes of luck are the authors' own account; the observation that they concede insufficiency is the extractor's, recorded as a caveat on sk_r22_0044. The country-perception pairs are the stereotypes of a particular period and readership.
confounders: reading country of origin as a factual matter of where a product is made; the authors are explicit that it is a matter of name and connotation
assuming the mistranslation anecdotes later in the chapter carry argumentative weight; they are widely circulated marketing stories reproduced without any source

treating Corona as confirming the two conditions; that case works through an association with Mexican cuisine and a visible citrus wedge, which is a third route the chapter does not fold into the rule

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 97-98 (Ch. 19, 'The Law of Consistency', the Tanqueray and Coca-Cola beer passages)
qa_items.question: A leading gin brand watches a durable trend toward premium vodka and proposes launching its own vodka under the same name. Give the authors' answer, the two questions they use to reach it, and the reductio they run alongside.
qa_items.answer: Their answer is to stick with gin and hope the market swings back — when the market swings another way you have a choice between following the fad and destroying the brand, or hanging in there, and in their experience hanging in is the better approach. The two questions are: will the new vodka cut into the leading vodka's market? Of course not. Will it undermine the gin business? Ultimately, yes. So the move can only take from itself. The reductio is Coca-Cola beer. They note that as children grow up they change their personality statements, moving from Coca-Cola to Budweiser, so if Coca-Cola tried to retain those customers by moving with the market it would logically introduce a beer — and they say that however foolish that sounds, it is conceptually no different from Tanqueray vodka, Coors water or Crystal Pepsi. Their governing line is that markets may change but brands should not, ever.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 97-98. Practitioner assertion; the Jack Daniel's beer and coolers cases in the same passage are reported as outcomes without figures. The authors' "in our experience" is the whole of the evidential basis for preferring to hang on.
confounders: the brand-stretch reasoning that a strong name in spirits transfers across spirits, which the passage rejects using the brown-goods/white-goods distinction
assuming 'ever' is final; the very next chapter opens by saying nothing in branding is absolute and sets out three permitted changes
reading the badge argument as demographic targeting; it is an argument for staying still while customers move on

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 98-100 (Ch. 19, the boredom passage and the Arch Deluxe)
qa_items.question: What cause do the authors give for most violations of the Law of Consistency, and what diagnostic error do they say a company makes after such a violation fails?
qa_items.answer: Boredom. Brand building is boring work, what works best is absolute consistency over an extended period, and when people do boring work they get bored — so every so often someone at a company like Volvo has a bright idea about branching out into exciting sports cars. They supply a verbal cue for the moment: run up a red flag whenever you hear the words "why should we limit ourselves?", because you should limit your brand, and that limitation is the essence of branding. The diagnostic error afterwards is misattribution: it is always the product that is declared a failure, never the branding concept. Their case is the Arch Deluxe — a hundred and fifty million dollars of advertising later it was declared a disaster and dropped, when on their reading McDonald's is understood as a kid-oriented family restaurant, so an adult hamburger might taste good in the mouth but was never going to taste good in the mind.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 98-100. Practitioner assertion. The durability examples in the same passage — Volvo selling safety for thirty-five years, BMW driving for twenty-five — are counts of years rather than measurements of effect, and the Little Caesars case attributes a fall to third place to one cause with no figures and no alternative considered.
confounders: attributing violations to competitive pressure or growth targets, which are the obvious causes and not the one the chapter names
assuming the product/concept distinction is testable as stated; the chapter offers no way to tell which failed in a given case
reading 'why should we limit ourselves' as a rhetorical flourish; the authors offer it as an operational cue to watch for

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 101-103 (Ch. 20, 'The Law of Change')
qa_items.question: Name the three situations in which the authors say changing a brand is feasible, and explain the mechanism they give for the third — including why they say it will not work in a fast-moving field.
qa_items.answer: First, where the brand is weak or non-existent in the mind: there is effectively no brand, so it can be used on any product in any category — who is to know? Intel leaving memory chips for microprocessors is their case, on the grounds that outside a handful of computer executives and purchasing agents nobody knew what Intel had stood for. Second, moving the brand permanently down the price ladder, which customers read as value received; going the other way, up the food chain, they call much harder if not impossible. Third, a slow-moving field where the change can be spread over a long period. The mechanism for the third is not persuasion but forgetting: Citicorp moved Citibank from a corporate to a consumer perception over twenty-five years, and the authors say little change actually occurred in any prospect's mind — instead of changing minds, enough time was allowed to pass for the natural process of forgetting to take place. That is why it will not work in computers or consumer electronics: there is not enough time for forgetting.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 101-103. Practitioner assertion with a stated mechanism. The Citicorp figures describe a business mix, not the state of any prospect's mind, which is what the claim concerns; the Intel case rests on an assertion about what the public knew.
confounders: assuming a repositioning campaign can do the work; the chapter's position is that customers reject the message that a brand is now something else — 'customers are never wrong'
reading the first situation as easy to identify; it is the judgement a company is least able to make about itself, and no test is offered
confusing moving down the price ladder with a discount promotion; the authors specify a permanent lowering

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 106-108 (Ch. 21, 'The Law of Mortality')
qa_items.question: An established brand faces a technology shift into a new category and asks whether to carry its name across. Apply the authors' position, including the valuation distinction they say managers get wrong.
qa_items.answer: They would say do not carry the name, and put the money into a new brand instead. Their reason is that a brand's power is confined to the meaning attached to its name and cannot be extended past it, which they argue through Kodak: Kodak stands for conventional photography, so the Kodak name has no power over videotape and, they predict, none over digital imaging. Their stronger claim is about succession — when a revolutionary new category develops, the inevitable winner is a revolutionary new brand name, as with Sony against the incumbent electronics names, Blockbuster against the incumbent retailers, and Dell against a long list of established computer makers. The valuation distinction managers get wrong is between how well known a brand is and what it stands for: a well-known brand that stands for nothing, or for something obsolete, has no value and has nowhere to go but down, while a brand that stands for something has value even if it is little known, because it can be worked with — especially in publicity.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 106-108. Practitioner assertion and a forecast made in the late 1990s about a transition then under way. The succession list is composed entirely of winners chosen after the fact; incumbents that did carry a name across a technology boundary are not examined. This bank deliberately records nothing about what became of Kodak — there is no source for it here.
confounders: answering with what actually happened afterwards; that is outside this copy and outside the question
assuming the authors advise abandoning the old business immediately; they distinguish investing from harvesting and object to spending on both sides of the street at once
reading 'euthanasia' as a criterion; the chapter gives no test for when a brand has reached that point

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed pp. 109-110 (Ch. 22, 'The Law of Singularity')
qa_items.question: The book closes with two answers to the question 'what is a brand?'. Give both, explain the test that goes with them, and state the caveat the authors attach about brands that have failed the test and are still trading.
qa_items.answer: A brand is a proper noun that can be used in place of a common word — instead of an imported beer you ask for a Heineken, instead of a safe car a Volvo, instead of a thick spaghetti sauce a Prego. And a brand is a singular idea or concept that you own inside the mind of the prospect. The test is the one that opened the book: say the name and see what comes back. What is a Chevrolet? A large, small, cheap, expensive car or truck. What is a Miller? A regular, light, draft, cheap, expensive beer. A name that returns a list of contradictory attributes has lost its singularity and, in their word, is burned out. The caveat is that such brands can remain on the marketing scene for many years because of the line-extension generosity of their competitors. Survival is therefore not evidence that singularity was retained — which is the fourth time in this span the authors use competitor weakness to keep an outcome from counting against them.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 109-110. The definitions and the caveat are the authors'. The observation that the caveat repeats the weak-competition move a fourth time is the extractor's; the other three are at printed pp. 7, 36 and 66.
confounders: reading the substitution test as being about generic trademark status; a brand can substitute for a phrase — a safe car, a driving machine — without owning the category word
assuming a surviving brand refutes the diagnosis; the caveat is written precisely to prevent that inference
treating this chapter as introducing something new; it restates the Law of Expansion and the Law of the Word, and was extracted for the closing definitions and the caveat

qa_items.source_title: Al Ries and Laura Ries, The 22 Immutable Laws of Branding (HarperBusiness, 2002 combined edition)
qa_items.source_locator: printed p. 101 (Ch. 20 opening), p. 105 (Ch. 21 opening), p. 77 (Ch. 15 opening)
qa_items.question: Someone cites 'immutable law' as a reason to weight a claim from this book heavily. Using three passages from inside the book itself, show what the authors actually claim about the status of their laws, and say what those concessions do and do not fix.
qa_items.answer: Chapter 20 opens by saying that nothing in life and nothing in branding is ever absolute, that there are always exceptions to every rule, and that the Law of Change is the biggest exception to the laws of branding — one member of the set is described as an exception to the others. Chapter 21 opens by narrowing immutability to the laws themselves and excluding brands, which are born, grow up, mature and die. Chapter 15 opens by stating what the laws seem to suggest about concentrating on a single brand, agreeing it is true, and then licensing a second, third and fourth. So the authors themselves do not hold the twenty-two as independent universal axioms. What the concessions fix is the reading that every law applies always. What they do not fix is testability: no criterion is given anywhere for when an exception applies, so the concessions widen the laws rather than making them checkable, and they are never reconciled with the Introduction, which asserts the laws apply equally everywhere and assigns each named failure to the violation of a numbered law. The word "immutable" is a title, and it supplies no evidence.
qa_items.support: Printed pp. 77, 101 and 105 — all three concessions are the authors' own sentences. The reading that they widen rather than test the laws is the extractor's, recorded in sk_r22_0049 and PROVENANCE.md §6. Nothing in this book is supported by measurement; see PROVENANCE.md §7 for the four candidate cases examined and rejected.
confounders: concluding the laws are worthless; practitioner assertion is a real category of knowledge and this is an articulate instance of it — the point is only about how it should be weighted
assuming the concessions make the laws falsifiable; they name exceptions without giving any test for when one applies

treating the Introduction's universal framing as the authors' considered position and the concessions as slips, or the reverse; both appear in the book, unreconciled, and this lane did not choose between them

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', opening argument (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara opens the chapter by describing grid use as "part of the status quo of designing." What exactly is his objection, and what is the harm he says follows from getting it wrong?
qa_items.answer: His objection is not to the grid but to defaulting to it. He calls grid use a convention and says that, like all conventions, it is suitable for achieving particular goals — not every goal. The designer's purpose is to facilitate the clearest and most compelling experience for the audience, and a grid may not be the best route there. The stated harm is specific: assuming a grid should be imposed may compromise the information's integrity. So the failure he names is imposing structure without asking whether this content wants it, and the damage lands on the content rather than on the aesthetics.
qa_items.support: Chapter 2 opening: grid use is the status quo and a convention suitable for particular goals; using one may not be the best solution and assuming one should be imposed may compromise the information's integrity.
confounders: reading the chapter as anti-grid; Samara attacks the default, not the device
assuming the harm he names is visual dullness — he names damage to the information itself
the modern default that breaking a grid is a matter of taste or brand personality; his stated warrant is about the content

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', opening argument (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara says clarity means different things in different contexts. What three cases does he name, and why does the list matter for deciding whether to use a grid?
qa_items.answer: He names three. Sometimes content has its own internal structure that must be upheld to be understood. Sometimes content must ignore structure altogether to create specific kinds of emotional reaction, or to invoke an important narrative association. And sometimes content requires a more complex intellectual involvement from the audience in order to resonate more profoundly. The list matters because it is his actual test: the question is not whether a layout looks clear but which of these kinds of clarity the content needs. Only the first case is obviously served by an imposed regular structure.
qa_items.support: Chapter 2 opening paragraph on clarity meaning different things in different contexts, listing internal structure, emotional or narrative reaction, and deeper intellectual involvement.
confounders: treating 'clarity' as a single quantity that a grid maximises
reading the third case as licence for difficulty as such; Samara ties it to resonating more profoundly, not to obscurity
collapsing the second and third cases — emotional reaction and intellectual involvement are separate entries on his list

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical, opening (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A designer cites this chapter to defend a layout as "intentionally unconventional" and dismisses a complaint that readers cannot navigate it. On Samara's own terms, has the designer finished the job?
qa_items.answer: No. Samara concedes the difficulty in full rather than denying it: any approach that flies in the face of convention will be fraught with difficulties, and he acknowledges that the usual objection is exactly this one — that the layout is too difficult to navigate. What he refuses is the inference that usability therefore precludes the approach. His answer is a duty, not a dismissal: identify the problematic aspects objectively and work to address them, after which even the most challenging solution may be resolved to a necessary level of practicality without necessarily diluting its inventiveness. A designer who cites the chapter to end the conversation is using the licence and skipping the obligation attached to it.
qa_items.support: "Considering the Practical in the Impractical" opening: the perceived challenge for viewers, including being too difficult to navigate; the refusal of the conclusion; objective identification of problematic aspects; a necessary level of practicality without necessarily diluting inventiveness.
confounders: the common reading of this chapter as 'anything goes'
assuming Samara denies the navigation problem exists; he grants it and assigns responsibility for it
assuming the fix must preserve the invention completely — his word is 'necessarily', which concedes it may cost some

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
qa_items.question: When an unconventional layout gives readers trouble, Samara says the fault is almost always in one of two places. Which two, and what does he claim about the tools available to fix them?
qa_items.answer: The two are optical differentiation — whether the reader can identify the most important elements, or the ones a sequence starts from — and eye path, also called compositional flow, meaning how the first element optically connects the reader to what comes next. His claim about the tools is that nothing new is required: every means of constructing a clear hierarchy in a grid-based layout remains the same in a layout built on an alternative approach, and there is no reason an unusual composition cannot also be a friendly one. The difference is one of degree, not of kind — he recommends applying the familiar size and weight differences to greater extremes than usual.
qa_items.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": hierarchy means carry over unchanged; the two aspects that tend most often to be the root of navigation trouble are optical differentiation and eye path; bigger and bolder usually means seen first, so push the differences further than normal.
confounders: assuming an unconventional layout needs a special hierarchy toolkit
confusing optical differentiation with legibility of the type itself
treating eye path as a fixed left-to-right scan; Samara derives it from contrast, and scopes the left-hand advice to Western readers

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Grid Deconstruction: Orthogonal, 'Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara gives a procedure for orthogonal grid deconstruction. What is the first step, and why is that step the part most often misread?
qa_items.answer: The first step is to install a base grid. Only then does the designer change how columns and rows relate to each other — separating them at irregular intervals, cutting through them in the opposing direction and sliding the parts horizontally or vertically, widening some but not others. It is misread because the chapter's title suggests the grid is the thing being escaped, whereas here the grid is the instrument: there is nothing to split, splice or shift until a structure exists. He recommends starting from a familiar structure, even a simple two- or three-column grid, as the introduction to alternative structure.
qa_items.support: "Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting": altering a familiar structure is an excellent introduction; first the designer installs a base grid, then changes how columns and rows relate.
confounders: assuming deconstruction begins from a blank page
confusing this with the non-orthogonal route, which changes the shapes of columns rather than their positions
assuming the base grid must be elaborate; he specifically suggests a simple two- or three-column one

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Grid Deconstruction: Orthogonal, 'Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Splicing and shifting move elements around. According to Samara, what is the actual payoff, and what does he tell the designer to do about it?
qa_items.answer: The payoff is relational rather than formal. When information that would normally appear in its expected place — marking a structural juncture in the grid — is moved and lands beside some other kind of information, a new verbal connection is created that did not exist before. If a change in size or density accompanies the move, the shifted information may end up behind or on top of other material, and the resulting optical confusion will often make foreground and background appear to swap places. His instruction is telling: he says it is important to watch what happens. The connections are observed after the fact, not specified in advance.
qa_items.support: "Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting": watching what happens when expected information is moved, the new verbal connection, and the foreground/background swap produced by optical confusion.
confounders: reading the operation as purely visual restructuring; Samara's stated payoff is a change in meaning
assuming the new connections are planned; his verb is 'watch'
confusing the figure-ground swap, presented here as a benefit, with the same effect treated as a hazard in the practicality section

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Grid Deconstruction: Non-Orthogonal, 'Deformation and Distortion' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: What distinguishes non-orthogonal deconstruction from splicing and shifting, and what optical effect does Samara say follows from it — including the condition that strengthens that effect?
qa_items.answer: Splicing and shifting move columns and rows while leaving their shapes intact; deformation and distortion alter the shapes themselves. Pulling the edges of columns and rows out of parallel alignment emphasises diagonal axes and makes the orthogonal underpinning far less apparent, which he describes as a far more organic effect. The optical consequence is an illusion of perspective as the newly created angles converge. The condition that greatly enhances it is that the content inside the columns changes in size or spacing to correspond with the perceived change in spatial location from near to far. He adds that columns and rows may be made curvilinear as well as angular — circles, waves, free-form organic shapes.
qa_items.support: "Deformation and Distortion": altering the actual shapes rather than the positions; diagonal emphasis; illusory perspective as angles converge, greatly enhanced if content changes size or spacing to match perceived depth; curvilinear as well as angular deformation.
confounders: treating deformation as a stronger version of shifting rather than a different operation
forgetting the content-scaling condition, without which Samara says the depth effect is weaker
assuming deformation must be angular; he explicitly includes curves and free-form shapes

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction (spine 6)
qa_items.question: You are laying out a transcript of a heated argument between three speakers. Using Samara's verbal deconstruction, what is the source of the layout's structure, and what specifically does he warn you are exchanging?
qa_items.answer: The structure comes from the speech itself. Samara says the natural rhythm of spoken language is often used as a guide for changing weight, size, colour or alignment among lines of type, with louder or faster words set larger, bolder or in italics to correspond to stresses and lulls in actual speech; giving a voice to visual language can push words out of paragraphs or force columns into relationships where the natural logic of the writing creates a visual order. His own example is a book of dialogue in which each character's voice is coded typographically and the columns are deconstructed by the quality of the speech — falling apart, becoming confused, interrupting each other. The exchange he names is explicit: breaking phrases and words apart in running text calls attention to the individual parts of speech and the presumed reading order may begin to change, which he says would generally interfere with reading; it is warranted only where the resulting ambiguity is appropriate to the content. A caption states the same trade in stronger terms — the verbal structure is brought into focus while the visual clarity is decreased.
qa_items.support: "Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction": speech rhythm guiding weight, size, colour and alignment; the dialogue book with typographically coded voices; the concession that fragmenting running text generally interferes with reading and is warranted where the ambiguity suits the content; the caption stating that verbal structure comes into focus as visual clarity decreases.
confounders: treating the typographic variation as decoration or emphasis rather than as the structure itself
assuming Samara considers the reading cost negligible — he concedes it twice
importing a modern accessibility argument as though it were his; he does not make one

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction, closing (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara suggests deconstruction "might even improve readability." What does he mean by readability there, and how confident is the claim?
qa_items.answer: He redefines the word. Readability in that sentence means the quality of, and the degree to which, the type engages its readers with the content — not the ease of decoding it. The claim is hedged: "might even", and it arrives immediately after his statement that these qualities should be made visual not merely as a tool for clarifying hierarchy and not just as intriguing eye candy, but to lay bare an author's methods and intent. It carries no reader evidence of any kind. Read as a claim about decoding ease it would flatly contradict his own admission that fragmenting text interferes with reading; read as a claim about engagement it does not.
qa_items.support: Closing of "Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction": the hedged suggestion about readability, with the source's own parenthetical definition of readability as engagement with the content.
confounders: reading 'readability' in the standard legibility sense, which makes the sentence contradict the same section
treating a hedged aside as one of the chapter's supported claims
confusing it with the accessibility sense of readability, which this book does not discuss

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Centered-Axis Structure (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Why does Samara call centred composition "structurally antithetical" to grid-based visualisation? Give his three reasons.
qa_items.answer: First, centring assumes only one governing alignment axis. Second, that axis is buried within the area of the material rather than being marked by its contours — unlike a grid, whose alignments show up at the edges of things. Third, the exterior contours, widths and depths of centred elements are mutually interdependent: they are not subject to predetermined intervals but driven by their fit and relative proportion as they come into central alignment. He allows that centred material may still have its proportions or positions guided by a grid, but the two allocate space by incompatible logics.
qa_items.support: "Centered-Axis Structure": the three stated reasons centring is structurally antithetical to grid-based visualisation, and the concession that a grid may still guide proportions or positions.
confounders: treating a centred layout as a one-column grid
assuming Samara rejects centring; he classes it as the classical page architecture and gives it its own section
confusing the buried-axis point with the fact that a grid's guides are also invisible in print — his point is where the alignment is legible, at the contour or inside the mass

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Centered-Axis Structure (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A centred layout for a cultural institution has been criticised as inert. Samara predicts this failure. What does he say causes it, and what are his remedies — noting which dimension the remedies are allowed to touch?
qa_items.answer: He says symmetry is unforgiving with regard to layout flexibility because it demands that every element adhere to a single axis, and elements that do not typically appear disunified from the whole. The resulting restfulness and uniformity are problematic relative to the goals of designed communication: a viewer is likely to gloss over the material and come to an intellectual rest quickly rather than investigate the work more intently. His remedies all work on the dimensions symmetry does not govern, because moving elements off the axis is precisely what is unavailable. Exaggerate contrasts in scale or proportion and in spacing, density and rhythm. Enlarge the symmetrically organised forms until they are clearly bigger than the remaining symmetrical spaces, so their confrontation with the format becomes tense and the static quality is reduced. Juxtapose dramatically different emphases in proportion, among both the forms and the spaces between them, under a defined logic of progression or alternation along the axis. And make radical changes in size or in lightness and darkness so that lateral movement is reordered as movement from near to far.
qa_items.support: "Centered-Axis Structure": symmetry unforgiving, elements off-axis appear disunified, viewer comes to intellectual rest quickly; exaggerating contrasts in scale and spacing as critical to optical vitality; oversized forms creating tension with the format; a logic of progression along the axis; radical size and value changes reordering movement dimensionally.
confounders: recommending that elements be moved off the axis, which is the one repair symmetry forecloses
assuming restfulness is the goal of a symmetrical layout; Samara treats it as the problem
reaching for colour variety in general — his named levers are scale, spacing/density, and lightness/darkness

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Centered-Axis Structure, caption to the paired advertisements (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Can symmetry and asymmetry be used in the same composition, on Samara's account? State his position and its condition exactly.
qa_items.answer: His position is that they rarely combine effectively, but that bringing the two kinds of organisational structure into confrontation can yield interesting results — on one condition, that the two compositional states remain distinct. He gives no test for how distinct is distinct enough. The condition is worth noticing because it is a rule shape that recurs through the chapter: a departure works while the state departed from is still legible as a separate state, which is also why he says a deconstructed grid should leave a recognisable vestige.
qa_items.support: Caption in "Centered-Axis Structure": symmetry and asymmetry rarely combine effectively, but confrontation can yield interesting results so long as the two compositional states are distinct.
confounders: reading it as a straight prohibition
reading it as unconditional permission — the condition is the whole content of the claim
assuming the two states should be blended into each other, which is the opposite of what he requires

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Other Kinds of Geometric Structure (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara claims that "being completely objective, the choice of one structural approach is no more valid, on a functional level, than that of another." What does he immediately require of the designer, and why does that requirement not contradict the claim?
qa_items.answer: He requires the designer to confront the issue of a structure's relevance on a communicative level. The two do not conflict because he separates function from meaning: every kind of structure will display content, so none is functionally better, but the different qualities of each impart extremely different perceptions of the content and therefore of its meaning — especially where the structure is one the viewer is likely to associate with a concrete experience. His example is blunt: if an arrangement is structured like a tree, the viewer will interpret it as a tree. So the freedom is real at the functional level and cancelled at the semantic one, which is where design decisions actually live.
qa_items.support: "Other Kinds of Geometric Structure": all structures equally valid functionally; different qualities imparting different perceptions of content and meaning; the tree example; the surviving obligation to confront a structure's communicative relevance.
confounders: quoting the functional-equality claim on its own as licence for arbitrary structure
reading the tree remark as being about literal illustration rather than about unavoidable association
assuming 'no more valid' means 'no different in effect'

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Other Kinds of Geometric Structure (spine 6)
qa_items.question: An arrangement shows no repetition or pattern among its parts. Does Samara consider it a structure? Give his reasoning.
qa_items.answer: Yes. His starting point is that inserting any form into a space — even a solitary one — creates structure, meaning a set of visual relationships between its contour, the shape of its outer boundary, and its axis, the imaginary line separating its halves, and those of other forms. He then says explicitly that any structure may be fluid and irregular in proportion or interval, and that simply because an arrangement presents no perceptible repetition or pattern among its parts does not discredit it as a structure. He notes that because of our orientation to Earth we typically perceive forms as expressing two primary axes, horizontal and vertical, but offers nature as the counter-catalogue — radial flower petals, the irregular axes of constellations, hexagonal crystal lattices, the helical whorl of DNA.
qa_items.support: "Other Kinds of Geometric Structure": any inserted form creates structure via contour and axis; orthogonal perception attributed to our orientation to Earth; nature's non-orthogonal structures; the explicit statement that absence of perceptible repetition does not discredit a structure.
confounders: equating structure with regularity or with a grid
assuming 'no pattern' means 'no structure', which is the specific inference he blocks
treating the natural examples as decorative rather than as his argument that geometricity does not require orthogonality

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Other Kinds of Geometric Structure (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Where does Samara say the intervals of a structure can come from, if not from a column grid? Name the sources he actually lists.
qa_items.answer: From outside the page. He names musical interval — the octave established by the seven unique tonal pitches of Western music, which he says book designers have used to create page divisions since the Middle Ages — and, by analogy, rhythmic or thematic alternation schemes applied to the distances between elements, in patterns such as A/B/A or A/B/A/C where each letter stands for one measurement. He also names any numeric progression or fractional relationship: odd-number ratios such as 1:3:5:7, and the Fibonacci progression in which each number is the sum of the preceding two, which he notes coincidentally drives the Golden Section. He closes by saying these approaches are neither comprehensive nor required to be used independently of one another.
qa_items.support: "Other Kinds of Geometric Structure": musical intervals used by book designers since the Middle Ages; A/B/A alternation applied to distances; numeric progressions including odd-number ratios and Fibonacci; the note that the approaches are neither comprehensive nor mutually exclusive.
confounders: attributing a preference for the Golden Section to him; he mentions it as a coincidence of the Fibonacci relationship
assuming these are historical curiosities rather than options he offers for use
assuming the schemes must be used one at a time — he says the opposite

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Intuitive, Relational, and Conceptual: 'Spontaneous Composition' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Spontaneous composition sounds like the absence of method. What is the step in Samara's own description that makes it a method, and what does he say about its relationship to grid-building?
qa_items.answer: The step is the adjustment pass. He describes the approach as starting fast and loose, the designer working as a painter does and making quick decisions as the material is put together and the relationships are first seen — and then, as the different optical qualities of the elements begin to interact, determining which qualities those initial decisions have affected and making adjustments to enhance or negate them in whatever way is most appropriate for the communication. The placement is intuitive; the correction is analytical. On grid-building, he says designers often use this method as a step in the process of building a grid, and that its use as an organisational idea on its own is just as valid — so he places it upstream of the conventional procedure rather than opposite to it.
qa_items.support: "Spontaneous Composition": intuitive placement based on formal aspects; starting fast and loose; the read-back-and-adjust step; the note that the method is often a step within grid-building and is equally valid on its own.
confounders: reading spontaneity as the absence of evaluation
assuming it is opposed to grid-building; he describes it as a phase within it
confusing it with chance operations, which import relationships the material did not already have

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Intuitive, Relational, and Conceptual: 'Imagery as a Source' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara asks what happens if the imagery is allowed to rule a layout. What reason does he give for expecting that inversion to be productive, and what are the two directions it can take?
qa_items.answer: His reason is an asymmetry of vocabulary: typography is always a pattern of lines, whereas images present a radically greater range of form languages. Applying an image's language to text therefore relieves the designer quickly of presumptions about how text should behave in a layout, or how layouts ought to be organised — presumptions he says are hard to dislodge because type and image are usually assumed to be mutually dominant and referential. The two directions are: one in which typographic elements become, in essence, part of the imagery; and one in which the imagery sets up the logic for how type responds to it pictorially, while the type retains its identity as a separate entity alongside the images.
qa_items.support: "Imagery as a Source": type and image notoriously challenging to combine; typography always a pattern of lines against images' greater range of form languages; the two named directions.
confounders: reading it as advice to make type look like a picture in general
assuming the type must always merge into the image — he names a second direction in which it stays separate
assuming the correspondence must be literal; elsewhere he says the mere fact of a shared quality is enough

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — 'Imagery as a Source' and Considering the Practical — 'Pictorial Strategies' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Two sections of this chapter address the relationship between an image and its layout, and they push in opposite directions. State both, and say what Samara offers for choosing between them.
qa_items.answer: In "Imagery as a Source" the image governs: its visual aspects determine the overall compositional structure and even the compositional and stylistic attributes of the type. In "Pictorial Strategies" the environment governs: crisp, naturalistic images inset in rectangles will often dis-unify from an expressive, gestural or spatially ambiguous environment, and the remedy is to manipulate those images so they take on visual characteristics found in the surrounding typographic or graphic forms, downplaying dissonance and promoting a perception of totality. He offers nothing for choosing between them. The two sections are written for different situations — one is a generative strategy at the start of a layout, the other a repair applied to a layout that already exists — but he never sets them side by side or states a rule.
qa_items.support: "Imagery as a Source" on letting imagery determine structure and type; "Pictorial Strategies" on crisp inset images dis-unifying and being given the surrounding forms' characteristics.
confounders: assuming the two sections say the same thing about integrating type and image
inventing a decision rule and attributing it to Samara; he gives none
assuming the pictorial repair means cropping or resizing — his instruction is to imbue the image with the environment's visual characteristics

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — 'Narrative Constructs: Pictorialization and Metaphorical Allusion' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Distinguish Samara's two narrative constructs, and say what he claims stays constant as a pictorialised layout runs across many pages.
qa_items.answer: In narrative pictorialisation the layout is made to look like something discussed in the text — elements arranged to give the impression of objects swept up in a flood, or to construct a literal image of a car or other machine; in simplest terms the layout becomes a kind of illustration. In metaphorical allusion the layout structure and the visual language of its forms refer instead to a tangential idea that supports or manipulates perception of the meaning; his example is a film festival promotion splicing repeated images to refer to film editing. What stays constant across a pictorialised sequence is the governing logic: as the content progresses or takes a different direction from page to page or screen to screen, the subject the layout depicts changes while the logic that decides how to depict it does not.
qa_items.support: "Narrative Constructs": pictorialisation as the layout looking like the text's subject and becoming a kind of illustration; allusion as reference to a tangential idea; the governing logic remaining the same as the depicted subject changes.
confounders: collapsing the two into one 'conceptual layout' idea
assuming the depicted subject must stay the same across a sequence — he says it changes and the logic does not
confusing metaphorical allusion with vernacularism, which borrows a style rather than depicting an idea

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — 'Narrative Allusions: Vernacularism' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: You are designing an invitation to an exclusive art auction and propose using the brush lettering and graphic devices of supermarket advertising banners. What is the mechanism Samara says makes this work, and what is the limit an extractor should attach to it?
qa_items.answer: That is Samara's own example. The mechanism is that vernacular imagery, or a vernacular compositional conceit, imposes the look of something else onto the communication and embeds it in that new context, either to draw a comparison or to comment on the subject being communicated. Because "vernacular" means the ordinary, such gestures often trade on forms associated with low culture or with undesigned visual experience, and the distance between the borrowed world and the actual subject is what carries the comment. He traces the practice to Pop Art, citing Warhol's Brillo boxes and Rosenquist's paintings of spaghetti and cleaning products. The limit is that the effect is entirely dependent on the audience holding the association: Hatch Show Prints signify the American Midwest, and Victorian illustrated books signify small independent trade, only to people who already read them that way. Samara does not discuss what happens when the borrowed style is simply read as itself.
qa_items.support: "Vernacularism": the auction-invitation example; imposing the look of something else to draw a comparison or comment; the low-culture note; the Pop Art lineage; the Hatch Show Prints and Victorian-illustration examples.
confounders: treating vernacular borrowing as retro styling for its own sake
assuming the association transfers across cultures — every one of his examples is culture-specific
confusing it with pictorialisation; vernacularism borrows a style, it does not depict the subject

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — 'Chance Operations: Random Physical Effect' and 'Programmatic Effect' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara's chance operations are often quoted as permission to place things arbitrarily. What does he actually say about control, and how do his two categories differ?
qa_items.answer: He says the opposite of arbitrariness. Conducting a chance operation implies that the chance is being controlled to a certain degree, and he adds that this is usually the case; by selecting the type of operation, a designer skews the results in their favour, ensuring appropriateness in the form while letting unpredictability create relationships structured thinking will not reach. The two categories differ in foreknowledge, not in whether control is exercised. Random physical effect involves randomness to a greater degree, resting on an action that prevents explicit control of the outcome — flinging paint, scattering or dropping cropped images from a height — where the designer knows what kinds of pattern the brush size or the gesture tends to produce but cannot predict or effect a specific result. Programmatic effect uses planned mechanical or mathematical procedures which equally deny explicit control, but whose mechanical nature guarantees greater foreknowledge of the results.
qa_items.support: "Chance Operations": chance controlled to a degree; selecting the operation type to skew results; random physical effect and its examples; programmatic effect and its greater foreknowledge.
confounders: reading chance operations as randomness without judgement
assuming programmatic chance gives the designer control of the outcome — it gives foreknowledge of the kind of outcome
assuming the benefit claimed is novelty; his stated benefit is seeing the material more clearly through unexpected juxtaposition

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — 'Chance Operations: Programmatic Effect' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Name three programmatic chance procedures Samara lists, and say what makes them programmatic rather than random.
qa_items.answer: From his list: dissecting an image in a pattern of intervals based on an arbitrarily applied grid or a mathematical formula; automatically photographing or scanning elements, or a layout in progress, from a particular viewpoint at predetermined times and inserting the captures as images; augmenting the point sizes of successive lines of type by an arbitrary multiplier; and printing two layouts on top of one another then deleting the instances where elements overlap. They are programmatic because the procedure is planned and mechanical or mathematical, so although the designer still cannot control the specific outcome, the nature of the procedure guarantees greater foreknowledge of what kind of result will appear.
qa_items.support: "Programmatic Effect": the four listed procedures and the statement that the mechanical nature of such procedures guarantees greater foreknowledge of results.
confounders: assuming a programmatic operation is deterministic in its result; it is deterministic in its rule
confusing the arbitrarily applied grid here with a grid derived from content, which is a different idea in this book
assuming these are digital techniques — he includes overprinting and physical capture

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Exhibits — Design Projects Without Grids, the 'Universal/Unique' book exhibit (spine 6)
qa_items.question: In one exhibit Samara says a grid produced an organic, seemingly random result. What is his stated reason, and why must an extractor be careful with this passage?
qa_items.answer: His reason is that the grid forces the deconstruction because its structure was created before the material it governs was assessed: the material ends up doing whatever it will as it is made to conform to predetermined criteria, and the result is a collage of texture, shadow, light and type that on closer inspection reveals its hidden order. Care is needed for two reasons. First, the same author elsewhere treats building a structure before reading the content as the error to avoid, so this is one author qualifying his own earlier position in a different context — not two sources disagreeing, and not a general licence to impose a grid blind. Second, the context is artificial: the project was made for an exhibition on the relationship between structure and freedom, whose brief required participants to use predetermined kernel elements — a grid, the word "word", and the image of an eye.
qa_items.support: Exhibit commentary on the "Universal/Unique" book: the master grid contributing to the organic quality; the grid forcing the deconstruction because it precedes assessment of the material; the exhibition brief and its predetermined kernel elements.
confounders: generalising a single exhibit under an artificial brief into a method
presenting this as a contradiction between two sources rather than as the same author writing about a different situation
assuming the resulting disorder has no structure — he says the hidden order is revealed on closer inspection

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A key label in a dense, structureless poster is partly obscured. A colleague proposes repeating it in a clear area of the page. What does Samara say about that move, and what does he prefer?
