qa_items.answer: He allows it and then withdraws most of the allowance. Repeating partially obscured information in an open area may help, he says, but it may also confuse a viewer with its redundancy — better to give the information a little extra room where it appears in sequence. So his preference is to fix the element in place rather than duplicate it. He pairs this with a general fallback: when in doubt, simplify, because if the same visual effect can be achieved with fewer elements or less interference, the element will differentiate itself more efficiently from within a complicated field.
qa_items.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": repetition of obscured information may help or may confuse through redundancy, with extra room in sequence preferred; and the when-in-doubt-simplify rule with its reason.
confounders: treating repetition as a straightforwardly safe redundancy strategy
assuming the fix is to increase the label's size, which is a different lever in his account
confusing this repetition with the repetition he recommends elsewhere, which marks which elements are alike in meaning

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara says hierarchy is not only about importance. What else does he say it is about, and which device carries that second job?
qa_items.answer: It is also about relation — establishing which elements are alike in meaning, whether or not they are important. The device that carries it is repetition: repetition assigns relative meaning to elements that will be understood as related no matter where they occur within the visual field, even when separated by material that is clearly different. This matters more in an unstructured layout than in a grid, because a grid encodes relatedness by position and a structureless layout has no position to encode it with.
qa_items.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy" diagram captions: repetition assigning relative meaning across the field; hierarchy as relation as well as level of importance.
confounders: treating hierarchy as a strict ranking only
assuming proximity or enclosure carries relatedness here; his named device is repetition
assuming repeated elements must be equally important — he says explicitly that they need not be important at all

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
qa_items.question: How does Samara account for the order in which a reader moves through a layout that has no reading structure, and what does that account let a designer do?
qa_items.answer: He accounts for it as a gradient. Compositional flow, or eye path, occurs as the viewer compares each hierarchic level's degree of contrast against the others and senses the difference as a decrease in optical resistance — contrast restated as resistance — so the eye moves from the area of greatest overall contrast to the least. Because the order is produced by a gradient rather than by position in a structure, a layout with no grid can still have a reading order, and the designer can support the direction by positioning axes or by using graphical forms to point. Practically, he adds that each element to be encountered next must either differentiate from its context to a similar degree, since like things attract attention, or be positioned near where the eye is likely to leave the previous element; and that graphical markers or anchoring points inserted at strategic locations help focus attention and direct the flow.
qa_items.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": compositional flow as decreasing optical resistance; the eye moving from greatest to least contrast; supporting the direction with axes and pointing forms; like things attracting attention; markers and anchoring points.
confounders: assuming reading order in an unstructured layout is arbitrary
treating eye path as a fixed scan pattern independent of the design
assuming the highest-contrast element is simply the largest; his variable is contrast against the field

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Which of Samara's navigation instructions is explicitly limited to a particular readership, and what is the correct way to record that limit?
qa_items.answer: The instruction to orient top-level elements toward the left-hand area of the layout. He states it as advice "for Western readers", and the related rule for type on a circular path — orient the entry point toward the upper left and, if possible, so that the first words are relatively horizontal — depends on the same convention. The correct handling is to keep the scoping attached to the claim: it is a reading convention, not a fact about perception, and it must not be carried over to readers of right-to-left or vertical scripts as though it were. Everything else in the same section — differentiation, contrast, the resistance gradient — is stated without that restriction.
qa_items.support: "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": the explicit "For Western readers" scoping on left-hand orientation, and the upper-left entry point for type set on a curve.
confounders: treating upper-left entry as a universal perceptual fact
assuming the whole section is culturally scoped; only the directional advice is
assuming Samara offers a substitute rule for other scripts — he does not discuss them

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Easing Dissonance, Enhancing Totality: 'Typographic Strategies' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: An expressive spread reads as a set of unrelated fragments. Samara's typographic remedy has a fallback for when the running text cannot take it. State the remedy and the fallback.
qa_items.answer: The remedy is to apply the layout's macro-level compositional gestures to micro-scale elements such as text, at a smaller scale — which he says creates greater cohesion among disparate parts and alleviates the fractured or dissonant quality that often attends alternative compositional approaches. He notes that text at a legible point size will withstand a degree of manipulation without sacrifice. The fallback is for when that seems too challenging: treat subheadings and callouts or decks as a bridge between the macro and micro scales, so the gesture is carried by an intermediate element and the running text is left alone.
qa_items.support: "Typographic Strategies": applying macro-level gestures to micro-scale elements; legible text withstanding a degree of manipulation; subheadings, callouts and decks as the bridge between macro and micro.
confounders: assuming the remedy is to reduce the expressiveness of the large forms
forgetting the fallback, which is the part that keeps body text readable
reading 'macro gestures at micro scale' as simply matching typeface or colour, rather than repeating the compositional gesture itself

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Integrating Information Design (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A financial table has to sit inside a loose, gestural annual-report spread and looks alien. Samara gives three moves in a definite order. What are they, and what is the standing limit on all three?
qa_items.answer: First, determine whether the data can take a form other than the one it was supplied in, since many kinds of statistical data can be visualised using different chart conventions; if it can, choose the data shape whose formal qualities most closely reflect those of the overall layout and recast the data into it. Second, if it cannot be recast, see whether the existing data structure is alterable enough to create adequate formal dialogue with the other elements. Third and only as a last resort, rotate the graph or table slightly, or position it over a more organic form, to diminish the presence of its corners and orthogonal axes. The standing limit is the data's integrity, which he attaches to the last move explicitly and which governs the whole sequence: the point of preferring re-encoding to rotation is that re-encoding removes the conflict at source, whereas rotation only disguises it.
qa_items.support: "Integrating Information Design": whether the data can take a different form; choosing the data shape reflecting the layout and recasting; altering the existing structure for formal dialogue; slight rotation or an organic backing as a last resort, without compromising the data's integrity.
confounders: reaching for rotation first, which is the move Samara ranks last
assuming the goal is to make the chart decorative; his limit is that the data's integrity must survive
assuming any chart type may be substituted freely — the first question is whether the data is permitted to change form at all

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Systematizing the Organic (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara gives exactly one numeric instruction in this chapter. What is it, what failure is it guarding against, and what is his stated mechanism?
qa_items.answer: Limit the rules to two or three in total — and limit the numbers, kinds and degrees of their variations as well. It guards against the system falling apart: he says the more rules there are, the greater the number of variables for each, and the more extreme the expression of each variable, the greater the potential for that collapse. The mechanism is multiplicative. Rule count, variables per rule and the extremity of each variable compound, so the space of permitted outcomes grows past the point where the set still reads as one system. He adds that the result of keeping to the limit is a more easily controllable and unified system, and that rules and their variations must be applied consistently among the corresponding parts.
qa_items.support: "Systematizing the Organic": the two-or-three limit including variations; the compounding of rules, variables and extremes; the more controllable and unified result; consistent application across corresponding parts.
confounders: reading the limit as being about visual minimalism rather than about the size of the rule set
assuming it applies to grid-based systems; he states it for irregular, alternative ones
forgetting that the limit covers the variations of each rule, not only the rules

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Systematizing the Organic (spine 6)
qa_items.question: You have designed eight spreads intuitively and now need rules so the rest of the book can be built by someone else. What is Samara's procedure, and what is unusual about the order it works in?
qa_items.answer: Analyse, as specifically as possible, which formal conditions are the most prevalent among all those present, using questions he supplies: what kind of images am I using; is geometry important in the shapes or relationships; is there spatial depth and, if so, what creates it — transparency, scale change, overlap; do I sense movement and, if so, is it lateral, vertical, frenzied, calm, repeated. The answers to those questions are the system's rules. Each rule is then given its permitted variables and their range — if cropping images into an irregular trapezoid is a rule, the trapezoids might all be one size and shape, or vary in size, or vary in the measures of their sides, or extend to parallelograms and triangles. What is unusual is the direction: the rules are read off work that already exists rather than being specified before it, which inverts the order in which a grid is normally derived. He also says a discrepancy should be treated as a prompt to reinvestigate the rules — edited out, or promoted into a new rule that must then be resolved among the existing elements.
qa_items.support: "Systematizing the Organic": analysing the most prevalent formal conditions; the four diagnostic questions; the answers as the system's rules; the trapezoid example of graded variation; treating a discrepancy as an incentive to reinvestigate the rules.
confounders: specifying rules in advance, which is the opposite of the procedure described
treating the four questions as a closed checklist; he calls them a way to begin
assuming a discrepancy must always be removed — he allows it to become a new rule

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Systematizing the Organic, the poster-series caption (spine 6)
qa_items.question: In a four-poster series the main title is rotated to a different angle on each poster. Samara says one version of this works and a nearby version does not. What is the difference, and what general problem does it illustrate?
qa_items.answer: The version that works has two titles oriented orthogonally and two diagonally, so the variation is controlled specifically against the fact that there are four posters: the system has a binary variation. The version that fails sets both diagonally rotated titles at the same angle, which he says would conflict with the logic of the other two, in which the angle differs in each. The general problem is that a variation repeating inconsistently among a system's components causes the layouts sharing a similar variation to disunify, and that the number of component parts is one factor in how such a discrepancy should be resolved. The underlying point is that a variation reads as a rule only when its pattern completes across the set; a half-applied variation reads as a mistake.
qa_items.support: "Systematizing the Organic" caption: inconsistent repetition of a variation causing disunity; component count as a factor; the four-poster binary variation and the conflicting alternative.
confounders: assuming more variation is always the risk; here the failure is variation that does not complete
assuming the rule scales unchanged to large sets — he says component count is a factor and does not generalise
reading the two diagonal titles at the same angle as the more consistent option; he says it conflicts with the logic of the other pair

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Interaction Design Without Grids (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara says screen work should be more hospitable to alternative layout than print, yet grids dominate online. What does he grant to the grid there, and what does he refuse to relax?
qa_items.answer: He grants that a grid readily addresses the requirements of responsive design and aids in rapidly templating multitudes of pages — but says there is no good reason those requirements cannot be equally well addressed through an alternative logic, and that screen-based interactivity, from scrolling to animation to flyout navigation to parallax, seems ready-made for alternative approaches. What he refuses to relax is the requirements themselves. He states that there really are no considerations or best practices for screen-based design from an alternative standpoint that diverge from those for conventional approaches, and lists them: content is of primary importance; navigation must be clearly different from content; text must be legible; users must be able to intuit functionality and page flow and trace the sequence of screens they have accessed; they must be able to get from any screen to any other; the site must load quickly; and it must be a compelling experience worthy of their time.
qa_items.support: "Interaction Design Without Grids": grid benefits for responsive design and templating; the claim that alternative logic could serve them; the explicit statement that no screen best practices diverge for alternative approaches, followed by the list.
confounders: assuming an unconventional site is held to a softer usability standard
reading his complaint as being about aesthetics; it is about an unexploited medium
treating his list as an accessibility standard — it is a designer's list and overlaps one without being one

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Interaction Design Without Grids (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A team wants to carry an unusual, spatial navigation concept down to phone screens. What does Samara say about that, and what does he deliberately leave unanswered?
qa_items.answer: He says the limited area of the smartphone screen, which is a benefit for the process of grid construction, may here be a hindrance, because unusual layouts and unusual navigation functionality typically require large areas. He then leaves the conclusion open, and does so as two questions rather than an answer: simply because one can design for device responsiveness, should one always; and is it important that viewers be able to access every kind of online content on their phones. Any resolution of those questions is not his. The most that can be attributed to him is the observation that the constraint is real and that he thought the usual assumption worth interrogating.
qa_items.support: "Interaction Design Without Grids": the smartphone screen as hindrance because unusual layouts require large areas; the two open questions about responsiveness and universal phone access.
confounders: attributing to Samara a recommendation against responsive design; he asks, he does not answer
assuming the constraint is technical; his stated constraint is available area
assuming he thinks small screens simply cannot carry alternative layouts — he shows a case where a card layout survives by pinning corners off-screen

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Pacing and Sequencing (spine 6)
qa_items.question: In a book with no consistent page structure, where can the structure live instead, on Samara's account?
qa_items.answer: In time, across the sequence. He says unconventional layout strategies tend to be more experiential than expository, and so lend themselves to other ways of thinking about sequence and pace: visual elements may relate to each other in time as though in frames of a film, with an image moving across a format or changing from page to page and affecting images or text that appear later. This kinetic structure comes to be recognised and understood as the viewer experiences the succession of frames. He adds that decisions about ebb and flow will often still be driven by the content's requirement for sequential clarity, but that a designer may treat sequence and pace as an idea in itself that establishes how the content ought to be delivered.
qa_items.support: "Pacing and Sequencing": unconventional strategies as more experiential than expository; elements relating in time as film frames; kinetic structure recognised through the succession of frames; sequence and pace as an organising idea.
confounders: assuming a layout without page structure has no structure at all
treating pacing purely as rhythm or variety rather than as a carrier of order
assuming content requirements are set aside — he says they often still drive the ebb and flow

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Exhibits — Design Projects Without Grids, commentary on the architecture-competition poster (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Two layouts are equally chaotic on first impression; one is praised in this book and the other would not be. Reading the exhibit commentaries, what does Samara consistently credit for the difference — and what is the honest limit on that reading?
qa_items.answer: He consistently credits a restricted substructure. In one commentary the designers attend to the parallel or divergent nature of axes and their junctures, distributing them along a limited selection of planar levels and directions, which he says ensures well-crafted, rhythmic cohesion instead of chaotic randomness. In another, spatial confusion and complicated interference between overlapping shapes and text are said to be underpinned by a rigorously controlled network of geometric axes in which the edges of every element line up with, or point to, those of other elements. In both cases the disorder is on the surface and something constrained survives underneath. The honest limit is that Samara says this about particular projects and never states it as a test; turning it into a diagnostic is a reader's generalisation, not his claim, and he offers no case anywhere in the chapter where apparent randomness turned out to be carelessness.
qa_items.support: Exhibit commentaries: axes distributed along a limited selection of planar levels and directions ensuring rhythmic cohesion instead of chaotic randomness; the rigorously controlled network of geometric axes underpinning apparent spatial confusion.
confounders: assuming the difference is the amount of visual disorder rather than what survives beneath it
attributing the generalisation to Samara; he describes projects and states no test
assuming a viewer can perceive the difference — the chapter asserts it and offers no reader evidence

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Exhibits — Design Projects Without Grids, commentaries on the exhibition catalogue and the improvisation poster (spine 6)
qa_items.question: What does Samara repeatedly report about how effortless-looking layouts were actually made, and why does that matter for judging a layout you did not watch being made?
qa_items.answer: He repeatedly reports that the effortlessness is expensive. An exhibition catalogue whose apparent simplicity looks at a glance not really designed is said to depend on almost obsessive attention to the selection, ordering, cropping, colour transitions and colour-reversal logic of its images. A poster with no baselines, alignments or margins, letters floating as though scattered, is described as a carefully randomised layout with two spatial levels added for control, its forms placed precisely enough that legibility survives the overlap of red and black letterforms close in optical colour. A third project's playful structure is called accessible because each part of the information is decisively located and components are separated so the eye can reach them. Why it matters is also the difficulty: what he is describing is process, not an inspectable property. Removing the grid removes the mechanism that placed things correctly by default, and that work transfers to the designer element by element — but a reader who arrives only at the finished artefact is given no test that separates the two cases.
qa_items.support: Exhibit commentaries: apparent simplicity belying almost obsessive attention; the carefully randomised improvisation poster whose precise placement preserves legibility; the playful structure accessible because each part is decisively located.
confounders: reading apparent randomness as evidence of low effort
assuming Samara supplies a test for the finished artefact; he describes how the work was made
assuming the exhibits are a fair sample — they are projects he selected and is commending, with no failure case shown

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — captions in 'Grid Deconstruction: Orthogonal' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A poster is built by overlaying and shifting a conventional calendar grid until almost none of it is visible. What does Samara say is doing the navigational work, and what general condition does the case illustrate?
qa_items.answer: He says the conventional calendar grid that gave rise to the overlapping layers remains as a vestige to help navigation: although only a hint of the modular structure is visible in the stepped movement of the informational chunks, the blue row structure directs reading from a familiar standpoint. The images that would originally have occupied left- and right-hand columns have been spliced and reordered into a strong vertical substructure. The general condition is the chapter's recurring one — the departure remains readable because the thing departed from is still partly legible. The same shape appears where he requires symmetry and asymmetry to stay distinct from each other, and where the exhibits credit cohesion to a surviving network of axes.
qa_items.support: Caption in "Grid Deconstruction: Orthogonal": the calendar grid remaining as a vestige to help navigation; the blue row structure directing reading from a familiar standpoint; images spliced and reordered into a vertical substructure.
confounders: assuming a thorough deconstruction should erase every trace of the original grid
assuming the vestige is a stylistic residue rather than a navigational aid
confusing 'a hint of the structure' with a merely faint or low-contrast rendering of it

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', On the Other Hand — A Historical Survey, 'From an Unexpected Quarter' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara says a magazine with no consistent editorial grid nonetheless had a system. What does he say defined it, and what does that imply about where cohesion can come from?
qa_items.answer: He says that in the magazine's design no overarching structure exists, and that the ferocity of the layouts and the continual destruction of conformity on every page visually define a system that is identifiable and understandable despite the lack of a consistent editorial grid structure. The implication he draws is that visual cohesion can be generated through intuitive, spontaneous relationships rather than through a repeated structure — that consistency of attitude can substitute for consistency of geometry. He distinguishes this from the earlier Cranbrook experiments, which he says were still referring to the idea of structure, whereas this work ignored it.
qa_items.support: "From an Unexpected Quarter": no overarching structure in the magazine; the continual destruction of conformity defining an identifiable and understandable system; the contrast with Cranbrook work that still referred to structure.
confounders: reading 'no structure' as 'no system'
assuming Samara treats this as the chapter's model case; he presents it as one point in a historical survey
assuming consistency of attitude replaces the practicality obligation he states later

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', On the Other Hand — A Historical Survey, 'Against the Establishment' and the survey's closing (spine 6)
qa_items.question: What conclusion does Samara draw from the history in this chapter, and why is that conclusion, rather than the history itself, the part worth keeping?
qa_items.answer: The conclusion is that rational structure — the grid — is one of many possible systems for organising visual material, and that context is an important factor in determining which system is best for a specific project. He closes the survey by saying that intuitive and idiosyncratic approaches now participate on equal terms with rational, grid-based ones, and that the designer's set of tools includes several methods from which the most appropriate for a given project can be chosen. That conclusion is the reusable part because the rest of the section is chronology — names, schools, dates — which carries no mechanism. The claim also does the load-bearing work for the chapter: it converts a historical narrative into the premise that selection, not habit, governs.
qa_items.support: "Against the Establishment" and the survey's closing: the grid as one of many possible systems with context determining which is best; intuitive approaches participating on equal terms; the designer's set of tools and choosing the most appropriate.
confounders: treating the historical narrative as the source's argument rather than as its setting
reading 'equal terms' as a claim that the approaches are interchangeable; his point is that selection is required
assuming the equality claim is about quality; it is about which system may legitimately be chosen

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Grid Deconstruction: Non-Orthogonal, 'Deformation and Distortion' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A long scrolling page feels monotonous. Samara offers a reason and a device drawn from grid deformation. What are they, and what does he say makes the effect register?
qa_items.answer: His reason is that the conventional scrolling function of webpages can rapidly regularise perceived movement into a vertically constrained stream. His device is grid deformation, which he says can introduce greater, unexpected lateral movement and a perception of deeper space for improved visual interest. What makes it register is the frame: as the altered shapes of columns or rows come into view within the browser area and then recede, their irregularity is abruptly reinforced by the orthogonal consistency of the browser window's edges. The deformation is read against the one rectangle that cannot be deformed.
qa_items.support: "Deformation and Distortion", the web paragraph: scrolling regularising movement into a vertically constrained stream; deformation introducing lateral movement and deeper space; the irregularity reinforced by the orthogonal consistency of the browser window's edges.
confounders: assuming the remedy for monotony is more content variety rather than a change of structure
missing the role of the browser frame, which is what he says supplies the contrast
generalising this to a full-bleed or frameless display, where the reference rectangle he relies on is absent

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Grid Deconstruction: Orthogonal, 'Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting' (spine 6)
qa_items.question: You want depth and directional ambiguity in a poster but not incoherence. Samara names a way to get ordered ambiguity from layering. What is it, and what detail does he say strengthens it?
qa_items.answer: Use more than one grid rather than none. He says a conventional grid structure repeated in different orientations can be used to explore a more dynamic architectural space by creating different axes of alignment, and that overlapping grids with modules of different proportions, or running at right angles to each other, can introduce a kind of order to the spatial and directional ambiguity that layering creates. The detail that strengthens it is that some elements should be oriented on both layers simultaneously — an element belonging to two structures at once is what ties the layers together instead of leaving them as separate sheets.
qa_items.support: "Splitting, Splicing, and Shifting": a conventional grid repeated in different orientations to create different alignment axes; overlapping grids of different module proportions or at right angles introducing order to the ambiguity layering creates, especially where some elements are oriented on both layers simultaneously.
confounders: assuming ambiguity must be reduced rather than ordered
assuming layering means transparency effects; his subject is overlapping alignment structures
omitting the shared-element condition, which is the part he says makes the ordering work

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy, diagram captions (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A poster has one element far more distinct than everything else, and the secondary material now reads as an undifferentiated mass. What does Samara say is happening?
qa_items.answer: He describes exactly this. An element that distinguishes itself from the others becomes a focal point and therefore assumes the greatest level of importance — but where the primary element disconnects visually to an extreme degree, that extremity diminishes the effect of the other contrasts evident in the secondary material. The contrasts among the secondary elements have not changed; they are being read against a much larger difference and so register less. The general controls he names are contrast in relative size and in relative spacing, meaning density against openness, which he says account for the most effective ways to establish a clear hierarchy, enhanced by hue or value change.
qa_items.support: Diagram captions in "Readability, Navigation, and Hierarchy": a distinguished element becoming a focal point of greatest importance; the extreme degree of disconnection diminishing the effect of other contrasts; size and spacing contrast as the most effective hierarchy controls.
confounders: assuming the secondary contrasts were poorly designed, when the stated cause is the primary element's extremity
assuming the remedy is more contrast everywhere; that is the change that produced the problem
confusing this with the source's general advice to push differences to greater extremes, which he gives for a complicated field

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Centered-Axis Structure, the responsive caption (spine 6)
qa_items.question: A centred layout that works on a desktop browser collapses on a phone. What does Samara say is lost, and what does he propose to recover some of it?
qa_items.answer: What is lost is the contrast in lateral emphasis. He says maintaining a logic of contrasting form widths and margin spaces is easily accomplished in the generously wide format of a desktop browser but is more challenging within the narrow confines of a smartphone screen. His proposal is to force text elements to occupy a narrower-than-optimal width and to introduce punctuating graphical forms, which he says permits some of the contrast in lateral emphasis to translate into the smaller viewing area. Note the concession embedded in it: he accepts a sub-optimal measure in order to preserve a compositional contrast, and says only that some of the contrast survives.
qa_items.support: Caption in "Centered-Axis Structure": contrasting form widths and margin spaces easy in a wide desktop browser and harder on a smartphone; forcing text to a narrower-than-optimal width and introducing punctuating graphical forms so some lateral contrast translates.
confounders: assuming the fix is to keep the optimal measure and drop the contrast
assuming the contrast fully survives; he says only that some of it translates
confusing this with his general advice to exaggerate contrast, which addresses inertness rather than width

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical, opening — the concrete-poems and cubistic-composition captions (spine 6)
qa_items.question: Samara shows two ways of keeping difficult layouts readable. Describe both, and say what principle they share.
qa_items.answer: In the first, a spread of concrete poems mitigates reading-sequence difficulty by positioning each poem's title so that it directs readers to the conventional location for text to start — upward and to the left; once the reader has entered from that familiar point, careful attention to the proximities of sequential words and phrases carries them through unexpected orientations, changes in spacing and other obstacles. In the second, a multi-plane cubistic composition integrates columns of relatively extensive text into its visual language while leaving the text situated primarily within open negative space, so it keeps its distinct identity and its legibility free of textural interference. The shared principle is that the difficulty is retained and localised rather than removed: one supplies a conventional entry point into an unconventional field, the other gives the text a protected zone inside a complex space. In neither case is the invention diluted; in both, one specific reading requirement is guaranteed.
qa_items.support: Captions in "Considering the Practical in the Impractical": the concrete-poem titles directing readers to the conventional starting point and proximity carrying them onward; the cubistic composition keeping text within open negative space to preserve identity and legibility.
confounders: assuming the repair means simplifying the whole layout
treating the entry point as a decorative device rather than as the navigational concession it is
assuming the text must be separated from the composition entirely; in the second case it is integrated into the visual language and only protected from textural interference

qa_items.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', whole chapter (spine 6) — read against Ch. 1's instructional sections
qa_items.question: Chapter 2 states several things that cut against positions taken in chapter 1 of the same book. Give two, and state the correct way to record such a conflict.
qa_items.answer: Two clear cases. First, on building a structure before assessing content: chapter 1's method treats the grid as a closed system that requires the content to be assessed first, whereas a chapter 2 exhibit commends a book in which the grid forces the deconstruction precisely because its structure was created before the material it governs was assessed. Second, on variation: chapter 2 says grid-based thinking, for all the variation it encourages, tends to engender systems that are characteristically consistent and programmatic and that expressing variation is more difficult — a cooler assessment than chapter 1's. A third, if wanted, is fragmenting running text, which chapter 2 concedes generally interferes with reading while also suggesting it might improve readability in the engagement sense. The correct record is that these are one author qualifying his own earlier statements across a chapter boundary within a single work, in different contexts and often for different purposes. They are not two sources disagreeing, and nothing in chapter 2 counts as independent corroboration of chapter 1 — it is the same author, the same book, the same edition.
qa_items.support: Chapter 2's "Universal/Unique" exhibit commentary on the grid preceding assessment of the material; "Systematizing the Organic" on grid-based thinking engendering consistent, programmatic systems in which variation is harder to express; "Verbal and Editorial Deconstruction" on interference with reading and the hedged readability remark.
confounders: presenting the two chapters as two sources in disagreement
treating chapter 2 as corroborating evidence for chapter 1 because both are about grids
assuming one chapter supersedes the other; the contexts differ and the author does not adjudicate

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Image-World", the passage on the photograph as a trace and the Shakespeare comparison (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Sontag locates photographic authority somewhere other than accuracy. Where, and what thought experiment does she use to isolate it?
qa_items.answer: In the photograph being a trace. A painting, however exact, is never more than the stating of an interpretation; a photograph is never less than the registering of an emanation — light reflected by objects — and is therefore a material vestige of its subject in a way no painting can be, something directly stencilled off the real like a footprint or a death mask. The thought experiment: offered a hypothetical Holbein portrait of Shakespeare or a hypothetical photograph of him, most would take the photograph — and not merely because it would show what he looked like, since even a faded, barely legible brownish shadow would still be preferred. Her phrase for why is that having it would be like having a nail from the True Cross. The authority is relic-like: what is credited is the causal link, not the likeness, which is why a degraded photograph keeps an authority a perfect painting never acquires.
qa_items.support: The Image-World: a photograph is not only an image, an interpretation of the real, it is also a trace, something directly stencilled off the real; a photograph is never less than the registering of an emanation, a material vestige of its subject in a way no painting can be; having a photograph of Shakespeare would be like having a nail from the True Cross.
confounders: locating the authority in accuracy or detail, which the faded-photograph case is designed to rule out
reading 'trace' as a metaphor; her argument turns on it being physical
assuming she therefore endorses the authority — she is explaining it, and elsewhere attacks what it licenses

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "Photographs furnish evidence" (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Sontag says a photograph is received differently from a written account or a drawing. State the difference precisely, and give the two features of the presumption she insists on.
qa_items.answer: What is written about a person or an event is frankly an interpretation, and so are handmade visual statements like paintings and drawings; photographed images do not seem to be statements about the world so much as pieces of it, miniatures of reality. The two features she insists on: first, the presumption survives distortion — the picture may distort, and there is still always a presumption that something exists, or did exist, which is like what is in it; second, the presumption is indifferent to the maker. Whatever the limitations of amateurism or the pretensions of artistry, any photograph seems to have a more innocent, and therefore more accurate, relation to visible reality than other made images do. Her formulation of the consequence is that a photograph passes for incontrovertible proof that a given thing happened.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: photographs furnish evidence; a photograph passes for incontrovertible proof that a given thing happened; the picture may distort but there is always a presumption that something exists or did exist which is like what's in the picture; whatever the limitations or pretensions of the individual photographer, a photograph — any photograph — seems to have a more innocent, and therefore more accurate, relation to visible reality.
confounders: reading it as a claim that photographs are accurate; she says they are received as accurate
assuming skilled photographs carry more of the presumption; she says it is indifferent to the maker

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage on the presumption of veracity and the Farm Security Administration photographers (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Sontag's documentary example: photographers took dozens of frontal pictures of one subject until satisfied. What is the point of the example, and what does she say about photographers who work without discrimination?
qa_items.answer: The point is that a standard is imposed on the subject by a decision that leaves no visible trace. They shot until they had the precise expression that supported their own notions about poverty, light, dignity, texture, exploitation and geometry — so the surviving frame agrees with a prior idea, and the agreement was produced by selection. Her general form is that in deciding how a picture should look, and in preferring one exposure to another, photographers are always imposing standards on their subjects, and that even those most concerned with mirroring reality are haunted by tacit imperatives of taste and conscience. About undiscriminating work she closes the escape: occasions when picture-taking is relatively promiscuous or self-effacing do not lessen the didacticism of the enterprise, because the passivity and ubiquity of the photographic record is itself photography's message and its aggression. Note that the reading of what the photographers were satisfied by is entirely hers, offered with no account of how she knows.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: the FSA photographers would take dozens of frontal pictures until satisfied they had the right look — the precise expression that supported their own notions about poverty, dignity, texture, exploitation and geometry; in deciding how a picture should look, photographers are always imposing standards; this very passivity and ubiquity is photography's message, its aggression.
confounders: reading it as a criticism of those photographers rather than as a claim about all selection
assuming neutral or artless shooting escapes the argument; she closes that route explicitly

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passage on the consequences of lying (spine 8)
qa_items.question: "A fake painting falsifies the history of art. A fake photograph falsifies reality." Explain the asymmetry, and note the detail in her definition of a fake photograph that is easy to miss.
qa_items.answer: The asymmetry follows from what each kind of image claims. A photograph makes a claim to be true that a painting can never make, so the consequences of lying are more central for photography than they ever can be for painting. A forged painting is a false attribution — a question about art's history. A faked photograph corrupts a claim about the world. The detail that is easy to miss is inside her parenthesis: a fake photograph is one which has been retouched or tampered with, **or whose caption is false**. The false caption is placed inside the definition of the fake, not outside it, which means the claim covers words attached to an entirely unaltered image.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: a fake painting (one whose attribution is false) falsifies the history of art; a fake photograph (one which has been retouched or tampered with, or whose caption is false) falsifies reality; the consequences of lying have to be more central for photography because photographs make a claim to be true that paintings can never make.
confounders: restricting 'fake' to image manipulation and dropping the caption clause
reading the sentence as a rule Sontag is proposing; it is a statement about what the two kinds of image claim

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passage on anxiety before the camera and the invention of retouching (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Sontag reports that when retouching became publicly known in the 1850s, the appetite for being photographed rose. What does she say people want from a portrait, and what inference rule does she attach?
qa_items.answer: She reports that the news that the camera could lie made getting photographed much more popular. What people want, on her account, is the idealised image — a photograph of themselves looking their best — and they feel rebuked when the camera does not return an image of themselves as more attractive than they really are; few, she says, are lucky enough to look better in photographs than in life. The inference rule is a nice one: that photographs are often praised for their candour and honesty indicates that most photographs are not candid, since a property is remarked on where it is not the default. Note that the causal joining — that the appetite rose *because* people want flattery — is not something she states; she puts the two adjacent, and this bank records the connection as an interpretation rather than as her claim.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: many people are anxious when about to be photographed, not because they fear being violated but because they fear the camera's disapproval; people want the idealised image; they feel rebuked when the camera doesn't return an image of themselves as more attractive than they really are; the news that the camera could lie made getting photographed much more popular; that photographs are often praised for their candour indicates that most are not candid.
confounders: predicting the opposite effect, which a straightforward account of trust would give
treating the causal connection as Sontag's; she states the fact and the desire separately

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "A new sense of the notion of information has been constructed around the photographic image" (spine 5)
qa_items.question: What does Sontag mean by saying that in a world ruled by photographic images all borders seem arbitrary, and what does she say a photograph therefore invites?
qa_items.answer: A photograph is a thin slice of space as well as of time, so anything can be separated — made discontinuous — from anything else, since all that is necessary is to frame the subject differently; and conversely anything can be made adjacent to anything else. Her consequence is epistemic: the world becomes a series of unrelated, freestanding particles and history a set of anecdotes, a view that denies interconnectedness and continuity while conferring on each moment the character of a mystery. The camera, in her phrase, makes reality atomic, manageable and opaque. What a photograph therefore invites is not knowledge but speculation: because photographs cannot themselves explain anything, they are inexhaustible invitations to deduction, speculation and fantasy — the ultimate wisdom of the image being "there is the surface, now think, or rather feel, what the reality must be like if it looks this way."
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: the photograph is a thin slice of space as well as time; all borders (framing) seem arbitrary, anything can be separated from anything else, all that is necessary is to frame the subject differently; the world becomes a series of unrelated, freestanding particles; the camera makes reality atomic, manageable and opaque; photographs are inexhaustible invitations to deduction, speculation and fantasy.
confounders: reading 'arbitrary borders' as a complaint about bad cropping rather than as a property of framing as such
assuming the invitation to speculate is a virtue in her account; she opposes it to understanding

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passage beginning "Because each photograph is only a fragment" (spine 8)
qa_items.question: One photograph appears on a contact sheet, in a gallery, at a political demonstration, in a police file, in a news magazine and on a living-room wall. What does Sontag say has happened, and what formula does she borrow to state it?
qa_items.answer: Each situation suggests a different use for the photograph, and none of them can secure its meaning. Because each photograph is only a fragment, its moral and emotional weight depends on where it is inserted, and the image changes according to the context in which it is seen. She borrows Wittgenstein's formula for words and applies it directly: the meaning is the use. She then extends the point from placement to time — the context that shapes a photograph's immediate, and especially its political, use is inevitably succeeded by contexts in which that use is weakened, so original uses are modified and eventually supplanted, most notably by the discourse of art, into which she says any photograph can be absorbed.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: because each photograph is only a fragment, its moral and emotional weight depends on where it is inserted; a photograph changes according to the context in which it is seen; each of these situations suggests a different use but none can secure their meaning; as Wittgenstein argued for words, that the meaning is the use — so for each photograph.
confounders: answering that the photograph means different things to different audiences, which understates it; her claim is that no placement fixes the meaning at all
assuming the original context is the true one; she says it is the one most reliably lost

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passage on Benjamin, the caption and the film "A Letter to Jane" (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Sontag says two things about captions that pull in opposite directions. Give both, and say what goes wrong if only the first is taken.
qa_items.answer: First: a photograph is physically mute and talks through the mouth of the text written beneath it, and words do speak louder than pictures — captions tend to override the evidence of our eyes. Second: no caption can permanently restrict or secure a picture's meaning; even an entirely accurate caption is only one interpretation, and a limiting one, and the caption-glove slips on and off too easily to hold. What goes wrong if only the first is taken is that a claim about instability becomes a technique — the caption starts to look like a control on meaning, which is exactly the position she is arguing against. She reports and rejects Benjamin's proposal that the right caption could rescue a picture and confer a revolutionary use value on it, on the ground that the moralists are demanding a photograph do what no photograph can ever do, which is speak.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: this photograph, like any photograph, is physically mute, it talks through the mouth of the text written beneath it; words do speak louder than pictures, captions do tend to override the evidence of our eyes, but no caption can permanently restrict or secure a picture's meaning; even an entirely accurate caption is only one interpretation, necessarily a limiting one; what the moralists are demanding is that a photograph do what no photograph can ever do — speak.
confounders: taking only the override half and reading it as a technique for controlling meaning
attributing Benjamin's right-caption proposal to Sontag; she reports it and argues against it

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the account of a wartime photograph and the caption supplied for it (spine 8)
qa_items.question: A photograph is released by one party and published by another with its own caption. On Sontag's reading, what happens to it — and what does that case establish and not establish?
qa_items.answer: Its meaning can reverse. In her case a photograph released for one political purpose was published in a magazine whose caption gave it, in her account, close to the opposite meaning, and the revolutionary use-value it had for those who released it was sabotaged by what the magazine furnished as a caption. What the case establishes is her positive claim about asymmetry: the image supplies no assertion of its own, the text supplies one, and the text wins. What it does not establish is that captioning solves anything, because the same detachability that let the second caption override the first will let a third override that — which is why she insists the caption-glove slips on and off. Note the evidence: this is a film-essay's reading of one wartime photograph in one magazine, inside a specific political controversy of the early 1970s, doing the work of a general claim.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: what the photograph meant when it was published in the French picture magazine in some ways reverses the meaning it had for those who released it; even more decisive than the new setting is how its revolutionary use-value was sabotaged by what the magazine furnished as a caption; the caption-glove slips on and off so easily.
confounders: concluding that better captioning would have protected the image
treating a single contested case as demonstrated rather than argued

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "Photography implies that we know about the world if we accept it as the camera records it" (spine 5)
qa_items.question: "Photographs do not explain; they acknowledge." Give Sontag's reason — not the assertion, the argument — and the concession she makes in the same passage.
qa_items.answer: The argument is about the form of understanding. An amorous relation is based on how something looks; understanding is based on how something functions; functioning takes place in time and must be explained in time; and therefore only that which narrates can make us understand. A photograph is a slice of time, so the object of understanding is not merely underrepresented in it — it is absent in kind. She takes Brecht's example, that a photograph of a great armaments works reveals virtually nothing about that organisation, and generalises it: the camera's rendering of reality must always hide more than it discloses. The concession is real and should not be dropped: photographs do fill in blanks in our mental pictures of the present and the past, and she names the case — images of 1880s urban squalor are sharply instructive to someone unaware it was that bad. Filling a blank is not explaining.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: strictly speaking, one never understands anything from a photograph; the camera's rendering of reality must always hide more than it discloses; a photograph of the Krupp works reveals virtually nothing about that organisation; understanding is based on how it functions, and functioning takes place in time — only that which narrates can make us understand; photographs do fill in blanks in our mental pictures.
confounders: answering that photographs lack detail or context, which is not her argument
dropping the concession and reading her as saying photographs convey nothing
attributing the armaments-works example to Sontag; it is Brecht's, reported by her

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passage beginning "The painter constructs, the photographer discloses" (spine 8)
qa_items.question: You are asked to judge a tightly cropped photograph in which the subject is not identifiable — it reads as an abstract form. On Sontag's account, what has to happen before any judgement is possible, and what does that imply about the standing of formal qualities in photography?
qa_items.answer: On her account the subject has to be identified first, and until it is, the judgement cannot be made at all. Her evidence is exactly this case: a photograph seen too closely or too distantly cannot be reacted to at all until the viewer knows what piece of the world it is. Two cases carry it. A photographed cabbage leaf reads as a fall of gathered cloth and needs a title to identify it — and the image then works in two ways, the form pleases and it is, surprisingly, a cabbage leaf, where gathered cloth would not have been beautiful because that beauty is already known from the fine arts. And a shape resembling a bare coronet becomes far more interesting once one learns it is a splash of milk. Her conclusion: the painter constructs and the photographer discloses, so the formal qualities of style — the central issue in painting — are at most of secondary importance in photography, while what a photograph is of is always of primary importance.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: the identification of the subject of a photograph always dominates our perception of it, as it does not necessarily in a painting; the painter constructs, the photographer discloses; the subject of the cabbage-leaf photograph looks like gathered cloth and a title is needed; if it were gathered cloth it wouldn't be so beautiful; what looks like a bare coronet becomes far more interesting when we find out it is a splash of milk.
confounders: reading it as advice about titling or captioning images; she is describing how they are processed
assuming she is dismissing composition; her claim is about the order in which the two questions are asked

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the opening passage and the passage quoting Benjamin on the camera's incapacity (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Sontag says photography beautifies. What makes this a claim about the medium rather than about photographers, and what route does she give for subjects that offer no beauty to find?
qa_items.answer: It is a claim about the medium because it covers work that sets out to refuse beauty: notwithstanding the declared aims of indiscreet, unposed, often harsh photography to reveal truth and not beauty, photography still beautifies. Intending otherwise does not exempt you. She quotes Benjamin's 1934 statement that the camera is by then incapable of photographing a tenement or a rubbish-heap without transfiguring it, and that it has turned abject poverty itself, handled in a modish and technically perfect way, into an object of enjoyment. The route for unpromising subjects is her own sentence: the most enduring triumph of photography has been its aptitude for discovering beauty in the humble, the inane and the decrepit — because at the very least the real has a pathos, and that pathos is beauty. She opens the essay with the corollary: nobody ever discovered ugliness through photographs, but many, through photographs, have discovered beauty.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: nobody ever discovered ugliness through photographs; photography still beautifies notwithstanding the declared aims of harsh photography to reveal truth, not beauty; the most enduring triumph of photography has been its aptitude for discovering beauty in the humble, the inane, the decrepit; at the very least, the real has a pathos, and that pathos is beauty. Benjamin, quoted: incapable of photographing a tenement or a rubbish-heap without transfiguring it.
confounders: reading it as a criticism of particular photographers rather than of the medium
converting it into a recommendation about what to photograph or how — she makes none, and neither does this bank

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the closing passages beginning "In a consumer society, even the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work" (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Sontag's claim about images of suffering is that the medium works against the effect they were made to have. State it precisely, note the clause about intention, and say what it is not.
qa_items.answer: Precisely: photographs can and do distress — protected inhabitants of the more affluent parts of the world learn about the world's horrors mainly through the camera — but the aestheticising tendency of photography is such that the medium which conveys distress ends by neutralising it. Two routes: cameras miniaturise experience and transform history into spectacle; and as much as photographs create sympathy they also cut sympathy and distance the emotions, producing a realism that is in the long run morally analgesic while remaining sensorially stimulating. The clause about intention is the part that bites: she says this of even the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work, so neither good intention nor accurate captioning exempts an image. What it is not: it is not advice. She does not say that images of difficulty should be composed differently, framed differently or avoided, and she recommends nothing at all here. Anything of that form would be an addition to what she wrote.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: in a consumer society, even the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work of photographers issues in the discovery of beauty; photographs can and do distress, but the aestheticizing tendency is such that the medium which conveys distress ends by neutralizing it; cameras miniaturize experience, transform history into spectacle; as much as they create sympathy, photographs cut sympathy, distance the emotions.
confounders: converting it into a rule about depicting difficult subjects, which is the characteristic way of misusing this source
assuming better intentions or accurate captions escape the tendency; she rules both out by name

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the opening passage on beauty being used up (spine 8)
qa_items.question: "Photographs create the beautiful and—over generations of picture-taking—use it up." What is the mechanism, and what qualification does Sontag put on her own explanation?
qa_items.answer: The mechanism is assimilation, not boredom. A way of seeing is startling only against a habit it violates; challenged by the revelations of photographers, seeing accommodates to photographs, so photographic seeing has to be constantly renewed with new shocks — of subject matter or of technique — in order to keep producing the impression of violating ordinary vision. Each success therefore removes the condition that made it work. Her worked case is a generation of rigorous close-up studies — plants, shells, leaves, weathered wood, workers' hands — which became clichés of a merely photographic way of seeing: what once took a very intelligent eye to see, anyone can see now. Her example of the same thing happening to a subject is sunsets, which the image-surfeited find corny because they now look too much like photographs. The qualification is against her own tidiness: increased familiarity does not entirely explain why certain conventions of beauty get used up while others remain, and the attrition is moral as well as perceptual — a residue she does not analyse.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: photographs create the beautiful and, over generations of picture-taking, use it up; the image-surfeited are likely to find sunsets corny, they now look too much like photographs; photographic seeing has to be constantly renewed with new shocks; the close-up studies have become clichés of a merely photographic way of seeing; what it once took a very intelligent eye to see, anyone can see now; increased familiarity does not entirely explain it, the attrition is moral as well as perceptual.
confounders: reading it as advice to seek novelty; she treats the search for new shocks as a treadmill, not a strategy
dropping her qualification and presenting familiarity as the whole explanation

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "The quality of feeling ... also depends on the degree of their familiarity with these images" (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Sontag's attrition argument has two parts, and only the second makes it a mechanism. Give both, and give her comparative example.
qa_items.answer: First: photographs shock insofar as they show something novel, and the shock of photographed atrocity wears off with repeated viewing — she places it beside pornography, where the surprise of the first encounter also wears off after a few more. Second, and this is what makes it a mechanism rather than an observation: the ante keeps getting raised, partly through the very proliferation of such images. The supply of images draws down the stock of novelty on which any response depends, so the level required to produce a response rises with the number of images produced. Her example is two famine reportages a generation apart, the later having less impact for some viewers because such images had become banal, and a further set that she says must have seemed to many like an unbearable replay of a now familiar atrocity exhibition. Her conclusion is that concerned photography has, in recent decades, done at least as much to deaden conscience as to arouse it.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: photographs shock insofar as they show something novel; unfortunately the ante keeps getting raised, partly through the very proliferation of such images of horror; the shock of photographed atrocities wears off with repeated viewings, just as the surprise of a pornographic movie does; the later famine photographs had less impact because those images had become banal; concerned photography has done at least as much to deaden conscience as to arouse it.
confounders: giving only the wearing-off half, which is an observation and not a mechanism
reading it as advice about frequency or variation; she recommends nothing
assuming the effect is about the viewer's callousness rather than about the supply of images

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "The ethical content of photographs is fragile" (spine 5)
qa_items.question: An archive photograph that once moved people because of what it showed now reads mainly as poignant and old. Which of Sontag's two decays is this, how do you tell it from the other, and what exception does she allow?
qa_items.answer: This is decay by time, not decay by repetition: it acts on every photograph rather than only on ones an audience has seen before, and you tell them apart by what changes — repetition lowers the response to a subject, whereas time changes what the image is affecting FOR. The ethical content of photographs is fragile and most do not keep their emotional charge; the demonstration is a substitution of what the image is affecting *for*. A photograph of 1900 that was affecting then because of its subject would today be more likely to move us because it is a photograph taken in 1900. The particular qualities and intentions of photographs are swallowed up in the generalised pathos of time past; aesthetic distance is built into the experience of looking at photographs, if not immediately then certainly with time; and time eventually positions most photographs, even the most amateurish, at the level of art. The exception she allows: photographs of certain horrors have gained the status of ethical reference points, and those do keep their charge.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: the ethical content of photographs is fragile; with the possible exception of photographs of those horrors that have gained the status of ethical reference points, most photographs do not keep their emotional charge; a photograph of 1900 that was affecting then because of its subject would today be more likely to move us because it is a photograph taken in 1900; time eventually positions most photographs at the level of art.
confounders: conflating this with attrition by repetition; the drivers and the scope differ
missing the ethical-reference-point exception

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "A photograph that brings news of some unsuspected zone of misery" (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Sontag says photographs cannot create a moral position. State the claim exactly, give the claim about order that follows from it, and name the case she sets against her own argument.
qa_items.answer: Exactly: photographs cannot create a moral position, but they can reinforce one — and can help build a nascent one. An image bringing news of an unsuspected zone of misery cannot make a dent in public opinion unless an appropriate context of feeling and attitude already exists, and what determines the possibility of being affected morally is the existence of a relevant political consciousness; without a politics, such photographs are most likely experienced as simply unreal or as a demoralising emotional blow. The claim about order is sharper: it is never photographic evidence that constructs — more properly, identifies — an event; the contribution of photography always follows the naming of the event. The case she sets against herself is a single wartime photograph of a wounded child, which she says probably did more to increase public revulsion against a war than a hundred hours of televised barbarities. She does not reconcile the two.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: photographs cannot create a moral position, but they can reinforce one — and can help build a nascent one; a photograph that brings news of some unsuspected zone of misery cannot make a dent in public opinion unless there is an appropriate context of feeling and attitude; the contribution of photography always follows the naming of the event; the 1972 photograph probably did more to increase public revulsion than a hundred hours of televised barbarities.
confounders: reading it as saying images have no effect; she says they reinforce and can help build
missing the ordering claim, which is the strong version
assuming she resolves the counter-case; she states both and leaves them

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the comparison of two wars and the discussion of internment photographs (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Two sets of photographs of comparable events reach the same public and only one changes anything. Reconstruct Sontag's explanation, and state what she says the other set's absence was caused by.
qa_items.answer: Her explanation is that the reception was determined by the political understanding already in place, not by the images. Photographs of one war's suffering circulated because journalists felt backed in obtaining them, the event having been defined by a significant number of people as a savage colonialist war; the other war was understood as part of a just struggle, and given that characterisation photographs of the cruelty of unlimited firepower would have been irrelevant. That is what she says caused the absence — not censorship but the absence of a place for such images: ideologically, there was no space for them, so nobody brought back photographs showing that the enemy had a human face. Her other case runs the same way through time rather than across two events: photographs of a wartime internment were read as a crime by Americans who had arrived at a political understanding two decades later, and could not have been read that way by people who saw them at the time, because the grounds for that judgement were covered over by a pro-war consensus.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: the public did not see such photographs because there was, ideologically, no space for them; Americans did have access to photographs of the suffering of the Vietnamese because journalists felt backed in their efforts, the event having been defined by a significant number of people as a savage colonialist war; the Korean War was understood differently, and given that characterisation such photographs would have been irrelevant; few people who saw the internment photographs in the 1940s could have had so unequivocal a reaction.
confounders: explaining the difference by the quality or availability of the photographs
explaining it by censorship alone; her claim is that there was no place for the images to land

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Image-World", the passage beginning "Photography is acquisition in several forms" (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Sontag separates three forms of photographic acquisition. Name them, and say which she calls the most inclusive and why.
qa_items.answer: First, in its simplest form, surrogate possession of a cherished person or thing — which she says gives photographs some of the character of unique objects. Second, a consumer's relation to events, both those that are part of our experience and those that are not, a distinction she says habit-forming consumership blurs. Third, and the one she calls the most inclusive: acquiring something as information rather than as experience, through image-making and image-duplicating machines.
