It is the most inclusive because the others follow from it — the importance of photographic images as the medium through which events enter our experience is, she says, only a by-product of their effectiveness in furnishing knowledge dissociated from and independent of experience. Through being photographed, something is fitted into schemes of classification and storage, and reality is redefined as an item for exhibition, a record for scrutiny and a target for surveillance.
qa_items.support: The Image-World: photography is acquisition in several forms — surrogate possession of a cherished person or thing; a consumer's relation to events, a distinction such habit-forming consumership blurs; and, most inclusively, acquiring something as information rather than experience; reality as such is redefined — as an item for exhibition, as a record for scrutiny, as a target for surveillance.
confounders: collapsing the three into 'photographs are possessions'
assuming the first is the most important; she says the third is the most inclusive

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "As photographs give people an imaginary possession of a past that is unreal" (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Sontag says the camera both certifies experience and refuses it. Explain how one act does both, and give the second, anxiety-based function she attributes to it.
qa_items.answer: It does both because what certifies the experience is precisely the object that replaced it. Photographs offer indisputable evidence that the trip was made, the programme carried out, the fun had; and taking them refuses the experience by limiting it to a search for the photogenic and converting it into an image, a souvenir — so travel becomes a strategy for accumulating photographs. The anxiety function is separate and she is explicit about it: the very activity of taking pictures is soothing and assuages the disorientation travel is likely to exacerbate. Tourists unsure of other responses put the camera between themselves and whatever is remarkable, which gives shape to the experience — stop, take a photograph, and move on. She adds that the method especially appeals to the work-driven, for whom photographing is a friendly imitation of work that appeases the anxiety of not working while on holiday. That passage is loaded with the national caricatures of its period, which are noted rather than repeated here.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: a way of certifying experience, taking photographs is also a way of refusing it — by limiting experience to a search for the photogenic, by converting experience into an image, a souvenir; travel becomes a strategy for accumulating photographs; the very activity of taking pictures is soothing; most tourists feel compelled to put the camera between themselves and whatever is remarkable; stop, take a photograph, and move on.
confounders: treating certifying and refusing as two separate effects rather than one act
reading the anxiety claim as evidenced; it is asserted about inner states

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passages on photographic seeing and on Weston's claims (spine 8)
qa_items.question: What does Sontag mean by "photographic seeing", what does she grant it, and where does she directly contradict the photographers she is discussing?
qa_items.answer: Photographic seeing is both a new way for people to see and a new activity for them to perform, and its content is the mentality that looks at the world as a set of potential photographs. She grants it two things: an aptitude for discovering beauty in what everybody sees but neglects as too ordinary, and a freedom from the narrow choices painters had to make about what was worth contemplating, because cameras record anything quickly. The direct contradiction is of the photographers' own accounts: one of them described photography as a way of identifying oneself with nature, and Sontag replies that contrary to what he asserts, the habit of looking at reality as an array of potential photographs creates estrangement from, rather than union with, what is seen — and that photographic seeing, examined, turns out to be mainly a kind of dissociative seeing. She offers argument rather than evidence for preferring her account of their experience to theirs.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: photographic seeing was both a new way for people to see and a new activity for them to perform; it meant an aptitude for discovering beauty in what everybody sees but neglects as too ordinary; contrary to what Weston asserts, the habit of photographic seeing — of looking at reality as an array of potential photographs — creates estrangement from, rather than union with, nature; photographic seeing turns out to be mainly the practice of a kind of dissociative seeing.
confounders: reading photographic seeing as a skill she recommends
missing that she is contradicting the practitioners' own testimony about their experience

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Image-World", the passage beginning "Photography does not simply reproduce the real, it recycles it" (spine 10)
qa_items.question: An image of one thing is placed in an advertisement for something entirely unrelated, and the pairing works. Name the quality Sontag says photography specialises in producing, give her formula for it, and give the single sentence with which she shows how far the erasure goes.
qa_items.answer: The quality is "the interesting", and the pairing works because interest is relational. The formula: what makes something interesting is that it can be seen to be like, or analogous to, something else — so interest is relational rather than a property of the thing. Her surrounding claim is that photography does not simply reproduce the real, it recycles it: things and events are put to new uses and assigned new meanings which go beyond the distinctions between the beautiful and the ugly, the true and the false, the useful and the useless, good taste and bad. Clichés recycled become meta-clichés; the recycling makes clichés out of unique objects and distinctive artefacts out of clichés. The sentence showing how far the erasure goes: in the form of a photograph, the explosion of an atomic bomb can be used to advertise a safe. She adds the underlying condition — images are always compatible, or can be made compatible, even when the realities they depict are not.
qa_items.support: The Image-World: photography does not simply reproduce the real, it recycles it; photography is one of the chief means for producing that quality which erases these distinctions — "the interesting"; what makes something interesting is that it can be seen to be like, or analogous to, something else; clichés, recycled, become meta-clichés; in the form of a photograph the explosion of an A-bomb can be used to advertise a safe; images are always compatible, or can be made compatible, even when the realities they depict are not.
confounders: treating 'the interesting' as ordinary interest rather than as her quasi-technical term
reading the recycling claim as being about reuse of assets rather than about the erasure of distinctions

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the opening passages on photographs as the standard of the beautiful (spine 8), and "The Image-World", the passage on how reality has come to seem (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Sontag describes a reversal between the image and what it depicts. State it, give her example about the self, and give the boundary she puts on the claim.
qa_items.answer: The reversal is that the copy becomes the measure: photographs, rather than the world, have become the standard of the beautiful, and instead of just recording reality photographs have become the norm for the way things appear to us — so it is reality which is scrutinised and evaluated for its fidelity to photographs. Her example about the self is exact: we learn to see ourselves photographically, so that to regard oneself as attractive is precisely to judge that one would look good in a photograph. She also reports the reversal in ordinary speech — people describing a violent event they were caught up in as having seemed like a movie, said not to diminish it but because other descriptions seem insufficient: it is how they explain how real it was. The boundary is hers and it matters: she says that in some non-industrialised countries people still felt apprehensive at being photographed, sensing a trespass, whereas people in industrialised countries seek to have their photographs taken and feel they are made real by them. The claim is scoped to the second case.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: photographs, rather than the world, have become the standard of the beautiful; we learn to see ourselves photographically; instead of just recording reality, photographs have become the norm for the way things appear to us; it is reality which is scrutinized and evaluated for its fidelity to photographs. The Image-World: reality has come to seem more and more like what we are shown by cameras; "it seemed like a movie" is said in order to explain how real it was.
confounders: reading it as a claim that people confuse images with reality; her claim is about which is the reference
dropping the scope, which she states explicitly

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the passage beginning "Photographs may be more memorable than moving images" (spine 5), with "The Image-World", the account of an operation watched in person and on film (spine 10)
qa_items.question: Sontag contrasts the still with the moving image. Give her contrast, her account of what a film takes from the viewer, and the cost she attributes to the still's stasis.
qa_items.answer: The contrast: photographs may be more memorable than moving images because they are a neat slice of time rather than a flow — a stream of underselected images cancels each predecessor with its successor, whereas a still is a privileged moment turned into a slim object one can keep and look at again, whose force is that it keeps open to scrutiny instants the normal flow of time immediately replaces. What a film takes is agency, and she draws it from her own experience of the same procedure watched in person and on film: in the room she was the one who changed focus and made the close-ups and the medium shots, while on film the camera had already looked for her and obliged her to look, leaving as her only option not to look — with the sequence condensed and arranged to stir or shock. The cost of the still's stasis is stated just as plainly: the truths that can be rendered in a dissociated moment, however significant or decisive, have a very narrow relation to the needs of understanding. Note that "may be more memorable" is her hedge, and that the unification of these passages under a single idea about who controls the duration of looking is a reading, not something she states.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: photographs may be more memorable than moving images, because they are a neat slice of time, not a flow; television is a stream of underselected images, each of which cancels its predecessor; each still photograph is a privileged moment. The Image-World: in the operating room I am the one who changes focus and makes the close-ups; in the theatre the camera looks for me and obliges me to look, leaving as my only option not to look. The Heroism of Vision: the truths rendered in a dissociated moment have a very narrow relation to the needs of understanding.
confounders: treating the memorability claim as established; 'may be' is her hedge and she offers one contrast
assuming she prefers the still; she states its cost in the same book

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passages on the caption and on meaning as use (spine 8)
qa_items.question: An image is being assessed on its own, and it will be published with a headline. Using only what Sontag claims, what is wrong with that assessment — and what is NOT fixed by assessing the pair together?
qa_items.answer: What is wrong is the unit. A photograph is physically mute and talks through the mouth of the text placed with it, and words do speak louder than pictures — captions tend to override the evidence of our eyes. So an image assessed without the words it will travel with is not a weaker assessment of the same artefact; it is an assessment of a different one from the thing anyone will encounter. What assessing the pair together does not fix is the meaning itself. No caption can permanently restrict or secure a picture's meaning; even an entirely accurate caption is only one interpretation, and a limiting one; and the caption-glove slips on and off, so the next placement supplies its own. Assessing the pair removes an error that is certain and settles nothing beyond that. Note that Sontag prescribes nothing here — this is her account of how images are read, and the inference about the unit of assessment is drawn from it rather than stated by her.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: this photograph, like any photograph, is physically mute, it talks through the mouth of the text written beneath it; words do speak louder than pictures; captions do tend to override the evidence of our eyes; but no caption can permanently restrict or secure a picture's meaning; even an entirely accurate caption is only one interpretation.
confounders: concluding that a well-written caption controls the reading
treating the inference about the unit of assessment as Sontag's own recommendation

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave", the attrition passage (spine 5), and "The Heroism of Vision", the passage on conventions being used up (spine 8)
qa_items.question: Someone summarises Sontag as "people get numb to images they see a lot of". Which two of her claims does that collapse into one, and what does she say that makes the collapse a mistake?
qa_items.answer: It collapses attrition of *response* into attrition of *convention*, and they have different drivers and different objects. The first is about a subject: photographs shock insofar as they show something novel, the shock of atrocity wears off with repeated viewing, and the ante keeps getting raised partly through the very proliferation of the images. The second is about a way of seeing: photographs create the beautiful and, over generations, use it up, because seeing accommodates to photographs — what once took a very intelligent eye to see, anyone can see now. What makes the collapse a mistake is her own qualification: increased familiarity does not entirely explain why certain conventions of beauty get used up while others remain, and the attrition is moral as well as perceptual. She names a residue that familiarity cannot account for, and does not analyse it — so a summary that reduces both to numbness through exposure discards the part of her argument she flags as unfinished.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: photographs shock insofar as they show something novel; the ante keeps getting raised; the shock wears off with repeated viewings. The Heroism of Vision: photographs create the beautiful and use it up; seeing tends to accommodate to photographs; what it once took a very intelligent eye to see, anyone can see now; increased familiarity does not entirely explain why certain conventions of beauty get used up while others remain — the attrition is moral as well as perceptual.
confounders: treating the two as one habituation effect, which is the collapse the question is about
supplying a modern account of feed fatigue in place of her claims; she wrote in 1977 and this bank adds nothing to what she says

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "In Plato's Cave" (spine 5) and "The Image-World" (spine 10), across the passages on evidence, on the trace, and on what photographs cannot do
qa_items.question: Sontag holds that a photograph is credited with a more innocent relation to reality than other made images, and also that photographs are as much an interpretation as paintings are. Is that a contradiction, and what does it tell you about how to use this source?
qa_items.answer: It is a tension she states deliberately and does not resolve, and her essay runs on the friction between the two. Both are claims about different things: the first is about reception — how a photograph is taken by the people who look at it — and the second is about production, what went into making it. Her whole argument about authority depends on the gap between them, which is why the passage moves straight from the presumption of veracity to photographers imposing standards on their subjects. What it tells you about using the source is that its claims come in pairs and the pairs must be kept together: taking the reception claim alone makes her sound credulous about photographic truth, and taking the production claim alone makes her sound as though the presumption does not exist. Neither half is her position.
qa_items.support: In Plato's Cave: a photograph — any photograph — seems to have a more innocent, and therefore more accurate, relation to visible reality than do other mimetic objects; although there is a sense in which the camera does indeed capture reality, photographs are as much an interpretation of the world as paintings and drawings are. Both appear within a few sentences of each other.
confounders: resolving the tension in one direction, which loses the argument
treating it as an inconsistency to be corrected rather than as the structure of her case

qa_items.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
qa_items.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the aestheticisation passages (spine 8), against "In Plato's Cave", the passage on moral position (spine 5)
qa_items.question: Someone cites Sontag to argue that a particular photograph should have been composed differently so as not to aestheticise its subject. Is that a use of her argument? Answer from the text.
qa_items.answer: No, and the reason is in the shape of the claim rather than in a matter of taste. Her claim is that photography still beautifies notwithstanding the declared aims of harsh, unposed photography to reveal truth and not beauty, and that this holds for the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work. A tendency that survives the intention to defeat it, and survives accurate captioning, is not one a different composition escapes — so the claim cannot ground a recommendation about composing. She also nowhere recommends anything: she describes what the medium does to a viewer's relation to a subject and stops. Her related claim about what images can accomplish runs the same way — photographs reinforce a moral position and do not create one, which is a statement about what determines an image's effect, not a specification for making one. Using her to prescribe a composition attributes to her a kind of statement she does not make anywhere in the book.
qa_items.support: The Heroism of Vision: notwithstanding the declared aims of indiscreet, unposed, often harsh photography to reveal truth, not beauty, photography still beautifies; in a consumer society, even the most well-intentioned and properly captioned work issues in the discovery of beauty. In Plato's Cave: photographs cannot create a moral position, but they can reinforce one.
confounders: reading the aestheticisation claim as an instruction, which is the standard misuse of this source
assuming that because she disapproves of an effect she must be recommending against a technique
concluding instead that she thinks such images should not be made; she says nothing of the kind

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'The Virtues of Simplicity', section 'Make sure the fuse on your idea isn't too long or too short' (spine 19)
qa_items.question: Sullivan calls comprehension speed the "Speed of the Get" and likens it to a fuse. Most advice about clarity treats slowness as the only failure. What is the second failure he names, and why does he say it is a failure at all?
qa_items.answer: The fuse can be too short. An idea that resolves before the viewer has begun attending goes off with what he calls a quick, clueless bang, and that instant resolution tells the viewer there is nothing there worth being interested in. His example of the failure state is a STOP sign: an instant read with too little substance to have any effect. So the target is an optimum rather than a minimum. He immediately adds the asymmetry he actually observes in student work — almost all of it errs long, produced by over-complicating and thereby "encoding" the idea, giving a get that takes three or four beats longer than it should.
qa_items.support: Stated claim, with the source's own two named failure directions and his stated judgement that students almost always err on the slow side. No measurement of either bound is offered.
confounders: reading the fuse metaphor as 'faster is always better', which is exactly the reading the STOP-sign example is there to block
confusing this with the simplicity argument — reduction is his method for shortening a fuse, not the same claim as the fuse itself
assuming the too-short failure is the common one; he says the opposite about the work he sees

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'The Virtues of Simplicity', section 'Keep paring away until you have the essence of your idea' (spine 19)
qa_items.question: Sullivan reports Neil French's arithmetic of a layout. State it in both directions, and say precisely what quantity it is a claim about.
qa_items.answer: Every element added to an idea reduces the importance of all the other elements, and every item subtracted raises the visibility and importance of what is left. The quantity is relative prominence inside one composition — attention treated as fixed and divided among the elements present — not how much information a reader can absorb and not the piece's overall effect. This is why the removal test has force: an element that can be taken out without loss was not merely idle, it was diluting everything that stayed. French's demonstration removes body copy by making the headline work harder, then the tagline if it adds no new information, then attempts a visual that delivers the message alone with the logo absorbed into it.
qa_items.support: Reported from a conversation with Neil French and endorsed by Sullivan, with a reproduced hand-drawn sequence. Asserted, not measured: no eye-tracking, recall or response data appears anywhere in the chapter.
confounders: reading it as a claim about cognitive load or reading capacity rather than about salience within one layout
treating 'fewer elements' as the goal; the stated goal is that what remains should dominate
assuming the endpoint is always reachable — Sullivan concedes he reduced a print concept to a single image exactly once in a career

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'The Virtues of Simplicity', section 'Make sure the fuse on your idea isn't too long or too short' (spine 19)
qa_items.question: A team is arguing about whether a supporting line should stay in a poster. One says it adds warmth; the other says it clutters. What operation does Sullivan give for settling this, and what does he call the element if the operation returns a particular result?
qa_items.answer: Take it out and see whether the idea still works. If the idea fails without it, that element was what he calls a load-bearing beam and it stays. If the idea still holds up, the element was not needed and should go. The test replaces argument with subtraction, and Sullivan applies it to any element of any concept — image, phrase, word, headline, tagline, logo. Note what the test does not settle: it establishes necessity, not merit, and it depends entirely on the tester's own judgement of whether the idea "still works", for which he offers no external check.
qa_items.support: Stated remedy, in the source's own words. The same term is reused later as a description of damage: he says less experienced clients are particularly good at asking for the removal of the load-bearing beam.
confounders: answering 'ask whether it is on strategy' — a different check that this source keeps separate
treating the removal test as a taste judgement about whether the line is good; it asks only whether the idea survives without it
assuming a load-bearing beam is always the largest or most prominent element

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'First say it straight, then say it great' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan's clear-and-clever diagram is often summarised as "be clear but also interesting". What does his own explanation add that this summary loses?
qa_items.answer: That the two demands are owed to different parties, which is why neither can be traded against the other. Clarity is owed to the client, who is paying for a message to arrive and is entitled to expect it. Interest is owed to the reader, who owes the advertisement nothing and, in his phrase, is not out there looking for "clear" — what customers notice is what is interesting. So the target is an intersection of two sets rather than a point on one scale, and each half has its own named failure: quoting George Felton, "I've seen that before" for the too-obvious end and "I don't get it" for the too-weird end. He is explicit that nothing tells you where the borders of the overlap lie in a given case, and that finding them is where essentially all the working time goes.
qa_items.support: Stated claim plus a reproduced two-circle diagram; the two rejections are quoted from George Felton's textbook. Presented as a diagram rather than as a procedure, and the source says so.
confounders: treating it as a single dial running from dull to clever, which is what the two-party argument denies
assuming the clever half is the hard one; his stated view is that both borders are hard and that finding them is the entire job
confusing the two rejections — 'I've seen that before' is the clarity-only failure, not the cleverness failure

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'The architecture of ideas' — 'A smile in the mind' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Quoting McAlhone and Stuart, Sullivan says a witty idea does not travel all the way to its audience. What is the mechanism he claims this serves, and what does it cost?
qa_items.answer: The audience must travel somewhere between five and forty percent of the way to unlock the idea, and their own act of completing it is the mechanism, not a side effect: it puts the mind in gear, and he reports the authors' claim that an idea that happens in the mind stays in the mind and leaves a stronger trace, because the person can re-create the pleasure by recalling it. He adds a gloss of his own about a small dopamine release at the moment of resolution. The cost is comprehension time — the distance the viewer travels is exactly what lengthens the fuse — so wit trades directly against his own Speed of the Get. Leave too much out and you mystify; put too much in and you bore.
qa_items.support: Quoted from A Smile in the Mind and endorsed. The five-to-forty-percent range is a figure of speech from that book, not a measurement, and nothing in Sullivan operationalises it. The dopamine connection is his own, linking a general research item about effort evaluation to advertising comprehension; the cited research is not about advertising.
confounders: treating the percentage range as a specification that could be applied
assuming Sullivan wants every idea to be witty; he claims only that this is how wit works when it is used
missing the trade-off with his fuse argument, which is the reason his simplicity chapter and his wit section are in tension

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'The paraprosdokian and the parallelism: Tension and release in a sentence' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan names two sentence architectures for a headline and insists they are different. What does each require, and what single instruction applies to both?
qa_items.answer: A paraprosdokian requires reinterpretation: the second half is unexpected in a way that forces the reader to reframe the first half, because the brain has already auto-filled a likely ending and the actual ending overturns it. A parallelism requires no reinterpretation at all — only opposition. Following Felton, you look for "two-fers": this versus that, this plus that, this but not that, not only this but that — a contrast that throws the benefit into relief. The shared instruction is positional: push the key words to the very end of the sentence, so the line goes off when the writer intends, like a firecracker at the end of a fuse. He adds that full reinterpretation is not always necessary; simply delaying the operative word can achieve a similar effect.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with worked headline examples for each structure. All the evidence is a selected set of celebrated headlines; no line that used the same structures and failed is discussed.
confounders: collapsing the two into 'surprise endings', which loses the source's explicit point that a parallelism needs opposition and not surprise
assuming the delayed-key-word device is a third structure; he presents it as a weaker form of the same positional rule
treating the structures as sufficient — his own framing is that they build tension, not that they make a line good

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Why Is the Bad Guy Always More Interesting?', section 'Brand platforms: the mother of stories' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: A client asks for "a campaign that will last". Using Sullivan's own definitions, what is the difference between a campaign and a platform, and what property decides how long the thing keeps producing?
qa_items.answer: A campaign, in his working definition, is a series of executions held together by similar messaging, typography, art direction, tone and architecture. A platform is a world with its own internal rules, and those rules can be used again and again to spin further stories — prequels, sequels, spin-offs. The property that decides longevity is the richness of the rule set: the more rules to your world, the more stories can be pulled out of it, which is why he says platforms outlast campaigns. He applies this to his own examples rather than exempting them: a One Show-winning parking-assistance campaign is excellent and is a world with essentially one rule — change what is on either side of the space — whereas a soft-drink platform that imported the entire rule set of the legal world kept generating spin-offs, a web mechanic and billboards.
qa_items.support: Stated definitions, explicitly offered "for the purposes of discussion" rather than as industry standard terms, with two named campaigns compared by inspection. Rule count is never defined or counted.
confounders: answering in terms of duration or budget rather than in terms of a generative rule set
assuming a platform must be bigger or more expensive; his distinction is structural
treating Ogilvy's thirty-year durability test as the same idea — that is a criterion for a big idea, not an account of why a rule set keeps producing

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Why Is the Bad Guy Always More Interesting?', section 'Two signs you have a platform' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: Sullivan gives two signs that an idea has reached platform size. Name both, and say which one you should distrust most and why.
qa_items.answer: First, it fits on a sticky note: a big idea can be summed up in a sentence, and needing more than a sentence or two to set it up means it is probably not there yet. Second, once spoken aloud its rules start talking and the platform unpacks itself — other people in the room begin generating executions unprompted. The second is the one to distrust, because it is a social measurement: it is confounded by who is in the room and by the enthusiasm of whoever is presenting, and Sullivan does not address this. He also hedges the first himself, calling it "kind of weird" and framing the whole formula around it as a tool rather than a rule.
qa_items.support: Both signs are stated claims, demonstrated on his own example and on classroom work. The weakness of the second is an extractor observation about a confound the source leaves unexamined; the hedge on the first is his own.
confounders: reporting the sticky-note sign as a length limit for a tagline; it is a test of whether the idea has one centre
treating spontaneous generation in a room as evidence about audiences rather than about colleagues
assuming these are tests of quality; they test for size and legibility of the rule set

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Why Is the Bad Guy Always More Interesting?', section 'Truth + conflicts = platform' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: A student is working on a footwear brand the client describes as "comfortable". Walk through Sullivan's two-step generator on that assignment and say what the second step is actually supposed to deliver.
qa_items.answer: Step one is the truest thing that can be said about the brand — not the client's preferred truth. For his worked case the client's truth was "comfortable" and the class's truth was "ugly". Step two is to look for the conflicts that arise as a consequence of that truth: wearing ugly shoes makes you look stupid, or costs you your evening. The student's page read UGLY + YOU WON'T GET LAID. What the second step delivers, in Sullivan's own single word, is focus: the campaign now has three fixed requirements — communicate comfort, acknowledge that the shoes are ugly, admit that wearing them removes sex appeal — instead of an open field. The resulting platform borrowed its whole rule set from the world of contraception while still delivering the comfort message the client needed.
qa_items.support: The worked example is the source's own classroom case. He explicitly refuses the word formula and calls it a tool — "use it if it works for you". The campaign was never produced and no outcome is reported.
confounders: starting from the client's stated benefit, which is the step the exercise exists to displace
treating the conflict as something to be found in the category; here it is a consequence of the truth
concluding the client's message gets abandoned — the platform is required to still deliver comfort

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Why Is the Bad Guy Always More Interesting?', section 'When everything is okay, we aren't interested' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: A brief reads: "We believe fresh food means better health." Sullivan's team could not work with this. What exactly is wrong with it on his account, and what is the general diagnosis?
qa_items.answer: It states a solution, not a problem. His stated principle is that creativity happens in response to a problem, so a brief phrased as a solution gives the maker nothing to respond to — solutions, in his phrase, are about as interesting as filled-in crossword puzzles, because the interesting part is over. The general diagnosis is that most briefs cut to the end of the movie: they describe life after purchase, a world with no cavities and no breakdowns, which removes the opposing force that a story runs on. His headline test for the same point is that nobody reads "Area Bank Not Robbed" — not because readers are morbid, but because attention tunes out an unchanged status quo.
qa_items.support: The brief and the team's failure to work with it are the source's own report. The underlying story claim is drawn from Robert McKee's screenwriting book and from a trade book's argument about interspecies alarm calls; neither is evidence about advertising.
confounders: diagnosing the brief as vague — it is specific, and its problem is structural
reading the argument as a case for negative advertising, which Sullivan explicitly denies in the same section
assuming any conflict will do; his exemplars all tie the conflict to the product's actual role

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Why Is the Bad Guy Always More Interesting?', sections 'To spark story, start with this versus that' and 'If a conflict isn't immediately apparent, make one up' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: You are handed an undifferentiated commodity — bananas — and asked for a campaign. Sullivan says the open assignment freezes his pen. What device does he impose, and what does he do when the category itself contains no conflict?
qa_items.answer: He draws a rectangle with a line down the middle, treats the line as the word "versus", and fills either side with any opposition that comes to mind — life with the product versus without it, our product versus theirs, or anything else. He reports that the same assignment stated as an opposition ("Coke versus Pepsi") starts producing ideas where the open version produced nothing. When no in-category conflict exists, his instruction is to invent one, and for bananas specifically to go outside the category: good food versus junk food, has its own wrapper versus canned foods, ready to eat versus food you have to cook. His stated point is that any of these could carry a story more interesting than "bananas have potassium", which he calls "milk builds strong bones all over again".
qa_items.support: Stated device, demonstrated on his own worked list. The evidence that the framing helps is his introspective report of what his own pen does; no comparison of output under the two framings is offered.
confounders: assuming the conflict has to be true of the category — he explicitly permits inventing one
treating this as competitive positioning; the opposition may have nothing to do with a competitor
answering with the truth-plus-conflicts formula, which is a different move that starts from a brand truth

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 7 'Why Is the Bad Guy Always More Interesting?', section 'Brand as archetype' (spine 21)
qa_items.question: Sullivan suggests casting a brand as an archetype from the Hero's Journey. He then adds a role assignment that most brand advertising gets backwards. What is it, and why does the archetype device work at all?
qa_items.answer: The brand is not the hero. The customer is the hero, and the brand is the archetype the hero meets — the figure who teaches a lesson or grants a power before the hero returns transformed. The device works because archetypes are shared: the audience already knows how a Caregiver, a Trickster or a Magician behaves, so casting the brand as one imports a stock of expected behaviour that does not have to be established first, and the character traits start suggesting stories. He notes the related compressions — Wieden's and Dru's "brands are verbs" (IBM solves, Nike exhorts, Sony dreams) and his own "brand = adjective".
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a figure of his own brand-archetype pairings, which he presents as his and invites the reader to disagree with.
confounders: casting the brand as the hero, which is the default the instruction is written against
treating archetype, verb and adjective as three names for one technique; they operate at different levels
assuming archetypes are universal — the stock of expected behaviour is culturally supplied

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'Three final notes on strategy' — 'Insist on a precise strategy' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Norman Berry's line is that vague strategies inhibit and precise strategies liberate. Sullivan endorses it and then qualifies it. What is the qualification, and what pair of questions does he want used to detect both failures?
qa_items.answer: A strategy can become too precise. When there is no play in the wheel, an over-specified strategy demands so narrow a range of executions that it has become, by proxy, an execution itself. So there is a workable band with a failure at each end, and the strategy can be moved along a continuum between meaningless breadth and purse-lipped dictums. His stated test is Jean-Marie Dru's mirrored pair. Could the campaign have been created without the brief? If yes, the campaign is lacking in content. Is the campaign merely a transcription of the brief? If yes, there has been no creative leap and it lacks executional force. His summary is that the strategy should be evident in the campaign, but the campaign should not be evident in the strategy.
qa_items.support: Berry and Dru are quoted; the qualification about over-precision is Sullivan's own. No test is offered for locating the band in a given case beyond the two questions.
confounders: reporting only the 'precise strategies liberate' half, which is the received version and is the half he qualifies
treating the two Dru questions as the same question asked twice; they detect opposite failures
confusing this with his separate allowance that a big idea may land off strategy

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'Start with a central human truth' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Sullivan separates facts from truths and says the distinction decides whether a campaign has anywhere to go. Give his standing example of each, and say what kind of work produced the truth.
qa_items.answer: The fact is "milk builds strong bones" — measurable, chart-friendly, which is why he says clients love facts, and, on his account, something nobody has ever acted on. The truth, which produced the campaign that sold milk by the trainload, is that milk is bought because it goes with things: nobody sits down to a bowl of milk, they sit down to cereal or cookies or a sandwich. It came from ethnographic work — researchers placed in paid participants' homes to shop and cook with the families — not from a survey. The general form is that a fact describes the object while a truth describes the buyer's actual relationship to it, which is where the purchase is decided. He adds that clients frequently pay to uncover such truths and then, frightened, cover them back up, because the client does not own the truth; customers do.
qa_items.support: Stated claim illustrated by one celebrated campaign reported second-hand. The inference from that single case to a general rule about facts and truths is the source's.
confounders: treating a truth as simply a more emotional fact; his distinction is about whose relationship is being described
assuming truths come from research — he says you generally know a truth instinctively and that it is almost never in the brief
taking his recommendation to study stand-up comedians as a research method; it produces observations about a comedian's audience, not a client's customers

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'The Creative Process', section 'Brand = adjective'; and Ch. 6 opening argument (spines 11, 19)
qa_items.question: Sullivan reports that audiences in every city he has lectured in answer "safety" when asked what Volvo stands for, and adds that Volvo has not recently appeared in lists of the safest cars. He reads this as evidence of one thing. What second reading does his own evidence permit that he does not draw?
qa_items.answer: He reads it as the power of simplicity: a brand that successfully welded one adjective to its marque rides the benefit of that position in customers' minds long after its products stopped meriting the distinction. The reading he does not draw is the uncomfortable one — that a successfully installed brand adjective can survive the loss of the underlying truth, which makes the same mechanism a way of sustaining a claim the product no longer supports. His own argument elsewhere in the book is that advertising must be built on truth and that customers, not clients, own it; the Volvo case is a place where those two commitments pull against each other and he does not reconcile them.
qa_items.support: The audience-poll result and the observation about safety rankings are both his. The second reading is an extractor observation about a tension the source leaves open, not a claim he makes.
confounders: treating the audience poll as a measurement; it is an informal show of hands at his own lectures, an audience already interested in advertising
concluding that Sullivan endorses making claims a product no longer supports — he does not raise the question at all
assuming the adjective must be the strongest available attribute; his advice where good adjectives are taken is to try a polar opposite or a flanking move

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Work fast. Fail faster.' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan grants that a beginner can write a beautiful headline. Where does he locate a senior writer's actual advantage, and what arithmetic follows from it?
qa_items.answer: Not in the quality of the first idea but in the speed of discard. He says he knows when to abandon an approach that is not working, and how to pick up an idea, inspect its possibilities and decide quickly to keep it or drop it. The arithmetic he states is that he can produce fifty really horrible ideas in the time it takes a junior to produce ten, and that the quantity produced in a fixed period is what raises the odds of striking quality sooner. Because the search is iterative — he quotes "all art is a series of recoveries from the first line drawn" — the bottleneck is evaluation speed, not generation quality.
qa_items.support: Self-report about his own working speed, with no external measurement; the fifty-versus-ten figure is illustrative. He does not address the possibility that fast discard also discards good ideas faster.
confounders: answering that experience produces better ideas, which is the claim he explicitly declines to make
reading 'fail faster' as tolerance of failure rather than as speed of judgement
confusing this with his separate rule that judgement is suspended during generation — the discard he means here is within the generating pass

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'If the idea needs a headline, write 100' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan sets a volume target rather than a quality target for headline writing. State the target and the two conditions he attaches, one of which is usually dropped when this advice is repeated.
qa_items.answer: Write a hundred lines, across several sessions. The first condition is that they all have to be pretty good — the target is a hundred workable lines ranging from decent to very strong, not a hundred attempts, and this is the condition usually dropped. The second is that between rounds you start over on a clean page and constantly pretend you have nothing so far. His argument for the number is that we cannot seriously believe a ticket-selling, brand-building campaign has been crafted after nineteen tries, and that a couple of hundred will be needed. He also gives the reason the target has to be set in advance: around half past two in the morning, "good" starts to look like "great", and volume produced earlier is what lets you refuse it.
qa_items.support: Stated target, illustrated by a reprinted working list of roughly fifty motorcycle headlines behind five finished advertisements. The hundred is a working figure he sets, not a measured optimum, and the reprinted list is the surviving work behind award-selected advertisements.
confounders: reporting it as 'write a lot', which loses the quality condition that distinguishes it from undirected output
assuming one session; he explicitly spreads it across several
reading the reprinted list as a natural sample of a writer's output rather than as the working list behind five successful advertisements

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Low-hanging fruit, the barren wasteland, and eureka' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Ideas are arriving easily in the first hour of a session and the team feels it is going well. What does Sullivan say this means, and what does he instruct?
qa_items.answer: He says to distrust it. Early ideas that come quickly are easy, and his objection is availability rather than quality: pretty much everybody else working the same problem will see the same easy solutions. The instruction is not to discard them but to write down every too-easy idea and move on, because one may later be convertible into something new. He then names what comes next and says there is no shortcut through it — the stretch where nothing usable arrives, which he maps onto the incubation step of James Webb Young's five-step model and treats as an expected stage rather than as failure. His summary of the ordering is that the breakthrough arrives only after the slog.
qa_items.support: Stated claim. The availability argument is asserted, not shown — no instance is given of the same easy idea appearing independently. The incubation account is inherited from a 1940s copywriter's model that he endorses without testing, and he says plainly he does not know where ideas come from.
confounders: treating ease as a sign of a strong idea, which is the intuition the passage is written against
discarding the easy ideas rather than recording them; he says to write them down
confusing the barren stretch with a failure of the assignment, which is exactly what he says it is not

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Dig shallow holes everywhere' and 'Review all the ideas so far and look for patterns' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan's search runs in two phases and then reverses. Describe the phases, say what the first is looking for, and say what he does when the second phase fails.
qa_items.answer: First, dig shallow holes all over the brief's territory: quick sketches against simple executions — a billboard, a tagline, a script — and do not stop to develop even a promising find. What that phase is looking for is stated precisely in the book he quotes: proof of concept, just enough validation to know a direction could be worth digging into, not a finished idea. Second, once a direction is chosen, the Deep Dig drives it everywhere the brand meets people, which the quoted agency extends past advertising into store design, uniforms, customer experience, internal communications and product ideas. When the deep phase fails — and he says an idea that looks huge can resist being enlarged — the move is to go back to digging shallow holes and create more ideas. He describes the same alternation in the language of convergent thinking, which groups possibilities, and divergent thinking, which creates them.
qa_items.support: Stated procedure; the two-phase account and the Deep Dig terminology are quoted from another agency's book and endorsed. No criterion is offered for how many shallow holes is enough.
confounders: treating the shallow phase as brainstorming for volume; its stated purpose is proof of concept per direction
assuming the sequence runs once; he is explicit that it oscillates
confusing the Deep Dig with production — it is idea development across every brand touchpoint

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Review all the ideas so far and look for patterns' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Most advice on campaigns starts by specifying the campaign idea. Sullivan's route runs the other way. Describe it, and name the sentence he repeats twice as its summary.
qa_items.answer: After the wall is covered and the herd thinned by a cold edit, you stand back and look for overlaps between the surviving ideas — visual, verbal, or by medium — reposition similar ones into clusters and keep looking. His repeated summary is: patterns are campaigns trying to come to life. Once a cluster of even two ideas that plainly belong together appears, the gears reverse: the pair is treated as the main idea and further ideas are pulled out of it. The campaign is treated as latent in the work already made rather than as something specified in advance — his image is a handful of pearls on a table with the thread still to be found.
qa_items.support: Stated procedure, with the summary line printed twice in the chapter. He concedes the divergent phase may fail, so a pattern found this way is not guaranteed to be a campaign.
confounders: assuming clustering by resemblance is the same as clustering by shared mechanism; the source does not distinguish them
placing this step before the cold edit rather than after it
reading a found pattern as a platform — his platform criteria are separate and stronger

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', sections 'Try being half-rational, half-random' and 'Don't just start writing headlines willy-nilly' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: You have a spirits brand whose product description mentions a Kentucky creek, charred oak barrels and nine years of ageing. Apply Sullivan's two named session devices and say what metric he actually cares about.
qa_items.answer: First the collider. Build a BRAND list straight from the description — hand-bottled, smooth, expensive, warming, nine years, strong — and a second list from one theme the product implies, say KENTUCKY, filled with every word and idiom the theme brings up: pure water, moonshine, creek, jug, hillbillies, old-fashioned, white lightning. Then let the eye jump between the lists pairing items, half by systematic permutation and half by accident. Crossing "expensive" with the feud imagery gave him "What the Hatfields would serve the Rockefellers." Second, the door-rattling method: work one attribute at a time — age, then what else happens in nine years, then place, then how the drink is taken — grouping output under each heading before moving on. The metric he states is not line count: it is how many different doors you went through, how many different ways you looked at the same problem.
qa_items.support: Both devices and the worked lists are the source's own, from his files. He notes the printed lines conceal about five scratched-out starts each, and says the technique becomes automatic with practice — scaffolding rather than a permanent method.
confounders: measuring the session by how many headlines were produced, which is the metric he explicitly displaces
assuming the second list must be distant from the product; in this device it is drawn from the product's own associations
treating the associations as portable — his Kentucky list runs on American regional stereotypes and folklore

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'Rewiring Your Brain', section 'Monahan's Intergalactic Thinking' (spine 23)
qa_items.question: Intergalactic Thinking and the word collider both work by colliding two lists. What single setting differs between them, and what does Monahan say about how the second domain should be chosen?
qa_items.answer: The distance of the second list. The collider draws it from the product's own associations; the intergalactic technique deliberately chooses a domain as far from the problem as possible. Monahan's stated selection criteria for that domain are three: fairly familiar to you, very unrelated to your line of work, and containing many data points — he names the farm, the ocean and the circus as good, and rejects backgammon, taxidermy and Russian musical instruments not because they are related but because they are thin. The underlying rule Sullivan quotes is that the promising connective question is not "what if we combine A and B" but "what if we combine A and Z". Sullivan's own near-domain variant runs the same machinery in reverse to produce a short telegraphic name for a campaign first, and then writes the campaign from the name.
qa_items.support: Quoted at length from Monahan's book with permission and endorsed. Sullivan's own live demonstration produces material he immediately says does not work; the one fully worked case reached a campaign that, he records in a footnote, the client killed within two minutes.
confounders: assuming any unrelated subject will serve; thinness of the domain is Monahan's stated disqualifier
conflating the two variants, which differ precisely in the distance setting
treating the naming variant as a hashtag tactic; the claim is about producing the idea, not about distribution

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'Rewiring Your Brain', section 'Tom Monahan's wonderful exercise: Ask a better question' (spine 23)
qa_items.question: Monahan's ladder has a precise terminal condition. State the three rungs by what kind of answer each admits, and say what Sullivan instructs the first question and first answer to be.
qa_items.answer: Rung one is a basic question relevant to the problem for which there is a correct answer, so no creativity is involved. Rung two is derived from the previous answer and admits only an educated guess, so some creativity is involved. Rung three is derived again and has no correct answer that can be known or even guessed, so creativity is required — and that is the better question. Sullivan instructs that the first question always be "why should people buy this brand?" and the first answer be the key message you were given, so the ladder starts inside the brief and climbs out of it. He notes the search is not linear: many threads dead-end, and the move is to back up, rephrase the last question and continue. He calls it, in his own coinage, the Toddler Socratic Method.
qa_items.support: Lifted whole from Monahan's book with permission; the teaching frame and the worked cases are Sullivan's. Monahan's own stated mechanism is that ordinary questions let the answerer stay inside the known, because an answer is by definition something that already exists.
confounders: treating the three rungs as a fixed length; Sullivan says finding the right question can take thirty or forty rounds
starting from a creative ambition rather than from the brief's key message
assuming any unanswerable question qualifies; it must be derived from the previous answer and stay on the problem

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'Rewiring Your Brain', section 'Try rewriting the brief's key message as a key question' (spine 23)
qa_items.question: Sullivan proposes replacing the key message on a brief with a key question. What is his argument, and what does he say the word "message" quietly presupposes?
qa_items.answer: His argument is about potential energy. A key message is fully cooked and asks nothing of the maker; a question is unfinished, which is what gives it spring — it is a riddle that produces an itch a creative person will want to scratch with ideas. He also names the presupposition: the word "messaging" presupposes that the solution to the client's business problem is a message, which it may not be, and creatives compound this by reading the line item on the brief as the solution rather than as an input. He reports that a famous milk campaign's brief took exactly this form — not "milk builds strong bones" but "what happens if there's no milk?" — and describes the moment the right question is handed over as the point where "why" turns into "what if".
qa_items.support: Stated position, with one reported case. This is a proposal about how briefs should be written, argued from the psychology of the maker rather than from any evidence about outcomes.
confounders: treating this as a claim that briefs should be vaguer; a key question is required to come out of the heart of the issue and be as clear and naked as possible
assuming the question replaces strategy; it replaces the message line item
reading it as advice for a junior's first week — he places problem-finding after the brief has been answered

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 8 'Rewiring Your Brain', section 'Why solve problems when finding problems is way cooler?' (spine 23)
qa_items.question: Sullivan distinguishes problem-solving from problem-finding and then concedes something that largely defeats his own recommendation. What is the distinction, and what is the concession?
qa_items.answer: Problem-solving answers the question the brief asked, and he characterises most agency work as maintenance of that kind — inventory changes, expired music licences, a client changing their mind. Problem-finding challenges the question: the team steps back, questions its own assumptions, and studies the client's customers, stores, data and systems for bottlenecks, redundancies and unmet needs, and once it finds a problem the client did not know it had, the work becomes problem-solving again. He states why no brief will ever ask for it: you cannot place an order for something that does not exist yet. The concession is structural — agencies, like most businesses, hire only enough staff to service current business, so creatives rarely have the hours to think deeply about a client's bigger issues, and it is problem-solving around the clock. His practical placement is therefore: do it after delivering what the brief asked for.
qa_items.support: Stated claim and stated concession, both his. His assertion that most agency leaders' biggest successes did not come from a brief is offered as something they would admit if honest — a claim about a counterfactual with nothing supporting it.
confounders: treating problem-finding as a synonym for creative ambition; it is a specific activity aimed at the client's business rather than at the communication
missing the concession, which is what turns this from advice into an argument about how agencies are staffed
assuming a junior should do it instead of the brief rather than after it

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Allow your partner to come up with terrible ideas. Don't play devil's advocate.' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan permits devil's advocacy in one place and forbids it in another, and he names one specific behaviour that must never happen. What is the split, what is the behaviour, and what does it actually cost?
qa_items.answer: Devil's advocacy is legitimate when road-testing an idea before taking it to a client, and has no place in the early creative process, where the substitute is the angel's advocate: ask what is good about the idea and what you like about it. The forbidden behaviour is smirking or rolling your eyes at a bad idea — never, even when the idea is genuinely bad; the prescribed reply is a neutral "Hmmm, that's interesting" and moving on. The cost is not to the dismissed idea but to future supply: he reports getting stuck on a half-idea his partner then carried over the line, so an idea one person cannot advance may be advanceable by the other. Visible contempt stops the partner offering half-ideas at all.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with his own reported experience. Practice wisdom from his teams; no study of team behaviour is cited. He separately warns against the opposite excess — saying aloud every thought that arrives.
confounders: reading it as a general ban on criticism; the pre-client road test is explicitly exempted
locating the cost in the rejected idea rather than in the partner's future contributions
confusing it with his instruction not to talk about work in the hallway, which concerns broadcasting, not the partner

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Work. Don't talk. Work.' and 'Be objective' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan tells makers not to talk about work in progress but prescribes one exception. Give the two costs he names and the exact terms of the exception.
qa_items.answer: The first cost is to the maker: talking converts energy that could go into being creative into talking about being creative. The second is to the idea's reception — an idea described is never as exciting as the idea itself, so early description spends the listener's enthusiasm at the worst exchange rate. The exception is late and narrowly framed: once ideas are on paper and polished to your satisfaction, walk them round the hallways before the creative director sees them, explicitly not seeking consensus but running a disaster check, and treat a problem raised independently by two people as probably real. The reason it comes after polish is the second cost — an unfinished idea has to be reconstructed in the listener's head from an account that does not carry what makes it work.
qa_items.support: Stated rule and stated exception. The two-people-agree heuristic is offered as "chances are it's real", a probability judgement rather than a rule.
confounders: reading the rule as applying to the writing partner, which would contradict his account of teamwork
treating the hallway round as seeking approval; he says explicitly it is not a search for consensus
running the disaster check before the work is polished, which is what the second cost argues against

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 'Creative Mind Versus Monkey Mind', section 'What to do when you're stuck' (spine 37)
qa_items.question: A team has half a notebook of unfinished approaches, none of which is working, and two days left. Which of Sullivan's repair moves fits this specific situation, and what is his stated reason?
qa_items.answer: Blow it all up and start on a fresh pad. His stated reason is that the old half-ideas may be serving only to muddy the waters, and that the maker may be subconsciously holding on to some approach they want to work but which never will. He gives a second move for a different symptom — if you are stuck mid-problem, change something: solve the same problem as if it were a different medium, or as if the budget were nearly nothing, then come back. And a third for a different symptom again: an idea that has been forced onto paper after hours of wrestling bears the dents of the fight and lacks the elegance of one that arrived, so abandon it rather than repair it. Note the tension he leaves unresolved — his other advice is to stay in the room and suffer through it, and he gives no rule for choosing between persisting and changing.
qa_items.support: Stated remedies, each attached by the source to a different symptom. The unresolved tension between persisting and changing is an extractor observation.
confounders: applying 'start from where you are', which is his move for a project too large to begin, not for a notebook of failed approaches
trying to rescue the best of the half-ideas, which is the behaviour the muddy-waters argument warns against
reading 'change something' as changing the strategy; his examples change the medium or the budget, leaving the problem fixed

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 15 'Creative Mind Versus Monkey Mind', section 'What to do when you're stuck' — 'Start from where you are' (spine 37)
qa_items.question: Sullivan borrows Anne Lamott's "start from where you are" for large projects. What is the mechanism he claims for it, and what does he offer as his own demonstration?
qa_items.answer: The mechanism is that you cannot see the other doors until you go through the first one — he attributes the phenomenon, calling it creative adjacencies, to Steven Johnson. Faced with a project too large to begin, you reach into the pile and take the piece that interests you most, regardless of where it belongs in the whole, because interest is what will get you started; and as soon as one idea exists on that piece, doors open on either side of it that were invisible before. His demonstration is the book itself: he began writing at what became its sixth chapter, on simplicity, because that was the part he most wanted to write, and left the opening chapters until later.
qa_items.support: Borrowed from a novelist's writing advice and endorsed; the demonstration is his own writing of this book, not an advertising project.
confounders: reading it as advice to do the easy part first; the criterion is interest, not ease
assuming the running order must then be preserved; the point is that sequence can be resolved afterwards
confusing it with his instruction to just start, which addresses resistance rather than scale

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Write hot. Edit cold.'; repeated in Ch. 5 'Flow and readability' (spines 15, 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan repeats "write hot, edit cold" in two chapters. What is the mechanism he gives for the hot half, and what does he actually prescribe for the cold half?
qa_items.answer: The mechanism for the hot half is mechanical and specific: if you try to edit too much in your head, your pen will stop moving. So generate without editing and let the words come out any way they want. The cold half is not merely "edit later" — he prescribes a cooling interval first, so the second pass is done with distance, and then a three-way sort: keep only the A-plus work, put the A-minus and B-plus in a separate pile to revisit, and either kill or shelve everything below. His strong form is that all first drafts are crap and all good copywriting is rewriting. What he does not supply is any criterion for what counts as A-plus; the grading is left entirely to the maker.
qa_items.support: Stated rule, printed in both the concepting and copywriting chapters. The grading scale is his own shorthand with no defined criteria.
confounders: treating it as a preference for speed rather than as a claim about what simultaneous judgement does to production
omitting the cooling interval, which is what he says makes the cold pass cold
assuming everything below the top tier is discarded; two of the three tiers are retained

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'The clever-headline, straight-visual rule' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: A poster shows a cracked windscreen; the headline reads "Your windscreen is cracked." A reviewer calls it clear and on-brief. What does Sullivan call this, and where does he locate the fault?
qa_items.answer: A see-say advertisement — the rookie error of showing the headline. He describes the symptom as every element trying too hard and either repeating or tripping over one another, and states the rule in both directions: never show what you are saying or say what you are showing. The fault is not in either element individually but in the relation: he treats the distance between what is said and what is shown as the variable that sets the size of the shift in the reader's head, so a visual that closes that distance to zero leaves the reader nothing to do and wastes the second element. His requirement is that the visual amplify the headline or reinterpret it. He grants that a supporting element may be deliberately straight — his own preferred pattern is one clever element and one straight one — but the straight element must still add something, and he supplies no test for where support becomes restatement.
qa_items.support: Stated failure with the source's own name for it, alongside his clever/straight rule. His positive example — a motorcycle advertisement whose visual alone is tame and whose headline alone is almost meaningless — is a reproduced image this extraction could not inspect.
confounders: judging it acceptable because it is clear and on-brief, which is the reviewer position the diagnosis is written against
confusing the see-say with the clever-headline/straight-visual rule, which permits a plain visual that adds
locating the fault in the headline alone rather than in the relation between the two elements

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Get the visual clichés out of your system right away'; and Ch. 3 'Look at the competitors' advertising' (spines 15, 13)
qa_items.question: Sullivan says visual clichés are not general but category-specific. What working procedure does that imply, and what stops this from being a blanket ban on familiar imagery?
qa_items.answer: It implies research rather than taste: go and learn which images your category is currently using — visit the competitors' sites, watch their videos, study what they post — and then do not use those. His examples are category-bound: grandfathers flying kites with grandchildren in insurance, earnest bespectacled people with a screen reflected in their glasses in technology. The mechanism is availability, the same argument he makes about early ideas: a cliché is what the whole category already reaches for, so using it puts the brand inside the category's existing visual field rather than distinguishing it from it. What stops it being a blanket ban is his own endorsement of borrowed image equity: an established image given a spin and used in a new and unexpected way that relates to the product advantage is the metaphor he recommends. The prohibition is on unmodified reuse, not on familiar imagery.
qa_items.support: Stated procedure and stated examples. Which images count as tired is judged by inspection and is time- and market-bound; his examples are American category conventions of his period.
confounders: treating the cliché list as universal rather than as something to be assembled per category
reading it as a prohibition on recognisable imagery, which his metaphor advice contradicts
assuming novelty alone resolves it — his metaphor condition requires the new use to relate to the product advantage

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Think it through before you settle for the ol' exaggeration thing' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan puts exaggeration last on his list of concepting techniques. Is he prohibiting it? State his actual position and the one condition he attaches.
qa_items.answer: No. He says explicitly that great ideas do use exaggeration and that it is not off-limits; his objection is frequency and thoughtlessness.
