He places it last because it is used so commonly that it is the first technique juniors apply, and its first hundred outputs are predictable inversions of the benefit — his caricature is a water-heater brainstorm producing ice cubes from the tap, repeated because the water is cold. The requirement is awareness: just be aware when you are using it. The condition, taken from Pete Barry, is that an exaggeration must be based on a truth; without one, what remains is a silly contrivance. He names the degenerate form, quoting Teressa Iezzi: the advertisement in which someone is so distracted by the product that they fail to notice some outrageous event.
qa_items.support: Stated position with his own explicit qualification. The 'based on a truth' condition is quoted from another author, and no test is given for when an exaggeration is sufficiently grounded.
confounders: reporting it as a prohibition, which he takes care to deny in the same paragraph
assuming the objection is that exaggeration is untruthful; the objection is that it is reached for before thinking
confusing the technique with hyperbole in copy — he is discussing a concepting lens applied to the message

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'Authority gets replaced with fake' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: A pack promises "Made with real cheese" and a truck advertisement carries an asterisked monthly payment. Sullivan says both work against themselves. What is the shared inference, and what does he say created the audience that makes it?
qa_items.answer: The shared inference is that the reassurance is evidence against the claim it defends: if the product were authentically cheese, it would not need to say so — his reductio is that nobody sells a phone by saying it is made with real phone — and an asterisk announces that a briefcase of qualifications is propping the number up, so the line can legitimately be read as saying "we're lying". Each is a defensive move that would be unnecessary if the claim were secure, so a reader who has learned the pattern treats the defence as a symptom. He grounds the learned pattern historically: the collapse of institutional authority, which he dates from a presidential resignation and traces through a chain of fallen public figures, produced what he calls a nation of eye-rollers and sceptics who no longer accept "because we said so". He places the same family: the exclamation point, the invented customer name, the stock photograph.
qa_items.support: Stated claim. The causal history is a sweeping cultural narrative offered without evidence and is specific to the United States; the asterisk reading is a rhetorical move rather than a claim about how most readers process fine print.
confounders: reading the objection as legal or ethical rather than as a claim about inference
assuming the remedy is to remove the qualifier, when his stated remedies are to have a claim that does not need one, or to embrace the weakness directly
treating the historical account as established; it is asserted

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'Embracing the suck' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: A client's product has an obvious, well-known weakness, and the brief asks you to work around it. What does Sullivan recommend instead, and what does he say about client-mandated elements the team wants to bury?
qa_items.answer: Take the weakness and use it to accentuate the product's main strength — what he calls embracing the suck. His modern example is a cough syrup whose campaign compared its own taste to public restroom puddle water and signed off "It tastes awful. It works." He treats admitting weakness as a way of disarming distrust, alongside admitting the commercial has an agenda at all, and reports a pizza brand opening a campaign by replaying focus-group video of its own customers saying the product was bad before promising to fix it. He extends the same move to a different case: when what sucks is not the product but a client mandate — a weak tagline, a jingle, a spokesperson — tackle it directly rather than doing something you think is cool and burying the mandated element in a corner or in the last ten seconds, because, quoting Jason Elm, good ideas often spill out of the very thing your instincts tell you to avoid.
qa_items.support: Stated remedy with two named campaigns. The pizza case is reported with a share-price comparison across fourteen years, which is not a controlled attribution and the source does not present it as one.
confounders: reading it as self-deprecation for its own sake; the weakness has to be turned to accentuate a strength
applying it only to product faults and missing the client-mandate case, which is where it is most immediately usable
treating the share-price figure as evidence that the campaign caused the change

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'To thine own brand, be true' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: You have written: "Discover how the flavours of ancient Italy tantalise your tongue." What portable test does Sullivan give for copy like this, and what does the test actually detect?
qa_items.answer: The bar-stool test: imagine sitting with a friend in a bar who asks why she should go there, and try to say your line to her face with a straight expression. His prediction for exactly this line is that she blinks and says "Duuude." The test works by changing the audience from an imagined public to a specific person who can react, because the register is adopted for an audience the writer cannot see, and a visible listener makes its emptiness audible. What it detects is a register failure — what he calls, quoting Mike Troiano, Official Marketing Bullshit mode — and only that. It says nothing about whether the claim is true or the strategy right. His instruction behind it: stop "writing ads"; do not write, talk — talk to the page, as if to someone capable of detecting nonsense.
qa_items.support: Stated test with the source's own worked line. The conversational register he prescribes is itself a convention of a particular market and period, not a neutral default.
confounders: reading the test as a check on truthfulness or strategy, which it does not perform
assuming the remedy is shorter copy; the remedy is a different register
confusing it with reading aloud, which he prescribes separately and which detects cadence rather than register

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Don't have a pre-ramble' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: A junior's body copy opens by explaining what the headline meant. Sullivan's diagnosis points somewhere other than the copy. Where, and what does he prescribe instead?
qa_items.answer: At the headline. Reporting Thomas Kemeny's observation that body copy is too often treated as an explanation of the headline, he converts it into a test of the headline: if your headline needs to be explained, it is not working. That inverts the usual direction of blame — the explanatory copy is a symptom whose cause sits upstream, so editing the copy cannot fix it. He names the parallel junior error of opening by restating what the headline already said. The prescription is journalistic: get to the point and put the most interesting, surprising or persuasive point in the first line, following the inverted pyramid, and do not bury the lead.
qa_items.support: Reported from Kemeny and endorsed; the inverted-pyramid remedy is Sullivan's. A rule of thumb applied to one failure pattern — he does not address copy that legitimately develops a headline rather than explaining it.
confounders: rewriting the opening paragraph, which treats the symptom
assuming all body copy following a headline is a pre-ramble; the fault is explanation or repetition specifically
confusing this with his instruction to keep the set-up short when presenting to a client, where he uses the same word

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Never, ever, not even once, or even just a little bit, ever use exclamation points anywhere, ever' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan bans the exclamation point. His objection is not that it is inelegant. What is the claim, and how does he demonstrate it?
qa_items.answer: The claim is about a mismatch between intention and reception: the writer intends it to sound excited, and the reader receives a brand that sounds desperate. He calls it the used-car salesperson of advertising sentences, the jazz hands of punctuation, and kryptonite to authenticity — which ties it to his wider argument that a signal of enthusiasm supplied by the sender rather than earned by the content is read as a claim the content could not support. He demonstrates by making the point emphatically in the preceding sentence without using one, and then observing that he did.
qa_items.support: Stated position. No evidence is offered that readers make this inference; the claim rests on the author's ear and is delivered in a joke, which makes the intended absoluteness hard to read — though the surrounding argument suggests he means it.
confounders: treating it as a style preference rather than as a claim about how the mark is received
assuming it applies only to headlines; he states it for advertising copy generally
missing the link to his reassurance-signal family, which is what makes it more than a peeve

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Never use fake names in a headline' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan objects to both invented customer names and product model numbers in headlines, but for different reasons. Give both mechanisms, and say which of the two objections he qualifies.
qa_items.answer: The fake name fails by detection: readers recognise the fabrication immediately, and an irritating kind of fabrication — his comparison is the stock relatives supplied inside shop-bought picture frames — and the judgement transfers to the advertiser. The model number fails by processing: a string like "TX-17" is not read as language, so it forces the reader to change gear mid-sentence and functions as a speed bump; and he names why makers are blind to it, which is that they work on the account and it feels familiar to them. He qualifies the first, not the second. There are times when using a person's name is the only way the concept will work, and in the hands of a seasoned team it can be done beautifully — it comes down, in his words, to how gracefully and believably you pull it off.
qa_items.support: Stated claims. The speed-bump account is asserted from his own reading experience with no reading measurement cited. His exception for names is unusually candid and is not a rule anyone can apply in advance.
confounders: treating both as the same objection to artificiality
reporting the name prohibition as absolute, which he explicitly relaxes
assuming the model-number objection is about brand consistency rather than about reading

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Get puns out of your system right away' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan's line on puns is unusually flat. State it, and then state honestly what kind of claim it is.
qa_items.answer: He says puns have no persuasive value, calls them the lowest thing on the joke food chain, and adds that any headline that rhymes is beyond saving. His instruction is not to avoid thinking of them but to clear them early: it is fine to write them down, provided they then go where they belong. What kind of claim it is: a strong professional prohibition stated in the grammar of a finding. He gives no mechanism and cites nothing, and it is one of the clearest places in the book where a taste position is delivered as fact. There is also an unstated tension — some of the work he admires uses wordplay close to punning, so the boundary he is actually drawing seems to be between wordplay that carries the argument and wordplay that replaces it, but he does not say so.
qa_items.support: Stated prohibition, with no mechanism and no evidence. The observation about the unstated boundary is an extractor observation, not a claim he makes.
confounders: reporting it as an established finding about persuasion rather than as this practitioner's position
concluding that wordplay in general is prohibited, which his own admired examples contradict
assuming he forbids writing them; he explicitly permits writing them down and then discarding them

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Viral, Naughty, and Rong', section 'Making ideas that blow up. Or, advertising as vandalism' (spine 25)
qa_items.question: A piece of work is on strategy, correctly targeted and contains no identifiable fault. Sullivan has a name for it anyway. What is it, what is the underlying claim, and what is the risk in using this diagnosis?
qa_items.answer: He calls it an obedient idea — work that dutifully ticks all the boxes about what an advertisement should be and then just lies there, asking to be looked at. The underlying claim is that brief-conformance is necessary and not sufficient: conformance checks are negative, they can rule work out but not in, and nothing in a brief requires the work to be interesting. It is the diagnostic counterpart of his argument that a campaign which is merely a transcription of the brief contains no creative leap. The risk is that "obedient" is his own coinage identified entirely by the reviewer's taste — no check is offered that distinguishes an inert idea from one the reviewer simply dislikes — and it appears in a chapter urging provocation, so it can easily become licence to reject correct work. His own limit is stated elsewhere: the replacement must still be relevant.
qa_items.support: Stated claim, from his experience as a creative director and a teacher. The caution about reviewer taste is an extractor observation about a gap he does not close.
confounders: assuming that passing every brief requirement settles the question, which is the position the diagnosis is written against
reading it as permission to reject any work that is not provocative, without his relevance constraint
confusing it with work that fails one of his named surface faults; the obedient idea has none of them

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', sections 'Insist on a relevant strategy' and 'Try to make your message incontestable' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Sullivan names the two things people fire back at an advertisement and attaches a different repair to each. Give both pairs, and state what he says to do if the second repair is unavailable.
qa_items.answer: "Yeah, riiiight" is a credibility failure, repaired by a message that is truthful, incontestable or measurably provable — for which he offers Pete Barry's stress test: imagine the loud man at the bar arguing back and build the comeback that sinks his boat. "So what?" is a relevance failure, repaired only by having something that matters to somebody: something customers want, or a problem they have. Execution repairs neither, which is why both checks sit upstream of the creative work. If the second repair is unavailable — if there is nothing relevant to say — his instruction is to tell the client to put their money away, because no matter how well it is executed an unimportant message has no receiver. He does concede a limit on the first: the incontestability advice does not apply to products that are all image or have no real difference worth hanging a hat on, and he names paper cups.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with a stated concession. The two-rebuttal scheme is a memorable heuristic, not a taxonomy; nothing establishes that these are the only two ways a message fails.
confounders: matching the repairs to the wrong rebuttals — relevance does not fix disbelief and proof does not fix indifference
assuming better execution can rescue either, which is what he explicitly denies
missing the concession about parity products, which is where the incontestability advice stops applying

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'Whenever you can, go for an absolute' (spine 13)
qa_items.question: Sullivan prefers an "-est" to an "-er". What is the argument, and what does he say happens when the absolute is not available?
qa_items.answer: His argument is a claim about what is retained: quietest, fastest and cleanest are what people are going to remember, and all the claims in the middle ground — quieter, faster, cleaner — are grey and forgettable. Best is better than good, and where the product genuinely is the best, set up camp there. What happens when it is not available is the failure he describes rather than a remedy he offers: the client or agency ends up trying to leverage some rice-paper-thin difference nobody cares about, often because legal will not permit anything stronger. His instruction is to try your hardest not to settle for an "-er", and his related advice where a category's good adjectives are already taken is to try a polar opposite or a flanking move rather than the second best, because second best will not be different enough.
qa_items.support: Stated preference with an asserted claim about memory and no evidence. His flanking example — a condiment brand claiming "slowest" in a category competing to be the most tomato-ish, with sales reported up and staying up — is a single case relayed without a source.
confounders: reading it as advice to overclaim; he requires the absolute to be true, and treats the parity case separately
assuming the answer to an unavailable absolute is a comparative, which is what he argues against
confusing the flanking move with de-positioning a competitor, which he discusses separately

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 3 'Tell the Truth and Run', section 'Listen to customers talk'; and Ch. 16 'Creative testing: be afraid. Be very afraid.' (spines 13, 39)
qa_items.question: Sullivan is hostile to focus groups and enthusiastic about listening to customers. These sound contradictory. What line is he actually drawing, and what is the strongest objection to his position that he does not raise?
qa_items.answer: The line is between research used to generate ideas and research used to judge them. Listening — in reviews, forums, chat rooms, bars, malls, on social platforms, unprompted and unpaid — he calls the best way to learn what customers think and something it has become too easy not to do; it belongs at the beginning, to find out what to say. Asking recruited, paid participants to critique finished creative he rejects, and his single stated rule is that when research is used to determine how to say it, great ideas suffer. He also exempts product, location, flavour, packaging and name testing, which he says pays off. The objection he does not raise is that he is not disinterested: he is a member of the profession whose work such testing evaluates, and nowhere in either passage does he acknowledge the interest. A second unraised tension is that his own founding argument rests on survey research about dislike and believability.
qa_items.support: Stated position across two chapters, with his own stated exemptions. The interest objection and the tension with his founding argument are extractor observations about gaps he leaves open.
confounders: reporting him as anti-research, which his enthusiasm for listening and his product-testing exemption both contradict
treating his objections as findings; he offers them as arguments for a client conversation and calls the process capricious rather than disproven
assuming he proposes a replacement check on work before it runs — he prescribes only an internal hallway disaster check

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', section 'Creative testing: be afraid. Be very afraid.' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: Sullivan lists specific mechanisms by which he says creative testing distorts what it measures. Give four of them, and name the common structure he claims underlies all of them.
qa_items.answer: Any four of: testing by its nature looks for what is wrong rather than what is right, and will find something; it assumes an intellectual reaction where the real reaction is visceral and instantaneous; it asks people what they will like before they have seen it in the world; it rewards work that is happy, vague and fuzzy because that does not challenge the viewer; it rewards the derivative, because a familiar feel scores higher than the unique, strange or new; it cannot convey tone, because a dozen pictures pasted to a board are not footage, voice-over and music; and it recruits ordinary people as advertising experts, after which they feel obliged to prove it. The common structure he claims is a reversal of direction: quoting Bernbach that we are so busy measuring public opinion we forget we can mould it, he says that in the testing room the dynamic of a commercial reaching viewers is replaced by viewers telling the commercial what to say. He names a second misuse separately — permission research, showing concepts and asking whether people like them, whose consensus and compromise he says grind ideas into vanilla or nonsense.
qa_items.support: Stated arguments, offered by the source explicitly as ammunition for a client conversation rather than as established findings. No evidence is offered for any of the listed mechanisms, and the conceptual-art illustration he uses is not a study of advertising testing.
confounders: reporting these as demonstrated effects rather than as arguments
confusing permission research with pre-testing; he treats them as two different misuses
missing his own concession that clients test everything else and that much of that testing pays off

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Remember, something has to dominate the page' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan says every design needs a boss. Roy Grace's version, which he quotes, makes the requirement about something other than the layout. What?
qa_items.answer: About an agreement between the makers. Grace's formulation is that there has to be a point on every page where the art director and the writer want you to start — whether the centre, the top right corner or the left — and there has to be an understanding, an agreement, and a logical reason for where you want people to look first. So the requirement is a decision taken and shared, not a property discovered afterwards. Sullivan's own version is that whether it is a big headline, a large visual or a single word floating in white space, somebody has to be the boss, and that there must be an overall visual hierarchy — an implied order of the relative importance of the elements. He restates the requirement inside the letter-or-postcard decision, which is what makes it a precondition rather than one recommendation among others.
qa_items.support: Stated requirement, with the operational version quoted from an art director in a case-history collection. No method for establishing dominance is given beyond scale and isolation.
confounders: treating it as a rule about which element should dominate; the requirement is that one be designated, not which
assuming the dominant element must be the visual
confusing it with balance or composition; the claim is about reading order

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Do I want to write a letter or send a postcard?' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Aitchison's letter-or-postcard fork, as Sullivan reports it, is decided by one variable and carries one claim that has nothing to do with reading. Give both.
qa_items.answer: The variable is message complexity: a postcard is visually led, one visual and sometimes a little copy, and suits one thought; a letter is predominantly copy-driven and suits a more complex message. The claim that has nothing to do with reading is about long copy specifically — the sheer weight of the body copy adds a sense of gravitas to the product regardless of whether the reader takes in a word of it. He frames the decision as a position on a sliding scale from all-visual to all-verbal, taken early rather than arrived at, and repeats that something must dominate either way. Note that the gravitas claim sits awkwardly against his own insistence elsewhere that anything not carrying meaning should be removed; he does not reconcile them.
qa_items.support: Framework quoted from Jim Aitchison and endorsed, illustrated with a matched pair for one brand. The gravitas-without-reading claim is offered with no evidence.
confounders: treating the choice as an outcome of execution rather than as a fork taken early
assuming Sullivan prefers the postcard; he reproduces and praises a 630-word advertisement in the same chapter
reading the gravitas claim as being about credibility of content rather than about the visible mass of type

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Can the solution be entirely visual?' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: A team decides to run a visually led execution. Sullivan states the consequence rather than the advantage. What does the decision oblige them to do, and what is the stated failure if they do not?
qa_items.answer: Relying on the image means the image assumes added responsibilities: it has to carry the idea, and the main selling idea cannot be buried down in the copy — it must be baked right into the visual. The stated failure is terminal rather than partial: if readers do not get what you are trying to say from the visual, they will not get it, and they will move on. His mechanism is that visuals work fast, so the visual is where a reader giving the piece one pass will take meaning from. He allows the other direction — a good visual or headline may earn a reader who then goes on to read the copy — and he adds a second reason with a stated scope: as brands are marketed globally, visual solutions matter more because they translate better than words.
qa_items.support: Stated claim, alongside a quoted provocation from another agency that people do not read advertisements — a position Sullivan does not hold in its strong form, since he praises long copy in the same chapter. The translation claim is asserted with no evidence.
confounders: reading it as a general claim that visuals beat words, which his own long-copy examples contradict
assuming the copy can still carry the selling idea as a backstop; that is precisely what he forbids
treating the translation argument as settled — it would not survive contact with the culturally specific imagery he relies on elsewhere

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Tension and release in an idea' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan states a scaling claim about the relationship between headline and visual. State it, and then state the two bounds that stop it recommending maximum distance.
qa_items.answer: The claim, reporting Pete Barry, is that the greater the polarity between headline and visual, the bigger the shift in the reader's head — the idea is revealed by the visual and the unexpectedness is what creates the tension between the two elements. The lower bound is his own see-say failure: polarity at zero wastes the second element and leaves the reader nothing to resolve. The upper bound is his fuse argument: the distance the reader travels is exactly what lengthens the fuse, so polarity beyond the medium's dwell time means the idea does not resolve at all. He also notes the relation is reversible — tension in a headline can be released by the visual, or a dominant visual can be reframed by the headline that follows it.
qa_items.support: Reported from Pete Barry and endorsed. "Polarity" is never defined or measured, so the scaling claim is directional and cannot be applied quantitatively; the two bounds come from elsewhere in the same book and the source does not connect them himself.
confounders: applying the claim without bounds, which would recommend maximum distance and contradict his own simplicity chapter
assuming the headline always sets up the visual; he states the reverse ordering too
treating polarity as a measurable quantity because the claim is phrased as a scaling relation

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Metaphors must've been invented for advertising' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan recommends borrowed image equity and elsewhere forbids the visual cliché. Both concern familiar images. Where exactly does he put the line, and what makes a metaphor worth using in the first place?
qa_items.answer: The line is re-angling. Picking up a ready-made image or meme and setting it down next to the client's logo will not work; taking an established image, putting some spin on it, and using it in a new and unexpected way that relates to the product advantage is what he recommends. The prohibition is on unmodified reuse, not on familiar imagery. What makes a metaphor worth using is compression: certain images have acquired fixed associations — the trade calls that accumulated meaning the image's equity — so the maker does not have to establish them, and one image can say what would otherwise take twenty words. He adds that this is particularly valuable where the product is intangible, since a metaphor makes it tangible, and that verbal metaphors work equally well.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with worked examples. His appeal to Jung is decorative rather than load-bearing and is uncited; the listed equities are culturally specific — colour associations in particular do not hold across cultures — and he presents them as general.
confounders: concluding that familiar imagery is banned, which the equity argument denies
treating novelty as the criterion; the criterion is a new use that relates to the product advantage
assuming the listed associations are universal

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Coax an interesting visual out of your product or its benefit' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan gives a systematic generator for visual ideas built on transforming the product. Give the operations, and state the constraint without which the exercise becomes something he elsewhere condemns.
qa_items.answer: Rotate it, invert it, scale it up or down, make its image rubber and stretch it, marry it with other visuals and icons, put a door in it, give it legs or a brain, set it on fire, ask what other thing it looks like, what could be substituted for it, and what the perfectly wrong way to use it would be. He derives the exercise from watching a child reinterpret a toy car as a motorcycle, a boat and a rocket purely by which surface faced the ground. The constraint, stated throughout, is that you are trying to coax out of the product a dramatic image with a selling benefit: the transformation must dramatise a customer benefit, not merely alter the object. Without it the exercise becomes the graphic acrobatics he elsewhere condemns, quoting Bernbach, as running the imagination riot rather than harnessing it.
qa_items.support: Stated device with the source's own anecdote as illustration rather than as evidence. The benefit constraint is his and is stated in the same passage.
confounders: treating the transformations as a stylistic device rather than as a search for a benefit-carrying image
dropping the benefit constraint, which is what separates it from arbitrary manipulation
assuming the product must appear in the finished work; the exercise generates the resemblance, not the layout

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Show, don't tell' and 'Can you use the physical environment as your visual?' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan's favourite demonstration advertisement is a phone advertisement on a magazine's back cover. What makes it work on his account, and what does he say a demonstration does to the headline?
qa_items.answer: It works by making the magazine's own front cover the evidence: the line states only that the cover photograph was shot with the advertised product's portrait mode. It is simultaneously his "show, don't tell" case and his "use the environment as the visual" case — the site of the execution is an element of the concept rather than a container for it. What a demonstration does to the headline is remove the need for a clever one: because the piece is not telling us, it did not need one. His deeper mechanism is that a demonstration is evidence rather than a claim, so it does not have to be believed on the advertiser's authority — which connects it to his argument about the collapse of authority. He gives a second case where what is shown is the cause and the reader supplies the consequence: an anti-slip skate advertisement whose mental image of children landing on their backsides he says is stronger than showing them that way.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with two reproduced advertisements this extraction could not inspect; the argument turns on what those images do. He does not separate the force of the demonstration from the force of the placement.
confounders: reading 'show, don't tell' as a preference for imagery over copy generally
missing the second case, where the strongest version withholds the consequence rather than depicting it
assuming every product can be demonstrated; he does not claim that

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Can your brand own something visual?' and 'Avoid style. Focus on substance.' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan endorses Krone's twenty-foot test and then makes a stronger claim of his own. State both, and identify the tension between this and his instruction to study a category's current visual conventions.
qa_items.answer: Krone's requirement is a page style: you should be able to tell whose advertisement it is from a distance of twenty feet — and Sullivan notes what is interesting about it, which is that Krone was talking about print advertisements, not billboards. Sullivan's stronger claim is that the longer he is in the business the more convinced he is that art direction is where the major battle for brand building happens, because once a look is established and a design territory staked out, nobody else can use it without looking like your brand. He pairs it with an instruction to pull the look from the brand's own DNA rather than from current fashion, since riding every passing fad makes work trendy and derivative. The tension: knowing and avoiding a category's current clichés requires close attention to exactly the conventions this instruction says to ignore. He states both and does not reconcile them.
qa_items.support: Krone is quoted from a 1968 trade interview; the stronger claim is Sullivan's own opinion, flagged by his phrasing, with no evidence. The colour-ownership examples are assertions about market perception with nothing measuring them. The tension is an extractor observation.
confounders: treating the twenty-foot test as calibrated; no viewing condition is specified
reading 'avoid style' as indifference to craft rather than as a warning against period fashion
assuming ownership of a colour or a look is established rather than asserted

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 6 'The Virtues of Simplicity', section 'A few words about outdoor. (Few being the key word.)' (spine 19)
qa_items.question: You have a campaign that includes a roadside board and a subway poster. Sullivan treats these differently. What is the differentiating variable, what does he permit for each, and what two tests does he give?
qa_items.answer: The variable is how long the audience dwells with the medium. For roadside boards he reports the received limit of about seven words, notes the logo adds two or three, calls ten pushing it, and says eleven can work with the right execution — helped by having no visual. For subway postings and bus stops he says concepts can risk a slightly longer fuse, because the audience dwells. The two tests: show it to someone for two seconds, take it away and ask what it said; and view the layout from ten feet away as a legibility check. His craft advice follows the same logic — when a campaign includes outdoor, start there and pretend there is no photography budget, because being forced to carry the idea in words boils the thinking down.
qa_items.support: Stated claims and stated tests. The seven-word limit is reported as something that has been said, not as a measurement he made. His own count that he can read fewer than ten percent of the billboards he passes is an informal personal observation, from which he reaches a strong conclusion — that highway outdoor may be best used only for directions.
confounders: applying the same word limit to both placements, which is exactly the distinction he draws
treating seven words as a measured threshold
missing that his section is also a polemic — he quotes Gossage's argument that a billboard is not a medium at all, and notes cities that have banned them

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Or pretend you're writing a letter' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan reports a specific physical trick used to produce a famous car brand's copy voice. Describe it, and say what he claims it prevents.
qa_items.answer: Bob Levenson is reported as writing "Dear Charlie" at the top of the copy and composing as though talking to his best friend, signing off "Yours sincerely, Bob" — then deleting the salutation and the sign-off. What is left is the voice. Sullivan's claim for the device is that it is intimate and that it keeps you from lecturing: the best copy feels more like a conversation than a speech, one person talking to another. It is his prescribed fallback when voice eludes a writer, and it sits alongside his general instruction to write to one person rather than to the masses, since it is one person reading the words.
qa_items.support: Reported second-hand from an art director who was at the agency, via a video interview. Anecdote about one writer's method, endorsed as a technique.
confounders: treating it as a format for the finished copy rather than as a drafting device
assuming it produces informality; what he claims it produces is address to a single person
confusing it with the bar-stool test, which checks a line rather than generating a voice

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Once you lay your sentences down, spackle between the joints' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan gives a test for whether body copy is properly joined. State the test, and name the other test in this source that has the same structure.
qa_items.answer: When it is done well, you should not be able to take out any sentence without disrupting the flow and structure of the entire piece. The other test with the same structure is the removal test for concept elements — take an image, phrase or word out and see whether the idea still works — and in both cases necessity is established by subtraction. He surrounds it with the structural requirement: read body copy as an essay, an opening line that pulls the reader in, a middle that supports it with facts, a closing call to action, with transitions carrying each sentence out of the one before, what Pete Barry calls an invisible thread. Note the difference in direction: applied to concept elements the removal test is a diagnostic for cutting; applied to copy it is a target to write toward, and a piece can pass it by being tightly written around nothing — which the source does not address.
qa_items.support: Stated test in both places. The observation that the same structure serves as a diagnostic in one chapter and as a target in another, and that the target can be met vacuously, is an extractor observation.
confounders: reading the test as an instruction to write short copy; it is about joinery, not length
confusing it with the cut-by-a-third rule, which is a separate finishing operation
assuming a piece that passes must therefore be good

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', sections 'When you're done writing the copy, read it aloud' and 'When you've finished writing something, go back and cut it by a third' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan gives two finishing operations. What does each detect or achieve, and what does he say the cut is actually for?
qa_items.answer: Reading aloud detects weak writing by changing the channel: the stop-and-start cadences and jagged segues that the eye skates over are audible. He learned it presenting copy to five clients and discovering its weakness only while speaking it, and he extends the instruction beyond radio scripts to print, online and anything else. The cut of one third is not about making less to read — quoting Thomas Kemeny, condensing and editing is about making any length of copy more interesting to read. So the purpose is density: removing a third raises the interest per line of what remains. His general principle is that there is hardly anything that cannot be improved by making it shorter.
qa_items.support: Stated operations, one with his own reported experience. One third is a working proportion, not a measured optimum; he offers it alongside a nineteenth-century writer's advice to strike out every other word, which is rhetorical rather than calibrated.
confounders: reading the cut as a brevity rule rather than as a density rule, which is the distinction he draws
limiting the aloud read to spoken formats, which he explicitly widens
treating one third as a specification

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'If you have to have one, make your tagline an anthem' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan's tagline advice is conditional. What is the condition, when in the process does he place the work, and what two tests must the line pass?
qa_items.answer: The condition is in the heading: if you have to have one. His framing throughout is that a tagline may not be needed, and his reduction exercise names it as the first element to remove if it brings no new information. If one is required, he places the work last — save it until the campaign is well started, possibly to the very end — then put the work on the wall and boil its essence down. The two tests: plug it into the actual executions and see whether it finishes the argument, and check that it works all by itself with only the logo to keep it company. He also endorses Adam Tucker's counter-position against wordplay: a good tagline is a summation of your idea, the full stop to your thinking, and the most famous of them contain no puns or trickery at all.
qa_items.support: Stated conditional advice, with the ordering constraint stated explicitly. 'Own some high ground' is offered with a single celebrated example and no account of when altitude becomes vacuity.
confounders: reading this as a recommendation to have a tagline, which the conditional framing and the reduction exercise both resist
writing the tagline first as a campaign anchor, which is the ordering he argues against
assuming cleverness is the aim; the quoted position is explicitly against wordplay

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Brevity Is the Soul of Wit', section 'Don't set out to be funny. Set out to be interesting.' (spine 17)
qa_items.question: Sullivan is a practitioner of comic advertising and writes this instruction against his own default. What is the claim, and what constrains the choice of register?
qa_items.answer: That funny is a subset of interesting: funny is not a language, it is an accent, and it may not even be the right accent for your client. Funny, serious and heartfelt are all irrelevant unless the work is interesting first, so interest is the necessary condition and humour is one available means to it. What constrains the register is the pairing he states elsewhere: the emotional choice is always a combination of what the product is and who is being addressed, and his negative case is that pie-in-the-face humour should not be on the list for a hospital's website. He recommends deciding the mood early — thoughtful, angry, stark — on the ground that the decision itself gives focus, while noting you can change your mind later.
qa_items.support: Stated position. The subset relation is a definition offered as an argument; nothing establishes it beyond his assertion. His own examples throughout the book are overwhelmingly comic, which his stated position does not require.
confounders: reading it as advice against humour, which it is not
treating interest as one option among funny, serious and heartfelt rather than as the condition all three must meet
assuming the register is chosen by the brand alone; he pairs product with audience

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Make sure every piece in the campaign makes sense all by itself' (spine 15)
qa_items.question: Sullivan requires every element of a campaign to be understandable on its own. What fact does he derive this from, and what does it sit awkwardly against elsewhere in the book?
qa_items.answer: From the fact that the maker does not control encounter order. There is no walking a customer through a portfolio saying which piece kicks off the campaign, so any piece may be the first one someone meets, and every single element must therefore be completely understandable and whole in and of itself — his image is that each cell contains the DNA for the whole organism. He pairs it with the requirement that a piece end by leading somewhere, with a call to action, rather than at a dead end. It sits awkwardly against his enthusiasm for platforms, whose later executions gain from rules the earlier ones established, and against his description of the brand story as a long open-ended tale told over time. He states both and reconciles neither.
qa_items.support: Stated requirement with a stated derivation. The tension with his platform material is an extractor observation. 'End with a call to action' is a near-universal trade convention rather than a claim particular to this source, and no evidence is offered for it.
confounders: assuming the pieces must therefore be identical or interchangeable, which contradicts his same-yet-different requirement
reading it as an argument against sequencing a campaign at all
missing the tension with his platform argument, which is the interesting part

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'A Brief History of Why Everybody Hates Advertising', opening argument (spine 9)
qa_items.question: The campaign Sullivan names in his title was, by his own account, measurably successful. Set out both halves of the record he reports, and state the position he takes.
qa_items.answer: On one side: it sold billions of rolls, displaced the previous category leader, ran to 504 executions between 1964 and 1990, and in a 1975 survey its actor was reported as the second-most-recognised face in America. On the other: research he cites found it among the most disliked commercials of its decade and last in believability across years of studies, and the agency that created the character spent years trying and failing to replace him. His position is that effectiveness does not settle the question. Quoting Norman Berry: advertising that does not sell is lousy by any definition, but sales achieved with work that is in bad taste or is intellectual garbage should not be applauded no matter how much it sells, because offensive, dull, abrasive, stupid advertising is bad for the industry and for business generally. His own rebuttal to the sales defence is a question — spitting on the table would also get your attention, so would you?
qa_items.support: Stated position, which he presents as his own — the opinions of one writer, and, in his words, "God knows, they aren't rules". The empirical material is reported second-hand from three trade books and a survey, and the sales attribution to the campaign specifically is not established by anything he cites.
confounders: reading him as denying that the campaign worked, which he concedes at length
reading him as denying that advertising should sell, which the quoted position explicitly affirms
treating this as a finding about effectiveness rather than as an argument about sufficiency

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 1 'A Brief History of Why Everybody Hates Advertising', opening argument (spine 9)
qa_items.question: Sullivan's alternative to the campaign he attacks rests on one claim he never defends. Identify it, and say why it matters to the whole book.
qa_items.answer: The claim is that the creative route arrives at the same commercial destination. He describes a fork in the road and says his path "leads to the same place — enduring brands and market leadership — but it gets there without costing anybody their dignity". That is the load-bearing step: without it his argument reduces to a preference, and with it the whole book becomes a claim about effectiveness as well as about taste. It is also the least supported step in the argument. No comparison of outcomes between the two schools appears anywhere in the book, and the evidence he does supply for his own tradition is a run of celebrated campaigns selected after the fact.
qa_items.support: The claim is stated in his own words in the first chapter. The observation that it is undefended and load-bearing is an extractor observation, not something the source raises.
confounders: assuming he supplies evidence later; the celebrated examples throughout are a selected sample and are never compared against anything
treating the claim as obviously true because the named campaigns are famous, which is the survivorship the observation is about
confusing this with his separate concession that clients have the right to their opinion

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Viral, Naughty, and Rong', section 'Rong means going 180˚ against common sense' (spine 25)
qa_items.question: Sullivan recommends being "perfectly wrong". He then states a degree condition that is the actual substance of the advice. What is it, and what stops this from being novelty for its own sake?
qa_items.answer: The degree condition: designing something wrong is easy, a little wrong is no good, and a lot wrong is even worse — what works is an idea in direct opposition to all prevailing wisdom in the category. The word doing the work is "perfectly". Partial deviation is still read inside the convention and buys nothing; only full inversion is unpredicted. What stops it being novelty for its own sake is his explicit refusal, quoting Bernbach: be provocative, but be sure your provocativeness stems from your product. Standing a man on his head to get attention is wrong; doing it to show that your product keeps things from falling out of his pockets is right. Merely letting the imagination run riot is not being creative — the creative person has harnessed and disciplined it.
qa_items.support: Stated claim, with the degree condition borrowed from Winsor and Bogusky and the constraint quoted from Bernbach. His most detailed example is a food campaign built on filming the product rotting, whose success is reported as being talked about worldwide rather than as a sales figure; he concedes such work is often polarising.
confounders: reading it as licence to be different, which the degree condition and the Bernbach constraint both refuse
assuming a partial deviation is a safer version of the same move; he says it is worse
missing the survivorship — the chapter's examples are award winners, and inversions that failed are not shown

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Viral, Naughty, and Rong', section 'Are you sure they'll even let us do this idea?' (spine 25)
qa_items.question: You have an idea and catch yourself thinking "they'll never let us do this." What does Sullivan say you should conclude, what is his reasoning, and what is the obvious weakness in the heuristic?
qa_items.answer: He says that if you find yourself wondering whether they will even let you do it, you should definitely do it — sit down and work out how to execute it and how you will sell it up the line. His reasoning is that we ask the question because we sense the idea could get a huge reaction, and that merely thinking about it summons the voices of all its enemies; the forces you sense assembling against an idea may be a measure of how much commotion it would cause if you pulled it off. He adds a division of labour: rejecting ideas is the client's job, not yours. The weakness is that the signal cannot distinguish resistance provoked by strength from resistance provoked by badness — an idea can be unbuyable because it is dangerous or because it is bad, and the heuristic reads both the same way. He does not address this.
qa_items.support: Stated heuristic. The weakness is an extractor observation about a gap he leaves open. It sits alongside a related instruction elsewhere: do not leave your best work on the agency floor — go as far as you can and let the client bring you back.
confounders: treating the anticipation of resistance as evidence the idea is good
reading it as advice to present unbuyable work without a plan; he requires you to work out how to sell it
confusing it with his separate instruction never to show a client work you do not want them to buy

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Viral, Naughty, and Rong', section 'What is the press release of your idea?' (spine 25)
qa_items.question: Describe the idea-as-press-release process, the bar Sullivan sets for it, and the reframe he says is the biggest thing in the chapter.
qa_items.answer: Before making the idea, write the press release for it — picture what the story in the newspaper will be after you implement it. Its origin, as he reports it, was an agency principal tired of hearing teams open with what happens in the commercial, on the grounds that the press covers news, and news is what the agency is trying to make for its clients. The bar he sets is explicit: not a story in the trade press, but the evening news. The reframe, which he attributes to strategist Gareth Kay and flags as the big one, is to stop trying to come up with advertising ideas and work instead on coming up with ideas worth advertising. It pairs with his other go/no-go question, from Alex Bogusky: if you cannot imagine anybody writing or talking about the campaign you are about to spend money on, rethink it.
qa_items.support: Stated process, quoted from an internal agency memo and endorsed. The reported outcome for his example is a sales claim without a figure followed by online view counts, which measure attention rather than effect.
confounders: reading the press release as a communications deliverable rather than as a design constraint on the idea
setting the bar at trade coverage, which he explicitly excludes
treating talkability as equivalent to effectiveness, which is not what the chapter establishes even though it reads that way

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Viral, Naughty, and Rong', opening section on paid, owned and earned media (spine 25)
qa_items.question: A client asks for a viral video. What does Sullivan instruct you to say, and what does that imply about how "viral" should be treated in a brief?
qa_items.answer: Politely point out that nobody makes viral videos: it is customers who make things viral, not us. Viral is not a strategy — it is a result of first coming up with a genuinely great idea. The implication is that "go viral" cannot be an objective on a brief, because it names an outcome that is not under the maker's control; what a brief can specify is the idea's quality and its designed shareability. He supports the point with his own counter-example: the creatives behind a print advertisement that became widely shared had no request to go viral on their brief, they simply pushed their thinking to the edge — and his stated lesson is that anything can blow up, including a print advertisement.
qa_items.support: Stated position with one named case. The paid/owned/earned vocabulary he uses around it is a trade taxonomy of the writing period; the substantive claim — that virality is an outcome, not an instruction — does not depend on it.
confounders: accepting 'go viral' as a specifiable objective, which is exactly what he refuses
assuming only video or social formats can spread, which his print example contradicts
confusing the refusal with indifference to earned attention, which he prizes

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 9 'Viral, Naughty, and Rong', sections 'Advice on working way out past the edge' and 'Build a small, cozy fire with the rule books' (spine 25)
qa_items.question: Sullivan ends by telling readers to throw out every rule in his own book, then names one exception. What is it, what is his statement of the consequence, and what does he concede in the same passage that makes the exception hard to apply?
qa_items.answer: The exception is relevance: even out in deep space, you must be relevant, and you are never going to get so far out there that you can dare not to be. His statement of the consequence concedes the aesthetic while refusing the professional claim — no matter how creative you think an idea is, if it has no meaning to your audience you do not have an advertisement; you may have art, but you do not have an idea. What he concedes in the same passage is that at that altitude judgement fails. Quoting Helmut Krone: when something is genuinely new you have no frame of reference, you distrust it, everybody distrusts it, and very often it takes somebody else to tell you it has merit. So the one rule he keeps is also the one he says you may be unable to apply at the moment it matters, and he supplies no test for it.
qa_items.support: Stated exception and stated concession, both his. The observation that the exception is untestable and that the concession undermines its application is an extractor observation.
confounders: reading 'throw out the rules' without the exception, which is the half that makes the chapter coherent
assuming relevance is defined; it is left undefined and could mean anything from meeting a stated need to being culturally legible
treating the Krone quotation as encouragement rather than as a concession about the limits of self-assessment

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', section 'Protecting your work' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: A client returns twenty comments: colour changes, copy rewrites, and one request to remove the single visual the concept depends on. Apply Sullivan's triage rule, and give his stopping condition.
qa_items.answer: Concede the first two classes and defend only the third. His rule is explicit: if they want to mess with your body copy, let them; if they want to change red to green, let them; protect the pyramid — if you get out with the big idea intact, consider yourself a genius. The request to remove the load-bearing element is the one to fight, and he names less experienced clients as particularly good at asking for exactly that. His stopping condition is unusual and worth stating: if one too many changes have hurt the original idea, pull the trigger yourself and kill it. He frames the whole thing as choosing battles — the moral being not to win battles and lose the war, since squabbling over body copy is not where advertising battles are won.
qa_items.support: Stated rule with a stated stopping condition. He frames it inside an explicit concession that advertising is a service industry and that clients have paid for the right to their opinion.
confounders: defending every comment, which the triage rule exists to prevent
conceding the structural change because it is one comment among twenty
missing the stopping condition, which is the part that distinguishes triage from endless accommodation

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', section 'Base your defense on strategy' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: Sullivan says to defend work on strategy rather than on its creativity. What is his reason, and what fact about clients does he offer in support?
qa_items.answer: His reason is that strategy is the ground the client can actually evaluate, and it is something they had a hand in authoring — so keeping the conversation there gives the work its best chance. Quoting Alastair Crompton: think like a creative person, but talk like an accountant. He wants the team able to track, step by step, how they arrived at the campaign, with the relevant product, market and customer facts at hand. The supporting fact is about how clients actually spend their time: marketing directors for consumer-products companies may spend as little as five percent of it on advertising issues, the rest on manufacturing, distribution, financing and product development, and the managerial strengths that got them the job likely had nothing to do with judging advertising. His conclusion is blunt: it is not a client's job to know great work when they see it.
qa_items.support: Stated claim, with the five-percent figure asserted without a source. The advice is quoted from a 1979 copywriting manual and endorsed.
confounders: reading it as advice to abandon creative ambition rather than to change the register of the argument
treating the five-percent figure as sourced; it is asserted
assuming the point is that clients are unsophisticated; his point is that judging advertising was never their job

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', sections 'Do not try to solve the problem in the meeting' and 'Never show a client work you don't want them to buy' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: Give two of Sullivan's presentation rules that constrain what happens inside the meeting itself, and state the reasoning behind each.
qa_items.answer: First: do not try to solve the problem in the meeting. When a client asks for a change you are not required to fix it or refute it on the spot — listen, write the issues down, play them back so both sides know they were heard, and take it away. Easy and obvious fixes are fine; major work in the room is not. Second: never show work you do not want bought, because clients gravitate to what they feel safer with and less scared by, and that is always the second-rate work — so presenting filler to round out a presentation is how the filler gets approved. Two related rules sit alongside: do not hand out materials before presenting, because the moment you hand someone a document you are competing with it; and do not describe your campaign as risk-taking, because clients want certainty and the word is close to the worst thing you can say to someone with a job on the line.
qa_items.support: Stated rules. The claim that clients gravitate to second-rate work is drawn from his own experience of presenting filler; no counting is offered.
confounders: reading the first rule as refusing the change rather than deferring the work
treating filler as harmless presentation padding, which is the specific belief he reports holding and abandoning
confusing 'don't be slick' with 'don't prepare' — he insists on rehearsal and on anticipating every objection

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', section 'They may be right' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: Sullivan reports Bernbach's pocket note and then goes further. What is the note, what is his stronger version, and what does he claim it buys?
qa_items.answer: The note Bernbach is said to have carried and consulted during disagreements with clients read: "They may be right." Sullivan's version starts, in his phrase, a few rungs further down the humility ladder — always enter any discussion, with clients, account executives or anyone, believing there is a fifty percent chance you are dead wrong, and really believe it. What he claims it buys is persuasive force: it adds a strong underpinning to the argument because to listeners it does not feel like you are forcing your opinion on them. His illustration is two kinds of minister — the quiet one who invites you to explore his faith, and the sweaty televised one telling you what happens if you do not repent — and the question of which is more persuasive.
qa_items.support: Reported as agency legend for Bernbach; the stronger version and the claim about persuasiveness are Sullivan's own. Offered simultaneously as a posture and as a sincere belief, which is a demanding and unfalsifiable instruction.
confounders: reading it as advice to concede, which his triage rule and his 'articulate defender' instruction both contradict
treating it as a rhetorical technique only; he says to really believe it
confusing it with 'listening doesn't mean saying yes', which he states separately as a distinct point

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', sections 'Somebody asks to cram more stuff into the idea' and 'Outlast the objections' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: A client wants one advertisement to cover their full product range. Give Sullivan's rebuttal and his stated reason, then give the fallback he offers when no argument works at all.
qa_items.answer: The rebuttal is a redirection rather than a refusal: if the client has three important things to say, tell them they need three advertisements. His stated reason is customer behaviour — customers never go shopping for full lines of products, they have specific needs, so advertisements addressing specific needs are more effective. He calls full-line advertisements effective only as magazine thickener and quotes the proverb about the hunter who chases two rabbits catching neither. The fallback when nothing works is persistence, and he specifies its shape: not digging in your heels, but rolling past the resistance like a stream around a rock. His illustration is a year in which he presented fourteen campaigns to one difficult client on a single assignment; they killed thirteen, and the point of the story is that fourteen were presented.
qa_items.support: Stated rebuttal and stated reason; the fourteen-campaign account is his own anecdote. He also states plainly that much of the time nothing you say will pull a concept out of the fire, and that clients' reasons for disliking work often defy analysis.
confounders: refusing the request rather than converting it into a larger deliverable
reading persistence as holding out for the original idea; he means returning with new work
assuming the argument always succeeds — he says most of the time it will not

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', section 'Somebody says, Negative approaches are wrong' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: A client objects that your campaign is negative. Sullivan supplies a rebuttal and a reassurance. Give both, and state the condition he attaches.
qa_items.answer: The rebuttal is the argument from drama: the most basic tenet of it is conflict, and without conflict there is no story and therefore no interest. He illustrates with a relentlessly positive photograph — happiness, camaraderie, everyone enjoying the product — which he says is boring precisely because there is no tension, no unanswered question, no story. He generalises: people do not slow down to look at the highway, they slow down to look at the accident, not out of morbidity but because we are wired to scan for interruptions to the status quo. The reassurance, and the condition, is the same sentence: as long as the client's product is ultimately portrayed in a positive light or is seen to solve a customer problem, the net takeaway is positive — because, quoting Tom Monahan, the true communication is not what you say but what the receiver takes away.
qa_items.support: Stated rebuttal with a reproduced photograph as the negative example. The underlying story claim is the same borrowed material as his storytelling chapter; the condition about net takeaway is asserted, with no measurement of what receivers actually take away.
confounders: arguing that negativity is effective in itself, which the condition rules out
omitting the condition, which is what makes the rebuttal usable with a nervous client
confusing this with fear-based advertising; his claim is about dramatic structure, not about threat

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 16 'Pecked to Death by Ducks', section 'Somebody asks, Why are we wasting 25 seconds of our TV spot entertaining people?' (spine 39)
qa_items.question: A client asks why the commercial spends most of its length entertaining rather than selling. Reconstruct Sullivan's answer, including the sequence he claims and the starting position he says you are in.
qa_items.answer: His answer is that there is no entitlement to the customer's attention; it is earned. The sequence he claims is ordered and each step depends on the one before: you are not welcome until customers like you, they will not like you until they listen to you, and they will not listen if you open with bulleted copy points about your product's superiority. So the "wasted" time is in fact the active ingredient. He adds the starting position: because of decades of bad advertising you are not starting from zero with customers but from below it, and there is a high wall around every customer with another brick added daily. His analogy is a door-to-door salesman — a client who says lose all the entertainment is proposing to skip the doorbell, jimmy the lock and walk into the kitchen with a fistful of facts.
qa_items.support: Stated argument. The like-then-listen sequence is asserted as a mechanism with no evidence attached; the below-zero starting position is his characterisation of the audience, consistent with his opening chapter but not measured.
confounders: conceding the point and moving the product mention earlier, which is the request the argument is written against
reversing the sequence — he claims liking precedes listening, not the other way round
treating the argument as a claim about entertainment being effective in itself, rather than about earning attention

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'Make the Idea Bigger, Not the Logo', section 'The hard part: come up with something that works from both an entertainment and a marketing perspective' (spine 29)
qa_items.question: Branded content has to satisfy two criteria at once. State them, state the failure Sullivan names for leaning too far one way, and give the test he quotes for whether a piece has succeeded.
qa_items.answer: It must work as entertainment and as marketing. The named failure of leaning too far into the narrative is that viewers may enjoy the idea and take away no brand message — the entertained audience must not leave without somehow knowing the brand was involved in the joy. He states the strong form of the requirement: the idea cannot be a "brought to you by the makers of" attachment, it must come from, be inspired by and carry the brand's own material, and it must be relevant to the audience. His own image is giving a dog a pill — the medicine cannot sit beside the treat, the two have to be one thing. The test he quotes, from PJ Pereira: if you make it impossible to talk about the idea without the brand, yet interesting enough to generate some buzz, you have something special.
qa_items.support: Stated claim with the test quoted and endorsed. The founding example — a car brand spending a year's whole budget on short films — is the single most celebrated case of its kind, presented as having changed the field; no comparable attempt that failed is discussed anywhere.
confounders: treating entertainment quality alone as the criterion, which is the failure he names
reading brand presence as sponsorship or logo placement, which the strong form explicitly excludes
assuming the reported returns are measured; they are the client's or agency's own figures relayed second-hand

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 11 'Make the Idea Bigger, Not the Logo', section 'Use do-invite-capture-share'; and Ch. 12 'Mastering good social media practices' (spines 29, 31)
qa_items.question: Sullivan reports a four-step participation sequence and one bounding condition that is easy to skip. Give the sequence, say which step he calls the hard one, and give the condition.
qa_items.answer: Edward Boches's sequence: do something really interesting that communicates the value of your brand; conceive the idea so people can participate and find a way to invite them in; capture what is created or document the event so it lives beyond it; and make it shareable across every relevant channel. He names the first step as the hard one, because it cannot be an advertisement — it has to be, in his phrase, radioactively creative — and it is where his idea-worth-advertising reframe applies. The bounding condition, quoted from Scott Prindle, is about the exchange: whenever you ask customers for time or effort you must come through with a payoff, and it needs to be equal to or greater in value than the time contributed, or usage rates are very low.
