qa_items.support: Reported from Boches and endorsed, with the payoff condition quoted from another practitioner. The supporting cases are award-circuit campaigns described after their success.
confounders: treating capture and share as the substance; the source names the first step as the hard one
omitting the payoff condition, which is the part that predicts whether anyone participates
attributing the sequence to Sullivan; he credits Boches, a co-author of an earlier edition

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 12 'Concepting for the Hive Mind', section 'Mastering good social media practices' (spine 31)
qa_items.question: Sullivan's social-platform chapter mixes a durable claim with a great deal of dated specifics. Separate them: what survives, and name three kinds of material that should be labelled as contingent on the platforms of the writing period?
qa_items.answer: What survives is the prime directive and the competitive frame behind it: be interesting, entertaining or useful, because — quoting Andy Blood — your competitive set is not other advertisers, it is all the content people care about. That is the same argument he makes about attention everywhere else in the book. What should be labelled contingent: first, per-platform tagging mechanics and ceilings, including how many are permitted and how a recommendation engine is said to respond; second, which named network's features to exploit and how influencer arrangements work; third, the content-scheduling vocabulary — he uses a stock-and-flow distinction and footnotes it himself as dating from around 2011 and no longer in wide use. Also contingent: the specific ratios in the rule-of-thirds content mix he reports. None of this should be presented as durable, and none of it is evidence about how any current platform behaves.
qa_items.support: The prime directive is his stated claim. The contingency judgement is an extractor observation, supported by the source's own footnote conceding one of his terms is out of use. Nothing in this material is evidence about what any automated or generative system can produce.
confounders: carrying platform-specific numbers forward as current practice
treating the prime directive as social-media-specific; it restates his general attention argument
assuming that because some of the chapter is dated, the whole of it is — the competitive frame is the same one that runs through the book

qa_items.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
qa_items.source_locator: Ch. 2 'The Creative Process', section 'Why nobody ever chooses Brand X' (spine 11)
qa_items.question: Sullivan warns against the gimmick and then names what he claims is the only legitimate source of material. What is the distinction, and what does he say you already have to work with?
qa_items.answer: A gimmick captures attention for a few seconds and is unrelated to the product — his example is the manufactured sales event at a used-car dealership — and once the ruse is over the customer only resents you. His distinction: the best answers always arise out of the problem itself, out of the product, the customer, or the realities of the buying situation. Any shtick dragged into the situation that is not organically part of the product or customer reality will not be authentic and will ring false. What you already have, on his list, is more than enough: the client's product with its brand equities and benefits, the competitor's product and its weaknesses, the price-quality-value arithmetic of the two, and what the customer brings — pride, greed, vanity, envy, insecurity and a hundred other wants, one of which the product satisfies. Those, he says, are the only paints you have, and they are all you need.
qa_items.support: Stated claim. Asserted rather than demonstrated; the inventory of human motives is a mid-century list offered without derivation.
confounders: reading the objection to gimmicks as an objection to entertainment, which he defends at length elsewhere
treating 'arises out of the problem' as a requirement to be literal; his own examples are highly figurative
confusing this with the Rong chapter's licence to invert conventions, which he also bounds by the requirement that provocation stem from the product

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: text
qa_items.question: WCAG 2.2 defines "text" in its glossary rather than relying on the ordinary sense of the word. What two conditions must both hold, and name something made entirely of characters that fails the definition.
qa_items.answer: Both conditions are required: the sequence of characters must be programmatically determinable, and the sequence must be expressing something in human language. Characters used for their appearance rather than to express language fail the second condition even though they satisfy the first. The source's own examples of things that are not text in this sense are ASCII art, emoticons and leetspeak, listed under the definition of non-text content; and the Understanding note for SC 1.4.11 adds that an uppercase X used as a close button, or a greater-than character used as a right-pointing arrow, count as non-text symbols. The consequence is that the same glyph can be governed by SC 1.4.3 in one use and SC 1.4.11 in another, depending on whether it is expressing language.
qa_items.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "text" and of "non-text content". The symbolic-characters example is from the non-normative Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Symbolic text characters".
confounders: reading 'text' as 'anything a person can read', which would wrongly include a wordmark rendered as an image
assuming 'programmatically determined' alone is sufficient — it is one of two conditions
confusing this with the definition of 'image of text', which is about rendering rather than about language

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: essential
qa_items.question: A designer claims an image of text qualifies for the "Essential" exception because the typeface is central to the brand's identity. What does the glossary definition of essential actually require, and which half of the test does that claim not address?
qa_items.answer: The definition has two conjoined halves. Removing the thing would have to fundamentally change the information or functionality of the content — and the information and functionality must be unachievable in another way that would conform. The brand-identity claim speaks only to the first half. It says nothing about whether the same information could be delivered by a conforming route, which is the half that usually defeats such claims. The source does grant one case by fiat rather than by test: a note under SC 1.4.5 and SC 1.4.9 declares logotypes — text that is part of a logo or brand name — to be essential, which short-circuits the test for the mark itself. The Understanding note for SC 1.4.3 draws the boundary explicitly: corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.
qa_items.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "essential", and the notes to SC 1.4.5 and SC 1.4.9 declaring logotypes essential. The statement that brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are excluded is non-normative, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: treating 'essential' as a synonym for 'important to us', which is the first half only
extending the logotype note to a whole brand type system — the source explicitly excludes it
confusing 'essential' with 'pure decoration'; both exempt, on opposite grounds

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: pure decoration
qa_items.question: WCAG gives a single-sentence operational test for whether *text* is purely decorative. State it, and say why it is stricter than it first appears.
qa_items.answer: Text is only purely decorative if the words can be rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose. The general definition — serving only an aesthetic purpose, providing no information and having no functionality — is joined to that substitution test for text specifically. It is strict because it turns on the identity of the words, not on their visual treatment. Words chosen because they are those words are carrying something, so they are not decoration however faint, small or ornamental the setting. The source's illustration is a dictionary cover with random words in very light text in the background: any words would do, so they are decoration.
qa_items.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "pure decoration", its note and its example.
confounders: treating faintness or ornamental styling as evidence of decoration — the test is about substitutability, not appearance
assuming a tagline set as background texture is decorative; a tagline cannot be substituted without changing its purpose
confusing the decoration exemption with the incidental exemption for text inside a photograph

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: contrast ratio (definition and Note 1)
qa_items.question: Write the contrast ratio formula as WCAG defines it, state the bounds it can take, and explain why black text on white and white text on black yield the same figure.
qa_items.answer: Contrast ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the relative luminance of the lighter of the two colours and L2 that of the darker. Note 1 gives the bounds: ratios range from 1 to 21, commonly written 1:1 to 21:1. The measure is symmetric because the assignment is by lightness, not by role — the lighter colour is always the numerator, whether it is the type or the ground. So the formula cannot distinguish dark-on-light from light-on-dark, and the standard sets no different threshold for the two. The 0.05 term is not cosmetic: the Understanding note explains it as the contribution from ambient light, taken from the Typical Viewing Flare value in IEC/4WD 61966-2-1, included because the ANSI/HFS standard behind the formula calls for it.
qa_items.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "contrast ratio" and its Note 1. The explanation of the 0.05 flare term is non-normative, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Notes on formula".
confounders: assuming the ratio runs 0 to 1, or is a percentage
assuming light-on-dark is treated differently from dark-on-light — the formula makes them identical
reading the 0.05 as an arbitrary constant to avoid division by zero rather than as a viewing-flare term

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: large scale (text), Note 5
qa_items.question: Where do the figures 18 point and 14 point bold come from? What does the source say about how the equivalent sizes are established for Chinese, Japanese and Korean?
qa_items.answer: They are not derived from a contrast experiment. Note 5 states that the 18 and 14 point sizes for roman text are taken from existing large-print conventions: 14 point is the minimum size for large print and 18 point the larger standard font size. For other scripts such as CJK, the "equivalent" sizes are defined the same way — the minimum large-print size used for those languages, and the next larger standard large-print size. This is why the CJK case is stated as an equivalence rather than as a converted point value: the numbers travel by convention, not by arithmetic. The non-normative Understanding note cites the American Printing House for the Blind large-printing guidelines and the Library of Congress large-print reference guide as the sources behind these sizes.
qa_items.support: Normative — Note 5 to the glossary definition of "large scale (text)". The cited large-print guidelines appear in the non-normative Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent" and "Related Resources".
confounders: assuming 18pt was determined empirically as the point at which 3:1 becomes sufficient
converting 18pt to a CJK point size arithmetically — the source defines the CJK case by large-print convention instead
treating these as general typographic minimums rather than as thresholds for one exception

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: relative luminance
qa_items.question: In the sRGB relative luminance formula the three channels carry very different weights. Give them, and say what the unequal weighting means for two colours that differ only in blue.
qa_items.answer: L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, computed on channel values first linearised from their 8-bit form by a piecewise transform with a breakpoint at 0.04045. Green carries roughly seven tenths of the luminance, red about a fifth, blue about seven hundredths. Two colours differing only in their blue channel therefore differ very little in relative luminance, so their contrast ratio stays near 1:1 however different they look — which is exactly the case the standard is built to catch, since a difference the formula cannot see is a difference some readers cannot see either. The source adds that authors should evaluate in sRGB unless another colour space is known to be in use, and records that the 0.04045 breakpoint was 0.03928 before May 2021 with no practical effect on results.
qa_items.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "relative luminance", Notes 1 to 3.
confounders: assuming equal channel weights, or averaging RGB
computing luminance on raw 8-bit values without the linearisation step
assuming a large perceived colour difference implies a large contrast ratio

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: large scale (text), and Notes 2-4
qa_items.question: "Large scale text is text at 18 point or above." Why is that statement of the definition incomplete in at least three separate ways?
qa_items.answer: First, weight is part of the test: 14 point bold also qualifies, so a 14 point setting can be large scale or not depending only on its weight. Second, script is part of the test: the definition ends with "or font size that would yield equivalent size for Chinese, Japanese and Korean (CJK) fonts", so CJK is settled by equivalence rather than by the same numbers. Third, which measurement of size counts is specified: Note 2 says font size means the size when the content is delivered and excludes resizing done by the user, and Note 3 says the point size should be obtained from the user agent, or calculated from font metrics the way a user agent does, because the size a reader sees depends on the author's setting and on the user's display and user-agent settings together. Note 3 gives working equivalences — for many mainstream body fonts, 14 and 18 point are roughly 1.2 and 1.5 em, or 120% and 150% of the default body size — and instructs authors to check them for the particular fonts in use rather than treat them as constants.
qa_items.support: Normative — the glossary definition of "large scale (text)" and its Notes 2, 3 and 4.
confounders: treating the definition as a single point-size cutoff
using the em or percentage equivalences as fixed conversions rather than as approximations to be checked
measuring the size after user zoom rather than at delivery

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.3, Rationale for the Ratios Chosen
qa_items.question: Reconstruct the derivation W3C gives for 4.5:1 and 7:1. What is the baseline, what multiplies it, and what does the chain imply about what those numbers are measuring?
qa_items.answer: The baseline is 3:1, described as the minimum level recommended by ISO 9241-3 and ANSI/HFES 100-1988 for standard text and normal vision. The multiplier is contrast sensitivity loss associated with acuity: the cited population finding is that 20/40 acuity carries a contrast sensitivity loss of roughly 1.5, so a reader at 20/40 needs 3 x 1.5 = 4.5:1 — the Level AA value. Following the same logic, a reader at 20/80 needs about 7:1, which is Level AAA. The note adds that 20/40 is commonly reported as typical visual acuity at roughly age 80, and that people with worse loss than 20/80 usually use assistive technology with contrast enhancement and magnification built in, which is why the ladder stops there. What the numbers measure is therefore compensation: how much extra luminance separation restores, for a reader with a specified acuity loss, the contrast experience a normally sighted reader gets at 3:1. There is no term in the chain for attention, appeal or communication effect, and the source claims none.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Rationale for the Ratios Chosen", a W3C Working Group Note. The thresholds it explains are normative (SC 1.4.3, SC 1.4.6); the derivation is not.
confounders: assuming 4.5:1 was chosen by testing reading speed at various ratios
assuming it is a threshold of general readability rather than a compensation factor for a stated acuity loss
treating the derivation as normative — it appears only in a Working Group Note

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent and Rationale for the Ratios Chosen
qa_items.question: The WCAG contrast measure has no term for hue at all. Give the reasoning W3C states for that choice, and name the one case where the source says the reasoning breaks down.
qa_items.answer: The stated reasoning has three steps. For people with colour vision deficiency who cannot distinguish certain shades, hue and saturation have minimal or no effect on legibility as assessed by reading performance; and the inability to distinguish shades does not itself damage light-dark contrast perception. Colour deficiencies are too diverse for prescribing effective general-use colour pairs from quantitative data to be feasible. Requiring luminance contrast instead accommodates the whole population with one number, because most of the luminance contribution comes from the mid and long wave receptors, which largely overlap in their spectral responses. The stated exception is predominantly long-wavelength colours against darker colours — generally appearing black — for readers with protanopia, and the source responds with an advisory technique on avoiding red on black rather than with a requirement. So a red-on-black pair can pass the normative test while the source's own note counsels against it.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent" and "Rationale for the Ratios Chosen". The hue-free formula it explains is normative (Glossary: contrast ratio, relative luminance).
confounders: assuming hue is ignored because it does not matter perceptually, rather than because it cannot be generalised over
assuming a luminance-passing pair is therefore safe for all colour vision — the source names protanopia and red on black as an exception
confusing this with SC 1.4.1, which is about colour carrying meaning, not about contrast computation

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent
qa_items.question: Why does WCAG allow large text a lower contrast ratio, and what second reason — a design-side one — does W3C give for the carve-out?
qa_items.answer: The stated perceptual reason is that text which is larger and has wider character strokes is easier to read at lower contrast, so the requirement can be relaxed. The second reason is stated openly and is about authors rather than readers: the lower requirement lets authors use a wider range of colour choices for large text, which the note says is helpful for the design of pages, particularly titles. The note also marks the limit of the concession — "18 point" and "bold" can mean different things in different fonts, but should be sufficient except for very thin or unusual fonts, which is why a warning about thin strokes is attached to the definition of large scale rather than to the criterion.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent". The carve-out it explains is normative (SC 1.4.3, "Large Text"); the thin-stroke warning is normative (Glossary: large scale (text), Note 1).
confounders: assuming the concession is purely perceptual — the source also names authorial colour latitude
assuming stroke width is not part of the reasoning, when it is the mechanism given
reading the concession as unconditional, when the source names thin and unusual fonts as its limit

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: contrast ratio, Notes 3 and 4
qa_items.question: WCAG assumes white where no background colour is specified — and separately calls it a failure to specify a text colour without a background colour. Why are those two statements not in conflict?
qa_items.answer: They govern different situations. Note 3 supplies a default for evaluation: for SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6, contrast is measured against the specified background over which the text is rendered in normal usage, and if no background colour is specified, white is assumed. Note 4 addresses what an author has done rather than how an evaluator proceeds: specifying a text colour while leaving the background unspecified is a failure, because the unspecified half falls to a user default that is unknown and cannot be evaluated for sufficient contrast. The failure is symmetric — specifying a background without specifying a text colour fails for the same reason. Crucially, the source's own sufficient technique G148 permits the opposite strategy: specify neither colour, and do not use technology features that change the defaults. Leaving both unspecified is a different act from leaving one unspecified, and the standard treats them differently. This is a failure of specification, not of appearance — the page can look perfectly readable to its author and still fail.
qa_items.support: Normative — Notes 3 and 4 to the glossary definition of "contrast ratio". The documented failure F24 and the technique G148 are listed in the non-normative Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Failures" and "Sufficient Techniques".
confounders: concluding that the white default rescues content that specifies only a text colour — it does not; that is F24
assuming that if the rendered result is legible, the specification cannot fail
missing the symmetry — specifying only a background colour fails too

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: contrast ratio, Note 5
qa_items.question: A letterform carries an outline. WCAG says the same device can end up on either side of the contrast calculation. State the rule and the mechanism behind it.
qa_items.answer: A border around a letter can add contrast and is used in calculating the contrast between the letter and its background. A narrow border is used as the letter — it joins the foreground. A wide border that fills in the inner details of the letters acts as a halo and is considered background. The mechanism is what the reader is actually distinguishing: once a border is heavy enough to fill the counters and interior detail of the letterform, the perceptual comparison is no longer letter against page but letter against halo, so the halo becomes the effective background. The note gives no numeric boundary between narrow and wide; the stated test is whether the border fills the inner details of the letters.
qa_items.support: Normative — Note 5 to the glossary definition of "contrast ratio".
confounders: assuming an outline always helps, or always counts as foreground
looking for a stated pixel or point threshold separating narrow from wide — the source gives a functional test instead
assuming the underlying page colour remains the background once a heavy halo is present

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: contrast ratio, Note 2; Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent
qa_items.question: WCAG permits contrast to be evaluated with anti-aliasing turned off. What is the stated reason, and what problem does the source itself admit this creates?
qa_items.answer: The stated reason is authorial control: authors do not control user settings for text rendering, including font smoothing and anti-aliasing, so the measurement is defined on what the author did specify. The Understanding note extends this into an evaluation instruction — refer to the foreground and background colours obtained from the user agent, or from the underlying markup and stylesheets, rather than to the text as presented on screen. The admitted cost follows directly: because anti-aliasing can render particularly thin or unusual fonts much fainter than the colour declared in the CSS, text can have a contrast ratio that nominally passes the Success Criterion but has much lower contrast in practice. The note's response is best practice, not requirement: choose a font with stronger, thicker lines, or aim for a colour combination that exceeds the normative requirement. The same warning is repeated for thin lines and shapes under SC 1.4.11. This is the standard conceding, in its own words, that conformance and perceived legibility can come apart.
qa_items.support: Normative for the allowance — Glossary: contrast ratio, Note 2. NON-NORMATIVE for the nominal-pass problem and the remedy — Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent", and Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Intent".
confounders: assuming the standard requires measuring the rendered pixels a reader actually sees
presenting 'exceed the threshold' as a requirement — it is best-practice advice in a Working Group Note
assuming a nominal pass guarantees perceived contrast, which is precisely what the source denies

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.8 Visual Presentation; Understanding SC 1.4.8, Intent
qa_items.question: SC 1.4.8 sets a line width of no more than 80 characters, but 40 if CJK. Why half, and what reason does the source give for limiting line width at all?
qa_items.answer: The stated reason for halving is width per character: the note says studies have shown CJK characters are approximately twice as wide as non-CJK characters when both are displayed with characteristics that achieve the same readability, so the maximum line width for CJK is half. The reason for limiting line width at all is a reading-process failure rather than an aesthetic one: for people with some reading or vision disabilities, long lines are a significant barrier because they have trouble keeping their place and following the flow of text, and a narrow block makes it easier to continue to the next line. The criterion's word is "glyphs", defined in the note as the element of writing in the writing system for the text — so the limit is counted in units of the script, not in characters of English. Note that the studies behind the CJK claim are not cited in the document.
qa_items.support: Normative for the values — SC 1.4.8, at Level AAA. NON-NORMATIVE for the reasoning — Understanding SC 1.4.8, "Intent".
confounders: citing the classic 45-75 character measure from typographic practice, which this source does not use
reading 80 characters as an authoring instruction — SC 1.4.8 requires that a mechanism be available, not that content use the value
assuming the CJK halving is about character count rather than rendered width at equal readability

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing, Note 1; Understanding SC 1.4.12, Author Responsibility
qa_items.question: SC 1.4.12 names four spacing values — 1.5x line height, 2x paragraph spacing, 0.12x letter spacing, 0.16x word spacing — and then says content is not required to use them. What is the requirement, then, and what does failure look like?
qa_items.answer: The requirement is resilience, not typography. The criterion is that no loss of content or functionality occurs when a user sets all four properties to those values and changes no other style property. Note 1 states it plainly: content is not required to use these values; the requirement is that when a user overrides the authored text spacing, content or functionality is not lost. The Understanding note frames the author's duty as twofold — not interfering with the user's ability to override, and ensuring the overridden content does not break. Failure is a layout failure, and the source illustrates three kinds: text cut off vertically, text cut off horizontally, and text overlapping other content. The note adds that the values are a baseline rather than a ceiling, and that ellipsised truncation can still conform provided a mechanism reveals the truncated content — if there is no such mechanism, it fails. A separate normative exception allows human languages and scripts that do not use one or more of these properties to conform using only the properties that exist for that language and script.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.12 and its Note 1, and its language-and-script exception. NON-NORMATIVE for the author/user split, the ellipsis allowance and the illustrated failures — Understanding SC 1.4.12, "Author Responsibility", "Use of ellipses" and "Effects".
confounders: reading the four values as a required type specification
confusing them with SC 1.4.8's leading provisions, which are an availability requirement for blocks of text
assuming any truncation fails — the source permits it where a mechanism reveals the content

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.5, Intent; Understanding SC 1.4.4, Intent
qa_items.question: What reason does W3C give for preferring real text to images of text? Name the specific capabilities that are lost.
qa_items.answer: The reason is user adjustability, not fidelity. The intent stated for SC 1.4.5 is to let people who require a particular visual presentation of text adjust it as needed — the note lists font size, foreground and background colour, font family, line spacing and alignment. An image of text takes all of those out of the reader's hands. The Understanding notes for SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.4 add two consequences: images of text do not scale as well as text because they tend to pixelate, and it is harder to change foreground and background contrast and colour combinations for images of text, which some users need. This is why SC 1.4.4 excepts images of text from the 200 percent resize requirement — not as a concession, but because they cannot satisfy it. The stated beneficiaries are people with low vision, people with visual tracking difficulties who need to change line spacing or alignment, and people with cognitive disabilities affecting reading who need to restyle text.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.5, "Intent" and "Benefits"; Understanding SC 1.4.4, "Intent". The criteria themselves (SC 1.4.5, SC 1.4.4) are normative and state no reason.
confounders: assuming the objection is that images of text cannot be read by screen readers — that is SC 1.1.1's concern, and images of text may carry text alternatives
assuming the objection is image quality or file size
assuming SC 1.4.4's exception for images of text is a permission rather than an acknowledgement that they cannot comply

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.5 Images of Text; SC 1.4.9 Images of Text (No Exception); Understanding SC 1.4.5, Intent
qa_items.question: SC 1.4.5 and SC 1.4.9 have nearly the same subject. Set out precisely what differs, including the condition one of them carries that the other does not.
qa_items.answer: Three differences, all in the escape routes. First, SC 1.4.5 applies only "if the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation"; SC 1.4.9 carries no such condition. Second, SC 1.4.5 excepts images of text that can be visually customised to the user's requirements; SC 1.4.9 drops that exception entirely. Third, SC 1.4.9 admits pure decoration as a permitted use, which SC 1.4.5 does not need to name because it only governs text used to convey information. What is common: both except a particular presentation of text that is essential, and both carry a note declaring logotypes essential. The Understanding note adds a distinction stated nowhere in either criterion: SC 1.4.5 is met where an image of text is used in addition to the same information as text and both are presented to the user, whereas SC 1.4.9 applies to all images of text regardless of whether they duplicate text. SC 1.4.5 is Level AA; SC 1.4.9 is Level AAA.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.5 and SC 1.4.9 including their notes. The "in addition to text" distinction is NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.5, "Intent".
confounders: assuming the only difference is the conformance level
assuming SC 1.4.9 forbids all images of text — it permits decoration and essential presentation
carrying SC 1.4.5's technology condition across to SC 1.4.9, where it does not exist

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.8 Visual Presentation, Note 1; SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing, Note 1
qa_items.question: SC 1.4.8 and SC 1.4.12 both mention line spacing at around one and a half times. Why are they not the same requirement, and what would it take to satisfy each?
qa_items.answer: They impose different kinds of obligation on different objects. SC 1.4.8 concerns blocks of text — defined as more than one sentence — and requires that a *mechanism be available* to achieve line spacing of at least space-and-a-half within paragraphs, with paragraph spacing at least 1.5 times the line spacing, alongside four other presentation aspects. Its Note 1 says content is not required to use these values, and that the mechanism may be provided by the browser or another user agent rather than by the content — so a page can satisfy it without the author doing anything to the type, if a user agent supplies the mechanism. SC 1.4.12 concerns whether content *survives* a user setting line height to at least 1.5 times the font size, along with three other properties, changing no other property. Its Note 1 likewise says content need not use the values. Satisfying SC 1.4.8 is about availability of control; satisfying SC 1.4.12 is about the layout not cutting off or overlapping when control is exercised. SC 1.4.8 is Level AAA, SC 1.4.12 Level AA.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.8 and its Note 1; SC 1.4.12 and its Note 1.
confounders: reading either as an instruction to set 1.5 line height
assuming that meeting one implies meeting the other
missing that SC 1.4.8's mechanism may be supplied by the user agent, not the content

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Relationship with Use of Color
qa_items.question: A five-star rating shows each star with a black outline, filled yellow when earned and white when not. A second version shows pale yellow stars on white with no outline. Which criterion does each version fail, and why is it not the same one?
qa_items.answer: The first fails SC 1.4.1 Use of Color. The distinction between earned and unearned depends on recognising yellow versus white; the form of the star is unchanged, so hue alone carries the state. The second fails SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: the source gives the pale yellow as #FFF000 against white at a contrast ratio of 1.2:1, so the stars are not discernible at all. The two failures are genuinely different. The first version's stars are perfectly visible — you can see every star, you just cannot tell which are filled. The second version's stars are barely visible as shapes. The source's stated passes make the boundary sharper still: a solid fill indicating the checked state that has contrast passes, and so does a yellow fill combined with a thicker border, because the border is a second, non-hue cue.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Relationship with Use of Color", with the stated colour values and ratios; the two criteria it separates (SC 1.4.1, SC 1.4.11) are normative. The figures themselves were not inspected in this extraction; the captions state the values.
confounders: calling both a contrast failure, which loses the distinction the source draws
assuming raising the yellow's contrast fixes the first version — it does not; the state is still carried by hue alone
assuming adding a text label is the only remedy; the source accepts a thicker border as a sufficient second cue

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: normative; Glossary: informative; Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent
qa_items.question: An auditor writes: "WCAG requires you to exceed 4.5:1 when using a thin typeface." Using the source's own definitions of its authority levels, say what is wrong with that sentence and what a correct version would be.
qa_items.answer: The advice exists but it is not a requirement. WCAG's glossary defines normative as "required for conformance" and informative as "for information purposes and not required for conformance", and states that content identified as informative or non-normative is never required for conformance. The Understanding documents are W3C Working Group Notes, and it is there — not in any Success Criterion — that the advice appears: where anti-aliasing renders a thin or unusual font much fainter than its declared colour, "best practice would be for authors to choose a font with stronger/thicker lines, or to aim for a foreground/background color combination that exceeds the normative requirements of this success criterion." A correct version: SC 1.4.3 normatively requires 4.5:1, computed on the specified colours; W3C's non-normative Understanding note additionally advises exceeding that figure, or choosing a heavier face, when a thin typeface may render fainter than specified. The distinction matters practically: a conformance claim cannot be failed on the strength of a Working Group Note.
qa_items.support: Normative for the authority definitions — Glossary: "normative" and "informative". The advice itself is NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: treating the Understanding documents as part of the Recommendation
assuming that because the advice is sensible it must be binding
over-correcting and discarding the note entirely — it is W3C's own published guidance, just at a weaker level

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Required for Understanding and Pie Charts
qa_items.question: Two pie charts convey the same data. Chart A labels each slice with a name only. Chart B labels each slice with a name and its value. In both, adjacent slices contrast at about 1.8:1. What does SC 1.4.11 say about each, and what does that reveal about how the criterion is scoped?
qa_items.answer: Chart A fails. It passes SC 1.4.1 because the slices are labelled rather than distinguished by colour alone, but the reader still has to discern the edges between slices to grasp the proportions — so those edges are graphical objects required to understand the content, and at 1.8:1 they do not meet 3:1. Chart B is not applicable rather than passing: its visible labels and values convey information equivalent to the slices, so the slices are no longer required for understanding and the criterion has nothing to bite on. The scoping lesson is that SC 1.4.11 does not attach to graphics as such. It attaches to whatever is load-bearing for comprehension, and that set shrinks as information is supplied in other conforming ways. The source lists four such ways: text embedded or overlaid conveying the same information, aesthetic-only graphics, information available in another form such as a following table or long description, and logos or brand names. It adds that text within a graphic must itself meet SC 1.4.3.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Required for Understanding" and the "Pie Charts" worked examples. The criterion's phrase "required to understand the content" is normative (SC 1.4.11). The figures themselves were not inspected; the captions state the verdicts.
confounders: assuming labelling a chart is always enough — labels alone leave the proportions to the slice edges
assuming every slice must contrast with every other slice regardless of what else is shown
reporting Chart B as a pass rather than as not applicable, which loses why it is out of scope

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), 'Logotypes' and 'Incidental' exceptions
qa_items.question: WCAG says logotype text "has no contrast requirement". What exactly does that sentence assert, and what does it not assert?
qa_items.answer: It asserts that the criterion does not apply — the text is removed from the scope of the measurement. It does not assert that the text is readable, that it is readable enough, or that its contrast is acceptable. The standard withdraws its test; it does not certify the outcome. The same reading applies to the Incidental group: text in an inactive user interface component, pure decoration, text not visible to anyone, and text inside a picture with significant other visual content all have "no contrast requirement" in exactly this sense. The source's own non-normative notes make the gap explicit for logos: the exemption is granted on the assumption that logos must comply with stricter colour choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines, and the notes go on to call the situation problematic when a logo also acts as a user interface component, recommending a higher-contrast variant or an equivalent control. An evaluator should therefore record such cases as excluded, not as passed.
qa_items.support: Normative — the "Logotypes" and "Incidental" exceptions in SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6. The rationale and the best-practice recommendation are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent", and Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Logos".
confounders: reading the exemption as a judgement that low-contrast logotypes are fine
recording an exempt element as a pass in an audit, which misreports the asset
extending the exemption to all brand-coloured text on the page — the source limits it to the logo and logotype

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.4 Resize Text; SC 1.4.10 Reflow
qa_items.question: Distinguish SC 1.4.4 Resize Text from SC 1.4.10 Reflow. What is each measuring, and what does each except?
qa_items.answer: SC 1.4.4 is about magnitude: text must be resizable without assistive technology up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality, and it excepts captions and images of text. SC 1.4.10 is about layout under constraint: content must be presentable without loss of information or functionality and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions, at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels for vertically scrolling content or a height equivalent to 256 CSS pixels for horizontally scrolling content. It excepts parts of the content that require two-dimensional layout for usage or meaning, and names examples — images required for understanding such as maps and diagrams, video, games, presentations, data tables (not individual cells), and interfaces where a toolbar must stay in view. The Reflow numbers are zoom-derived: the note states 320 CSS pixels is equivalent to a 1280 CSS pixel viewport at 400% zoom. A CSS pixel is itself defined as a visual angle of about 0.0213 degrees, not a hardware pixel. Both are Level AA.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.4, SC 1.4.10 and its Notes 1 and 2, and Glossary: "CSS pixel".
confounders: treating 320 CSS pixels as a phone screen width rather than as a zoom-derived viewport equivalence
assuming Reflow forbids all horizontal scrolling, when it forbids scrolling in two dimensions and excepts content needing two-dimensional layout
carrying SC 1.4.4's captions and images-of-text exception across to SC 1.4.10, where it does not appear

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.3, 'Large Text'; Glossary: large scale (text), Note 1; Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent
qa_items.question: Taking the 3:1 large-text branch buys something and costs something. State both sides as the source presents them, and say when the trade goes bad.
qa_items.answer: What it buys is stated openly: a lower requirement lets authors use a wider range of colour choices for large text, which the note says is helpful for the design of pages and particularly for titles. What it costs is contrast headroom — the type is now permitted to sit at a ratio the standard itself considers insufficient for body text, and there is no margin left for anything that reduces effective contrast. The source names when the trade goes bad. Note 1 to the definition of large scale states that fonts with extraordinarily thin strokes, or unusual features that reduce the familiarity of their letterforms, are harder to read, especially at lower contrast levels — which is exactly the condition the branch creates. The Understanding note reinforces it: "18 point" and "bold" can mean different things in different fonts but should be sufficient except for very thin or unusual fonts. So the branch is safest for a large, conventionally weighted face and least safe for the thin display face a designer is most likely to want at title size.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.3's Large Text exception and Note 1 to the glossary definition of "large scale (text)". The colour-latitude benefit and the thin-font caution are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: treating the 3:1 branch as a free concession with no stated downside
assuming the thin-stroke note creates a testable requirement — it does not; no criterion converts it into one
assuming point size alone decides whether the branch is available

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), 'Incidental' and 'Logotypes'; Glossary: pure decoration; Glossary: image of text
qa_items.question: Four pieces of text appear in one page. (a) A wordmark in the header. (b) A street sign visible in a photograph of a high street. (c) A heading saved as a PNG so a licensed display face could be used. (d) Faint words tiled behind a hero section, chosen at random from a thesaurus. Which have a contrast requirement under SC 1.4.3, and on what ground?
qa_items.answer: Only (c). (a) is exempt under the Logotypes exception — text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement. (b) is exempt under the Incidental exception as text that is part of a picture containing significant other visual content; the Understanding note uses almost this example, saying incidental text such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign is not included. (d) is exempt as pure decoration, but only because the words satisfy the substitution test — chosen at random, they can be rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose; had they been the brand's values or a tagline, the exemption would fail. (c) is squarely in scope: it is an image of text under the glossary definition, text rendered in a non-text form to achieve a particular visual effect, and the criterion applies to images of text as it does to text. Note that (c) would additionally engage SC 1.4.5, since the presentation could be achieved with a web font.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.3's Incidental and Logotypes exceptions, and the glossary definitions of "pure decoration" and "image of text". The street-sign illustration is NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: exempting (c) because it is 'an image' — the criterion covers images of text explicitly
exempting (d) on the strength of its faintness rather than the substitutability of the words
treating (b) as an image of text; the glossary note excludes text inside a picture with significant other visual content

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Logos
qa_items.question: Under SC 1.4.11, when does a logo *lose* its exemption from the contrast requirement? Give the source's stated condition and its worked case.
qa_items.answer: The exemption rests on the assumption that logos must comply with stricter colour choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines — that is, on a constraint the author cannot alter. The source states the consequence directly: where a logo is presented with insufficient contrast but that presentation was an author choice rather than mandated by brand guidelines, the low-contrast presentation is not "essential", and the logo is not exempt. The worked case is an author who displays partner or company logos at low contrast by default and raises the contrast only on hover; being logos does not rescue that, because the initial low-contrast presentation was chosen, not mandated. The source separately flags that the exemption is problematic when a logo acts as a user interface component such as a link, and recommends as best practice a higher-contrast logo variant where brand guidelines allow, or an equivalent control that meets the requirements. Caution on authority: this narrowing is non-normative, and it sits alongside SC 1.4.3's normative clause that exempts logotype text with no condition attached.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Logos", including its Figure 40 caption, and Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent". The unconditional exemption it narrows is normative (SC 1.4.3, "Logotypes"). The figure itself was not inspected.
confounders: assuming 'it is a logo' is always sufficient — the source ties the exemption to a brand mandate
presenting the narrowing as a normative requirement when it appears in a Working Group Note
assuming a hover state that restores contrast cures the default presentation

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: image of text (note); Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent; Understanding SC 1.4.11, Required for Understanding
qa_items.question: A bar chart is delivered as a single PNG. It contains axis labels, data values printed on the bars, and a title. A colleague argues all of it is exempt because the chart is "a picture that contains significant other visual content". Is that right?
qa_items.answer: No. The exclusion does apply to the classification of the graphic — a chart is one of the source's own examples of a picture with significant other visual content, alongside screenshots and diagrams, so the chart as a whole is not an "image of text". But the exclusion does not carry the labels out of scope. The Understanding note for SC 1.4.11 states plainly that text within a graphic must meet SC 1.4.3, and the SC 1.4.3 note frames the intent of the picture exception as separating pictures that have text in them from images of text made to replace text in order to get a particular look — with the contrast requirement applying where images of text were intended to be understood as text. Axis labels and printed data values are unambiguously intended to be understood as text. So the labels and values carry the text contrast requirement, and separately the bars and gridlines are graphical objects assessed at 3:1 under SC 1.4.11 unless the printed values make them unnecessary for understanding.
qa_items.support: Normative for the classification — the note to Glossary: "image of text". The text-within-a-graphic rule and the intent of the exception are NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Required for Understanding", and Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: applying the picture exception to everything inside the picture
assuming a chart delivered as an image is entirely out of scope of Guideline 1.4
missing that supplying printed values can remove the bars themselves from scope under SC 1.4.11 while leaving the values in scope under SC 1.4.3

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.1, Intent
qa_items.question: Visited and unvisited links are distinguished by colour alone, and the two colours contrast at less than 3:1 with each other. Does this fail SC 1.4.1? Give the source's reasoning.
qa_items.answer: No — the source states that it does not fail, and gives four technical reasons why setting or conveying a link's visited status is not treated as an author responsibility. User agents constrain exposure of the visited state for privacy reasons, so author queries report all links as unvisited. Any such information would be inaccurate anyway, being browser- and history-dependent. Authors can only use colour to modify the :visited pseudo-class — the technology constrains non-colour styling — and palette limits make it impossible to achieve 3:1 between link and non-link text and between visited and unvisited links while also achieving 4.5:1 for all of them. And authors cannot set the visited state, so SC 1.3.1 and SC 4.1.2 cannot be met for it either. The source is explicit that this carve-out does not relieve the general obligation: authors must still ensure all text links meet the contrast minimum against the page background under SC 1.4.3.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.1, "Intent", a W3C Working Group Note. SC 1.4.1 itself is normative and states no such carve-out.
confounders: applying the general colour-alone rule mechanically and reporting a failure
generalising the carve-out to other state distinctions such as selected or active, which have no such technical constraint
concluding the links are exempt from contrast requirements altogether — SC 1.4.3 still applies against the page background

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Hover states and Boundaries
qa_items.question: SC 1.4.11 requires 3:1 for "visual information required to identify user interface components and states". Does a custom hover highlight have to meet 3:1? And does a button need a visible boundary?
qa_items.answer: Neither, on the same reasoning: the criterion covers what is *required* to identify something, and in both cases something else already does that job. For hover, the source observes that many native HTML components display no hover effect at all — the pointer's own location is the indicator of hovering. An author-supplied hover treatment is therefore supplemental rather than required to identify the state, and need not itself reach 3:1. The stated condition is that it must not cause the component to lose sufficient contrast against adjacent colours, or cause the indicators for other states such as focus or selection to lose theirs. The source's worked pass is a checkbox with a black border that gains a subtle grey hover fill at #DEDEDE: the border still has 15:1 against it, so the checkbox remains identifiable. For boundaries, the criterion does not require a visible boundary marking the hit area — if a control has visible content such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon that identifies it, no border is required and none is assessed. A boundary is required only where there is no other visual way to identify that the control exists, and then it must meet the ratio. The source adds two caveats: a control still needs a sufficiently contrasting focus indication regardless, and delineating all control boundaries remains a best practice for people with cognitive disabilities.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Hover states" and "Boundaries". The criterion's phrase "required to identify" is normative (SC 1.4.11). Figures were not inspected; captions state the values.
confounders: assuming every state change must meet 3:1
assuming every button needs a 3:1 border
missing the condition on hover effects — they must not push the component or its other state indicators below the ratio

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: contrast ratio, Note 6
qa_items.question: Which colour pairs does WCAG say should be evaluated for conformance, and what does it explicitly say authors need not consider?
qa_items.answer: Conformance should be evaluated for colour pairs specified in the content that an author would expect to appear adjacent in typical presentation. Authors need not consider unusual presentations, such as colour changes made by the user agent — except where those changes are caused by the authors' own code. The evaluation set is therefore bounded by what the author specified and would expect, not by every combination the content could theoretically produce under some rendering. The boundary is a judgement rather than a rule: the source does not define "typical presentation".
qa_items.support: Normative — Note 6 to the glossary definition of "contrast ratio".
confounders: assuming every possible pairing of every declared colour must be tested
assuming user-agent colour overrides such as forced-colours modes must be accounted for
missing the carve-back — author code that causes an unusual presentation does put it back in scope

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.11, Essential Exception
qa_items.question: Name the categories W3C gives for the Essential exception to SC 1.4.11, and state the underlying principle that unites them.
qa_items.answer: The principle is destructive interference: the exception is intended to apply where there is no way of presenting the graphic with sufficient contrast without undermining the meaning. Since the remedy for low contrast is to change colours, the exception covers cases where changing colours destroys what the graphic exists to carry. The named categories are logos and logotypes, presented in a brand's specific colours; flags, which may not be identifiable if their colours are changed; sensory content — the source states there is no requirement to change pictures of real-life scenes such as photos of people or scenery; and things that cannot be represented any other way, for which it names screenshots demonstrating how a website appeared, medical diagrams using the colours found in biology, and colour gradients representing a measurement such as heat maps. As with the logo case, the exception is an exemption from a requirement, not a finding that these graphics are easily perceived.
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Essential Exception". The criterion's essential- presentation exception is normative (SC 1.4.11, "Graphical Objects") but names no categories.
confounders: assuming any photograph or brand asset is automatically exempt without the meaning-destruction reasoning
assuming the exception means the graphic is perceivable
conflating this with SC 1.4.3's Incidental exception, which is about text rather than graphics

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.5 Images of Text; Understanding SC 1.4.5, Examples and Intent
qa_items.question: A community group must upload an event poster — a JPEG containing all the event details — to a council website whose CMS cannot reproduce the poster's layout in HTML. What does SC 1.4.5 require here, and would the same solution satisfy SC 1.4.9?
qa_items.answer: SC 1.4.5 is satisfied by adding the poster's information as regular text alongside the image. The source uses almost exactly this case: a user must upload an event poster containing text to an events calendar, the CMS is too limited to allow a custom HTML/CSS/SVG recreation, so they post both the poster image and the text it contains, and the text is shown next to the poster on the calendar page. Two separate grounds support this. The criterion applies only if the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, and here they cannot. And the Understanding note states that where images of text are used in addition to text conveying the same information, and both are presented to the user, the criterion is met — which lets authors keep the styling they want while the information remains manipulable as text. That same solution would not satisfy SC 1.4.9, which the note contrasts explicitly: SC 1.4.9 applies to all images of text regardless of whether they are used in addition to text, so the poster would have to be pure decoration or its presentation essential.
qa_items.support: Normative for the criteria and the technology condition — SC 1.4.5, SC 1.4.9. The worked poster example and the "in addition to text" allowance are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.5, "Examples" and "Intent".
confounders: requiring the poster to be removed, when the source permits it alongside text
assuming a text alternative on the image is sufficient — the note's route is presenting the information as text to all users
assuming what satisfies SC 1.4.5 satisfies SC 1.4.9

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent; Glossary: contrast ratio, Note 2; Glossary: large scale (text), Note 1
qa_items.question: A caption is set in a hairline geometric sans at 11pt, in a grey computing to 4.6:1 against white. A reviewer says WCAG has nothing to say about it because it passes. What does the source actually say about this case, and what does it stop short of saying?
qa_items.answer: It passes SC 1.4.3 as computed — 4.6:1 exceeds 4.5:1, and computed values are not rounded, so it is a real pass rather than a marginal one. But the source raises two related concerns and states both as concerns rather than requirements. Note 1 to the definition of large scale says fonts with extraordinarily thin strokes or unusual features that reduce the familiarity of their letterforms are harder to read, especially at lower contrast levels. And the Understanding note explains why the number can flatter this setting: because the contrast ratio may be evaluated with anti-aliasing turned off, and because evaluation refers to the colours in the markup rather than the text as presented, a thin face rendered by a user agent with anti-aliasing may appear much fainter than its declared colour — producing text that nominally passes while having much lower contrast in practice. The note's response is best practice, not obligation: choose a font with stronger, thicker lines, or aim for a combination that exceeds the normative requirement. What the source stops short of saying is that this caption fails anything. It has no test for stroke weight, no requirement to exceed a threshold, and no claim about whether the caption reads well.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.3, and Note 1 to Glossary: "large scale (text)", and Note 2 to Glossary: "contrast ratio". The nominal-pass account and the remedy are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: reporting a failure on the strength of the thin-stroke note, which creates no requirement
reporting nothing at all, which discards the source's own stated concern
assuming the 4.6:1 figure describes what the reader perceives

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: large scale (text), Notes 2-4; Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent
qa_items.question: A designer says: "The subhead is 20px, so it is large text and 3:1 is enough." Diagnose everything wrong with that reasoning using the source's own definition.
qa_items.answer: Three problems. First, the unit: the definition is in points, not pixels. The Understanding note gives the conversion — 1pt = 1.333px, so 14pt and 18pt are approximately 18.5px and 24px. At 20px the subhead is about 15pt, below the 18 point threshold. Second, weight: 14 point bold also qualifies, so if the subhead is bold the question becomes whether it reaches roughly 18.5px, which 20px does. The claim cannot be settled without knowing the weight, and the designer has not stated it. Third, the measurement: Note 2 says the size meant is the size when the content is delivered, excluding user resizing, and Note 3 says the point size should be obtained from the user agent or calculated from font metrics as user agents do — so a figure taken from a design file is not automatically the figure the criterion is asking about, particularly where sizes are set in relative units and the user agent computes them. The correct answer is therefore: 20px regular is not large scale and needs 4.5:1; 20px bold plausibly is, subject to confirming the computed size.
qa_items.support: Normative — Glossary: "large scale (text)" and its Notes 2, 3 and 4. The 1pt = 1.333px conversion and the 18.5px / 24px equivalences are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent".
confounders: treating px and pt as interchangeable
ignoring weight, which can move 14pt into the large-scale category
taking the size from a design file rather than from the delivered, user-agent-computed size

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Glossary: contrast ratio, Note 3; Understanding SC 1.4.3, Failures (F83); Understanding SC 1.4.11, Gradients
qa_items.question: White type is set over a photograph that runs from bright sky to dark foliage. What does WCAG actually give you for measuring this, and what does it not give you?
qa_items.answer: It gives you a failure and a partial method, not a measurement procedure. The failure is F83: failure of SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6 due to using background images that do not provide sufficient contrast with foreground text or images of text. The measurement rule assumes a specified background — Note 3 says contrast is measured with respect to the specified background over which the text is rendered in normal usage, with white assumed if none is specified — and a photograph is not a specified colour. The nearest thing to a method is in the non-normative note on graphical objects: where there are multiple colours or a gradient, test the least-contrasting area, and if that area falls below the ratio, assume it is invisible and ask whether the object is still understandable. That transfers naturally to worst-case testing of text over an image, but the source frames it for graphical objects, not for text over photographs. What the source does not give you is a defined value for the whole setting, a rule for averaging, or a threshold for how much of a glyph may fall below the ratio. It does supply one relevant device: Note 5 on letter borders, under which a narrow outline joins the letter and a wide halo becomes the effective background — which is why scrims and outlines can change the answer rather than merely improve the appearance.
qa_items.support: Normative — Glossary: "contrast ratio", Notes 3 and 5. F83 and the least-contrasting-area method are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Failures", and Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Gradients" and "Testing Principles".
confounders: computing an average background colour and reporting a single ratio as though the standard defined one
assuming the white-background default of Note 3 applies — it applies when no background is specified, not when the background is an image
assuming the graphical-object gradient method is the standard's stated method for text

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum); Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent and Rationale for the Ratios Chosen
qa_items.question: A brand team asks: "Our campaign key visual has a headline at 3.8:1. Does WCAG say our advertisement is illegible?" Answer using only what the source claims.
qa_items.answer: No. WCAG makes no claim of that kind about anything. SC 1.4.3 is a conformance criterion for web content, and what a shortfall means is that the content does not satisfy that criterion at Level AA — assuming the headline is not large scale, in which case the applicable figure would be 3:1 and 3.8:1 would meet it. The criterion's stated purpose is narrow and specific: to provide enough contrast between text and its background so it can be read by people with moderately low vision or impaired contrast perception, without contrast-enhancing assistive technology. The numbers are derived as compensation for a stated contrast sensitivity loss at a given visual acuity. There is no claim in the document that meeting a threshold makes a message effective, noticeable or attractive, and no claim that missing one makes a design bad. The honest statement to the brand team is: at this size the headline would not meet the Level AA web threshold, which concerns readers with low vision; whether it works as advertising is a question this standard does not address and does not answer.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.3 and its Large Text exception. The purpose statement and the derivation are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Intent" and "Rationale for the Ratios Chosen".
confounders: translating 'fails WCAG' into 'is illegible' or 'is bad advertising'
forgetting to check whether the large-scale branch applies, which would change the applicable figure
treating a web conformance standard as a general legibility authority for print or film

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast; Understanding SC 1.4.11, Graphical Objects and Testing Principles
qa_items.question: A dashboard shows a row of status icons with no accompanying text. One is a light grey warning triangle on a white card, measuring 2.4:1. Walk through how the source says to assess it, and name what would take it out of scope.
qa_items.answer: First identify the graphical object: for a simple single-colour icon, the source says the entire image is one graphical object, so here it is the triangle itself. Then check its contrast against its adjacent colours — the white card — which gives 2.4:1, below the 3:1 the criterion requires, and the source states the ratio is a threshold that is not rounded. Then apply the comprehension test: assume the sub-threshold area is invisible and ask whether the graphic is still understandable. With the triangle gone there is nothing left, so it fails. Two things would take it out of scope. If text embedded or overlaid conveyed the same information — a visible "Warning" label beside the icon — the icon would no longer be required for understanding; the source's example of this is labels and values on a chart, and the note adds that such text must itself meet SC 1.4.3. Or if the information were available in another conforming form, such as a table that follows, or a long description revealed by a control. Aesthetic-only graphics and logos are the other two exclusions the source names, and neither applies to a status icon.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.11, "Graphical Objects". The graphical-object definition, the invisibility test, the four out-of-scope situations and the no-rounding rule are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.11, "Graphical Objects", "Required for Understanding", "Testing Principles" and "Intent".
confounders: measuring the icon against the page background rather than against its adjacent colours
assuming a text alternative in the markup takes it out of scope — the exclusion is visible text conveying the same information
rounding 2.9x figures up to the threshold, which the source explicitly forbids

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.1 Use of Color; Understanding SC 1.4.1, Intent and Examples
qa_items.question: A form marks required fields by colouring their labels red, and states at the top that required fields are shown in red. Does that satisfy SC 1.4.1? What minimal change would, and what would also work without adding any icon or text?
qa_items.answer: Not on its own. "Required fields are red" is the source's own example of information conveyed by colour differences, and an instruction in text explaining the colour code does not give a sighted reader who cannot distinguish the hues any way to tell which labels are red. The source's worked passing example adds a second visible cue at the field: instructions explain that required fields are labelled with red text *and* with an icon, so readers who cannot perceive the colour difference still see the icon. The minimal change is therefore a per-field non-colour cue — an icon, an asterisk, or the word "required". Without adding any mark, one other route works: if the red differs from the surrounding label colour not only in hue but significantly in lightness, with a relative luminance difference giving a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater between them, the source counts that lightness difference as the additional visual distinction. The limit on that route is stated too — where the reader must accurately perceive or differentiate a particular colour, as with green for valid versus red for invalid, an additional indicator is required regardless of the ratio.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.1. The examples, the 3:1 lightness-difference allowance and its limit are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.1, "Intent" and "Examples".
confounders: assuming a legend or key explaining the colour code is sufficient
assuming a programmatic marker such as aria-required satisfies it — the note states the criterion requires a visible alternative and does not directly address assistive-technology users
assuming better contrast against the page background helps, when the relevant comparison is between the two label colours

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: SC 1.4.3, 'Incidental'; Understanding SC 1.4.11, Inactive User Interface Components
qa_items.question: An audit flags a disabled "Continue" button — grey text on a grey fill, about 2:1 — as a contrast failure. Is the audit right, and what reason does W3C give for its position?
qa_items.answer: The audit is wrong on the letter of the standard. Text that is part of an inactive user interface component falls under the Incidental exception to SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6 and has no contrast requirement, and SC 1.4.11 likewise excepts inactive components. The source defines the case precisely — an inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable — and offers exactly this example: a submit button at the foot of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until the required fields are complete. Its reason for the exemption is candid rather than principled: it would be beneficial to some people to discern inactive controls, but a one-size-fits-all solution has been very difficult to establish, and the note anticipates a future approach varying the presentation of disabled controls by user preference, such as adding an icon. So the correct audit finding is "excluded — inactive component", not "pass" and not "fail", and the source's own note is the place to record that the exclusion is a known compromise.
qa_items.support: Normative — the Incidental exception in SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.6, and the inactive-component exception in SC 1.4.11. The definition, the example and the reasoning are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.3 and SC 1.4.11, "Inactive User Interface Components".
confounders: applying the contrast requirement to every visible control regardless of state
recording the outcome as a pass rather than as an exclusion
assuming a control that merely looks greyed out is inactive — the test is that it is not currently operable

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.12, Use of ellipses and Effects
qa_items.question: Applying the SC 1.4.12 spacing values, a card component's heading is clipped mid-word and its body text overlaps the card below. Which of these fails, and what repairs does the source accept short of redesigning the layout?
qa_items.answer: Both fail. The source illustrates three failure types under this criterion — text cut off vertically, text cut off horizontally, and text overlapping other content — and the described case contains two of them. The repairs the source accepts stop short of redesign in one specific circumstance: where a text container cannot expand because of a design constraint, such as a maximum width for a left navigation or a table column header, truncation with an ellipsis can still meet the requirement provided the content remains available. The source names two acceptable routes: a mechanism reveals the truncated text on the page, for instance on focus or on activation; or, where the ellipsis is part of a section containing a link, the truncated text is revealed on the linked page. It is explicit about the converse — where text is not truncated normally but is when spacing is applied, and no mechanism shows the truncated text, that fails. Overlapping text has no equivalent concession. Note also what the criterion does not demand: the author is not required to use these spacing values, nor to build a mechanism for users to set them.
qa_items.support: Normative — SC 1.4.12 and its Note 1. The illustrated failures and the ellipsis allowance are NON-NORMATIVE, from Understanding SC 1.4.12, "Effects" and "Use of ellipses".
confounders: assuming any truncation fails the criterion
assuming the fix is to set the content's own spacing to the SC values, which the criterion explicitly does not require
extending the ellipsis concession to overlapping text, which the source does not

qa_items.source_title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, W3C Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
qa_items.source_locator: Understanding SC 1.4.3, Intent (note on adjustable colours); Understanding SC 1.4.8, Intent
qa_items.question: A product team wants to ship a reading mode whose colour presets fall below 4.5:1. Someone objects that this cannot be allowed. What does WCAG actually say about user-chosen low-contrast combinations?
qa_items.answer: The source not only allows this, it encourages the underlying capability. Its note states that some people with cognitive disabilities require colour combinations or hues that have low contrast, and that authors are therefore allowed and encouraged to provide mechanisms to adjust the foreground and background colours of the content — and that some combinations a user chooses may fall below the specified levels without that being a violation of the criterion, provided there is a mechanism that returns to the required values. SC 1.4.8 makes the same point from the other side: for blocks of text a mechanism must be available for the user to select foreground and background colours, and its Understanding note observes that such users sometimes choose combinations that seem unintuitive to someone without that disability, sometimes with very low contrast, and that only very specific combinations work for them. The condition is the one to keep: a route back to the conforming values must exist. So the correct framing is not "low contrast is forbidden" but "the conforming presentation must remain reachable".
qa_items.support: NON-NORMATIVE — Understanding SC 1.4.3, "Rationale for the Ratios Chosen" (the note on adjustable colours), and Understanding SC 1.4.8, "Intent". SC 1.4.8's requirement that a mechanism be available for user-selected colours is normative, at Level AAA.
confounders: reading the contrast criteria as prohibiting any low-contrast presentation under any circumstances
dropping the condition that a mechanism must return to the required values
assuming this permission covers the author's default presentation rather than a user-chosen one
